Summary

Bitten by a werewolf when she was twelve years old, Kara soon finds herself kicked out of Ilvermorny and abandoned by her mother with no home to return to. Taken in by family friends and dragged halfway across the world to start fresh as a Second-Year at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, Kara struggles to balance school, grief and Lycanthropy as she adjusts to her new life.

It's at Hogwarts where she meets a First-Year Slytherin by accident and strikes up an unlikely, secret friendship that spans their years at school and finds them on opposite sides of the brewing First and Second Wizarding Wars as family loyalties, secrets, promises and fears keep them apart. As the years drag by with frequent crossing paths, just how long can they stay loyal to their cause while their hidden feelings threaten to ruin everything?

Chapter 1

            Bare feet thundered on the stairs as a young girl checked the worn leather watch strapped to her wrist, blonde hair falling around her face in straggly curls as her wire-rimmed glasses slid down her nose. Her plaid shirt was buttoned unevenly in her distracted haste and she brimmed with excitement as she made for the front door of the modest, gabled farmhouse.

 

            “Kara,” her mother called out, dishes clattering in the kitchen as they washed themselves in the sink, and Kara bit back a sigh, swinging around the end of the staircase and stepping through into the kitchen. 

 

            Her mother was sitting at the table, still wearing her scarlet MACUSA robes as she pored over the notes of a case, quill in hand and ink staining her fingertips. She looked up at Kara and raised her eyebrows, dark eyes serious as she set aside a scroll of parchment and dipped the quill into ink.

 

            “Where are you running off to at this time of night?”

 

            Wincing sheepishly, Kara shifted from foot to foot as she twisted the small field notebook in her hands, a quill poking out of her shirt pocket as she gave Alura a pleading look. “It’s a full moon - the Mooncalves will be out tonight. I was going to study them-”

 

            “Exactly, it’s a full moon . It’s not a night for being out chasing after silly creatures.”

 

            Sighing heavily, Kara rolled her eyes and gestured wildly, “it’s not silly. It’s for my Magizoology research.”

 

            “It’s late.”

 

            “It’s summer vacation!” Kara protested.

 

            Lowering his copy of The New York Ghost , Zorel gave his wife a faint smile, “it’s Wisconsin , my love, let her run through wheat fields and have her fun. It won’t do her any harm; she won’t go far and the wards-”

 

            “You know it isn’t saf-”

 

            “Sweetheart,” he gently, yet firmly cut her off, “let’s not.”

 

            His eyes - Kara’s eyes - strayed over to his daughter, who was still looking hopeful and a little confused at the secret conversation her parents were having as she lingered in the doorway to the kitchen. They’d been like that for the past few weeks, since she’d come back from Ilvermorny for summer break. Something had happened while she was away at school, that much was apparent, but no amount of badgering them would reveal what it was exactly.

 

            “Fine,” Alura relented, gesturing dismissively before shaking her head and returning to her work.

 

            Beaming at her father, who gave her a quick wink as he reached for the enamel mug of coffee on the table, she turned on her heel and made for the front door.

 

            “Make sure you put a robe on,” her mother called after her as an afterthought. “And shoes.”

 

            Deigning not to respond with the fact that it was the middle of summer, Kara snagged her school robe from the hook near the door and slipped it on over her head, buttoning up the top three buttons and flattening the collar. The emblem of the Thunderbird house was stitched on the breast pocket. She skipped the shoes, her muddy boots on the rack beside the door, opting to run around barefoot as often as she could get away with. Kara found that as she got older it became more and more inexcusable.

 

            Grabbing her camera, she slipped out into the night, the full moon hanging bright and big overhead, casting a silvery tint to the trees and fields spread out from the farmhouse. A faint mist gave the night a strange quality and she shivered as her face clouded briefly, before her earlier haste took over and she ran out into the thin border of forest separating the land, cold grass between her toes.

 

            The fog coalesced here, obscuring her feet and the shadows of tree trunks that loomed out of the darkness, and Kara breathed in the scent of pine and spruce and oak as she followed the familiar path. Appearing on the other side, her skin prickled with the sensation of being watched and she looked around, finding nothing unwelcome in the night.

 

            Hurrying onwards, she made for the fields spreading out around her in a patchwork blanket. Wheat came up to her shoulder as she dashed into the rippling stalks, her pace slowing as she took caution, not wanting to scare the Mooncalves off. 

 

            An hour of fruitless wandering and the young girl was starting to lose hope, circling back around the way she’d come. The trees that nestled the farmhouse from view were dark and shrouded in an even thicker fog than when she’d left, the moon sitting higher in the sky and casting its bleaching light over the night as she carefully wound through the trees, fingertips brushing rough bark as she relied on memory alone to pick her way back, over roots and through the underbrush and bracken.

 

            Disappointment knifed through Kara as she took in the sight of the illuminated house, its white clapboard and brick chimney, quaint wraparound porch beckoning her home. She’d hoped for more, for anything, but hadn’t seen so much as a ghoul or a boggart as she’d wandered around in the moonlight.

 

            Still, it was a beautiful night. Mystery and the thrill of being out so late left Kara reluctant to return home just yet, safely through the trees and within the wards her parents had set up to hide their home from the No-Maj’s in the nearby town. Spreading her arms wide open, she drank in the sight of the gleaming white full moon and the bright stars dotting the velvet sky as they illuminated everything within the clearing the house resided in, to the very tips of the towering trees.

 

            The spectacle made her feel so small, the expanse of sky stretching above her as she breathed in the smell of fields and trees and the nearby dirigible plum bushes. Sinking down to the grass, she lay on her back, staring up at the stars as she ran through the constellations; Astronomy was one of her favourite subjects at school and there was something about the unknowable secrets of the universe that compelled her to try and know .

 

            She found Perseus and Cassiopeia, Eridanus and Hydrus, and the last one she found was Lupus. Still drawing the lines between the stars that made up the wolf, Kara heard a rustling in the trees behind her and bolted up into a sitting position, a smile lighting up her young face at the thought of Mooncalves in the trees.

 

            Scrambling to her feet, camera in hand and her movements quiet as she crept forward in a crouch, Kara stepped into the shadows of the trees. She could see nothing though, no signs of movement, and she wondered for a second if it had been her father’s owl up in the branches when a low growl made the hair on her body stand on end.

 

            Whipping around, Kara’s eyes blindly searched the fog as she swallowed thickly. “Hello?”

 

            From out of the darkness of the trees, she saw a dark, furry shape emerge. The shape looked like a huge, black dog with a grey streak running along its hunched back. It bared its sharp, pearly white teeth that sparkled with saliva in the moonlight, and growled even louder. 

 

            Kara was so terrified she couldn’t move. In fact, the only movement that continued anywhere in her body was that of her fiercely pounding heart. Even her lungs were still, panic gripping her so tightly that she couldn’t even bring herself to draw in a breath.

 

            The feral creature reared back its head and howled hauntingly - it was a sound that, for a moment, took Kara’s fear away and replaced it with wonder, yet the fear returned as the beast charged. The most Kara could manage in an attempt at flight from it was a single staggering step backwards, out of the confines of the trees but not quite past the boundary line of the protection wards. 

 

            As she stumbled backwards, she tripped over the uneven ground and went down as the hulking monster advanced on her, forcing Kara to shrink down even further. She didn’t make a sound as it loomed over her, massive paws pinning her to the ground, claws digging in through her robe and shirt.

 

            The pressure of it seemed to knock the breath out of Kara as she trembled violently, closing her eyes as her bottom lip wobbled and the werewolf’s rancid breath made her feel sick. Its muzzle pulled back as it softly snarled and Kara let out a small whimper as the brutish animal slowly crushed her chest, leaning in so close that its snout was almost pressed against the young girl’s cheek.

 

            It raised one paw and slashed at her right shoulder. Kara let out a strangled scream with a sharp intake of breath as fresh pain seared where the claws had torn at her flesh. The rip of cloth told her that her shoulder was vulnerably exposed, the strange feeling of warmth soaking into the cloth letting her know that she was bleeding. Even with her closed eyes, Kara’s perception of the world seemed to pitch, unconsciousness furring the edges of her mind as she lay pinned to the earth.

 

            Distantly, she heard a woman scream her name, fraught with terror, and a deeper voice bellowing a curse as footsteps grew louder.

 

            “Kara!”

 

            “Alura, stay back!”

 

            Her father was halfway across the yard, wand raised and a spell already forming as he slung it wordlessly at the monster. “Get away from my daughter!”

 

            But it seemed the hexes weren’t powerful enough, and only worked to irk the beast. Snarling, as Zorel stepped beyond the wards, it hunched lower and sprang at him, claws tearing through his abdomen as the creature went straight for the jugular, teeth clamping down hard as they bit through the flesh and tossed the slumped man aside like a rag doll.

 

            “Zorel!”

 

            “Dad,” Kara hoarsely croaked, her eyes open as she’d watched the whole thing happen through her tilting vision, a sob building in her throat.

 

            She waited for him to climb to his feet and hex the werewolf until it ran away, her hand grasping at grass and mud as her eyes swam with tears.

 

            But he didn’t, and a moment later a soft gasp escaped her limp body as fresh pain tore through her other shoulder. It was a burning pain, pointed teeth renting the flesh and digging into bone with a single, fleeting bite that lasted a mere second - yet the agony was so exquisite that it felt like an eternity, existing in that moment of being bitten for aeons, as time had suspended and left her to suffer.

 

            Even long after the thing had pounded away, retreating into the darkness, it felt like it was still there, in her as her blood soaked its jaw. She was barely holding onto consciousness, camera abandoned near her hand and the sky overhead visible through slitted eyes as footsteps thundered towards her. The last thing Kara saw that night was the full silver moon looming ominously overhead.

 

            “Mom. Dad,” she murmured before darkness enclosed her.

 

 

            Harsh sunlight fell across her face and woke Kara with a pucker of annoyance between her eyebrows. A soft groan slipped through her lips as she rolled over, exhaustion keeping her mind half asleep, before white-hot pain lanced through her and shocked her to wakefulness.

 

            Vision blurry, Kara reached out with a fumbling hand for her glasses, but they weren’t on the nightstand beside her bed. And as she shifted she realised the narrow, lumpy mattress wasn’t hers and the scratchy striped blankets weren’t either. Panic knifed through her and she found it difficult to swallow, her throat dry and the coppery taste of blood caught at the back of her throat.

 

            “Mom?”

 

            Her voice came out hoarse and weak and there was the sound of quick motion, shoes quietly scuffing the tiles floor before a hand was clapped over Kara’s mouth. She struggled as panic welled up inside her, the blurry shape of someone with dark hair looming over her indistinguishable without her glasses, and Kara only stilled as pain flared up again.

 

            “Sh. I’m trying to listen,” a quiet, familiar voice ordered her.

 

            Kara swallowed as her eyes slid closed and she took a moment to allow everything to settle, the ringing in her ears receding and the sense of vertigo diminishing. Only then was she able to tune into the conversation beyond the small room she was in, voices slightly muffled but barely controlled, as if they were trying not to yell.

 

            “Alura-“

 

            “I can’t. I will not-“

 

            “She’s your daughter.”

 

            “She stopped being my daughter the moment that beast-“

 

            A flash of memory struck Kara like she’d been slapped across the face; bared teeth, her father’s crumpled form, the crushing weight of something. It all felt veiled in fog, much like the night before, hiding something from her sight as she lay in the narrow bed and listened.

 

            “What are you going to do?”

 

            “I don’t know. I don’t know, Eliza. Send her back to Ilvermorny.”

 

            “You know they won’t take her-“

 

            Kara’s heart hammered in her chest as she drew in shallow breaths, squeezing her eyes shut as she twisted the sheets in her hands.

 

            “I don’t care,” Alura hissed. “I will not have a daughter who’s a- a werewolf.”

 

            The word was deafening in Kara’s head, blotting out any other thought as her stomach twisted nauseously. With startling clarity, the events of the night before settled into order in her mind, and she reeled as she made sense of what had happened.

 

            “And what are you going to tell her? First Zorel and now-“

 

            “I won’t tell her anything. She can think I died too.”

 

            “Alura,” Eliza exclaimed, aghast.

 

            “You wouldn’t understand. If it was your daughter-“

 

            “If it was my daughter, I would love her all the same.”

 

            “You take her then, if it’s nothing to you.”

 

            With a scathing sound of contempt, Eliza’s voice grew more distant, as if she was following Alura down the hall, pursuing her as she pleaded and cursed her out.

 

            “You care too much for your blood status; it’s not going to save you-“

 

            The rest of the conversation became too muffled for Kara to hear and she lay there for a moment, staring blindly up at the ceiling as her heart pulsed in her throat.

 

            “Alex?” she hesitantly guessed.

 

            “Here.”

 

            Her glasses were slid onto her nose and the room was thrown into focus, a faded blue curtain drawn around the bed and the brick walls emanating coldness. Turning her head to the side, she took in the sight of a teenage girl with shoulder-length russet hair sitting in a rickety wooden chair as she picked at a loose thread in the torn knees of her faded jeans.

 

            “Your mom is here?”

 

            Shrugging, Alex gave her a wary look, canvas shoes squeaking on the edge of the chair as she wrapped her arms around her drawn-up knees.

 

            “Your mom sent an owl.”

 

            They were the closest neighbours to the farmhouse, their mother’s old friends, a leftover remnant from their days at Ilvermorny, and Kara had grown up spending the odd holiday with the Danvers family. Alex was two years older than her and in Wampus at school, so they’d never really gotten to know each other all that well, but at Christmas and Thanksgiving she was always patient with Kara, putting up with her enthusiastic tailing along and proudly showing off her wand the year she’d turned eleven and started school.

 

            Swallowing thickly, Kara blinked back tears as she ran her fingers over the sheets. “Do you know what the Healers said?”

 

            “My mom said not to talk about it,” Alex said as her mouth thinned.

 

            She picked up her copy of Quidditch Through The Ages and went back to her reading as Kara was left to stare up at the ceiling, waiting. It was a torturous wait, the minutes stretching out like hours for a twelve-year-old whose world had fallen apart overnight.

 

            “My dad’s dead, isn’t he?” Kara asked after a few minutes.

 

            “Yeah. Sorry.”

 

            Closing her eyes, Kara jerkily nodded as her chin dimpled with the effort it took to hold her sob at bay. Quietly grumbling, Alex climbed to her feet and moved over to the bed, poking Kara’s arm.

 

            “Hey, it’ll be okay. My dad’s dead too.”

 

            Kara choked on a laugh as tears ran down her temples and into her hair. The door squeaked open before she could reply, a Healer tearing back the curtain as a pale looking Eliza peered out from behind the woman. Pity welled up in her blue eyes and it was all the answer Kara needed as she forced herself to swallow.  Eliza softly clicked her tongue and moved over to the bed, brushing Kara’s frizzy curls out of her face as she gave her a heartbroken look of dismay. Eyes closing, she couldn’t stop herself from crying then, clapping a hand over her mouth as she shook.

 

            “It’ll be alright,” Eliza comforted her. “Don’t you worry, okay? You just focus on getting better and then we’ll get you back home.”

 

            “It bit me. It bit me; I remember-“

 

            “Hey, sh, it’s okay, sweetheart. The Healers have taken good care of you, you’re going to be fine.”

 

            But Kara knew that there was no cure for Lycanthropy, and even though the Healers had saved her life, had sealed the bite with silver and Dittany, the saliva was in her bloodstream. Yes, she’d live, but as an infected werewolf, transforming with the full moon.

 

            The tenderness and pity in Eliza’s voice made Kara cry harder, confusion and disgust and hurt making her chest hurt as her shoulders burned with white-hot pain. She couldn’t stop, couldn’t catch her breath, and the Healer was silent as she took a needle and filled it with the shimmering silver liquid in a vial, plunging it into Kara’s arm until her body went limp and darkness crept in on her mind.

 

            The next time she woke she was disoriented and clumsy, her tongue thick in her mouth and her body heavy. She couldn’t speak, couldn’t form any words as she made slurred sounds and failed to do more than move her hands an inch. There was that awareness of someone else in the room with her though, but even when she managed to open her heavy eyes a fraction, her poor vision made it too hard for her to make out anything.

 

            In the end, Kara spent four days at the hospital, the bite and scratch wounds healing quickly under the attention of the Healers as they fed her various potions and cleaned out the wounds. By the time she was discharged, stiff and sore and weak, only thin, silvery raised scars remained and her mother hadn’t come to see her.

 

            Eliza was there with some of Alex’s borrowed clothes for Kara to wear, a little too big for her but clean, and as she changed, she ran her fingers over the scars and wanted to cry. Slipping the navy and mustard Fitchburg Finches Quidditch t-shirt on, Kara tucked it into the old jeans and put on the boots, a size too big, and hid the scars from sight. She couldn’t even bring herself to look at them in the mirror.

 

            With her glasses on and her wand in her pocket, Kara stepped out of the room to find Eliza waiting for her, Alex a little further down as she leaned against the wall with her arms folded over her chest as scowled. Confused, Kara looked at Eliza and fiddled anxiously with her fingers.

 

            “So, I- where’s … is she coming? I mean …”

 

            Gently resting a hand on Kara’s shoulder, Eliza swallowed thickly. “You’re going to come and stay with us for a little while, okay?”

 

            “Until school starts?”

 

            “We’ll talk at home.”

 

            It struck Kara as wrong that she would be going home to a different house, not to the farmhouse she’d been raised in. Her room up in the eaves of the gabled roof with its charts of the stars and photos of magical creatures was home to her; she didn’t want to go somewhere else.

 

            “But my mom-“

 

            “She’s at work right now; we’ll send her an owl at home, okay?”

 

            Blinking back the stinging in her eyes, Kara nodded. She let Eliza shepherd her towards the lobby and over to the fire. With a handful of Floo powder, Kara stepped into the emerald flames after Alex and closed her eyes to the whirling grates passing by before she stepped out into the cramped kitchen of the Danvers home.

 

            Eliza was a Herbologist and the small house burst with an array of plants she tended to and sold for potions, greeting her as she dusted herself off and watched as Eliza came through behind her. Kara knew they were from a long line of Pureblood witches and wizards, much like her own family, but looking around at the faded homeliness of the kitchen, it was clear that their blood status hadn’t afforded them the same wealth and privilege that Kara had grown up with on their hidden acres out in the countryside.

 

            “Alright, you should take it easy; sit, sit. Alex, why don’t you go upstairs and clear out your dad’s old office. We’ll have to squeeze a bed in.”

 

            Oblivious to the angry look shot at her by the other young girl, Kara looked at Eliza with anxious blue eyes. “I’m not- I mean … I won’t be here long, will I?”

 

            “I’ll visit your mom tomorrow, okay? You just rest up; that attack must’ve taken it out of you.”

 

            Reaching up, Kara rubbed at the tender bite wound on her shoulder, some phantom pain of teeth lingering on the edges of her mind. Swallowing, she nodded, too afraid to even voice her fears about being bitten, about what came next. Any magical child grew up knowing about werewolves, about how they transformed into beastly creatures with the full moon, how aggressive and vicious they were, targeting people and tearing them apart, drinking their blood. There was a reason they were classified as XXXXX by the Ministry. 

 

            Sitting at the kitchen table, watching Eliza move around the cramped space, talking to her plants as they trailed after her, Kara was left alone with her awful thoughts. Even at twelve, there was the sense of knowing her life was over, that everything had fallen apart over the course of one night, and how she should’ve listened to her mother. Of course, Kara hadn’t any reason to heed Alura’s warning, the worry behind her mother’s words seeming trivial.

 

            Even now, she didn’t know that her mother had pissed off a werewolf during a court session at work, that Selena had left with a thirst for revenge after being put on the Werewolf Registry, restricting her freedom and costing her her job. She didn’t know that her mother’s prejudices, as she’d made it mandatory for the werewolf to subject herself to government control, had been the cause for the revenge, promised to her as the woman had been dragged from the courtroom. 

 

            Perhaps if she’d known, she might’ve never gone outside on a full moon, but she still didn’t know, and as she sat there in the vaguely familiar kitchen, out of place and terrified, all Kara could think was why? She couldn’t even comprehend her father’s death yet, a numbness as reality refused to sink in, leading her to view it all from some outside perspective, as if her mind shielded her from the obvious truth.

 

            “I’m a werewolf, aren’t I?” Kara hoarsely asked twenty minutes later, her knees hugged to her chest as she stared blankly at the fireplace.

 

            Eliza knocked over the tin of Conjure Cocoa and hesitated before picking it up. With a wave of her wand, she had three mugs filled and sent them drifting over to the table. One was set down before Kara but she didn’t touch it as she gave Eliza a mournful look.

 

            With a resigned sigh, the other woman sank down onto the seat perpendicular to her. “Yes.”

 

            She’d already known, of course, had remembered it and overheard her mother, but it still took her a moment to absorb the truth voiced by someone else. There was another gripping fear though as she leaned her forehead against her knees, shoulders taut with panic.

 

            “Will I be able to go back to school?”

 

            “Not to Ilvermorny.”

 

            The gentle letdown felt earthshattering, on top of the Lycanthropy. There weren’t many jobs a witch could get without some sort of formal education, and being a werewolf would mean she’d be shunned from every opportunity. Kara could still remember the son of her parent’s friends who’d turned out to be a Squib and how bad it had turned out for him ; Lycanthropy was an even worse curse, even still having her magic.

 

            “But … I wrote to other schools. I received a letter from one of them; you’ll be accepted there.”

 

            “There aren’t any other American schools,” Kara said with confusion as her brow creased.

            

            “It’s in Scotland. All of the U.K. witches and wizards go there. I’ve heard it’s quite good.”

 

            “Scotland?” Kara rasped, feeling faint, feeling sick. “My mom won’t let me go there . How-”

 

            Placing a hand on her arm, Eliza swallowed thickly, her eyes bright with tears as she devastated her one last time. “Kara, your mom … isn’t coming back for you.”

 

            “My mom’s … not coming back?” she echoed, her childish face crumpling with confusion as her brows drew together over the rims of her glasses. “I- what- no. She- she has to, she’s … my mom. I want my mom.”

 

            She started crying then, unable to feel embarrassed as she sobbed into the borrowed jeans, shaking with the effort as tears turned her eyes bloodshot and cheeks blotchy. Eliza climbed to her feet and moved over to her chair, wrapping an arm around Kara’s shoulders as she held her, until Kara was grabbing a fistful of her denim shirt in her hand and sobbing into the fabric, leaving a large damp patch.

 

            “It’s alright; it’ll be okay. You won’t be alone - I’ll take care of you. I’ll take you to Hogwarts.”

Chapter 2

            Sitting in the middle of the open field, the brisk wind ruffling her hair and her stomach twisting itself into knots, Kara stared out at the row of grey-brick houses, terraced and drab, much like most of England. They’d been there for two weeks, settling into the cramped, narrow house wedged between two identical ones, just outside of Falmouth in Cornwall. It was remote enough that they had some freedom to exist without coming under scrutiny, a rather sizable magical population dwelling there too, but close enough that they could walk to the nearby Asda with Eliza, marveling at the electricity and the British food. 

 

            London had been too expensive for Eliza to afford on her savings and the sale of the small home in Wisconsin, a widowed mother who’d been saddled with the responsibility of two daughters now, and Kara felt a stab of guilt as she picked a dandelion from the long grass and twirled it between two tanned fingers. She doubted she’d ever get used to the English countryside and its rather damp climate, even if Cornwall wasn’t quite as dismal. In the two weeks since they’d been uprooted and moved to the other side of the world, it had only rained three times but even that small bit of luck wasn’t enough to endear her to the foreign land. 

 

            Alex had ignored her for the most part, stiff and angry as she blamed Kara for them having to move, which was true but stung nevertheless. The start of the school year at Hogwarts wasn’t due to start for a little more than a week which left them with too much time at home together to co-exist in the small house. Kara had resorted to spending all day, every day outside, wandering the narrow streets, walking through the rain as she kicked empty beer cans along the street, watching No-Maj - no, Muggles - kick a ball back and forth in the park while a mother waited on the side of the road for a bus. It all felt so strange and unfamiliar to her. 

 

            The only place that felt peaceful was the open strip of fields between one cluster of houses and the open countryside, or the sandy beaches and coves on the eastern side of the city. Kara preferred the open fields, almost familiar, although it was achingly evident she wasn’t in Wisconsin. She spent hours wandering aimlessly, picking flowers, watching squirrels run up trees and frogs croak in the grimy shallows of the riverbed. She even thought she caught sight of a Grindylow in a stagnant pond, a ghastly green creature amidst the brown ditchwater which quickly ducked behind the neon orange of a submerged traffic cone.

 

            Yet, with each passing day, Kara was saddled with growing anxiety as the moon inched closer to full. She’d yet to transform for the first time and it filled her with dread, her face pinched with fear as she grew quieter. Not that she’d had much to say anyway - she missed her home and her mom, and as kind as Eliza was, Kara couldn’t help but stay up half of the night, crying into her pillow so she didn’t wake Alex, who had been forced to share a room with her. Alura hadn’t so much as sent a letter , it was like Kara had ceased to exist to her that night, and Eliza had been left to hastily pack what she could at the farmhouse and bring it home to Kara with an apologetic look on her face.

 

            It was just another thing to add to Kara’s silent anger, stewing in her thoughts as she counted down the days, waiting for the day she’d transform into a monster. No amount of gentle reassurances at the table crammed into their dim kitchen over a meal of meatloaf that she barely touched could quell the growing nausea as her stomach tied itself into knots. Eliza’s maternal bearing was futile and Kara could see her adoptive mother grow more concerned with each passing day. Even she couldn’t lie about the horror that loomed closer every day.

 

            Until the day was upon them and Kara woke, feeling exhausted already as if her body knew it in her bones that this was the day of the full moon. She woke red-eyed and disheveled, shoving her wire-rimmed glasses onto her face and then curling up under the blankets as she avoided rising until Alex left the room an hour later, ignoring her although Kara felt that she knew she was awake. Cherishing the time to herself, Kara sat up and ran a hand over her face, looking at the small room, two single beds wedged up against opposite walls, while a set of drawers were pushed up at the ends and a single desk in between them. Alex had put up posters of the Fitchburg Finches Quidditch team, Weird Sisters, and moving photos that included a man that Kara dimly knew was Jeremiah from the handful of times she’d met him.

 

            For her own half of the bedroom, Kara had nothing to show for her life. Her clothes were neatly put away, her trunk of school supplies - soon to be replaced - was under the bed and the bristles of her Nimbus 1001 broomstick stuck out slightly. Picking up her copy of Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them , Kara flipped to the well-worn chapter on werewolves, her stomach lurching at the sight of the hairy beast with its XXXXX rating. She ran her fingertips over the face of the monster and swallowed thickly.

 

            There was a light rap on the bedroom door a few minutes later, before it opened and Eliza poked her head around it. Her wary expression brightened at the sight of Kara sprawled on the bed, knees up and book on her stomach. Smiling softly, she cocked her head to the side.

 

            “I thought you were up. Mind if I come in?”

 

            She took Kara’s silence as agreement and stepped inside, shutting the door behind herself and crossing over to Alex’s unmade bed to sit down. The gap between the beds was so narrow that if they’d both reached out they would’ve been able to touch. Leaning forward, elbows braced on her knees, blonde strands of hair falling about her face as her wand held her bun in place, Eliza fixed her with a searching stare.

 

            “How about some breakfast?”

 

            Kara always had an appetite but it had escaped her the last few weeks, making her look gangly and thin, her grief giving her a bowed posture while her fear pinched her face. She shook her head, slumping further down the pillows beneath her head as she hid behind her book.

 

            “Kara … I know you’re scared. That’s normal .”

 

            Silent, Kara blinked back the burning pressure behind her eyes and drew in a shallow breath, scowling at the creamy pages, thumbing the worn edge. Her heart pounded in her chest and her senses felt overwhelmed, slightly heightened since the attack - although her eyesight was still poor enough to warrant glasses - and she felt the maelstrom of emotions inside her like a hurricane. That was another thing that she wasn’t used to, too many emotions rioting inside for her to parse through. All Kara knew was that it hurt .

 

            “I was thinking … not tomorrow, maybe the day after, we could go to this Diagon Alley,” Eliza said, waving the yellowed parchment letter that had been delivered via owl with information about the requirements for Hogwarts. “We can get all of your new school things.”

 

            “I don’t have any money,” Kara murmured.

 

            “Well … that’s alright.”

 

            Kara didn’t say anything else and Eliza sighed softly, patient but only to a certain extent as she leaned across the space between them and gently pulled the book from Kara’s hands. She shut it with a quiet thud and set it down on the mattress beside her, staring expectedly at her new daughter.

 

            “I don’t want to go to Hogwarts,” Kara petulantly replied after a moment, folding her arms over her chest. 

 

            “It’s a good school, from what I’ve heard.”

 

            “I want to go home.”

 

            Mouth thinning with regret and guilt, Eliza brushed a strand of hair out of her face, “I’m sorry she left you.”

 

            Kara’s chin dimpled as her mouth turned down at the corners, her face crumpling as the urge to cry built. Turning on her side, she closed her eyes and tried to pretend she was alone, in her own bed. She heard the thin mattress groan across from her as Eliza climbed to her feet and then her warm hand gently touched Kara’s arm before her book was set down beside her.

 

            “Eat something. We’ll leave for St. Mungo’s at five.”

 

            Stomach twisting at the very thought, Kara squeezed her eyes shut tighter and heard the door click shut. Letting out a pent-up breath, she gripped the book in her hand and lay there for a little while longer. Eventually, she climbed to her feet and went through to the small bathroom, the grout between the ghastly navy tiles still somewhat greyish despite Eliza’s deep clean with the aid of magic, and ran a bath into the narrow tub. It was bewildering to her that there were two knobs, but the water was always on the cooler side as the boiler took an age to kick in and Kara spent half of her bath shivering as she grit her teeth.

 

            Changing into a sky blue t-shirt and a pair of jeans, she laced up her tennis shoes and disappeared outside. The sky was a shade deeper than her shirt and she squinted as she set off through the fields. Her wand was stuck into her back pocket, although she very well couldn’t make much use of it, and she set about her aimless wandering, fingertips skimming the long grasses and the rough trunks, so different to Wisconsin but more familiar than their new home.

 

            She whittled away the hours, walking along the muddy riverbank, skirting around trash as she watched ducks splash in the water. The sun was warm and she sat in the shade of the trees before finally sitting in the open field to the back of the grey row of houses, waiting until the sun started sinking lower. She didn’t risk it getting too low though - sunset was still a way off, but she blew the head off a dandelion and watched the seeds scatter on the wind before climbing to her feet and wearily making her way home.

 

            Eliza was in the living room and leaped to her feet at the sound of the front door opening, a harried look on her face as she smoothed her hands over the cotton shirt she was wearing. Kara stared at her and quickly ducked her head down, scuffing the toe of her shoe over the linoleum, eliciting a high-pitched squeak.

 

            “We should leave soon,” Eliza said.

 

            Nodding, Kara tugged at the hem of her t-shirt, her mouth dry and the cool air in the hallway making her arms prickle with goosebumps. She caught sight of Alex at the top of the staircase as she looked up at the flicker of motion, watching her sister’s face darken with annoyance before she vanished into their bedroom.

 

            “You need to eat first.”

 

            Kara shook her head as Eliza walked out of the room, putting an arm around her shoulder and guiding her to the kitchen. An array of magical plants had taken over the place, growing from every available surface for Eliza’s herbology work, and she shifted a freshly potted Wiggentree as she dragged a chair out and propelled Kara down onto it.

 

            Dinner was a simple fare of scrambled eggs and bacon on toast and Kara ate only a mouthful, the grease of the bacon too overwhelming, not to mention the fact that it was round instead of brittle strips. Eventually, when it became apparent she wouldn’t eat anymore and the afternoon was growing later, Eliza flicked her wand at the plate and the food dumped itself in the trash.

 

            Pulling a deep blue robe on over her cotton shirt and jeans, Eliza gave her a wan smile and Kara pulled on a beige corduroy jacket, her hands trembling slightly as she buried them deep in her pockets. Moving into the living room, she was dimly aware of Eliza calling upstairs to tell Alex not to answer the door to anyone before she joined Kara and reached for the pot of Floo powder. 

 

            The fireplace turned emerald green and Eliza hesitated as if wondering whether Kara would follow her through or choose elsewhere to vanish to. After a moment, she ducked into the low grate and clearly stated the name of the hospital they’d been given at the Ministry of Magic when she’d taken Kara to get registered. It was the safest option, they’d been assured, with trained Healers to contain and treat her overnight, but Kara still hesitated as Eliza vanished and she was left to go next.

 

            “You won’t even remember it.”

 

            Whirling around, Kara stared at Alex with wide eyes, taking in the form of her sister leaning against the doorframe, a pucker on her brow as she appraised her with brown eyes. She didn’t say it unkindly, just stated it as a fact, and Kara swallowed, nodding as she wondered if that was true.

 

            “Good luck.”

 

            Pushing off the door frame, Alex walked towards the kitchen, leaving Kara to grab a handful of Floo powder and toss it into the grate. She ducked beneath the mantlepiece and forced herself to speak, the words coming out as a croak as her dry throat refused to cooperate.

 

            “St. Mungo’s.”

 

            A minute later, Kara was ejected into the waiting room of the hospital, and if she hadn’t already been feeling nauseous from fear, she was sure the dizzying speed at which she passed a hundred grates would have made her feel so. Eliza was at her side a moment later, brushing soot off her and then leading her over to the reception area, where witches and wizards were sitting on rows of rickety, mismatched chairs, reading copies of Witch Weekly and The Daily Prophet or else nursing an array of injuries, from nasty dragon burns to someone with their head on back to front and another sprouting feathers from his face. 

 

            “Excuse me, my … daughter is here for her first- you see, she was … bitten on the last full moon, so this is- it’s her first transformation. We were told to come here-”

 

            “Dai Llewellyn Ward. First Floor,” the bored witch said with a lazy flick of her fingers towards the elevator as she scratched in an answer on her crossword with a quill.

 

            Hand on her shoulder, Eliza steered Kara over to the elevator and they climbed in with a Healer in sea-green robes. The hospital’s crest was stitched on the breast of the robe, a wand and a bone crossing each other. She swallowed thickly, breathing in the smell of dittany and bleach as they made their way up to the Creature Induced Injuries corridor of the hospital, the elevator dinging before they parted to reveal signs on the wall.

 

            Making left, they passed by more Healers and patients being wheeled on gurneys, in wheelchairs, past wards where someone was screaming. The sound made Kara’s heart pound in her chest, her breaths rapid and her palms clammy as her face turned ashen. Eliza took her hand, sensing her panic, and squeezed tightly. The simple act made Kara want to cry and her bottom lip wobbled as she clenched her teeth.

 

            They came to the Dai Llewellyn ward a minute later, with Kara realising it was for serious bites, and stepped into the small, dingy space. A single small window across the other side of the ward cast late afternoon light into the space, made darker by the oak paneling on the walls. The only glimpse of decoration was a portrait of some Urquhart Rackharrow hanging on one wall and Kara stared around at the empty beds.

 

            A trainee Healer greeted them a moment later and sobered up at the mention of their visit, turning brusque as Kara was set behind a curtain and given a hospital robe to change into, ordered to leave all of her clothes on the bed. Behind the privacy curtain, she undressed with shaking hands, kicking off her tennis shoes, shivering as the cold air hit her exposed back. It was frightening and she could feel her pulse pounding in her ears as her throat constricted. 

 

            The gown was paper thin and the floor was cold beneath her feet as she pulled back the curtain and Eliza gave her a strained smile. She was worried too, Kara realised, the thought making it even harder to swallow. 

 

            “You should take your glasses off, too. And leave your wand,” the Healer ordered her before turning to Eliza, holding out a clipboard and a quill. “If you can fill out the form.”

 

            Dutifully filling out Kara’s details, the quick scratching of the quill was the only sound that filled the small room as Kara stared at Eliza. She felt dizzy, felt like there wasn’t enough air in the room, and she broke out in a cold sweat. Signing with a flourish, Eliza handed the clipboard back to the Healer.

 

            “If you’ll follow me, I’ll take you down to one of the cells.”

 

            When Kara glanced at Eliza, eyes wide with terror, the Healer hesitated and frowned slightly.

 

            “Oh. You can probably go. She’ll be out of it all night, and she won’t come around for a few hours after dawn. Probably not until tea time, to be honest. The first one really takes it out of them.”

 

            Kara visibly paled at the Healer’s words and Eliza fixed the young man with a hard stare. “I’ll stay.”

 

            “Alright then. You can’t stay with her in the cell though.”

 

            “I’ll just see her down there.”

 

            “As you wish.”

 

            Kara tightly gripped Eliza’s hand, her adoptive-mother uncomplaining even though it must have hurt, and they were led downstairs, past the ground floor and down to the lower levels, where the Alchemy Rooms were, resident Healers poring over cauldrons and researching the properties of plants down one end, while the other end held separate wards with cells. The purpose of them was to hold dangerous prisoners requiring care, those who were too volatile to stay on a normal ward, or those who would transform into a vicious beast. 

 

            “Here,” the Healer said, stopping before a door and tapping it with his wand.

 

            A series of locks and bars slid back and the door squeaked open on noisy hinges to reveal a small space with grey stone floor and walls. There were no windows and the only light came from a dozen floating candles up near the vaulted ceiling of the cell. Perhaps it was her imagination but Kara’s nose tickled with the smell of old blood and harsh bleach as she stared at the space she was to be confined to.

 

            “This- this is it?” Eliza asked, quietly aghast.

 

            “It’s secure enough to hold them when they transform. We keep Healers down here to keep an eye on the patients down here; don’t worry.”

 

            Looking stricken, Eliza looked down at Kara and squeezed her hand. Inhaling shakily, she gave her a pained smile. “It’ll be okay.”

 

            “I don’t want to go in there,” Kara said, her voice pitifully small.

 

            Letting out a resigned sigh, Eliza cupped her face in her hands and gave her a mournful look as she sank down to a half-crouch. “I know you don’t, sweetheart. It’s too dangerous to leave you outside though - you might hurt someone. This way … we can keep you and everyone else safe.”

 

            Tears blurred Kara’s eyes and her chin wobbled as she drew in a breathless sob. Shaking her head, blonde curls bouncing at the movement, she gripped the sleeves of Eliza’s robe. “Please don’t leave.”

 

            “I’ll be right upstairs waiting for you to wake up, okay?” Eliza assured her, climbing to her feet and letting Kara bury her face into the front of her robe. Hugging her closely, she gently shushed her and ran a hand over her curls. “It’ll be okay; you’re so brave. It’ll all be over before you know it.”

 

            Through her hiccuping sobs and blinding tears, Kara was made aware of the Healer guiding Eliza into the cell with her, the stone floor freezing to the touch, the air damp and frigid, and she grabbed fistfuls of her robe as she clung to her for a moment longer. But Kara knew she couldn’t stand to hurt anyone if she transformed around them - she was too naïve to consider that the Healer would have stunned her before letting that happen - and she forced herself to let go.

 

            Wiping her tears with the cuffs of her robes, Eliza kissed her brow and hugged her gently, murmuring kind reassurances into Kara’s hair before she was left alone. The door grated shut, the locks sliding into place, the metal thick and reinforced, the sound ominous and chilling, and Kara stood in the middle of the room, feeling the cold seep into her bones, along with the dread, before sinking down to the stone floor. It was colder there but she hugged her knees to her chest and quietly cried while she waited for the nightmare to begin.

 

            In the windowless cell, illuminated by a circle of candlelight, she had no way of knowing how fast time was slipping by and how high the moon had crept into the sky, but she felt it. It could’ve been minutes or hours later, but Kara knew the exact moment the change crept upon her. A dull roar sounded in her ears, deafening as her blood pounded in her head, and her body became rigid, her shoulders hunching as she curled in on herself, pain erupting in the pit of her stomach and quickly spreading. 

 

            On her knees, doubled over so her sweating forehead nearly touched the stone floor, Kara let out a breathless gasp of pain, arms wrapped around her midsection, and she grit her teeth. It spread rapidly, the terrible agonising sensation that every atom of her being was being violently ripped apart and she let out a choked shout as she rocked herself. Eyes stinging with the pain, although she might’ve been crying again, Kara swallowed the sour taste of bile and let out a strangled yelp as her shoulder hunched, the sound of cracking bones filling the space. She retched then, bringing up nothing as she’d eaten nothing all day, and scrabbled at the stone floor with her fingernails, which were slowly darkening and lengthening into claws.

 

            Tendons taut and skin stretching, Kara couldn’t stop the first genuine scream as she seemed to convulse on the cold floor, the stone gritty against her pallid cheek as her bones shattered and reformed themselves, muscles rent and then sewed themselves into new shapes, her entire body shifting with excruciating pain. At some point during the transformation, as grey hair sprouted from her skin, Kara’s screams became whines, dog-like and inhuman, and her appearance became that of a wolf, rather than a young girl. Still, there were distinct differences to a plain wolf - the tail that had formed was bushier, the snarling snout elongating her face was shorter, and her eyes were shockingly human, still as blue as ever. There was even a sandy undercoat to the grey pelt that was springing forth, a remnant of her blonde hair lingering even now.

 

            The pain reached its peak as her spine hunched and then formed with a sickening crack, and she remained conscious up until that point before her mind was completely lost to the darkness and the wolf stood in the cramped space, head tipping back to let out an eerie howl. 

 

            And then Kara was conscious again as if the whole thing had only lasted a second, her whole body on fire, too weak to even move. She couldn’t even open her eyes, her head pounding and the pain so all-consuming that it was all she could do to draw in a shallow breath. Her chest and head hurt the most, although all of her limbs were leaden, and Kara was struck with the thought that Alex had lied - she remembered it all.

 

            “Hey,” a gentle voice was greeting her then, a hand brushing hair out of her face.

 

            Kara flinched at the contact, her eyes still shut, and let out a pitiful whimper. “It’s okay. You’re okay.”

 

            Eliza. The name filled her mind as relief flooded through her, her body limp on the thin hospital bed. A moment later there was another voice, that of an unfamiliar woman, at her bedside and Kara found herself too deep in her pain to concentrate on what was being said. Everything hurt, her ears were ringing and she felt like her head had been split open. 

 

            She must have slept awhile and the next time she woke she was able to open her eyes to narrow slits. A woman with red hair was bending over her, holding a vial to her lips and Kara drank the Blood-Replenishing Potion in spluttering mouthfuls, oblivious to what it was before another vial was taking its place and a Wiggenweld Potion to replenish her strength.

 

            It was still another twenty minutes before she could open her eyes properly, blinking slowly as she stared up at the fuzzy ceiling. Blankets were covering her and a lumpy pillow was beneath her head and Kara let her head loll to the side, taking in the blurred figure sitting in the chair beside her, watching her closely with an anxious look on her face.

 

            “Good morning,” Eliza murmured. “How’re you feeling?”

 

            “I … don’t know. It hurts.”

 

            “The Healers are taking good care of you. You’ll be- you’ll be fine , okay?”

 

            Letting out a soft, spent sigh, Kara made a humming sound, dubious and tired. Eliza didn’t say much but Kara could hear her soft breathing and her skin prickled with the feeling of being watched. She dozed again for another hour before she roused herself after lunch, her appetite evading her but more alert after sleeping off the long night. 

 

            Sitting up against her pillows, she was offered her glasses by Eliza and took in the thick bandages on her arms, swallowing thickly as she eyed them. She knew, of course. Kara could remember the searing pain of clawing at her own flesh, rending it open with her claws, snarling and staggering around the cell in a frenzy, her fear and hatred of herself, of what she’d become, only heightened in her mindless state. She’d torn at herself, trying to get it out , soaking the cell with her blood. The memories existed through a sort of haze, bloodlust and fear and dread clouding them all with a palpable fog, and Kara pressed her lips into a thin line as she stared down at her hidden body beneath the blankets, wondering how much of her was scarred.

 

            A Healer came by an hour later to check her bandages and Kara saw just how much then. Hitching up the new gown - the last one had been shredded and soaked with her blood when they’d recovered her unconscious body just after dawn - the Healer peeled back the bandages to reveal angry red lines, still weeping in places as the curse of a lycanthropes bite or scratch stopped it from healing easily. The woman used silver and dittany to help close it up more, the wound stinging and smoking faintly as Kara hissed and writhed on the bed.

 

            Most of them were shallow and would heal to nothing with another round of silver and dittany, but there were two deep parallel lines starting on the left of her rib cage and down to her hips, and another on her right shoulder. They were still pink, but Kara knew they would fade to white scars like the bite wound that had infected her. She was afraid to see her face, removing her glasses and screwing her eyes shut as she bared her teeth against the stinging pain of dittany in the cuts there, knowing that her face would be scarred too.

 

            It was a long day, and she drifted in and out of sleep all afternoon, her wounds regularly treated and a sleeping draught given to her when the pain medication started wearing off. Eliza was quiet beside her the entire time, looking just as tired as she looked at Kara’s restless form, grey face sweating as she writhed on the bed, lips murmuring soundlessly. 

 

            They kept her late, considering it was her first time - the worst time, they assured her - and it was almost dinner time when she stiffly rose from the bed, her small body sagging beneath shaky legs as if she’d aged decades overnight. Frail and cold, she hugged her arms to herself over her worn clothes, Eliza’s arm around her shoulders as she led her down the hallway and into the elevator. It was an effort, taking all of her strength, and when she went through the wide fireplace with a pinch of Floo powder, she sprawled on the tiles of the kitchen floor, face down and breathing heavily through the blinding pain.

 

            Hands helped drag her to her feet and Kara met Alex’s concerned brown eyes, watching as her sister flinched slightly at the sight of her. Letting her go, Alex moved away, that wary resentment threading through her again as she hovered uncertainly and waited for Eliza to appear a moment later. 

 

            “Let’s get you up to bed,” Eliza murmured, a hand pressed between Kara’s shoulders as she urged her along.

 

            Each plodding step upstairs made her body ache and as Eliza helped her down onto her bed, she sank heavily into the mattress, a hand pressed to her ribs as her chest rose and fell with quick, shallow breaths. Sinking down to her knees, Eliza unlaced her shoes for her and eased them off before helping her under the blankets. Kara didn’t even have the energy to take her jacket off, the sheepskin collar soft against her jaw as she blinked black spots away.

 

            Making sure she was comfortable, Eliza left her to rest alone for a while and Kara slept gladly, eager to escape the haunting memories of last night. She woke an hour later, cheeks flushed and pink, more colour in her face than there had been that morning, and squinted through the dim evening, the room grey as a rectangle of light from the landing seeping in through the open doorway, silhouetting a small outline.

 

            Alex stepped into the room and set down a cup of hot chocolate on the desk beside Kara, her face a blur in the dark as she loomed over Kara. “Mom made casserole for dinner … if you’re hungry.”

 

            Kara rolled over onto her side, staring at the bare wall, and ignored her. Alex stood there awkwardly for a moment before leaving, unsure of her new sister, resentful of her even as she pitied her. Laying in the dark for a while, she finally pushed the blankets back and rose, unsteady on her feet for a moment before she made for the drawers at the foot of her bed and pulled out flannel pyjamas. 

 

            Making her way to the small bathroom, Kara switched on the light and stared at her reflection in the mirror. A white scar cut across the bridge of her nose and her left cheek and Kara gingerly pressed her fingers to it as she swallowed thickly. Shedding the rest of her clothes as water drummed into the bathtub, she ran her fingers over the ridges of the new pale scars, and the old ones too, and blinked back tears.

 

            Scrubbing her skin clean, hard enough to turn her pink, as if it would erase what she’d become, she eventually climbed out and changed into pyjamas. Making her way back into the bedroom, ignoring the sounds of dishes in the kitchen and the sound of Alex’s owl - an American Barn Owl named Maximus, after the Seeker and Captain of the Fitchburg Finches. Climbing back into bed, she let sleep drag her under and didn’t stir until Alex was climbing out of bed the next morning, kicking her quaffle and tripping.

 

            Rubbing the sleep from her eyes, Kara squinted at her and Alex held the red ball and sheepishly palmed it as she found her awake. “Oh … sorry.”

 

            “What time is it?” Kara rasped, her stomach aching with hunger.

 

            “I don’t know. Mom’s up though.”

 

            “Oh. Okay.”

 

            Swinging her legs out of bed, Kara climbed to her feet and stretched, her muscles aching dully but marginally better than yesterday. She was still a little washed out and exhausted, but she had an appetite and made her way downstairs, cautious and agitated as she fiddled with her fingers, taking in the sight of Eliza making clippings of snakeweed as a spelled radio played Celestina Warbeck.

 

            “Good morning,” Eliza warmly greeted her, dusting soil off the front of her shirt and setting down her shears. “Breakfast?”

 

            By nine o’clock they were eating together at the table, with clouds of steam from the kettle as Eliza brewed tea, the clattering of plates and cups a replacement for conversation, and sunlight billowing through the back window.

 

            Kara couldn’t stomach much more than plain toast, despite her appetite, but she ate it all and washed it down with pumpkin juice, which seemed to satisfy Eliza. As the dishes washed themselves in the sink, Eliza gave her a searching look and a small smile.

 

            “Feeling up to Diagon Alley today?”

 

            “Sure,” Kara murmured, unbothered.

 

            “We’ll leave as soon as we’re ready. I heard the entrance is a pub so we can have lunch there. See what’s so good about this English food, huh?”

 

            Mouth turning down slightly at the corners, Kara stared at the scarred wood of the table, years of herbology practiced there, and she saw the leather case with an undetectable extension charm on it, full of plants and herbs and fungi that Eliza cared for, ready to be sold. They would need that money to buy their school supplies and Kara felt guilt well up inside her again - she had no money to pay for herself.

 

            Getting ready upstairs, Kara pulled on a long-sleeved striped shirt and tucked it into her jeans, pulling on her corduroy jacket and her tennis shoes again before leaving her blonde curls unkempt as she pocketed her wand. They were still waiting on Alex, who, at fourteen, took ages to do anything, but eventually emerged in an oversized leather jacket that had once been Jeremiah’s and scuffed leather boots.

 

            Grumbling at the old jacket, Eliza sighed and shook her head, and directed them out the front door. Locking up, she walked down the garden path in her blue robe, leather case in hand, and stopped on the pavement, thrusting out her wand hand. With the sound of a bang, a purple, triple-decker bus materialised down the other end of the street and hurled towards them before coming to a screeching halt.

 

            A bored conductor rattled off a spiel before charging them eleven Sickles each for a ticket and letting them board. Kara looked around sceptically at the interior, an assortment of chairs - none of them bolted securely to the floor - filling the space and occupied by an assortment of witches and wizards. An old man near her was knitting something in a ghastly shade of pink while a young witch was reading a book called The Scars of Salem. The trio sat in three empty seats and no sooner had they settled down did they find themselves careening down the street, chairs sliding all over the place before there was another bang and they were streaking down a country road.

 

            Clutching the arms of her chair with a stricken look on her face, Kara watched as they cycled through half a dozen roads, passengers coming and going as they stopped in Hogsmeade, outside Thunderbolt headquarters in Manchester, at a red telephone box for the Ministry of Magic and then finally outside the Leaky Cauldron. 

 

            They slipped through the door of the pub, unseen by Muggle eyes, and found the place small, dingy and welcoming, filled with all manner of magical folk as they paused to gossip and have a drink before going about their business in Diagon Alley. They didn’t linger inside but made their way out to the courtyard out back, where Eliza tapped a brick and an archway materialised before them as the red bricks receded.

 

            Kara looked around with interest at the array of stores lining the cobblestone street as other shoppers passed by, a riot of colours and sounds filling the narrow space. The street was cast into shadow by the tall, crooked buildings and she took in all manner of stores, from books and owls to robes and sweets and tea shops, as well as an assortment of tents, stands and carts wedged into the narrow alleys between shops. People crowded around them, buying singing flowers or roasting chestnuts and goods that had most likely been stolen.

 

            Their first stop was to Slug and Jiggers Apothecary, where Eliza managed to sell a few of her potion ingredients before the owner sent her off to Noltie’s Botanical Novelties and Mulligrubs Materia Medica to sell what they wouldn’t take. Purse weighed down with a few extra galleons, Eliza took them to a store with a sign displaying Madam Malkin’s Robes For All Occasions on the North Side of Diagon Alley. They passed by an archway leading through a narrow and dark alleyway with a sign reading Knockturn Alley.

 

            Inside the robe shop, both girls were made to stand on small stools while tape measures flitted around them, measuring armpit to wrist, head to toe, shoulder to shoulder. All the while, a squat old lady in mauve chatted away to Eliza, pulling out robes and starched white shirts and grey skirts. In short order, they had been fitted with three black robes each, black winter cloaks with silver fastenings, starched white shirts and grey skirts with plain grey ties. They’d been assured that the uniforms were spelled to change colours once they had been sorted into their houses. 

 

            Most of their supplies from Ilvermorney would suffice - pewter cauldrons rather standard, and a few of their textbooks matching the curriculum - still, there were new textbooks for Alex’s electives and Kara was to be given her old copy of The Standard Book Of Spells: Grade 2. They went from shop to shop, Eliza trying not to wince as the cost stacked up, before they started heading back towards the Leaky Cauldron, laden with packages wrapped in brown paper.

 

            Kara tried the steak and kidney pie for lunch and the Tongue Tying Lemon Squash, while Eliza had pea soup and Alex the House Soup Leaky, which was rather unassuming to the latter until the peppercorns exploded in her mouth and turned her face red as steam shot out of her ears. Kara bit back a smile and cut into her pie, feeling a little better after the morning’s events. 

 

            Still, as they rode the Knight Bus home after lunch, she surreptitiously ran her fingers over the new scar on her face and stared at the ever-changing scenery as her stomach tied itself into knots. The start of the school year was only a week away and she clung to the handful of days with desperation as unease threaded through her, the thought of a new school with no friends making her long for home and Ilvermorney almost as keenly as she longed for Alura.

Chapter 3

            Kara followed her new sister down the length of the scarlet locomotive as a foggy mist, reminiscent of nights on a full moon, plumed from it, giving Platform Nine and Three-Quarters a rather mysterious air. 

 

            Swallowing her nerves, Kara pushed her trolley and heavy trunk through the noisy crowd, her stomach sinking at the sight of so many students who would become her classmates. Nobody except Dumbledore, the Hogwarts staff and her sister knew that she was a werewolf - a new one at that - and Kara was sure they’d be able to see something off about her - and not just the fact that she was an American. 

 

            There was something strange and dark about her now, something that would speak to the subconscious mind and make her classmates avoid her, seeing that part of her soul that had been tainted that night, weeks ago now. She’d only turned once and the fear was still new, the memory of so much pain and waking to new scars and twisting nausea still sharp in her mind. Alex was confident as she cut through the crowd of parents and students parting ways, and Kara followed in her shadow, looking around at the other children and feeling a sense of isolation, now firmly placed as other due to her lycanthropic burden, yet she enjoyed watching them anyway. It was the closest she’d ever come to knowing any of them.

 

            She bumped her trolley into that of another student’s as she tried to navigate around it and was given a sharp look by a young man with a shaved head, dressed in a fine black suit as he held a black cane topped with a silver serpent’s head. He scowled at her and turned away, and Kara glanced sideways at the young girl dressed in a black sweater and skirt, being berated by the older woman who Kara assumed was her mother.

 

            Eliza’s hand gently pressed into her back, urging her along as she spoke softly, “come on, let’s find you a compartment and stow your trunk. Where’s your sister gone?”

 

            Kara winced at the mention of Alex being her sister - she couldn’t imagine that she’d ever get used to having another family, let alone having any sort of relationship with Alex that went beyond disdain and accusation. Still, she was silent as she allowed her new mother to shepherd her towards the train, peering over the heads of milling students to catch sight of her daughter lugging her own trunk into an empty compartment. 

 

            Climbing onto the train, Kara tried to help Eliza with the trunk, before Alex sighed impatiently and nudged her aside, dragging it in and stowing it beneath the seat. Fiddling with her fingers, Kara’s throat constricted at the thought of being sent away, alone. She didn’t want to go to Hogwarts, she wanted to cling to the only familiar thing in her life anymore - Eliza, her mother’s old friend, only vaguely known but better than nothing. Her eyes prickled with tears and she looked down, dirty blonde hair hiding her face as she hunched her shoulders.

 

            Wiping her hands on her jeans, Eliza smiled encouragingly, “well, we’d better say goodbye before it hits eleven. I’ve heard it leaves on the dot.”

 

            Alex jumped down and rolled her eyes as her mom hugged her tightly, brushing her hair back and kissing her cheek as she reminded her to be good. Standing inside the compartment, stomach swooping and palms clammy as the moment of departure came upon them, Kara found herself lost. As Alex climbed back up, shouldering past her, Eliza stepped forward and held out a hand to her.

 

            Looking up, Kara’s eyebrows raised slightly, a mournful expression on her face. She climbed off the train and stood before Eliza, head ducked down and gently urged up by the warm, calloused hands cupping her face. Giving her a strained smile, Eliza brushed her blonde hair out of her face, revealing the pale scars that Kara tried to hide in vain.

 

            “You’re going to be great,” Eliza firmly told her, giving her face a gentle squeeze in her hands.

 

            Kara’s eyes filled with tears and she couldn’t bring herself to speak, swallowing past the lump in her throat. She hesitantly nodded and Eliza sighed, face etched with worry, as she pulled her into a hug, Kara’s face pressed against her shoulder. Kissing her brow, Eliza let her go and gave her a tight-lipped smile.

 

            “Stay out of trouble and focus on the work, okay?”

 

            She nodded again and climbed back into the compartment, settling down in the corner on a comfortably worn padded bench. A sharp whistle pierced the air as the last minute call for boarding sounded through the station, the remaining first-years looking nervous and pale as they said their last goodbyes. Alex dragged the exterior compartment door shut and then poked her head out the window, heeding her mother’s last minute warnings before the train started to pull forward on the tracks, gradually gathering speed before it started to round the corner and she withdrew back into the compartment. Platform Nine-and-Three-Quarters vanished behind them.

 

            Heaving a sigh, Alex flopped down onto the bench across from Kara, turning so that her back was to the wall and her legs were stretched out before her. Neither of them spoke and Kara curled up into a ball, removing the well-worn copy of Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them and thumbing through the pages. Students passed by in the corridor, a mixture of accents clamouring together, distinctly British even though Kara had no hope of parsing through the regional differences.

 

            Students stopped at the door and moved on once they saw that it was occupied, and the two of them lapsed into a heavy silence. Pretending to read her book, the page open to the chapter on Lethifolds, Kara couldn’t concentrate at all, but when the compartment door jerked open a minute later, she startled at the intrusion.

 

            “Oh,” said the tall boy with brown skin and a shaved head, filling the doorway. Glancing back over his shoulder, he raised his eyebrows to someone out in the corridor. “Looks like our compartment’s been taken.”

 

            “Well kick them out,” another guy drawled.

 

            “Don’t be an arse, Mike,” a girl tutted, pushing forward.

 

            She ducked under the boy’s arm and smiled tentatively. “Hi. Is it alright if we sit in here?”

 

            Alex slowly lowered her feet to the floor and shifted across the bench, a wary look on her face as they watched a retinue of teenagers file in. It quickly became crowded and Kara found herself pressed up against the far wall as a boy her age dressed in a uniform sporting a blue and brown tie, his dark hair brushing his shirt collar, sat beside her.

 

            “Anyone know these two?” the first boy asked, leaning forward to peer at Kara and Alex, his face crumpling slightly with confusion. “You’re not First Years - God, you’re not Slytherin’s are you?”

 

            “We’re new,” Alex curtly replied. 

 

            “Oh. Strange.”

 

            “I’m Kelly,” the first girl introduced herself with a shy smile, gesturing dismissively to the boy. “That’s my brother, James. That’s Mike, Imra, Querl, Lucy and Winn.”

 

            Alex nodded and Kara kept her head ducked down, peering at them all through the curtain of her hair as she clutched her book tightly. They were of varying ages - some, like James, older, while the boy beside her, Querl, looked to be Kara’s age.

 

            “I’m Alex. This is Kara.”

 

            “Sisters?” 

 

            With a shrug and a flicker of annoyance in her eyes, Alex’s lips twisted slightly. “Sort of.”

 

            “What’re you reading?”

 

            Kara startled at the voice beside her and looked up, her glasses slipping down her nose as she looked at the boy with wide blue eyes. “Oh, um, it’s Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them.”

 

            He nodded and the attention quickly moved on from her as she tried to make herself small and hidden, tucked away in the corner. They were clearly a close-knit group of friends, gossiping about what they’d heard over the summer holidays in the letters swapped between them all, complaining about teachers and getting into a heated discussion about Quidditch. From what Kara could tell, they were a mixture of three Houses and varying years - Querl was in Ravenclaw and had grown up not far from Mike, a Fourth-Year Hufflepuff, which explained his presence, James, Lucy and Imra were all in Gryffindor and Kelly a Third-Year Ravenclaw with Winn. There were no Slytherin’s.

 

            For all they didn’t know the two newcomers, they were welcoming and tried their best to include them in conversation, although Kara was firmly avoiding it as she kept her head in her book, not even reading it as she remained on the same page on Lethifolds. 

 

            “What House do you think you’ll be in?” Imra asked.

 

            “Gryffindor,” Alex immediately replied. “I was a Wampus back at Ilvermorny; I’ve heard they’re similar.”

 

            Imra was a Fourth-Year as well and she nodded eagerly at the thought of Alex being her new housemate. She turned her piercing blue eyes on Kara a moment later and raised her eyebrows.

 

            “What about you?”

 

            Kara was ignoring them and didn’t respond until Alex kicked her boot, frowning slightly as if she willed her new sister not to ruin things for her. Flushing slightly, which only made her pale scars stand out more, she shifted uncomfortably.

 

            “Well … I don’t know. How do they sort you here?”

 

            “With a hat.”

 

            “A hat?” Kara echoed as her face crumpled.

 

            “You’ll see,” James said with a kind smile, looking to the door as it was opened to reveal a witch pushing a snack trolley.

 

            There was a rush of motion inside the compartment, all of the kids rummaging through pockets for money as they made a disorderly queue. Mike bought the most, his arms full of pumpkin pasties, cauldron cakes, licorice wands, Droobles’ Best-Blowing Gum, Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans, and chocolate frogs, as well as other sweets that Kara had never seen before. 

 

            Eliza had given the two of them some money for the train, and Alex a little more for weekend visits to Hogsmeade - Kara was disgruntled that she was still too young to go - but it was a pittance compared to the money that some of them handed over to the witch. Kara bought herself a Chocolate Frog with the little money she had, chocolate being her one great weakness when it came to sweets.

 

            She curled back up in her corner and opened the box, catching the frog before it could leap away and bit off a leg. Staring down at the card, she tucked it into her pocket, the motion noticed by Querl, who was sorting through his Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans with unnerving confidence, handing off the bad ones to Mike, who seemed oblivious as he tipped a handful of ear wax, tripe and soap flavoured ones back and chewed with no reaction. 

 

            “Who’d you get?”

 

            “Marlowe Forfang,” Kara murmured.

 

            “Who’s that?” Lucy asked. 

 

            Finding herself pinned beneath the expectant gazes of half a dozen of her new peers, Kara opened and closed her mouth, slinking down in his seat. Querl perked up, an eager look on his face as he held the answer on the tip of his tongue.

 

            “He was a wizard who died trying to find a cure for lycanthropy.”

 

            “What’s that?” Mike asked, scoffing down a licorice wand as he frowned with confusion.

 

            “Seriously?” Kelly coolly asked him. “How are you a Fourth-Year and you don’t know what lycanthropy is?”

 

            “Dunno,” he shrugged.

 

            “It’s … what a werewolf has,” Kara quietly replied. “It’s the condition they get when they’re bitten.” 

 

            “It’s a technical term,” Querl supplied.

 

            Mike had already moved on from the conversation and was trying to cram a whole pumpkin pastie into his mouth as Imra elbowed him, rolling her eyes. There was an ease between them all as they talked and Alex fit right in, while Kara was practically forgotten about in the corner for the next few hours as the train chugged through the English countryside, heading northwards to Scotland.

 

            It was starting to get dark beyond the windows, shadows lengthening and the sky a deep blue as the first few stars winked through the streaks of grey clouds. James declared they’d be there soon, within the hour at least, and everyone went off in search of their uniforms, leaving Kara and Alex to pull their own out of their trunks and join the queue for the toilets. Her tie was crooked when she emerged, curly hair positively unruly and a pinched look of worry to her face as she carried her clothes back to her compartment, losing her way and walking in on a group of Seventh-Years who gave her an odd look before she stammered and blushed and felt an arm around her shoulders.

 

            “Next one,” Kelly softly told her, steering her along.

 

            “Oh,” Kara said with a strained laugh, pushing her slipping glasses back up her nose.

 

            “Are you okay?” the other girl asked with surprise, looking at Kara with mild panic on her face. She was rather short, almost of a height with Kara, who was quite tall for her age at almost thirteen. “God, you’ve gone very white. Shall I get your sister?”

 

            Kara clenched her teeth and closed her eyes. “She’s not my sister.”

 

            “Oh. Well …”
