            “I’m fine.” she murmured, ducking her head and making for the door to the compartment, weaving past Lucy and Imra, who were fixing eachother’s hair and ties.

 

            The boys already looked dishevelled, Mike’s shirt untucked, Winn’s hair standing up as if he’d anxiously raked his fingers through it, and there was a newcomer as well with a shock of white hair and deathly pale skin. Kara almost thought him an albino before she let out a yelp of surprise as she watched his skin turn green, leaping away from him and almost into Alex’s lap.

 

            Laughter filled the compartment and Kelly ruffled the boy’s longish hair before dropping into the seat across from him while Alex shoved Kara back into her corner with a scowl. “Querl, don’t terrorise her on her first day.”

 

            “You’re a Metamorphmagus,” Kara said with surprise and no small amount of awe in her voice as she gave her a wary look.

 

            “Yes,” he simply replied, his appearance melting back into one of dark eyes, dark hair and tanned skin.

 

            The train started to slow then, a screeching sound from the tracks as everyone was jolted, those not sitting almost toppling into laps, and they all squeezed onto the benches while Kara stared out at the darkness that had crept in, finding herself staring at what looked like a hundred illuminated windows piercing the night. With a hiss and a final jolt, the Hogwarts Express came to a final stop and James moved to open the door.

 

            As Alex started to reach for her cage housing Maximus, the owl ruffling his feathers, she was told to leave everything there and Kara tucked her battered book into the pocket of her black robe as she climbed off the train. Kara looked around, feeling lost amidst a sea of black robes with touches of colour to signify which House they’d been sorted into - save for the First Years in the same black and white as Kara and Alex.

 

            “Firs’ years!” a voice cried out. “Firs’ years! Over here!” 

 

            “You’d better go with him,” Winn said, nudging Alex and nodding towards the gigantic man walking through the crowd of students, head and shoulders above even the tallest Seventh Year. “Hagrid, the Groundskeeper,” he said by way of explanation before hurrying off towards a carriage.

 

            “He’s so tall,” Alex said with shock, speaking aloud instead of to her sister. “He must have giant’s blood in him.”

 

            They followed the stream of First Years following after Hargrid, his lantern lighting the way as he led them to the lakeshore where a fleet of small rowing boats were waiting. There was a moment of uncertainty as people boarded the boats, people getting shafted to the next one as the spots filled up. Kara’s stomach lurched as Alex climbed into one and she hurried to climb in next to her, the boat rocking nauseatingly.

 

            Once everyone was seated in a boat, Hagrid tapped the side of the boat with an umbrella and they started smoothly gliding across the surface of the lake, and Kara watched the castle loom closer. It was drastically different to the old red-brick buildings of Ilvermorny, a relatively new school in comparison, and even though she couldn’t see much of the castle, the black outline against the dark sky was impressive and a little daunting.

 

            The boats docked in a small underground cavern, the air dank and sconces on the wall illuminating the space as they all clambered onto the stone berth, a flight of stone steps leading up to a set of giant oak doors. Ushered through by Hagrid, he left them waiting in a large entrance hall and there was a restless nervousness to the new students, Alex looking comically tall next to the crop of eleven-year-olds, although she was a little paler than usual, for all her blustering and confidence.

 

            A woman appeared a short while later, dressed in dark robes with dark hair pulled back into a severe bun. Her accent was distinctly Scottish and too thick for Kara to understand much of what she said as a faint ringing sound filled her ears, the uniform too stuffy, even in the chill, airy hall. A ghost wandered through a moment later and Kara’s attention snagged on the man dressed like a monk, spectrally grey as he glided through the opposite wall. 

 

            “Follow me, please,” said Professor McGonagall, turning and making for the doors, which opened at the swish of her wand.

 

            Towards the back of the two neat rows of students, Kara entered the Great Hall with a slack look of surprise on her face, spellbound by the ceiling and the hundreds of floating candles. Four tables, sorted by Houses she realised, were parallel with the path the new students took towards the front, where a raised platform held the High Table occupied by a dozen teachers. In the centre was an old man with a long beard and piercing blue eyes, and he smiled faintly as the students assembled before the platform and Professor McGonagall fetched a stool and a ragged hat. She placed this on the stool and it startled Kara by producing a song . Whoever had heard of a singing hat before?

 

            Once it had finished, McGonagall unfurled a roll of parchment with a list of names on it and called out the first one. A young boy stumbled forward, shaking as he sat on the stool and the hat was placed on his head. A moment later he was sorted into Ravenclaw and the process started anew with the new student.

 

            “Danvers, Alexandra.”

 

            Alex swallowed thickly and walked forward, mounting the steps and sitting on the stool as the Sorting Hat was lowered onto her head. Kara had noticed that some took longer than others to be sorted, but the hat had barely touched her sister’s head when it cried, “GRYFFINDOR!” 

 

            She clapped along with the other students, the rowdiness from the scarlet table particularly loud, and then Kara realised it was her turn as McGonagall shouted her name out, the cheers dying down. 

 

            “Danvers, Kara.”

 

            Her throat closed up and she had to clench her hands to stop them trembling as she took a jerky step towards the stool, feeling everyone’s eyes drilling into her back. She felt the eyes of the staff before her too, knew that they were all thinking about how she was the little werewolf who Dumbledore had permitted to attend.

 

            She felt a cold sweat break out on her skin as she turned and sank onto the stool, squeezing her eyes shut to the sea of black staring back at her. And then a voice murmured in her ear, making her stiffen with uneasy surprise.

 

            “Well, well, what do we have here? A little werewolf, how unusual. I’ve never had one of you before. Hm, let’s take a look, shall we? Oh, yes, you’re clever - very clever - perhaps Ravenclaw would suit you. But wait … brave as well, yes. Anyone who can weather the full moon has to be brave. But no … you’re afraid of your little secret, aren’t you? I can sense your fear. You have a need to prove yourself, to fit in; I can see you being a hard worker to achieve what you want, and, yes, patient too. You understand more than most; you’re a rare kind soul. How odd for someone who has been dealt an unjust hand, and yet, there’s no blame in your heart for your mother. You could be ambitious, but Slytherin is out of the question - you’d never make friends there, even with your Pureblood lineage, and that’s what you want, isn’t it? Someone to be loyal to, somewhere you belong where you can prove yourself, rise above what was done to you and dedicate yourself to something … worthier. You really could be good in Ravenclaw, you know, but you’ll be great in HUFFLEPUFF!”

 

            The last word was shouted to the hall and a cheer went up, the hat removed from Kara’s blonde head as she rose on unsteady legs, feeling pale and faint as she blinked. There was a part of her that was frightened that she’d been sorted into a different House to Alex, to be left alone to make friends with a bunch of strangers already in their second year. Still, she made her way over to the table of black and yellow, seeing the face of the boy from the train and falling down onto the bench beside him, willing herself to shrink down into her robes as she captured the attention of everyone in the nearby vicinity, before the sorting continued and she was spared.

 

            It seemed like forever before the last student was called up and then the tables before them were suddenly filled with an array of food. Kara’s stomach had been rumbling quietly for the past five minutes and she blinked at the mountains of chicken drumsticks and potatoes, slowly reaching out to place some on her plate.

 

            Chatter and laughter filled the room, friends reuniting after the summer holidays apart, classmates catching up and the new students introducing themselves. Kara kept to herself and ate in silence, refilling her pumpkin juice, helping herself to some more peas and lamb chops. Dessert arrived shortly after the plates emptied and she tried sticky toffee pudding and felt far too full and tired by the time the meal came to a close.

 

            Once everyone had finished, it was time for bed and Kara was left following the stream of Hufflepuffs as a Prefect called out, shepherding them out of the Great Hall. The older girl made for a wide staircase heading downstairs and they were taken down to the basement, introducing herself as Julia Freeman, a Sixth Year. 

 

            They made a left turn and followed a corridor through the basement before they made another left. “We call this kitchen corridor,” Julia called out, gesturing to the numerous paintings of food on the walls. “We’re lucky; access to the kitchens is nearby. I’m sure you’ll all find out the secret to getting in by the end of your first year. Now, our Common Room is just over here.”

 

            They were led to a little nook on the far right of the wide, cosy hallway, where a stack of large barrels lay on their sides. The lids facing them were wider across than Kara was tall. Julia gave them all a wide smile and turned towards the barrels.

 

            “The other Common Rooms have passwords and riddles - ours is easier than that. All you have to do is tap the middle barrel on the bottom row in the rhythm of Helga Hufflepuff.”

 

            The Prefect tapped along as she spoke and the wide lid of the barrel swung open to reveal the Common Room beyond. Stepping inside, Julie hesitated and then glanced back over her shoulder.

 

            “Make sure you tap the middle barrel lid and use the right rhythm; the other ones will cover you in vinegar and you won't be let in.”

 

            Kara frowned at how bizarre this school seemed to be, her fleeting glimpse at dozens of moving paintings and suits of armour making it seem more medieval than Ilvermorny had. And riddles and passwords? The thought of how many secrets must lay in the school made her intrigued; Kara loved a good puzzle and was quickly taken with the idea of exploring - another pastime of hers.

 

            Inside, the Common Room was circular with a low ceiling. Light from a dozen lamps and the cheerful fire in the massive hearth, with a honey coloured wooden mantelpiece carved with badgers framing it, bathed the room in a warm glow. The light glinted on the abundance of burnished copper and the comfortable yellow of the room. There was an earthy smell too, rich and green, from the plants that seemed to be everywhere.

 

            Above the fireplace was a painting of someone Kara instantly knew to be Helga Hufflepuff. Students were already milling about on overstuffed sofas and upholstered armchairs of yellow and black and Kara felt instantly at home. She’d been expecting something austere and unfriendly, yet there were a dozen smiles and greetings thrown the way of the new students as the First Years were led through a round door leading off the Common Room.

 

            Standing there cluelessly for a moment, an older girl with tanned skin, brown hair and hazel eyes wandered over. “You’re not a First Year are you?”

 

            “Second,” Kara murmured.

 

            “Oh, American,” the girl said with mild surprise. “I’m Sam. Third Year. Your dorm is through that door.”

 

            She pointed it out to Kara and gave her a warm smile before wandering over to the door beside it and stepping into her own dorm. Swallowing thickly, Kara walked over to the door and pulled it open, finding herself staring at a small round antechamber with more doors branching off it. 

 

            Pausing for a moment, Kara noticed plaques on the wooden doors and hesitantly moved over to one reading the list of five names. Relief washed through her and she moved onto another door and then another. There were eight doors in total and Kara found her name on the fifth one, just after the one with a plaque that read Bathroom.

 

            The other four girls were Eve, Belinda, Mackenzie and Izzy. Kara swallowed thickly before she reached for the door handle set into the centre of the round door and turned it. The door opened on well-oiled hinges, creaking faintly as the chatter inside died.

 

            Kara found herself greeted by four faces staring at her from four-poster beds made with yellow drapes and patchwork quilts. Copper lamps cast a warm glow over the space and a small wood burner was burning in the middle of the round room. Only one bed remained empty and Kara noticed her trunk was already sitting at the foot of it, the nightstand empty and the quilt taut over the mattress.

 

            “New girl, come in,” one of them called out, giving her a slow smile.

 

            A blonde with springy curls and blue eyes eagerly climbed to her feet, beaming at Kara. “I’m Eve Tesmacher.”

 

            “Oh, um, hi. I’m Kara,” she shyly murmured, keeping her head down. “Danvers,” she added a bit belatedly, the surname getting stuck in her throat, unfamiliar and unnatural.

 

            “That’s Mackenzie,” Eve said, gesturing to the girl who’d spoken first. “And Izzy and Belinda.”

 

            The one called Belinda stared at Kara for a long moment, her expression seeming irate, as if she was annoyed at having a new roommate. 

 

            “What happened to your face?” she bluntly asked after a moment.

 

            Kara winced slightly and swallowed thickly. “Fell off my broomstick,” she whispered in reply.

 

            Belinda let out a snort of laughter and Eve let out a strained laugh as she moved over to Kara, grabbing her by the sleeve of her robe and dragging her over to her bed.

 

            “They’ve already brought your things up. Bathroom is just next door.”

 

            Nodding, Kara moved over to her trunk and fished out sweatpants and a worn Ilvermorny T-shirt with a Thunderbird on the front. Making her way to the bathroom next door, Kara changed in a toilet stall and brushed her teeth at a porcelain sink, catching the eyes of a few other Second Year girls in the black-spotted mirror.

 

            She ducked her head down and avoided everyone before making her way back to her new dorm. The girls quickly cut off as she walked back in, giving her the distinct impression that they’d been talking about her, and Kara caught them staring at the Thunderbird emblazoned on her T-shirt as she crossed over to her bed, the one to the right of the door.

 

            Stowing her uniform, Kara climbed onto her bed tucked away in the corner, one side pushed up against the stone wall, and clutched her copy of Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them. She didn’t want to be rude, but these girls were friends already and Kara knew she’d never fit into their group on any deep and meaningful level.

 

            She remained quiet and absorbed in her book until the other girls dimmed their lamps and climbed into bed, pulling the hangings around theirs. Kara stayed up a while longer, reading by the glow of her own lamp before she set it down on the nightstand beside her wand, removed her glasses and put the lamp out. 

 

            Drawing the hangings around her bed, she climbed beneath the soft quilt and lay on the piles of pillows. It was comfortable and warm, yet Kara couldn’t sleep, her body tense and her mind racing as she awaited tomorrow. The first day of school.

Chapter 4

            The first few weeks at Hogwarts passed in a whirlwind of confusion for Kara. She found herself behind in classes, the Hogwarts curriculum ahead of what she’d been learning in some classes at Ilvermorny, while some classes she wouldn’t take at Hogwarts until next year - Kara was dismayed to find that Care of Magical Creatures wasn’t allowed until Third Year - and Charms was the only one she was currently excelling at. Then there was the castle itself, a maze of corridors and moving staircases and some unhelpful paintings that would never tell her where she was or where to go. 

 

            In her first week, Kara had tapped the barrel to the Hufflepuff common room out of rhythm and found herself doused in vinegar and locked out until the Third-Year she’d met on her first night, Sam, had arrived and let her in. Then there had been Quidditch tryouts, something that Kara was eagerly excited for, hoping to make the house team and find something to enjoy in this unfamiliar place she’d been banished to, but she’d been the smallest one there looking to be a Beater and had lost out to a Seventh-Year who’d been on the team for years. Overall, Kara was thoroughly defeated by Hogwarts so far, and that was without the full moon approaching.

 

            It was on the 20th of September, a few days before her thirteenth birthday, and she grew more anxious with each passing day. She’d received a few letters from Eliza so far, owls swooping in at breakfast and depositing them on her plate of toast or bowl of porridge, and she’d read them at night while tucked up in bed, but hadn’t replied so far. She’d barely seen Alex either, her new sister slipping in with the group they’d met on the train, and making the Gryffindor Quidditch team as a Chaser, Kara had heard. So far, she hadn’t made any of her own friends, although most of the Hufflepuff students she’d crossed paths with had been friendly enough - save Belinda, who was often mocking towards Kara, although Eve usually tried to smooth it over, nervous and eager to please. 

 

            What Eve didn’t seem to understand was that Kara didn’t want friends. She’d had her own at Ilvermorny - Thara, Kenny - and missed her best friends, more than she’d thought she would. Kara hadn’t even had time to say goodbye, never wrote a letter or explained her absence. To them, it would be as if she’d simply vanished, and she thought it was better that way. Still, it didn’t stop her from feeling lonely as she woke each day to a dorm of strangers, showered and dressed and sat beside strangers in her shared classes, not speaking as she kept her scarred face down, squeezing into empty spots at mealtimes and wandering the grounds alone.

 

            That was one thing Kara did like about Hogwarts; the sprawling grounds were rich with places to explore. The weather was still slightly warm enough for her to do her homework outdoors while the light lingered a moment before dinner time, sitting against the trunk of a tree on the edge of the Forbidden Forest - although she dared not enter, upon the strong warning they’d been given at the welcome feast - or walked along one section of the lake, peering into the murky depths to catch sight of mermaids or grindylows. Students threw a Quaffle back and forth or did their homework, a few of the older ones sneaking puffs of smuggled cigarettes with colourful smoke, the younger ones playing Gobstones or trading Chocolate Frog cards. She liked to observe them, as alone as she was, the indecipherable accents blending together, finding them shockingly different to the Americans she was used to.

 

            On the morning of the full moon, Kara woke to the leaden feeling of the night ahead of her deep in her bones. Pale and feeling the weakness of the full moon awaiting her, she could barely stomach a few mouthfuls at breakfast and thought she ought to be glad that she has no friends to notice how ashen her complexion was. As it was, Kara was prone to keeping her scarred face down, and as she left the Great Hall, she almost collided with Alex who had cut her off just outside the wide doors.

 

            Grabbing her by the sleeve or her robes, Alex towed Kara off to one side so they weren’t blocking the stream of students and Kara peeked up at her. She wasn’t sure if Alex was avoiding her, but this was the first time she’d gone out of her way to cross paths with Kara.

 

            “You look awful,” Alex noted.

 

            Lips twitching as she pushed her glasses up her nose, Kara swallowed thickly. “It’s-“

 

            “I know what today is. Mom asked me to check up on you - she said you haven’t answered any of her letters.”

 

            “There’s not a lot to say.”

 

            “Well … she’s worried about you. Do me a favour and write back to her so she stops asking me how you’re doing. I’ll even let you borrow Maximus to send your letters.”

 

            Dipping her head in a small nod, Kara’s mouth thinned and she felt her stomach twist. Closing her eyes, she drew in a shallow breath. “Right.”

 

            “Hey, are you good?”

 

            Shaking herself out of that nauseous feeling that had crept up on her as soon as she’d woken up that morning, Kara hitched her bag up higher on her shoulder. She didn’t look at Alex as she spoke, her eyes training on Julia, the Hufflepuff Prefect, as she watched her walk past, casting Kara a curious look.

 

            “Fine. Congratulations on making the Quidditch team by the way,” Kara said, trying to steer the conversation away.

 

            “Thanks,” Alex awkwardly replied, a confused frown pinching her face. “I heard you tried out.”

 

            “Maybe next year,” Kara murmured, shifting restlessly. “I have to go.”

 

            She walked off without another word, hunching her shoulders and making for the staircase. Transfiguration was her first class of the day and she was early, taking a seat at the front, where she could keep her head bent low over her work and remain unnoticed by everyone else. Pulling out her copy of A Beginner’s Guide To Transfiguration, Kara opened to the chapter detailing how to turn a beetle into a button, which they’d been working on in the last lesson. She’d managed to make her button grow legs, but not the full transformation yet, but she was determined to throw herself into her studies. 

 

            She might be stuck in Scotland until she graduated, but she’d work as hard as possible to her good enough grades to do whatever she wanted. It wasn’t lost on her that being a werewolf was something that would hold her back, but Kara had always been smart. Being behind in the curriculum just meant that she’d have to devote more time to studying, and seeing as she had no other distractions, she had every intention of doing so.

 

            Still, being the day of the full moon, she was woefully ill-equipped for lessons, a headache growing behind her eyes, a tension to her muscles that made her body ache. History of Magic was her next lesson and Kara didn’t hear a word that Professor Binns said as she sat at the front of Classroom 4F on the ground floor. In Charms, her hand shook as she tried to take notes and she skipped lunch in favour of walking down to the greenhouses.

 

            Herbology was next, and she’d hung around outside Greenhouse Three, drinking in the cool air as she tried to ignore the way her stomach twisted nauseously. As the day wore on, her pallor became almost greyish, her eyes sunken and a cold sweat on her skin. Her assigned partner for the year was Querl Dox, the Metamorphmagus from the train, and she almost burned his finger off casting the Incendio Duo spell on a Flesh-Eating Slug while they worked on a Puffapod plant together.

 

            “Are you alright?” Querl asked, his hair turning blue and standing on end with surprise as he looked at her face. “You look awfully pale.”

 

            Bloodless lips drawing into a thin line, Kara tersely nodded, her voice a bare whisper as she replied. “I’m fine.”

 

            “Is it the Puffapod spores? They cause dizziness, you know.”

 

            “That must be it,” Kara agreed, harvesting a pink seed pod.

 

            She hoped to dissuade any other attempts of conversation but she’d come to realise upon the first lesson they’d been paired together that Querl loved to talk. Normally, Kara didn’t mind it so much, especially with the Ravenclaw boy’s intelligence helping her out with the unfamiliar British plants she’d never encountered before, but she was wary of that intelligence. Would he be smart enough to realise what she was if she allowed herself to make a friend of him? It wasn’t worth the risk.

 

            The day ended with double Potions in the dungeons, Professor Slughorn a little scattered as he had them brewing a Hair-Raising potion in pairs - Kara unfortunately paired up with Belinda, who added too many rat tails to their potion - before he assigned them an essay on the potion and classes ended for the day.

 

            The thought of dinner made Kara queasy so she made straight for the library. It was a place of great solace to her, the orderly rows of bookshelves towering above her and pressing in on either side making it so easy for Kara to slip away to some forgotten corner and read and do her homework. She spent hours there, especially on the weekend, her battered copy of Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them substitutes for a dozen more books on werewolves, and other topics besides.

 

            Tucking herself away in an alcove with a narrow writing desk and a flickering lamp, Kara set out her inkwell and quill and a fresh roll of parchment and set about writing her essay for Slughorn as she waited until it was late enough to make her way to the Hospital Wing. It was there that she’d be taken outside and deep into the Forbidden Forest, to run where she would be of no harm to anyone or herself. It was the short-term solution Dumbledore had come up with for the time being and it made Kara shiver with the thought of being lost to the expansive forest sprawling across the Highlands. But after an hour or so, even the rustle of paper and the scent of old hardcovers wasn’t enough to slow the scurry of Kara’s pulse.

 

            When the waning light of day filtering through the windows started to turn the bluish of late afternoon, Kara started to pack up her things. Dinner would almost be over now, giving her enough time to change out of her robes and disappear before her roommates could corner her, and she listened to the rustling of carefully turned pages; the smell of old leather and, underlying it, the whiff of burning candle wax. She wished she could stay for the rest of the evening and live in that infinite space between now and the full moon.

 

            Making her way through the hallways, she slipped downstairs and tapped the barrel in the correct rhythm, her hand shaking - part weakness and partly because she worried she’d get it wrong and be trapped outside - and was admitted to the comfortable Common Room. In the empty dormitory, Kara dumped her bag and changed out of her uniform, shedding her robes and changing into worn jeans and an old Thunderbird sweatshirt. Tucking her wand in her pocket, Kara made a swift exit and followed the directions she’d been given to the Hospital Wing.

 

            It was mostly empty - one student with a burnt face covered in a thick green paste asleep in a narrow cot - and Madam Pomfrey was brusque as she greeted Kara, rearranging tonics and potions in a large cabinet. Late afternoon sunlight slanted through the arched windows, casting long shadows on the stone floor, and Kara was shown to a narrow bed in the far corner, where Madam Pomfrey arranged a privacy screen around it.

 

            “Best leave your glasses and wand, dear,” she cautioned Kara.

 

            Slipping off the wire frames and setting them on the end table beside the bed, Kara narrowed her eyes against the sudden blurriness of her vision as she fished out her wand. Setting it down beside her glasses, Kara felt a pang of unease to go without her wand for the evening - ever since she’d received one for school, she hadn’t been parted from it, and to go wandering in a dark forest on a full moon seemed like a time when a witch should want her wand.

 

            “Now, if you’ll follow me.”

 

            Kara obeyed, her stomach tying itself into knots as Madam Pomfrey led her out of the Hospital Wing and down a corridor. They made a few turns and then she glanced around before tapping on a suit of armour, which stepped aside to allow the bricks to ripple into a passageway. Lighting her wand, Madam Pomfrey ducked inside and Kara was left to follow, the dark pressing in on each side as the worn stone steps went downwards, the secret staircase winding down and around through the castle. 

 

            It eventually levelled out and carried on, the air dank and chill and an uneasy feeling of claustrophobia leaving Kara a little panicked as she followed after Madam Pomfrey, staying close and clinging to the light of her wand. After ten minutes, the path sloped upwards and Kara braced herself against the old stones for balance as she walked upwards, a wooden trapdoor opening with a shower of leaves and dirt on the edge of the Herbology greenhouses bordering the Forbidden Forest.

 

            “Professor Dumbledore has discussed the plan with you?”

 

            “Professor Sprout did, ma’am,” Kara explained.

 

            The head of Hufflepuff had sought her out after Herbology that afternoon to reiterate the plan they’d discussed during her first week. 

 

            “Good. Right, well, off you go then.”

 

            Kara stared at her blankly, faltering for a moment as she stared into the shadows of the trees, the sky a deepening blue overhead as the lingering rays of sunlight peeked over the mountains ringing the castle. Swallowing thickly, her throat dry, Kara opened and closed her mouth.

 

            “How far do I go?”

 

            “All exits to the castle will be locked tonight as a precaution; I’d suggest walking until the moon rises. Not so deep that you get lost though, hm? I’ll be back at dawn to fetch you. Good luck.”

 

            Nodding, Kara felt sick as she took a stumbling step towards the trees. The long groan of rusting hinges cut through the sound of the wind cutting through the forest, followed by the soft thump of the trapdoor closing a moment later, and Kara walked past the first rough trunks of the ancient trees. It was thick and overgrown, the path forward a struggle as she pushed past oak, beech, pine, yew as knotgrass and thorns inhibited her. 

 

            The evening was cool and the fading sunlight struggled to pierce the thick canopy overhead as she let her feet find their own path, stepping over roots and passing by stagnant pools of water and the occasional clearing. Black flowers grew in patches and everything was mossy and green, patches of lichen covering rocks and trunks and Kara’s shoes sinking into black dirt.

 

            The deeper she went, the sicker she felt and Kara felt her gorge rise as her stomach twisted sharply with a painful pinching sensation. She was already feeling faint from eating too little that morning, and nothing for the rest of the day, and her shallow breaths seemed too loud in the stillness of the forest as her skin prickled. A cold sweat covered her body and she knew when afternoon tipped into night, the dusk giving way as the sun finally slipped over the horizon. The full moon was rising, the feeling so sharp that Kara could feel it in her back teeth.

 

            Unsure of how deep she’d gone but knowing that she wouldn’t be able to walk much further, she started tearing at her clothes, kicking off her shoes and leaving everything in a pile on the forest floor before staggering forward, arms wrapped around herself, and falling to her knees. The pain blossomed and she cried out to the gloomy forest. The moon was hidden behind the canopy but the change came on as it rose higher in the sky, her bones cracking, her body stretching and breaking and reforming.

 

            The pain was blinding and Kara scrabbled at the dirt, caking her fingers before they turned into claws, fur sprouting and her back hunching. A strangled whine escaped her, inhuman, and that was all that Kara was aware of until she came to the next morning to the rotting smell of foliage strong in her nose. It was disorienting to go from white-hot pain, a pain that seemed unbearable at the time as she screamed herself hoarse, to the still, foggy morning of the silent forest, her body aching and leaden but no longer screaming in protest.

 

            Kara was rather surprised, almost pleasantly so, to find that she could push herself to her knees without the incapacitating pain of her first transformation. Not because it was easier but because she hadn’t bitten and scratched herself, her pale skin filthy but otherwise no worse for wear, aside from a few scratches and bruises from tearing through the forest all night. Her skin hadn’t been rent, blood pooling beneath her, and while it was still agonising, she could at least walk. Mud caked her bare skin and her blonde curls were damp as they hung limply, clinging to her skin, and the dank smell of water clung to her, leading Kara to think she’d bounded through at least one puddle.

 

            Finding herself in a different part of the forest to where she’d started, Kara worried she’d gone too deep to find her way back, the thought of traipsing through the forest for hours making her blanch, as weak as she was. But some subconscious part of her werewolf mind had led her not far from where she’d started, the ground torn up and furrowed, trees showing signs of her claws and it was relatively easy to follow the furrowed ground back the way she’d come from.

 

            The morning was apple-crisp as she walked onwards, arms wrapped around herself as she shivered. The air was cold and Kara felt like it cleaned her body from the inside, scraping out her lungs with each abrasive breath, her body alert and tense. She couldn’t imagine what those mornings would be like during winter, waking to frost on the ground and her breath pluming like white clouds. And it hurt. A sick, nauseating pain, like pushing on a broken bone, but she forced herself through it, dots of black and red swimming in front of her eyes as she put one foot in front of the other.

 

            The light filtering in was dim and pale, early morning waking her before she normally would have risen for class, and she stumbled upon a fleeing fox as she followed the way back, but was otherwise left alone. Kara knew there were things more dangerous than foxes in the Forbidden Forest, but she had no memory of crossing paths with them the night before and was glad for it.

 

            Eventually, she came upon her discarded clothes and let out a huff of eager delight, quickly changing into her jeans and sweatshirt before pulling her socks and shoes on. Feeling warmer and more human, although her reflection would have disagreed with the latter if she’d seen it, she walked the rest of the way back to the edge of the Forbidden Forest with a banging headache.

 

            Madam Pomfrey was already waiting beside the trapdoor for her and gave Kara a quick once over and handed her a vial of Wiggenweld Potion to restore her. Tipping it back and feeling some of the aches in her body recede, Kara followed Madam Pomfrey down the steps and made the return journey up to the Hospital Wing.

 

            It was still early and most students hadn't risen to her ready for breakfast and classes yet, which made it easy for Kara to slip in and sit heavily onto her bed. Slipping her glasses onto her face, she blinked at the sudden clarity and let Madam Pomfrey usher her down onto the bed.

 

            After a brief assessment, Kara was confined to the bed for the time being, although she was desperate for a shower, and a tray laden with breakfast appeared for her a short while later. Propped up on pillows, sipping pumpkin juice and picking at the sausages and bacon on her piled plate, wistful for some of Ilvermorny’s pancakes with maple syrup, Professor Sprout appeared to check on her. Kara was shy and quiet, but she liked the head of Hufflepuff, always covered in a little bit of dirt, showing up at the Common Room with a new potted plant to add and giving a lecture to whichever students were about. She was bold and Frank but kind, and as she patted Kara’s shoulder and told her to rest up, Kara didn’t feel quite so ashamed.

 

            Still, she was made to skip classes and given a sleeping draught to recover over the course of the morning, and after eating a pumpkin pastie and a small fruit salad, she was discharged to spend the rest of the day in bed at her Common Room. Kara was quick to make herself scarce, quickly vanishing downstairs and fetching things to shower. 

 

            Scrubbing herself clean and wincing at how sensitive her skin was, exhaustion making her shoulders slumped and eyes heavy, Kara felt better once the dirt and the dankness of brackish water had been washed down the drain. Leaving her damp hair to dry into a frizz of blonde curls, she pulled on grey sweatpants and a knitted sweater before needing a distraction.

 

            Kara didn’t want to sleep again, felt too restless and frustrated for that without the aid of another potion, but she didn’t want to be outside either. Sticking to the castle, she decided to wander the halls and explore, something that had become a favourite pastime of hers in between classes, poking her head into rooms to find equipment, abandoned classrooms, forgotten sitting rooms and secret passages behind paintings and the like. 

 

            Dark circles ringed her eyes and her clothes felt itchy, which was perhaps why she’d forgotten to put shoes on over her shocks, ordinarily hating the confining feeling of them anyway but the thought unbearable as her sensitive skin crawled. It was like the werewolf inside her was anxious to get out, fighting against the moon, which was now waning. It left Kara feeling depleted and restless.

 

            Classes were still in session so Kara wandered all the way up to the Astronomy Tower, knowing it would be abandoned. It was the highest tower at Hogwarts, and she enjoyed the midnight lessons with Professor Sinistra, mapping the night sky and finding planets through her telescope. 

 

            Walking up the spiralling staircase, she opened doors to classrooms with dusty chalkboards and rooms with wide windows overlooking the grounds, cramped study rooms with star charts on the walls. At a portrait of Hesper Starkey, an Astronomer with dark hair and eyes, who’d studied how the phases of the moon affected potion-making, Kara noticed a hinge on the edge of the tall portrait.

 

            “What’s behind your portrait?” she shyly asked the woman.

 

            “Who says there’s anything behind my portrait?” the witch coyly replied.

 

            “It has hinges. If you look closely.”

 

            “Ah. An astute witch. Very well. I shall give you the password to find out if you can answer this question; what phase was the moon in last night?”

 

            Kara’s stomach jolted and she imagined she visibly paled, although the question seemed innocuous, given the witch’s legendary research. Swallowing thickly, Kara gave her a faint smile.

 

            “It was the full moon last night.”

 

            “Correct, little Hufflepuff. And now the password; Lunartickle.”

 

            “Lunartickle,” Kara echoed, a hum of curiosity in her quiet voice as she committed the password to memory.

 

            The portrait winked and swung open on silent hinges to reveal a room behind. Hesitating, Kara stepped through the open frame and into the room beyond, finding it full of numerous astronomy tools. It was positively crowded with armillary spheres, celestial globes and orreries, the metal rings and gloves, bewitched floating planets and lunascopes. 

 

            It was a small room still, and as Kara padded through the room in her socks, inspecting the astronomy equipment with interest, she came to the sudden realisation that she wasn’t alone. Letting out a quiet yelp as she backed into an orrery, Kara startled the young girl sitting on the wide window ledge in her uniform. 

 

            A pale face surrounded by raven hair and piercing bloodshot green eyes stared back at Kara, who flushed red as she looked down at the stone floor of the secret room. She was immediately embarrassed at the realisation that the girl had clearly been crying and she’d barged in on such a private moment.

 

            “I- sorry,” Kara replied, tongue-tired. “I thought-“

 

            “What’re you doing here?” the girl demanded, turning even whiter as she hurriedly climbed down from the windowsill. 

 

            She was small, the silver and green of her tie, robes and edged knitted vest presenting her as a Slytherin. Her accent, while holding the slight edge of a brogue, was polished and prim, similar to the lofty way Kara had come to realise the purebloods of old money spoke. No doubt this young witch was much the same.

 

            “I was … exploring.”

 

            “Exploring? Shouldn’t you be in class?”

 

            “Shouldn’t you?”

 

            Pale cheeks turned rosy as she raised her chin in a haughty manner that wasn’t quite so intimidating as Kara thought the young girl imagined. She seemed almost shy, even in her imperiousness, her voice quiet despite its demanding tone.

 

            “Professor Binns didn’t even notice when he died; I doubt he’ll realise I’m not there,” she said, her brusqueness softening as she grew quieter, running a thumb over the corner of the small book she held.

 

            Kara laughed quietly, nose scrunching slightly as she ducked her head down, hiding her scars as her unruly blonde curls fell into her face. She gripped one of the metal rings, turning the structure a little as the joints of it groaned.

 

            “I was at the Hospital Wing,” Kara confessed.

 

            “Why?”

 

            Gesturing vaguely, Kara smiled thinly. “I’ve been unwell.”

 

            “You do look rather sick,” the girl noted.

 

            Humming in agreement, Kara hid her hands inside the sleeves of her navy sweater, fingers toying with the cuffs. The girl eyed her for a moment, wary and reserved.

 

            “You’re not a Slytherin,” she commented.

 

            Cracking a quick smile, Kara shook her head, pushing her glasses up her nose. “No, I’m- I’m a Hufflepuff. Second-Year.”

 

            “Oh. I probably shouldn’t be talking to you then.”

 

            “I shouldn’t be talking to you either.”

 

            They cast furtive glances at each other as the silence dragged on for a moment, taking the measure of each other as they both lingered uncertainly. 

 

            “You’re not wearing shoes,” the other girl eventually blurted out.

 

            Looking down at her socked feet, Kara wriggled her toes and let out an awkward laugh. “I don’t like shoes.”

 

            The girl snorted, “I think winter here will change your mind.”

 

            Kara’s cheek dimpled as she smiled crookedly, skimming her sock along the floor as she buried her hands in her jeans pockets. “It gets colder in New England than in Scotland.”

 

            “So my mother tells me.”

 

            “She’s American?” Kara asked with surprise.

 

            Shrugging indifferently, the girl ducked her dark head and parted the book in her hands before snapping it closed again. “Yes. She went to Ilvermorny too.”

 

            “But you’re … English?”

 

            “Irish.”

 

            “Sorry, I’m not really good with accents yet.”

 

            A thin smile crossed the girl's face. “What made you transfer to Hogwarts?”

 

            Kara opened and closed her mouth, her face flushing, making her pale scars stark against the rising colour in her cheeks. She stammered as she replied, rubbing at the back of her neck.

 

            “I- well, my … mom, she, uh, she moved us here for work so …” Clearing her throat, Kara ducked her head down.

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “Are you okay?” she suddenly asked as they lapsed back into silence. “You looked upset when I came in.”

 

            “Just a letter.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            Sinking back down onto the windowsill, the girl parted the small book again and Kara noticed a letter slipped in between the pages. Pressing her lips into a flat line, Kara toyed with the orrery, eyeing the layout of the planets.

 

            “What’re you reading?”

 

            “Common Magical Ailments and Afflictions.”

 

            Kara’s face crumpled slightly with bewilderment at such a boring and dense book for a First-Year to be passing the time with. The girl let out a quick laugh, holding it up and giving her a shy, wry smile.

 

            “I’d like to be a Healer after school.”

 

            Eyebrows rising slightly, Kara hummed in surprise. She still wasn’t quite sure what she’d like to be after school; a Magizoologist, a reporter, a Quidditch player, an Auror. She’d entertained a few career choices growing up, and, a day away from thirteen, thought herself still too young to really know what she wanted to do. Especially now with lycanthropy throwing a wrench in things.

 

            “I guess … that’s the Slytherin ambition or whatever your House traits are.”

 

            Brow creasing slightly, the girl cocked her head to the side. “You don’t sound nearly as hateful as everyone else.”

 

            “Why would I hate you? We’ve only just met; I don’t even know your name.”

 

            She let out a laugh in response. “That doesn’t matter, does it? It’s a House rivalry.”

 

            “I don’t think Hufflepuff has a rivalry with anyone.”

 

            “Or you’re just too new to realise it.”

 

            “Aren’t you a First-Year?” Kara laughed, amusement creasing her face. “You’re new too.”

 

            “Yes,” the girl murmured, fiddling idly with a silver ring on her index finger, emblazoned with a snake entwined with an L. “But my family has been in Slytherin for generations - on my father’s side - so I know how it all works.”

 

            Crossing her arms over her chest, Kara cocked her head to the side. “I don’t really care about knowing how it all works.”

 

            “You won’t make friends here if you’re seen with a Slytherin.”

 

            “Well, I haven’t made friends anyway, and it’s a secret room.”

 

            A clouded look crossed the girl’s face. “How did you get in here?”

 

            Kara grinned, eyes creasing at the corners. “I asked what was behind it and the portrait gave me the password after answering a question.”

 

            “She must like you.”

 

            “It was an easy question.”

 

            “What was it?”

 

            “What phase of the moon was it last night?”

 

            “Full moon,” the girl immediately replied.

 

            Stomach lurching, Kara’s throat tightened and she smiled thinly. There was a tremor in her hands as she curled her fingers into the wool of her sweater, feeling unbalanced by the ready answer of the other student.

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “Are you okay? You look a little pale.”

 

            “I- well, Madam Pomfrey told me to stay in bed, but I didn’t want to. I think I should’ve listened.”

 

            “You should sit down.”

 

            With another wan smile, Kara sank down to the stone floor and wrapped her arms around her drawn-up legs as she pressed her forehead against her knees. Drawing in a shallow breath, Kara raised her head again and rested her chin on top.

 

            “Better?”

 

            “It’s just- I think I’m coming down with the flu. I’ll be fine; I had some Pepperup Potion.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, the girl studied her closely. “There’s no steam coming out of your ears.”

 

            “Oh … well, I had it last night so it’s worn off now. Just in time.”

 

            “In time for what.”

 

            “It’s my birthday tomorrow.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            Uncrossing her arms, Kara struggled back to her feet then, wiping her palms on her jeans. “I should go. Sorry for bothering you.”

 

            “It’s alright. No one really bothers me.”

 

            There was a pang of loneliness in her quiet voice and Kara studied her for a moment. Although she seemed lofty, it was in a gentle and shy way, as if used to getting what she wanted but only as one who lingered on the outskirts of life. It was rather like Kara’s childhood; her family had been well-respected purebloods with enough money that Kara was given expensive trinkets for birthdays and Christmas and then left to entertain herself as her parents worked. It struck her that the girl must not have had any friends either.

 

            Giving her a wavering smile, Kara shrugged, “still, I’ll leave you to your book.”

 

            She stepped back, almost colliding with a celestial globe and sheepishly righting it as the girl muffled a laugh. Letting out an embarrassed laugh as her cheeks flamed, Kara ducked around it, the girl hidden from her view, and then turned around.

 

            “Bye,” she softly called out.

 

            Slipping back through the room without another word, Kara pushed open the portrait and stepped back onto the staircase, blinking herself back to reality. Glancing at the portrait of Hesper Starkey, she frowned, as if not entirely believing the encounter had been real.

 

            After a moment, she shook her head to clear her mind, making her temples pulse with a lingering headache, and then decided to make her way back down to the Common Room. Curling up on an armchair, she read over a chapter for Defence Against The Dark Arts and finished off her Potions essay on the Hair-Raising Potion before students started streaming in after the last class of the day.  Eve spotted her and made a bee-line for her before heading to their shared dormitory, a puckered look on her face.

 

            “There you are! Where have you been?”

 

            “Hospital Wing,” Kara murmured, keeping her head bent low over her homework. “Madam Pomfrey just let me out.”

 

            “Are you alright?”

 

            “Just the flu.”

 

            “Oh. Belinda said you probably had Dragon Pox.”

 

            “Why would she say that?”

 

            “She said you looked green in Herbology yesterday.”

 

            Looking up, Kara gave her a fleeting smile. “Nope. Just the flu.”

 

            “You can sit with us at dinner, you know.”

 

            Starting to pack away her things, screwing the lid on her pot of ink and shuffling rolls of parchment, Kara made a faint sound of acknowledgement. “Right. Thanks. I should go down.”

 

            Stowing her bag at the foot of her bed, Kara slipped back out and through the barrels, making her way through the hallways and upstairs to the Great Hall. Her mind was distracted as she walked in, straying over to the Slytherin table to try and catch sight of the girl from the secret room in the tower, but if she was there, Kara didn’t see her.

 

            Taking a seat on the bench at her house table, Kara helped herself to some shepherd’s pie with peas and chips and then some trifle for dessert, poking at the layers dubiously but finding her appetite returned, even if her whole body ached and she felt exhausted. It was something she’d have to get used to, something she’d have to push through and manage, relying on potions like the ones Madam Pomfrey had given her to make it through the day after the full moon so she could be back in class the following day.

 

            But despite her exhaustion, Kara’s sleep that night was plagued with nightmares. It has become an increasingly frequent thing, for her to wake in a cold sweat to the lingering memory of snarls and teeth and claws, the taste of blood, her father’s shout, her own screams echoing in her ears. While the full moon had depleted her body, it had dredged up memories she wished to forget but were still too fresh for that. 

 

            Maybe with time, with years, she’d forget the vivid details of it all, but for now, her sleep was disturbed and she woke on her thirteenth birthday to a steel grey dawn in a quiet dormitory. Pushing back her patchwork quilt to find the copper stove lit and heating the room, Kara fetched her uniform and went to shower and get ready for classes.

 

            Fixing her tie in the mirror and donning her yellow-hooded robe, she returned to her room and picked up her school bag and took her wand from the nightstand. Slipping out, she made her way downstairs and out into the Transfiguration courtyard, seeking the bracing Highland air and the damp dewy morning as she sat on a stone bench and let the memories be scoured away by morning.

 

            She was early to breakfast, pouring a bowl of Cheeri Owls and marmalade on toast and sipping tea as the Great Hall slowly filled. An owl deposited a parcel before her and she tore off the brown paper to find a brown leather diary and a small box labelled Scrivenshaft’s Quill Shop, which she opened to reveal a black and gold eagle feather quill. There was also a box of homemade fudge brownies and a birthday card which Kara tore open.

 

To Kara,

 

Happy 13th birthday! I hope you have a wonderful day celebrating with your friends.

 

I know it’s not much, but I thought you might like these to write down your thoughts, and I know you always used to like my fudge brownies when you were younger. 

 

Please write back soon. I’d like to know how it went the other night and know you’re settling in okay.

 

Love Eliza x

 

            The card made her eyes sting and she quickly shut the card, jamming it back into the envelope and shoving it to the bottom of her bag. It was too much to hope that her mom might send her a gift, especially after two months of silence from her, but she was touched that Eliza had sent something.  There was also a flicker of guilt as well, knowing she should’ve written back sooner, and after a moment’s hesitation, Kara fished a scrap of parchment out of her bag, along with an inkwell, and dipped her new quill into it. Halfway through scrawling out a thank you note with a quick reassurance about how well she was settling in, Kara felt something bump into her forehead and fall to the table, narrowly missing her abandoned bowl of cereal.

 

            Setting her quill down, Kara frowned and picked up the piece of parchment folded to look like a butterfly. Its folded wings were still fluttering and she looked around to find where it had come from but didn’t find anyone nearby who was looking at her expectedly. Unfolding it, she smoothed out the creases and took in the surprisingly elegant script spelling out a short message.

 

Happy birthday

Chapter 5

            The first few weeks at Hogwarts passed by quickly, as fresh September days turned into bitter black October nights, and Lena adjusted to school with overwhelming relief. She shone in her classes, already far above the level of her peers from the brutal education she’d been raised with at home, earned Slytherin an abundance of points with her answers, her perfect potions and full marks on every assignment, and was free from the miserable estate she’d grown up on, which was perhaps the best part of all. While her classmates were homesick, sent weekly packages and near-daily letters from their parents, Lena was remarkably unaffected by being alone.

 

            If anything, she was painfully shy and craved her solitude. It had been during her first week, anxious to put as much distance between herself and the dim dungeons as possible, that she’d discovered that hidden room in the Astronomy Tower, and she spent most of her time tucked away there in secret, working on her essays and homework with books she’d checked out from the library, which was where she spent the remainder of her time.

 

            Not that she had anything against her fellow Housemates, or their Common Room, but Lena hated to be underground. It felt too stifling, too claustrophobic, the thought of being trapped so overwhelming that her breathing became shallow if she thought about it too much. From what she’d heard, and been told her entire childhood, Slytherin had the best Common Room out of the four Houses though.

 

            Their dorms were split into groups of five within each year, and Lena found herself in with a few girls from well-known Pureblood families, but she was relatively uninterested in befriending any of them. Their dorm was a long rectangular space with deep green wallpaper, occupied by five identical four-poster beds made from dark-stained walnut and hung with heavy emerald drapes and bedding. The mattresses sagged from years of use, small nicks in the furniture and stains, but the interior was undeniably beautiful in a moth-eaten way, an ode to lost grandeur. 

 

            They each had a nightstand beside their bed and a reasonably sized desk across from the foot of it, with a wardrobe wedged in beside it. It was comfortable and always moderately messy, strewn with socks and shirts, forgotten books, and two cats that sprawled on whichever bed they felt like, which Lena didn’t mind so much, even if she was allergic. She kept her own portion of the dorm tidy, her desk covered with strict rectilinear piles of notes and textbooks, her clothes hanging neatly arranged in her wardrobe like drab ghosts of varying dark shades.

 

            Each morning she woke to a tea tray on her nightstand, something she’d already gotten used to, the small emerald tray with a tarnished silver pot of tea and a teacup and saucer decorated with green snakes. It always came with a small shortbread biscuit bearing the House Crest and tasting of butter and sugar. She never ate the biscuit but enjoyed her cup of tea black while she read through one of the thick tomes on healing she always had within reach.

 

            It was a comfortable routine and, if anything, she seemed less timid, although she went unseen by the rest of her House. The other girls in her dorm, as well as other First-Years, eyed her with curiosity, whispering about her as she ignored them - and she was happy to. Her family may have been notorious but Lena had spent years trying to make herself invisible and small, unnoticed in the big manor house she’d been raised in, and it was a slow process to coax her out of the habit, a certain sweet sadness to the hunch of her shoulders and mournful softness of her face that spoke of reservations.

 

            Still, Lena was content and settled in with ease, observing the other students from the outskirts, exploring the castle and learning as much as she could. Even on the cusp of twelve years old, Lena knew that her life wouldn’t always be this way. She might be small and unnoticed now but she just had to get through the next seven years of school and then everything would be different. Her ambitions weren’t unfounded - Lena knew she’d get the marks to be accepted as a Trainee Healer - and she clung to the dream she’d created for herself.

 

            Before she knew it, it was November, the weather turning towards winter and her birthday passing by with little fanfare. Her brother’s owl, Ignatius, deposited a parcel before her at breakfast, unwrapped to reveal a birthday card bearing his name and their mother’s, both written in his hand, and two wrapped gifts in green paper. The first had been a book on hexes, Lex having taken to eagerly telling Lena all about his time on the Duelling Team and encouraging her to sign up prior to her starting at Hogwarts. The second was a silver cloak, slipping through her fingers like silk as she held it in her lap, recognising it instantly for what it was; the family invisibility cloak that had been passed onto her brother years ago.

 

Thought you might have more use for this now than I do. Enjoy! - Lex

 

            So far, the only use Lena had gotten out of it was breaking curfew to sneak more books out of the library or escape the rowdy Common Room when she should have been tucked away in the dungeons. If anyone noticed her absence, they never commented on it, and Lena welcomed the reprieve as she walked the quiet hallways, growing still whenever a patrolling teacher passed by. She hadn’t been caught yet and it brought another element of delight to being at Hogwarts.

 

            On a particularly bitter day, the sky a dismal grey and dead leaves skittering across the courtyard in the stiff breeze, Lena hurried to Charms, her final class of the day, and spent the whole period carefully jotting down notes from one of the healing textbooks she had hidden inside her Charms textbook. She’d already mastered making a feather float in her first week of classes, tearing through the syllabus with ease, and she knew she rightfully should have been grades ahead but Hogwarts didn’t allow for students to rush through their schooling. The most Lena had managed was cornering Professor Slughorn after Potions one day, clutching her books to her chest as she stared at the floor, the Head of Slytherin’s cheerful bumbling as she asked him to speak to her teachers for more coursework inspiring little confidence that anything would come of it. She’d taken it upon herself to excel her own education, practicing in her hidden room at the top of the Astronomy Tower.

 

            It was where she went after class ended, her footsteps on the stone steps as she wound up through the spiralling staircase, pausing at the painting to glance up and down in case someone else was coming. When she was sure the coast was clear, Lena fixed the smiling portrait of Hesper Starkey with a confident look and spoke.

 

            “Lunartickle.”

 

            It swung open on its hinges to reveal the comfortably packed room, the astronomy devices overshadowing the path cutting around to her favourite spot by the window. It offered a spectacular view of the surrounding scenery, the lake glistening like mercury in the grey weather, the mountains already capped with snow, the sprawling Forbidden Forest and the greenery of the Highlands. It painfully reminded Lena of Ireland in a way, of days spent outdoors to avoid being locked inside with her brutal studies, but she wouldn’t go back for anything.

 

            Rounding a brass telescope, Lena paused as she found her spot occupied though, blinking in surprise as her mouth opened and closed. It was that girl again, the one from last time, dressed in her uniform and wearing shoes this time, although she looked similarly worn out. At Lena’s sudden appearance, the girl startled.

 

            “You again,” Lena said with undisguised surprise.

 

            “You’re here,” the girl softly exclaimed, her face softening with delight as she scrambled off the window ledge, a book falling from her lap and onto the floor.

 

            She let out a sheepish laugh and ducked down to pick it up, the worn spine clasped in her hand as she straightened up and gave Lena a shy smile. Feeling a prickle of unease as she took in the yellow and black striped tie, the notes of Hufflepuff throughout the girl’s uniform marking her as a would-be enemy, if Lena had cared enough to involve herself in the house rivalries, she strayed another step closer. Expression clouding, Lena gave her a wary look.

 

            “I thought I’d dreamt you,” the girl said, her cheeks reddening.

 

            Pausing, Lena stared at her face. Pale freckles, pale skin, dark-blonde hair - untamable, frizzy - and eyes a weather-worn, spectral blue that made her feel uneasy, as if she looked into Lena’s very soul. There were faint scars, almost silver and striking against the colour that flooded her cheeks. The girl looked wan again, and Lena wondered if perhaps she was just homesick, not sleeping well at Hogwarts, the smudges under her eyes giving away her exhaustion.

 

            “Why would you think that?” Lena eventually replied, her dark eyebrows furrowing together.

 

            “I haven’t seen you since. I thought … maybe I was going mad.”

 

            A crooked smile graced Lena’s lips as she folded her arms over her chest, noting the ink stains on the girl's fingertips. “Well, you’re not mad and I’m not a dream.”

 

            Neither of them spoke for a moment as they faced each other, and Lena’s bag was growing heavy on her shoulders from the sheer amount of books stuffed in there, testing the integrity of the black dragonhide. 

 

            “What’s your name?” the girl eventually asked.

 

            “What’s yours?”

 

            She grinned, fleeting and shy, toying with the corner of her book as she dragged a scuffed shoe across the stone floor of the secret room. “Kara.”

 

            “I’m Lena.”

 

            “I always look for you at dinner,” Kara admitted, her cheeks still pink.

 

            “I’ve seen you around,” Lena shyly replied, “you spend a lot of time outdoors.”

 

            She blinked in surprise behind the wire glasses perched on her nose, a bewildered look on her face as she smiled faintly. “Yes.”

 

            Fiddling with the Slytherin ring on her forefinger, Lena bit her lip and glanced at the book that Kara was holding, her curiosity piqued. She jerked her chin toward it, her eyebrows rising a fraction.

 

            “What’re you reading?”

 

            “Oh, it’s, uh, Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them.”

 

            “You like creatures?”

 

            Shrugging, Kara smiled ruefully. “Sure. I like a lot of things.”

 

            She sank back down onto the wide ledge of the window, turning over the battered copy in her hands. Lena shifted restlessly and ended up swinging her bag off her shoulder, setting it on the ground beside her to give her sore muscles a break. Cocking her head to the side, Lena hesitated, unsure if she wanted to prolong the interaction, somewhat torn between wishing she was alone in her secret room so she could do her homework and practice and wanting the girl to stay.

 

            “How was your birthday?”

 

            “It was good,” Kara murmured, letting the book part in her palms to reveal a folded piece of parchment. She plucked it from between the pages and held it up to show off the butterfly. “Was this you?”

 

            Cheeks reddening, Lena’s nose wrinkled as she ducked her head. “Yes.”

 

            “Oh … thanks. How’d you do it?”

 

            “My brother taught me.”

 

            “Is he at Hogwarts too?”

 

            Shaking her head as she sank down beside her bag, pulling out a scrap of parchment, Lena’s mouth thinned as she straightened back up. “No, he graduated last year.”

 

            Moving over to her side, Lena hesitated and then sank down onto the window ledge beside her, smoothing the piece of parchment in her lap. “Like this.”

 

            She made a few creases and then started to fold the parchment until she had a simple butterfly. Holding it up in her cupped hands, Lena softly blew on it and watched it flap across the space, a smile creasing her face.

 

            “I can do a crane too.”

 

            Kara frowned as she pulled a piece of parchment out of her brown leather satchel, finely made and only showing a few signs of use, before she copied Lena’s movements and found herself holding her own butterfly. When she blew on it, the folded piece of paper just glided down to the floor and Kara’s expression fell.

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “You have to think with intention,” Lena gently instructed her.

 

            Picking it up again, Kara tried a second time, the butterfly wobbling for a few moments as it flapped its wings out of sync before tumbling back to the floor. Making a disconcerting sound, Kara stooped down to snatch it back up.

 

            “It might be a bit advanced for me,” she said with a sheepish smile.

 

            “You’ll get it if you keep trying.”

 

            Nodding, Kara tucked in back between the pages of her book and snapped it shut with the intention of trying again later that night. Lena studied her from the corner of her eye as she held her butterfly in her hands and fiddled with the corner of a wing.

 

            “Can I ask you something?” Kara shyly asked, drawing her knees up to her chest as she set her book aside and wrapped her arms around her legs. She leaned her cheek on her knee as she looked at Lena with a clouded expression on her face.

 

            Blinking in surprise, Lena shifted away slightly but angled herself more towards Kara in the process. “Okay.”

 

            “Do you … like it here?”

 

            “At Hogwarts? Yes.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            Face crumpling slightly, Lena cocked her head to the side, observing the guarded look. “You don’t?”

 

            Wrinkling her nose as she bared her teeth in a pained look, Kara shrugged half-heartedly. Her smile didn’t reach her sad blue eyes when she looked at Lena. “I … it’s not- I just- I miss my old life. And it’s so much harder here than it was at Ilvermorny. I thought- I thought when I found you crying … you might be homesick too.”

 

            Kara winced as Lena stiffened at the mention of her crying, a delicate pink flush in her cheeks as she bristled, swallowing thickly. Her lips were a thin line as she tightly replied. “I have to go.”

 

            She quickly rose from the window, her patent shoes squeaking as she stooped to snatch up her bag, head ducked down low. Kara made a small sound of surprise behind her, shoes scuffing as she scrambled to her feet, shifting awkwardly as she grimaced.

 

            “Wait- I’m sorry, I didn’t mean- I just … it’s lonely.”

 

            Lena paused at the roughness of Kara’s voice and turned, a stricken look on her face as she took in the blue eyes filled with tears. Panicked, she dropped her bag with a heavy thump and opened and closed her mouth.

 

            “Are you alright?” she asked, shock colouring her voice.

 

            Angrily rubbing at her eyes, her glasses nudged up from the motion, Kara’s mouth screwed up into a pout as she fought hard not to cry. “I’m fine,” she replied, her voice wavering slightly. 

 

            Feeling uncomfortable by her tears, Lena cleared her throat and toyed with the cuff of her robes in an anxious habit, inhaling as if to speak but remaining silent. She repeated that a couple of times over the following minute of silence before she spoke.

 

            “I don’t have any friends here,” she confessed. “But I like it here. It’s better than being at home.”

 

            Kara didn’t reply, staring down at her shoes as she sniffed and rubbed at her face, which was red with embarrassment, making the pale scars stark against her skin again. Lena wondered where she’d gotten them, but it felt rude to ask.

 

            “Look, I can help you with your homework if you want me to,” Lena offered. 

 

            Swallowing as she looked at her, dry-eyed but bloodshot, Kara’s brow puckered. She looked confused by the offer and let out a strained laugh. “I’m a Second-Year.”

 

            “I know, but I’m … smart,” Lena awkwardly replied, seemingly embarrassed by the admission. “I already know most of the syllabus so I can help you study.”

 

            “Why?”

 

            Shrugging, Lena chewed on her lip and pressed her thumb to her forearm over the sleeve of her robe. Her lips thinned and a ripple of guilt and fear crossed her face before she cleared her throat. 

 

            “You need help.”

 

            “I thought we weren’t allowed to be friends.”

 

            Lena jutted her chin forward, scowling slightly. “We’re not friends . We’ll just- we’ll be studying together. In here . No one else has to find out.”

 

            “Okay,” Kara said after a momentary pause, rubbing at the scar on her cheek as she tried to mask her delight. “That’s- thank you. So … will we just meet here?”

 

            Mouth thinning with exasperation as her eyebrows drew together over guarded jade eyes, Lena nodded. “Tuesdays and Thursdays. After dinner.”

 

            “Okay.”

 

            “If you see me in the hallways …”

 

            “I’ll ignore you,” Kara finished with a solemn nod.

 

            “Good.”

 

            Still, there was a certain lightness to her face now, the relieved slump of her shoulders making her look less burdened, although Lena could see the exhaustion weighing her down. She gave Lena a warm smile that caught her off-balance and she grabbed her satchel, shoving her book into the bag.

 

            “Okay, well … I’ll leave you alone then,” Kara said. “And I’ll see you Tuesday.”

 

            Lena silently nodded, picking up her bag again and moving over to the ledge, setting it down and pulling out her half-written essay for Herbology as she sank down onto the wall. Dinner wouldn’t be for another hour at least, which left her enough time to finish off the essay and practice a wand-lighting spell she’d been trying to work. 

 

            “Bye.”

 

            Kara’s head bobbed in another nod and she stumbled back a step, almost tripping over her feet as she ducked beneath the lunascope. “See you.”

 

            An odd look of amusement crossed Lena’s face as she watched Kara turn and disappear. Shaking her head as she narrowed her eyes, a crease forming between her eyebrows, Lena snorted and a small smile curled her lips. She wasn’t sure why she’d offered to help her - maybe so she wouldn’t dissolve into outright crying - but Lena had sensed the desperation, how lost Kara was, and felt a kindred pang. Lena hadn’t been moved across the world to a new school, but she’d grown up in a home where she’d felt just the same.

 

            Carefully finishing off her essay in her neat calligraphy, the slow scratching of the quill comforting and familiar, Lena’s mind occasionally strayed to thoughts of Kara and she was rather unproductive in comparison to her usual work ethic. As she idly practiced lighting her wand, her muttered Lumos producing a glow at the tip of her wand with sporadic success, Lena considered the Hufflepuff girl and winced at the thought of what her family would think if they knew she was spending time with someone who wasn’t in Slytherin. 

 

            Was Kara even a Pureblood? Not that Lena put much stock in all of that, only a Halfblood herself, although that was a tightly kept secret in itself, but she could imagine what her punishment would be if she was hanging around with a Hufflepuff who wasn’t even a Pureblood. Not that anyone paid her much attention, and inter-House friendships weren’t uncommon, but it was different in Slytherin. They were a closed group, all of them raised within the same circle, knowing of each other long before they started at Hogwarts.

 

            Eventually, it grew too dark for her to continue doing her homework, night falling rapidly as far north as they were and so late in the year. The night wasn’t as black and impenetrable as it would be later on, the dark firs on the mountainside brushed with snow, and the white caps indenting the sky, which was almost phosphorescent indigo, turning a deep blue. The moon was almost full, hanging low and full like a silver penny, while the lake shimmered as a breeze rippled its surface.

 

            Making her way down to dinner, Lena ate soup and a small slice of pumpkin pie and went to the library to read some more. She stayed late, slipping on her invisibility cloak and curling up in an armchair as she read an advanced book on the medicinal properties of magical creature parts before her eyes started burning and she realised how late it was. 

 

            Returning to the Slytherin Common Room with that familiar cagey feeling as her skin prickled with unease. She gave the password - Parseltongue - and stepped inside, the air from the fire burning in the wide fireplace stifling as it chased away the damp chill of the dungeon hallways. The ceiling was high and green globes of light were bracketed on the walls and hanging from chains. The wide, stained glass windows depicted snakes in shades of green and grey on either side of the carved marble fireplace, and no light filtered in through them. Their Common Room was situated partially under the lake, and in the daytime watery green light filtered in, giving the place an eerie tint. The impenetrable blackness of so much water looming beyond the windows did little to quell Lena’s unease of the place. She wasn’t sure which was worse; underwater or underground.

 

            Slipping into her dorm, she slowly unpacked her school bag and grabbed her pyjamas to change out of her uniform. In the bathroom, she locked herself in a stall and shed her robe, removing the small snake tie pin and loosening it around her neck. Undressing, Lena pulled on her embroidered black silk pyjamas and paused before slipping her left arm in, catching sight of the old scar on her forearm. It was small and pale, but still noticeable against her porcelain skin, almost silvery and written in her neat calligraphy.

 

            I am a failure

 

            Swallowing thickly, her mouth dry, Lena closed her eyes and slipped her arm in before her fingers fumbled with the buttons of her shirt. Padding back to her dorm in her slippers, she left the green desk lamp lit, unable to bear leaving the room in darkness as she joined her classmates and went to bed. Drawing the drapes around the bed, Lena pulled the blankets over herself and gripped her left arm as she waited for sleep to claim her.

Chapter 6

            As promised, Kara met Lena every Tuesday and Thursday to study in the secret room in the Astronomy Tower, and it quickly became one of Kara’s favourite parts of the week. It wasn’t that she wanted to get close to anyone - she had the opportunity to make friends but knew that her secret would inevitably come out if she did, and that was a risk she wasn’t willing to take - but it was nice to have company with low stakes.

 

            Lena wasn’t her friend. They’d both made that clear, their conversations usually focused on their homework and classes, and the occasional comment or question about other things, but Lena was a Slytherin and Kara was a Hufflepuff. It would have been impossible for two people so at odds to have become friends, even if they were too young to fully understand the depth of the house rivalries.

 

            Still, it made Kara feel less alone to spend a few hours with someone else each week, and she had a slight suspicion that Lena felt the same. Even better was that her grades quickly improved; she’d gone from a majority of Acceptable marks and a few Poor ones to an average of Exceeds Expectations.
