The first time she got an Outstanding she’d been pink-cheeked with shy delight as she handed Lena the Transfiguration essay on the Vera Verto spell she’d helped her with.

 

            They worked on spells too, with Lena poring over the theoretical work for some of the more advanced ones she was working on, while Kara practised the ones they were learning in her classes. She would watch Lena though, impressed and a little awed at how easy she seemed to find everything. It took Kara a few tries to turn a beetle into a button, but Lena managed it on her first go, explaining that she’d studied that one a few years ago before even getting her wand or Hogwarts acceptance letter.

 

            As December breezed by, the holidays fast approaching, Kara went to the tower straight from dinner for the last meeting for the term. It was Tuesday and the full moon was only a few days away, leaving her wearied as she plodded up each step. Still, she tried to mask it as she walked into the room to find Lena already there and quietly greeted her, trying to break the strange awkwardness that lingered between them, two young girls who weren’t really friends and didn’t know how to be.

 

            They settled in with their respective homework, Kara going through the steps of a potion they’d be brewing in class tomorrow before she moved on to a Charms essay that she’d started over the weekend.

 

            “That was a close game on Saturday, don’t you think?”

 

            Lena’s brow furrowed slightly and her mouth twitched at the corners as she gave Kara a solemn look. “I didn’t go.”

 

            “You didn’t go?”

 

            “I’m not a fan of Quidditch.”

 

            “What?”

 

            Lena let out a quiet huff of laughter, her cheeks turning faintly pink. She shrugged nonchalantly and continued scrawling out a sentence on her essay. “I don’t like flying - don’t like heights. And I’ve been to World Cup games but you can barely see anything and they’re so long and boring.”

 

            “But your house was playing!”

 

            “I know, they won.”

 

            There was an undercurrent of smug pride in her voice and Kara rolled her eyes, grimacing. “Well, maybe we’ll beat you next year.”

 

            “It doesn’t matter to me. I’m not on the team.”

 

            Kara let out a bewildered laugh, shaking her head as she picked up her Charms book and flipped the page. She tapped the end of the quill against her chin and was silent for a moment, keeping her head ducked down as she fiddled with the corner of the book.

 

            “I’d like to be on the team.”

 

            “Would you?” Lena asked with mild surprise.

 

            “I tried out but didn’t get it.”

 

            “What position?”

 

            Raising one shoulder in a crooked shrug, Kara’s cheek dimpled with dismay, “Beater.”

 

            “Oh. Well … maybe next year.”

 

            “Maybe.”

 

            “Are you done with your essay? I’ll check it for you.”

 

            Kara scrawled a closing sentence at the bottom of her roll of parchment and handed it over, drawing her knees to her chest and encircling them with her arms as she studied Lena. She watched her dip her quill into the pot of ink and spread the essay out over a book, smoothing it down and quickly scanning Kara’s writing as she made small corrections and comments. Kara had to admit that her marks had considerably improved over the last few weeks, her homework grades higher with the amount of studying she’d been putting in with Lena twice a week. 

 

            It wasn’t that Kara was stupid - she was actually very smart - but her diagnosis of lycanthropy had left her distracted, reluctant to try and somewhat stubbornly objecting to the way that Hogwarts was run. She was used to multiple-choice pop quizzes at Ilvermorny, of a curriculum that was generally easier, allowing her to score highly with minimal effort and more focus on extracurricular activity. So far, it seemed like Hogwarts offered only a few options - Quidditch, the chess team, gobstones team and the duelling club. Kara imagined she would have liked the last one, a popular choice for most of the older students who knew more complex spells, but she didn’t want to go alone.

 

            “Not bad. You should focus on the theoretical side more.”

 

            “Okay. Thanks.”

 

            Lena nodded and handed the essay back, Kara quickly reading over the neat annotations and editing before she pulled out a blank piece of parchment. 

 

            “And you need to check for u’s.”

 

            “Right.”

 

            Kara worked on rewriting it and flipping through her textbook, reading a few snippets allowed to gain Lena’s approval before she wove them in. The only sound that filled the secret room near the top of the Astronomy Tower was the sound of scratching quills, turning pages and the gentle clink of quill nibs against the rim of ink pots.

 

            They stayed until it was almost curfew and Kara was feeling a little tired. The full moon was only two days away and she didn’t tell Lena she wouldn’t be there on Thursday - what preemptive excuse could she give? Slowly slipping books into her satchel, she chewed on her lip as she considered whether she’d see her again before the holidays in a few days. 

 

            Climbing to her feet, she dragged the strap over her shoulder, the bag feeling particularly heavy as her body anticipated the full moon in two short days. Violet bags already ringed her eyes and she gave Lena a ghost of a smile as the Slytherin girl rose to her feet with her own bag and books.

 

            “Are you going home over Christmas?”

 

            “Me? No. I’m staying.”

 

            Kara’s eyebrows rose a fraction in surprise. It seemed like only those with no family or a strong attachment to Hogwarts stayed behind over the holidays, and while Lena loved being at the school, it was still surprising that she would have chosen to stay there alone rather than go home to what Kara could only assume was a very nice house. Lena hadn’t said it, but Kara had the distinct impression that her family was rich from the quality of her shoes, her bag, the brand new books, the magical tools and trinkets to aid with studying that seemed endless.

 

            “Are you?”

 

            “No, I’m not staying.”

 

            “And where’s home?”

 

            “Falmouth. Cornwall. What about you?”

 

            “Near Wicklow. Ireland.”

 

            Humming with interest, Kara started winding back through the path to the door, Lena following after her. She supposed she ought to say goodbye until the new year, but that would give away too much.

 

            “Do you like it there?” Kara blurted out, glancing back over her shoulder.

 

            “Sometimes. I like the countryside. We’re near the national park.”

 

            “Oh. That sounds nice.”

 

            Lena made a vague sound of agreement and they carried on walking, pausing at the door as they always did so they could sneak out individually. Kara hesitated and glanced back over her shoulder, adjusting her bag strap as she gave Lena a thin smile.

 

            “Thanks for helping me out.”

 

            “That's okay,” Lena murmured. 

 

            She was looking down at the stone floor and glanced up, doing a slight double-take as if she was seeing Kara for the first time. It was true that they rarely looked each other in the eye, Kara always so evasive on accounts of the pale scars she was so self-conscious about, and Lena always seemed like she wanted the ground to swallow her whole.

 

            A small frown clouded her face now though, a mild look of concern as she cocked her head to the side. “Are you okay?”

 

            “Fine, why?”

 

            “You look … pale.”

 

            “So do you.”

 

            Lena let out a surprised laugh, her expression smoothing out for a moment before she frowned again, her chin dimpling as she pursed her lips. It gave her childish face a petulant look, as if annoyed that she couldn’t quite figure out the answer to a puzzle.

 

            “You look tired.”

 

            “I didn’t sleep well last night,” Kara evasively replied with a shrug. 

 

            “Oh. Okay.”

 

            “I’ll see you on Thursday,” Kara quickly replied before pushing the portrait open and stepping out onto the staircase.

 

            She just heard Lena’s mumbled goodbye before the portrait swung closed and hid her from sight. Making her way back to the dorm, Kara went straight to bed and shut out the sound of the other girls whispering as she tried to get as much sleep as possible. Even if her sleeps were deep and restful, the full moon sapped her strength on the days either side of it and she hoped more sleep might stave off the exhaustion a little. It didn’t but she was too young and stubborn to give up.

 

            Her fifth transformation went much like the other few at Hogwarts, with Kara sent as deep into the Forbidden Forest as she could walk before she succumbed to the curse, left to roam free and awaken at dawn covered in mud and scrapes and bruises. She always seemed to find her way back to the area she’d transformed, the unconscious part of her mind rising to the surface as the moon started to sink back over the horizon, and Kara was grateful for that as the frigid winter weather left her bluish and shivering violently as she stumbled around on weak legs looking for her clothes.

 

            Madam Pomfrey made her stay in the Hospital Wing all morning again, Kara stomaching a small breakfast and then a lunch, sleeping in between with the help of a draught. The potions she was given for pain and to recoup her strength were always marginally effective and this time Madam Pomfrey had even given her hot chocolate with her breakfast to warm her up. By the time she left, Kara’s fingernails were no longer purple and she made her way to the Common Room and enjoyed the solitude.

 

            Choosing to pack her trunk to take with her for the holidays, she finished quickly with the meagre belongings she owned and stole a good seat near the wide hearth when she was done. Sam, the Third-Year who’d been kind to her on her first day, and was always rather kind in a shy way, had a free period and joined her a while later. She offered up a game of wizard’s chess but Kara didn’t have a set so they played exploding snap with a deck of cards that Sam pulled out of her backpack.

 

            The holidays started a day later, and Kara was almost regretful that she wouldn’t spend Christmas in the decorated castle. Large trees were arranged in the Great Hall with enchanted snow and festive tinsel and baubles hanging from the branches of the pines, the suits of armour wore Christmas hats and snow fell from the enchanted ceiling as they ate turkey and pudding for the week leading up to it. But she was also glad for the reprieve from staying away from her classmates, from isolating herself as much as possible and worrying about homework and classes.

 

            Her relief was short-lived as she made her way out to the courtyard, leaving her luggage with everyone else’s and making the walk down to the gate. She found Alex waiting there for her and silently hovered at her elbow. She hadn’t seen much of her sister around, usually just a nod when they passed in the hallways or the occasional request to use her owl to send Eliza a letter, but they would be travelling home together so Kara waited with her. Kelly, James and Mike were there too and Kelly kindly asked her about her classes, her voice warm and encouraging as Kara shied away from her, ducking her head down.

 

            “What’re those?” Kara whispered to Alex, tugging on the sleeve of her robe as she took in the skeletal horse pulling the carriages as they started arriving.

 

            Alex pulled her Gryffindor scarf down from over her mouth as she shot her a confused glance, hazel eyes narrowing a fraction. “What?”

 

            “The things pulling the carriages.”

 

            Looking at the carriages, her sister frowned and scoffed, shaking off her touch. “Very funny.”

 

            “What?”

 

            “There’s nothing pulling them.”

 

            “Yes, there is,” Kara quietly insisted, a stubborn set to her face. “Those skeleton horses.”

 

            “God, you’re so weird,” Alex scoffed, shaking her head.

 

            Wounded by the dismissal in her words, Kara’s mouth turned down at the corners and her cheeks flushed red as her blue eyes prickled with tears. But she was seeing them; they were right there, shuffling their wings and waiting patiently as the carriages were loaded with students to be taken down to the platform. She didn’t bring it up again though and was momentarily worried that maybe she was going mad - was there a side effect of lycanthropy? - but Kara still skirted away from the creature as she climbed into the carriage.

 

            On the Hogwarts Express, she didn’t follow her sister and her friends to the compartment they flocked to, but slipped away to find her own, still somewhat upset. The train wasn’t quite as packed as it had been on the way to Hogwarts and she was on one of the earlier carriages which meant she found an empty compartment. It didn’t stay empty for long as her Hufflepuff roommates found her and settled in with some of the other First-Years from other dorm rooms. 

 

            The train ride was long, and only two days after the full moon, Kara was still recovering from the sleepless night and the toll taken on her body. She slept through most of the ride and only woke to buy herself a pumpkin pastie before she fell back asleep, head leaning against the door as she shut out the noise of her fellow students exchanging Chocolate Frog cards and gossiping.

 

            When the train screeched to a halt at Platform Nine and Three-Quarters, Kara struggled with her trunk as the platform bustled with activity, families trying to locate each other. The noise was deafening and Kara looked around anxiously as she tried to spot Eliza. Standing beside the train with her trunk at her feet, she had no choice but to wait until she was found, and it was almost ten minutes later before Eliza pushed a trolley with Alex’s trunk and owl cage on it through the crowd. 

 

            Relief broke across her face as she spotted Kara and Eliza smiled warmly as she crossed over to her. “There you are!”

 

            “Hi.”

 

            Eliza let go of the trolley and wrapped an arm around her shoulder, cupping one side of her face. “You look tired. Are you feeling okay?”

 

            “I’m fine.”

 

            “Alex, get her trunk.”

 

            They rode the Knight Bus home, the purple triple-decker depositing them outside the small cottage outside of Falmouth, and Kara helped Alex drag both trunks up to their small room. After sharing with four other girls, it was downright silent in there, even if it was a fraction of the size of her dorm. Still, it was the closest thing she had to a home, even if she hadn’t had the opportunity to spend much time there, and it was with a sense of relief that she sank onto her bed.

 

            Alex disappeared back downstairs and Kara could hear the sound of movement and conversation but felt outside of it. Giving mother and daughter a few minutes to catch up, she toyed with the folded butterfly slipped from the pages of her worn book until she sighed and climbed to her feet. 

 

            The stairs squeaked as she walked downstairs and Kara hovered uncertainly on the threshold of the kitchen until Eliza noticed her and smiled, beckoning her in. The kitchen had become thoroughly overgrown with plants in her absence and Kara took a seat at the table as a kettle whistled on the stove.

 

            Hot chocolates were set down before both girls and dinner shortly followed, Eliza peppering them with questions, which Kara skirted around. She made vague comments about friends she didn’t have, classes that she was only just getting the hang of and assuring her that her transformations were something she was quickly getting used to, which was also a lie.

 

            She slept late the next day, grateful she didn’t have classes, and Kara washed the dishes after breakfast and then helped Eliza out in the garden. It was marginally warmer at the southern end of the U.K. compared to the Scottish Highlands in the middle of winter, and despite the stormy skies and rain sweeping in off the coast, she spent most of the Christmas break outside in the garden or in the surrounding damp fields.

 

            On Christmas Day, she woke early to the sound of Alex climbing out of bed. Blearily blinking as she scrabbled for her glasses, Kara sat up and pushed them on before she followed her sister downstairs. Eliza had found a small tree and decorated it and when Kara stepped into the living room there were presents beneath it.

 

            She’d bought two boxes of Bertie Bott’s Every Flavour Beans on the Hogwarts Express out of the few knuts she had leftover from the money Eliza had given her on the first day of school. Kara had wrapped them in parchment and put them under the tree the night before, the only gifts she could manage and she opened the ones labelled for her as she sat cross-legged on the floor, a fire blazing in the fireplace.

 

            Eliza had knitted her a yellow sweater with a black K on it in the colours of Hufflepuff, while Alex had a similar one with an A in the Gryffindor colours. There was also a chocolate bar from Honeydukes from Alex, much to Kara’s surprise, as well as homemade fudge and a small trimming from one of her plants, put in a little pot for Kara to take care of. 

 

            She was grateful and was hesitant as Eliza hugged her, but when she did, Kara sank into it with a sudden desperation for it to be her mom. Christmas should’ve been at her home, the big farmhouse and dozens of wrapped gifts that her parents could afford with their moderate wealth. There should have been deep snow and dinner with her parents' friends - the Danvers included. It made her eyes sting with tears and she couldn’t stop the painful ache in her chest as she longed for her mom and dad. Kara had spent all term suppressing her grief, but it was all so fresh over the holidays.

 

            Christmas with Eliza and Alex was a quiet affair but it wasn’t all bad; they played exploding snap with a battered deck Alex had and they all cooked dinner together. Eliza had splurged and they had turkey and a dozen sides, and it felt like home with the smell of cinnamon cookies resting and roast potatoes in the oven. Alex even taught her how to play Wizard’s Chess with an old set she had, thrashing Kara, who had never bothered to learn how to play before, but she enjoyed it all the same, even if she still harboured a prickle of resentment for her sister’s hot and cold treatment.

 

            It was still rather early, the dishes from dinner washed and put away, leftovers wrapped up for tomorrow and the darkness making it feel a lot later than it was, when Kara walked upstairs to fetch a sweater. She jumped at the sound of something tapping on the window when she walked into the room and frowned as she saw a Greater Sooty Owl sitting on the windowsill. It was deep grey and black and completely unfamiliar and she thought that one of Alex’s new friends might have sent her a gift as she made to open the window.

 

            The owl ruffled its feathers and then thrust out a leg, where a slim box was fastened to it. Untying the parcel, Kara stroked the owl’s head and smiled as it softly hooted before it soared off into the night. As she made to set the gift on Alex’s bed, Kara paused at the sight of the small folded butterfly. 

 

            Her stomach lurched as a shot of excitement ran through her and she quickly slipped the butterfly out from under the twine. It fluttered its wings twice in her palm and she unfolded it to find two words scrawled on the scrap of parchment.

 

Merry Christmas

 

            She carefully refolded the butterfly and pocketed it as a small smile curled her mouth as she turned over the wrapped gift. Kara hooked a finger under the twine wrapped around the box to slip it off. 

 

            “Who’s that from?”

 

            Kara jumped at the sound of Alex’s voice and made to hide the gift behind her back, a guilty look on her face as her cheeks reddened at being caught. “A … friend.”

 

            “We both know you don’t have any friends,” her sister shot back, not unkindly as she wandered further into their bedroom and sank down onto her bed, leaning back as she braced herself on the mattress. “Even if you tell mom you do.”

 

            Flushing an even deeper red, Kara sat down opposite her on her own bed, holding the brown paper wrapped gift in her lap, fingers digging into it as a flicker of annoyance towards her sister flared up. “And?”

 

            “Nothing. But … if you made more of an effort, you could have friends. Querl said you pretty much ignore him in class.”

 

            “I’m fine by myself.”

 

            “If you say so.”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Kara made for the bedroom door and walked downstairs, feet thundering on the steps, and winding through the cramped kitchen to slip out into the garden. Eliza had transformed it into a space filled with magical plants of various kinds, winding up trellises, sprouting from the dark earth, flowering and budding even in winter, some of them with vines creeping up the fence and stubby trees reaching skywards. Skirting a potted Dirigible Plum bush, Kara padded barefoot onto the dewy grass, relishing the feeling of it underfoot as she walked straight to the small bench hidden near the hedgerow at the back of the garden. 

 

            Sitting in the light of the waning moon, she slid the lid off the box and stared down at the quill nestled inside. There was another note and she picked it up and unfolded it, hunching over the words as she tried to make out the black ink in the dark.

 

It’s a spell-checking quill, to help catch your u’s.

 

            Quietly laughing, Kara slipped the lid back on and stayed outside a moment later, enjoying the cold. She wondered how Lena’s Christmas was at Hogwarts and if she wished she’d gone home, what kind of presents her parents had bought her and if she felt lonely.

 

            The rest of the holidays passed by quickly, the new year rolling in and another trip back to Platform Nine and Three-Quarters with their trunks. Allowing Eliza to hug her as she murmured a quiet reply and promised her she’d write more, Kara boarded the train and tucked herself in the corner of the compartment, her trunk already wedged in alongside Alex’s. They were joined by Alex’s friends and Kara avoided speaking unless directly spoken to, giving short, shy answers to James’s questions about her holidays. 

 

            It was a Tuesday and even though they arrived back at school late, riding the carriages pulled by skeletal horses that made Kara’s hair stand up on end as no one else seemed to see them, she wolfed down dinner and then went straight to the Astronomy Tower. She wasn’t sure if Lena would be there on account of it not being a school day, but it was her secret place first and foremost and while Kara only came there twice a week she knew Lena went there most days. Her instinct was right and Kara felt a blossoming warmth as she found the Slytherin girl reading a thick book.

 

            “Oh. Hello,” Lena said with mild surprise at Kara’s arrival.

 

            “Did you have a good Christmas?” Kara asked.

 

            “The best I’ve ever had.”

 

            Lena said it so quietly, so dismissively, that Kara wasn’t sure if she was being serious or not. She was like that often, saying things with such nonchalance that it could’ve been dry humour or jaded honesty, but Kara didn’t know her well enough to figure out which.

 

            “Thanks for the gift. I got you- well, I, uh, I wasn’t sure what- what you liked so …” Kara pulled a bag of Fizzing Whizzbees out of her pocket and held them out.

 

            A flicker of surprise crossed Lena’s face and she reached out to take it. She wouldn’t have known that Kara went without lunch for the duration of the train ride so she could spend the last of her money on the last-minute gift. Lena gave her a small smile.

 

            “Thank you,” Lena murmured, turning it over in her hands. “I was going to give you yours before the holidays but you didn’t show up on Thursday.”

 

            Flushing red, Kara ducked her head and rubbed the back of her neck. “Oh. Yeah. I, uh, I was- I got … detention.”

 

            “Detention? You don’t seem like the type.”

 

            “I forgot to hand in my essay on time and you know how strict Professor McGonagall is.”

 

            “Right.”

 

            They fell silent and Kara had a burning question on the tip of her tongue as she glanced up at Lena, a furrow forming between her eyebrows. She moved over to the windowsill and sank down onto it beside Lena.

 

            “This is going to sound crazy but … there are skeleton horses pulling the school carriages and no one else can see them,” Kara finally said.

 

            Setting her thick book aside, Lena frowned slightly. “You mean the Thestrals?”

 

            “What?”

 

            “Thestrals pull the carriages; I read about it in Hogwarts A History. Haven’t you read about them in Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them?”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Kara didn’t know how to explain to Lena that most of her time spent reading that book had been dedicated to the scant few pages dedicated to werewolves. 

 

            “I- maybe, but I don’t remember anything about them.”

 

            Blinking at her with a wariness to her expression, Lena grimaced and shifted uneasily. “The only people that can see them are people who’ve seen someone die.”

 

            Face flushing red as she turned her head aside, hiding the grief on her face, Kara’s throat constricted and she swallowed painfully. “Oh.”

 

            The silence was thick and uncomfortable, Kara’s grief still too raw and fresh for her to reveal the truth to someone she only knew in passing. The pain of losing her father and being abandoned by her mother was something she made a conscious effort to avoid thinking about; if she dwelled on it, Kara imagined that she’d just cry all the time, and she didn’t think she’d ever be anything other than miserable ever again.

 

            “I can see them too,” Lena quietly confessed, staring at the floor.

 

            Kara’s head turned sharply as surprise flashed across her face. She didn’t ask who, or for how long, but the tightness in her chest suddenly felt looser, and Kara exhaled slowly as she nodded. Somehow, she’d known on some level Lena was stuck in a deep sadness that could only be explained by something as consuming as grief. It made sense.

 

            “There’s a herd in the Forbidden Forest; I can take you to see them sometime, if you’d like,” Lena continued.

 

            “We’re not allowed in there. We’ll get caught and- what if we’re seen together?”

 

            Smiling slightly as her cheeks dimpled, there was a gleam in Lena’s green eyes as she raised her chin. “I’m too smart for that. But you have to promise to keep a secret.”

 

            “We’re already each other’s secret.”

 

            “Promise,” Lena solemnly pressed.

 

            Rolling her eyes as she grinned, Kara stuck her hand out for Lena to shake. Her hand was cool and small, and pale against Kara’s lingering summer tan from years spent outdoors. Lena pulled it back quickly and Kara’s smile grew a fraction.

 

            “There. I promise. Now it’s an oath.”

Chapter 7

            Kara’s grades bumped up as the new school term rolled by, essays and tests and practical lessons all blurring together as she studied ferociously in the Astronomy Tower with Lena, able to recall the uses of Mandrake’s with ease, brewing potions perfectly on the first try and how to banish pixies with little fuss. They were paltry spells in the grand scheme of things, Second-Years still very much mastering the basics of magic, but she was no longer lagging behind the rest of her class, sitting at the bottom of the ladder with her poor grades. Now, Kara was near the top, her natural intelligence allowing her to make up for the dismal effort she’d made at the beginning, so distracted by her lycanthropy that trying had felt meaningless as she drowned amidst her grief and guilt and homesickness.

 

            That hadn’t gone away though, only became managed. She didn’t cry, didn’t show it in any way that she was suffering through losing two parents, that she’d been saddled with a life-long curse with no hope of breaking it as it broke her just a little bit more each full moon. Of course, Lena noticed the sickly pallor of her skin and her exhaustion either side of the windows of the full moon, and her disappearance the following day, but she didn’t put the clues together, and she didn’t know the truth about Kara’s family. For all anyone knew, she was Kara Danvers , and she’d moved here with her mother and sister and started at Hogwarts without further question.

 

            The bitterness of winter started to lift and the snow melted on the school grounds, the beginnings of spring breaking through with the green smell of the gardens and the forest blown in on the breeze. The tentative layer of ice covering the grey lake thawed as well and Kara spent her free periods, afternoons and weekends skirting the edge of it that bordered the Forbidden Forest. Pine and moss were comforting smells to her, black earth on her hands and the knees of her jeans as she slipped more than once, and she enjoyed the solitude of it, although her mind turned to Lena often, imagining if they were real friends, taking walks and doing their homework outside on mild afternoons. 

 

            Instead, their time together was limited to Tuesday and Thursday evenings after classes and dinner, depending on whenever they both made it to the Astronomy Tower. Sunset was delayed longer with each passing day, the deep grey lightening to cloudy blue as the seasons turned and Easter was almost upon them when Lena finally deemed the weather nice enough for them to sneak into the Forbidden Forest and see the herd of Thestrals hidden away there. She knew the way, she insisted, and Kara was all too willingly trusting as they made plans for Saturday morning, just after dawn, before the Great Hall filled for breakfast, when they wouldn’t be missed.

 

            Bundled up in her Hufflepuff scarf, jeans and a sweater, Kara skirted the lake and slipped into the cover of the trees, warily making her way in deeper before she let out a sharp cry in the silence as a hand grabbed her arm. Eyes wide and her hand going to her wand, she found herself staring down at Lena, who was wearing a velvet black cloak over a black turtleneck, skirt and tights. She looked like a monochrome portrait, her pale skin seeming to glow in the dark - save for her eyes, piercing and mildly surprised at Kara’s panic.

 

            “Sorry.”

 

            Shoving her wand deeper into her pocket as she blushed, Kara brushed a wayward curl out of her face and flushed. “You scared me.”

 

            Nodding, Lena was silent for a moment before pointing off. “It’s this way.”

 

            “How’d you find out about this anyway?”

 

            “Oh, uh, I saw Hagrid leading one of the foals back to the herd and followed him. He’s good with creatures; my brother told me he got expelled a few decades ago for apparently killing a student with one of his pets. I think Professor Kettleburn lets him take care of the Thestrals though.”

 

            Kara’s eyebrows rose in shock at the rumour and looked at Lena as she hesitated, lowering her voice. “My sister thinks he must have giant’s blood in him.”

 

            “He has to ,” Lena eagerly agreed. “Humans don’t grow that tall and all creatures have key traits. Giants are obviously very big.”

 

            “Do they all though?”

 

            “Of course they do,” Lena softly scoffed. “You’d know it was a vampire if you saw their red eyes, wouldn’t you?”

 

            “What about werewolves?”

 

            “I mean, on a full moon, of course you’d notice. You probably wouldn’t survive though. My brother says they’re really dangerous.”

 

            Kara resisted the urge to rub at her scars, her throat closing up as she regretted broaching the topic. Lena was far too perceptive and intelligent for her to be skirting around such a dangerous topic, and Kara was reluctant to lose the only sort of friend she’d made so far.

 

            “You would,” Kara murmured, “you’d just be a werewolf too.”

 

            Lena gave her a smug smile. “Not me. I’d hex it. My brother taught me this spell - a Bat-Bogey hex. I think that’d distract a werewolf long enough for me to run away.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Kara gave her a strained smile. Lena said it so convincingly that she might have believed her if she hadn’t been the victim of such a brutal attack. A Bat-Bogey hex wouldn’t stop a werewolf, that much Kara was sure of as she was assaulted by memories of coppery blood and white-hot pain. She wished she’d even been afforded the time to try a spell before she’d been bitten, but it had all happened so fast.

 

            They lapsed into silence after that, the sound of their feet snapping twigs and the occasional hoot of an owl cutting through the quiet. The forest was peaceful in the early morning, a lingering fog swirling around their ankles as their breath misted before them. Kara would’ve been content to walk for hours, her imagined friendship with Lena made real for just a small amount of time.

 

            After ten minutes, Lena held her arm up to stop Kara in her tracks, both of them standing at the top of a short, gentle slope with a thick oak blocking their path. Quietly creeping around the gnarled roots, her hand dropping to find Kara’s, fingers cold and thin and brittle boned in Kara’s slightly warmer grasp, Lena guided her down. 

 

            As she stepped around the tree, Kara’s lips parted with surprise at the herd of black, skeletal winged horses. She shouldn’t have been surprised - this was the entire purpose of their covert visit into the Forbidden Forest - but Kara had almost forgotten that eerie sight of them as they’d pulled the carriages along. Empty eye sockets and whip-thin tails, the leathery wings almost translucent as greenish light filtered through the canopy and made the veins tracing through the thin skin stand out.

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “They’re quite pretty, aren’t they?” Lena shyly whispered, giving Kara a crooked smile.

 

            They were, in some sad, lonely way. No one would ever look at them and see anything other than death, but they were gentle as the two young girls wandered closer, Lena bolder than her, having visited them a few times before. She even patted one on the nose and let out a soft, shuddering laugh as a foal bumped against her with a quiet keening cry. It made the hair on Kara’s arms stand on end, a pang struck in her chest as it constricted. It was a beautiful curse to be able to see them.

 

            A lover of all creatures, Kara eventually inched closer and patted one on the bridge of its strange skull-like snout. It made her think of her father, bleeding in the dark as the light vanished from his eyes, her own vision dimming as blood soaked her shirt. And now she could see this creature, a bittersweet memory of her torn up life.

 

            “Who did you see die?” Lena asked after a long bout of silence.

 

            “My dad,” Kara eventually whispered, her eyes stinging fiercely.

 

            She tried to pretend that she wasn’t on the verge of crying, folding her arms as she jammed her cold fingers into her armpits, her bottom lip trembling - from the cold, she told herself. Thirteen was too old to be crying over nothing. Her mother had always hated it when she cried, found it a relief that her daughter was relatively happy all the time, adventurous and wild and barely needed supervision, which would come back to literally bite her later on. But that was before and now Kara was sad and lonely and missed the old house she’d been raised in.

 

            “When?”

 

            Lips pressed together for a long moment, unwilling to talk about it, Kara drew in a shuddering breath, staring at the skeletal winged horses as they calmly nosed around, so gentle that Kara couldn’t bring herself to feel terrified of them. They were scary to look at, but so was she in the right phase of the moon. She just hoped that someone might think that she was misunderstood too.

 

            “August. Last year,” Kara rasped, wiping her eyes on the cuff of her sweater, a fleeting, almost dismissive motion that made it seem like she wasn’t wiping her tears away.

 

            Her throat was closed up and it hurt to breathe, the cold like fire as she drew in shallow breaths, chest rising and falling quickly. Lena was beside her, quiet and small as she stared straight ahead, drowned by the finely cut cloak as her pale cheeks turned a gentle pink from the cold of the forest.

 

            “I’m sorry.”

 

            “What about you? Who’d you see?”

 

            Lena hesitated, her brow furrowing momentarily before her eyes dropped to the leaf-strewn floor. “My mum.”

 

            “Oh. I thought-”

 

            “She died when I was little. My dad was already married, so … I lived with them afterwards.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “Did you move here because your dad died?”

 

            Wincing slightly and trying to mask it by ducking her head down, Kara shrugged. “Kind of.”

 

            “Do you miss it back home?”

 

            It was getting hard to talk now and Kara’s response was hoarse. “All the time.”

 

            They stayed a while longer before following the winding path back towards the lake, parting ways as Kara lingered in the cold and let Lena make a head start back to the castle. She followed after, lagging behind, and took a seat at the Hufflepuff table as she thawed in the warmth of the hall. A hundred or so students were sitting on the benches, enjoying their breakfast, oblivious to the Thestrals and the loss of people, and how it was a small comfort to share that with someone in the middle of the forest on a cold spring morning.

 

            Neither of them mentioned their parents again as the weeks slipped by, and before Kara knew it, it was almost the end of term. She was dreading it this time; the full moon fell a few days before Easter, which meant she’d be home in Falmouth and require a trip to St. Mungos. The thought of being trapped in that stone cell, mauling herself in the small confines with nowhere to run, to scratch at trees and tear up the earth, running until she exhausted herself and the moon went down, was nauseating. It left Kara feeling hollow and sick as she passed the March full moon with two days out of class, pale and clammy and exhausted, wandering the halls barefoot as she let the cold stone of the old castle radiate up through her soles, grounding her.

 

            To make matters worse, it was only two days before she was due to ride the Hogwarts Express back to London when she found herself the cruel butt of a joke. It wasn’t surprising in any way, but Kara was already consumed with the misery of the next full moon and couldn’t even defend herself as she made her way to the Transfiguration classroom after lunch. She joined the queue waiting outside the locked door of McGonagall’s classroom and was busy gently stroking one of her pale scars when there was the sound of tearing leather.

 

            The strap of her bag snapped, books and parchment spilling out, inkpots shattering and quickly blotting the essay for Transfiguration and soaking into the white feather of her quill. Kara’s stomach sank and she dropped to her knees, biting back a sigh as snickers filled the hallway, students skirting around her on their way to classes. When she reached for her thick Charms textbook, it floated out of her reach and Kara frowned, looking up with confusion. It didn’t dawn on her that she was being made fun of, the butt of some joke as her school supplies started floating around her.

 

            As she looked up, the floating supplies dropped , and Kara wasn’t quick enough to duck her head down before being assaulted by the Charms textbook, hot pain radiating from her nose as it made her eyes water. Everything else crashed down around her, ink splashing over her hair and forehead and her worn copy of Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them striking her on the cheek hard enough to bruise. She let out a small cry, cupping her cheek as her glasses were knocked from her face.

 

            Squinting, she felt around in the mess before her, black ink staining her palms as she brushed over broken glass and ruined parchment before finding her glasses. Setting them back on her face, Kara blinked as her blurry vision clarified in time to watch as Belinda shrieked, bats erupting from her face as she swatted at them. Eyes wide and mouth falling open, Kara knelt before her mess and watched, slack-jawed, as blood trickled from her nose. 

 

            As Belinda ran from the queue forming outside the Transfiguration classroom, the hallway quietened and the laughter receded, replaced by excited whispers of gossip. As Kara quickly stacked her books, a small folded paper bat flapped its wings and fell on top of the ruined essay she held on top of the stack. It had a pair of eyes and a mouth drawn on in ink and one of the eyes winked.

 

            Looking up, a grave look on her face, Kara’s eyes scanned the crowd of students still milling about for their classes before they snagged on a small pale girl, face hard with anger and eyes sharp with delight. Kara didn’t have to ask who’d cast the hex but her stomach twisted with conflicting emotions - gratitude and excitement at the prospect of being defended, and wariness and discomfort at the casual way Lena had hexed Belinda, who was, of course, the source of Kara’s throbbing nose and ruined belongings.

 

            “What’s the meaning of all this fuss?”

 

            Kara blanched at the sight of Professor McGonagall sweeping down the hallway and her mouth went dry as the woman’s eyes landed on her. Wilting beneath the hard stare, Kara’s shoulders sagged and hung her head, hiding her scars as much as the fresh blood dripping from her nose.

 

            “Miss Danvers, care to explain?”

 

            “I … tripped, Professor.”

 

            “Is that right? Well … off to the Hospital Wing you go. Do you have your essay to turn in?”

 

            Miserably holding up the ink stained parchment, the words blotted out in places, Kara flushed as McGonagall gingerly took it, holding it between her fingers as she peered at the ruined assignment. 

 

            “Right, well,” she muttered, her eyes dropping to the shards of glass and puddle of ink before her mouth tightened at the corners with displeasure. Kara swallowed thickly but the Professor just waved her wand and wordlessly cleaned the mess, the ink pots reforming - albeit empty - and dropping on the stack in her arms before McGonagall siphoned the ink from her ruined essay, revealing the words she’d spent a painstaking two hours on the night before, with Lena’s help.

 

            “Off you go now. Everyone else get to class.”

 

            Walking over to the windowsill, Kara set her armful down and quickly shoved everything into her satchel with shaking hands. Afterwards, she walked to the Hospital Wing and let Madam Pomfrey check if her nose was broken - it wasn’t - and if she was alright- she wasn’t - before she wearily left. She didn’t make it further than the open door before Alex was bearing down on her, a scarlet and black bat.

 

            “What happened to you?”

 

            “Why are you here?” Kara asked at the same time, disgruntled as her cheeks flamed.

 

            A crease formed between Alex’s eyebrows. “Professor McGonagall had me pulled out of Potions and sent up here.”

 

            “Why?”

 

            Shrugging, Alex rolled her eyes and let out an exasperated sigh. “I don’t know, Kara, why don’t you tell me?”

 

            Holding her satchel with the broken strap, the leather wound tightly around her fist, Kara clenched her teeth and looked down at her scuffed shoes. Feeling claustraphobic and aching for the wild outdoors, to escape into the forest and perhaps even shed her human skin for the painful relief of forgetting for a few hours, Kara swallowed thickly.

 

            “It’s just one of the girls in my dorm. She … doesn’t like me. I don’t think so, anyway.”

 

            “Which one?”

 

            “You wouldn’t know her.”

 

            “But what’s her name?”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Kara hauled her heavy satchel up by the broken strap and hauled it over her shoulder before setting off. Alex easily kept pace with her, a few inches taller, and she sighed heavily before pulling the satchel, yanking Kara back with it. 

 

            “What?” Kara snapped, pink-cheeked and angry now.

 

            “Just … hold on.”

 

            “Go back to class. I just want to be alone.”

 

            “Tell me who did it,” Alex softly ordered her.

 

            Kara let out a strained laugh, “what’re you going to do? Hex her?”

 

            “I might.”

 

            “Don’t bother. Someone already did.”

 

            Blinking in surprise, Alex jerked back, Kara’s satchel going with her. “Wha-“

 

            “Just leave me alone. It’s not like you care anyway, so …”

 

            Kara’s eyes stung with tears as she mumbled, head ducked down and a lump in her throat. Alex’s mouth thinned and she clicked her tongue.

 

            “Well don’t cry about it.”

 

            “I’m not crying,” Kara bitingly replied, resisting the urge to angrily cross her arms over her chest and purse her lips on a petulant pout.

 

            Rolling her eyes, her sister stopped at one of the wide window sills overlooking the sprawling grounds and courtyards below. She set Kara’s satchel down and pulled out her wand, gently clearing her throat and pointing it at it.

 

            “Reparo.”

 

            The leather worked its way back together until the worn bag was as good as new. Kara pressed her lips into a flatter line, her hands balled into fists and lingering resentment simmering inside her.

 

            “Thanks,” she curtly replied, still sounding somewhat petulant.

 

            “Yeah, don’t worry about it,” Alex said with a sigh, sinking down onto the yellowed stone.

 

            After a long moment, Kara joined her. She kicked her legs, shoes bouncing off the wall in rhythmic thumps as silence swallowed them. Watching one of the paintings of an old man wander into the next frame, Kara tried to quell the frustration inside her. She wasn’t really annoyed with Alex - she just didn’t know where else to channel it all. She’d become so irritable these days, teenage angst settling in as she was forced to grow up faster than intended.

 

            “I’m sorry about the carriages as well, by the way,” Alex haltingly said, guilt creeping into her face as she looked down at her lap, avoiding Kara’s sharp look of surprise. “I asked Querl about it. He said they’re called … Thestrals?”

 

            “I know,” Kara murmured, “I figured it out myself.”

 

            That wasn’t entirely true, but she wasn’t going to tell Alex about Lena. That was her little secret, her little oath, and she was reluctant to share that with anyone.  

 

            “Only people who’ve watched someone die can see them,” Kara told her.

 

            Alex winced and grimaced as she looked up at the ceiling, the wan sunlight picking out strands of red in her hair. Things between them were strained and uncomfortable, all the pressure of looking out for each other, as siblings did, without none of the bond forged through growing up together. Sure, Alex had pandered to her when they saw each other occasionally, playing Exploding Snap and sharing licorice wands while their parents drank Firewhiskey and talked about the latest MACUSA news. They didn’t hate each other, they just weren’t sisters, and both of their lives had been uprooted. It wasn’t fair on either of them but Kara had definitely drawn the short straw.

 

            “Why can’t you just try to fit in more?” Alex asked with a sigh after a moment, her expression agonised as she looked at her sister.

 

            Kara flushed slightly, her scars stark against the red, and she chewed on her lip, the ghostly memory of her nose throbbing making her reach up to touch it as she looked down. “You know what I am.”

 

            “That doesn’t matter,” Alex firmly told her, a hard look of stubborn insistence on her face. “You don’t even have to tell anyone.”

 

            “They’ll figure it out.”

 

            “They won’t! Just … try and fit in, would you? Maybe they wouldn’t pick on you if you made more of an effort.”

 

            Scoffing as her ears burned, Kara climbed to her feet and grabbed her satchel, her gratitude towards Alex for fixing it extinguished at her words. Slinging it over her shoulder, Kara scowled at her, but it was more wounded than anger.

 

            “Thanks for that,” she snapped before stalking off, grateful that Alex didn’t come after her.

 

            Making her way back to the Hufflepuff Common Room, Kara waited until classes were over, spending an hour playing Gobstones with Sam Arias, the Third-Year who was always nice and had heard about Kara’s beating from her books. She was always nice anyway, but Kara thought she was taking pity on her as Sam shared some of the Honeydukes chocolate she had leftover from the last Hogsmeade’s trip with her before the fire.

 

            Once students started trickling back in, Kara excused herself and made her way through the castle, up to the Astronomy Tower and through the portrait. She knew Lena would be there even if it was Wednesday night, when they weren’t supposed to be meeting. Kara had been itching to see her all afternoon and she wasn’t disappointed as she wound through the equipment, finding the young girl curled up on the sill as usual. Lena was surprised to see her though.

 

            “You’re not supposed to be here,” she blurted out.

 

            “Yeah, I- I just- I saw you earlier.”

 

            “How’s your nose?” Lena asked, a sly look in her green eyes, her stare intense and sparking with smugness.

 

            Kara gave her a droll look, reflexively touching it as she blushed. Mouth turning down at the corners, her blonde, wayward curls fell into her face, hiding her displeased expression. “You shouldn’t have hexed her.”

 

            “You can’t prove it was me.”

 

            “I know it was you.”

 

            “Are you going to tell Professor Sprout and get me a detention?” Lena asked, a thin smile curling her mouth. 

 

            Rolling her eyes as she sank down onto the windowsill beside Lena, Kara grimaced. “You know I wouldn’t.”

 

            “You shouldn’t let people walk all over you, Kara,” Lena murmured, one hand gripping her forearm tightly as a dark look clouded her pinched, pale face, suddenly solemn.

 

            “I don’t. I’m just … not really interested in what other people say and do. Sometimes … I think I’d be happy to just be alone all the time.”

 

            A funny look crossed Lena’s face before she gave Kara a forced smile, eyes creasing at the corners. “Me too.”

 

            “Are you going home for Easter?”

 

            “No.”

 

            Kara’s mouth thinned slightly as she gave Lena a searching look. “What’re you going to do about summer?”

 

            Moonlight and soft candlelight illuminated the twist of Lena’s lips, absent any humour, as she looked at Kara, smoothing out her grey skirt as her robes pooled around her. “I’ll have to go home, won’t I?”

 

            “Is it really that bad there?”

 

            Quickly looking away, dark hair falling like a curtain between them, a muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw and she resisted the urge to cover her arm, right over that horrid scar. “Yes.”

 

            “Oh. They won’t let you stay here?”

 

            “No. But it’s okay; I’ve gotten good at staying out of the way.”

Chapter 8

            Spring blurred into verdant summer in the Irish countryside, the wide-spreading branches of the elm trees shading the lawn as bees hummed through the neat flowerbeds of the estate and clouds of gnats congregated in the damp, shaded corners of the garden. Lena spent hours that first week at home, behind the brick wall on the west side of the sprawling house, tangling rose bushes thriving in the mild warmth as neatly paved paths cut past the wide fountain and the singing daffodils. 

 

            After the vividness of Hogwarts, the merciful escape, being home felt sort of like living in the walls of a dead place. The first day back, she passed through dim parlours and the ballroom, kept pristine by their House Elf, Hope, through the deserted library with rare books on dark magic that Lena had snuck from the shelves while growing up. The main courtyard of the garden felt cold and grey beneath the pale blue sky and she felt as if she’d become a ghost upon returning, the life washed out of her as she wandered through the house, feeling shockingly out of place. 

 

            Her bedroom was spacious and worn, the furniture carved from dark wood, motifs of snakes carved along the mantle of the fireplace tiled in deep Slytherin green and the heavy covers of the bed were dove grey, reminiscent of the silver of her family’s house. There had never been any doubt that Lena would be a Slytherin as well - anything else wouldn’t have been allowed, even if she hadn’t been quite as ambitious, not as determined or clever. But no one would ever have said Lena wasn’t clever; her mother had made her life hell to avoid that.

 

            The bed was made with neat hospital corners and there were no personal items on display to let it be known that it was the bedroom of a young girl, not so much as a pair of abandoned shoes, a poster for a Quidditch team or a doll from her childhood. Despite the House Elf who took care of the real chores, mess had never been acceptable growing up, and Lena’s books were all neatly contained on a tall shelf near the armchair, her clothes all hanging in the armoire or folded in the drawers. Anything that could be considered personal - a few letters from her brother during the school year, the empty bag from the Fizzing Whizbees Kara had bought her, a creased photo of her in the arms of a red-haired woman - were all tucked in the drawer of her nightstand, right beside the stack of parchment tied with string, bearing the same sentence over and over again from the last three years.

 

            And there was Lena, slipping out, her shoes in hand as she eased her creaking door shut and walked on the emerald runner pinned to the wooden stairs. Down to the grand staircase, wide and sweeping down to the foyer, dimly lit even as early-summer sunlight swept in through the tall, arched windows. The marble was cool through her socks and she slipped right out the front door unnoticed, feeling like a ghost in her own home.

 

            The grass had been cut and gave off a warm, allergenic smell as she darted down the white polished marble steps and across the lawn, white socks staining green on the soles as the warm sun shone down on her. Dappled sunlight filtered through the leaves of the old elm trees that lined the long gravel driveway that split the trimmed lawn and eventually ended at a tall, wrought-iron gate.

 

            In the shade of a tree, hidden safely behind the trunk, Lena laced on her shoes and moved from trunk to trunk, down to the hedgerow enclosing the estate. Falling to hands and knees before a secret part in the hedge where the hedges hollowed out enough for her to crawl through at an angle, invisible when looking right at it, Lena came through on the other side with a quiet inhale. Her heart pounded in her chest and she scrambled to her feet, shooting off towards the mountains.

 

            Her family’s estate was right on the doorstep of the national park, the uplands a patchwork of vivid green and brown of blanket bogs, heath and grass. The valleys were crowded with trees and it was easy for Lena to get lost in them, watching a peregrine falcon hunt, red and grey squirrels scurry up trees and hares dart past. Summers there were mild and damp and while it was painfully familiar, she felt a pang of longing for Scotland.

 

            Her shoes became muddy as she trampled through mud and long grass and behind her the gate disappeared into a cope of black pines. The trees seemed so tall that they scraped against the blue sky and Lena felt the tightness in her chest ease. After months away from school, it felt even more torturous to be back home.

 

            Spending the day outdoors, Lena avoided the winding rivers and flat lakes shimmering blue. She found a nest of Knarl’s eating wild daisies, almost identical to hedgehogs, save their darker faces, spotted an Alihosty tree and avoided it at the memory of what the leaves could do, and ended up planted on the banks of a small lake. It was a different lake in her memories, the water murkier and greener, the feeling of tentacles lashing around her small limbs as she choked on brackish water. 

 

            Here, there was only the sun shining on the surface of it and the telltale signs of a Merrow lurking in the depths. She’d crossed paths with them before and found them rather fish-like and greenish in comparison to the beautiful merfolk that were occasionally seen in the lake at Hogwarts. They were dangerous, but Lena never got anywhere close to the edge of the water, her body tense and cold with fear.

 

            Staying outside until it started getting late, her stomach gnawing with the hunger of missed meals, she eventually traipsed back as afternoon dragged on. Although it was dinner time, the sun was still bright in the sky, summer delaying dusk as she made her way back to the estate and the knowledge that her mother was inside.

 

            Lena prayed for the days Lillian was at work, which was more often than not, too consumed with her job to pay attention to her daughter. It was the days at home that resulted in pain and she knew sneaking out all day would enact some sort of punishment. If she’d had any choice in the matter, Lena wouldn’t have gone home at all.

 

            At the end of the day, she was only twelve though - although she was thirteen that October, so she didn’t think of herself as completely helpless - and she had nowhere else to go. The thought of her own place one day was all the hope she had that it wouldn’t always be this way - that, and the overwhelming relief that she’d be back at Hogwarts in a few weeks. Contrary to most of her fellow classmates, that day couldn’t come soon enough.

 

            Sneaking back inside, her palms and knees muddy and her dirty shoes held in hand as she tried to creep through the foyer in her grass-stained socks, Lena shrank back at the appearance of her mother. Lillian stood imperiously in the doorway to the main sitting room, a hard look on her face as she crossed her arms over her chest. She was beautiful but cold and Lena wished she had her invisibility cloak on so that she might escape the piercing gaze of those pale eyes.

 

            “You snuck out,” Lillian noted.

 

            Lena knew better than to reply and stood there silently, waiting for her mother to continue. Reaching for her wand, Lillian flicked it in Lena’s direction, making her daughter flinch in anticipation of pain. Instead, the creases of Lena’s shirt smoothed themselves out, the flecks of grass clinging to her skirt vanished and the stains on her socks and bare knees were wiped away.

 

            “How many times have I told you you’re not to leave this house without my permission,” Lillian stopped. 

 

            Mouth clamped into a flat line, Lena hung her head apologetically, looking appropriately chastened as she held her shoes in hand.

 

            “Well?” Lillian demanded.

 

            “I’m sorry,” Lena whispered.

 

            “Seeing as you have plenty of spare time, how about some revision before dinner?”

 

            Mouth thinning at the corners, Lena didn’t speak as she followed her mother into the sitting room. Her brother was sprawled on a sofa in rumpled robes after a day of work and he gave her a quick grin before returning to the newspaper, some ghastly article about this new Pureblood fanatic Lex admired monopolising the front page. Lena set her shoes down on the carpet and stood before her mother with her hands clasped before her.

 

            Lillian sank down onto a sofa and leaned back. To anyone else, she might have seemed relaxed, indifferent, but Lena knew better than to allow herself to be lulled into a false sense of security. Although her mother had never attended Hogwarts, there was something serpentine about her flat stare and preternatural stillness that made Lena believe she would have embodied the worst Slytherin traits perfectly.

 

            “What’s Bubotuber pus used for?”

 

            Lena hesitated, frozen for a moment before a wave of calm swept through her, the answer coming to her. “Healing potions.”

 

            “Which spell can be used as a defence against Dementors?”

 

            “Expecto Patronum,” Lena confidently replied, her brow furrowed together in grim concentration.

 

            “And that’s Latin for?”

 

            “I expect a guardian.”

 

            Lillian fixed her with a piercing stare, a challenge glinting in her pale blue eyes. Her lips twitched faintly at the corners and she tilted her head to the side, surveying her daughter standing before her, looking pale and small and uncertain. Lena avoided her mother’s eye as she stared down at the carpet.

 

            “Look at me,” Lillian softly demanded.

 

            Peering up, Lena met her eyes and her stomach twisted. But she had more courage than she gave herself credit for, was more defiant than her mother expected her to be. Lillian’s smile was a cold twist of her lips, almost a sneer, as she gave her the next question.

 

            “What are the five Primary Exceptions to Gamp’s Law of Elemental Transfiguration?”

 

            Lena swallowed, shifting on her feet as her skin prickled, subdued panic rearing its head. She could almost feel the bite of the scar on her arm reopening, the scratch of the Blood Quill on the paper as she neatly wrote the words, over and over again until her mother told her to stop.

 

            “I don’t know,” Lena whispered, her mouth dry as she stared down at the dark floorboards.

 

            “Mother, please,” Lex drawled from the sofa, lowering his copy of The Daily Prophet to roll his eyes, “that’s hardly fair. I didn’t learn about that until Sixth -Year.”

 

            “She will be better than you,” Lillian curtly replied, glancing over at her son with a flicker of fond exasperation in her eyes. 

 

            He was smart, yes, and favoured as her precious oldest, her child, and so he had been allowed to shirk his studies, relying on his natural intelligence, his cool charm and ambition to carry him through his O.W.L.’s and N.E.W.T.’s. He’d done well and accepted the entry level job at the Ministry of Magic in the Department of International Magical Co-Operation to liaise with the International Confederation of Wizards. Still, he’d gotten that through their father pulling strings at the Ministry when Lex had graduated two years ago, right before Lionel had died, and Lillian was still somewhat put out at her son’s disinterest in medicine. 

 

            Whatever hopes and dreams she’d had for her son, they now belonged to Lena. Lena who could never do right in her mother’s eyes, who could get every answer correct and still not please Lillian. Her decision to be a Healer had in part been in an effort to appease her mother, to perhaps garner just a fraction of the love she showered Lex with, and yet deprived Lena of in the same instance.

 

            “Although, perhaps I’m wasting my time,” Lillian continued, her tone clipped and her expression holding contempt for her daughter. “I’ve overestimated your intelligence if you can’t remember the reading I assigned you last week .”

 

            “I read it but-”

 

            “Do not speak when I am speaking,” her mother shouted.

 

            Flinching slightly, Lena clasped her hands before her and hung her head, her skin prickling with a cold sweat as she clamped her mouth shut. It was no use arguing with her mother, knowing the punishment would only be worse - had been in the past, with hours lost to the stifling darkness of the dungeon while she was left to reflect on her shortcomings and childish tantrums.

 

            Inhaling sharply, Lillian pinched the bridge of her nose as she closed her eyes, stiff and imposing, before she exhaled and gestured dismissively. “Fetch the quill.”

 

            Lena’s stomach dropped with the sickening dread. Her palms were clammy and she swallowed the lump in her throat as she stood rooted to the spot. Opening her eyes as her hand dropped from her face, Lillian arched an eyebrow.

 

            “You know the rules. Get a question wrong and you’ll be punished. Now go.”

 

            Turning, Lena walked over towards the writing desk set against one wall, sunlight spilling through the parted curtains to illuminate the dark wood and the compartment on top with its small drawers hiding quills, ink and parchment. Dragging the chair out, Lena took a seat at the desk, her feet unable to touch the floor, and reached for one of the drawers with a shaking hand, lifting out a Blood Quill and then a fresh sheet of parchment from the one beneath it. She didn’t need any ink. 

 

            Smoothing the parchment down, she set the nib of the quill against it and hesitated before starting to write in her elegant script; I am a failure.

 

            Her mother’s punishments had been milder when she was younger - a quick slap, no dinner, days locked in her room - but they’d quickly accelerated at the realisation that Lena was smart. Not just smart, but eager to learn and please, easily malleable for someone like Lillian to shape into the perfect Healer. Her father had spent most of his time gone or drunk and might have been called volatile in one of his good moods; although she’d been his favourite, that favouritism had only extended so far, and he’d never cared enough to rein in Lillian’s severity.

 

            The old silvery scar on her left forearm stung fiercely as the letters reopened and then closed over, pinkish from the pain, and Lena curled the fingers of her left hand into a fist. Repeating the sentence again, the letters reopened and closed, turning redder with each line. She got to five before her chin started wobbling, ten before her eyes filled with stinging tears and she couldn’t help but sniffle.

 

            “You’d better not be crying,” Lillian warned her, the clink of crystal knocking as she poured herself Firewhiskey and listened to the scratch of the quill and her daughter’s suppressed sobs. “Or I’ll give you something to cry about.”

 

            Pressing her mouth into a flat line, her cheeks splotchy from her anger and pain, Lena continued, over and over again until she’d filled the sheet of parchment and reached for another one. She made it halfway through that one before Lillian softly ordered her to stop. Lena set the quill down and let out a pent up breath, sharp and breathless, picking up the pages - a few sentences were blurred from her tears - and climbing to her feet. Pushing in the chair and slipping the Blood Quill into its drawer, Lena made to leave.

 

            “Wait,” Lillian called out. “Come here.”

 

            Turning, Lena swallowed thickly and walked over to her mother, hanging her head as she stood before her. Lillian reached out and cupped her chin in a tight grasp, fingers digging in as she jerked Lena’s head up. Staring into her pale eyes, Lena felt diminished.

 

            “Tomorrow you’ll do better.”

 

            It wasn’t a question but a statement. Lena would have no other choice and she nodded quickly, the movement somewhat constricted by her mother’s tight grip. Giving her a thin smile, Lillian let go and stroked her dark hair out of her face, ignoring the petulant expression her daughter was giving her.

 

            “Good girl. Go and get cleaned up for dinner.”

 

            Fleeing as quickly as possible, Lena all but ran up to her room, shutting the door behind her and angrily rubbing at her eyes as she tried not to cry. As a distraction, she walked over to her drawer and added the new sheets of parchment to the stack, retying the bundle with shaking hands and then picked up the empty Fizzing Whizbees packet, turning it over in her fingers as she thought of Kara. She wondered what it was like down in Cornwall, near the sea with the warmer weather, a mother who loved her and weeks of summer holidays to look forward to.

 

            Shoving it back in the drawer and slamming it shut, Lena walked over to the closet, fading sunlight seeping in through the windows as she picked out clean clothes and cried as she changed for dinner. Once she was done, she moved over to the window. Her arm stung and her eyes were raw from crying as she curled up on the window seat, wishing it was the ledge of the Astronomy Tower, across the sea with miles between her and her mother. Miles from harm.

 

            Dusk was sweeping in and her owl, Morrigan, swooped down onto the window sill, ruffling her feathers as Lena unlatched the window and let her inside. Perching on Lena’s knee, she stared at her with unblinking yellow eyes and allowed the young girl to stroke her beak. Sometimes, Lena felt like she was her only friend but then a flash of blonde, of blue eyes and pale scars would cross her mind, before the thought was gone in an instant.

 

            There was a knock on the door and Lena scrubbed at her eyes with the sleeve of her shirt, listening to the sound of old hinges creaking open and the heavy thud of footsteps on the floorboards. They groaned beneath her brother’s weight and Lena looked up, pale with bloodshot eyes, and so small as she huddled against the windowpane with her owl in her lap.

 

            Lex sighed as he set down the wide, shallow bowl of blue solution on the side table set beside an emerald green armchair. He looked over at her and gestured. “Come on.”

 

            Resentful, Lena scowled at him for a moment before climbing to her feet, Morrigan flapping out the window and soaring off, and walking over to him. She unbuttoned the cuff of her shirt and rolled it up, exposing the fresh pink lines of the scar before she took a seat and set her arm in the bowl of Murtlap Essence. The cool solution took the sting right out of it and she let out a shuddering breath.

 

            “Why does she do it to me and not you?” Lena asked, her voice wavering.

 

            “Because it’s too late for me to be better. But you - she wants to make you exceptional.”

 

            “But it hurts.”

 

            Wiping at her cheeks, which flushed red with anger and humiliation, Lena pouted and Lex gave her a crooked smile as he sank down to a crouch beside the chair. His curls were cropped short and he was still boyish in the roundness of his face, on the cusp of twenty, and he was gentle as he rotated her arm slightly in the solution.

 

            “Ah, it’s not so bad,” he lightly murmured. “It’ll stop hurting in a bit. Then we can play some chess, if you feel like it.”

 

            Rolling her shoulders in a non-committal shrug, Lena chewed on the inside of her lip and sniffed. “Do you think you could write to Dumbledore and ask if I can stay at Hogwarts next summer?”

 

            With a heavy sigh, Lex climbed to his feet and hauled Lena up as well by her shoulders. She looked up at him with wide-eyed bewilderment on her young face, thinking her brother could solve all of her problems if he tried. He was the best person she knew, had her adoration from the moment she’d been brought to the big, quiet house, and had received numerous punishments in pursuit of his affection.

 

            But he frightened her then, his usual warmth hardening into exasperation, his face crumpled with annoyance as he seized her elbows and shook her. “Listen to me, we’re a family. We’re loyal to each other. No one gets to leave , okay? Do as you’re told and you’ll thank her for it one day. Things are going to be different soon, anyway. There’s change coming and we’ll all be better for it.”

 

            Staring up at him with confusion and hurt in her green, bloodshot eyes, Lena’s lips parted and she looked shockingly pale. As if coming back to himself, Lex let out a short laugh and let go, the places where his thumbs had pressed aching slightly in their absence. He smoothed her hair and gave her a crooked smile.

 

            “Come on. Let’s go and eat dinner.”

 

            Her arm was dripping Murtlap Essence all over the rug and she grabbed the small towel Lex had brought up with it and dried herself off. Rolling her sleeve down over the words, avoiding looking at them, Lena buttoned the cuff with clumsy fingers and followed her brother out of the room. Sitting at the king dinner table, Lena was ignored as her mother and brother discussed the rising attacks on Muggles with amusement, exchanging comments and sentiments about how the lax Ministry had afforded many of the minority groups too much power, rivalling that of the elite old Purebloods families.

 

            The days followed a similar pattern, depending on her mother’s work schedule. On the days she was gone, laughter rang through the rooms or the gardens as Lex showed her duelling stances on the gravel driveway or lounged in the library with her as she prepared for another quiz, wrote up essays Lillian requested and, occasionally, snuck through the hallways as her brother indulged her in hide and seek. On the days he worked, she snuck out through the hedges and trampled through the valleys and up the mountains, Hope making her a sandwich to take with her and cleaning up the telltale signs as Lena tracked mud through the house upon her return.

 

            When Lillian was home, she tried her best to stay out of her mother’s way, studiously hiding in the corner of the library with some book or essay. Her mother chose those days she remembered her existence to question her until Lena got an answer wrong. She could answer a dozen correctly but one wrong answer would find her parked at that writing desk, breathlessly sobbing her way through a page of words engrained in her brain deeper than they were in her arms.

 

            The only time she was allowed out was once the letter for her second year at Hogwarts came via owl post. Lillian took her one Wednesday morning, a handful of flu powder bringing them to The White Wyvern, dressed in black with her pale daughter trailing in her long shadow as they wound down Knockturn Alley, stopping at Mr Mulpepper’s Apothecary for potion ingredients. Lena was measured for a new uniform and basked in the smell of ink and parchment in Flourish and Blotts as Lillian paid for a copy of The Standard Book of Spells, Grade 2 . There was already a worn copy of Lex’s at home, used to teach Lena years ago, but nothing but brand new would be good enough - even for the disappointing youngest child Lillian had never asked for.

 

            They didn’t stay long, only a handful of hours necessary to get what they needed, but Lena was buoyed with the thought of returning to Hogwarts soon. It was only a few short weeks away, then a couple, then one. Lena had everything packed away in her trunk days before September 1st, anxious to be gone again, and even one last test resulting in a stinging slap across the face and three entire pages of sentences the night before wasn’t enough to dampen the intense relief of waking up the next morning knowing she’d be far away by the time she went to bed that night.

 

            Rising early in the morning, excitement twisting her stomach and leaving her with little appetite as she toyed with the yolk of her boiled egg and ate a measly mouthful of toast, Lena tried to calm herself as she let Hope run a bath for her and iron her clothes. It was warm for early September but Lena wore a thin cotton shirt, as always, her wardrobe lacking in anything short-sleeved.

 

            She was dressed and in the sitting room with the biggest fireplace, the one they always Flooed out of, her trunk at her feet and her Greater Sooty Owl in her cage. 

 

            “You should hear him talk, mother,” Lex’s voice drifted into the room, striding behind Lillian as he looped his tie around his neck, open robes flapping around him. “He’s quite inspiring. I think you’d agree with several of his points on blood purity and the power imbalance.”

 

            “Yes, yes,” Lillian dismissively replied as she strode ahead, tall and imposing, not even glancing at her daughter as she walked over to the fireplace. “I’ve heard all about this Dark Lord and his new war . I admit, I’d be interested to see if anything comes of his attempt to overthrow the Ministry. Merlin knows Gellert Grindelwald turned out to be a complete and utter disappointment.”

 

            “Come to his next meeting,” Lex encouraged her.

 

            Clicking her tongue, Lillian rolled her eyes. “Mm, I suppose I should see it for myself; I hear he’s very persuasive and the attacks of Muggles at least show that he’s serious.”

 

            She was pulling on a pair of black leather gloves and her eyes strayed over to Lena, giving her a cursory once over. Turning to Lex, Lillian gave his cheek a quick pat.

 

            “I’ll see you at dinner.”

 

            Turning to Lena, she gestured with her hand and Lena scooped a handful of Floo powder from the small vase kept on the mantle. Standing in the grate, Lena dashed her handful of powder at the sooty ground and spoke clearly.

 

            “Platform Nine and Three-Quarters!”

 

            She watched a dizzying torrent of open fireplaces spin past before she stepped out onto the platform and stepped aside, her mother coming through a minute later, her trunk and owl beside her. Lillian gestured with her wand to raise the trunk onto a trolley while Lena carefully lifted the owl cage on top and started wheeling it towards the scarlet train.
