            They were early, only a few dozen students and parents milling about, and Lena took an empty compartment near the front of the train. Stowing her trunk for her with a lazy flick of her wand, Lillian looked down at her daughter.

 

            “Remember, I want copies of all of your homework and essays,” Lillian sternly told her. 

 

            Lena nodded obediently, already knowing what was expected of her from last year. Her mother had criticised any wrong answers or less than perfect marks, which weren’t often but still happened. Lena was already dreading repeating it.

 

            “And don’t disappoint me.”

 

            “Yes, mother.”

 

            “And join the Duelling Club; physical skills are a valuable resource.”

 

            She nodded again and then Lillian sighed and her meek appearance, her mouth thinning as she reached into a pocket of her pristine robe and withdrew a bulging purse.

 

            “For the train,” she said, holding it between two fingers and letting it drop into Lena’s reluctant hand. “I’ll see you next summer.”

 

            With that, Lillian turned on her heel and strode off, her heels clicking on the stone before she vanished between one step and the next, Apparating out of King’s Cross. There was no sentimental goodbye or an ounce of affection, and as soon as she vanished, Lena breathed easier than she had in months.

 

            Sitting in her compartment, reading her copy of Healing at Home With Herbs by Phyllida Spore, Lena tuned out the sound of the platform filling and students cramming onto the train. It was inevitable that she’d have to share her compartment as the others were quickly filled and Lena tucked herself away in the corner as wide-eyed First-Years sought refuge in hers. It was a relatively quiet ride, most of the First-Years venturing hesitant questions and glancing at her with curiosity, trying to place whether she was one of them or not.

 

            Lena kept to herself and the hours passed by quickly, a pumpkin pastie and a cauldron cake tiding her over until dinner that evening, as well as a Chocolate Frog for Kara. The thought had come to her as she was perusing the trolley and she quickly added one to her purchase before tucking it into her pocket and returning to her book.

 

            After an early start that morning, excitement leaving her unable to sleep, Lena felt the prickling feeling of exhaustion behind her eyes as the train started pulling into the platform. She’d changed into her brand new Slytherin uniform a short while after getting onto the train and rubbed Morrigan’s beak through the cage as they came to a screeching halt before leaving her behind.

 

            It was futile to even try and catch a glimpse of Kara in the crowd of students, the sound of Hagrid’s booming voice cutting through the muffling steam as the young Groundskeeper herded First-Years towards the boats. Lena was left to take a carriage this time and patted a Thestral in passing before hauling herself up into a free one.

 

            Soon enough, she was sitting in between a Fourth-Year and Seventh-Year Slytherin in the Great Hall, chatter filling the place as they waited for the Sorting Ceremony. It seemed like an age as the dozens of students crowded before the raised dais took turns setting the hat on their head and joining their respective Houses, but eventually the tables flooded with food. Lena was partial to the thinly sliced roast beef and Yorkshire puddings and left enough room for trifle before the Welcome Feast was over. Seeking out a Prefect she knew from last year, she asked for the password to the Common Room and slipped away from the crowd in black and green making for the Dungeons.

 

            Hurrying upstairs, cutting through a secret passageway and away from the other students as she tried to remain unnoticed, Lena arrived at the portrait of Hesper Starkey and let herself into the Astronomy Tower. Lighting her wand, she moved through the room and then lit a few of the candelabras, a warm glow fending off the darkness, and sought comfort in the peace of being back. It felt like coming home.

 

            She wasn’t sure if she expected Kara to be there or not, just enjoying the comfort and solitude of being back at a place that felt safe, felt like a reprieve. But when she heard the sound of something clattering to the ground and the whispered curses following, she let out a quiet laugh, her solemn expression softening with anticipation.

 

            A minute later, Kara sheepishly rounded the corner and came into view as Lena lit a few more candles to brighten up the place.

 

            “You might consider using your wand, you know,” Lena greeted her.

 

            Kara let out a shy laugh, pushing her wire glasses up her nose as she ducked her head. “Hi.”

 

            “Hi.”

 

            “How was your summer?”

 

            Lena’s face crumpled as she smiled, her eyes creasing at the corners, cheeks dimpling, but it was an almost painful expression that lacked any real amusement. Her throat felt like it was closing up and she wanted to cry.  “I’m glad to be back. Yours?”

 

            Kara glanced up quickly and Lena’s lips parted slightly as her eyes widened with surprise. There was a new scar on Kara’s chin, as pale as the rest of them, and her eyes trained on it as she stammered for a moment, losing her train of thought.

 

            “It was okay,” Kara murmured.

 

            She’d grown at least an inch, looking a little broader in last year’s uniform, faded a little from too many washes. Her mother must have enlarged them a little to fit and Kara looked lankier in it.

 

            Blinking, Lena met her eyes and Kara gave her a pained smile. “It’s okay, you don’t have to be polite.”

 

            “I- did your mum do it to you?” Lena asked, her voice a ragged whisper as she curled her hand around her left arm.

 

            Unabashed shock flashed across Kara’s face so fast that Lena knew her reaction was genuine. “No. No, she would- she would never.”

 

            Some of the panic dissipated as Lena’s taut muscles relaxed and she smiled thinly. Only her mother would do something like that, apparently. She was glad that her mother was the cruel exception, and that her gentle maybe friend was spared the same harrowing fate.

 

            “Just… please don’t make me tell you,” Kara asked, her voice ragged as her mouth hitched into a sad, uneven smile.

 

            Swallowing, Lena reached into her pocket and pulled out the unopened Chocolate Frog, hesitating before holding it out. “I got this for you.”

 

            Another flicker of surprise crossed Kara’s face and her smile was more genuine as she took it, glancing up at Lena. “Why? I mean- thank you, but-“

 

            Shrugging half-heartedly, Lena looked down at her lap. “I don’t know. I know you like chocolate. And I wanted to write to you over the summer but I … didn’t.”

 

            “Why not?”

 

            “Why didn’t you write to me?” Lena evasively countered.

 

            Brow creasing slightly, Kara grimaced. “Oh. Well … I don’t have an owl. I could’ve borrowed Alex’s but that would’ve raised some questions, seeing as I don’t have any friends.”

 

            Lena’s mouth twitched faintly at the corners. “I didn’t write to you because I didn’t think we were friends.”

 

            Kara turned over the Chocolate Frog box in her hands and then looked up, rubbing at the new scar on her chin with a flicker of wariness in her pale blue eyes. “And the chocolate?”

 

            Hesitating, Lena twisted her fingers as her pale, thin cheeks were flooded with two patches of colour. “The chocolate is because … I think I’d like it if we were friends. Secret friends.”

 

            Settling down on the wide window ledge beside her, Kara gave her a shy smile. “Okay. Secret friends. Is that another promise?”

 

            “It can be. What if we promised to always be friends? No matter what? No House rivalries, no families, just us.”

 

            “I’d like that.”

 

            Extending a small hand, silver Slytherin signet ring flashing on her finger, Lena gave her a wan smile, and it felt like she was branded by Kara as they shook hands, her touch so warm that it seared something invisible and binding right into her very bones. Staring back at her, Lena felt like she’d just made her own decision for the first time in her life and it lit her from within with a spark of hope. 

 

            “Me too.”

Chapter 9

            “Did you hear?” Kara asked, rounding a particularly large lunascope with a wide smile on her face as she took in the sight of Lena curled up in her usual spot.

 

            It seemed like she was always there, still some figment of Kara’s imagination that showed up when she needed her, but there was something tangible about her and Kara’s grin widened a fraction as Lena looked up from her book. Holding her spot with her finger as she closed the book, Lena cocked her head to the side, taking in Kara’s pink cheeks, her damp curls, darkened by the water, and the new silvery scar on her cheek that she’d come back from the Christmas holidays with, making it look like a dimple when she smiled.

 

            Eyes glancing back down to the cover of her book, Lena hid a smile. “Yes, of course. You played very well.”

 

            Kara’s face furrowed as she quickly crossed over to the window, lankier from the sporadic growth spurts that had led her to fill out a little, snagging a spot on the Quidditch team with the help of a little extra strength her lycanthropy bestowed upon her. It just made her clumsier on two feet though, unused to the extra inches as her worn jeans showed a strip of her pale ankles as she cast down. She was wearing her Hufflepuff Quidditch sweater with pride after winning the match against Ravenclaw only an hour ago as she gave Lena a curious look.

 

            “How would you know? I doubt any of your lot we’re giving me any compliments.”

 

            Looking confused for a moment as she pressed her lips into a line, Lena softly cleared her throat and shifted. “Well … I came to watch you play.”

 

            “Really?” Kara blinked.

 

            Frown deepening, Lena nodded. “Of course. I went to the last one as well.”

 

            “But … you don’t like Quidditch.”

 

            “I don’t mind it, I just- I’d rather spend my time studying,” Lena murmured, thumbing the corner of her book. “I mean … it’s dead boring, but it’s also a distraction.”

 

            Kara’s expression was bemused, and she looked like she was going to laugh. There was something about Lena that made her seem years older than she was, as if she’d never treated anything as a joke since the day she was born. She’d turned thirteen in October, with Kara spending the last of her money on a packet of Jelly Slugs at Honeydukes as a gift, but the way she talked seemed so jaded and serious most of the time that it felt like she’d skipped childhood altogether.

 

            “Why’d you come then?” Kara asked, breaking a block of chocolate from the bar she’d bought herself and holding it out to Lena.

 

            Hesitating before breaking off a measly square and then sighing when Kara broke off more for her, Lena gave her a wry smile. “Because I wanted to see you play. That’s what friends do.”

 

            Humming in agreement as a glow of delight spread through her, Kara smiled. “Thanks.”

 

            “I see you’ve made more friends though,” Lena commented, the sting of jealousy in her words well masked.

 

            Shrugging half-heartedly, Kara’s smile turned lopsided. Ever since she’d made the team, she’d become somewhat popular in Hufflepuff. Mike Mathews, who was in Alex’s friend group and a couple of years ahead of Kara, was on the team too as a Chaser, which meant they spent a fair amount of time together with training sessions. As an extension of becoming friendly with everyone on the team, Kara had been subjected to Querl Dox being even friendlier in class together, the Ravenclaw so close to Mike that he seemed to think Kara was now a part of the friend group as an extension of him as well as Alex.

 

            In fact, it seemed that every day she was with one of her sister’s friends; Querl sat outside with her at lunchtime with Winn, and Mike during training sessions or when he invited her to throw a quaffle around with James, the Gryffindor Keeper. Imra and Kelly were more academically focused and would sit at the same table in the library as her and help with her homework, although the conversation was limited there. Even Alex had finally gotten over her annoyance at having her life uprooted for her new sister, reverting back to the previous kindness she’d shown Kara growing up, if nothing else.

 

            “Oh, um, I mean … kind of,” Kara haltingly replied. “I mean … they’re my sister’s friends. Mostly.”

 

            “That’s good,” Lena murmured, giving her a reserved smile. “You should have friends.”

 

            Kara nudged her patent shoe with her worn tennis shoes, her smile a little awkward as she rubbed at the scar on her chin. 

 

            “You’re my best friend though.”

 

            “Am I?” Lena asked with surprise.

 

            “Sure. Who else?”

 

            “I don’t know. I thought … well, you probably have friends in America.”

 

            “Yeah, but … I haven’t spoken to them since we moved,” Kara awkwardly explained. “And it was really only one friend. Kenny.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “And what about your friends?”

 

            Lena stared at her for a moment, unblinking, before opening and closing her mouth. “Pardon?”

 

            “Well, I never see you around, even though you always see me. Who are your other friends?”

 

            A v formed between Lena’s eyebrows and she ate the rest of the chocolate to buy herself a moment. Kara watched her duck her head down and waited patiently for a response.

 

            “I, uh, I don’t … I don’t really have any other friends.”

 

            “Oh,” Kara softly exclaimed with surprise. 

 

            Lena had said it before, last year when they’d first met, but it had been so close to the start of term that it wasn’t at all surprising to think she hadn’t made friends yet. Apparently, it wasn’t just Kara who’d had trouble on that front.

 

            “I thought- I mean …”

 

            “I didn’t come here to make friends.”

 

            “Oh. Okay.”

 

            Looking a little flustered as she tried to explain herself, Lena’s delicate features crumpled into a perplexed expression as she pouted slightly. Her eyes were piercing beneath her furrowed brows and she looked at Kara with a flicker of wariness before confessing.

 

            “It’s just in my nature to stay in my corner and watch other people. I enjoy it.”

 

            “So, you enjoy watching me?”

 

            Flushing with a prickle of embarrassment as she bristled with indignation, Lena quickly objected. “No, I- it’s not like I follow you around. I just see you sometimes when I’m studying outside. You’re always with that Metamorphmagus.”

 

            “That’s Querl. He’s … funny,” Kara haltingly replied, a small smile on her lips as she thought of him changing his appearance to amuse her. 

 

            “I know him. He’s in the Chess Club too. He’s smart.”

 

            “Yeah. Ravenclaw,” Kara said with a droll smile, her hair curly in disarray as she let her head roll to the side to look at Lena.

 

            “He’s especially smart for a Ravenclaw.”

 

            Kara gave her a quick grin and raised her eyebrows a fraction. “But not as smart as you. You should’ve been a Ravenclaw.”

 

            Scoffing as she tried not to be too flattered, Lena quickly blurted out the first thought that crossed her mind. “My mum was.”

 

            Face crumpling with confusion, Kara picked at the pilled cuff of her sweater. “I thought your mom went to Ilvermorny.”

 

            Blanching, Lena’s mouth opened and closed and she seemed to stiffen. Kara wasn’t sure what she’d said wrong but she could see the way Lena had tightened, her shoulders rigid, her mouth a hard line, something painful in her green eyes. But when she spoke, it was nonchalant, almost dismissive.

 

            “My other one. Remember I told you in the forest …” Lena trailed off and Kara closed her eyes, cringing at how she’d forgotten.

 

            “Right. Sorry.”

 

            “It’s okay,” Lena murmured, although her knuckles tightened as she gripped her book and a muscle twitched in her jaw. “It’s just … nobody knows.”

 

            She said the last part anxiously, her eyes opening to fix Kara with a firm stare. Quickly nodding, an unspoken message passing between them, Kara cleared her throat slightly as she shifted.

 

            “I, uh, you know how … my dad died?”

 

            “Mm.”

 

            Kara’s lips twisted as she paused for a moment, “well, I … lost my mom then too. At the same time. So, the mom that I moved here with … she’s not my mom. She was a friend and she took me in, and that’s why my sister hates me. Because before me, she was an only child, and she had friends and school and was nice to me when I was younger. And then I lost my parents and we had to come here.”

 

            “Why?” Lena softly asked. “Why did you have to move here? Couldn’t you have stayed?”

 

            Letting out a frayed laugh as pain blossomed in her chest, the urge to tell Lena the truth building in her throat, even though she knew she’d never be able to. What had happened to her was something Kara couldn’t even begin to put words to, to volunteer that information to the first person to show her a little kindness in this new school. It was terrifying to consider losing the only person she felt like she had, even now, with new friends.

 

            Rubbing her forehead, Kara cleared her throat. “I- it’s a long story. Maybe some other time.”

 

            “Right. I have to study anyway.”

 

            “Mhm. I’m surprised to hear that you study outside though.”

 

            “Why?”

 

            “I don’t know,” Kara shrugged, hugging her knees to her chest as she smiled slightly. “I can’t really imagine you anywhere but here. Or maybe the library.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lena fixed her with a droll look, “we’ve been into the Forbidden Forest together.”

 

            “I know. You still look like you belong in some corner, tucked away with your books. I bet you look even more normal in the library. Do you spend all of your time there? I mean, you’re always here when I come here, but you study so much so I figured you must go to the library, right? But I’ve never seen you there.”

 

            Patiently listening to her babble, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction when Kara finished. Giving her a sheepish smile, Kara pushed her glasses up her nose and Lena laughed slightly.

 

            “I’ve seen you there,” Lena admitted.

 

            Throwing her hands up, Kara laughed, “see! How come you always see me but I don’t see you?”

 

            “Maybe you’re just not looking close enough,” Lena whispered, although there was a look of amusement on her face that Kara could pierce, some secret she wasn’t privy to.

 

            Narrowing her eyes, she hummed for a second and then let it go, leaning back against the cold window pane.

 

            “Shouldn’t you be celebrating?” Lena asked as she reopened her book.

 

            “Yeah. There’s a party in the Common Room. Ravenclaw’s probably mourning their defeat as well.”

 

            “Aren’t you going to join in?” Lena asked, peering up.

 

            Kara hesitated and then smiled crookedly. “Yeah. I just- I wanted to come and see you first.”

 

            Lena blinked as she looked back at her, unable to parse through the strange feeling of having someone seek her out for good intentions. Kara couldn’t have known that though, couldn’t have read the inner turmoil of her friend, just as Lena was likewise oblivious to her own.

 

            Dusting off her thighs, Kara pushed herself to her feet and looked down at Lena, a soft smile curling her mouth. “You know, next time you see me outside, you could say hi.”

 

            “I thought we said we couldn’t.”

 

            “I know,” Kara murmured with a shrug. “But we could. Otherwise, I’ll have to join the Chess Club and I don’t know how to play chess.”

 

            Snorting, Lena gave her a withering look, effectively derisive for someone so young. “You don’t know how to play chess?”

 

            “It wasn’t as popular at Ilvermorny!” Kara protested, holding her hands up helplessly.

 

            “Okay, next Saturday meet me here after breakfast,” Lena brusquely ordered her. “I’ll have to teach you myself.”

 

            Kara laughed but readily agreed, rolling her eyes. “Alright. I’ll see you Tuesday.”

 

            “See you Tuesday. Enjoy your party.”

 

            Waving before rounding the corner, Kara disappeared from the tower and made her way back down to her Common Room where a party was in full swing. Someone was playing music and a few others had pilfered the kitchens, snacks crowding the tables. Kara plucked a pumpkin pastie from a tray and took a bite before Sam Arias handed off a bottle of butterbeer, which Kara had tried at The Three Broomsticks on her first Hogsmeade visit and loved.

 

            “Good game,” Sam said over the noise, the older girl nodding approvingly before letting out a quick laugh. “Especially knocking Lockhart off his broom like that. I’d say they wouldn’t have stood a chance without their Seeker, but he’s not a very good one anyway, so you probably evened the odds a bit in their favour.”

 

            Kara let out a quick laugh, flushing with delight. It had been a well-aimed shot on her part, the bludger striking him in his side, but she winced at the thought of him spending a night in the Hospital Wing thanks to her. Considering that he was rather average and not particularly well-liked, Kara resolved to not feel too bad about it and accepted congratulations and compliments from the rest of her House, feeling a glow of pride at being seen. Still, the whole time she thought about Lena.

 

            The week followed quickly, Kara’s schedule packed with the electives she’d chosen at the beginning of the school year. Now, halfway through her third year, she felt bogged down by her extra classes, electing to take Care of Magical Creatures and Study of Ancient Runes, writing essays about Flobberworms and the difference between different runic alphabets. Surprising to no one, Lena was a big help to Kara, despite being too young to have ever been allowed in Classroom 6A for a lesson on runes.

 

            After their meeting on Thursday night, Kara was feeling particularly peaky, her face had lost all colour and her hands developed a tremor as she held her quill. The full moon was tomorrow night and she was already feeling the characteristic effects of it but was grateful that this transformation would happen in the Forbidden Forest again. The one over Christmas, locked in a cell beneath St. Mungos, had been particularly nasty, Kara carving up her own stomach with nothing else to turn her attention to. She was beginning to worry that she’d become so scarred that she wouldn’t be able to recognise herself in the future.

 

            If Lena noticed how clammy and grey she was, she didn’t comment on it - not until Kara excused herself the excuse of a stomach ache, feigning a required trip to the Hospital Wing as an excuse to cut their studying short. Really, Kara just needed a moment’s reprieve before curfew had her return to her Common Room, with her nosy dorm mates, who’d gotten rather good at pretending she didn’t exist, but still made comments they thought she couldn’t hear.

 

            The next day was dreadful as she sat beside Querl in Ancient Runes and mistranslated half of the Futhark alphabet, mixing up Laguz and Teiwaz by sight. Kara felt so incredibly drained, a headache forming behind her eyes, that she messed up the Shrinking Solution Professor Slughorn had them brew and was saddled with an extra foot for her essay on it. 

 

            “Are you okay?” Querl asked after class, keeping his voice low as they hurried to Charms. “You look … off.”

 

            “Off?” Kara echoed, feigning ignorance as she gave him a weak smile.

 

            She watched as his features melted into a mirror of her own, a disorienting experience to witness, and took in the scattered scars and the sickly shade her skin had taken on. It was more unsettling than looking in the mirror and she quickly glanced away, hitching her bag higher on her shoulder.

 

            “I’m fine. We should get to class.”

 

            It wasn’t anything she hadn’t suffered through before, more than a dozen times by now, and she briefly thought about how this would be her life for decades to come. Well, perhaps not too many, considering everything she’d researched about lycanthropy and how it aged its victims at a rapid pace. It was an odd feeling to think that she’d go prematurely grey, that she’d be so worn down by this disease that it might shave years off her life. 

 

            Her mood was depressed for the rest of the day, and she picked at her casserole beside Mike as he regaled her with a story about the time he’d gone to a Quidditch match between the Wimbourne Wasps, who he favoured, and the Caerphilly Catapults. Kara was only half listening as her appetite evaded her, and after excusing herself from her half-eaten plate of food, she vanished outside for some fresh air and then made her way up to the Hospital Wing at the appropriate time.

 

            Following Madam Pomfrey through the tunnel, she came out beside the greenhouses, as usual, and smiled thinly at the kindly woman. As Madam Pomfrey made her way back inside the castle, Kara paused at the corner of the greenhouse and took in the view.

 

            It was early evening and the sky had turned a dusty lavender, against which the castle glowed a warm, inviting gold. She wished so desperately that she could be tucked away in her Common Room, enjoying a round of Exploding Snap with her housemates, something other than a freak . Sure, she had more friends now, perhaps could be doing that on any other night, but they wouldn’t feel the same if they knew the truth, and that was the real reason for her bitterness and isolation.

 

            The grass stretched before her as she lingered, black in the dark and damp from the cold. In the distance, the towers and jagged pine trees loomed, vicious black and sharp. The air smelled icy, like winter was lingering, even though February had arrived, and the night was gravely still as an owl hooted in the trees. 

 

            Turning, Kara made her way into the forest, a slip of a girl winding through the dark trunks as she shed her clothes along the way and shivered on her walk. Her vision was poor without glasses or wand light and she felt twigs gouge into the bottom of her feet as she felt the sickening prickle of the change creep upon her. Through the canopy of the trees, the moon, high in the sky, was white as a ghost.

 

            When she woke, it was to the pattering of rain on her reddened cheeks, her body so pale that one might’ve confused her for a corpse if there had been anyone around. Violently shivering and feeling sore and loose-limbed, Kara walked through the Forbidden Forest and gathered her strewn belongings, stumbling along as she dressed, feeling weak-kneed and in need of a good sleep.

 

            But sleep would have to wait; she’d promised Lena to meet her after breakfast to play chess, and Kara hated the idea of flaking on her. The last time she hadn’t shown up, the guilt had eaten away at her for a few days as she imagined Lena waiting for her. Instead, she made her way back to the greenhouse, where Madam Pomfrey was waiting for her in the lavender light of dawn and allowed herself to be examined and quickly patched up, a stinging salve rubbed into her cuts and gauze plastered over a cut on her ankle, perhaps from a rock, before promising to stay in bed in her dorm.

 

            Hurrying back, aching head to toe, Kara slipped into the empty bathroom ahead of most of the other Third-Year girls and teetered unsteadily as she removed the gauze from her wound and let the hot water scream over her scraped skin. She felt warmed through by the time she climbed out, dressing in a long-sleeved t-shirt that was too short at the cuff and a pair of worn jeans with her usual tennis shoes, which had started pinching her toes recently as she outgrew them.

 

            Rushing downstairs, Kara hastily made a few bacon sandwiches and wolfed down two with a cup of strong tea before making a swift exit with two more in hand. Before she could slip upstairs, a voice called out behind her and she turned in the Entrance Hall, feeling watched by the dozens of portraits as Alex walked towards her.

 

            “Hey,” Kara said, caught on the spot.

 

            “Hey. Just wanted to see how you are,” Alex awkwardly greeted her, closing the distance. “Want to step outside for a minute?”

 

            Kara hesitated, a sheepish look on her face, before suppressing a sigh and nodding. “Sure.”

 

            Her sister was looking a little more stressed these days, her chopped-off hair dishevelled and circles beneath her eyes as she struggled through the O.W.L. caseload of all Fifth-Year students. She’d chosen the subjects required to be an Auror and on the times Kara had seen her with the other Fifth-Years, they all seemed to be complaining about some essay or spell, some lesson or Professor. Kara didn’t envy any of them.

 

            They walked outside to a nearby courtyard, empty at that time in the morning. The sky was a harsh, unforgiving grey, and as Alex stopped at an open arch of the walkway, Kara mimicked her casual posture, the bricks they were leaning against numbing her shoulder as the cold seeped in.

 

            The daffodils were up now in flower beds beside the walkway, and the groups of white tulips beside them spoke of warmer weather to come, but it was a dismal day outside. It was still lightly raining, letting up from the heavier drops that had roused Kara on the forest floor, and she imagined it would be more pleasant inside by the fire.

 

            There was a sleepy air to everything, the cold blanketing a few of the lower points of the school grounds in a haze of fog. The wind whistled faintly against the castle, rattling the open doors, and the sun was buried behind the clouds as the rain misted around them, making Kara’s smaller curls stick to her cheeks. Her eyes ached and she held her cold sandwiches up before hesitating and handing one off to Alex, who glanced down and accepted it with a sigh.

 

            “Are you okay?” Kara slowly asked.

 

            “Fine,” her sister replied, mouth thinning. “It’s just O.W.L.s, you know. Well, I guess you wouldn’t but you should be glad about that.”

 

            “How’s the studying going?”

 

            Alex let out a short laugh. “Well, I might fail Potions, but other than that … not bad, I guess.”

 

            Her sister was smart, and always had perfect marks as far as Kara was aware, so she blinked in response to Alex’s comment. “Oh, uh, have you thought about a tutor, maybe?”

 

            Taking a bite of the sandwich, she raised her eyebrows as she waited for Alex to reply. “James has tried, but Potions isn’t his strong suit either. Better than me, sure, but …”

 

            “I might know someone,” Kara blurted out before she could stop herself. She swallowed the other half of her sandwich and coughed as it went down dry. “I mean- well, they’re a Second-Year-“

 

            Alex scoffed, her expression turning sour as her cheeks flushed red. “Nice. Thanks for that.”

 

            “No, no,” Kara quickly continued, nervously twirling her wand, running a thumb over the pattern of the vine wood as she cringed. “I mean … they’re really smart. Maybe they could help. They already know some N.E.W.T. stuff. Might be worth a shot?”

 

            Her voice hitched up at the end as if it was a question but Alex looked annoyed at the suggestion as she crossed her arms over her chest, her father’s jacket bunching up as she scowled. Straightening up, Kara shifted from foot to foot.

 

            “Or I could- I could help. Maybe not with the actual work, but if we studied together …”

 

            “I am studying!” Alex fiercely exclaimed, her brown eyes shining brightly as if she might cry over her frustration.

 

            “Okay, well, how about you give me your essays when you’re done and I’ll read over them? Just a fresh set of eyes. I’m actually pretty good at Potions now. Well … not yesterday but that’s because I was tired.”

 

            Sighing, Alex gestured dismissively as her mouth thinned. “Sure, Kara. You can read over them.”

 

            Perking up slightly, Kara smiled at her. “Really? Okay. Yeah, just … I don’t know, get Maximus to drop it off when you’re done.”

 

            “As opposed to … walking across to the Hufflepuff table and giving it to you?” Alex drily asked.

 

            Wincing sheepishly, Kara buried her hands in her pockets and shrugged, hunching her shoulders. “I don’t know. You never seem to … like me.”

 

            Pausing, Alex stared at her with a stiff, unreadable expression on her face before she let out a pent-up breath. Rubbing the back of her neck, Alex wrinkled her nose. 

 

            “Okay, I deserve that. Look, I know I’ve been … a bit of an ass. I’m sorry.”

 

            “It’s fine.”

 

            “No, it’s not,” Alex murmured, her cheeks reddening. “I know it hasn’t been easy for you either. Being here, with- with … everything. But I’m glad that you sit with us all. Querl really likes you, and Mike- well, Mike really likes you.”

 

            Kara wrinkled her nose slightly, her brows furrowing. “Yeah, everyone’s … nice.”

 

            “I’m just saying … you can hang out with us more. I won’t tell them about … you know.”

 

            “Right.”

 

            Nodding, Alex cleared her throat and let her gaze wander, her breath hanging in the air before her. After a moment of silence, Kara pressed her lips into a flat line and hesitated before jerking a thumb over her shoulder. “Well … I should go. I’m, uh, I’m meeting someone. Uh, study session, so …”

 

            “Right. Yeah. Freezing out here too,” Alex grumbled, hunching her shoulders and clapping Kara on the back as they turned back towards the castle. 

 

            It was perhaps the first sign of affection she’d shown Kara, and it stayed with her as she made her way to the kitchens, a tangible pressure between her shoulder blades, long after they’d parted ways. Chatting with the House Elves for a good ten minutes, Kara left the kitchens with a tea towel bursting with different biscuits, scones, muffins and pastries as she held the bundle tightly to her chest and hurried upstairs.

 

            Climbing into the secret room, she wove through the messy maze to their spot and smiled sheepishly as Lena looked up from the chessboard, where it looked like she was halfway through a game with herself.

 

            “Sorry, I know I’m late,” Kara breathlessly greeted her. “I got held up by Alex and … well, it’s a long story. I, um … overslept? But I brought food!”

 

            She brightened up as she finished her halting explanation, scurrying over to the windowsill and setting down her bundle before unknotting it, revealing the sweets inside. Sitting down beside it, she raised her eyebrows as she smiled at Lena.

 

            “None of that was at breakfast,” Lena commented, narrowing her eyes.

 

            “Perks of being so close to the kitchens,” Kara said with a sly smile as she boasted. “We know the secret way in.”

 

            Narrowing her eyes further, Lena hummed and selected a shortbread biscuit from the pile. “I’ll bring tea next time,” she said as she took a bite and brushed crumbs off the lap of her green plaid skirt.

 

            She was wearing another one of her black turtlenecks, perfectly tailored, and shirt white socks with loafers. It seemed antiquated compared to Kara’s comfortably worn jeans and t-shirt and the sweater she’d thrown on top, but from what she’s gathered of Lena’s upbringing, a Pureblood family with money and an estate, it was also fitting.

 

            “Where are you going to get tea from if you don’t know how to get into the kitchens?”

 

            “Who said I didn’t know how to get into the kitchens?” Lena countered with an arched eyebrow.

 

            “Do you?”

 

            She hesitated and sagged slightly. “No, but we get a fresh pot of tea every morning in my House.”

 

            Kara spluttered, “really?”

 

            “Mhm. I guess a House full of tradition has its perks. Shall we play?”

 

            Lena explained the rules to her and Kara quickly picked them up, the two of them going through a rudimentary game as Lena clicked her tongue and groaned as Kara fell into obvious traps. They talked and ate as they played, Kara reiterating school gossip that she’d heard, to Lena’s indifference, while Lena filled her in on decades of history her brother has passed on to her.

 

            Rain battered the window pane and the morning wore on, Kara looking worse for wear but managing for the sake of the company. She would’ve liked to be tucked up in bed, or perhaps sitting on one of the sagging sofas or moth-eaten armchairs, the soot-stained brick hearth keeping her warm as she rested, but sitting in a damp, abandoned secret room with Lena was worth more than any comfort.

 

            That line of thinking only made Kara worry that all the lies she kept hidden on the dark side of her heart would one day be washed into the open. These lies, her past, always kept her on guard around everyone, but she slipped up so often around Lena that she was terrified of the inevitable day that her friend figured out just what kind of monster she’d been consorting with. It sat like a stone in the pit of Kara’s stomach as the day dragged on towards lunch.

 

            “Hey, Lena?” Kara murmured after prodding her knight to E5, eliciting a hum of acknowledgement in response. “Do you- do you think we’d still be friends even if things were … different between us?”

 

            “Different how?” Lena distractedly asked, still eyeing the board for her next move.

 

            Licking her lips, Kara floundered for a moment. “Say … you know what they’re writing in the papers? About that new … Dark Lord? Well, apparently he’s a Pureblood fanatic and he’s getting lots of supporters who think the same thing. What if- what if that was us?”

 

            Looking up, her mouth a hard line and her stare brittle, Lena stiffened. “You mean what if I believed the same things as the rest of Slytherin?”

 

            With a sheepish, pained look on her face, Kara shrugged half-heartedly. “Sure. I mean, I don’t think you do, I just-“

 

            “I’m a half-blood,” Lena interrupted her, her forehead creasing with a solemn look of confusion. “My mum and dad aren’t but … my mum that died was Muggleborn, so … why would I think that?”

 

            That caught Kara off-guard and she faltered for a moment. “I don’t think you do,” she reiterated. “It’s just … what if there was something like that where we were on opposite sides?”

 

            “So … like the house rivalry?” Lena asked, raising an eyebrow.

 

            “Kind of. What if it was more serious than that? And you didn’t want to be friends with me anymore?”

 

            Lena was silent for a moment before she let out a heavy sigh and let forth a torrent of pent-up words, as if she’d been waiting for this moment. “Everyone here thinks that Slytherins are all bad people because most of us care about stuff like- like blood purity and we all love dark curses, but that’s not true. At least, I don’t think so, and wouldn’t I know? I’m one of them. But people still think that, even though they’re the ones who bully me sometimes.”

 

            “People bully you?” Kara softly asked, her eyes widening a fraction as a jolt of objection ran through her.

 

            “It doesn’t matter. Good and bad people are found everywhere, aren’t they? Not just in one place. So I don’t think it really matters if someone is good or bad, only if they’re trying to be better. Those girls that were picking on you last year … are they bad people?”

 

            Kara’s face screwed up as she considered it. “No. I don’t think so. I think … they just think it’s funny, and when they get older they won’t be like that anymore.”

 

            “Would you forgive them?”

 

            “Of course,” Kara quickly replied. In fact, she hadn’t ever held a real grudge against them.

 

            “Because you know that they’ve tried to become better.”

 

            “Sure,” she murmured, “but what if there’s no getting better?”

 

            Cocking her head to the side, Lena gave her such a scrutinising look before she smiled softly. “I don’t think you could ever do something so bad that I wouldn’t want to be your friend.”

 

            “Neither could you.”

 

            Giving her a fleeting smile, Lena nodded and looked back down at the chessboard. Kara sat there and watched her, dim sunlight filtering through the rainy windowpane, and she felt so at peace watching her. She believed Lena when she said there was nothing that could make them not friends, but she believed that opinion was born out of ignorance of the truth and resolved not to hold it against her when things came to light.

 

            For now, Kara was content to stay within that bubble of peace with her friend, taking in the fine, elegant features of her face, her delicately boned hands as she touched her slender fingers to her lips, considering her next move in the pale February daylight of a rainy morning. 

 

            And if Mike really liked her, she really really liked Lena.

 

 

            Lena sat in the shade of an elm tree set back from the banks of the Black Lake, a worn diary in her lap and library books scattered around her. She smoothed down the page, staring at the loose sheet of parchment with a lunar chart on it, and dipped her quill into the ink as she shaded in the full moon. It was partially for her Astronomy homework, but Lena had been suspicious since last November, and rifled through the other loose sheets before glancing down at her diary, where she’d made meticulous notes on lycanthropy.

 

            Glancing up, she squinted at the glare on the surface of the lake. It was early March and the soft afternoon light simmered on the lawn, students scattered around as they enjoyed the brief sunny spell after so little sunshine in recent weeks. Now that the shallows of the lake were thawing, the water wasn’t as pretty as it had been in the middle of winter. The banks were muddy and soggy, the smell of decomposing plants on the breeze, but everyone milled about on the damp grass, watching owls swoop overhead with ravens and sparrows, leaning against tree trunks as they performed small spells, or strolling along the paths, their robes and cloaks brushing over the dirty ground.

 

            Her eyes instinctively found Kara, sitting with a bigger group of friends than Lena was used to seeing her with. There was Querl Dox, his appearance shifting with encouragement and loud laughter, and Alex, Kara’s sister with her chestnut hair, so starkly different from her in looks, sitting on the opposite side of the sprawling circle beside a girl with dark skin and hair. There were a few others there too, a mix of robes and ages, but emerald green obviously absent. 

 

            Kara looked washed of all colour, her skin a shade paler than usual, her scars even whiter against her cheeks, her chin, her curls falling in her face in her usual effort to hide her face. Lena’s stare was scrutinising as she considered her theory, adding up the fact that Kara always seemed sick around the full moon, that she showed up with new scars after the holidays, and any number of hidden ones beneath her clothes too. Brow puckering with a thoughtful look, Lena tapped the end of her quill against her chin and watched her closely.

 

            Everything she’d read about werewolves was in direct contrast to who Kara was. She wasn’t dangerous, she wasn’t monstrous, she wasn’t some violent witch who wanted bloodshed. Kara was the most gentle person she’d ever met, filled with so much suppressed sadness that only her pale eyes revealed the depths of her feelings, and Lena finally felt like she understood why.  

 

            They’d been friends for a year and a half now, and Lena’s suspicions had finally grown too much for her to ignore it as she’d wondered over Kara’s bouts of illness, her excuses easily disproved as Lena stopped by the Hospital Wing to sit behind the screen and play Exploding Snap with her, only to find her somewhere else, her growing scars perhaps the most suspicious of all. It had taken all but a few trips to the library to scour the shelves for healing books on scars, detailing which ones couldn’t be fully healed, including those of a Werewolf scratch. From there, Lena had gone down a rabbit hole of numerous theories, crossing off each one until lycanthropy was left staring her in the face. But she wasn’t mad, wasn’t angry that Kara had kept it from her; she was only sad for her friend and resolved to keep her discovery to herself.

 

            As she thought that, still staring at Kara, Lena jolted as their eyes met across the lawn, watching the sun wink on Kara’s glasses, although she was undoubtedly staring right back at her. She didn’t wave at Kara, and Kara didn’t wave at her, but there was a tense moment of staring as the secret knowledge of their friendship bridged the space between them. Lena had to admit, it was rather thrilling to be noticed by her, seen by her when she ordinarily snuck about with her invisibility cloak on, watching Kara from afar as she wandered the grounds unobserved. That was how Lena had first found the Thestrals in the Forbidden Forest.

 

            A breath of wind caught at a page of Lena’s diary and broke her stare as she dropped her gaze, smoothing it back down with a flicker of impatience. When she looked back up, Kara’s attention had shifted to whatever the Hufflepuff boy was saying. A short while later, Lena packed up her things and retreated inside when the day cooled off, clouds sweeping in with the threat of rain, heading up to the library with her stack of borrowed books to return, confident in her theory of Kara’s injuries. 

 

            She returned them to the elderly librarian, who always gave her a funny look at the topics Lena borrowed and, more often, the frequency of her borrowing. After dropping off her returns, Lena turned to the voluminous stacks stretching as far as she could see in every direction and felt something akin to being at home. Here the air was as it should be, dry and edged with dust and leather and paper, the smell of ink clinging to the pages of the old books she cracked open, greedily drinking in the words filling them. Lena was hungry for knowledge, fuelling her ambition as she passed her days at Hogwarts with endless hours of reading.

 

            Making her way to the section on curses and the counter-spells for them, she pulled a book from the shelf and walked through to her favourite nook, a leather armchair so worn and cracked that it sagged in the lamplight. She felt distracted though, her mind turning to Kara as it so often did, and she spent a good fifteen minutes breathing in the smell of the place, something musty and indistinct that was simply time, before she gathered a stack of textbooks on her mental list and left the library behind.

 

            On Tuesday, after classes and dinner, Lena made her way up to the Astronomy Tower, wariness prickling up her spine as she thought of coming face to face with Kara again, knowing all that she did. Lena was unusually quiet as she padded through the room, lingering in the shadows for a moment as she took in the sight of Kara, illuminated by a few floating balls of light and pilfered candles as she frowned down at a roll of parchment. With her hunched shoulders and the way her hair curled around her face, at the nape of her neck where it escaped her bun, she looked small and so young and Lena’s chest ached dully for a moment. 

 

            She went unnoticed until Kara looked up, rubbing at the scar on her chin as she frowned and looked to the spot where Lena was standing as if impatiently awaiting her arrival. Only to find her there, watching her. Startling at the sight of her, and then flushing at the thought of being observed, as Lena likewise flushed at being caught staring, Kara smiled unevenly.

 

            “Oh. Hey. I didn’t hear you coming.”

 

            Lena hesitated a moment at the sheepish softness in Kara’s voice and a small smile twitched her lips in response as she stepped forward, lurching towards their spot and drawing up short. She faltered for a moment before giving Kara a quizzical smile, her green eyes clouded with confusion.

 

            “Hi,” Lena murmured, slowly sinking down onto the stone ledge. 

 

            She smoothed her hands over the pleated grey skirt and pulled her robes tighter around herself. They seemed to swallow her, pitch-black against her pale skin, in contrast to Kara’s washed-out ones, which were a deep grey after a year and a half of wear. Swallowing, Lena studied her closely, noting the circles beneath her eyes, lavender half-moons that made her look tired and gentle as she smiled shyly.

 

            “Hi,” Kara echoed again.

 

            Lena could tell what kind of day someone had had just by the way they said hello. She’d grown up in a house where understanding the tone of someone’s voice had meant suffering the anger or impatient frustration of one parent or another, had meant knowing when to tread lightly and when to make herself scarce. From Kara’s weary voice, Lena could tell it had been an exhausting day, or rather an exhausting night, the full moon high in the sky. She wanted to ask what Kara had done, where she went on those nights, but she just stared at her, looking for new scars, for any signs beyond the ragged look of a sleepless night.

 

            “You look tired,” she quietly commented.

 

            Kara hummed, nudging her glasses up to rub at her eyes. “Mm, I didn’t get much sleep last night. Um … Eve’s cat kept playing with my bed drapes.”

 

            “Oh. Annoying.”

 

            “Hey, can you do me a favour?” Kara quickly changed the topics, holding up the roll of parchment and smiling crookedly. “Could you give this a read-over?”

 

            Brow creasing with confusion, as this was their usual routine, and she would hardly have called it a favour, Lena plucked it from Kara’s hand. At a quick glance, it was written in a different hand entirely and Lena looked up, raising her eyebrows in a silent question.

 

            “Alex is … struggling a little. Her O.W.L.s are coming up and she’s worried about her Potions marks. I told her I knew someone but … I think she thought I was making fun of her when I said it was a Second-Year, but that’s because she doesn’t know you. I told her I’d take a look at it. Not sure why she trusted me .”

 

            Lena let out a quick laugh and scanned the essay, humming slightly as she dipped her quill into some ink and pulled a sheet of Kara’s blank parchment towards her. As she scanned Alex’s essay, she made notes and changes on the blank sheet and then handed it to Kara with instructions on what to tell her sister to improve upon. Kara blinked and then smiled brightly at her.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Nodding, Lena proceeded as usual, poring over her work as she briskly completed her essays and then turned to more interesting and complex topics, years ahead of what should have been her skill level. And yet, for all her knowledge of the theoretical side of magic, Lena could put it into effect as well, performing the spells Kara was learning quicker than her friend could. It wasn’t that Kara was a poor student - not after settling in and assimilating to her coursework - but rather Lena was exceptional because she wasn’t allowed to be anything else.

 

            Kara left just before curfew, looking like she could’ve fallen asleep tucked up against the window, undisturbed, and Lena stayed a while longer, curfew coming and going and her invisibility cloak guiding her safely back down to the Slytherin Common Room without incident. A few of her housemates cast her curious glances as she passed by, the aloof Luthor who didn’t have the time of day for anyone that wasn’t made of paper - or, she secretly thought, was a Hufflepuff Werewolf by the name of Kara - and went to the neat corner of her dormitory to work late at her desk, the oil in her lamp waning as the hour crept towards midnight and she filled the dark dorm with the sound of her scratching quill and rustling pages.

 

            Rising early the next morning, Lena fed Morrigan a slice of toast after her owl had dropped off that morning’s copy of The Daily Prophet , another article detailing the deaths of a few Muggles and this Dark Lord her brother had become enthralled by. It was happening with increasing frequency and weekly articles about his assaults, where before it had been more sporadic with the rare snippet near the back of the newspaper. Now, he was making the front page, had whole sections dedicated to attacks, and Lena wasn’t quite so distant from the rest of her House to not hear the whispers of brothers and sisters and parents throwing their lot in with him. Of course, there were those who were quiet and nervous about the news too, similar to how Lena felt as she was struck with a helpless weight in the pit of her stomach.

 

            Tucking her newspaper into her bag, she pondered over that article in particular with a furrowed look on her face, her attention drifting around the Great Hall. After the library, it was the biggest room at Hogwarts with long oak tables running from wall to wall, the high-pitched, barrel-vaulted enchanted ceiling echoing with the noise of laughter and conversation, clinking cutlery and the frenzied cry of swooping owls. Arched windows on either side let in the morning sunlight and the Professors lined the long table on the raised dais at the far end of the room.

 

            Later that evening, at eight o’clock on the dot, Lena was back in the Great Hall, the space emptied of the long tables and benches to make space for the padded mats and the long platform for the Duelling Club. Lena had joined at the start of the school year at her mother’s insistence and brother’s encouragement and had immediately been paired with opponents years ahead of her in size and skill. Still, without fail, she’d managed to win every duel so far and when Professor Flitwick, who boasted of his days as a duelling champion, bid them pair up this week, Lena hung back to wait for a partner to reveal themselves. 

 

            “Shall we, Luthor?” asked a Fifth-Year from her House. 

 

            He was tall and broad-shouldered, his brown skin and dark hair flopping in his face. He gave her a charming grin and raised his eyebrows, reaching up to push his hair out of his face. Jack Spheer. Lena knew him - everyone did, but it was especially hard not to in her own House. He’d been made Prefect this year and his badge glinted on his robes.

 

            Glancing up at him, feeling slightly dwarfed, she tersely nodded and gripped her wand in hand, following him to an empty space in the candlelight of the Great Hall. Jack’s face crumpled with a bewildered look and then he let out a laugh.

 

            “You might try talking, you know.”

 

            “I do,” Lena murmured, not defensively, just mildly surprised by the comment.

 

            He hummed and brandished his wand, eyebrows rising. “Ready?”

 

            Nodding again, Lena bowed as she held her wand up before her and then elegantly swished it away. As Jack mirrored her movements, Lena considered which spell to use before making the correct motion as she let the word spill from her tongue. “Stupefy!”

 

            Jack’s surprise was etched on his face as he keeled over, stunned. There was a lull in the room as the nearby students cast Lena stricken looks, confused as to how a scrawny Second-Year had one of her House’s star pupils laid out flat within mere seconds. Flushing as she watched tiny Professor Flitwick walk over to them, Lena fiddled with her wand - ivy and unicorn hair - with an anxious edge to her expression.

 

            “Dear me,” Professor Flitwick tutted, “poor boy should have used a Shield Charm.”

 

            He uttered Rennervate to awaken Jack, who frowned, puzzled, as he rubbed at the back of his head, still sprawled on the stone floor of the empty Great Hall. 

 

            “On your feet,” Professor Flitwick instructed him. “And might I suggest landing on one of the mats next time?”

 

            “I’ll try to have better aim next time I get stunned, Professor,” Jack replied, somewhat dryly and unnoticed by the tiny Professor as he picked himself up.

 

            “Quite right, Spheer,” Flitwick nodded, his eyes darting over to Lena. “You’re lucky Miss Luthor didn’t cast a stronger spell. I say, it’s rather remarkable she stunned you to begin with, yes.”

 

            The last part seemed a derailing of his own thoughts and Lena shifted uneasily as she waited for the attention to divert from her. At Flitwick’s instruction to carry on, she looked at Jack, feeling sheepish even if her impassive expression said otherwise.

 

            “Is that what you’re learning in those books you always have a nose stuck in?” Jack asked, his lips twisting with a smile as his brown eyes shone.

 

            “How do you know I always have my nose in a book?” Lena countered, her small voice haughty as she clutched her wand tightly.

 

            He gestured vaguely, “everyone does. It’s half of what Slytherin talks about. Lex Luthor’s little sister finally makes it to Hogwarts and blanks everyone dead the entire year.”

 

            Flushing, Lena ducked her head down. “Yes, that’s what’s in my books. Some of it, anyway.”

 

            “You know, you might try making a friend or two,” he suggested.

 

            “Maybe I already have one.”

 

            “Perhaps so, but it’s handy to have more in a pinch, I dare say. Besides, we’ve all been watching you duel for months now and we’re dying to know how you got so good. Did your brother give you private lessons?”

 

            Lena wanted to laugh at the suggestion, and not least of all because she couldn’t do magic outside of Hogwarts. The only private lesson she’d been given involved questions that felt like an interrogation and a Black Quill to gouge a reminder in her skin. She loved her brother but he only ever seemed to distract her, which only led to punishments for her - only her, never him.

 

            “No. I taught myself the spells,” she murmured.

 

            “Right,” he slowly replied, slightly sceptical. “Andrea Rojas bet me five galleons I couldn’t convince you to come and sit with us one evening. So, how about it?”

 

            Lena’s eyes drifted across the room to the Fourth-Year duelling Veronica Sinclair, a Third-Year. She knew practically all of her House by sight - or the ones from Pureblood families, at any rate, after years of hearing her family discuss who was who over dinner - and Andrea Rojas was immediately recognisable, pretty in an effortless way, her eyes a piercing shade of blue, not entirely different to Kara’s.

 

            “Maybe,” Lena evasively replied before they resumed their duelling.

 

            It wasn’t that she had anything against them in particular, only that Lena’s sole interest in Hogwarts was learning all that she could and limiting her distractions. Kara was already more than she’d bargained for, and Lena wasn’t sure she wanted to have other friends to eclipse the friendship she already had. Not to mention the fact that she had to put some stock in the nasty comments people said about her House, with the likes of Malfoy’s and Black’s in the upperclassmen, who bullied and looked down upon the other Houses.

 

            She followed the stream of Slytherin’s back to their Common Room and returned Jack’s nod as they parted ways. After that, she seemed to see him everywhere, greeting her with a passing nod, a regular duelling partner on Wednesday nights, and lounging with a circle of friends, all of them with an air of nonchalant superiority and wealth. She caught a few of them watching her on occasion as if they were waiting for something, expecting something of her. They never approached her though, and weeks slipped by, the end of the school year rapidly approaching as Lena furiously studied for exams she didn’t really have to study for at all.

 

            On top of that, she was helping Kara study for her own exams, as well as editing Alex’s Potions essays, and, when her marks started rising, other essays Kara sheepishly brought her as well. Lena didn’t mind it so much; she viewed it as studying for her future coursework, learning about Transfiguration spells that she hadn’t covered yet and Potions she’d only read about in passing. 

 

            On the last day of term, Lena sat in the Astronomy Tower as night lingered in the early hours of the morning. There was no moon and the stars were painfully bright, but the pain of knowing she’d be back home tomorrow was worse. She was drinking burnt black tea alone, the teapot she’d smuggled out of her bedroom steaming beside her with the fresh pot that had arrived on the tray beside her bed. Curfew was still in effect and Lena had crept upstairs beneath her invisibility cloak as she sought out the comforting solitude of the tower.

 

            The weather had warmed considerably over the last few weeks, damp spring suddenly turning to early summer. The Giant Squid could be seen snatching toast tossed by students from the surface of the Black Lake, the sun sparkling off the still surface as the surrounding mountains and forest bloomed with greenery and lingering snow caps melted off. Lena spent more than one day sneaking into the Forbidden Forest with her cloak on, when Kara had sent an owl with an apology that she couldn’t make it on Saturday for chess because of Quidditch practice, or was visiting Hogsmeade with her new friends. Amidst the Thestrals, Lena would read and enjoy the cool dampness of the forest, the smell of foliage and plants reminding her of the distant memory of her mother as she stared at the skeletal horses and felt the hollow pang in her chest.

 

            She didn’t get to see Kara before the holidays and spent the train ride home sitting in the end compartment with most of the Slytherins, tucked in the corner at a table, while two First-Years swapped Chocolate Frog cards and cast her nervous glances. Jack had caught her eye and smiled, raising his eyebrows invitingly, but Lena had turned her attention back to her book and tuned out the hum of conversation and laughter as last-minute spells went wrong, pranks were played and friends spent the last few hours enjoying each other’s company. And for all her talk of secrecy, Lena ached for the chance to sit with Kara, playing chess and sharing sweets, talking about their plans for the summer as Lena dreaded hers and wondered at Kara’s upcoming transformations. Instead, she sat alone and remained content with the mere idea of what it would be like to have a friend she didn’t have to hide.

 

            Lillian was waiting for her at Platform Nine and Three-Quarters when the Hogwarts Express screeched into King’s Cross, billowing clouds of white steam filling the air platform as students spilt out, dragging trunks and owls and cats with them. Lena followed suit, struggling with her trunk until someone materialised at her side, dressed in a black shirt and pressed pants, a black cat nestled in his arms. Jack gave her a small smile.

 

            “Allow me,” he said, slipping past Lena and lifting the end of her trunk with ease, lowering it down onto the platform.

 

            “Thanks.”

 

            “Have a good summer,” he said, before hauling his own trunk off and vanishing without another word.

 

            Dragging her trunk and the cage that held Morrigan, Lena sought out her mother, who was a dozen feet away, looking impatient and haughty, standing a head above most people on the platform, who gave her a wide berth. Lena visibly seemed to shrink in on herself as she made her way towards her mother, who blinked as she caught sight of her daughter.

 

            “Don’t slouch,” Lillian greeted her in a clipped tone, waving a hand at Lena’s trunk to make it drift behind her as she strode towards the fireplaces to Floo back home.

 

            Lena dutifully followed after her and spiralled through a dozen hearths before neatly stepping out into a sitting room in her house, a sense of vertigo staying with her for a moment. Hope was there, brushing soot off Lena’s black clothes before Lillian appeared behind her and was given the same service. 

 

            “Trunk. Upstairs,” Lillian curtly commanded the House Elf, giving Lena a dismissive look. “Take the owl too.”

 

            “Right away, mistress,” Hope squeaked, making herself scarce.

 

            Lena swallowed thickly and turned, hoping to escape the room with its sumptuous jade lounges, emerald rugs and bottle green vases filled with fresh flowers that filled the air with a cloyingly sweet smell. “Not you.”

 

            At her mother’s impatient tone, Lena turned back around, clasping her hands before her as she made herself meet her mother’s eyes, narrow shoulders squared and jaw clenched against the tremor in her chin. Walking over to the decanters and pouring herself some Firewhiskey, Lillian gracefully sank down onto a sofa and snapped her fingers, gesturing for Lena to stand before her.

 

            “What ingredients are used to make Felix Felicis?”

 

            “Ashwinder egg … um-”

 

            “Don’t say um.”

 

            “Murtlap tentacles … squill bulb …”

 

            “And?”

 

            Swallowing as she balled her hands into fists, Lena’s eyes shuttered and she suppressed a weary sigh, already tired from a long day and just wanting dinner and to go to bed. “I don’t know.”

 

            “You don’t know?” her mother echoed, her voice smooth and mocking before she let out a quiet laugh and clicked her tongue.

 

            “I’m tired, mother,” Lena murmured. 

 

            “Tired? From sitting on a train all day? One might think you would’ve used that time wisely-”

 

            “I did.”

 

            Pressing her fingertips to her forehead as she sighed heavily, Lillian set her glass down and then gave her daughter a frosty look. “You never make it easy , Lena. Do you?”

 

            It was rhetorical but Lena had to bite off the urge to stand up for herself as she wilted, hanging her head as she fiddled with her fingers. It wasn’t that she was particularly shy, or even quiet by nature, only that Lena had grown up making herself as small and unobtrusive as possible, so the mere idea of her standing up to her mother was terrifying. Lena wasn’t sure what punishment it would enact, only that it wouldn’t be very pleasant. 

 

            “Look at me when I speak to you,” Lillian said, her voice softening before she made a small sound of objection at the back of her throat. “Actually, don’t bother. Just get the quill.”

Chapter 10

            Kara entered her fourth year at Hogwarts with greyer robes, worn thin in places, and a few more scars, mostly hidden beneath her uniform, where she’d rent the smooth skin of her torso and arms and legs. She’d grown a bit over the summer and had a tan from painting the garden fence for Eliza and spending long days dozing in sunny fields as she tried to spot magical creatures. 

 

            Alex had gotten a job that summer at Quality Quidditch Supplies in Diagon Alley, selling broom polish and shirts for the national Quidditch teams to the witches and wizards that filtered through, which meant that Kara didn’t see much of her. When Alex was home, the small cottage was filled with the sound of the rock bands she favoured, played on her prized gramophone, and she sometimes brought home groceries from Tut’s Nuts or bargains she found at the markets at The Harpy’s Bazar . On the days she wasn’t home, Kara would borrow Maximum from his perch where he dozed and scrawled secret letters to Lena, bidding the owl to cover the distance to Ireland quick enough for her sister to not notice he’d been gone. 

 

            Sometimes he brought a letter back with him, tied to his ankle and without any names attached to it. Just a few sentences that overflowed with loneliness and longing, of that sad, aching way Lena had of speaking, her voice trembling with forced bravery that could’ve seen the small Slytherin girl in Gryffindor under different circumstances. Kara’s answers always spoke of how soon they’d be back at Hogwarts; Lena wasn’t the only one who ached for the castle, especially after the horrors of the full moon that left Kara tearfully wishing for the sprawling Forbidden Forest, where she’d be free to run instead of mutilating herself in a cell.

 

            The weeks dragged by and then the start of the term arrived suddenly, with a flurry of shopping at Diagon Alley, bartering for the best deals and combing through the secondhand stores for their textbooks and supplies. Kara inherited Alex’s textbooks and they watched Eliza scrounge together sickles and knuts for everything else. Kara’s stomach twisted with guilt at the added burden her adoption had put on her adoptive mother, who never did anything but make Kara feel welcome. 

 

            It had been different that summer, with just the two of them most days, Kara giving Eliza a hand with the plants that now positively overflowed the small house and the garden. She didn’t call her mom but there was a maternal warmth to Eliza that Kara was now realising Alura had lacked and she felt shy and uncertain around her, unused to the spontaneous hugs, the reassuring hand on her back as Eliza set a plate of bacon and eggs down in front of her for breakfast, the way she’d cup Kara’s face in her hands and give her a searching look after a full moon, tutting at the dark circles and pale complexion, smoothing her thumb over the silvery scars. Kara was getting used to this being her family now, but she still had nightmares.

 

            It was July and unusually warm as she stood in the garden, tanned and wearing a thin vest that showed the crisscrossing pale scars on her arms as she watered Eliza’s Dirigible bushes, her thumb over the end of the garden hose as she directed sheets of water over the leaves of the plants. Bees wove from flower to flower and Kara squinted as the sun winked on the lenses of her glasses, shading her eyes as she kept an eye out for Maximus returning with a letter for her, or perhaps Lena’s black owl, Morrigan, who occasionally brought a response.

 

            It was the last week of school and she’d finished all of her homework and was somewhat anxious to get back to Hogwarts. She’d become comfortable in Falmouth, for the weeks she spent there while not at school, but Kara felt like she was constantly reminded of her affliction there - Eliza worrying, days and nights spent at St. Mungos, Alex’s awkward attempts at friendship. At Hogwarts, nobody knew, aside from her sister and the teachers, and she was an outcast in a different way, of her own design. 

 

            “Hey.”

 

            She lowered her head and turned, watching as Alex pulled the back door shut, returning from a day of work. Directing the stream of water, Kara smiled slightly, her eyes bluer against the recent tan she’d gained over the holidays, trying to stave off the sickly pallor lycanthropy instilled her with.

 

            “Hey.”

 

            “Mom said you’re going to burn if you stay out here any longer.”

 

            Glancing down at her shoulders, which were starting to turn a little pink, Kara shrugged indifferently. She liked to stay outside and wait for letters, the slim hope of it keeping her busy as she tried to pretend she was outside for some other purpose; bringing a book with her, rereading that old passage from Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them, watering the plants or kicking a ball at the fence. She was on the cusp of fifteen and bored, the weeks spent at the cottage broken up by her brief stays at the hospital, stiff and exhausted.

 

            “I’ll be inside soon.”

 

            “Alright. I bought a new record as well, if you wanted to listen.”

 

            “Sure.”

 

            Alex lingered a second, studying her. “Can I ask you something?”

 

            Turning, the stream of water changing its trajectory, Kara raised her eyebrows expectedly. “Yeah.”

 

            “Who are the letters from? I mean, I know it’s not Querl, or Mike or anyone else’s owls. You’re not very good at sneaking around.”

 

            Kara’s cheeks flooded with red and she cleared her throat as she rubbed the back of her neck. Walking over to the tap on the wall, she turned it until the stream of water guttered and then stopped, coiling the hose neatly and then setting it on the grass before she turned to Alex.

 

            “Have you read them?”

 

            “No,” Alex quickly exclaimed. “I mean … Maximus brought me this one this morning and it didn’t have your name on it, so … yeah, I read it.”

 

            She pulled a folded note out of her pocket and handed it to Kara, who quickly snatched it from her. Turning around, she unfolded it with clumsy fingers, her cheeks flaming as she hunched over the words neatly scrawled in Lena’s penmanship.

 

I can’t wait for school to start again. I haven’t been allowed out much - my mum sets me more homework than all of our Professors combined - and I miss going to our spot together. I’ve been reading The Daily Prophet a lot and things are getting worse. My brother talks about it all the time and I don’t like the idea of a war but that’s what he says is going to happen if he doesn’t get what he wants. My mum tells me it’s for my own good that I’m stuck inside studying all the time, and that if I misbehave the Dark Lord will come and punish me. I know she’s lying but he sounds scary. Have you read about him? He’s got a lot of people following him and they’re getting these marks put on their arms and hurting Muggles. I’ll be glad to be at Hogwarts again soon where it’s safe and I can beat you at chess. I’ll see you next week.

 

            She hadn’t signed it but Kara knew her writing well and her mouth twitched slightly at the corners as she quickly folded it back up. She shoved it into the pockets of her jeans and cleared her throat.

 

            “Is it your boyfriend?”

 

            “No,” Kara quickly replied, her blush deepening. “It’s … a friend.”

 

            Giving her a droll look, Alex raised her eyebrows. “You can tell me, you know.”

 

            “I don’t have a boyfriend.”

 

            “Well, Mike likes you.”

 

            Gesturing helplessly, Kara spluttered, “and?”

 

            “I don’t know, Kara,” Alex wearily sighed, “maybe you should go to Madam Puddifoot’s with him to drink tea. Do something normal . ”

 

            “Normal?”

 

            “Yeah, normal. Stop letting your, you know, thing get in the way of things. You’re almost fifteen and you spend most of your time cooped up somewhere studying . It’s sad.”

 

            Crossing her wiry arms over her chest, Kara scowled. “Not all of my time; I have Quidditch.”

 

            “I said most ,” Alex pointed out. “You should join the Duelling Club this year. I’ll teach you how to disarm people; I’m getting good at it now. No one will mess with you then. Maybe you’ll come out of your shell more.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Kara hummed dubiously and Alex put an arm around her shoulders, slowing her escape back to the house as she led them at a leisurely pace. “Just think about it. And you should invite your friend to sit with us as well. No one will bite. They sound kind of … sad.”

 

            Letting out a rough bark of laughter, Kara couldn’t help but smile at the thought of Lena sitting with their friends, out of place in her Slytherin robes and her solemn demeanour. She was so serious all the time, always had her nose in a book and ink on the tips of her fingers, and she would be starkly out of place with the rowdy group of teenagers from other Houses. 

 

            “I don’t think she’d want to.”

 

            “Oh, she , is it?” Alex said with intrigue.

 

            Gently shoving her, Kara scoffed and grabbed the door handle, pulling it open to the aroma of a chicken roasting in the oven. Eliza was in the living room, watering the plants on the windowsill and mantelpiece while the table bore signs of her packaging up her wares to be sold to the shops she catered to. Alex lowered her voice but pressed on.

 

            “It’s not one of those losers in your dorm, is it?”

 

            “No.”

 

            “Are they still giving you trouble?”

 

            Wincing slightly at the memory of Lena hexing Belinda, Kara shook her head. They’d mostly left her alone after that, blanking her dead instead of the taunts and muffled laughter behind their hands, and she was happier for it. 

 

            “No, they’re … fine.”

 

            “Good. Come on; come and listen to my album.”

 

            Sighing, Kara hesitated in the kitchen and then followed her sister upstairs to their shared bedroom, the small space cluttered with their belongings. She was barefoot, as was her preference, and the soles of her feet were tinged green with grass stains as she sprawled out on her narrow bed, shoving aside a worn shirt she’d borrowed from Alex and a few school books.

 

            Days later, they traded the unusual arrangement of sharing a room for the familiarity of their dorms with the girls they spent the majority of the year living with. Dressed in her worn robes and sitting beside Mike on the Hogwarts Express, she left Eliza behind with a hug and the promise to write and looked forward to seeing Lena again, a handful of letters tucked safely in her case for safekeeping. 

 

            She went straight to the Astronomy Tower after dinner and the Sorting Ceremony, listening to Dumbledore’s solemn speech about dire times and the importance of staying safe. Kara didn’t know it then, but this was the year where students would be pulled out of class, informed of the deaths of family members as the war progressed.
