It all happened at a distance, so removed from Kara’s life that if it wasn’t for The Daily Prophet and whispered rumours flying from student to student via letters received from home, she wouldn’t have known it was even happening. Even in Cornwall, they’d seemed so removed from it all, away from Diagon Alley and the Ministry of Magic and the centres of social and political power in the Wizarding World.

 

            Lena wasn’t in their secret room when she got there though and disappointment deflated Kara as time slipped past and it was evident she wouldn’t be meeting her. Instead, she went upstairs, to the top floor, for a little while, enjoying the deep blue as night fell with no moon. Those were the nights she loved the most, where she didn’t even have to see the stages at all, although the new moon meant she was halfway through the cycle, and that was its own kind of torment. The stars were painfully bright and Kara stood at the top of the Astronomy Tower and breathed in the frigid air of autumn in Scotland.             

 

            Slipping back downstairs before curfew, Kara changed into her pyjamas and went to sleep early, slipping back into the routine of Hogwarts as if she’d never left. When she woke, it was to the expectations of a Fourth-Year, with a full schedule and Quidditch tryouts looming before her. Still half-asleep, she shovelled her breakfast into her mouth, trying to wake up with a cup of tea and pumpkin juice.

 

            “Alright, Danvers?” Mike asked, swinging his leg over the bench and sitting heavily beside her. 

 

            He gave her a crooked smile and Kara returned it, nodding as she took a bite of her toast. Loading up his plate, Mike chatted away about his holidays and Quidditch and how he was trying to bulk up and his O.W.L.s starting this year and Kara listened with polite interest. They were friends, of a sort, by extension of the other people they were friends with, but Kara didn’t like how everyone kept making comments about Mike liking her. Truthfully, she didn’t like him like that but she was content enough to talk Quidditch with him, both of them hoping to make it back onto the team again this year.

 

            She had class afterwards, heading straight to History of Magic and scratching down the odd comment from Binns as everyone struggled to stay awake. Kara already knew that would be the class she struggled with most this year, the early lectures from the old ghost enough to send anyone to sleep. Her next class was Ancient Runes and she fumbled through the phonetic ties of the Futhark alphabet to the current spells they used, and how it all tied in with Latin, which Kara admittedly wasn’t very well-versed in. The rest of her day passed by in a similar fashion, all of the teachers jumping straight into the Fourth-Year curriculum with no pause for the students to try and settle back into school.

 

            By the time dinner arrived, Kara was tired and hungry, filling her plate with an assortment of vegetables and cuts of meat and then finishing off with treacle tart. Seemingly in a rush, she rose from the table the moment she’d cleared her plate and left the Great Hall, sneaking upstairs instead of down to the dungeons to her Common Room. She gave the password and stepped through the portrait, hoping to find Lena there this time. 

 

            She was rewarded by the sight of her, a warm delight filling her chest as her face softened with a smile. “You’re here! You weren’t here last night.”

 

            “Hi,” Lena quietly greeted her, closing her book and smiling slightly. “No, I, uh, I was … tired last night.”

 

            Kara could see the guarded look in her eyes but didn’t pursue it. She didn’t need to know that Lena’s arm had been stinging fiercely and she’d knocked herself out with a potion, no Murtlap essence to help with the pain. She’d slept early but the shadows beneath her eyes were still clear in her thin face. There was always something sullen about her expression, some brooding sadness that Kara occasionally pierced before it fell back into place. They’d been friends for a couple of years now, growing increasingly closer, but there were still times when Kara felt like she didn’t know Lena all that well at all.

 

            “Long train ride, huh? How were your holidays?”

 

            Lena shrugged, her mouth turning down at the corners. “I spent most of it studying.”

 

            “Surely you already know everything ,” Kara teased with a grin.

 

            Choking on a quiet laugh, Lena arched an eyebrow as she closed her eyes. She did look tired and worn out, her pallor impossibly paler and a reserved quietness to her. “I missed you,” Lena whispered, looking confused as she said it.

 

            She always wore her pin-straight hair parted in the middle, two dark curtains on either side of her sharp-boned face, and she looked up through her lashes as she hugged her knees to her chest. Kara’s face softened with surprise, her shoulders slumped as she gripped her ankles, sitting cross-legged with her wild blonde curls and her glasses slipping down her scarred face.

 

            “I missed you too,” she confessed. “It’s weird not seeing you all the time. But thanks for writing; I liked your letters. Well, I liked that you wrote.”

 

            “Sorry I couldn’t say much. If my mum saw them … she wouldn’t be very happy.”

 

            “No, I know. I just- I wish your holidays were more fun for you.”

 

            “I’d rather be here. I have fun with you.”

 

            Kara pursed her lips slightly, hesitating as she picked at the pilled grey robe, shabby in comparison to Lena’s pristine new set. “Well … maybe we could hang out more.”

 

            “Hang out?” Lena echoed, a sarcastic edge to the affected American accent. 

 

            “We’re friends. We could meet up every night like normal friends do.”

 

            “We’re not normal friends.”

 

            “But we could hang out more. Even if it’s just to study together. Or play chess. I’ll even let you practise your hexes on me.”

 

            Lena gave her a wary look, “every night?”

 

            “You’re up here anyway, aren’t you? Maybe it doesn’t have to be every night but … I like spending time with you.”

 

            Feeling shy as she admitted it, Kara softly cleared her throat and fixed her tie, loosening it a little bit. Lena was quiet for a moment and Kara pushed her curls out of her face and rubbed at the faded scar on her cheek as she waited.

 

            “Alright,” Lena finally agreed, her voice a quiet murmur before she gave Kara a small smile. “But I have Duelling Club and you have Quidditch so we can’t do those days.”

 

            “Well, I’m thinking of joining the Duelling Club. Alex thinks I should so I can defend myself better. But I don’t think I need to if you’re around.”

 

            She laughed and tapped her shoe against Lena’s, her lips twisting into a playful smile. Lena rolled her eyes and leaned back against the stone wall of the windowsill, reaching out to toy with the latch of the window.

 

            “I’ll go easy on you if we get paired up.”

 

            “Thanks.”

 

            Kara stayed until curfew was minutes away and hesitated when Lena didn’t move, before she said a hurried goodbye and ran down through the castle, getting a stitch in her side and her cheeks turning pink as she hauled her heavy book bag along with her. She made it back to the Common Room a few minutes late but no one was the wiser, except Sam, who saw her come in and gave her a sly wink, her new Prefect badge shining on the breast of her robes.

 

 

            Lena stayed in the Astronomy Tower a while longer, jotting down notes in the margins on her textbooks from her classes that day, crossing out instructions in the Potions one and annotating it to fit the steps she’d tweaked on her own time, brewing all sorts of things in her bedroom at home as she practised. When she finally packed up to leave, it wasn’t to the Slytherin Common Room but the library that she went to, covered by her invisibility cloak as she eased open the heavy door and slipped inside 

 

            She hadn’t been to the library yesterday but stepping through the door and into the dark, dusty room with the endless rows of leather-bound books and old wood, felt like a second homecoming after stepping back into Hogwarts itself. Out of all the places at the school, aside from the privacy of her secret room in the Astronomy Tower, the library was her utmost favourite place, offering a hushed environment for Lena to exist around other people without the need to talk. Walking down a row towards the section on Ancient Runes, she ran her fingers along the bumps of the spines and pulled one free at random.

 

            She took the book off the shelf and sank down onto the nearest armchair, turning the lamp on to read before turning it back off. Her exhaustion was creeping up on her and she didn’t really feel like reading, but just being there, amidst the smell of paper and leather, was comforting. The library was a strange place at night, so vast and quiet, the mere whisper of disturbed air seeming loud in the space. Yet it was a comfort to Lena as she curled up on the armchair with her invisibility cloak draped over her, hugging the heavy tome to her chest. The air had the faint smell of something musty and indistinct that was simply time, the furniture polish and leather and wood reminding the young girl of everything she’d missed while she’d been back home. She stayed there until past midnight, basking in the emptiness of the cavernous library, tucked away in the corner by herself.

 

            Rising early, Lena sipped a cup of burnt black tea, poured from the enamel teapot waiting beside her bed, feeling dreadfully tired but filled with aching relief to be back at Hogwarts, back into her usual routine of long days of studying and hours spent skulking around the library after hours to drink in more knowledge. She was keen to immerse herself back in the monotony of school, with her classes and extracurricular groups, study sessions at the library and the added allowance of Hogsmeade weekends on occasion. 

 

            Slipping out of her shared dorm dressed for classes, she found the Common Room mostly empty, the sumptuous emerald lounges free from the huddles of students gossiping over The Daily Prophet and the Dark Lord’s rise to power as they whispered about who in their family had joined him, which of them were supportive of his actions. Crossing the thick emerald rugs and the wide mouth of the hearth, where House Elves had already stoked the fire, she stepped out into the rest of the dungeons and made her way upstairs.

 

            The Great Hall hosted a few dozen early risers, sipping tea and eating bacon and porridge and cereal, but Lena didn’t linger. It was warm in there but she buttered two slices of toast and hauled her bag outside with her, sitting on the damp sloping lawn leading down to the murky lake, where her Common Room bordered upon. Hogwarts was so vastly different to the greenness of the lawn at her home estate, with the sharp lines of mortar between the bricks of the manor house, the rustling row of trees in the light summer breeze as they lined the gravel path from the gates to the front door. Instead, Hogwarts was craggy and overgrown, the banks of the lake muddy and smelling sweet with decomposing plants.

 

            The early morning light shimmered on the dew of the lawns, a snaking wisp of smoke rising from the gamekeeper’s hut as the chill air of early September filled Lena with life. There had been few opportunities for her to go outside that summer, with Lillian’s strict rules reinforced with Lex absent for most of the day and the doors spelled shut to keep Lena from sneaking out. She sat on the grass and enjoyed what was surely the last of the sunny weather as she read through her textbook for Potions. Lena had always excelled there and wondered if it was inherited from her dead mother, the potion maker who’d spent the first four years of Lena’s life telling her daughter about herbs and ingredients and potions, while Lena watched the bubbling concoctions or played with the stems of discarded plants on the floor. Until she’d killed herself, of course, and left Lena with an altogether different kind of mother.

 

            Consumed by her thoughts for a moment, a breath of wind caught the page of Lena’s book and she smoothed it down impatiently with her hand, a brooding look on her face. Her arm burned beneath the sleeves of her uniform, a parting gift from her mother, and she tried to distract herself from the stinging pain of it as she revised what she already knew in preparation for her classes. As a Third-Year, Lena had chosen her electives - or rather, Lillian had chosen them for her - and she was enrolled in Arithmancy, Ancient Runes and Care of Magical Creatures, assuring her Professors that she’d be able to manage the workload. They were convinced, considering her impeccable marks over the last two years.

 

            She’d had her first Arithmancy class yesterday and found herself unsurprisingly good at the logical side of divining meaning from numbers. Lillian had insisted that it was an essential requirement to be a good Healer to be able to infer meaning from numbers that would be associated with patients and their charts, helping diagnose them and treat them. Likewise, it was important to know the root of languages and how that translated to magic and Lena was looking forward to her first Ancient Runes class that afternoon. Care of Magical Creatures was first up that morning, the chill of the grounds promising to keep them all shivering as they learnt about the properties of animals, information for Lena to file away for future use when healing people. 

 

            Alchemy was another subject Lillian had informed her she’d need to take, but that wasn’t offered until Sixth-Year, which gave Lena time to focus on her core subjects first. By the time she was a Sixth-Year, she’d be able to drop Astronomy and History of Magic to make room for more important classes. Lillian had already mapped out her entire education at Hogwarts, through her O.W.L.s and N.E.W.T.s and into her W.O.M.B.A.T.s for her post-Hogwarts education. Lena knew she was already well above the rest of her peers, perhaps a few years ahead, but Lillian had insisted she go through her schooling at a normal pace to maximise her time to learn as much as possible. Lena was just grateful she’d have more time at Hogwarts to escape home.

 

            Her first Ancient Runes class was easy and left her feeling somewhat bored as she read from the later chapters she was already well-versed in while Professor Babbling lectured from the front of the class, drawing the alphabet on the chalkboard for the new students who hadn’t bothered to learn the readings by heart, if at all. When she was called on to answer a question, she earned Slytherin ten points for her correct answer and Professor Babbling quickly warmed to her. It was her last lesson for the day and she spent two hours tucked away in the corner of the Common Room, getting a head start on her homework as Jack Spheer waved at her from the sprawling group of upperclassmen he was trying to get her to join.

 

            Lena studiously ignored him and eventually went into her dorm to sit at the small desk at the foot of her bed when a group of Second-Years got too noisy. When she grew hungry she followed the stream of students down to the Great Hall and filled a bowl with a lamb and leek stew and ate with a book in one hand and a spoon in the other.

 

            “Don’t you ever put that thing down?” Jack drawled as he sank down beside her.

 

            “Yes. I just pick up another one,” Lena quickly retorted.

 

            He let out a warm laugh and helped himself to pork chops. Spooning stew into her mouth, Lena kept her eyes trained on the page she was reading and Jack glanced at her before leaning in and craning his neck to see what she was reading.

 

            “What book is this? Merlin, you’re not taking Ancient Runes , are you?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            He rolled his eyes and let out an exasperated huff, “you should have taken Divination instead; it’s an easy pass. Trelawney’s cracked and will pass you on anything if you make up some symbol in the bottom of your tea leaves.” 

 

            “I prefer Arithmancy. It’s more scientific.”

 

            “What, that Muggle rubbish?” he sceptically asked.

 

            Lena gave him a withering look and he smiled, raking a hand through his hair, neatly parted on one side and falling across his brown forehead. “How was your summer?”

 

            Lips twisting, Lena looked down at her bowl, her dark hair falling between them. “Good. Yours?”

 

            “Very good. I spent a week in India with my parents and watched the Tornadoes thrash the Cannons. Which team do you go for?”

 

            “I don’t like Quidditch.”

 

            “How can you not like Quidditch?”

 

            “I don’t like flying.”

 

            “Scared of heights?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            He seemed surprised by her candour and blinked, pausing only for a brief moment. “Oh. Well, that’s okay. You’re not the one flying when you’re watching.”

 

            “I don’t like sports either.”

 

            “What do you like? Except for books.”

 

            Chewing her lip, Lena was silent for a long while, staring blankly at her book without taking anything in. “I like … werewolves.”

 

            “What?”

 

            “They’re interesting.”

 

            “They’re monsters. ”

 

            Shrugging indifferently, Lena softly sighed and closed her book, giving up on the pretence of ignoring the boy. “I don’t think so. And there are human monsters too. Have you seen the news?”

 

            “You mean the Dark Lord? Snape says he’s just passionate.”

 

            “My brother said Snape’s an idiot. What do you think?”

 

            “About Snape?”

 

            Lena’s eyes cut to him, a contemptuous look on her face as she reached for her pumpkin juice. Jack just laughed, cutting into his dinner and chewing before he replied, ducking his head in close. “What have the Muggles ever done to me?”

 

            Giving him a shrewd look, Lena’s frostiness thawed a little as a small smile twitched the corners of her mouth. She didn’t respond but Jack forged onwards.

 

            “You could sit with us, you know.”

 

            “I know.”

 

            “Good.”

 

            He nodded to himself as if he’d satisfied his objective, and Lena returned to her book a few minutes later when he didn’t pursue any further conversation. She pushed a few stray leeks around the bottom of her bowl and then ate a small slice of sponge cake before she saw Kara rise from the Hufflepuff table and leave. Gathering up her own things, Lena said goodbye to Jack and followed the tall girl from the Great Hall, staying silent as she shadowed her up through the castle at a safe distance.

 

            Stepping into the room a few minutes after she’d watched Kara arrive, Lena made her way over to her window and watched her friend from the shadows for a moment. Lena had been surprised by her appearance yesterday, looking tanned from a summer evidently spent outdoors, but a slightly harrowed edge to her expression as she’d smiled, her blue eyes swimming with relief. She wondered whether it was the full moon or if something else had affected Kara’s summer, but Lena was happy she was back.

 

            “Hi,” she said, stepping forward.

 

            Kara startled and then let out a sheepish laugh, rubbing at the scar on her chin. “Oh. Didn’t see you there.”

 

            Lena could tell what kind of day someone had had by the way they said hello, by the way their footsteps fell, so attuned to the minute shifts in moods out of self-preservation that she was able to read Kara immediately. She hadn’t realised she knew her so well, but she could see the ease in the slack slope of Kara’s shoulders, the contented way she leaned against the wall, at peace in the round room of the tower. 

 

            Smiling slightly, Lena walked over to her and sank down onto the windowsill, setting her bag down beside her. It was brand new, made from dragon skin and expensive enough to make Lena feel guilty as she eyed Kara’s scratched and worn leather satchel. 

 

            “You’re here early,” Lena noted.

 

            “Oh, yeah,” Kara murmured, her ears turning pink as a blush crept up her neck and into her cheeks. “I’m trying to avoid someone.”

 

            “Your roommates?”

 

            “No, uh, my, uh, teammate. He’s friends with my sister’s friends.” Kara pulled a face and glanced out of the window at the falling dusk sweeping over the mountains and the dark, sprawling forest.

 

            “Oh.”

 

            Lena started to pull out her books and fresh rolls of parchment, lighting a lamp with her wand and then safely setting aside a pot of ink and fishing out her favourite quill. Kara eyed the stack of textbooks and tried to read the spines as she opened the limp flap of her satchel and reached for the Defence Against the Dark Arts homework she’d been issued that morning.

 

            “What electives did you pick?”

 

            “Arithmancy, Ancient Runes and Care of Magical Creatures.”

 

            “Three?” Kara exclaimed. “Are you planning on studying all year?”

 

            Giving her a thin smile, Lena’s eyes shuttered for a moment. “Probably. I’ll need them to be a Healer. At least you’ll be able to help me with my Ancient Runes and Magical Creatures homework.”

 

            “Yeah right,” Kara scoffed. “You’re probably already ahead of me and you’ve only had one class so far.”

 

            Lena let out a soft laugh and didn’t object - they both knew it was true. “Did you stick with both of them?”

 

            “Yeah. I, uh, I’ve been thinking about what to do after school though.”

 

            “That’s a bit early.”

 

            “You already know what you want to do.”

 

            Delicately wrinkling her nose, Lena picked at the knee of her grey tights. “Well, my mum’s a Healer. My brother didn’t want to be one so … um, well, I know it’ll please her if I do it.”

 

            “Do you want to be a Healer?”

 

            “Yes,” Lena firmly replied, “I want to help people. I don’t- I don’t want to hurt them.”

 

            “You wouldn’t hurt people,” Kara said with an easy smile, “you’re too nice.”

 

            Letting out an awkward laugh, Lena brushed her hair out of her face as she stared down at her lap, fiddling with the signet ring on her finger. “I want to help people. There are a lot of bad people so …”

 

            “You mean that Dark Lord? Eliza just says it’s terrorism and the Ministry will stop him soon,” Kara said with more conviction than she felt. 

 

            She was still somewhat confused by the whole thing, this young man who’d swooped in to seize power around the time they’d arrived in the U.K., earning more for himself as political strife over blood purity made things unstable. Only a week ago, she’d snagged Eliza’s copy of The Daily Prophet, reading about how a werewolf attack was supposedly linked to this Dark Lord’s spreading propaganda. It was obvious that his influence was spreading to more dangerous parties, the confidence of his followers making them bolder with their attacks, no longer seemingly limited to Muggles, but to Muggleborns as well.

 

            “I don’t think so,” Lena slowly said, “at least … my brother doesn’t think so.”

 

            “Oh,” Kara murmured, “does … does your brother agree?”

 

            Wincing slightly as she turned her head aside, resting her cheek on her knee, Lena made a sound of annoyance. “He talks about him a lot. Over the summer … I didn’t like the way he talked about it. He said his followers have given themselves a name now - Death Eaters. Lex said they’re taking all the powerful spots and then they’re going to overthrow Minister Jenkins.”

 

            “Is he- has he joined him?”

 

            “No. No, I don’t think so. Not yet. But … I’m scared that he will. My brother doesn’t do bad things but … if he believes those things the Dark Lord is saying … that means he’s bad, doesn’t it? You- you can’t be good and think those things.”

 

            “No, you can’t,” Kara murmured, a clouded look of consideration giving her a distracted air about her. “But … you’re not like that. I know no one likes Slytherin’s but-”

 

            Lena let out a choked laugh, her green eyes bright with irritation as she gave Kara a cutting look. “But I’m different?”

 

            “You are. You’re … nice. You’re lovely.”

 

            Two spots of pink coloured Lena’s cheeks and her mouth twisted slightly as she glanced back out of the window. It was dark out now, with curfew not far off. She had no intention of leaving just yet. They lapsed into silence for a moment and it wasn’t awkward but she could feel Kara restlessly scrambling for something to say to fill it. 

 

            “So … you can go to Hogsmeade now,” Kara conversationally started.

 

            “I guess so.”

 

            Her eyes slid sideways to Lena and she pushed the wire glasses up her nose, her tanned, freckled cheeks flushing slightly. “We could meet each other if you don’t have plans already. Maybe Madam Puddifoot’s for tea. Alex said it’s usually pretty empty so no one will see us.”

 

            Lena smiled slightly, her chin propped up on her knees as she hesitated, her green eyes flickering with wariness. “Will you- I mean … are you going next time?”

 

            “Yeah, of course . You should see all the shops they have. It’s so much fun. Better than the library,” Kara teased, wrinkling her nose as she nudged Lena’s polished shoe with her foot.

 

            “But it’s-”

 

            She cut herself off, biting her lip and giving Kara a crooked, aching smile as her eyes softened with understanding. “Won’t you be in the hospital?”

 

            Kara shrank back slightly, her face crumpling with confusion. “What?”

 

            “You can tell me,” Lena earnestly assured her, straightening as she crossed her legs and cocked her head to the side, trying to see past the curtain of Kara’s wayward curls. “It’s okay.”

 

            Blanching as fear knifed through her, Kara’s voice was hoarse and her stomach lurched with breathless nausea. She tried to feign ignorance, a weak smile unevenly curling her lips as she let out a strained laugh.

 

            “Tell you what?”

 

            Lena blinked and then frowned, her lips curling into a smile. “I’m not stupid, you know.”

 

            “I know,” Kara said with a forced smile, “you’re the smartest person I know.”

 

            “Then why are you pretending I’m stupid?” Lena asked, her forehead puckering with confusion.

 

            “I’m not. I just … I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

 

            Kara licked her dry lips, her heart pounding in her chest as her eyes darted around in a panicked manner. Reaching out, Lena pulled Kara’s worn copy of Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them from her open school bag, letting it part naturally to the page on werewolves. She gently set it down on Kara’s lap and hesitated.

 

            “It’s a full moon, the night before the Hogsmeade weekend,” Lena murmured.

 

            The air was forced from Kara’s lungs as surprise shot through her, the sound scornful and disbelieving. She couldn’t even respond as her throat closed up, the blood draining from her face. Standing quickly, startling Lena slightly, she tightly gripped her book as she snapped it closed in one hand and grabbed her bag with the other, abandoning the beginnings of her homework as she turned.

 

            Kara walked out. What else could she do? She slung the leather strap of her bag over her shoulder and rounded the astrological devices too quickly for Lena to stop her, eyes stinging with frightened tears as her whole body trembled. Then she was through the portrait and on the spiral staircase, taking the steps two at a time as her long legs bore her downstairs, until she slipped behind a tapestry and into a narrow, secret passageway. Her hands were balled into shaking fists, tendons stretching taut under her skin as she fought to swallow the lump in her throat. Facing a wall, she pressed her forehead against the cold stone and let out a breathless sob. 

 

 

            She avoided Lena for weeks afterwards, which wasn’t hard considering they were in different Houses, different classes, and made a point to ignore each other in public. But she stopped going to their secret room, didn’t try and catch glimpses of her at the Slytherin table at meal times, her grades slipping as she bit her nails down to nothing, worried about when the whispers would start. 

 

            They didn’t though, and Kara turned fifteen and Lena turned fourteen without a word passing between them and no talk of the werewolf in their midst. November arrived, cold and even wetter, the late autumn colours unusually subdued as dark clouds swept in and storms battered the castle. She ordinally liked to spend time outdoors, taking off her shoes and walking on the grass or along the fringes of the Forbidden Forest or the soft earth of the lake shore, but even Kara was driven inside by hail and rain and spent many afternoons near the Common Room fire, placing Exploding Snap with Sam or returning from Quidditch practice splattered with mud and almost blue to look at as she joined the rest of the team to talk strategy over the cups of tea someone brought up from the kitchens.

 

            Whispers circulated, but they weren’t about the Fourth-Year werewolf in Hufflepuff, but they were far more troubling in the grand scheme of things. Minister Jenkins was deposed, just like Lena’s brother had said, and things took a turn for the worst. Dumbledore was rarely seen at Hogwarts, and strangers came and went from meetings in his office with him when he was there. Rumours started to spread about him creating his own force of witches and wizards to take on these so-called Death Eaters and Alex was excited by the idea, insisting that if things grew into an all-out war, she’d join them after she finished school. That was another year and a half away and all of them hoped it would be over by then. 

 

            The second week of November, Kara was leaving Greenhouse Four after Herbology, in conversation with Querl, who was sporting blonde hair lately - unless his emotions made themselves known - and carefully picked her way up the steps as she wondered at their homework assignment aloud. She was already drafting a mental letter to Eliza to ask about the properties of Bubotuber plants, wondering if she might be able to offer some more insight than the standard textbooks that she’d have to check out at the library. Mid-sentence, Kara felt something overwhelm her and a cold, dry hand clapped over her mouth as she tried to let out a squawk of protest, dragged into the bushes before she could react.

 

            “Four feet is a long essay for Professor Sprout, especially when we have to touch the pus . Don’t forget your gloves next- Kara?” Querl continued before he pulled up short, noticing she wasn’t beside him and turning to look. 

 

            He looked stumped, his blonde hair darkening to violet as his eyes turned grey. Rubbing the back of his head, his mouth turned down at the corners and Kara tried to make a muffled response, stepping forward and feeling the weight of the person behind her get dragged along. Querl just made a sound of bewilderment and kept walking, craning his neck to see over the heads of their classmates, in case she’d ducked ahead without him seeing.

 

            Annoyed, Kara elbowed the person behind her and heard the sharp exhale as she got them in the sternum, feeling the person stagger backwards. Something liquid and light dragged over her skin and she shivered involuntarily, staring through the gloomy light of the Forbidden Forest as she tried to spot her attacker. Slipping her wand out of the pocket of her robe, she slowly raised it and then let out a yelp as Lena suddenly appeared before her, windswept and disgruntled, balling something silvery in her arms.

 

            Clapping a hand over her mouth, Kara closed her eyes and tipped her head back as her wand arm fell limply to her side. “Merlin, Lena, what the- what are you doing? I could’ve hexed you.”

 

            Letting out a short laugh, surprise flashed across Lena’s face and she rubbed at the middle of her torso. “I would’ve used a shield charm.”

 

            Spluttering, Kara’s cheeks reddened and her eyes ran over Lena, wary and reserved. “What are you doing?”

 

            “You’ve been avoiding me.”

 

            “I haven’t.”

 

            “Yes, you have,” Lena sharply insisted, a stubborn, petulant set to her jaw as she took a step forward. “Don’t lie to me. I’m not stupid.”

 

            “I didn’t say you were stupid.”

 

            “But you are avoiding me. I thought … I thought we were friends.”

 

            Her voice was small and soft, sadness threading through her response as her anger burned out quickly. She deflated before Kara’s eyes, her shoulders drooping beneath the voluminous trappings over her Slytherin robes. Swallowing thickly, Kara looked down at her feet, her bag slipping off her shoulder and the toe of her school shoes scuffed and pinching slightly - she should’ve let Eliza enlarge them a bit more.

 

            “We are-”

 

            “Then why haven’t I seen you-”

 

            “We’re not supposed to see each other, are we?” Kara countered evasively. “We’re supposed to pretend we don't know each other. That’s what we said.”

 

            Lena scoffed and angrily crossed her arms over her chest. “Stop it . That’s not it; it’s because I said you’re a were-”

 

            Surging forward as panic seized her, Kara covered Lena’s mouth with her hand, cutting her off before she could finish the word. Her blue eyes were wide and her face reddened as she grew flustered and embarrassed, making the silvery scars stark against the pallor of her skin. Mouth dry and a lump in her throat, Kara loomed over Lena, her growth spurt lending her some added height, and the smaller girl’s brow puckered as she wrapped her thin fingers around Kara’s wrist and tried to pry her hand away.

 

            As if coming to her senses, Kara swallowed thickly and removed her hand, watching Lena’s pulse flutter at the side of her throat as she breathed in the clean smell of soap and ink that always seemed to cling to her. Still standing imposingly close, she looked her in the eye and broke the quiet tension.

 

            “Don’t,” she whispered, part warning as well as a plea.

 

            “It’s okay,” Lena rasped, a tentative smile faintly creeping onto her lips. “I’m not scared of you. I don’t care.”

 

            Scoffing, Kara had to look away, ducking her head down slightly as her lips twisted wryly. “You can’t not care that I- that I’m-”

 

            “I don’t,” Lena firmly insisted.

 

            Kara’s bottom lip trembled slightly as she nudged her glasses up, rubbing at her eyes. They stung fiercely and she could feel her throat closing up, the urge to cry building in her chest. Alex’s friends were nice but Lena was her friend, and she’d been struck with confusion and fear about her finding out, wondering how , scared to lose the first friend she’d made at the school.

 

            “You’re my friend,” Lena continued, speaking simply in the way that kids, too young to have learned how to hate yet, did. “It’s only one night, isn’t it? You’re nice the rest of the time. You’re the nicest person I know. If- if you weren’t my friend … I wouldn’t know what to do.”

            

            Hesitating for a moment as she wrestled with the urge to cry, Kara tipped her head back, eyes squeezed shut as she kept a hand pressed over her mouth. Lena watched her with wide eyes, waiting as she brimmed with restless impatience. And then Kara lowered her head, ducking it down as she squared her shoulders and seemed to rock on her heels for a moment before pitching herself forward into a motion that Lena didn’t recognise was a hug until Kara engulfed her. 

 

            Lena stiffened with shock as Kara buried her face in her shoulders, hunched over slightly with her added height. She couldn’t remember the last time she’d been hugged - had it been when Lex had seen her off to Hogwarts in her first year? He didn’t have much time for her now, her brother consumed with his darker vices - and she didn’t know how to react. Her arms hung limply at her sides as the silvery invisibility cloak slithered to the leaf-strewn floor. It took a long moment before her body relaxed and she hesitantly wound her arms around Kara, breathing in the smell of the greenhouses and the detergent her robes had been washed in. 

 

            Pulling back a moment later, pink-cheeked and her dry eyes red, Kara cleared her throat. She brushed her hair out of her eyes, looking contrite as she warily looked at Lena. “How long have you known?”

 

            Shrugging, Lena’s brow puckered. “The start of the year. You were sick a lot and I figured it out in Astronomy because we were doing lunar charts. I started keeping track of it and was sure by the end of term.”

 

            “You didn’t tell me you knew,” Kara rasped.

 

            “You didn’t tell me.”

 

            “I … was scared. I don’t- it’s … people would be scared of me.”

 

            “I’m not scared,” Lena stubbornly insisted.

 

            Turning away, Kara pressed her lips into a flat line and scuffed her shoe through the autumn leaves blanketing the fringes of the forest. She was aware that she had Transfiguration in a few minutes, and wouldn’t want to bring on Professor McGonagall’s ire, but lingered anyway.

 

            “You should go,” Kara said after a moment. “Don’t you have class?”

 

            “No, I have a study period.”

 

            “Oh. We might be seen.”

 

            “In the forest?”

 

            “Maybe.”

 

            Lena smiled slightly, “okay, let’s go somewhere else then.”

 

            She picked up the invisibility cloak and threw it over herself, vanishing before Kara’s eyes, until she threw it over Kara as well and they both stood face to face beneath the shimmering fabric of it. With a coy grin on her lips, impishly mischievous in a way that Lena’s solemn face rarely was, she grabbed Kara’s hand, her own paper dry and cold against the clammy warmth of her friend’s, and she towed her forward as Kara hitched her satchel higher on her shoulder.

 

            Instead of making their way back to the castle, or to the more secluded spots on the grounds, like the boathouse or the empty courtyards, where it was common to see couples and groups slip away to for privacy, Lena turned towards the greenhouses. She stopped outside one of the ones they’d never been inside and raised her wand, murmuring a quiet Alohomora to unlock it. 

 

            “What are you doing?” Kara hissed. “This is Greenhouse Seven; we’re not allowed in here yet.”

 

            The old door opened with the soft sigh of well-oiled hinges to admit them and Lena glanced sideways at her. “No one has to know we were in here.”

 

            The greenhouse was peaceful inside, the wind muffled by the yellowed glass panes and a few degrees warmer to keep the abundance of plants insulated. Stepping around a stack of terracotta pots, Kara slipped out from underneath the invisibility cloak and followed the left path, past rows of black laurel and 

 

            Wolfsbane and oleander hung from the ceiling, dangerous and enticing, and the place smelled richly of dirt and damp and something green. Kara liked the greenhouses but the plants in this one were unfamiliar to her as she eyed them warily, 

 

            “I tried to pretend like I didn’t know,” Lena said after a long moment, passing down the right path, creeping plants and shrubs and cuttings filling the space between them, obscuring her from sight at times as the shadowed leaves and vines hid her. “I didn’t want things to change.”

 

            “Does it have to?” Kara apprehensively asked.

 

            Lena hesitated, “no. But it will, won’t it?”

 

            Kara swallowed thickly around the lump in her throat. “Yeah.”

 

            “I’m sorry about what happened to you.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Kara slipped down a narrow path between overgrown aconite and asphodel and stepped onto the same path as Lena. “It didn't happen to me. It was … done to me.”

 

            “Oh. Yes. I guess so,” Lena murmured with a clouded look on her face. “How did it happen?”

 

            Toying with the leaf of a Venomous Tentacula until it snapped at her fingers, Kara shrugged, a petulant look on her face as she looked down at the soil spilling across the paving stones underfoot. “I was outside, looking for Mooncalves. My mom made some werewolf mad so … they wanted to get back at her. They were waiting outside our house and bit me in the garden. My dad got bitten too but …”

 

            “Oh. That’s how he …”

 

            “Yeah. And then my mom didn’t want me anymore. I’m … half- orphaned. Our neighbours took me in - Alex and her mom - and I- Ilvermorny wouldn’t let me back in so she moved us here. So I could go to school. Dumbledore said it was okay.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            She looked on the verge of tears, a pouting look of frustration and grief mixed together in a confusing, tangled web in her chest. Rubbing at her eyes, Kara scowled and jutted her chin forward in a stubborn manner. 

 

            “No one else knows - except Alex . And the Professors, obviously but …”

 

            “Is that why she didn’t like you?”

 

            “Not in that way. She just didn’t want to move or have a sister, but … my mom left me. She just- she left and my dad … my dad is dead and I miss them.”

 

            Kara found it hard to talk about her parents without her voice catching, but Lena couldn’t talk about her mum at all, so she didn’t hold the tremor in her words against Kara. It had only been two years, just twenty-four full moons, since the attack, a handful of days in the grand scheme of things, but so much agony squeezed into so little time.

 

            “How is Alex? Does she need help with her homework?” Lena asked, changing the topic.

 

            Kara let out a quick laugh and pulled her face, shaking her head with fond amusement. “She’s such a Gryffindor. Nice to me but ready to fight anyone. Sometimes an ass. Sorry, arse.”

 

            Lena laughed at the affected accent, a crooked smile twisting her lips. “Sounds like she’ll be a good Auror.”

 

            “She’s already trying to sign up to fight in this war.”

 

            “It’s not a war yet ,” Lena murmured, her voice thick with worry as uneasiness wound through her.

 

            “It’s getting worse. You were right. I’m surprised we can still go to Hogsmeade.”

 

            “I’m not really allowed to go to Hogsmeade anyway,” Lena confessed, her right hand closing over the forearm of her left arm as she looked down at the floor. 

 

            “What do you mean?”

 

            “My mum wouldn’t sign my form. She thinks it’s a waste of time. I should use my free time to study more.”

 

            Kara’s mouth fell open and she floundered for a moment, “what do you mean?”

 

            Giving her a thin smile, Lena raised one shoulder in a lopsided shrug. “She’s quite strict, you know. She makes me send her all of my essays and homework once I get them back, so she can keep track of my marks. If I- if I don’t get full marks … she’s not very happy when I go home.”

 

            Making a choked sound at the back of her throat, Kara frowned. “Okay, um … well, you, uh, you can sneak out, with your cloak.”

 

            A mischievous smile curled Lena’s lips and her eyes were half-lidded as she made a small sound of amusement in her chest. “I said she wouldn’t sign my form, not that I didn’t get my form signed.”

 

            “Oh. Did your brother-”

 

            Shaking her head, Lena’s smile became a smirk, “no, I forged it myself.”

 

            “So … will you have tea with me?”

 

            Hesitating, Lena’s brow furrowed for a moment. “The next one-”

 

            “I know,” Kara whispered, ducking her head with shame. 

 

            “You’ll be tired, so maybe we should wait until next time. And I’ll work on my disguise.”

 

            “Disguise?” Kara snorted, her face crumpling with bewildered amusement. “I guess that’s a good idea. That way no one will notice us. You can’t wear your robes though.”

 

            “I won’t.”

 

            A slow grin spread across Kara’s face and she nodded, holding out her hand. “Alright, next time then.”

 

            “Next time,” Lena agreed, reaching out to shake on it.

Chapter 11

            The next full moon was near the end of November, a wet day and a bitter evening as Kara was ushered through the tunnel after she’d picked at her dinner, left to undress in the dimness of the forest and slip between the trees. The earth was freezing beneath her bare soles and drops of frigid rain fell from the high canopy overhead, splashing over her pimpled skin as she hugged her arms to herself and shivered violently as her teeth chattered.

 

            It hindered her somewhat, and Kara wasn’t as deep into the forest as she usually managed to get before the transformation stole over her, her stomach churning until she brought up what little dinner she’d managed to force down. Bracing herself against the rough trunk of a wide tree, she coughed and spluttered and then cried out as her back hunched with a painful crack, the bones splitting and restructuring. 

 

            She forgot about the cold as ragged cries of pain tore free from her throat, her body contorting as it changed, lengthening and sprouting grey hair. The last thing she was aware of was the dark forest, the scent of old leaves and damp moss filling her nose and the sour taste of bile filling her mouth. 

 

            When she came to the next morning, later on in the morning thanks to the approaching winter bringing early sunsets and late sunrises, Kara couldn’t feel her body. Face-down in freezing mud, her lips were tinged blue and her fingernails were lavender beneath the dirt as her eyelids fluttered past the bone-leaden feeling. A shine of dew lingered in the patches of grass thrusting up, and the mist and chill permeated the forest as the sky lightened to a milky blue overhead.

 

            Somehow finding her feet, Kara shivered violently as she stumbled onwards, the bitter wind screaming through the trees making her feel like she was being slapped. Her eyes watered and her hands burned from the cold and she moved blindly through the dark trunks of the towering trees, her vision blurred without her glasses as she tried to follow the brightening light towards the thinning edges of the forest, trying to orient herself with the foggy memories of last night.

 

            Kara stumbled upon the Thestrals then, closer to the lake than the greenhouses, and she shivered as she stood on the fringes of the herd for a moment, staring at the blurred shapes of the horses that reminded her of why she was in the forest, naked and in pain. A painful breath escaped her and she wiped at her muddy cheek, her chest aching with grief and her lungs burning from the cold. One of the foals approached her and she pressed her trembling fingers to its skeletal face for a moment, feeling the leathery hide over hard bone before she turned and followed the vaguely familiar route back to the castle grounds.

 

            Finding her clothes at the usual hollow in the roots of a wide tree, she pulled them on, cringing at the damp wool chafing her skin, the wet cotton socks over filthy feet and slipped her glasses on. Madam Pomfrey was already waiting at the tunnel and Kara followed her through to the hospital wing, where she was tucked away in a bed in the far corner and given a number of potions to help warm her up and send her to sleep.

 

            She woke past lunch, feverish and aching as if she’d come down with the flu. It was a familiar sensation post-full moon now, but it didn’t make it any more bearable as she let out a listless sigh, her heavy eyelids refusing to open. Her pale cheek was etched with the crosshatched pattern of the hospital blanket placed over the starched sheets and Kara pushed them away from her face as she stirred.

 

            Her eyes were slitted as she came back to her own body, and through her lashes, she could see the outline of someone sitting beside her. Face pinched with confusion, she struggled to open her eyes further and gentle fingers brushed her cheek as her wire glasses were set on her face, helping to clarify things. It brought a lump to Kara’s throat, reminding her of waking up in the hospital that first time, with Alex slipping her glasses on for her, quietening her as they listened to Alura leave her.

 

            She thought it was Alex for a moment, but Alex didn’t come and sit with her. She would meet her afterwards when Kara was discharged, checking to see how she was once she’d had time to sleep off the transformation. But it was a Hogsmeade weekend, and Kara had already insisted that she enjoy her freedom from the castle; she’d just be sleeping anyway. No, it wasn’t Alex. 

 

            Sitting on a chair beside the narrow hospital bed, a book open in her lap and a grave look of pitiful worry, Lena stared at her. Meeting her gaze, blue eyes piercing, ringed by circles of exhaustion and set in a thin face made pale from a long night, Kara let out a sharp breath of surprise. Her throat was so sore that she couldn’t speak and her eyes watered as the urge to cry stole upon her.

 

            Clenching her teeth as her face crumpled, she screwed her eyes shut and shook with quiet sobs, her breath hitching in her throat as she inhaled. Lena reached out and took her hand, soft and warm and pale against Kara’s, with dirt trapped beneath her fingernails and worn into the grooves of her palms. She felt like a feral, frayed thing beside the polished perfection of her loyal friend.

 

            “It’s alright,” Lena murmured.

 

            Kara’s chin dimpled with the effort to stifle the sobs and she wiped at her wet cheeks with clumsy fingers. A part of her was embarrassed and angry at her tears but Lena just held her hand and waited until she fought it, her sons easing into shuddering gasps, her cheeks turning pink and splotchy and her eyes red-rimmed. The Hospital Wing was empty save for a Seventh-Year Gryffindor boy who was always there behind a curtain the day after the full moon, which afforded Kara some privacy as she tried to wrestle with the overwhelming surprise of Lena sitting beside her through the aftermath of something so horrifying.

 

            “What-“ Kara rasped before trailing off, giving Lena a mystified look.

 

            “I wanted to make sure you were alright.”

 

            “You should be in Hogsmeade.”

 

            Shrugging dismissively, Lena frowned slightly. “I went this morning to get what I needed. It didn’t take very long. But I got you this.”

 

            Pulling a Chocolate Frog from the pocket of her dark green cloak, Lena set it down on the blankets covering Kara’s lap. “I heard chocolate’s good for you after … you know.”

 

            A small smile graced Kara’s face as her heavy eyelids shuttered. “Thank you.”

 

            With fumbling fingers, she opened it and was too slow to catch the frog, leaving it up to Lena, who set it down in the box, the enchantment broken. Kara turned the card over in her hands.

 

            “Who did you get?”

 

            “Falco Aesalon. The first recorded Animagus. Have you ever thought about being one?”

 

            “Sometimes. I don’t know what I would be though. What if I turned into something horrible?”

 

            “Do you get to choose?”

 

            “No. It’s whatever form the magic thinks suits you. I heard that a student at the Uagadou school turned into a dragon. It’s really hard to become one but they let them do it when they’re still at school. My brother said Professor McGonagall became one at seventeen.”

 

            “I bet you could do it,” Kara firmly replied. “And … I think you’d be something nice, like a cat. I like cats.”

 

            “Do you?”

 

            Smiling thinly, Kara hummed in agreement. “Yeah. I think … if I got to pick, I’d like to be a cat.”

 

            “Have they taught you how to do a Patronus yet? I’ve read that they’re usually the same as your Animagus.”

 

            “No, not yet. What’s yours?”

 

            Shifting slightly, Lena frowned, “I don’t know. I can’t do one.”

 

            “Your mom hasn’t shown you yet?”

 

            Looking a little surly and embarrassed, Lena’s mouth tightened at the corners. “No, I just haven’t been able to do the spell. I’ve tried. It’s really advanced but … I’m usually really good at hard spells. I’ve done loads that are hard. Nothing happens though.”

 

            The truth was, Lena didn’t have any memories happy enough to conjure a Patronus, corporeal or non-corporeal, although she didn’t know that was the source of her failure. She’d spent futile hours since the start of term trying to make something appear, even a faint wisp to be proud of, to report to her mother, but nothing ever happened. It was a sore point that left her put out, but she didn’t dwell on it too long, knowing she’d get it eventually.

 

            “Well, maybe you should become an Animagus and then you’ll know. Unless it’s different. But who cares? You’ll be an Animagus. We can try it together if you want, but you’ll have to teach me how to do it.”

 

            A pained, sheepish look softened Lena’s face. “One of- one of the steps means … you have to keep a mandrake leaf in your mouth for a whole month so- well, you have to spit it out on the full moon so …”

 

            “Oh,” Kara murmured, her enthusiasm slipping away quickly as she wilted, sagging back against the pillows. 

 

            She smoothed her hands over the blankets and swallowed, her throat dry. “Well …”

 

            “I can help you with your Patronus though. If you wanted to know …”

 

            “Maybe,” Kara murmured, her cheeks shallowly dimpling with a ghost of a smile.

 

            It was full of bitterness though and she turned her head to stare up at the ceiling for a moment, blinking back the stinging in her eyes as she felt disappointment knot in her stomach. Lena shifted on the chair, reaching down to her bag and pulling out a wooden box, raising her eyes suggestively as she rattled it, pieces inside clattering.

 

            “I brought chess, in case you wanted to play while you waited to get out. Madam Pomfrey said I wasn’t allowed to disturb you but … I told her I figured it out and she likes me anyway because I told her I wanted to be a Healer when I had to come in for a Pepper-Up Potion last year. She said as long as you rest I can stay.”

 

            “Go on then,” Kara hoarsely relented, weakly pushing herself up onto the thin pillows as Lena dragged the trolley with the tray between them and set up the pieces. 

 

            Lena always went black so Kara made the first move and they fell into the familiar routine of Lena thrashing Kara at chess. Kara didn’t mind though; she’d joined the Duelling Club, as promised, and it turned out she was even better at offensive magic than Lena was, and when they’d been paired up last week, Kara had hit her with a Jelly-Legs jinx that had left Lena’s proud ego a little bruised when Kara had gleefully teased her later on that evening. Lena could keep her chess and all the things she was better at; Kara would make sure no one would ever touch her again.

 

            “I should be getting out soon,” Kara murmured after their third game.

 

            It was the middle of the afternoon and she probably could have weaselled her way out of the Hospital Wing a couple of hours ago if she’d tried but she’d been content to sit with Lena and play chess. It had distracted her to the point where she might have forgotten it had been a full moon last night, if not for the haunting toll on her body.

 

            Lena nodded and gathered up the marble chess pieces in her small hands, letting them tumble back into the box the board made once folded in half. “Can I come next time?”

 

            Kara hesitated, “if- if you want to.”

 

            “Okay.” 

 

            Packing the chess set into her bag, Lena gave her a crooked smile and was gone a few minutes later. After she left, Madam Pomfrey came over to check on Kara and allowed her to leave. Shoving her feet into her shoes and desperate for a shower, Kara slipped her wand into her back pocket and the Chocolate Frog card into the other one before shuffling out of the ward, her muscles aching and joints stiff. 

 

            The next full moon, Lena was there again the following morning with a block of chocolate and her chess set as the two of them played and spoke quietly. There was a privacy screen around Kara’s bed, hiding them from the view of the rest of the ward, and she felt a little better having Lena there, even if she was sad that she’d be going home tomorrow for the Christmas holidays. Lena would be staying, of course, and Kara promised to write and gave her the present she’d managed to trade a rare Chocolate Frog card and a month of homework for - a copy of The Healer's Helpmate by H. Pollingtonious. Lena opened it and smiled as she leafed through the pages, earnestly thanking her before presenting Kara with her gift, carefully pulled from a box in her bag.

 

            Depositing it on the sheets, Lena smiled faintly, her green eyes watchful and wary as Kara stared at the tiny little kitten clawing at the hospital blankets. Lena had purchased it from Jack Spheer’s cat, who’d recently had a litter, after she’d managed to convince him to take two Galleons and offered to be his Duelling Club partner for the rest of the year.

 

            “Are you serious?” Kara softly exclaimed, scooping the little kitten up.

 

            “You said you liked cats and one of my housemates had kittens. I thought- I mean, you don’t have an owl, and no one wants a toad , so …”

 

            “It’s perfect,” Kara murmured, holding the tiny ball of fur up. “Thank you.”

            

            She lifted it to her face and the kitten pressed its nose against her cheek and let out a quiet cry, opening its mouth to show tiny needle-like teeth and a pink tongue. Its fur was pitch black and there was a smudge of white on its brow.

 

            “You need to think of a name,” Lena said, reaching out to stroke the velvety ears of the kitten.

 

            “Hmm, how about Streaky?”

 

            “Streaky?” Lena scoffed.

 

            “Yeah, for this little white streak,” Kara explained, smoothing the patch.

 

            Its green eyes slitted and she set it down on her chest, the kitten splaying its legs and laying on its belly. Lena wrinkled her nose at the suggestion and Kara rolled her eyes.

 

            “Well, how did you come up with Morrigan?”

 

            “She’s from Irish mythology. Usually as a trio of sisters for death and war and that sort of stuff. But they’re seen as a crow so I thought it was a good fit even though she’s an owl, not a crow.”

 

            “How do you know all this stuff?”

 

            “I have a book from my mum. She was Irish too and my dad gave it to me after she died. All of these myths and stories about Celtic folklore.”

 

            “Is there a Celtic cat god?”

 

            “Not really. There’s a Welsh one who has white cats around her but I don’t think that fits this one.”

 

            Lena tickled the cat under the chin and Kara smiled as she watched her. Stroking the bridge of its nose, her fingertip grazed the white smudge and Lena hummed with consideration.

 

            “It kind of looks like a crescent moon, don’t you think?”

 

            She moved her finger away and Kara studied the smudge, a little uneven but somewhat reminiscent of a crescent moon. “A little. Is there a moon god?”

 

            “Elatha. For the sun and moon. But this is a girl. You could go for the Welsh one but it’s a mouthful. Arianrhod. Or the Egyptian cat goddess is Bastet. Or Luna is the Roman goddess of the moon.”

 

            Kara made a rasping sound at the back of her throat as she deliberated. “Which one do you think? I’m not very good at choosing things.”

 

            A smile twitched Lena’s lips. “I think … Bastet.”

 

            “Okay. Bastet then.”

 

            Looking pleased with herself, Lena nodded. She left a short while later with the reassurance that she would enjoy Christmas at Hogwarts more than she would at home, and Kara was struck with the sudden urge to ask if she wanted to come home with her. She didn’t ask though and promised to see Lena in the new year.

 

            Christmas passed by quickly, rainy weather and brewing discontent keeping them indoors as they decorated the tree Eliza had brought home, the smell of gingerbread and cinnamon filling the small cottage. They played Exploding Snap and listened to music, Eliza knitting them new sweaters and making their clothes just a little bit bigger. She’d tutted and fussed over Kara when she’d picked them up from the station, how she was almost as tall as Alex now and wouldn’t be able to take her hand-me-downs for much longer. On Christmas morning, they swapped their gifts for each other, with Kara getting a new journal and socks from Eliza, as well as some homemade treats and her new sweater, while Alex bought her a Sneakoscope, insisting that it would come in handy as things got worse.

 

            Kara bought her sister new gloves for Quidditch and had stolen a clipping of a Floo plant, thinking that Eliza could extract the Floo powder from the flowers and sell it to Floo-Pow for some extra money. Eliza was very enthusiastic about it and kissed her cheek as she cupped the other side of Kara’s face, thanking her and then moving the plant safely out of the way of an adventurous kitten that had been in her daughter’s arms when she stepped off the train. 

 

            They made the most of their holidays together, just the three of them, making do with what little money Eliza scraped together throughout the year to buy them something. Kara always felt a prickle of guilt in addition to her gratitude, and she never complained, not even when her toes were pinched in her shoes and her socks started showing holes. She could have been on the streets, abandoned by her mom, but she was in that little cottage with a family who loved her like she was their own, even if it had taken some of them a while to get there. 

 

            It felt like they were barely in Cornwall before they were gone again, back on the train, catching up with friends who’d gone to France for the holidays or Christmas galas with their parents or just spent it with their extended family. The older ones in their group complained about resuming their classes and how badly they were doing in their studies, about how they didn’t think they were going to get the grades to be an Auror or a Banker or whatever it was they were planning on doing. Kara still didn’t really know what she wanted to do, and she had until the end of the year to decide, her fifth year determining the kind of future she’d have, which wasn’t looking optimistic with the prejudice toward lycanthropy. 

 

            She saw Lena the next night, who gave her an uninspiring summary of her Christmas, attending Slughorn’s annual Christmas party with other well-off students he used to forge future connections, regaling Lena with stories about how intelligent her brother was. Kara shared the gingerbread and fudge gifted to her by Eliza as they sat by the window, pitch-black outside and a chill seeping in through the edges of the warped glass. Lena seemed indifferent to spending the holidays at Hogwarts, but Kara knew it couldn’t have been better than spending it with good people. For all her family’s evident wealth and power, they deprived her friend of the most vital things a child could want, and it was clear to see in the reserved, flinching way Lena had of evading anything personal, anything that could hurt.

 

            Two days before the next full moon, they had another Hogsmeade weekend, the mid-January bringing deep snow drifts that they waded through, bundled up in cloaks and jumpers and scarves. Kara’s breath plumed before her as she struggled down the long road to Hogsmeade with Imra on one side and Kelly on the other. Alex walked behind them with a Gryffindor Seventh-Year called Maggie whom Alex had confessed to Kara she was seeing when they’d been back home. They were both on the Gryffindor Quidditch Team and Alex had hit Maggie with her broomstick and promised to visit her every day in the infirmary until she got better. Kara had the distinct impression that her sister’s girlfriend didn’t like her.

 

            “Coming to The Three Broomsticks?” Imra asked, raising her eyebrows suggestively.

 

            “Oh, um, maybe.”

 

            “First round is on me.”

 

            Kara gave her a quick smile, only feeling a little embarrassed by the offer. She needed the few knuts she had left for Madam Puddifoot’s, where she was meeting Lena soon. “I just need to go to a few shops first. I might meet you there after.”

 

            “Okay. You’ll want a hot Butterbeer in this weather though.”

 

            Imra wasn’t wrong; Kara’s hands were already cold inside her woollen gloves and even her new socks weren’t enough to keep her feet warm. She nodded in agreement but still parted ways with the group once they reached the town, watching as Imra fell into step beside Mike and Kelly looping her arms through James and Querl’s, while Alex dragged Maggie over to Zonko’s first. Slipping down to Madam Puddifoot’s, Kara claimed the furthest table in the shadowed corner, away from the door and windows, and pretended to study a menu as she kept an eye on the door. 

 

            It was ten minutes before the door opened and Alex stepped inside. A black cloak hid her clothes and her eyes landed on Kara as she smiled and wound her way through the tables to approach her. Dragging one of the wooden chairs out, Alex sat down across from her and arched an eyebrow in an expression that looked strange on her sister’s face, so unlike her usual expressions.

 

            “I thought you were with Maggie,” Kara said, a frown creasing her forehead as she set her menu down.”

 

            “Who’s Maggie?”

 

            It was definitely Alex’s voice, but the words came out with a distinctly polished accent with a lilting hint of Irish. Kara blinked, leaning back in her seat as surprise shot through her. Leaning in again, she squinted, trying to figure out what Lena had done.

 

            “Polyjuice Potion,” her friend supplied. 

 

            Kara was only vaguely familiar with the notion and frowned. “How?”

 

            “I brewed it,” Lena said with a quick laugh. “Took a while but it should last a few hours.”

 

            Kara didn’t need to know how she’d brewed the lacewing flies for weeks and snuck out to one of the Greenhouses to steal some fluxweed under a full moon. Or how she’d gotten herself paired with Alex during Duelling Club and stolen a hair to complete the transformation.

 

            “You’re … a genius,” Kara said after a moment, a smile spreading across her face. “I just hope Alex doesn’t come in here with her girlfriend now, or that’s going to be hard to explain.”

 

            “I didn’t know who else to pick. It wouldn’t seem weird if you were here with your sister.”

 

            “It’s perfect.”

 

            Alex’s mouth twisted into an uneven smile that left Kara feeling odd, trying to reconcile Lena with her sister’s face. “Shall we order?” Lena suggested.

 

            Kara ordered tea and Lena got a black coffee, which made Kara wrinkle her nose, surprised that she could drink it. She added two sugars to her own tea, making it strong as the approaching full moon left her feeling weak already, clammy and congested as if the flu was settling in her chest. She felt too tired to even protest when Lena insisted on paying, slipping coins from her full purse as she tried to hide the contents from Kara.

 

            They talked about school and gossip and the next Quidditch match - Slytherin vs Ravenclaw - which Lena wasn’t really interested in but was going for her House all the same. Making sure to keep their voices down so no one would get suspicious about their conversation, they instinctively leaned toward each other and their cups soon grew empty. Lena ordered another pot of tea, this time for two, her coffee cup whisked away and a china teacup replacing it. She poured the tea for them and they fell back into conversation.

 

            It was the best Hogsmeade trip Kara had had so far, the two of them hidden behind the fogged-up windows, in the far corner, warm and happy. They could’ve stayed there all afternoon, but it was a couple of hours later that Lena’s face started to twitch slightly, and then it looked like it was bubbling. She drained the dregs of her tea and gave Kara an apologetic look before ducking out into the street and vanishing.

 

            Still reeling slightly, Kara lingered a while longer before she eventually walked the beaten path to The Three Broomsticks and joined her friends. James bought her a Butterbeer and she sat beside him, small and unobtrusive unless spoken to, her face seeming to grow paler by the hour as she sipped her drink. Excusing herself when Kelly asked if she was feeling okay, she trekked back to the castle by herself and napped for the rest of the afternoon before picking at her steak and kidney pie at dinner.

 

            The full moon came around with its usual horrific toll on her body, the snow leaving her shivering in the mud, curled in on herself until a blanket was placed over her, someone kneeling beside her on the pile of rotting leaves and pine needles. Madam Pomfrey had her on a stretcher, floating back towards the greenhouses and her clothes by the time her eyelashes fluttered open. She managed to dress and stiffly make the walk back through the tunnel, a sharp pain in her chest from the cold.

 

            Kara ended up in the Hospital Wing for three days after this one, fighting a bout of pneumonia and recovering quickly with the potions and tonics fed to her. Lena visited every day during her study periods and after dinner, when it was late enough for her friends to have come and gone and retired to their respective Common Rooms for the evening. She’d stay until Madam Pomfrey kicked her out, helping Kara with the homework Querl brought her and sneaking her sweets to brighten her mood.

 

            It was Friday afternoon, just after lunch, when Kara was finally discharged, a cardigan pulled on over the long-sleeved shirt and worn plimsolls, the knees of her jeans faded and thin. Hugging her arms to herself, she left the Hospital Wing and slowed. In an alcove halfway down the corridor, she spotted Alex leaning against the wall as she stared out the window and kicked her scuffed sneakers against the stone, looking agitated. Approaching, Kara gave her a tired smile and then raised her eyebrows expectedly.

 

            “What’s got your wand in a knot?”

 

            “Why was a Slytherin sitting next to you?”

 

            Kara aimed for nonchalance, rubbing her eyes as she nudged her glasses up. “Oh, her? Some Third-Year stuck in detention. She was cleaning bedpans for most of the time but Madam Pomfrey made her bring me some water.”

 

            Staring at her for a long moment, Alex let out a scathing sound of disbelief. “Detention?”

 

            Shrugging, Kara grimaced and splayed her hands helplessly. “I don’t know. I didn’t really talk to her.”

 

            “Yeah, well, she’s a Luthor, and there’s plenty of bad stuff to say about her family,” Alex darkly informed Kara, as if she was ignorant of her own friend.

 

            “Says who?”

 

            “James was telling me stuff about her dad and how her brother was really into dark magic when he was here. Graduated a few years ago but was a proper Slytherin. I bet she’s just the same.”

 

            “Oh. Yeah. Maybe.”

 

            Alex lightly slapped her arm, “stay away from her, okay? All this trouble going on … it’s going to spread here soon and we all know which side that house is going to be on. Keep your Sneakoscope with you.”

 

            Kara rolled her eyes but didn’t object to any of her sister’s claims. She’d learnt that it was easier to just agree with Alex than fight her on it sometimes, and Lena was her secret to keep, so it didn’t matter what anyone else thought about her. Kara liked her just fine.

 

 

            Lex manoeuvred the luggage trolley through the crowded station, impatiently gesturing for Lena to hurry up as he made towards the wide fireplaces. Abandoning the trolley and then snapping at Lena to leave it when she made to return it to the trolley bay, he grabbed her arm in a tight grip that made Lena wince. Dragged into the fireplace with him and her trunk, Lena briefly caught sight of Kara’s wide-eyed look of surprise before emerald flames whirled around them and she endured the nauseating trip back to the manor house.

 

            Stepping out of the fireplace, Lena allowed Hope to brush the soot from her, smiling shyly at the House Elf who squeaked delights at her return home. She was perhaps the only one who was pleased that Lena was home, including Lena. Lex strode through the house without another word, distracted and annoyed, leaving Lena to pick up the cage with Morrigan nestled inside, while the House Elf snapped her fingers and sent the trunk upstairs.

 

            The sitting room was dim, no lamps lit and wrongly angled to allow any sunlight to seep into the opulent space, leaving it feeling dingy instead. Moving over to the window with the cage, Lena unhooked the latch and pushed the pane open, staring out at the long path bordered by trailing willow trees, the perfectly manicured hedges beyond skirting around the grounds of the estate. Opening the cage, Lena stroked her owl’s beak and watched her fly outside, knowing she’d be hunting all night, leaving the girl without a single friend at home.

 

            Holing herself up in her bedroom to stay out of trouble, Lena read by lamplight, reclining on her bed as the last few rays of sunlight slipped through gaps in the heavy emerald curtains, highlighting the ancient wooden furniture in the gloom. She could hear a blackbird singing in the garden and it was cold in her room, making Lena feel like she should open the windows to let in the warmer summer air beyond. But it was always cold in that house. Doors that were left ajar slammed, earning many punishments for Lena as a child until she learned to shut things behind her, the gutters clogged with rain in autumn and the damp seeping into the walls in winter, weeds cropping up in the gardens in spring. She’d always thought the house beautiful in a dark and disturbing way, the marble floor of the foyer betraying every step and whispered sound up to the vaulted ceiling, causing more punishments as her attempts to sneak about failed.

 

            She knew when her mother got home, the sound of the front door slamming shut announcing her arrival through the warren of corridors. It wasn’t long before Hope knocked on the tightly shut bedroom door and stepped inside, hunched with fear.

 

            “Mistress has asked to see you in her study, Miss.”

 

            Throat closing up, Lena set her book aside and sat up on the rumpled bedsheets. Taking a moment to run her hands over her creased shirt and pull the cuffs of her white cotton shirt down, she slipped her feet into her loafers and whispered for the House Elf to go to the kitchens and get started on dinner, hoping to dissuade her mother’s ire from the tiny servant. Her footsteps were loud on the wooden steps as she made her way down a servant’s stairwell to her mother’s office, lingering outside a moment before she steeled herself enough to knock, knowing it wouldn’t do to keep Lillian waiting.

 

            Her knuckles rapped on the polished wood and she waited for the sound of her mother’s voice. “Come in.”

 

            Opening the door, Lena stepped inside and eased it shut behind her. Crossing over to the wide mahogany desk, she stood before it and kept her eyes downturned, focused on the sheaves of paper littering the surface, covered with her mother’s neat script. 

 

            “Won’t you give your mother a kiss?” Lillian said with an edge of sarcasm.

 

            Balling her hands into fists, Lena rounded the desk and kissed her cheek, dry and powdery from her makeup. The sweet smell of it mingled with her perfume, a nauseating familiar thing that made Lena’s stomach squirm as she retreated back around to the front of the desk. 

 

            “All O’s again,” Lillian said, plucking Lena’s school report from amidst the ordered mess of her desk, peering down at the perfect grades and then dropping it. 

 

            She rooted through the other papers and pulled up a Potions essay, smoothing it down flat and clicking her tongue. “But a ninety-eight on your essay for a Shrinking Solution. This is rudimentary; I would have expected a hundred percent. You disappoint me.”

            

            “Professor Slughorn took a mark off for-”

 

            “I’m well aware of where you lost marks. Too many stirs in your instructions.”

 

            “But it makes the potion better,” Lena earnestly insisted.

 

            “It’s wrong .”

 

            “I know but-”

 

            “If there is a but , I hear nothing more than excuses,” Lillian drawled, dragging a thick, heavy book towards her as she flicked her fingers dismissively at her daughter. “Get the quill.”

 

            Clenching her teeth, Lena swallowed dryly, stubbornly arguing her point. “My mum’s instructions said an extra stir makes it more potent and-”

 

            Lillian shut her book and held it in a white-knuckled grip, rising from her seat to give herself more force as she slammed the thick tome down on Lena’s right hand, braced against the desk as she tried to make her case. A breathless sound of shock escaped Lena as immediate, white-hot pain filled her hand, the small bones of her fingers breaking as they were crushed beneath the weight and then pinned in place by Lillian.

 

            “I am your mother,” she coldly replied. “And you will obey my instructions.”
