            Fighting back, shallow, breathless sobs, telling herself not to make a sound, Lena stared at Lillian with watery eyes, her face grey with the nauseous urge to vomit over her mother’s papers. No doubt that would earn her an even worse punishment and Lena struggled to swallow as her gorge rose. This quiet part of Lillian’s anger had always been the most frightening for Lena as a child. She felt flayed by her own helplessness.

 

            “Do you understand?” Lillian asked.

 

            “Yes. Yes,” Lena hurriedly replied, a plea in her voice as her eyes filled with tears.

 

            A small, hitching sob escaped her and Lillian let out a withering sigh. Lifting the book, she freed her daughter’s hand and set the book down heavily to the side before sinking back down onto her chair. Welling tears overfilling, they splashed down onto the polished wood.

 

            “Don’t,” Lillian warned her. “Don’t look at me like that.”

 

            Cradling her hand to her stomach, Lena sniffed and pressed her lips together, trying to rein in her pain. With another sigh, Lillian held out her hand, crooking her fingers in an impatient, beckoning motion until Lena held out the trembling, slightly crooked fingers of her right hand. 

 

            “You know better than to provoke me with that woman,” Lillian chided her, smoothing her fingers along Lena’s hand, carefully turning it this way and that as she inspected it. “It’s very ungrateful, after everything I’ve done for you.”

 

            “I’m sorry,” Lena gasped, the pain in her fingers making her vision dim at the edges.

 

            “Of course you are,” Lilliam murmured, her voice softening to a croon as she cast non-verbal spells over her daughter’s hand, the light touch of her fingers almost tender as they glided down the lengths of Lena’s hand, straightening out the crooked extremities.

 

            It hurt like hell, and Lena’s hand shook in Lillian’s tight grip as she moved her other hand around, undoing the harm she’d caused. The pain faded after a few minutes, but the ghost of it lingered and Lena choked on another sob, swallowing it as her throat constricted around it. It hurt as well and she wished she could cry without earning her mother’s contempt.

 

            Rising from her seat as she kept a hold of her daughter’s hand, Lillian rounded the side of the desk and pulled Lena. “Come.”

 

            Tripping over her feet as she was tugged forward, Lena squeezed her eyes shut as Lillian let go of her hand and then wrapped an arm around her shoulders, pinning her against her chest. She was so small compared to her mother, her height increased by her heels as well, and Lena’s bottom lip trembled as her resolve crumpled and she let out a ragged sob. Lillian hushed her as she stroked Lena’s dark hair, a farce of maternal instinct.

 

            Sighing, Lillian let her sob into the front of her shirt for a few moments, a rare show of guilt as she tried to absolve her own conscience of the harm she’d inflicted. But she soon tired of Lena’s crying, her shirt damp from the tears and wrinkled where her daughter had gripped a handful of the thin cotton in her tight grasp.

 

            “Never again, do you hear me? You’ll not cry over silly hurts ever again. You must understand that there’s no room for failure,” Lillian said, cutting through Lena’s quiet sobs. “I’m not being cruel , but you’re too weak . You’ll thank me for it one day.”

 

            Lena didn’t think there would be a time when she would ever thank her mother for what she did. She could understand getting good grades at school, studying and working hard to get a good job, but Lillian’s casual violence was beyond that. The way she inflicted it with cool indifference was chilling and Lena took no comfort in her embrace, a cold, unfeeling thing that left her stiff with the anticipation of more pain.

 

            “Now, wipe your face and go to bed,” Lillian gently instructed her, pulling away. “We’ll chalk this up to a long day; we’ll revise tomorrow.”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            Lillian reached up and gripped Lena’s chin in a tight grasp, jerking her head up so Lena was forced to meet her piercing gaze, flat like a snake. Forcing down the lump in her throat, she pressed her lips into a flat line to stop her chin from wobbling. Turning her head to the side, Lillian pressed her lips to Lena’s cheek and then let go of her, brushing her hair behind her ear and smiling sharply.

 

            “Good girl.”

 

            Retreating to the safety of her bedroom, Lena curled up in bed, the blue light of dusk making her room feel cold and unwelcoming. It was too early for her to sleep and she hadn’t eaten since the train, a pumpkin pastie bought from the trolley and washed down with juice, but it was a punishment in its own right, no tray brought up for her and no disturbances. 

            

            Summer had quickly become Lena’s most dreaded time of the year, a time where childish freedom to explore the countryside and the nearby national park, to relax without school work for a few weeks, turned into something else. She’d been locked in the pitch black cellar three times so far after her mother’s overwhelming demands had left her stammering and confused, shoulders hunched in shame as she was cowed by a lengthy berating. Lillian didn’t touch her again but Lena scrawled those words into her arm on a near-daily basis, the pain no longer as sharp, having been dulled by years of familiarity. It was almost comforting in a way.

 

            Days became weeks and they passed into the tail-end of summer, night beginning to fall earlier and the dull autumn weather on the horizon, bringing a chill to the house that didn’t leave while Lena was still there. Wind beat the windows and whistled through cracks in the windows and under doorways, the fireplaces in every room lit to stave off the cold as they let out pools of heat that never spread far enough into the damp corners Lena lurked in. She traded her starched shirts and pinafores for knitted vests and tailored pants, feeling clammy but cold as fall sharply arrived, leaving her shivering beneath a sky gone a hard grey. When Lillian wasn’t home, leaving her locked in her bedroom, Lena stayed in bed and slept for hours, the House Elf sneaking her forbidden food and Morrigan bringing the occasional letter from Kara, which was safely stowed with the tied stacks of lines written over and over again, a mirror to her scar. She wrote back, keeping the worst of it to herself as she gave Kara vague snippets of her holidays and didn’t sign it.

 

            Lillian took her to Knockturn Alley for most of her supplies, striding down the narrow, dark streets with a haughty air of command about her. They had to go to Diagon Alley for a few things and Lena’s eyes strayed towards a shabby shop with the sign The Junk Shop , where Kara told her she’d gotten a job over the summer. She wondered if she could slip away for a minute, wind through the overcrowded, precariously stacked secondhand items to catch a glimpse of her friend, maybe even purchase some trivial item while they pretended not to know each other. The thought was thrilling.            

 

            She didn’t, of course, but Lena basked in the feeling of Diagon Alley anyway, free from the prison of a house. It was a breath of fresh air for her and Lena enjoyed the twisting alleys that connected different streets and districts of shops. There was something charming about it, perhaps the way the buildings didn’t match the height or face of the ones beside them, the irregularity of it making each one unique. Lena liked the ramshackle stalls and vendors and food stands, smoke drifting throughout, the tang of blood and animals and the spark of magic acrid to her nose. It was a taste of her inevitable freedom when she’d be able to come and go at her leisure, basking in the colourful riot of magic and people without the long shadow of her mother’s disapproval.

 

            It was still another week and a half before she was set to start her fourth year at Hogwarts and Lena was gloomy and surly as she impatiently waited. She yearned for the library and the open grounds, the dismal weather that meant she wasn’t at home, where the grass was green and she was locked indoors. She would take winter in the Scottish Highlands, with its snow and sleet and rain, over a mild summer day in Ireland, which was its own kind of sadness, so much hatred for her own country as a by-product of her mother’s hurt. 

 

            On the train ride back to school, she sat in the usual compartment with the dignified Slytherins in their new robes or pressed suits, shaking hands and recounting summers spent flying through the moors or valleys near their homes, camping in forests and overseas trips with their parents - various dignitaries and politicians. Lena sat undisturbed with her book, for the most part, a few comments thrown at her by Andrea Rojas and Veronica Sinclair, trying to goad her into reacting but ultimately ignored.

 

            After the Sorting Ceremony and a dinner that she picked at, her cheek propped up in her hand and a brooding air about her, Lena slipped away to the library, the hub of the castle in her mind. The doors opened to the sprawling space crammed with desks and shelves, absent the hushed noise of people whispering, crying, napping on sofas, Madam Pince organising books on a trolley while others floated around, organising themselves. In one of the far corners of the endless room, hidden behind a bookcase, was a forgotten reading room, a tiny alcove with a green lamp and a sagging leather armchair, and Lena sat for a while, breathing in the smell of dust and sweet ageing of paper until she retired to the Common Room.

 

            The next morning, she woke early and walked the labyrinthine corridors of the ancient castle, as if convincing herself that she was safe within the familiar stone walls. Its warren of corridors and ever-changing staircases left only a hazy impression of the castle’s true layout and Lena wished she could map it, uncover every secret as she got pleasantly lost, going from empty classroom to broom closet to trophy room to secret sitting room. Eventually, she made her way up to the Astronomy Tower, where she could look over the courtyards and gardens below, worn stone and wilting plants and dense woods of black maples and pines and the long pathway down to the iron gates enclosing them within the grounds.

 

            Making her way back downstairs, she took her breakfast outside with her, wedging bacon between slices of buttered bread and tomato sauce, and stepped off the path to walk across the slowing grass. The sky was a weak grey with clouds hanging low on the horizon and her whole body felt heavy with relief. She walked for a while, over stretches of the grounds until she reached the treeline and skirted the edges of the forest. Blackberry brambles clustered around the trunks of wide trees and she picked some to eat as she walked, breathing in the sweet decay smell of the forest as she filled her pockets and ate her sandwich. Pine needles crunched beneath her feet and weeds and vines snagged at her feet. 

 

            There were two new foals and Lena coaxed them forward with slivers of bacon from her sandwich, thinking that she should have brought more, and she felt a sense of peace as she sat with the Thestrals for a while, the morning lightening more until she was sure she was about to miss her classes. She went back to the castle and met her classmates at Greenhouse Four for her first lesson and all day she was filled with the anticipation of seeing Kara, eager for the soothing balm of her presence.

 

            It cut through her so keenly that when she arrived at the Astronomy Tower after dinner, Lena had the bizarre urge to hug her, cling to her and know that there was someone good in her life. Someone who would never hurt her.

 

 

            Winter passed by with grey, miserable weather. Slush congregated in the gutters and the lake welled up, colds sweeping through the students and Professors from the chill of the hallways and the outdoor lessons and Quidditch practices. Their birthdays and Christmas came and went and Kara struggled through the caseload of her O.W.L.s with the rest of her peers. 

 

            She’d dropped Care of Magical Creatures at the start of the year and taken up Arithmancy after coming to a decision at the start of the school year that she’d like to be an Unspeakable. She had a natural curiosity and an interest in unravelling mysteries and when Professor Sprout had sat her down to consider her future, she’d proposed it to Kara, who’d taken to it with surprising determination. While she loved her creatures, Kara would need the Arithmancy grades for her N.E.W.T.s and had a lot to catch up on.

 

            These days, she spent most of her time studying in the library with Querl, Alex, Kelly, Lucy and Imra. James had graduated last year and was now at an entry-level position at the Ministry of Magic in the Department of Magical Accidents and Catastrophes as a trainee member of the Accidental Magic Reversal Squad. Mike was always off playing Quidditch and coasting through on his average games, insisting that he’d be a professional Quidditch player once he graduated, so he was rarely around. Nia was a new First-Year who knew Winn, and she joined them wherever they went as well. Alex and Lucy were on the last leg of their Hogwarts education now and they always looked stressed and exhausted as they checked out stacks of books to rival the amount Kara knew Lena withdrew. If she wasn’t studying with her friends, she was studying with Lena instead.

 

            They’d spent hours together in their secret room trying to cast Patronus charms, thinking of their happiest memories to no avail. The truth was, Kara’s happiest memories were childish things, and then she’d been bitten and there hadn’t been very many of them since. Lena didn’t have any to begin with. Occasionally, they would set their homework aside and sit together, knees almost touching as they both grew too big to comfortably sit on the ledge together. Kara was taller than Alex now, who’d tapered off at 5’6, and she’d spent all of her hard-earned wages over the summer for a newer set of secondhand robes and some clothes, easing the financial burden on Eliza a little, but her ankles still showed beneath the hem of her corduroy pants when she crossed her legs.

 

            “Hey,” Kara said one evening, reaching forward for Lena’s hand as she toyed with the fingers on her right hand, an anxious mannerism she’d picked up in the last six months. 

 

            Lena flinched slightly but then relaxed, letting her hand go limp in Kara’s, sinking back against the wall. Kara toyed with her fingers and smiled crookedly. “Have you been writing too much?” she lightly teased. “Fingers hurting?”

 

            “Something like that,” Lena vaguely replied, her eyes half-lidded and then cutting to Kara as her lips curled with a wry smile.

 

            At fifteen, her quiet sullenness had turned into brooding sarcasm, and Kara occasionally found her heart spasming in her chest when they touched, when Lena looked at her just a moment too long. She didn’t know how to cope with it so she’d kissed Mike in the Quidditch changing rooms after they’d won their last game, and it had only served to confuse her further. But sitting there, toying with Lena’s fingers, she felt her stomach flutter and she resisted the urge to kiss her fingertips. 

 

            It was dark outside, grubby mounds of snow glowing white in the dark, the edges brown and slushy up close but looking picturesque at night time. A snowstorm had blown through at the start of the week and blanketed the castle, making it look like something out of a postcard, and Kara was glad to be back after the Christmas holidays, January already fading into February.

 

            “Going home for the next holidays too?” Lena asked.

 

            “Mhm. You know … you could come with me. My mum wouldn’t mind.”

 

            Lena let out a small laugh, “I couldn’t.”

 

            “No one would have to know.”

 

            A muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw and she pulled her hand back, hunching her shoulders as she sat cross-legged, her dark head ducked down. Lena traced over the rough lines of the fabric on her pants with her index finger, the thick wool warm and nubbly in places from wear. 

 

            “Are you okay?”

 

            “Yes,” Lena rasped, “I just- I don’t want to go home.”

 

            “Oh. Do you- is there anywhere else you can go?”

            

            Lena shook her head, her terror so plain to see that Kara’s stomach jolted with panic. 

 

            “Why do you hate going home so much?” Kara quietly asked, three years into their friendship and still at a loss about the things that haunted Lena, kept her up at night and left her pale and silent at times.

 

            Shrugging, Lena’s lips twisted with discontent. “It’s just better here.”

 

            “But why?”

 

            Frustrated, Lena scrubbed her fingers over her face and scalp, letting her nails drag across her skin. So was the cold as the chill stone beneath her burrowed into her, her clothes doing little to keep her from shivering.             “Why do you like being here so much?” Lena evasively countered.

 

            Kara’s mouth opened and closed and she swallowed thickly as she hesitated. “When I’m home,” she hoarsely started, “I’m not allowed out … when it’s a full moon. I … hurt myself.”

 

            As she spoke, Kara pushed up the sleeve of her sweater and the long-sleeved cotton shirt beneath, exposing the scar cutting across her forearm, the first of a few parallel lines. Lena’s eyes darted down to the silvery scars against her skin, almost luminescent in the dimness of the room, shiny and thin but permanent.

 

            Gesturing to her face, which burned with embarrassment, making the scars livid, Kara let out a strained laugh, a sheepish smile on her lips. “These are the better ones.”

            

            Lena reached out and cradled Kara’s forearm in her hands before the sleeve could be pulled back down. Allowing her left hand to take the weight, she traced her fingertip along the pale scar and Kara shivered, the blonde hairs standing on end. She jerked her arm back, pulling the sleeves down and drawing her knees to her chest, hugging them defensively. 

 

            Setting her hands back in her laugh, Lena pressed her lips into a flat line before eventually speaking, her voice a low rumble of unease. “Going home gives me scars too.”

            

            “Your mum-”

 

            “Mum,” Lena echoed with a scoff of laughter, her eyes darting to Kara, “look at you . We’re rubbing off on you.”

 

            Kara rolled her eyes but gave her a fleeting grin. “What’s she like? You never talk about her.”

 

            Shrugging, Lena shifted, getting more comfortable. “She’s just my mum. Sometimes she's nasty. Sometimes she can be nice.”

 

            “Do you love her?”

 

            “Of course,” Lena quickly replied. “She’s my mum. You … you should love your mum.”

 

            “No, you shouldn’t,” Kara murmured, “not if they’re not very nice.”

 

            “Do you love your mum? She wasn’t very nice to you.”

 

            Kara hesitated, her face clouding with conflicting feelings. “I guess so. But … I’m mad at her too.”

 

            “Yes,” Lena wearily sighed, rubbing her tired eyes. “I’m mad at my mum too.”

 

 

            The end of the year rapidly approached and Kara knew the first few grey hairs she spotted in the mirror one day weren’t because of the stress of her impending O.W.L.s. It was a shocking, bitter blow, not yet even seventeen and already showing the toll that lycanthropy was taking on her, aside from the scars. There wasn’t much she could do, except swallow the grief that filled her chest as she finished brushing her teeth and went about her day.

 

            Her first exam was Defence Against the Dark Arts, Kara’s best subject, aside from Herbology, and she felt confident coming out of it, flexing her stiff fingers and chatting with Querl as they escaped out into the early summer weather as it tilted towards warm. Puffy clouds trailed across the sky and Kara fretted about her other exams and wondered if they would even matter soon enough. Last week, Winn had been pulled out of Potions to the news that his mother had been killed in an attack, and in March, James and Kelly had received word that their dad had died fighting for the Order. Alex was even more determined to join up once she graduated, only weeks away now, and it filled Kara with anxious fear that her strong-headed sister would jump headfirst into trouble.

 

            Astronomy was next, and then Transfiguration, showcasing her talents by turning a Lovebird into a Lovenote and casting a successful Vanishing spell, much to her relief. She thought she did quite well, all things considered, especially on the practical side. History of Magic was her final one, sitting in the glow of the candlelit Great Hall and its ceiling displaying the day outside, the hour seeming to drag on indefinitely as the neat rows of students hunched over their papers and filled the space with the sound of scratching quills.

 

            Freedom and weightless relief greeted Kara as she left her final exam, and she spotted Lena leaning against a wall with the morning newspaper tucked under her arm, wearing her Slytherin scarf loosely draped around her neck as she smiled slightly. Kara’s heart thudded in her chest and she returned her smile, cocking her head to the side as her blue eyes shone behind her glasses. Setting off towards the dungeons, she kept a leisurely pace so Lena could catch up to her and they could pretend they were walking toward their respective Common Rooms.

 

            Stopping to pretend to stare out the window, Kara’s eyes tracked Lena as she passed her by. Tenderly, it seemed almost longingly, they smiled at one another, saying nothing as they passed by, so close that it had to have been intentional in the wide, empty hallway. And there, Kara’s fingers touched the back of Lena’s hand as she passed, making her jerk in surprise before catching her fingers.

            

            “How’d it go?” Lena murmured.

 

            “Good, I hope.”

 

            Lena nodded and sank down to her knees, pretending to fix the strap of her bag, while Kara continued to stare out the window. They spoke quietly, even though the hallways were empty, and when Lena straightened up, there was a folded butterfly note abandoned on the flagstones. Stooping down to pick it up, Kara didn’t have time to unfold the note before a voice called out.

 

            “Hey.”

 

            Kara looked up, her eyebrows rising slightly at the arrival of her sister in her rumpled robes, slinging her satchel across her chest and pocketing the butterfly. “Hey.”

 

            “How’d it go?”

 

            A smile curled Kara’s lips. “Better than I was hoping.”

 

            “Good.”

 

            “You?”

 

            “I’m ready to graduate,” Alex said, exhaling as her shoulders slumped and she grinned with excitement.

 

            Kara let out a quick laugh and she hugged her sister, a rare thing for them but the moment deserving of it, Alex returning it before slinging an arm around Kara’s shoulders and looking around the place.

 

            “I’m going to miss it here, I think.”

 

            “Yeah. It’s going to be weird without you next year.”

 

            “You’ll be fine. Just don’t go getting yourself into any trouble. I won’t be here to kick their ass for you.”

 

            Kara scoffed, shaking her head before she leaned into her sister. She was already a couple of inches taller, which Alex didn’t like, but it was funny to think about how much things had changed in a few short years. They’d gone through some uncomfortable growing and now the thought of not skimming rocks on the surface of the lake or sharing sweets from Hogsmeade as a group in a tucked away sitting room as they played Exploding Snap seemed weird.

 

            “Come on, why don’t you finally show me the kitchens before I leave for good?”

 

            “Okay, but you can’t tell anyone. It’s a proudly guarded Hufflepuff secret.”

 

            “Fair enough.”

 

            Escorting her to the corridor with the paintings of food lining the walls, Kara showed her where to tickle the pear to get into the kitchens and they ate jam tarts and profiteroles as Alex told her Maggie had broken up with her and Kara told her she wanted to be an Unspeakable at the Department of Mysteries. 

 

            The two of them sat together for a while as the House Elves worked around them and kept dropping off freshly baked desserts and pots of tea, and Alex took advantage of the abundance of food while she could. Eliza did the best that she could but there wasn’t enough money for them to eat as well as they did at Hogwarts, but Kara still had a lean edge to her thanks to her monthly transformations and her fluctuating appetite.

 

            When they didn’t think they could eat anything else, they went down to the Quidditch pitch with their friends and played what was the last game for a few of them, the afternoon waning as the sun started to set and they were all grass stained and muddy, breathlessly laughing and carrying their brooms. The warmth of the day filled the air with the sweet smell of grass and warm water and Kara breathed it all in, a pang of sadness for her sister as she imagined giving all of this up.

 

            The Seventh-Years graduated two weeks later, dressed in their robes and their pointed hats with family filling the Great Hall with the rest of the students - although a few were glaringly absent as the early days of the war took its toll. There was a feast afterwards and then a ball, and Kara slipped away after Mike had tried to convince her to dance with him on his last night at Hogwarts. She’d excused herself to get a glass of butterbeer and then kissed Eliza goodbye and vanished upstairs to the secret room, knowing Lena would be there because she didn’t have any graduating family so wasn’t invited to the graduation ball. She was there, of course, sitting near the window, her quill scratching across the pages of her book.

 

            She looked up at the sound of Kara’s shoes on stone. “Oh. Shouldn’t you be with your sister?”

 

            “She’s having fun with her friends,” Kara said, slowly drifting closer, almost hesitant. “And I had to escape the dancing.”

 

            “You don’t dance?”

 

            Kara choked on a laugh, giving Lena a droll look and burying her hands in the pockets of her robes. “Do I look like I dance?”

 

            “I don’t know. Maybe. I think if the right person asked you.”

 

            “Would you ask?”

 

            “Me? I’d rather not dance,” Lena snorted, closing her book and setting it aside. “There’s a reason why I prefer books to anything physical; two left feet.”

 

            “I don’t believe you,” Kara murmured.

 

            “No?”

 

            “Prove it. Dance with me.”

 

            Lena rolled her eyes and looked away as a huff of laughter escaped her. A wry smile twisted her lips and then her eyes cut back to Kara, piercing in the gloom. “With what music?”

 

            “Use your imagination.”

 

            Her voice was teasing and low and Lena hesitated before rising to her feet, smoothing a hand over her pressed trousers and then folding her arms over the thin knit of her sweater. “You’ll laugh at me.”

 

            “I won’t, I promise.”

 

            “When I trip and fall, then?”

 

            “I won’t let you fall.”

 

            Wariness crept into the lines of Lena’s face and she hummed a moment before Kara took a slow step towards her, holding out a hand. Hesitating, Lena’s lips twitched slightly and her eyes shuttered before she softly sighed.

 

            Her hand was cool in Kara’s as she drew her forward, and Kara splayed her fingers across Lena’s back, feeling her ribs, her spine, and the warmth of her as they stood close together. They’d gotten comfortable around each other over the last four years, their touches no longer self-conscious fleeting things but lingering, familiar. After that first hug where Kara had nearly bowled Lena over, she’d hugged her goodbye before every holiday and Lena had grown used to it with a frightening yearning for more. 

 

            And now, slow dancing to no music, pressed close, they were drawn to each other. The air was thick with anticipation and Kara let her forehead fall against Lena’s, the two of them swaying, not so much dancing but neither of them minded. Her throat closed up with the painful ache to kiss Lena, and she could feel her breath ghosting over her lips, shallow and warm. She was going to kiss her, Kara could see how inevitable it was, the anticipation of it making her pulse stutter and her lips part. 

 

            And then they slowly swayed back so she was facing the window, catching a glimpse of her reflection against the dark window panes out of the corner of her eye. It was like being doused in cold water, her pale reflection, inches taller than Lena, and the breath caught in Kara’s throat as she closed her eyes and pulled back slightly. The poor werewolf would never be good enough for the beautiful rich girl and it was a bitter realisation to swallow.

 

            She pecked her on the cheek instead and then wrapped her in a brief hug before letting her go. Lena looked at her with sharp confusion as Kara cleared her throat and gave her a wavering smile. Reaching up to fix her ponytail, Kara ducked her head slightly.

 

            “I might have an early night.”

 

            “Oh. Okay, um …”

 

            “Have a good summer, yeah?” Kara murmured, her chest hurting as she avoided Lena’s eyes.

 

            Lena let out a choked laugh, slightly breathless with disbelief. “Mm, I’m sure I will,” she dryly replied. 

 

            Kara cringed slightly, her cheeks heating as she rubbed the back of her neck. “Okay, well … I’ll miss you.”

Chapter 12

            Kara didn’t see Lena again before the holidays started and it left her feeling uncertain about the awkward way they’d left things. Mostly silent on the train ride home, her knees hugged to her chest as she brooded, picking at the stitching on the seat cover, she said goodbye to her friends once they pulled into the station, hugging them before following Alex off in search of Eliza as they towed their trunks and she cradled Bastet in one arm.

 

            Back at home, she unpacked her clothes and let the cat roam freely and then sat on the edge of her bed, fiddling with the refolded butterfly note Lena had dropped for her. Alex was making a mess of her side of the room and paused in between tossing out old essays and broken quills to glance over at Kara.

 

            “What’s the matter with you?”

 

            “What? Nothing,” Kara quickly replied, looking guilty over nothing.

 

            “You’ve been acting weird all day.”

 

            “Oh. Just … worried about N.E.W.T.s, I guess.”

 

            Alex’s shoulders slumped as she gave her sister a sceptical look. “Really? Do you think I’m that daft? You’re worried about school when your summer holidays have just started? Out with it.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Kara flopped back on her bed, staring up at the ceiling and letting out a heavy sigh. “How do you know if you like someone?” Kara blurted out.

 

            Letting out a snort of laughter, Alex crossed the narrow gap between their beds and sat down on Kara’s, jostling the mattress. “Really? That’s what’s bothering you? Who is it? Mike?”

 

            “Will you stop going on about Mike,” Kara exasperatedly replied. “He’s … I don’t know. He’s a bit boring, isn’t he?”

 

            “You could do worse than boring.”

 

            “Because I’m a werewolf and no one will ever want to go out with me?”

 

            “What? No. I just mean, well … he’s alright, isn’t he? He’d be nice to you, so you should give it a go.”

 

            But Kara was scared of the idea of being rejected by Lena, of seeing a flicker of condescending amusement in green eyes at the idea that she would ever like Kara, or even worse, the disgusted rejection because of her lycanthropy. In the end, she resolved to keep her feelings for Lena to herself and pursue alternative options.

 

            She worked at The Junk Shop almost every day to make some extra money, standing amidst the dusty shelves and old pieces, shelves of worn books and stacks of battered trunks and lamps that brightened and dimmed with the trajectory of the sun, Sneakoscopes and burnished telescopes and all manner of cauldrons and Hogwarts uniforms donated by the sackful at the end of each school year. Things were bad that summer and they’d been raided a few times, Kara hiding in a cupboard as the shop was trashed and items were damaged, dark figures with silver masks setting fires all along the street as the windows burst and a few unlucky souls were killed in the attacks.

 

            It didn’t stop Kara from working there though, despite her mother and sister trying to talk her out of it. Truthfully, they needed the money, and Kara took pride in buying herself a new pair of sturdy leather boots, a little big at the toe but enough room for her to grow into before she stopped. It was Eliza’s birthday as well, and Kara splurged on a gold ring for her, a little sapphire set into the band. It wasn’t much, but it felt good to afford something nice with her own hard-earned money, and she was always coming home with trinkets for her mother and sister, handing Alex battered vinyls and Eliza tiny plant clippings bought at The Harpy’s Bazar .

 

            It wasn’t that Kara earned a lot, but that she didn’t have to spend money on herself, so she saved it for gifts and her Hogwarts supplies for her Sixth-Year. In the end, she took Alex’s advice down to the word and borrowed Maximus to write Mike a letter, which led to more letters. He started to meet her every day after her shift, apparating into Diagon Alley to take her to Florean Fortescue’s for ice cream on the days when things seemed normal, or butterbeer and pea soup at The Leaky Cauldron , kissing her goodbye until, eventually, she let him take her home to his house while his parents were at work. 

 

            Afterwards, she stared up at the ceiling and confessed she was a werewolf when he asked about all of her scars, glad her poor eyesight spared her seeing his expression. He stopped meeting her the last week before school started, sending her an owl saying he was busy with his training regime as he tried to get scouted for one of the Quidditch league teams. Kara didn’t mind; she’d just wanted to know what it felt like to be wanted by someone. Just once.

 

            It made her quiet and brooding for the last week of the holidays, and she could’ve told Alex but kept it to herself instead. It was confusing for Kara; she didn’t even like Mike like that, and he hadn’t been the one she’d wanted to kiss, but he’d been there and interested and Kara didn’t really care what he thought about her. She hadn’t stuck around long enough to find out if the abundance of scars repulsed him, to make him promise not to tell anyone. She’d just gone home instead and had to deal with her sister’s antics as she struggled to contain it all.

 

            “You’re miserable today, aren’t you?”

 

            “Stop,” Kara mumbled as Alex pushed her socked foot against her arm.

 

            “Merlin, is that- grey hair?” Alex exclaimed, sitting on the kitchen counters as she drank a glass of water after a day of Auror training, the last rays of sunlight slanting in to highlight the undeniably grey streak in her sister’s hair.

 

            She jumped down and grabbed Kara’s head in her hands, pulling her head down to eye it as Kara slapped at her hands, cheeks flaming, and came up looking dishevelled and pissed. Eliza let out an exasperated sound of annoyance.

 

            “Alex, leave your sister alone.”

 

            “Mum,” Alex pressed, “she has grey hairs. She’s not even seventeen.”

 

            “It’s fine,” Kara mumbled, rubbing at her red cheek, a silvery scar livid against her evident embarrassment.

 

            Eliza frowned though, slinging the tea towel over her shoulder and rounding the table, beckoning for Kara to come to her. She cradled her head in her hands, infinitely gentler than Alex had been as she tilted her head down and caught the offending strand of hair in her fingers. Smoothing it back into place, Eliza squeezed Kara’s face between her palms in an affectionate manner, although her smile didn’t reach her worried blue eyes.

 

            Kara covered a hand with her own and gave Eliza a tight smile. “Mum, it’s fine.”

 

            Nodding, Eliza pulled her hand free and then swiped it through her hair, grey at the temples and peppered throughout the rest of the blonde. “I got my first grey hair when I was twenty-five. We all go grey early in this family.”

 

            They all knew it was a side effect of lycanthropy but Kara let Eliza lump her in with the long line of Danvers as if she was one of them, grateful for her comfort all the same. She’d started calling her mum last year, the word just slipping out when they’d been home for Easter and Kara had asked Alex where she was. They’d frozen but Kara didn’t make any excuses for it, and they quickly got used to it, the word feeling different to Kara than mom did, decidedly British and separate from the woman who’d abandoned her.

 

            Still, that night, Kara stood in the tiny bathroom and combed her fingers through her hair, taking in the few silvery strands, knowing it would get worse. She was tired. Each month sapped more of her strength and carved up more of her body when she was forced to go to St. Mungo’s, and there were still times she wanted to curl up into a ball and sob. 

 

 

            Lena despised being back home again, her hatred increasing with each passing year, every summer bringing fresh torture to her as she was forced to abide by her mother’s rules as her brother drifted further and further away from the person he’d been in her childhood. This time, he picked her up from the station with a shaved head that made him look oddly skeletal and severe, a cold, haughtiness to his face that Lena didn’t like.

 

            They’d barely gotten back home before he’d grabbed her arm in a tight grip, eliciting a small gasp of affronted pain as she turned around and wrenched her arm back. Lex was indifferent to her as he unbuttoned the cuff of his starched shirt.

 

            “Look,” Lex said, an almost manic grin on his face as he pulled his left sleeve up over his forearm.

 

            The pale skin was marked with a symbol that seemed to be everywhere these days, above houses of freshly dead Muggleborns and Muggles, people deemed threats or traitors or half-breeds. A black skull with a snake coming out of its mouth, twisted in a loop. It made Lena's stomach twist with horror and she quickly looked up at Lex, her expression unreadable. 

 

            “You joined.”

 

            “It’s eye-opening,” he feverishly gushed, “the way he explains it all. We’re downtrodden, made weak by keeping ourselves hidden from the Muggles. But he’s going to change all of that and we’ll have so much power. He’s already doing so much for our kind.”

 

            “Yes,” Lena replied, her brow furrowing, “killing people.”

 

            Lex waved a hand dismissively, “he’s just thinning out the traitors, the ones in charge who are trying to keep us pinned down. You’ll see. You should join once you’re out of school. He’d love how smart you are; just think about what you could help him achieve.”

 

            “He probably wouldn’t let me join,” Lena scoffed, trying to be evasive in light of Lex’s manic behaviour. “I’m a Half-Blood.”

 

            “Oh, well, don’t worry about that. He let Snape join and rumour has it his dad was a Muggle. At least your mum was a Muggleborn witch. And the Luthor family can trace our lineage all the way back to Salazar Slytherin, just like the Dark Lord. Think about that - we’re technically related.”

 

            That wasn’t true, it was just something their dad used to tell them, a sort of bedtime story of the great power of the Luthor family and the generations of Slytherins who’d gone through Hogwarts. Lena had believed him, of course, until she’d read through a genealogy book in the untouched library and traced their family back too many generations with no sign of Salazar Slytherin anywhere in there. When she’d tried to bring it up at dinner, her father had split her lip with the signet ring he wore with the force of his slap.

            

            “Right,” Lena slowly murmured. “Maybe. I doubt mum would let me though.”

 

            “Oh, she would. I don’t know why she doesn’t join herself . She believes in his ideology as much as the rest of us; it’s almost insulting for her to sit there and let us all risk our lives for her rights. Reaping the benefits of it while she’s busy at the hospital. But not you; you’re not a coward, are you?”

 

            “No,” she whispered, although she didn’t believe that herself. “I, uh, I should study before she gets home. She’ll want to quiz me.”

 

            As she’d guessed, Lillian did quiz her, arriving home late after a long shift, the faint tang of the hospital clinging to her coat when she swept into Lena’s room, curtly beckoning her without further greeting. Lena had been studying at her desk, revising the Seventh-Year and beyond magic that Lillian would unfairly test her on when she hadn’t even started her O.W.L.s yet. 

 

            Following her mother downstairs, Lena stood in the living room and recited Potion ingredients and lists of runes, answered questions about Alchemy, which she hadn’t even studied yet, and wouldn’t for another year, her voice flat and monotone as she stood rooted to the spot, careful not to fidget. It didn’t matter though; her mother was full of criticisms, from the way she enunciated certain spells, to the way her shoulders slumped as the evening dragged on, to the way Lena jutted her chin forward in a look that Lillian said was arrogant. Then there were the questions themselves, endless as she got each one right, an hour passing by and then two, and the more, Lena’s eyes burning as the clock inched towards midnight.

 

            “You’re yawning. Pathetic . How do you expect to conduct twelve-hour healing sessions on the worst injuries and curses you’ve ever seen? Hm? You can’t even stay awake to answer a few measly questions.”

 

            “I’ll probably drink coffee,” Lena couldn’t help but retort, cranky after a sleepless night in wake of coming home, “or perhaps sleep.”

 

            Lillian’s gaze was cutting and Lena clenched her teeth, a muscle flexing in her jaw as she swallowed, her whole body already tensed for what came next as the tendons stood rigid at her neck. But Lena wasn’t frightened; what would she do? Make her write lines? She’d been doing that since she was eight, the words so ingrained in her skin that she thought they must be bone-deep by now. Would she break the fingers of her hand again? Lena wouldn’t cry this time.

 

            “You’ve inherited your worst qualities from your mother,” Lillian said with contempt. “Including your attitude .”

 

            Her disappointment bored into Lena, who remained frozen, gripping the folds of her skirt until her knuckles whitened with the effort. This was the point where Lillian became dangerous, her disdain for her daughter plain as she rose from her seat, setting her glass of Firewhiskey down on the coffee table and rising to her full height. She had a hand in the pocket of her flared pants, no doubt fingering her wand, and Lena quickly looked down at the rug as her mother’s heels sounded her slow, lazy approach.

 

            “Do you think I do this because I enjoy it?” Lillian asked.

 

            Lena didn’t reply, keeping her jaw clenched shut and her eyes cast downwards. Normally silence was the best way to go when dealing with her mother, but now it only served to fan the flames of Lillian’s cold disapproval. Her sullen scowl betrayed her true feelings though, not quite schooled into the blank look of indifference she usually tried to keep in place. If she looked up, Lillian would be able to read her daughter’s opinion of her clearly in her eyes.

 

            “I asked you a question, Lena. Stop this ridiculous petulance and answer me.”

 

            Gripping her arm, her skin clammy at her lower back, anticipating the cutting sting of the quill, Lena swallowed, her throat dry. Her voice was hoarse when she replied, brittle and haughty. “What would you like me to say?”

 

            Lillian glared at her. “I’ve grown weary of your insolence.”

 

            Looking up, she smiled wanly, a mere twitch of her lips and a haunted look on her face as she met her mother’s eyes, a challenge there. “I’ll get the quill.”

 

            Her mother let out a bark of disbelieving laughter before her expression turned livid. Lena backed up a moment too late as Lillian lunged forward, grabbing a fistful of her daughter’s dark hair, and yanking down to tilt her head up. Lena’s breaths turned quick and shallow as her heart pounded in her chest.

 

            “You think you’re so clever? You think this is amusing?”

 

            Lena’s bottom lip trembled then, betraying the flicker of fear as she wondered if perhaps she’d underestimated her mother. Of course, Lena knew the worst parts of her, all the ways she’d hurt her daughter, but now she doubted if that was the worst of it, if perhaps Lillian had been lenient with her punishments. But what could be worse than what she’d already done to her?

 

            “I’ll knock that smug look off your face and we’ll see how funny it really is,” Lillian harshly continued, dragging Lena along with her by a handful of her hair, leaving her daughter scrambling to keep up with her long steps as her scalp prickled with pain.

 

            Propelling her over to the steps leading down to the dark cellar, where Lena had spent many nights curled up on the freezing, damp stone floor, hungry and with wet cheeks as her arm stung, Lillian all but dragged her down the steps as Lena tried to twist out of her grasp. 

 

            “Let me go,” Lena said through her teeth, her voice rough with panic as she dug her nails into her mother’s arms, trying to make her stop.

 

            “You will not defy me,” Lillian hissed, ducking her head close to Lena’s as she said it, before shoving her forward and letting her go.

 

            Stumbling down the last couple of steps, Lena caught herself on the door as the air rushed out of her lungs. Lillian waved a hand to open the door and Lena fell over the threshold, the dank smell of the cellar greeting her with that old fear of dark places. She thought her nights spent down there would have numbed her to the cold, ominous feeling of the space, but each time it made her skin prickle with unease and this time was no different.

 

            “Your lack of manners is appalling,” Lillian continued, her voice harsh and derisive. “That school has done nothing but make you soft. Weak. I should have fought your father harder on sending you to Ilvermorny - even Beauxbatons would have been better. That’s Dumbledore and his soft teaching for you; you would have benefited from a good slap and fewer meals.”

 

            She grabbed the shoulder of Lena’s shirt and forced her further inside, sending her sprawling, arms windmilling for balance as a cold sweat crept over her skin. Turning slowly, hunched like a cornered animal, her hand twitched for her wand but she wasn’t seventeen yet. It would be certain expulsion to curse her mother, and Hogwarts was the only reprieve Lena had from the hell of her home. Curling her hands into fists, she surrendered to her fate and let it happen.

 

            The door slammed shut a moment later and Lena launched herself at it, numbing the sides of her fists as she pounded on the aged wood and wordlessly shouted. Her chest hurt from the panic and her clothes were too thin for the chill of the draughty space as it seeped into her, making her stiff and shivering. It wasn’t long before her mother returned with her brother. He was shorter than her and Lena had never truly been afraid of him - until now.

 

            It was the way he held himself, his average build seeming broad and tense as he filled the doorway with his dark form. His face was hidden by the shadows but Lena could feel the grim malice emanating from him as he stepped inside, Lillian lingering in the doorway, backlit by the weak light filtering down from upstairs.

 

            “Dad had a specific knack for instilling respect in us, but it seems you’ve forgotten that. I guess that’s what growing up without a father does to a person, but that’s no way to speak to your mother.”

 

            “Lex,” Lena whispered, the sound a ragged plea.

 

            Squinting through the dark, she watched him toy with his wand, nervous despite his resolute approach. Even then, she still didn’t quite believe that her brother would hurt her - not badly. But then the word spilt from his lips, too gentle for the evil behind it.

 

            “Crucio.”

 

            The spell hit her squarely in the chest, illuminating the cellar for a brief moment before Lena’s face was wrenched with agony. Her legs buckled and a ragged sound of pain escaped her before it cut off, leaving her chest rising and falling with panicked breaths as she struggled to fill her lungs, her body in shock.

 

            “No, that won’t do,” Lillian clicked her tongue, “you have to feel it, mean it. Try again.”

 

            He did it again. Blinding white pain slammed into her, driving her down to the floor, her knees scraping against the stone as she hunched over on all fours. All of his resentment and anger and glee was put into it, and later she would go over the fact that he seemed to enjoy it. Her brother who’d read her The Tales of Beedle The Bard and helped her catch garden gnomes liked the sound of her ragged screams that she couldn’t quite swallow. He did it again and again, Lillian vanishing somewhere upstairs to let him enact her punishment. 

 

            She let it hurt until it couldn’t hurt anymore.

 

 

            Kara’s sixth year started without her sister, dropped off at Platform Nine and Three-Quarters by Eliza, who hugged her goodbye and held her for a brief moment longer, dark times making everyone fear every goodbye would be the last one. It was the start of her N.E.W.T.s and she was apprehensive about how difficult her classes were about to get, although she’d done quite well in her O.W.L.s - Outstanding in Herbology and Defence Against the Dark Arts and Exceeds Expectations in everything else. This year, she’d be able to drop History of Magic and free up some extra time for studying.

 

            Climbing onto the train just before eleven o’clock, noticing it was less crowded than usual as students were withdrawn out of fear, she worked her way down the narrow corridor to her usual compartment. Sliding open the door, Kara watched as five pairs of eyes turned to face her, all of her friends sitting back in unison as they tried to pretend like they hadn’t just been gossiping. Stepping inside, Kara pushed her satchel onto the rack above their heads and took a seat beside Querl.

 

            “Hi. Good summer, yeah?” she asked, her eyes moving from face to face. 

 

            They all exchanged looks with each other and Querl’s hair changed from pure white to a violet shade that Kara knew signified worry. He seemed a little agitated as he ran his thumb over the edge of his letter.

 

            “Did I miss something?”

 

            “Is it true?” Imra asked, cocking her head to the side as she stared at Kara.

 

            “What?”

 

            “Mike told us.”

 

            Kara flushed slightly as she shifted, “Mike told you what?”

 

            There were multiple things she didn’t want him sharing, and while she realistically knew one could ruin her life infinitely more than the other, to an embarrassed teenager, one was as important as the other. Kelly gave her a strained smile, reaching across to touch her fingers to the knee of Kara’s pants.

 

            “He sent Querl a letter.”

 

            It was the letter in her friend’s hands and Kara quickly plucked it from him before he could stop her. Her eyes scanned the messy writing, trying to make sense of it all.

 

            “That word is transformation,” Querl whispered, pointing it out.

 

            Kara blanched and then let out a strained laugh, letting the letter flutter back into Querl’s lap. “He told you I’m a werewolf?”

 

            “I saw him at The Leaky Cauldron as well,” Imra said, “he said the same thing.”

 

            “Mike’s not smart enough to figure that out for himself,” Kelly scoffed.

 

            Rubbing her scarred cheek, Kara spent an agonising moment deliberating before she swallowed. “He didn’t figure it out; I told him.”

 

            There was a tense moment as her words settled over the compartment. Looking at her with pitying dark eyes, Kelly’s mouth thinned slightly. “So … it’s true?”

 

            “Yeah. Yeah, it’s true,” Kara whispered.

 

            “Oh. Well … are you okay?”

 

            A shuddering laugh of bewilderment escaped Kara as she closed her eyes and tipped her head back against the padded train bench. “Not really.”

 

            No one spoke for a moment and Kara opened her eyes, climbing to her feet. “I think I’m going to go and-“

 

            “Wait,” Winn said, throwing his arm out to stop her. “We don’t mind.”

 

            Blinking, Kara’s expression clouded with confusion. “What?”

 

            “We’re not going to tell anyone,” Nia chimed in. “You’re our friend.”

 

            Sinking back down onto the seat, it took Kara a moment to absorb it. She’d thought Lena was a one-off acceptance, that no one outside of her or Alex or Eliza would feel kindly towards her kind, and she’d spent years on the outskirts of the friend group, knowing it was a tentative thing hinging on one big secret. Apparently that had all been for nothing.

 

            “Oh. Okay.”

 

            “I can’t believe you told Mike first,” Querl said, sounding a little put out.

 

            “Oh, uh, we, uh, I saw him a couple of times over the holidays.”

 

            No one said anything to that, although there were telling looks and Kara couldn’t bring herself to explain how they were right but it wasn’t like that . In the end, she settled down, sharing Nia’s box of Bertie Bott’s Every Flavour Beans and watching the scenery roll by until it got too dark to see much. They were talking about the war and Barty Crouch, who’d taken over the Department of Magical Law Enforcement, making headway in the war, as James reported back to Kelly. Things were looking grim and the anonymous Death Eaters were more elusive than the Ministry liked, although the Order of the Phoenix were similarly just as anonymous and elusive and were doing their own work in counter-terrorism.

 

            After the Sorting Ceremony and feast that night, she deliberated over going to see Lena, eager to see her again but wary after the way things had left off. She couldn’t help but feel like Lena would be able to see right through her and it made Kara flustered as she paced up and down the steps to the tower before ultimately going back to her Common Room, seeking solace in the round room, practically overgrown with plants and comfortable sofas, the warm stone giving the place a homely feeling as she sat tucked away in a corner with Bastet curled up on her lap.

 

            She saw Lena the next night, knowing she couldn’t stay away from her for long. Her footsteps announced her arrival long before she rounded the cramped room but Lena still didn’t look up when she approached, and it made Kara’s stomach tie itself into knots, wondering if Lena was mad at her for the almost kiss. Surely she’d known, surely it had been written on Kara’s face, as plain as day.

 

            “Hi,” she murmured, hesitating before sinking down onto the window seat. 

 

            “Hi,” Lena replied, staring out the window as she avoided looking at her. 

 

            Kara nudged her shoe with her knee, a wavering smile on her lips. “How’re you?”

 

            “Fine.”

 

            “How were the holidays?”

 

            Lena shrugged and Kara felt her stomach sink with dismay. Her throat closed up and her mouth went dry as she scrambled for something else to say, something that would provoke a response. And then her eyes landed on the badge pinned to Lena’s robes. She blinked in surprise - Lena hadn’t mentioned that in her letters.

 

            “Oh! Prefect. Congratulations, you must be thrilled.”

 

            Shrugging again, Lena made a vague sound of agreement at the back of her throat, but sounded anything other than thrilled. Sitting silently for a moment, Kara rubbed her forehead, smoothing out the furrowed crease of confusion.

 

            “Look, I know that things … it was weird before the holidays, but did I- did I do something or …?”

 

            That caught Lena’s attention, her head sharply turning to look at her, her green eyes jaded as her lips twisted ruefully. “What could you have done?” she asked, her tone gentle but patronising.

 

            Gesturing helplessly, Kara shook her head, mystified. “I don’t know.”

 

            But then she got a good look at Lena, at how pale she was, at the dark circles beneath her eyes. Lips twisting into a crooked smile, Kara’s shoulders slumped and she raised her eyebrows slightly. “You look tired; do you even sleep anymore, or do you sit up all night reading?”

 

            Reaching up, Lena touched her fingers to the circles beneath her eyes and hummed in agreement. “Something like that.”

 

            Kara didn’t need to know they were old bruises covered with makeup from a broken nose hastily healed two nights before. It didn’t even hurt much anymore, unless she touched it. Dropping her hand, Lena turned her attention back to beyond the window, the dark night not offering much of a distraction.

 

            “So … O.W.L.s.” Kara continued, “how’re you feeling about them?”

 

            Rolling her eyes as she started to thaw in the presence of her thread, Lena gave her an exasperated look. “Like they’re a bit overdue. I could’ve done them years ago. I should be done with this place; I could be … somewhere else.”

 

            “Why didn’t you try to graduate earlier?”

 

            “My mum didn’t think there was much point if I couldn’t do magic outside of school. And she thinks I need to emotionally mature first. That’s what all her lessons are for.”

 

            Lena couldn’t keep the bitterness out of her voice but Kara couldn’t have known the real reason for it. All she knew was that Lena’s mum made her study a lot, that because of her, Lena preferred to be at Hogwarts instead.

 

            “Well, she must be proud of you. I bet you’re going to get all O’s.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena’s eyes were hard as her lips twitched derisively. “Of course I will. I wouldn’t be allowed to get anything lower. It won’t make her proud though; it’s expected . And even that won’t be good enough really.”

 

            Shifting closer to her, Kara frowned, “hey, it will be.”

 

            Turning her head aside and twisting her torso, Lena leaned into the window, away from her. Kara inched closer, wary as she watched Lena tense, the lines of her curled-up body taut, wondering what was so awful that she’d react like that, like she was frightened of Kara.

 

            “Maybe- maybe you were born into a family that doesn’t appreciate you but … one day things are going to be very different.”

 

            “You can’t know that.”

 

            “I do,” Kara softly insisted, touching her knee. “We- we don’t have to stay here. We can go wherever we want. I can- I can get a place when I graduate, and you can come and stay with me over the holidays. You won’t have to go back home again if you don’t want to.”

 

            Turning her head slightly, glancing sideways at Kara, Lena’s mouth flattened and uncertainty crossed her face. “I couldn’t-“

 

            “I would want you to. I- you’re my best friend, I- I-“ Kara faltered, looking down at her hand on Lena’s knee before she swallowed and hoarsely continued. “Come here.”

 

            Her voice lowered to a whisper and she reached for Lena, who shifted away from the window, allowing Kara to wrap her arms around her. They sat there for a moment, neither of them speaking as they revelled in the feeling of each other, the comfort of each other’s company, and Kara had a distinct feeling that if she wasn’t so stoic, Lena would be crying. She felt like she had to tell her it was okay.

 

            “You can cry, you know.”

 

            “Why would I cry? I’m not in any pain.”

 

            Kara frowned slightly, her chin on Lena’s shoulder. “You don’t have to be in pain to cry.”

 

            “Just … don’t let go,” Lena rasped, and that was all the explanation Kara needed to know that she was in pain, just not physically - not anymore.

 

            “I won’t.”

 

 

            Kara turned seventeen and opened the worn velvet box delivered by Maximus to reveal a battered leather watch with a face bearing the phases of the moon instead of numbers. It made her stomach twist with loathing for her condition but the watch itself was a beautifully touching gift and she quickly buckled it onto her wrist, the soft leather wrinkled with previous use and fitting comfortably on her arm. Alex gifted her a camera, a compact black and silver thing with a flash bulb on the front and a pack of film rolls and a developing potion. Kara tested it out on Bastet, the black cat playing with the brown paper the gifts were wrapped in.

 

            There were cards too and other presents from her friends, who were there to celebrate her birthday with her, and Lena gave her a gift that night, another velvet box handed out by the shy girl who’d snuck away in Diagon Alley to find the perfect present for a special birthday. Lillian had been angry when she’d found her; Lena had spent the night in the cellar again, slipping the box out of her pocket to stroke the velvet, knowing she would’ve done it again for the price of no dinner and a cold, sleepless night.

 

            “Happy birthday,” she said as Kara opened the box, revealing a gold necklace with a moonstone set in gold hanging from it.

 

            Kara touched her fingertips to the moonstone and felt her throat close up with affection. No one had ever bought her something so nice, something brand new and expensive and all for her. In her hand-me-down clothes that had been enlarged numerous times and were ill-fitting and thin from years of wear, it felt like the most expensive thing in the world to her. 

 

            “It’s beautiful. Thank you.”

 

            “It’s a moonstone,” Lena explained. “I thought- well, the moon is beautiful, even when it’s full, and I know … you don’t like it, but I saw it and I thought of you.”

 

            “I love it,” Kara shyly smiled. “Help me put it on?”

 

            Nodding, Lena plucked it from the box and Kara turned, scooping her curls up in one hand to expose her neck. Standing close behind her, her fingers brushed the back of Kara’s neck, gentle and cool, making goosebumps creep across Kara’s skin. Lena fastened it quickly and Kara let her hair back down, turning to smile at her as she touched the pendant.

 

            “How is it?”

 

            “Beautiful.”

 

            Stepping in, Kara wrapped her in a hug, “thank you.”

 

            Lena made a strained, dismissive sound at the back of her throat before giving Kara’s cheek a quick peck and pulling back. They shared crooked smiles and then Kara showed her the camera she’d been gifted by Alex, insisting that Lena let her take her photo to develop. Kara did it later that night, dipping it into the potion with the others she’d taken that morning and watching Lena’s rosy-cheeked embarrassment as she smiled and then held a hand up, turning away from the flash of the camera, shy.

 

            After that, Kara took as many opportunities to photograph her as she could, carrying the camera around with her everywhere. It wasn’t just Lena that she took photos of, but everything at Hogwarts, from her friends to the castle and ghosts and Quidditch games, the Thestrals when she went with Lena again, managing to sneak a shot of her friend petting one, and the owlery when she went to send her weekly letter to Eliza and Alex. She developed them all and was pleased to look at them, to see a vibrant life at school, despite the torture that crept up on her every month.

 

            Lena turned sixteen and Kara bought her a quill that was more expensive than she could really afford, but she’d just have to skip lunch on the Hogwarts Express on the trips back and forth home for the holidays. It was worth it to see Lena’s bright smile as she unwrapped the diary as well, Kara thinking that perhaps she could make good use of it for her troubled thoughts, just like Eliza had done for her when she’d first started school. It was beginning to worry Kara, the brooding discontent within her friend that made her fear for what was to come. Was it just her family, or was it this war? Lena was kind and Kara didn’t think for a second that she’d ever be on the side of bad people, like the rest of her House, but she knew the Dark Lord was manipulative and Lena was a prize. More than anything, she just wanted to keep her friend safe, wishing they could hide up in their tower and let it all pass them by in peace.

 

            The first Hogsmeade visit came around with a smaller turnout than usual, with a lot of students opting to stay within the safety of the castle grounds as things worsened. It was a near-daily thing for a teacher to pull a student out of class, or for a letter to arrive, breaking the news of a family member’s death. Every letter that came for Kara, she felt a brief buzz of panic at what would be inside it. Alex had joined the Order of the Phoenix the second she’d left school, tight-lipped about what she was getting up to but coming home dirty and tired, staying out late and occasionally wincing and limping as she got ready for Auror training the next day. She worried she’d get a letter from Eliza saying she’d been killed during one of her scraps with the Death Eaters. Or maybe it would be Eliza, visiting Diagon Alley during one of the increasingly frequent raids and attacks.

 

            Word never came and so she ventured down to the little magical town to meet Lena, as they’d done every month since that first one. But Alex wasn’t at school anymore so it would look odd if Kara was getting tea with her sister, who undoubtedly would not apparate into Hogsmeade to get a cup of tea with her sister. They’d migrated from Madam Puddifoot’s to a lesser used pub, The Hog’s Head , and were served by a surly barkeeper with piercing, strangely familiar blue eyes, as they nursed dusty bottles of Butterbeer with Lena appearing to be a dark-haired boy with light brown skin and dark eyes. It was Querl’s real appearance, Metamorphmagus powers aside, and no one ever bothered them there, with mostly older locals sitting in dingy corners. 

 

            Kara would occasionally touch her hand across the worn table and counted out her Knuts to buy them another round, that odd feeling in her stomach as she tried to reconcile her friend with her other friend who didn’t even know about her. Lena confessed that she’d stolen a hair from him during Chess Club and used it in her Polyjuice Potion stores; Kara had known it was her the moment she’d walked into the pub. She thought she would recognise Lena anywhere, in any disguise, so tuned into her mannerisms that they were as familiar to her as her own.

 

 

            A few weeks before the Christmas holidays, things drastically changed for Lena, and she wasn’t sure if things would ever be the same again.

 

            After Charms, she was making her way to the library for a free study period and spotted a certain Hufflepuff walking down an empty corridor near the library and felt warmth bloom in her chest. Lena coveted the rare moments in public when they were together, even if it was just passing each other in the hallways, and she quickened her pace to catch up. She came up behind Kara and tugged on the end of her ponytail, a smirk on her lips as her eyes slid sideways at her, falling into step. Lena didn’t even have time to murmur a quick hello and continue on her way before a loud shout sounded behind her.

 

            “Oi! Leave her alone.”

 

            Turning, mild surprise crossing her face, Lena wasn’t quick enough to draw her wand before she was blown backwards off her feet, forced back a dozen feet until she slammed into the stone floor of the corridor. Her head painfully bounced against the flagstones and she bit into her tongue hard enough to draw blood, black spots dancing across her vision for a moment. 

 

            Blinking as she struggled to sit up, hot anger lashed through Lena and she slipped her wand into her hand, the polished ivy smooth in her grasp as she pushed herself to her feet, green eyes sharp with danger.

 

            “Winn,” Kara barked, panicked and surprised. “Don’t.”

 

            While Kara was busy staring at the group of her friends who’d just rounded the corner of the corridor, leaving the library at a slower pace than she had, Lena stepped out from behind her willowy form and pointed her wand at the mousy Seventh-Year in Ravenclaw robes. Swallowing the mouthful of blood, she bared her teeth as she cast a non-verbal stunning spell, shooting straight past Kara, who stumbled to the side with wide eyes.

 

            Winn blocked it and sent a disarming spell back, a volley of sparks flying back and forth. It quickly became three against one, Imra and Nia pulling out their wands while Kelly and Querl tried to talk them down. Kara did the same to Lena, bearing down on her, the solid bulk of her Beater’s body helping her wrap her arms around Lena as she propelled her backwards.

 

            “Please,” Kara whispered. 

 

            Lena shoved back against her, a hard look of anger on her face, her eyes flitting over Kara’s face as she looked at her with wounded betrayal. Then Kara’s head snapped back, a burst of blood splattering on Lena’s face, muffled curses slipping past the hands that Kara cupped over her face, doubling over. Glancing over her shoulder, Lena watched as Andrea Rojas lowered her wand and sauntered forward.

 

            She set off an Ear-Shrivelling curse, which caught Imra, who clapped her hands over her ears, and then pointed her wand at Kara, who straightened up with a scowl on her scarred face. Blanching, Kara dropped her hands from her face and whipped her wand out of her pocket, pointing it at the Seventh-Year Slytherin. Lena pushed Andrea out of the way as Kara hexed her, taking it in the face, which went numb with pain as if she’d been punched. She watched realisation dawn on Kara’s face, her wand arm lowering and her lips parting, an apology already on the tip of her tongue.

 

            Ignoring her, Lena turned her attention to the group behind, Winn already halfway through mouthing a spell. Her stomach jolted with panic and Lena plucked a spell she’d never used from the list in her mind, one that the Slytherins had been passing around at the end of the last school year, which hadn’t been used as far as Lena knew.

 

            “Sectumsempra,” Lena cried as she made a cutting motion with her wand, watching as the spell struck Winn in the chest.

 

            He staggered backwards and went down, his face deathly pale as red blossomed on the front of his rumpled school shirt. Everyone froze and even Lena paused, her wand arm lowering as dread pooled in her stomach. She took a step forward, her legs numb as she almost tripped herself up, but a hand grabbed a fistful of her robe and dragged her away.

 

            Twisting in Andrea’s grasp, Lena’s bottom lip trembled as she managed to keep walking, hauled away by the Seventh-Year who was giving her a sideways glance of renewed interest. At the next girl's bathroom, Andrea pushed her inside and over to a stall, anticipating what the green tinge to the young girl’s face meant. She nudged Lena’s knees out from under her. They bit into the tiled floor and Lena managed to catch the edge of the toilet before she vomited up her breakfast.

 

            “Merlin, Luthor.”

 

            “I’m sorry.”

 

            “It’s fine … you’re in deep shit though. I didn’t know you were so ruthless.”

 

            Lena made a rasping hum at the back of her throat, wondering if this was worthy of expulsion or a lot of detention. It wouldn’t matter who had started it; House rivalries were a bitter thing that transcended their time at Hogwarts and she knew those reputations were to blame for Kara’s friends lashing out at the mere sight of her even touching their friend. 

 

            Leaning against the door, Andrea watched her for a few minutes until Lena climbed to her feet and closed the lid of the toilet, pulling the chain and swallowing, the bitter taste of bile and blood mingling on her tongue. She walked over to the porcelain sinks and washed her hands, keeping her head ducked down, and then dried them off before Andrea grabbed a few more from the dispenser and wet them. Lena blinked as the older girl grabbed her face in a tight grasp and tutted, muttering in Spanish as she wiped the flecks of Kara’s blood from Lena’s cheeks and chin.

 

            Tossing the damp paper towels in the bin, Andrea clapped a hand on Lena’s shoulder and then tilted her head to the side. “Come on, then. May as well await our punishments in comfort.”

 

            Brow furrowing, Lena walked towards the door and hesitated as she opened it. “Thanks, by the way.”

 

            “You know, if you’d bothered to make any friends, you would know that Housemates stick together. Especially against the Gryffindors; nasty pieces of work all dressed up as courageous for being twats to anyone wearing green.”

 

            Lena let out a hoarse bark of laughter and rubbed her eyes, her tongue thick in her mouth and stinging. Dishevelled and tense, she followed Andrea back to their Common Room and tried to slip off to her room, before the hood of her robe was snagged and Andrea bodily manoeuvred her towards her group of friends monopolising the sofas and armchairs by the wide hearth. 

 

            Veronica set down the copy of Witch Weekly that she was leafing through and turned her head, still in Gayle’s lap, to watch them approach. Half a dozen eyes latched onto Lena with interest and Andrea let her go as she stepped over Gayle’s legs, slipping between the sofa and the cluttered coffee table.

 

            “Who’s this?” Veronica drawled, although they all knew very well who Lena was. 

 

            “A stray,” Andrea almost purred, stroking Lena’s cheek and chuckling as she walked over to a sofa and sprawled on the cushions. Lena scoffed, her lips twitching as she shook her head.

 

            Her Housemates welcomed her with a few handshakes and hellos - Slytherins were nothing if not dignified - and she sat back in an armchair, her legs crossed at the knee and her chin propped up in her hand as she brooded. 

 

            “Go on then, Luthor,” Veronica called out, raising her eyebrows as she grinned. “What’s your deal?”

 

            “My deal?” Lena snorted, her lips twisting.

 

            “We’ve been in school together for five years and this is the first conversation we’ve ever had.”

 

            Letting out a quiet huff of laughter, Lena narrowed her eyes slightly. “I just prefer to spend my time studying.”

 

            “Surely you’ve read every book in the bloody place by now,” Gayle rolled her eyes.

 

            “Almost.”

 

            “Why the sudden change of heart? Realised you’d leave school with no friends if you turned your nose up at us, hm?” Veronica goadingly asked.

 

            Gesturing to Andrea, Lena’s mouth turned into a wry smile. “I didn’t have much say in the matter.”

 

            “Caught her duelling with a bunch of the other houses. You remember James Olsen and Alex Danvers? Pretty sure it was their sisters and some of their friends,” Andrea said. “Luthor got one of them nicely, that’s for sure. Think twice before getting on her bad side, darling.”

 

            “I always thought she had a bit of a dark streak, that one,” Veronica said, giving Lena a sly wink.

 

            Shifting uncomfortably, Lena ran her clammy palms over her thighs, her eyes shifting evasively around the opulent Common Room as she waited. It wasn’t long before Professor Slughorn stepped inside, a harried look on his face as he scanned the room. He was usually cheerfully bumbling but now he looked like he was regretting his career choice as a teacher, having to deal with students' duelling and other hassles.

 

            “Miss Luthor,” he wearily called out as he spotted her amidst the group. “Miss Rojas.”

 

            Andrea let out a theatrical sigh and gave Lena a quick wink before standing with a dramatic flourish. Lena was more subdued as she followed after her, small and sheepish in her shadow.

 

            “Well, I can’t say I’m surprised at you duelling, Andrea Rojas, but this is a first for you, Miss Luthor,” he babbled as he escorted them out of the Common Room. “A tiresome matter which reflects badly on your House. Very badly indeed, girls. Especially from my prized Prefect. Come along then; Professor Dumbledore’s asked to see you in his office.”

 

            “Honestly, Professor, it wasn’t even fair odds. If we weren’t such good duellers, we’d probably be in the Hospital Wing by now. Lena got hit with a stinging hex to the face.”

 

            “Is that so?” he murmured, peering at her face. 

 

            Lena had regained the feeling already but she self-consciously rubbed at her cheek, humming with disconcertion. He continued on with his lecture then, and Lena viewed him as a sort of kindly grandfather, having no experience with them herself, and was content to let him continue his spiel about dignity and respect.

 

            They reached a statue of a gargoyle, innocuous considering they were in Gargoyle Corridor, and Lena patiently waited for Slughorn to give the password, which turned out to be Ice Mice after the sweets Lena had seen at Honeydukes .
