The gargoyle revealed a twisting staircase that carried them upwards and they came to a stop at a door, where Slughorn knocked and they were admitted.

 

            “Thank you, Horace,” Dumbledore greeted him, waving them inside. 

 

            They weren’t the only ones there, the cluttered office feeling cramped by the sheer amount of people filling the space. Professor McGonagall, Professor Sprout and Professor Flitwick, bring all the Heads together, as well as Kara, Kelly, Imra, Querl and Nia. They were standing or sitting depending on seat availability, and Lena stood beside Andrea as she gripped her left arm, her thumb stroking over the words through her robes.

 

            “Ordinarily, I would leave it up to the Heads of your Houses to determine punishments, but considering the severity of the duel, I’d like to hear what transpired from each of you beforehand. Who would like to go first?”

 

            “I was just defending my Housemate, sir,” Andrea piped up first, “she was outnumbered six to one.”

 

            “Kelly and Querl weren’t duelling,” Kara murmured, her voice sounding thick and slow. “They were trying to stop us.”

 

            Nodding, Professor Dumbledore dismissed the two students, who were quick to make their exits, before continuing. Kara rubbed at her slightly swollen nose as she haltingly interjected, supplying facts or correcting Imra and Nia. 

 

            “Winn started it.”

 

            “No, I was trying to stop them.”

 

            “Yes, I cast a stinging hex. It hit Lena in the face.”

 

            In the end, they all got a week of detention, except for Lena, who was slapped with a month. She hadn’t started it but she thought it was fair, standing pale and meek as she winced with the thought of carving up the Ravenclaw boy without a second thought. Her Latin was good, but she hadn’t even considered the translation - to cut always - it had just been a spell doing the rounds, courtesy of Snape.

 

            “You may go,” Dumbledore gravely informed them, the group of students making for the door. Lena stiffened as she continued. “Except for you, Miss Luthor.”

 

            Turning, Lena felt sick as she walked back over to his desk, standing in front of him with her eyes trained on the carved wood. All of the Heads left as well, except for Professor McGonagall, his Deputy, and she couldn’t bring herself to meet the Headmaster’s piercing pale stare.

 

            “Please, sit.”

 

            She sank down onto an overstuffed chair and fiddled with the silver snake ring on her index finger, her hands trembling. 

 

            “Your teachers speak very highly of your skill, Miss Luthor,” Dumbledore started, his voice soft and curious as he appraised the small girl across from him. “No doubt you’ll earn perfect grades on your O.W.L.s - with the right guidance. Professor McGonagall thinks you’d potentially even earn higher grades than our N.E.W.T. students, which is very high praise indeed.”

 

            Ducking her head, the flattery going straight over her head, despite the truth to his words. She felt decidedly undeserving of it and couldn’t look up from her lap.

 

            “Look at me,” Dumbledore gently ordered her.

 

            She stared at her lap for a few moments before peering up through her lashes and then raising her head. Swallowing thickly, her green eyes full of fear and apprehension, she licked her lips, the taste of blood lingering at the back of her throat as she tried to make her voice work.

 

            “I didn’t mean to-”

 

            “You’re not in any further trouble, and you have no need to convince me of your sincerity,” he cut her off, raising a withered hand to silence her. “Quite the opposite, in fact. I feel I must do my due diligence in providing the best opportunities for my students, and your potential is too great to waste, and too valuable for the Dark Lord to ignore for long.”

 

            Lena’s gaze sharpened at the mention of him. Her mouth went dry and she grit her teeth, twisting her robes in her hands.

 

            “Professor Slughorn tells me you’d like to be a Healer after school. It’s a very noble profession, to dedicate your life to helping other people. Perhaps … there would be another way to help people as well.”

 

            Professor McGonagall was tight-lipped with disapproval but remained silent. They’d clearly argued about this before but Professor Dumbledore seemed unaffected by her objection to his plan.

 

            “If you were interested.”

 

            Looking up at him again, Lena’s brow furrowed with confusion, but she hesitantly nodded. He smiled slightly, and nodded in return as he steepled his fingers, leaning closer to her across the desk. Lena studied the elaborate embroidery of his robes as she looked down from his half-moon glasses.

 

            A jolt of surprise made Lena’s stomach lurch as she looked up, meeting his eyes for a quick moment. “You mean … you want me to fight the Dark Lord?”

 

            He smiled slightly, gesturing with his hand. “Perhaps not as directly as you may be thinking; you’re too young at any rate. There are those who do fight, skilled duellers - of which I’m assured you’re quite adept - but … I think you could help in a different way. One which would be invaluable to us.”

 

            She didn’t speak, confused and nervous before him as she fiddled with her ring and trembled slightly from the adrenaline of the moment. Raising his white eyebrows and giving her a stern look down the length of his nose, Dumbledore gave her an expectant look that she knew was a test. Lena was good at tests.

 

            “Tell me, Lena, your brother … do you know if he’s joined Lord Voldemort?”

 

            She flinched at the name and couldn’t speak, settling for a quick nod as she looked away. 

 

            “You’re certain? It’s imperative that you’re sure. He’ll be a danger to many people if he’s chosen to join Lord Voldemort.”

 

            “Yes,” she whispered. “I’ve seen his Dark Mark.”

 

            Nodding, Dumbledore glanced at Professor McGonagall, “she’ll do quite nicely, I think, Minerva.”

 

            Whatever Professor McGonagall’s thoughts, she didn’t express them in front of her student. Turning his attention back to her, Professor Dumbledore leaned back in his seat and gave her an appraising look.

 

            “I’m in need of people inside the enemy’s circle. I need people with the ear of Death Eaters and their plans, and I think you would be a good fit.”

 

            Lena looked pale and frightened as she slowly shook her head, her hand covering her forearm, the thought of another mark there chilling. “No, I- I don’t- I don’t want to become one of them.”

 

            He held up a hand to placate her, “I wouldn’t ask you to become one, only ingratiate yourself with your brother, some of your fellow Housemates, anyone you think might have some insight into valuable information. I’ve been attempting to gather information on my former student for years, to learn what his plans are, and what he will do next. He’s very clever, to perhaps even rival yourself, and everything he does is deliberate and with purpose, even if that purpose is for his own satisfaction. So far, I’ve been unsuccessful in my attempts to infiltrate his circle but I believe you would make a good candidate.”

 

            “You want me to … be a spy?” she asked.

 

            “I suppose so,” he said with thin amusement. “You wouldn’t be allowed to tell anyone. Not even your closest friend. For all intents and purposes, you would be on the Dark Lord’s side, a loyal servant without the mark. You’re too young for him to take any interest in you yet; that would change once you finished with school, but in the meantime, you could gather information and report it to us. Anything, even the most minuscule detail could be the difference between someone dying at his hand. You could help save people, in a different way to being a Healer, but no less important. No one would be allowed to know of your bravery, and you’d have to compromise yourself and your morals on occasion, but it would be for the greater good.”

 

            “I- but … how?”

 

            “It’ll be difficult for you to attain anything of substance while at Hogwarts, but even rumours are valuable to us. If you kept an ear out around your Housemates and reported back to me, or Professor McGonagall, it would be a big help. A very big help. Write letters to your brother, question him when you go home for Christmas, over the summer. Find out which of your Housemates have family members who have joined Lord Voldemort.”

 

            Chewing on her lip, Lena considered it for a moment. “What if … I say no?”

 

            “Then I hope you understand I’ll have to wipe your memories of this conversation for the safety of others. But, if you do wish to aid us, as an outside source that even the majority of our network won’t know about, you’ll be a force for good, helping to put a stop to this war.”

 

            Hesitating, Lena felt her throat constrict as her heart pounded in her chest. But he’d known exactly where to press to convince her, coercing her with the idea of being seen as good , of being a hero on the right side of the war. He didn’t tell her that she’d be hated for it, that she’d risk her life and do horrible things that would make her hate herself. Dumbledore was looking at the bigger picture and she was a tiny, infinitesimal thread in the intricate plot he’d woven. Lena was nothing, she was disposable, and if anything happened to her, no one would even know what she’d been doing. Barely sixteen, she only understood a sliver of how convoluted the whole idea was but she was angry, she was smart, and she was frightened of her mother and her brother and what the Dark Lord would mean for her if things got worse.

 

            “Okay. Yes, I’ll do it.”

 

 

            Kara paced back and forth in the cramped room in the Astronomy Tower. Her hair was in disarray from the number of times she’d raked her hand through her curls, her face almost pale enough to rival her pallor on a full moon, which was still weeks away yet, and she waited for Lena to come. She undoubtedly would . 

 

            It wasn’t long before she heard the scuff of shoes and turned to meet her, already bearing down on the weary figure of her friend, who pulled up short. Understanding welled in Lena’s eyes and her lips curled into a wry smile as she let out a quiet huff. Kara didn’t speak as bewilderment crumpled her scarred face.

 

            “Go on,” Lena quietly urged her. 

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Kara stared at her at a loss, spreading her hands helplessly. “Why- you hurt him. Badly. I- why would you do that?”

 

            A sour taste filled Lena’s mouth and a prickle of anger towards her friend bloomed in her chest. “Me? He attacked me. You attacked me.”

 

            Kara blanched and quickly took a step forward, reaching out for her, her fingertips just managing to graze Lena’s cheek before her friend jerked herself backwards, a scornful look on her face. “I didn’t mean to hit you.”

 

            “Just Andrea?”

 

            Stammering as her mouth opened and closed, Kara looked appropriately ashamed as her lips twisted ruefully. “I’m sorry. It all just … got a bit out of hand.”

 

            “Yes, it did,” Lena curtly agreed. “But I will not be made to feel bad for defending myself. You want to blame someone? Fine , blame your friends. ”

 

            “She broke my fucking nose,” Kara exclaimed, making a cutting motion with her hand.

 

            Lena turned her brooding eyes to Kara’s face as she pouted, annoyed as she crossed her arms over her chest. Madam Pomfrey had clearly seen to it; it looked the same as ever, just perhaps a little pinker than usual from the ordeal.

 

            “You hexed my face.”

 

            “I didn’t mean to-”

 

            “But you did. So how is that any better?”

 

            “Are you seriously defending her?” Kara spluttered. “I thought you didn’t like any of the people in your House. I thought I was your friend.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Lena’s eyebrows furrowed together as she smiled uncertainly, cocking her head to the side. “You are , but … you didn’t even defend me. She’s not my friend but she had my back, but you- you’re my friend and you let me face them alone .”

 

            “I tried to stop them,” Kara gravelly insisted, a bright sheen in her eyes as she curled her fingers into fists, resisting the urge to reach out for Lena. “I never would have let them hurt you.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena gave her a bitter sneer, so much scorn in her expression that it drove the breath from Kara’s lungs. “No, you’ll just do it yourself, won’t you?”

 

            With that, she turned and stalked out, leaving Kara devastated as her mouth opened and closed without anything coming out. By the time Christmas rolled around a few weeks later, Lena hadn’t spoken to her since and Kara didn’t have the opportunity to question what she was doing when she saw her friend climbing into a carriage to go home for the holidays. 

Chapter 13

            Lena arrived home to an empty house, lugging her trunk through King’s Cross Station and flagging down the Knight Bus with the others travelling via the purple triple-decker. She sat at the back, Morrigan’s cage clutched tightly in a white-knuckled grasp as the chairs careened about with alarming danger, until the bus eventually emerged on a narrow country road in the Irish countryside. It was familiar, but a mile away from the manor house, at least. Lena would have to walk.

 

            It was already getting late and she staggered along the rutted road, poorly maintained with only a few adventurous campers and the like heading out on the dirt track in their big cars. Lena had seen them on occasion, or the farmers with their trucks and their sheepdogs in the back, tending to their cattle on the dairy farms. None of them crossed her path now so she dragged her trunk alone and let Morrigan free to save her the uncomfortable journey home in the confines of her cage.

 

            There was the faintest sliver of daylight lingering on the horizon when Lena reached the gate, touching her hand to it and watching them open on creaking hinges, the sound loud in the stillness of the night. She was tired and it was freezing, her robes doing little to keep out the bitter wind of the Irish moors. Moonlight highlighted the unwelcoming house and her feet crunched the gravel of the path to the front door, where she steeled herself and knocked.

 

            Hope answered it, surprise making her voice squeakier as she pulled the door open wider to admit Lena to the foyer. Her trunk was whisked away upstairs and she turned, pale and haughty, to watch as Lillian stepped out of the living room. 

 

            “You’re home,” she commented, out of character, seeing as her mother hated unhelpful statements.

 

            “I thought I could make better use of my time here,” she replied, the words scraping her throat as she forced them out, pale and stiff and wishing she was anywhere else.

 

            Nodding, Lillian gestured her into the dining room and followed after her. Hope brought a shallow bowl of soup, which Lena listlessly spooned into her mouth in the wan glow of the dimmed chandelier overhead. She kept her head ducked down over her food, sitting rigidly as Lillian idly tapped a pointed nail on the lacquered wood. The room was airy and frigid in the winter, reminding Lena of the damp wintry months spent at home before Hogwarts. 

 

            Despite Christmas being days away, there wasn’t a single solitary sign of the holidays present in the house. No cinnamon and nutmeg perfuming the air, no pine trees decorated with ornaments, no mistletoe and boughs of holly or wrapped gifts in the corner. It’s how it had always been for her, a childhood absent of laughter and love and family. She’d been given gifts - too many of them when Lionel had been alive - but they were set at the foot of her bed by Hope, with no fuss and none of the magic of Christmas. Lena ached for Hogwarts.

 

            “How are classes?”

 

            She glanced up at her mother, setting her spoon down against the rim of the bowl as she softly cleared her throat. “Fine.”

 

            “Your essay on Confundus charms could have been better.”

 

            “It was one mark off perfect.”

 

            “Professor Flitwick has always been an easy grader,” Lillian sniffed. “It could have been better.”

 

            Ducking her head back down, Lena’s mouth tightened at the corner and she wanted to fling her bowl of soup. Instead, she picked up her spoon and scooped up a small amount of soup, trying to pretend that she was even remotely hungry. Her stomach was in knots, her throat dry and the nauseous unease of being home stole any appetite that might have filled her. 

 

            “You’ll write a new one for me before tomorrow morning. I have work early; I’ll read it at breakfast.”

 

            Nodding, Lena forced down her mouthful. After a few minutes, Lillian cleared her throat and pushed the chair back, leaving her to finish her meal alone. The second she was out of the room, Lena let the spoon clatter into the bowl and nudged it away. Wiping her mouth on her napkin she set it down on the table and stood up, pushing the chair back in and slipping out of the room.

 

            Upstairs, she ran a scalding bath in the enamel tub in the room adjacent to her bedroom. Sinking into the steaming water, stinging against the chill that made her skin ripple with goosebumps, she gripped the side of it and closed her eyes, her chest rising and falling quickly as she steeled herself and then slipped underwater. Lena hated being submerged, hated the panicked tightness in her chest at the feeling of being unable to breathe, the burning of her lungs as she squeezed her eyes shut and gripped the edge of the tub.

 

            It warmed her through though, and she washed off the muck of the damp walk home through stagnant puddles of frigid water that had spattered her with thin mud. Her skin was pink when she emerged, her dark hair dripping as she dried her face and stared at her wan reflection in the steamed mirror. Pulling on emerald green flannelette pyjamas and thick socks, and a thick dressing gown and slippers on top to fend off the cold and dampness, she pulled the desk chair out and pulled a blank roll of parchment towards herself. Finding a quill and a pot of ink, she unscrewed the lid and dipped the nib into the dark liquid, hesitating before she started to write.

 

            It wasn’t her essay, it was a fleeting letter to Kara to send off with her Christmas present - a novel that she’d found in Hogsmeade called Hairy Snout, Human Heart by an anonymous author. It was a story about lycanthropy and Lena had read it first, intrigued by the humanising of the monstrous disease, although she’d never viewed it as such. She wanted to know how it felt to be Kara, how it felt to have your skin shred and bones splinter every month, the weakening feeling of the full moon creeping up on her. Lena felt just a little bit broken for Kara once she’d finished reading it. 

 

            They hadn’t talked in the weeks leading up to Christmas and it left Lena feeling surly and unbalanced. Since the very start of school, Kara had been a constant, her one friend in it all while she shrugged off the company of others, but things had been growing increasingly tense and uncomfortable between them over the last six months. It had started before the end of Lena’s fourth year, when she’d thought - just for a brief, fleeting moment - that Kara was going to kiss her. Only she didn’t, and Lena had to stifle the confusing disappointment that welled up inside when she’d pulled away and hadn’t left her since.

 

            Setting her letter aside for when Morrigan got back, Lena started on the essay for her mother. Her eyes were itching and her fingers cramping from the small, tight script filling the lengths of parchment. She knew better than to skimp on the detail or make her writing bigger to make it seem like she’d written more. Lena’s arm used to sting from the blood quill punishment for her shortcuts, until she learnt to try her hardest to mitigate the pain.

 

            Now, the quill didn’t hurt so much. She’d gotten used to it, numbed herself to the prickle of pain as the words cut themselves open again and again, unaffected as she filled pages with the same sentence over and over. It was the other spells now, the torture so casually inflicted upon her, the occasional broken bone when it went too far. Sometimes she felt a phantom pain in her jaw from over the summer, when Lex had broken it and Lillian had healed it after letting her suffer through a day of blinding agony. It had been healed properly, of course, but Lena sometimes still thought she could feel the ghost of it.

 

            A large part of her was apprehensive, being home over the holidays and opening herself up to more opportunities to get hurt, but she had work to do. She stayed up until the early hours of the morning, scattered pages drying across her desk as ink stained her fingertips and her shoulders ached from hunching over for so long. Stealing a few hours of sleep, she stuck a pin in the burning candle on the nightstand so it would drop and wake her up before Lillian was awake, yawning and rubbing her eyes as she walked downstairs in the pitch black with a sheath of papers in her hand, slippers scuffing the floor.

 

            Her mother came down ten minutes later, sitting at the head of the table with the silver tray bearing her breakfast brought in by the tiny House Elf. The top of a boiled egg had been cut off and Lillian sipped her coffee, skimming through Lena’s essay with quick cutting motions of her pale snake eyes.

 

            “Better,” she determined before climbing to her feet and heading off to work.

 

            Before she swept out of the room, she threw the pages into the crackling fireplace, a dismissive act, as if it hadn’t taken Lena hours to write, staying up until the early hours of the morning as she wished for bed. 

 

            She left without another word and Lena swallowed her resentment and went back up to bed, sleeping away half of the day, until her bedroom door was abruptly opened. Scowling as she pushed herself up, blearily blinking through the grey daylight seeping past the heavy curtains. Lex smirked as he crossed his arms over his chest, the trim black suit and severely shaved head ageing him, despite being only twenty-three, still so young for malice to have twisted him so much.

 

            “You are home,” he said in greeting. “I thought mum was joking when she said you were.”

 

            Lena had never come home for any holidays except the summer, in contrast to her brother who’d come home every time. It hadn’t even been mentioned before, no letters asking if she was coming the first Christmas in her first year, no lamenting about her missing out. It had just been assumed, the inconvenience of her done away with by leaving her holed away at the boarding school.

 

            She threw a pillow at him and scoffs, “I’m trying to sleep.”

 

            He caught the pillow and sauntered further inside as Lena pressed her face into the remaining pillows. Pulling the blankets back as he hummed a tune, Lex laughed as she kicked out, the heavy blankets shaken out from the movement before he reached down and pulled her hair. It stung at the roots and Lena slapped his hand away as she turned, her eyes blazing as she staggered onto her knees. 

 

            Laughing, Lex’s hand shot out and grabbed her throat, squeezing tight as Lena made a soft choking sound of surprise. “You’re no fun anymore,” he complained.

 

            He let her go, and for a brief moment, her neck bore the imprint of his fingers before fading away. Falling back, Lena raked the hair out of her face and pressed the heels of her palms into her eyes, wide away now.

 

            “Merlin, do you have to be such an arse?”

 

            “I was only coming to see if you wanted to thrash me at chess, but if you’re going to be sour about it …”

 

            Hesitating, Lena looked up at him, lowering her hands. “Don’t you have more important things to be doing?”

 

            He shrugged nonchalantly, grinning with his hands in his pockets. “I’m meeting Lockwood and Graves tonight, so not until then.”

 

            “Drinking at The White Wyvern again?” she snorted.

 

            Winking, a slow smile spread across his face. “Something more important than that.”

 

            She tried to pretend that she wasn’t leaping at the opportunity to coax more information out of him and feigned a heavy sigh - which wasn’t entirely fake - before climbing out of bed and slipping her cold feet into her soft slippers. Fetching her dressing gown, she pulled it on and tied it tightly at the waist.

 

            “One game,” she reluctantly agreed, “and only to make sure you haven’t forgotten how good I am.”

 

            Chuckling as he clapped a hand on her shoulder, Lex kissed the side of her head. “I’ve missed you.”

 

            Lena doubted that but she replied similarly, making her way downstairs and taking a seat before the marble chess set she’d first learnt on. Trying to prolong their time together as she sipped the hot tea Hope brought her and eyed the board, tapping her lip as she considered her moves, Lena let the conversation flow easily between them as she fell into her sulky little sister role and let Lex boast and condescend, his smugness almost insufferable.

 

            Afterwards, she went upstairs and penned a letter to the Headmaster and watched Morrigan fly away. 

 

 

            Kara spent her Christmas trying to convince Alex to vouch for her to join the Order, to no avail. Her sister insisted that she wasn’t allowed to join, that she was too young, still at school. But things were getting worse and their other friends had joined. James had been the first, older than them all, and then Alex afterwards, James vouching for her the moment she’d graduated. Why shouldn’t Kara be allowed to join? She was seventeen, she was legally an adult.

 

            Eliza agreed with Alex though, gently but firmly telling her she couldn’t join, she had school to think about, she’d be safe at Hogwarts. But two nights before she was due to head back to Hogwarts, she heard her mum and her sister arguing in the living room, trying to keep their voices down as Kara lay stretched out on her narrow bed. Creeping to the top of the carpeted stairs, she sat and eavesdropped and felt her stomach lurch with guilt.

 

            “Everyone is dying. It’s too dangerous to stay,” Alex said, trying to keep her voice down.

 

            “I have no other choice.”

 

            “Yes, you do. Go back home. Wisconsin is safer than here; the war hasn’t spread that far.”

 

            She heard Eliza let out a weary sigh, “Kara has school. The whole reason why we moved here was because Ilvermorny wouldn’t take her back; there’s nowhere else for her to go.”

 

            “Who cares about school? This is about your lives!”

 

            “Even if I wanted to, I can’t afford it . I spent all the money from our old house on buying this place, and I can’t afford to do it again, Alex.”

 

            Alex let out a spluttering cough and Kara could envision her clearly, her indignation and frustration. “And what about when he comes here? You won’t be able to stop him.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Eliza softly sighed and Kara leaned forward at the top of the stairs, straining her sensitive hearing to catch her mother’s response. “Now, what would the Dark Lord want with a poor herbalist? Some gillyweed to grow gills?”

 

            Her mother’s humour didn’t go over well with Alex. She made a few choice comments and stormed out of the living room, pausing at the bottom of the stairs as her eyes drifted up to meet her sister’s tense expression, shoulders curled inwards, a few inches of her ankles visible past the short hems of the thinly worn sweatpants. Grabbing her robe off the hook, Alex slipped it on and then apparated right out of the narrow hallway.

 

            Creeping downstairs five minutes later, Kara made two cups of tea and joined Eliza in the cramped living room, waiting for her to finish watering the plants. Side by side on the sagging sofa, Kara curled into Eliza, head on her shoulder as she cradled her cup of tea between her cool palms and they listened to the Wizarding Wireless Network News as they listed recent deaths across the isles. It was devastatingly long.

 

            Eliza kissed her frizzy curls and softly sighed. “She’s just scared.”

 

            “She’s a Gryffindor; I didn’t think she got scared.”

 

            “Courage isn’t the absence of fear, it’s doing things even if you’re scared. This is something your sister can’t confront and that’s what scares her. She’ll be alright though, and you’re safest at Hogwarts, where Dumbledore can protect you.”

 

            “What about you?”

 

            “Me? I’m fine here. I’m Secret Keeper; no one can find me if I don’t tell them where we live.”

 

            It soothed Kara’s fears a little and she didn’t feel quite so bad leaving again. Alex was there anyway, on the occasions that she wasn’t at Auror training in the days or out tailing Death Eaters and duelling in the dead of night, coming in late to wake Kara, covered in filth and blood and cursing as she dabbed Dittany on her cuts and scrapes, lucky to be alive. Each time it made Kara’s stomach jolt and it was a relief to go back to Hogwarts, away from those midnight interruptions, but also a thing that filled her with dread, waiting for a letter, waiting for news instead of being there herself.

 

            The first night back in the draughty castle, she went up to their secret room and curled up on the window seat, waiting. It wasn’t long before Lena arrived, a slip of a shadow in a deep green turtleneck and a black and white houndstooth patterned skirt. It was too cold for the thinness of her jumper but Lena didn’t seem to feel it, thin and pale in the moonlight as she crossed her arms over her stomach and stared down at the grey stone floor.

 

            “Hi,” Kara murmured, standing up.

 

            She pulled at the edge of her sweater, baggy and worn out of shape as the wool pulled thin in places, her scuffed shoes squeaking as she fidgeted restlessly.

 

            “Hi.”

 

            “You went home for the holidays.”

 

            Lena glanced up, a gleam in her green eyes, and Kara shrugged, her cheek shallowly dimpling as her mouth thinned.

 

            “I saw you getting into a carriage.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “Why? I thought …”

 

            Shrugging, Lena smiled wryly, mocking in her tight response. “Quality time with my family.”

 

            Kara opened and closed her mouth, her eyes flitting over Lena’s appearance as a stab of unease filled her. Lena’s expression was not quite anger, not quite fear, but a yawning kind of grief. There was nothing physically wrong with her, but Kara couldn’t shake the feeling that something was wrong, a deep-seated discomfort sitting heavily in her stomach like a stone.

 

            “But … why?”

 

            “Why not?” Lena evasively replied, pacing a few steps in a dawdling manner.

 

            Mystified, Kara’s forehead creased as she ran her thumb over the pilled wool of her sleeve. “Why are you acting like this is- this is nothing? I mean … you never go home and then … suddenly you act as if it’s normal.”

 

            “Maybe my mum was just worried for my safety. I’m glad to be back here though,” Lena said, rolling her eyes and trying to play it off as airy exasperation as she flicked her sleek dark hair off her shoulder. “I’ve missed you.”

 

            Curling her hands into fists, her thumb running over the small scars on her knuckles, Kara didn’t know what to say. It took her a moment to form a response.

 

            “I’ve missed you too.”

 

            “How was your Christmas?”

 

            “I- yeah, it, uh, it was … fine.”

 

            “Full moon got you good?” Lena guessed.

 

            Kara had a new scar on her hip and her hand self-consciously moved to linger over the puckered, silvery skin. She hummed in agreement and tried to change the subject. It just felt off though. Wanting to chalk it up to that argument before the holidays, Kara tried to get past it, but she knew deep down this was something else. In a way, the fight had been the catalyst for everything that came afterwards, she just didn’t know it at the time.

 

            “Eliza wouldn’t let me work over Christmas,” Kara sighed, “apparently Diagon Alley keeps getting raided.”

 

            “Mm, The Daily Prophet reported that Flourish and Blott’s windows were blown in. Three died and two people had to go to St. Mungo’s for superficial wounds.”

 

            Of course Lena would be interested in their injuries, probably coming up with her own method on how to treat them. The thought made Kara smile slightly as she sank back down onto the window ledge. They stayed late, talking until it was past curfew and Kara knew that she would probably get detention for being out of the Common Room so late if she was caught, but they ended up leaving together, under the invisibility cloak with Kara hunching slightly to make sure her ankles didn’t show. 

 

            Lena walked her all the way down to the stack of barrels and Kara hesitated, turning and wrapping her arms tightly around her friend. She could feel the ridges of Lena’s spine, her shoulder blades, her ribs, and held her tighter as she dug her chin into her shoulder, feeling sad for her friend, even though she didn’t know why. Lena hugged her back after a moment, the silky feeling of the invisibility cloak blanketing them both before she pulled back and Kara slipped out from under it.

 

            Tapping the barrels in rhythm, still feeling Lena’s eyes on her, although she couldn’t see her anymore, Kara slipped into the Common Room. 

 

            They fell back into their usual routine of studying together, both of them trying to manage their heavy workload on top of Chess Club, Quidditch practice, the Duelling Club and the rare Hogsmeade weekends. They didn’t meet on the next one in January but Kara saw Lena with a group of Slytherins, small and pale in her black robe and pressed pants as the others laughed in their arrogant way, enchanting snowballs to bombard the Third Years from other houses. 

 

            Kara knew most of them, of course, and had Arithmancy with Veronica Sinclair. Some of them weren’t bad, just haughty and sly, but a few had bad reputations, going back to their siblings and parents as well. Lestrange. Black. Dolohov. Rookwood. Rowle. Kara wondered how many of them had marks on their arms, the seventeen-year-olds who were old enough to do magic outside of school, terrorising Muggles and Muggleborns on the holidays with their family. 

 

            Watching her friend slip into The Three Broomsticks, Kara followed with her own group and situated herself at their table so she could watch Lena. Clutching her Butterbeer tightly, she barely paid attention to the conversation as her eyes drilled a hole between Lena’s shoulder blades, and when Querl asked what she was looking at, she made some vague excuse about spotting one of her Housemates was across the pub and averted her gaze.

 

            Later that evening, Kara was unusually surly. They sat with their backs to the stone walls of the window ledge, knees pulled up to their chests as they balanced books on their laps and marked the arrangement of planets or wrote about Inferi. Eventually, Kara broke the peaceful quiet between them, looking up from her essay with a clouded look in her eyes.

 

            “Why are you hanging out with those people?”

 

            Looking up with mild surprise on her face, Lena set her quill down in the ink pot. “They’re my Housemates.”

 

            “They’re not good people.”

 

            “You don’t know them.”

 

            “Do you?”

 

            “Well, I’ve been sharing a Common Room with them for five years, so … better than you do.”

 

            Kara’s mouth thinned and she trained her eyes back on her work, but Lena let out an impatient sigh, plucking her essay away from her and giving her an insistent look. 

 

            “Go on. Say it.”

 

            “I- it’s just … I don’t like them.”

 

            “What if I said I didn’t like your friends?”

 

            Letting out a weary sigh, Kara closed her eyes. “That’s different. It was a- a misunderstanding. They’re nice, really.”

 

            Snorting, Lena arched an eyebrow, “you know what? You’re a hypocrite.”

 

            “What?” Kara spluttered.

 

            “You don’t like me having other friends, do you? You’re allowed other friends but not me? Are you jealous?”

 

            Flushing, because she was - just a little - Kara snatched her essay back, rubbing the scars on her cheek, which were stark against her red cheeks. Disgruntled, Kara looked out the dark window, smoothing her fingers over the roll of parchment.

 

            “You’re being ridiculous,” she muttered with a quiet scoff.

 

            “You’re being an arse,” Lena shot back, nettled.

 

            Sharply looking at her, a v formed between Kara’s eyebrows. “I’m trying to protect you. If you want to keep us a secret, that’s fine, but-“

 

            “Don’t act like you’d want your friends to find out either.”

 

            Jutting her chin forward in a stubborn manner, Kara pouted slightly. “I’d tell them if you wanted me to.”

 

            Lena made a scathing sound at the back of her throat and they lapsed into silence. Then she exhaled heavily and reached for her quill, tapping the nib on the rim of the ink pot and slowly packing her things away with care. There was a slight tremor in her voice when she replied and Kara didn’t know if it was barely concealed anger or something else.

 

            “I need to go to the library. Need a different book for my essay on Boggarts.”

 

                        Kara didn’t mention how Boggarts were a Third Year Defence Against the Dark Arts subject. Yes, it was revised in their fourth and fifth years too, but there was nothing Lena could learn from a book that she didn’t already know about them. But Kara let the lie go and watched Lena pack up, slinging her bag strap over her shoulder after climbing to her feet.

 

 

            Annoyed, Lena made her way down to the dungeons, unaware of her surroundings as the cold settled into her bones and she brooded over her conversation with Kara. Lena wished she could tell her the real reason for her sudden burgeoning friendships with her Housemates, why she’d taken a sudden interest in them five years into her schooling at Hogwarts. Of course, she didn’t say a thing. Lena kept it to herself as she coaxed out information as a quiet hang-on of the multiple cliques Slytherin House split itself into.

 

            She’d sent multiple letters over Christmas as she refilled Lex’s glass of Firewhisky and made mental notes about the people he was around. Surely they were in on it too, if her brother with the mark on his arm was spending so much time with them. Some of them were the parents or older siblings of the students she’d started paying particular attention to. They didn’t mind her presence so much, even tried engaging her in their ideology on blood purity, with Lena making a few vague comments of agreement, wanting to wince at the stab of guilt.

 

            They got used to her and they slipped up around her. In Hogsmeade, only that morning, Amycus Carrow, a fellow Fifth-Year, made a contemptuous comment about the Dark Lord allowing half-breeds to join the lower ranks and went on a rant about the information his older sister had told him about a werewolf called Fenrir Greyback becoming a Death Eater. He wasn’t high enough in Voldemort’s circle to warrant a Dark Mark but it was a startling piece of information for Lena to put in a letter for Dumbledore, sending Morrigan to his office window with it tied to her leg.

 

            In truth, she knew Kara was right about her new friends. Only a few seemed genuinely nice enough, and her mind was preoccupied with thoughts about what she was getting herself into, and annoyed with her friend’s hypocrisy on top of that. Lena did believe that Kara was at least slightly jealous that she had new friends, that she’d blown off their ritual of sneaking away together in Hogsmeade in disguise. She was still brooding over her when she reached the wide hallway bracketed by lit sconces, with someone walking behind her.

 

            “Lena,” Andrea lightly called out, her voice smooth and amused. “You’re walking rather … murderously. Finally embracing our apparent House qualities?”

 

            Looking up, Lena’s brow furrowed, distracted. “Oh. Hi.”

 

            “What’s got your wand in a knot? Surely not homework?” 

 

            “Nothing.”

 

            “Well, you look miserable. Come with me; I’ve got just the thing.”

 

            She could stop the older girl from looping her arm through hers and towing her towards the Common Room entrance, drawling the password and hauling her inside. Lena avoided looking at the windows, the night so dark that there was nothing but a chilling blackness behind the thick glass, which made her stomach churn with unease. All that pressure, all that power, held back by an inch of glass. It made her want to shiver, her eyelids shuttering as her mouth went dry. Lena hadn’t confronted a real Boggart in class, but she knew what form hers would take, without a shadow of a doubt. Swallowing, careful not to let the Mandrake leaf tucked under her tongue for the last three weeks go down her throat, she let Andrea drag her over to the girl’s Seventh-Year dorms. 

 

            It was a mirror of the Fifth-Year dorms, and she walked over to the door Andrea opened and stepped inside. Her bedsheets were rumpled and the desk across from the foot of it was in disarray with makeup, perfume, bent quills and crumpled pieces of paper scattered on top of open textbooks. Andrea rummaged around in the drawer of the nightstand as Lena eyed the spine of a book; Extreme Incantations.

 

            “So … what’re you planning on doing after school?” Lena conversationally asked.

 

            They were alone in the dorm and Andrea straightened up, grinning at the flask she’d scrounged up from the cluttered drawer. She sank onto the edge of her bed and shrugged indifferently, unscrewing the cap.

 

            “My dad owns a quill manufacturing company with offices in London and Argentina and a few printing businesses in London too. Probably working for one of them until I inherit them.”

 

            “Oh. Is that what you’re doing there?” Lena asked, nodding at the broken quills on the desk.

 

            Andrea tipped the flask back and winced slightly before holding it out to Lena. “A bit, yeah. Thought I might come up with a quill that captures your thoughts without you having to dictate. Here. Drink.”

 

            Lena took the flask and sniffed it. Firewhisky. Hesitating, she took a small sip and coughed as it burned down her throat. It was appropriately named. Wiping her mouth on the back of her hand, she held the flask back out to Andrea, who laughed.

 

            “You’re sweet,” Andrea said with amusement.

 

            Scoffing, Lena sank down on the mattress beside her. She was still in her uniform, with her bag on her shoulder, Firewhisky warming her insides, and beside the only Housemate here that she thought might genuinely be good. Andrea seemed uninterested in the war, either side of it, more consumed with the latest edition of Witch Weekly and her rabid interest in Charms class than anything else. Lena eyed her sideways as she watched Andrea take another sip of Firewhisky.

 

            “Have you ever kissed someone?” Lena asked, indifferent as her dark hair hung in her face.

 

            She turned, a coy look in her green eyes as she met Andrea’s amused stare. Her blue eyes were like the sky, like Kara’s, and far too innocent for someone so cunning as her housemate. Andrea arched an eyebrow as she smiled.

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “Have you ever kissed a girl?”

 

            “Yes,” she replied, her voice lilting with laughter.

 

            Lena reached out and wrapped her fingers around the green and silver striped tie, pulling Andrea closer. “Good.”

 

            Pressing her lips to the other girl’s, Lena felt a slow warmth prickle in her stomach, Andrea’s mouth soft beneath her own. It was quick and gentle and the other girl laughed when Lena pulled back, making her bristle.

 

            “Oh, no, darling. Not like that.”

 

            She kissed Lena again and it was hard not to wish it was someone else, someone who stoked the hurt and anger in her chest, made her heart lurch and her chest ache. She was barely sixteen, and didn’t know what it was like to be loved or love someone - really love someone - but she felt so tense around Kara, all the pent-up tension between them clouding the air, making it hard for it to be easy like it had once been.

 

            And there was Andrea, beautiful and confident and more like the girls Lena knew her mum would approve of, if Lillian ever felt such a thing. She liked her, but she didn’t know her. Lena didn’t know what Andrea looked like when she was concentrating on an essay, didn’t know the reason behind that scar on her forehead, or what secrets she held. Granted, Andrea didn’t know that about her either, and perhaps that was what made it easier to kiss her back and feel a sense of agency in the act.

 

            She went back to her dorm a short while after that, a few more sips of Firewhisky in her and a bee-stung swell to her lips. Lena avoided Kara for a week afterwards out of guilt, until they were paired together in Duelling Club, two of the most adept duellers at Hogwarts and relishing the challenge to one-up each other while pretending they weren’t the closest of friends. Well, perhaps not anymore, but they still holed up in their secret room with books, and blankets and tea on particularly cold days, quizzing each other for Lena’s O.W.L.s and Kara’s end-of-year exams, approaching quicker than they liked. They would review essays and answers and late in the night they’d play chess, but it wasn’t like it was before.

 

            Things had gotten too complicated without either of them being able to voice it. Lena could no more reveal her spying anymore than Kara could admit her feelings. They were stuck at an awkward impasse of trying to pretend things were the same as ever while knowing it wasn’t. It was like they were acting out preordained roles in some play of their lives and it frustrated them both. It frustrated Lena so much that she spent more and more time with Andrea, meaningless afternoons spent out on the trimmed lawn as the weather turned to spring, her friend’s head in her lap as Lena cupped blades of grass in her hands and gently blew on them, wordlessly transforming them into white butterflies that fluttered away. She wished it was Kara with her head in her lap, laughing at the butterflies as her curls caught in the breeze.

 

            The next time there was a storm, she stood outside and chanted the spell she’d said twice a day for weeks now, biding her time for this moment, after months of preparation and difficulty, stealing supplies from various teachers with her invisibility cloak, braving the full moon outside and collecting dew and ensuring it didn’t see sunlight or human touch for a week straight. Eventually, on an early May night, a spring storm blowing through with flickering lightning and thunder that shook loud enough to make her teeth rattle, Lena finally transformed into a black raven with distinctive green eyes.

 

            She hadn’t told a soul what she was doing, not even Kara, and when her avian form was caught by a forceful gust of wind, which sent her sailing towards the still violence of the Whomping Willow, breaking her right wing as she struggled to work out the mechanics of flight and overcome her fear of heights, Lena lied to Madam Pomfrey and said she’d been flying on a broomstick she didn’t have. Her arm was set straight and she wore a sling for two days until the aches subsided, an odd sensation filling her at the thought of what she’d turned into. Kara’s question had sparked the beginning of the process of becoming an Animagus, with Lena thinking that it would make it easier to spy, depending on what she turned into, and she resolved not to remain unregistered, and not tell anyone.

 

            She didn’t know she was a raven - not yet - only that she was some sort of bird, which felt ironic, considering Lena preferred her own two feet planted firmly on the ground. She also didn’t know about the symbiotic relationship between ravens and wolves, two animals that shouldn’t have gotten along so well, feeding into each other with the most unlikely of relationships. And of course, considering that neither of them had conjured a Patronus, she couldn’t have known that Kara’s was a wolf, for reasons other than her Lycanthropy, and that hers would have taken the form of a raven as well, tying them both together in some unspeakable way that transcended humanity. 

 

            For some inexplicable reason, she decided not to tell Kara she’d managed to complete the process of becoming an Animagus. It wasn’t for a lack of trust, but something held her back. The next time she saw Kara, her arm free of the sling, she made up an irritable lie about some spell gone wrong by one of her classmates, which had caught her in the crossfire. And then later that night, once Kara had gone, she changed again and fluttered around the tower, trying to gain control of her body in that form as she got used to the disorienting feeling of flying. That became her routine.

 

            At the end of the term, Lena finished her O.W.L.s with little to no sense of achievement, knowing that she’d gotten near-perfect grades on both the theoretical and practical portions of each subject. It didn’t leave her feeling proud or relieved that they were over, that she’d tried her hardest, it just left her feeling drained and weary of the fact that no matter if she got straight Os, it still wouldn’t be good enough. Still, Kara brought her a knotted tea towel of all of her favourite cakes and tarts from the kitchens and celebrated the end of her exams with a few rounds of Exploding Snap and bottles of Butterbeer the House Elves had willingly offered up as well. 

 

            She hugged her friend goodbye and went home for the summer, dreading every second that she was there.

 

 

            Lena returned to Hogwarts with the overwhelming feeling of relief, wanting to cry as she climbed onto the half-empty train, silent and cowed after perhaps the worst summer of her life. She thought it would get better the older she got, the more she proved herself, but that only served to add to her punishments. Instead of pride over her daughter’s accomplishments, Lillian had been indifferent and stood by as Lex took his petty spite out on her for her perfect O.W.L. grades, which he hadn’t managed to achieve for himself. 

 

            Students had slowly been withdrawn from Hogwarts over the last few years, barely imperceptible at the start, but now it was glaringly obvious how few were returning this year. There were no disgruntled arguments over train compartments or crowded seats as students piled in where they could fit, and Lena sat with Veronica Sinclair now that Andrea had graduated and gone to work at her father’s company. They’d written a couple of letters over the summer, apparently their friendship transcending the occasional rendezvous in dark classrooms, and she thought she might miss her friend this year, despite only really speaking to her over the last year. To make matters worse, it was Kara’s last year as well, and Lena would truly know what loneliness was like next year. 

 

            She didn’t have to wonder if she’d be coming to school next year. Voldemort could seize control of Hogwarts and Lillian would still make her go to school. It wasn’t that her mother thought it was safer there, which it was, and her general opinion of Dumbledore was that he was an old hack who should’ve been replaced years ago, but she didn’t care for her daughter’s safety enough to delay her education. That was the most important thing to Lillian, that Lena graduated with the marks to go to Healer School. Nothing short of bringing the castle down would persuade her otherwise, and even then, Lena imagined she’d be shipped off to Durmstrang or Ilvermorny. 

 

            Kara had already written to let her know she would be returning for her final year, completing her N.E.W.T.s from within the bubble of safety Dumbledore’s presence provided. There were many others who didn’t return and Lena stared out the window to watch the grey countryside roll past. The weather seemed off these days, conflated with the increasing terror sweeping the nation, and she saw the unsettling figures of Dementors in the distance on more than one occasion as they rattled northbound. 

 

            With fewer students, Lena had to all but beg for them to allow her to take Alchemy, joining the couple of Seventh-Years - Kara included - for their lessons and left to catch up to speed, which wasn’t especially difficult for her. In the tiny classroom, she ended up beside her friend, careful not to touch her, not to acknowledge her, as they wrote about the transformative properties of metal and the theoretical process of immortality. They’d never shared a class before and Lena found herself distracted by her closeness at times, the two of them sitting at the back, swapping fluttering butterfly notes and helping each other with their shared assignments. It was thrilling and Lena wished they’d gone through Hogwarts together, side by side, as open friends. But it would have been impossible, tarnishing the thing that had only blossomed because of their isolation from outside interference.

 

            It wasn’t long before Kara turned eighteen and Lena turned seventeen, the latter receiving a silver watch with a black dragonhide strap, two silver and green ouroboros snakes inside the watch face in the place of hands, the points where their mouths consumed their tails indicating the hour and minute as they rotated clockwise. It was her mother’s old watch and she was surprised by the sentimentality of it, delivered by Lex’s owl, Ignatius, along with a few other gifts from her brother, who hadn’t forgotten her entirely. Kara bought her a hair-thin silver bracelet with a little onyx gemstone embedded in it, clasping it around Lena’s wrist for her. Lena had hugged her - for the last time - and held her just a little bit longer than she usually did, seeking comfort in the rarity of human contact. She would never have let go if she knew how bad things were going to get.

 

            The first Hogsmeade weekend fast approached in early November, on the heels of a chain of attacks. Kara had been red-eyed and raw-voiced when she told Lena that her friend, Nia, had lost her mother in an attack at the start of term. She was a seer who dealt in prophecies and it had seemed like a coordinated attack, leaving her daughter with her own prophetic dreams to deal with. Her other friend, Winn - the one who’d attacked Lena - was on the other end of the grieving spectrum, when it came out that his father was a supporter of the Dark Lord and had blown himself up, along with his narrow inventor’s workshop in Diagon Alley, taking two buildings and a dozen Aurors and shoppers with him. Kara’s sister had been there, shadowing one of the senior Aurors as part of her training. She’d come out with a few scratches and written a shaky letter to her sister.

 

            It was outright war now, the late 1970s bringing the worst of the fighting. It was hard to hold out hope, to think that her efforts were helping, in some small way, when Death Eaters and their sympathisers outranked the people fighting against them twenty to one. But Lena counted herself amongst one of those Order members, even if she wasn’t allowed to join and was operating outside of it, ignorant of their existence in any official capacity. Once she graduated, perhaps Dumbledore would fully induct her into it, allowing Lena to help in a more hands-on fashion. If the war was still ongoing.

 

            The next Hogsmeade weekend stumped Lena though, clouding the idealistic view she had of the Order. She was too smart to not know that’s who she was aiding, but on Thursday evening, sitting near the fireplace with her new friends, she pretended not to listen to one of her Housemates whisper about a rumoured attack in the village on Saturday. Lena’s stomach plummeted and she stayed up until everyone else went to bed, before donning her invisibility cloak and making her way to Professor McGonagall’s office, her quarters adjoining it.

 

            The severe woman opened the door with a look of irate disapproval tightening her mouth, holding her lit wand aloft. Her dark hair was plaited and she had a tartan robe over her pyjamas but didn’t look as if she’d been sleeping, even though it was almost midnight.

 

            “Miss Luthor, I assume I don’t need to remind a Prefect that it’s past curfew.”

 

            “Sorry, Professor McGonagall, I- it’s  … important,” she quietly said, an anxious look in her green eyes as she met her teacher’s gaze. “I need to speak with Professor Dumbledore immediately.”

 

            Hesitating, her steely gaze piercing, McGonagall let out a withering sigh and gestured Lena ahead of her. Walking through the dark castle at the professor’s wand light, Lena bundled her invisibility cloak in her arms and followed alongside her, feeling nervous as dread sat heavily in her stomach.

 

            Taking her up to Dumbledore’s office, where Lena hadn’t had the audacity to go alone, McGonagall spoke the password to the gargoyle before they rode the staircase up to the Headmaster’s Tower. Despite the lateness of the night, the Headmaster was still awake, pacing before an item Lena recognised as a Pensieve. He smiled slightly at the sight of her, a weariness to his pale blue eyes as he stared over his half-moon glasses.

 

            “Miss Luthor. It’s late; I trust you’re here for a good reason.”

 

            “Yes, Professor. I- one of my Housemates - Amycus Carrow - was talking about an attack. This weekend in Hogsmeade. Apparently, it’s going to be targeted towards the Muggleborns, sir.”

 

            “You’re sure of this?”

 

            “Yes, sir. He was talking about it with Black. His older sister told him. I thought- I thought I should tell you straight away so you could … I don’t know, cancel the weekend.”

 

            He smiled faintly again and resumed his slow pacing. Lena’s eyes darted towards the Phoenix perched behind his desk, in the prime of its cycle, and Professor Dumbledore eyed her closely as he considered what she’d told him.

 

            “This is troubling news. Thank you for bringing it to my attention.”

 

            It sounded like a dismissal and Lena’s mouth opened and closed, a small sound of confusion stuck at the back of her throat.

 

            “Will you alert the Order or-“

 

            “You’ve done your part,” he gently told her, “leave it with me now. You’ve done well, Lena.”

 

            Her throat closed up at the praise and she gripped her left arm tightly in her right, pinning the invisibility cloak to her chest.

 

            “I want to do more,” she blurted out.

 

            Chuckling, he closed the cupboard with the Pensieve and turned to face her. “All in good time. It wouldn’t do for you to get caught out; this is very dangerous work, as it is. It’s delicate work, to ensure we counteract their plots without revealing a spy in their midst. If suspicion should fall upon you, I fear the Dark Lord would use Legilimency to reveal your true allegiances and compromise us all.”

 

            His eyes narrowed and he hummed softly with intrigue. “Although  … yes, I believe you’d be rather adept at Occlumency if given the chance. I shall instruct Horace to give you private lessons. He’s a most accomplished practitioner of the defence. For now, keep your ears open, Miss Luthor. Good night.”

 

            Left feeling stumped and confused, Lena stammered a goodnight and followed Professor McGonagall back down the moving staircase. Her brow furrowed and her mouth turned down at the corners, leaving her perplexed about what he intended to do with the alarming news. He seemed rather unbothered by it and Lena felt uneasy.

 

            The next few days passed by quickly and Lena sent Kara a letter at breakfast on Saturday morning, a sleepless night spent worrying as no cancellation was forthcoming from the Headmaster preceding over their evening meals. Her eyes were bloodshot and she looked terrible as she watched her owl land before the Hufflepuff girl, little regard for who might recognise her distinctive Morrigan, watching Kara scan the note with increasing confusion, her head rising and her eyes scanning the scant occupants of the Slytherin table. There used to be thousands of students at Hogwarts, but now they were reduced to the hundreds as people died and families moved away. 

 

            Their eyes meet for the briefest moment before Lena slipped away from her uneaten breakfast and untouched black coffee that had cooled considerably. Pacing in the empty courtyard, she all but lunged at Kara, dragging her into a dark alcove the moment she stepped outside into the chilly November grey. Slush gathered on the ground and Lena’s cheeks were red from the cold as her breath faintly plumed before her.

 

            “You can’t go to Hogsmeade today,” she rasped, her voice hoarse from a lack of sleep, her eyes almost manic.

 

            “What?” Kara echoed, her face crumpling as a smile twitched the corners of her mouth.

 

            “You can’t go today,” Lena firmly insisted, swallowing thickly before continuing. “You need to stay at the castle, okay? We can- we can drink hot chocolate and I’ll- I’ll do your Astronomy homework for you. Just … stay with me today. Please.”

 

            Uneasiness wound through Kara and she drew back slightly, her smile diminishing as she hunched her shoulders in her wool coat, dipping her chin so her mouth was hidden by her yellow and black scarf. 

 

            “Are you okay? Has- has something happened?”

 

            Agonised, Lena squeezed her eyes shut. “I just … I have a bad feeling.”

 

            Letting out a small bark of laughter, Kara cocked her head to the side, her wire-frame glasses lopsided on her face. “Funny. That’s what Nia said this morning as well.”

 

            “You should listen to her. Didn’t you say her dreams are prophetic?”

 

            “Sort of. Not very accurate though; she’d only just started taking Divination classes so she doesn’t really know what it all means.”

 

            “Well … listen to her today,” Lena raggedly said, a plea in her voice as she reached out to grab Kara’s cold fingers, holding them tight, unconcerned with any prying eyes. That didn’t matter right now.

 

            Wariness bloomed in Kara’s blue eyes and she nodded with uncertainty. Lena supposed it was her desperation that convinced her friend, some loyalty convincing her to stay by Lena’s side and see her through whatever had her so frantic, presuming the pressure of her N.E.W.T.s was maybe pushing her to the breaking point. Slipping her fingers from Lena’s grasp, Kara gave her a thin smile.

 

            “Okay. Okay, um, just … give me five minutes to tell my friends. It’s the full moon tomorrow anyway so they won’t be suspicious.”

 

            Lena had almost forgotten that in her panic, seeing the sallow tint to Kara’s skin, the dark smudges beneath her eyes and the way her tall frame stooped slightly. Nodding, Lena swallowed thickly, relief keenly cutting through her.

 

            “Okay. I’ll meet you upstairs, okay?”

 

            Nodding, Kara smiled again, her eyes creasing at the corners. “Okay.”

 

            Remaining outside a minute longer as Kara vanished back into the draughty protection of the castle, Lena let out a shaky breath and then composed herself before following after her. She walked down to the dungeons to gather her things and walked upstairs to the secret room, setting out her things with precision and flipping through her copy of Flesh-Eating Trees of the World to find the chapter on Snargaluff plants for her essay on harvesting the pods. They’d spent yesterday’s Herbology lesson wrestling the stumps in pairs for the practical side of it and Lena was only slightly relieved that she wasn’t overly interested in Herbology - aside from how the store-bought ingredients could be used in potions.

 

            Ten minutes after she arrived there, Kara appeared, two cups in hand and an anxious edge to her expression. It brightened with a smile as she walked over to the ledge, setting both cups of hot chocolate down and letting her bag slip from her shoulder. Sitting down, she took a sip of her steaming drink and then cocked her head to the side.

 

            “Do you want to talk about it?”

 

            Hesitating, Lena shook her head, keeping it ducked down. As promised, she helped Kara with her Astronomy homework - not quite doing it all for her - and they spoke about their plans for Christmas, with Lena going home again and Kara avoiding any comments on the new routine. They lamented over Lena not knowing how to Apparate yet, with the Ministry run course not starting until after Christmas and the test not until April, and Kara knew her friend didn’t have the freedom to Floo out of her home on a whim. Lena had never let on how bad it was, but it was clear her mother wouldn’t let her. Even if she could Apparate to some predetermined destination, Lena didn’t think she’d risk Lillian’s wrath. 

 

            It was still nice to fantasise about what they’d do together, with Kara telling Lena she’d show her around the Junk Shop and the Harpy’s Bazar , where Lillian would never deign to visit, mentioning the awful food at The Leaky Cauldron , while Lena drew comparisons with The White Wyvern , which Lillian approved of. They got distracted from their homework talking about going to Carkitt Market, down a side street from Diagon Alley to visit the Museum of Muggle Curiosities Lena had had the burning desire to step inside, ever since they’d gone to the outdoor shopping arcade to get her ivy wand from Gregorovitch’s. Kara teased her about visiting her in Ireland and taking her to see the Ballycastle Bats play a match, making Lena roll her eyes as she fought back a smile, and they felt the afternoon slip by with surprising ease.

 

            As it approached lunchtime, they snuck down to the kitchens together, using all manner of secret passageways behind tapestries and spiralling staircases behind statues to remain unseen. In the company of a score of House Elves, they ate ham sandwiches and jam tarts and drank cups of tea before going to the library. With the majority of the students at Hogsmeade, and few remaining ones wishing to spend their weekend holed up amidst the stacks of books, they practically had the place to themselves, pretending that they weren’t together as they stood back to back in the rows of shelves, thumbing through dusty times and keeping up a whispered conversation before tucking themselves away in Lena’s favourite forgotten corner.

 

            They actually did do some homework then and let the afternoon pass them by until it was dinner time. Then they left separately, returning to their Common Rooms with their bags. Lena had barely stepped through the doors before the whispers caught her attention, the whiff of smoke, the hitching sobs of Third-Years, the pale faces. Her stomach twisted with guilt and regret and she watched as some of the older students, the ones grooming themselves for a Dark Mark after graduation, sneered and taunted the ashen lower years as they huddled in their small groups with wide eyes.

 

            Piecing together what had happened as she sat beside Veronica Sinclair, who lazily stroked the side of her neck and drawled indifferent comments about the injured Muggleborns, Lena had to swallow the sour taste rising at the back of her throat. Her faith in Dumbledore wavered then, her self-righteous belief that she was on the right side, that she was saving people, turning to ash. She couldn’t bear to go down to dinner after that and vanished back up to her secret room, far away from the oppressive feeling of the underwater Common Room.

 

            It was an hour later when boots squeaked on the stone floor and Kara appeared, white-faced and wide-eyed with bewildered panic. Her knuckles were white and she had to try a few times to get the words out.

 

            “You knew, didn’t you?” she hollowly asked.

 

            “Knew what?” Lena asked, her voice wavering as she raised her eyebrows, a feigned look of innocence on her sharp-boned face.

 

            A choked hysterical sound caught at the back of Kara’s throat, turning breathless as she covered her mouth with her hand. Tipping her head back, she stood still for a moment and Lena silently rose to her feet, her heart hammering in her chest.

 

            “Six people are dead,” Kara told her, her voice deathly quiet.

 

            Lena inhaled sharply, gouging half-moons into her palms as she clenched her jaw. “What happened?”

 

            “You tell me,” Kara demanded, lowering her head and giving Lena an accusing look. “You begged me not to go. Why is that?”

 

            Lena was exhausted and didn’t want the argument that was sure to follow, but she gave her friend the one answer that she knew Kara wouldn’t accept.

 

            “I can’t tell you.” 

 

            Her voice sounded dull, even to her own ears, and Kara’s disbelieving silence was deafening as Lena avoided looking at her. The tension in the air was unbearable and Lena didn’t know how to dispel it, how to make Kara trust her, trust that she hadn’t been complicit in it, that she was just caught in the middle of it all, trying to do her best to help.

 

            “How-“ Kara started and then faltered, taking a hand through her hair and then gesturing helplessly. She tried again. “How could you- how could you let that happen? How did you know? I- you should’ve told someone.”

 

            Her hair was shot with grey, not just the pale gold of a summer spent in the sun. Lycanthropy was taking its toll on Kara, in the thinness of her face, the sickly pallor of her skin, no matter how much of a tan she had. The full moon was the following night and Kara looked hollow and frail as she stood before Lena, at a loss for words at her friend’s failings.

 

            “I couldn’t have stopped it,” Lena said instead of trying to defend herself, instead of revealing her attempt to go to Dumbledore. 

 

            She’d been naïve to think he’d do everything in his power to protect the students - or maybe he had and he just wasn’t powerful enough - and she tried to swallow her guilt. There had been Order members there, amidst the Death Eaters that had Apparated in to target students they presumed to be Muggleborns or the children of. The students had quickly sought cover in the shops as the adults were left to duel away, but not before a few casualties had struck, including four students. 

 

            Lena had heard all of this secondhand in the Common Room. Three Death Eaters had been taken in by Ministry Aurors who’d arrived in the midst of the quick attack, and two Hogwarts Professors - she didn’t know which - had ushered students back towards the castle while casting protective shield charms around them all. It had lasted all of five minutes and Lena imagined the screams that had filled the small magical town, while they’d been safely tucked away inside their tower.

 

            “How did you know?” Kara brusquely asked. “How did you know? Did your brother- are you- are you with them?”

 

            Aghast, Lena choked on a breath of surprise as she blinked at Kara’s audacity to ask her that. They’d been friends for years, they knew each other better than anyone. But that amounted to nothing the moment suspicion was cast upon her.

 

            “Show me-” Kara started, taking a step forward as Lena flinched back. “Show me your arm,” she demanded.

 

            Lena backed away again as Kara made a grab for her sleeve. They repeated this again, twice more, before Kara’s wiry fingers encircled Lena’s wrist and they struggled for a moment, Lena trying to pull herself free as Kara fumbled with the cuff of her sweater, trying to tug it up over her forearm. Teeth grit, Lena pulled back but Kara was taller and stronger, years of being a beater on the Hufflepuff Quidditch team adding lean muscle to her tall frame, and used the momentum to step forward and move behind Lena, her chest to her back.

 

            Pushing back against her, Lena wrenched her arm in Kara’s grasp and ducked out from under her, her wrist burning from the friction of the cinched fabric. She would not let Kara pull up her sleeve. She tried to pull back again and Kara’s mouth thinned with annoyance, but she was angry and afraid for her friend and managed to grab her arm with her other hand.

 

            It all happened quickly, not even a minute of struggling before Lena was digging her nails into Kara’s arm to try and stop her from exposing the words etched on her skin. Kara couldn’t have known - why would she have? Lena’s struggling incensed her to believe that there was a Dark Mark branding her skin, the vivid black skull and snake of evil tattooed there as a secret nod to her allegiance. She couldn’t have known it was the mortifying fear over those words in her own hand, written over and over again over countless years, that was what she was trying to hide.

 

            When her sleeve was wrenched up a moment later, exposing the pale scar, they both went still, Kara’s hands still tight around her arm as realisation dawned on her. Her face turned ashen as her eyes took in the words, confusion turning to shock and then white-faced horror.

 

I am a failure

 

            In the time it took Kara to study the pale words scarred into an even paler arm, Lena had pulled her wand from her pocket and now rammed the tip of it up under Kara’s jaw. Her face was tight with fear, her eyes flat and her voice trembling as she spoke in a dangerously low voice.

 

            “Don’t. Touch me.”

 

            Kara swallowed thickly, a shaky breath exhaled through her nose as Lena’s wand jerked her head back slightly, hurting at the base of her skull. Slowly unclenching her fingers, heedless of the deep half-moons gouged in her skin, Kara opened and closed her mouth.

 

            “What-” she managed to get out, the word a croak that cut off.

 

            She swallowed, her mouth dry and throat closed up, and tried again. 

 

            “What’s that?”

 

            Shaking the sleeve back down as she pulled her wand back, Lena’s face twisted, a flicker of hatred in her green eyes. Heat spread up her neck and into her cheeks as she stepped back, reaching out to cover the spot on her arm, over her sleeve, in a gesture that was intimately familiar to Kara, who blanched with realisation. Kara’s throat tightened. Her mouth opened, but nothing came out, just a rush of air, an angry breath.

 

            “Lena,” she said, her voice cracking as she cocked her head to the side, her eyes darting up as her eyes prickled with the burning urge to cry. “What is that?”

 

            “It’s nothing,” Lena harshly replied, fear and embarrassment making her voice ugly.

 

            Taking a stumbling step forward, Kara reached for her but Lena roughly shrugged away from her touch, her patent loafers squeaking as she almost tripped over her own feet in her haste. She didn’t like being touched when she was wounded and this was her biggest wound, a raw pain that she’d hidden for so long.

 

            “Did she-”

 

            “I did it to myself,” Lena snapped. 

 

            It wasn’t entirely a lie but she hated to shoulder the blame for what had been done to her. Still, she needed to loyally tie herself to her family, or pretend to at least, and she couldn’t do that if someone knew what had been done to her. And Kara knew - she was far too perceptive not to - the tears springing unbidden to her eyes and spilling down her cheeks.

 

            “No, you- it’s not your fault.”

 

            Trying to force out the right words, Lena let out a broken laugh as she gestured to herself. “This is how I survive , do you understand? It’s how my mother taught me. It’s what works .”

 

            Kara made a strangled sound deep in her throat, like a whimper. Her broad shoulders squared as she turned her body to face the window, rubbing her forehead as her heart raced in her chest. Lena wondered how much restraint it was taking to stop her from going beyond the confines of the school grounds and apparating to Ireland to rip Lillian’s head off. Lena wouldn’t stop her if she’d tried to do it.

 

            But her face burned hot. She felt embarrassed by the fact that Kara knew, had seen the deep pain Lena had spent years swimming in, unable to drag herself out, and resentment rose up inside her at her friend. And she knew that this was the moment that she lost her, and it should have felt like the least of her worries, knowing how risky it was to spy on her Housemates and her family. Losing Kara shouldn’t hurt as much as the possibility of dying, of losing the war, of letting everything she was trying to secretly work for be in vain. But it cut Lena clean through and it hurt to breathe as she gripped her head on either side of her temples.

 

            She’d grown up being mistreated and there was a sense of comfort, of safety, in the mistreatment she suffered at home, driving home those awful thoughts about herself that only seemed to quieten around Kara. Now, to be exposed to someone that she loved, Lena felt threatened, her heart pounding in her chest, trapped by the accusations of the one person who’d managed to make her feel like she wasn’t horrible, wasn’t a failure or evil or anything that her family and the other Houses said. But now Kara was blaming her, assuming the worst, when the only thing Lena was guilty of was suffering at the hands of her family’s expectations. She could not be anything less than exceptional and it had been marked on her skin, a stark contrast to the mark Kara had expected to find there instead.
