            “Go to Professor Dumbledore,” Kara begged, “he can’t make you go home to her.”

 

            “She’s not … awful,” Lena murmured, her voice flat as she trailed off.

 

            Kara’s face creased with bewilderment and sadness. “You’re too kind and too loyal to see it.”

 

            Giving her a pained, crooked smile, Lena narrowed her eyes, perplexed. “She’s the only one who’s ever taken care of me.”

 

            “Taken care of you?” Kara echoed, aghast, “you spend six weeks at home with her in the summers while she’s at work and this is what she does to you? How much does she really look after you?”

 

            “You don’t even know what you’re talking about,” Lena scoffed, her voice turning icy. “Sorry that you like going home because your mum loves you-“

 

            “My mom loves me? She abandoned me. She thinks I’m a monster , so don’t act like it’s been great for me, okay? My life is hell.”

 

            Lena made a choked sound at the back of her throat. “You think that mine is easy? Just because I don’t transform into a werewolf once a month? You know what, I wish I did. I wish I was repulsive to her so she would ignore my existence. Instead … instead I’m stuck.”

 

            Fear gripped her so tightly that it made her do things she ordinarily wouldn’t, say things she would regret saying for the rest of her life, but Lena was helpless to stop it. She didn’t think Kara was repulsive, she thought she was the singular most beautiful person she’d ever seen, but there was such a rift between them that she never could have said that. And Lena couldn’t take her words back, even if it hadn’t been her meaning.

 

            “Repulsive?” Kara breathlessly echoed, wounded betrayal sharpening her eyes.

 

            Swallowing thickly, Lena looked down at the floor, running her tongue over her teeth as she steeled herself to push it even further, the bitter taste of her anger filling her mouth. “That’s what you think everyone thinks of you. That’s what you think about me, isn’t it? How repulsive I am, how I must have a mark on my arm because I’m a conniving Slytherin who wants Muggleborns and half-breeds dead . And you know what, maybe I am like them. That’s what you think, right?”

 

            “I- no. You’re nothing like them, like the people who can’t- who can’t love you,” Kara insisted, her voice hoarse as it scraped her throat, a plea in her voice. 

 

            “Oh, now I’m nothing like them? You don’t even trust me. You won’t even believe me when I tell you I don’t have a Dark Mark but I’m supposed to believe we’re friends? You’ve never thought I was good enough; you would never want to be seen with a Slytherin, because deep down … you think I’m just like the rest of them.”

 

            The air was stolen from Kara’s lungs and she stammered wordlessly, her blue eyes filling with tears as she numbly shook her head. “That’s not true. I’ve always been on your side - until today.”

 

            The meaning behind Kara’s words was plain. Lena might not have a Dark Mark on her arm, but she’d known what was going to happen, and that could only have meant one thing. She knew what the Death Eaters were going to do, which meant she was running in the same circles as them, and Kara had grumbled and scorned Lena’s new friends for their reputations and actions, connecting the dots now and turning her back on years of earned trust. Lena would have forgiven her if she’d just asked, but instead, Kara had forced her hand, forced her to show the shameful scar on her arm and then hastily back-tracked, but it was too late for that now. Lena’s pride wouldn’t allow her to look Kara in the eye with any of the same trust and tenderness as before.

 

            Gritting her teeth against the raw pain in her chest, the urge to cry building, making her breath bottom out as it hitched in her throat, Lena forced the lump in her throat down. She wouldn’t cry, she refused to cry, had experienced pain that far outweighed the sting of Kara’s doubt cast upon her, but it devastated Lena. So she did the only thing she knew how to do and severed her ties to her emotions out of self-preservation. She cut herself off from the only person she thought might have genuinely cared for her, and Lena couldn’t even tell her how wrong her judgement was.

 

            Licking her chapped lips, she raised her wand again, betrayal bright in her green eyes as she hardened herself against her heart. She’d suffered too much to let someone else be the cause of her weakness now so she made Kara go, the only way she could force her to.

 

            “Get. Out,” Lena slowly ground out, the wand shaking slightly in her hand. “Before I make you.”

 

            “Are you going to hurt me?” Kara softly asked, surprise blooming on her face as her hands hung limply at her sides.

 

            “You don’t want to find out what I’m capable of.”

 

            Kara’s lips twitched with a derisive hint of a smile, bitter and sad as her hand reached up to touch her chest, the spot where Lena had cut Winn deeply with a spell she hadn’t known the true depths of. “I already know.”

 

            Her throat constricting as her stomach lurched, the final blow dealt by the last person she expected to hurt her, Lena’s wand arm lowered as she watched Kara leave without another word. 

 

            They didn’t speak to each other again for four years.

Chapter 14

            Kara expected a few days to pass by before they both cooled off, their anger diminishing to sheepish apologies and then endurance of that awkward tension that had plagued them for more than a year now. But she was wrong. Arriving back at the Hufflepuff Common Room hours after leaving the Astronomy Tower, red-eyed and brimming with an odd sense of grief, she felt her last bit of hope gutter at the sight of dozens of students sitting around, pale-faced and hollow-eyed. 

 

            One of the dead students had been a Third-Year Hufflepuff, and once again, Kara was devastated by the fact that Lena had known. For a brief, panicked moment, she’d been so sure of what she’d find on her arm, terrified as she’d dragged the cuff up as Lena struggled. But there was a different mark, one in her friend’s own hand, and Kara felt sick.

 

            Pushing through the crowded Common Room, every Hufflepuff student left at Hogwarts coming together to seek out comfort and a false sense of safety, she made her way to the bathroom and fell to her knees before the toilet, retching. Kara might have thought it was the early effects of the full moon tomorrow night, leaving her nauseous and weak, as usual, but there was an extra edge to it that night. Sitting there, clammy and numb with dread, she stifled the urge to cry over her friend again. Was that even the right word to use any more?

 

            That fact was further solidified when Kara woke in the Hospital Wing two mornings later, alone in the narrow bed with the lingering aches and pains of the transformation. It was the first time she’d awoken without Lena at her bedside since her friend had confessed to knowing and Kara felt a yawning ache of loneliness well up. Madam Pomfrey thought she was suffering from an especially painful transformation when she checked on her and found the young witch breathlessly trying to swallow her sobs. She kept her in an extra night and knocked her out with a potion, leaving her oblivious to the small, dark-haired figure lurking in the corridor outside, debating whether she should go in or not.

 

            In the end, pride won Lena over and she kept walking. In the end, their pride was too great for them both and neither of them could bring themselves to confront the other first. Lena was irrevocably upset by Kara’s unfounded accusations, and Kara was equally as mortified and confused by what she’d done and whether or not Lena had some ties to the Death Eaters, even if she didn’t have a mark. Kara scathingly thought that her brother must have joined, and if he was passing information onto Lena about attacks and she was doing nothing to stop them, didn’t that make her complicit?

 

            But Kara’s heart ached in her chest as she walked around missing her friend. She didn’t have the courage to go back to their secret room, which had been Lena’s first, so she only ever saw Lena in the Great Hall, or in their Alchemy classes, where she’d taken a new spot at the front of the class, leaving Kara staring forlornly at her back. She was still walking around with all of those friends Kara hated so much, the ground dwindling down as students had graduated or been pulled out of school, and there were flurries of duels occurring in the hallways between all the Houses and Slytherin. 

 

            These small targeted attacks were often brutal and out of the blue, and Kara had wound up in a few, defending brash Fourth-Years who were loyal to a fault and selfless enough to take a hex for a fellow Housemate or a Ravenclaw or Gryffindor being attacked. She was a good dueller and usually helped finish it off quickly, but more than once she’d been confronted by Lena’s friends, bristling and ready to fight as her throat closed up at the sight of her friend, looking haunted and exhausted. Lena had stopped the duels each time, making haughty, dismissive comments about how she wasn’t worth their time, her hands all over Veronica Sinclair as Kara flushed and turned her back on them.

 

            Christmas was something of a relief, getting a break from the constant reminders of Lena, although she moped around the cottage with nothing to do. It was too dangerous for her to work to scrape together a few Sickles over the short winter break, and she couldn’t stop brooding over the gift she’d already bought for Lena - a new quill she ended up giving to Eliza as another gift instead. Confined to the protected cottage, Kara spent most of her time in the small, overgrown garden tending to plants and sitting on the damp grass as she practised spells and finished off her homework.

 

            School started back and it felt like she’d barely been home at all, focusing on Quidditch practice with the upcoming game and spending every other moment studying with Querl for their upcoming N.E.W.T.s. He didn’t question the sudden increase in their time spent together, and he was the next smartest student at Hogwarts, after Lena, so he helped her with her homework and failed to fill the hole in her heart.

 

            It was 1981, the last year of the war, although no one knew it and it all felt bleak and hopeless. Red-nosed with a lingering cold and sore from all of her Quidditch training in the January snows and abundance of sleet and rain, Kara was feeling hopeless as the darkness crept in. She was receiving almost daily letters from Alex now, who’d told her over the holidays that she’d gotten engaged to Maggie. Kara hadn’t even known they were dating again, and Alex confessed it had only been a few months at that, but people were feeling the impending doom and were becoming rash. 

 

            There had been rumours of students who’d been at Hogwarts only a year or two ago, now married and pregnant or already seen carrying a child or two around Diagon Alley over the school holidays. Kara hadn’t imagined her sister would be one of the hasty lot but she loved her sister enough to be happy for her, even if she didn’t really like Maggie. They planned to do it at Easter, when Kara would be home for the holidays and their friends could all get together.

 

            By the time the Easter holidays arrived, Kara went home to comfort her heartbroken sister instead, left by Maggie a week before they’d planned to get married. The other woman was leaving the country, sick of the war and unable to be persuaded to stay by her fiancée. She hadn’t even asked Alex to go with her.

 

            Kara didn’t know what to say, too inexperienced with the hardships of love to offer any insight. She just made copious amounts of tea for them all while Eliza sat at the foot of Alex’s bed and tried to talk sense into her. She went back to school for the last leg of her education before her final exams with uneasiness leaving her distracted. The high demand of her coursework left Kara with little time to dwell on other things though and she was grateful for Querl and Nia’s steadfast company in the library as she spent what felt like her every waking hour there with the former.

 

            Becoming an Unspeakable in the Department of Mysteries meant it was vital that Kara did well in her exams, needing at least five Exceeds Expectations grades to even be considered for a position. She knew that being a werewolf meant she’d need to do better than five Es though, worried her application wouldn’t even be glanced at if she didn’t do better than that. Her extracurricular classes in Magical Theory and Ancient studies would count though, and she’d picked up History of Magic again in her Seventh-Year in the hopes that it would help her over the line with more opportunities to showcase her breadth of knowledge. 

 

            She didn’t have to sit exams for them all, but Kara decided to try her luck, and when May arrived with the taste of freedom as the school year came to a close, she found herself panicking. This was it, her last year, graduation only weeks away, and it was dawning on Kara that this was her opportunity to do well. If she failed, she wouldn’t have the same opportunities as her classmates, would only have her W.O.M.B.A.T.s to take, if she felt like it, and they didn’t hold the same weight as her school exams.

 

            Pale and tense, Kara went to every exam exhausted and terrified, her hands covered with ink and her eyes dry itching and dry as she tried to formulate her essay on Protean Charms, tried to demonstrate her skill in Transfiguration by turning a king into a rook, writing about the Fundamental Laws of Magic and brewing a near perfect Draught of Living Death potion.

 

            Once her last one was over, she felt a sense of accomplishment and felt the familiar anger at her loneliness as she was seized by the adrenaline-fuelled rush to go to Lena. They hadn’t spoken since last November, hadn’t so much as written a letter, exchanged more than the briefest moment of eye contact, and yet every part of Kara ached for her. There was no congratulatory secret moment in their room with food pilfered from the kitchens, no one to enjoy the last days at Hogwarts with, even though she still had a few friends there. She felt lonelier than she had in those first few months of starting at the school, with everyone gone and graduated and her best friend blanking her dead. 

 

            The day of her graduation ceremony was vastly different to Alex’s. They didn’t allow family in, the risk of being infiltrated and attacked too great - they’d already cancelled any remaining Hogsmeade weekends and had Aurors guarding the perimeter and town for months now - which meant Kara was all alone. It was in alphabetical order by surname so she was seated near enough to Querl for them both to make the most of the moment together, dressed in her Hogwarts robes for the last time with her pointy hat saved for special occasions. Tomorrow, they’d leave for good on the fleet of little rowing boats, like how they’d all arrived there at the beginning.

 

            Kara felt unusually morose, her throat closing up as she listened to their names called individually, going up to collect their certificates from Professor Dumbledore. All of the teachers and students were present but Kara didn’t notice the Slytherin girl standing at the back, waiting until her name had been called and she’d walked up to get her certificate and shaken the hand of the Headmaster before she’d vanished back to her secret room. Lena had thought she owed her old friend that much, holding onto the oath she’d made to her all those years ago, even if it had never meant so much to Kara.

 

            She didn’t sleep that last night at Hogwarts. Staying up all night, long after the feast had ended and curfew had come into effect, Kara wandered the hallways in her socks, taking in the classrooms that she’d oddly miss, the grounds that had made her transformations a little bit bearable and the tower she’d found her first bit of comfort there. She deliberated for a long while about going into the room, scared that she might encounter Lena, and not quite sure how to feel about it, still harbouring anger towards her for her cowardice that had gotten people killed. In the end, she went inside and found the signs of her scattered on the window ledge to come back to. Hesitating, Kara had picked up a scrap of parchment and folded it into a crane, like Lena had shown her, leaving the paper bird behind for her as a goodbye. She didn’t think she’d see her again.

 

            Red-eyed and exhausted, she ate her final breakfast at Hogwarts and made sure her things were all packed away in the battered trunk before carrying Bastet downstairs in her arms. The cat was a painful reminder of Lena’s thoughtfulness and Kara hugged her a little bit tighter as she followed everyone down to the boathouse. Sitting in a boat beside Querl, she watched the castle retreat behind them as she left Hogwarts behind and felt a certain sense of homesickness already setting in.

 

            Riding the train back to London, Kara was met by Eliza, even though she could have apparated herself home, and she hugged her mother tightly. They were the same height now, and had the same amount of grey sprinkled through their blonde hair, despite the decades between their ages. People wouldn’t have been remiss to think they were mother and daughter, and she fussed over Kara with her congratulations and her worry over how pale and tired she looked as they made their way over to the wide fireplaces to Floo home instead.

 

            Once Kara had directed her trunk up to her room and let Bastet free to roam around the small house, Eliza vanished upstairs as she told her to stay put. Sitting at the kitchen table, Kara noticed a piece of paper sitting beside the ink pot and picked it up, freezing at the sight of her mother’s name at the top.

 

Alura,

 

It’s been six years now and I know you haven’t replied to any of my letters, but you should know about our daughter. She’s just graduated and I couldn’t be there with the war, but I’m so incredibly proud of her. You turned your back on her, the same as Ilvermorny did, but she’s proven you all wrong, despite what she is. She’s applying to be an Unspeakable once she’s home and I have no doubt she’ll have the marks for it. Our daughter is smart and it breaks my heart that you’ve willingly given up on the privilege to be a mother to her. You’ve missed out on so much and I hope my letters have made you regret it. Clearly not enough if you never came back for her, but I want you to know that she’s been loved and cherished and I’ve been more than generous to you, but this will be the last letter from me. Kara’s old enough to seek you out herself, if that’s what she wants, and if she doesn’t, she knows she has a mother who loves her right here. I hope it angers you to know how much she’s thriving here, away from you. 

 

Your old friend,

 

Eliza

 

            Letting the page slip from her fingers and flutter back down to the table, Kara looked up, white-faced, as Eliza walked back in. She was holding a brown-wrapped parcel in her arms and her expression fell at the look on Kara’s face. Eyes dropping down to the letter, her face rippled with pain.

 

            Setting the parcel down, she clicked her tongue and picked up her finished letter. “I should know better than to leave things lying around. I don’t know where my head is these days.”

 

            “I didn’t know you wrote to her,” Kara hoarsely murmured.

 

            “Only on occasion. I thought- well, at first, I thought she might change her mind. Then I thought I could convince her, but … she never replied. I’m not sure if they ever reached her.”

 

            “They did,” Kara murmured, certain of herself.

 

            Smoothing a hand over Kara’s hair, Eliza gave her a strained smile, the fine wrinkles at the corners of her eyes deepening slightly. 

 

            “I thought one last letter to tell her how well you’ve done would make her regret not being here to feel as proud as I do. You’ve done very well.”

 

            Kara let out a hollow laugh, looking down. “I haven’t gotten my marks back yet.”

 

            “It’s not the marks that count; you’ve tried your hardest and that’s something to be proud of. Now, open your present.”

 

            Eliza nudged it closer to her and Kara slowly unwrapped the twine and paper, a deep blue robe slipping out. She rose to her feet and held it out, the fine wool of it soft in her fingers as she smiled.

 

            “I thought you’d need something for your first day of work,” Eliza said. “You’ll need to look smart at the Ministry.”

 

            “It’s perfect. Thank you,” Kara earnestly replied, giving her a grateful hug.

            

            “Go on. Try it on.”

 

            She slipped the deep blue robe over her jeans and shirt and fastened the clasp at the front. It was a simple cut, without any of the embroidery or embellishments of more expensive pieces, but it was new and Kara had so few new things that it made her chest warm with gratitude.

 

            “Now I just need to get a job,” Kara laughed, looking down at herself as she spread her arms, the wide sleeves falling back slightly.

 

            They ate dinner together as the late spring warmth blew in through the open back door, the sun lingering on the horizon and casting long shadows over their roast chicken. Alex came home late, dressed in a long leather coat with her short hair rumpled from a long day doing who knew what. Kara rose from the table to hug her tightly, taller than her now, which she knew annoyed Alex. 

 

            Alex gifted her a new notebook and a peacock quill that matched the deep blue of her new robe, telling Kara they were for writing down all of the mysteries she solved. Their unwavering confidence that she’d get a job in the Department of Mysteries made her nervous as she feared disappointing them, but she was pleased all the same that they believed in her.

 

            After she’d flicked her wand at the dishes, she went out to the back garden with Alex, sitting on the worn wooden bench with her legs folded beneath her as her sister offered her a flask. It was Firewhisky, which Kara had never tried before, and wasn’t particularly fond of, it seemed. Still, she sipped it as Alex lit up a cigarette that trailed grey smoke.

 

            “Sorry. Bad habit, I know,” her sister mumbled. “Too much coffee and smoking in being an Auror, I tell you. J’onn said it took him twenty years to kick it after his training was done.”

 

            “Don’t let mum catch you.”

 

            Alex laughed, exhaling a breath of green. “She found out a couple of weeks ago. Had a fit, but I told her I’d pack it in, so don’t tell her.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Kara gently elbowed her. “Fine. Anyway, so … when can I join?”

 

            “Join what?” Alex evasively replied.

 

            Scoffing, Kara turned on the bench, grimacing as she narrowed her eyes. Moonlight winked off her glasses and Alex sighed, giving her an exasperated look.

 

            “You have to be invited.”

 

            “Okay, so invite me.”

 

            “By Dumbledore. And you’re not supposed to know who’s a member. It’s like … proper secret shit, alright? I know our loud-mouthed friends have told you they’re in it, and, yeah, me too, but it’s dangerous.”

 

            “I know it’s dangerous, I’m not dense,” Kara rolled her eyes. “I want to help.”

 

            “Yeah, well, my hands are tied, kid. Unless Dumbledore wants you in, there’s nothing I can do. And, trust me, it’s probably better that way. Too many of us are dying-“

 

            “That’s even more reason to let me join so I can make up for numbers. I’m a good dueller; you can vouch for me.”

 

            “You think they’re all not good duellers? That counts for fuck all when you’re jumped by seven Death Eaters in an ally at night. They got Benjy Fenwick good a couple of weeks ago. Blasting curse. We went looking for his body but we only found bits of him.”

 

            Kara was stubborn though, and she pestered Alex for a week straight until her exam results came in. Between all of her classes - including the extracurricular ones - she managed to get five Es and three Os, the delight of her achievement distracting her from her dogged insistence that she was ready to join the Order. With her results came the confirmation of an interview at the Department of Mysteries at the end of July. Her application had been sent in while she was still at Hogwarts, a painstaking Saturday spent writing a cover letter and then outlining her O.W.L. grades, her position on the Hufflepuff Quidditch Team, as a Duelling Club member and her part-time work on the holidays, trying to present a good case for herself. Lycanthropy was glaringly obvious at first glance though and she was shocked to hear back from them.

 

            With a few weeks to prepare for her interview and brush up on any topics they might ask her about, Kara had a big enough distraction to consume her attention, which was why it was surprising to receive a note one day from an unrecognisable owl. It was sparse, with just an address written on it in looping handwriting that Kara had never seen before and she frowned for a moment, setting down her quill and kneeling on the overgrown grass in the garden as she looked around, confused.

 

            Alex arrived home just after dinner, a scrape on her chin and a moody look in her eyes before her expression softened, eyebrows rising inquisitively. 

 

            “All ready for later?”

 

            “Are you talking about the cryptic letter I got earlier?”

 

            Shrugging indifferently, Alex filled a cup with water and knocked it back. “Might be.”

 

            “What’s with all the secrecy?”

 

            “Apart from being a secret organisation?”

 

            “Yeah, but I already know about it.”

 

            Alex gently slapped her shoulder as she walked past, dragging out a chair. “Everyone knows about it, you drip. That doesn’t mean everyone’s in it. Mum’s a sympathiser, but she won’t join up. Plenty of other people are backing the cause, but they don’t want to do the fighting and they don’t get to know who’s who and what’s what.”

 

            “Alright, alright. Can I get something a little more straightforward then?”

 

            “Tonight.”

 

            “When? I didn’t even get a bloody time.”

 

            Snorting, Alex glanced down at her watch. “I’ve got the time. We’ve got about an hour and then we can go. Make sure you eat; there’ll be drinking.”

 

            “Drinking? What is it, a party?”

 

            "Sometimes. Bunch of young people about to die? What else do you think we’re going to do while we sit around and wait for You Know Who to pop us off?”

 

            Kara’s mouth turned down at the corners as she considered it for a moment and found it made a lot of sense. She supposed the looming threat of death as they all spied and duelled wore off a bit, dimming their grand illusions of battle. Most of them would be jaded by now, seeing their fair share of the worst of the fighting, and these were the younger recruits who’d only been at it for a year or so. And Kara would be the freshest of them all.

 

            At seven o’clock, once the sky was dark and they’d eaten their dinner, they donned cloaks and boots and kissed their mother goodbye as Eliza fretted over them both. They left with a stern warning from their mother to look after each other. Alex grabbed Kara’s arm and apparated them to a street in Manchester. 

 

            It was dark but noisy and they slunk past a row of terraced houses, black sacks of rubbish spilling across the pavement and overgrown gardens sporting rusting bikes and shopping trolleys. Passersby drifted up and down the pavement, paying them little attention as they walked shoulder to shoulder, hands on their wands in their pockets. A tight knot of people huddled outside one of the houses, drinking and smoking as a party raged on inside and music leaked through an open window.

 

            “It’s not far,” Alex whispered. “Just better to walk there in case we’re being followed.”

 

            Kara made to turn her head and her sister’s hand clamped down hard on her arm as she hissed through her teeth. “Don’t be stupid. Don’t look. Never look .”

 

            Swallowing, her mouth dry, Kara cleared her throat. “Where are we going?”

 

            “A safe house. A few of the girls live in a flat nearby. You’ll know most of them from school; Imra and Lucy moved in but Marlene McKinnon’s there too. Might be too old for you to remember.”

 

            Alex crossed the street and ducked down a narrow gully before they came out near a dark park. A row of shops, some with neon signs announcing a Chinese takeaway or a green sign declaring Spar, lined the dimly lit street, lamp posts casting wan pools of orange across the pavement as Alex stopped in front of a smooth wall between two closed-down shops with boarded over windows. 

 

            As Kara looked, she found brass numbers attached to a peeling black door that seemed to melt out of the brickwork. Alex wandlessly opened it and stepped into a narrow entryway with a staircase going upstairs. It was bare and made Kara feel slightly claustrophobic as she followed her sister upstairs, greeted by another door. Alex opened that one as well, announcing herself as she stepped inside.

 

            Kara followed her into the open living room, where a group of young women sat on sofas and armchairs or cross-legged on the scuffed wooden floor, drinking cups of coffee as they prepared for a long night on watch or nursed cheap wine and beer after a long day. Feeling a little nervous, Kara raised her hand in a half-hearted wave as her cheeks reddened. There were a few familiar faces though and once Alex had introduced her to everyone, Kara walked over to a tweed armchair where Kelly was sitting and sat on the arm of it.

 

            That was her first foray into the Order business, drinking her first beer and taking tepid puffs of the cigarettes passed around while she listened to who’d been raided last night and who was staking out where tomorrow. It wasn’t as exciting as she’d anticipated, and it would be a while yet before she was allowed to the main Order headquarters and given any real tasks, but Kara was filled with adrenaline as she settled in amongst the other young women fighting for good.

 

 

            The moment Kara left their secret room, Lena deflated slightly. She knew she’d made the wrong choice, telling her to go, but she couldn’t bring herself to think rationally for a moment and see how it all looked from Kara’s perspective. In her eyes, her friend had jumped to the wrong conclusion and hurt her feelings, and if there was one thing Lena could do, it was to harden herself against the people who caused her pain. 

 

            Still, that didn’t stop the childish game that sprang to mind as Kara walked out without so much as a glance back over her shoulder. If you love me you’ll come back. If you’re my friend you’ll say sorry. If you didn’t mean it you’ll come and tell me.

 

            But Kara didn’t answer her thoughts and Lena was too proud to go to her herself, too injured and stubborn to swallow her hurts and be the bigger person. Instead, she went to the one person she could take her anger out on, the person who’d shocked Lena and been the catalyst for her losing the only friend she had. Bypassing McGonagall this time, she went straight to the gargoyle statue and spoke the password, the door admitting her almost as soon as the spiral staircase deposited her at the top.

 

            “Ah, Miss Luthor, good evening. Come in, come in.”

 

            His kindly old man appearance didn’t fool her anymore, a cunning mind hidden behind ice blue eyes and half-moon glasses. Still, she stepped into his office, her hands curled into fists and a hard set to her jaw as her eyes burned bright. One might have believed it to be a sheen of tears, but Lena didn’t cry anymore.

 

            “You let them die,” she harshly stated, a tremor in her voice as she gave him a betrayed look.

 

            “War has casualties,” Dumbledore softly lamented, “and it comes at a great cost to us all.”

 

            “I told you-“

 

            He softly sighed at her narrow-minded view of things and steepled his fingers. Lena thought the act was infuriating and ground her teeth together as she stood in the middle of his office, wanting to break his silver, steaming apparatus, her chest rising and falling quickly.

 

            “Your warning helped us prepare in advance, but to cancel the Hogsmeade weekend would have announced a spy in their midst. It would have removed the window of opportunity we had to apprehend a number of their own.”

 

            “You- they’re dead. I- why am I telling you all these things if- if you won’t even listen?”

 

            “I take your reports very seriously, Lena. You’ve become a valuable asset and I’m very grateful for your help.”

 

            “Grateful,” she scoffed, her face bone white and devastated.

 

            “But there is a nasty side to this, and it stains us all. We can’t save everyone, and we must sacrifice a few to save many. For the greater good. I believe it won’t be long before the remainder of this war plays out, for good or ill. You’re young, and I admit that I must seem ancient to you, but with my age comes invaluable experience to know when to play my hand. There are lessons you’re yet to learn, and I hope you forgive me for making you complicit in the hardest one yet.”

 

            Mouth opening and closing soundlessly, Lena couldn’t believe he could so calmly discuss letting innocent people die. A small, pathetic sound escaped her before she clamped her lips together.

 

            “You’ve done very well, Lena.”

 

            “I don’t want to do this anymore,” she murmured, her voice trembling. “Not if I can’t help people.”

 

            “You’ve helped a great many people,” Dumbledore gently assured her. “And you could help many more before the end. The list of Death Eaters you’ve given me, if you could help gather evidence to prove their guilt, they’ll spend their lives in Azkaban once this is all over. You would be a hero. You would have stopped evil itself from spreading across Britain and beyond. You’re free to make your own decision, and I understand how difficult it must be for you, but I will only ask you to reconsider and continue to help.”

 

            She couldn’t formulate a response, and even though some part of her knew she was being manipulated, Lena tersely nodded and then saw herself out before the old man could say anything else. Downstairs, near the statue of the gargoyle, she punched a wall hard enough to split her knuckles and let the pain punish her almost as much as her broken heart before making her way down to her Common Room.

 

            Christmas came and went quickly with letters sent to Dumbledore with the passing comments mentioned by Lex, and Lena returned to Hogwarts with hatred settling into her heart. She could feel how empty she was becoming, the people she was consorting with chipping away at the image of herself she had in her head. Could she still think she was good for hanging around with the people she did? Kissing Veronica Sinclair to steal her letters and coax secrets out of her, duelling with other Houses in solidarity with the more ruthless Slytherins, lamenting about the state of Hogwarts and making loud proclamations about how her brother would help her join the Dark Lord once she graduated to garner trust with the children of other Death Eaters. 

 

            Every day, she hated herself just a little bit more, failed herself to the point where she started writing the lines in between her study sessions. She didn’t have her mother’s quill and a part of her craved the pain of the letters opening up on her arm, but she was left with her lines instead, self-loathing and years of discipline leaving her volatile and angry.

 

            The year passed by quickly with Lena studying hard and avoiding Kara in their Alchemy classes. When she wasn’t in class, she was studying. When she wasn’t studying, she was at Duelling Club, another extracurricular class, or her private Occlumancy lessons with Slughorn. Otherwise, Lena’s time was dedicated to spying on Slytherins and any other students she’d heard had turned from the other Houses. It was shockingly easy to gather intel on them, with the use of her invisibility cloak or perching as a raven on a windowsill, in a tree, in a courtyard, ruffling her feathers and cawing as she stored the information away for later reporting.

 

            Before she knew it, her end-of-year exams were over and Lena just felt empty inside. It wasn’t with any real sense of accomplishment, it wasn’t with relief, knowing she’d endure another summer of studying regardless of it being the holidays, and she found herself missing her friend even more than usual as she sat in her tower by herself. 

 

            Graduation followed soon after, with all the remaining students feeling like a pathetically small group inside the cavernous Great Hall. They wouldn’t allow any parents this year and Lena watched from back until Kara’s name was called and she shook Dumbledore’s hand, her cheeks dimpling with delight as she rejoined the sea of black robes and hats. Lena left then, not even bothering to stick around for Veronica’s. 

 

            The next day she was due to go home and Lena was tense and sullen as she apparated to the gates of the manor house, letting herself inside and finding herself mercifully alone. Hope greeted her and Lena smiled faintly down at the little House Elf, turning down the offer of a late lunch and making the most of her alone time to search her brother’s bedroom. Finding scattered letters in various places, Lena memorised the contents and dates and left everything as it was before scrawling down everything, no matter how inconsequential, and sending it off to Dumbledore. 

 

            Lillian was home first, barely acknowledging her existence, save to ask how her exams had gone. They ate dinner together and then Lillian had her perform a few practical spells, her scorn becoming evident when Lena couldn’t manage even a wisp of a Patronus.

 

            It was only when Lena stiffly muttered a retort to her mother’s disdain that Lillian gave pause. “I haven’t been given much cause to have good memories, have I?”

 

            “You’ve been given a roof over your head, food and clothes. A better education than you get at that school. Everything you’ve ever asked for. Are you really so ungrateful, after everything I’ve done for you?”

 

            “No,” Lena murmured.

 

            Fixing her with a sharp look, Lillian’s mouth thinned and her eyes narrowed. “I don’t like your tone.”

 

            “I think you’d be hard-pressed to find something you did like about me. It’d be a shorter list, that’s for sure.”

 

            “Careful,” Lillian warned her, a lighthearted lilt to her tone that let Lena know she was on thin ice. “Or have you gotten cocky since you’ve turned seventeen? I’ll still have you obey me at my mercy, regardless of whether you can twirl your silly little wand around without fearing expulsion.”

 

            Hesitating, wondering whether she could actually take on her own mother in a duel and deciding she didn’t want to find out, Lena smiled slightly. 

 

            “I’m tired. I think I’ll go to my room and study a bit before bed.”

 

            “A wise choice.”

 

            Brusquely making her exit, Lena changed into her pyjamas and lit the lamps before doing as she’d said and read in bed until her eyelids grew heavy. She woke the next morning to an empty house again and decided to go to Knockturn Alley for the day, wondering how much she’d be able to overhear at The White Wyvern over a bottle of butterbeer.

 

            That became her routine for the summer, reading various healing books and finishing off her essays in the back corner of the pub, while regulars came and went. Shockingly, her mother left her relatively alone that summer and Lena wasn’t sure if it was because she was seventeen and could legally hex her to bits if Lillian tried anything or if her mother was just so rushed off her feet at work that she didn’t have as much time to torture her daughter into submission. As it was, Lena had had to deal with multiple attacks and duels as she sat in the pub, and she wondered how overrun St. Mungo’s was with the injured lately. 

 

            Lena was sometimes joined at her table by various school friends - although she used that term lightly - and her brother and his older friends on a few occasions. Lex would always mock her, stealing her homework and laughing with his oafish friends, all of them thinking themselves so important with their puffed-out chests and hidden marks. She put up with it on the off chance they spilt something important over glasses of Dragon Barrel Brandy.

 

            A part of Lena had always been waiting for her brother to realise his responsibilities and his potential and step up, to put his brains to good use. He was the eldest, and was smart enough, although Lillian had been slack with him and that’s why Lena resented him at times, for pointing their mother’s ire towards her. But if Lex wouldn’t do it, wouldn’t pander to their mother’s dreams that he’d be a Healer like her, wouldn’t do anything but work the job their father had pulled strings to get him and drink with his Death Eater friends around terrorising the country, Lena would. Lena would do what he wouldn’t, and while she was at it, she would make sure she did it better than he ever could have. Lena Luthor was not a failure.

 

            But she was weak, or rather thought of herself as such, because at the end of July, when she got word that the McKinnon’s were on Voldemort’s list to be dealt with that night, she couldn’t stop herself from thinking about Kara. If Dumbledore put in the call and summoned the Order to try and turn the tide of the attack, would Kara be amongst them? Lena had wondered about it for weeks now, knowing that her old friend had wanted to join, but how hard was it to join? The Order was desperate for good people, genuinely on their side, as outnumbered as they were, but to let someone who’d graduated mere weeks ago sign up was really showing their hand.

 

            It would be bloody and dangerous and as the sun sank beneath the horizon of the Irish countryside, she paced in her room. It was grey outside and Lena hesitated before locking her bedroom door from the inside and casting a spell to make it sound like a quill was scratching and books being opened and closed. They’d already had dinner and Lillian was working that night, so Lena didn’t expect to see her again for a day or more.

 

            Still, she hesitated a moment longer, cracking her knuckles and pacing before the empty fireplace as her heart stuttered in her chest. One thing she knew was that she wouldn’t be able to live with herself if anything happened to Kara. She’d done what she could when Dumbledore had squandered her information and kept her friend back at the castle, and while they might not be friends anymore, might have grown to hate each other on some level, there was a deeper part of Lena that still loved her and would keep her promise to always be Kara’s friend. That meant stopping her from walking into danger.

 

            Opening the window before transforming into her raven form, Lena swooped out into the darkness of early dusk and swooped beyond the confines of the house grounds. Transforming back into her human form so she could apparate, she smoothed a hand over her black robes and tried to quell the nervous lurching in her stomach. She’d managed to find out from Lex where the McKinnon’s lived, and admittedly knew very little about them, other than their oldest daughter was a Gryffindor and she’d seen Kara’s sister around her a few times. No doubt Alex would be there tonight, and where Alex was, Kara was sure to follow along.

 

            Their house was set in the countryside, in a small town surrounded by fields and forest. Lena stowed her invisibility cloak and stuck to the trees as a raven for a while as she scouted out the area, having gotten quite good in her Animagus form and mercifully better at keeping her clothes with her when she transformed. The sound of her wings flapping in the stillness of the night felt too loud as she swooped from tree to tree and then across the fields as a black shadow overhead.

 

            She spotted a few figures dotted around the house, none of them wearing silver masks, and settled down behind the cover of a bush in sight of the red-brick semi-detached to wait in her human form, covered by her invisibility cloak. Hours passed by and Lena felt stiff and bored, the waning moon clouded over and a light fog gathered in the dips of the surrounding countryside. It felt very atmospheric, just a little eerie and weighted with anticipation as midnight came and went.

 

            The first sign of an attack wasn’t a shout or a scream but a flurry of colourful light from in the trees a hundred feet from the house. It could’ve been fireworks to a Muggle who didn’t know better, but Lena’s heart leapt into her throat as she crouched, waiting. Her cloak added a layer of protection to her 

 

            White-faced, Lena watched the fighting unfold as figures seemed to surround them everywhere. Silver masks caught fingers of moonlight from behind the cloud cover and she watched arcs of vivid green illuminate the gnarled forest. When a tree beside her split in half with a shower of splinters by an errant spell, Lena realised she wasn’t safe just because no one could see her beneath her cloak.

 

            Deciding to move, she kept her wand in hand and was quick and low as she hurried through the woods. It was too dark to see and she didn’t want to risk lighting her wand in case she needed to expose her arm and disarm someone, knock them unconscious or curse them into oblivion. That was how Lena wanted to help, but that wasn’t her priority that night. 

 

            Before long, she was cut and bruised from stumbling around, lost. The night was cold and her lips trembled as she stifled shivers, rain worming its way through the canopy as the fighting went on, leaving wizards and witches slipping in the mud, wrestling each other down as much as they were casting spells. She didn’t spot Kara amidst the fray and the light fog and it was only just getting started, making her worry about how bad things would get before long.

 

            Even as she crouched down near the base of a tree, trying to make out faces in the dark, she watched a Death Eater apparate in a cloud of black smoke, wand raised to take out a red-haired man. Lena was quicker though, her wand snapping out to stun the robed figure, who keeled over into the nettles as the red-haired man turned around. Another man appeared at his side, red-haired and smiling as he clapped the man who must have been his brother on the shoulder. Lena thought her spell had gone unnoticed, but she was wrong.

 

            “You shouldn’t be here, girl,” a grizzly man with a roving electric blue eye growled at her as he appeared out of the dark, limping towards Lena, who startled, scuttling backwards on her ground as she looked around. “Aye, I can see you under that cloak, and I know you, too. Dumbledore won’t be pleased to know you’re exposing yourself like this.”

 

            Lena scrambled to her feet, gathering the invisibility cloak around herself as she tried to settle her pounding heart. “Kara Danvers … is she here? If you can tell me that, I’ll go.”

 

            “Danvers? The blonde one? Werewolf, ain’t she? I know her but I can’t answer your question. Go on, now, off with you. Go home, girl.”

 

            He turned and limped off, and Lena blinked with the realisation that it was Alastor Moody. One of the best Aurors, who’d spent years of the war filling cells in Azkaban. Lena wondered if he’d be the one to catch her brother. Still, no matter who he was, she didn’t listen, setting back off through the trees, the scent of damp earth and tangled weeds filling her nose as screams split the night, filling her with terror. A curse shot past her head and she skidded on a patch of leaves, going down, the invisibility cloak hitching up over her calves before she scrambled to her feet, fingernails digging into soft mud and rotting leaves. 

 

            Lena’s breaths were sharp and quick, a stitch in her side, a tremor in her hands as she gripped her wand tightly and looked around at the madness. Her skin was clammy and cold and she was already filthy, disoriented and panicked as she moved through the fighting like a ghost, aware that any moment a spell could hit her, a flash of green life could end it all, but her mind was only focused on one thing - one person.

 

            And then she caught sight of blonde hair turned silver in the moonlight, a tall girl adept enough to take on two admittedly rather bad Death Eaters in a duel slashing her wand in rapid motions as she advanced on the duo. Kara was back-to-back with Alex, who was taking on another, more proficient dueller, terrifying as she viciously threw spell after spell at them. Lena hesitated, wondering whether she should take her too, but she watched as Alex finished off the Death Eater and plunged further into the fray, confident in her sister’s abilities as she was confronted by more of the enemy ripping through the forest in a torrent of black smoke to decimate the Order.

 

            Taking her opportunity, Lena hit one of the Death Eaters with Sectumsempra, knowing the effects now and showing no qualms about using it as the figure dropped, rent open by the spell. The other one she hit with a blasting spell that nearly took the cursing man’s arm off, and then she was almost barrelling Kara over as she slammed into her, arms wrapping tightly around her before she dragged her along in her apparating. Before Alex could even realise her sister wasn’t at her side anymore, Lena had taken her miles away to some empty field, overgrown with weeds and rubbish.

 

            She staggered as they landed, her foot catching the hem of her invisibility cloak and ripping it off her, and before Kara could even comprehend what had happened, Lena had her lain out flat in the grass, stunned into unconsciousness. Breathing heavily and covered in a cold sweat, Lena flopped down onto the grass beside her and let out a ragged breath, a broken sound of pure relief escaping her as she ran a dirty sleeve over her dirtier face.

 

            “I’m sorry. I’m just keeping you safe,” she whispered to her friend, looking at her and taking in the familiar scars and her crooked glasses.

 

            Reaching out, Lena fixed them and then turned her face to the cloudy sky, spotting a few stars and feeling incredibly small. She wondered if someone so small could really make a difference, if she should go back and sneak through the forest and incapacitate more Death Eaters, try her hardest to even the odds for the Order, go inside and get the McKinnon’s out before they were killed.

 

            Instead, she stayed in that field and felt the breathless urge to cry as she did nothing but sit with her friend, the one person she could keep safe, and waited it out. She had to stun Kara a few more times and it was a couple of hours before dawn that she saw the distant sign of the Dark Mark glowing eerily green above the house. She had to wonder how many had died in the trees and how many had escaped. She hoped the Order knew when to withdraw, when self-preservation won, outnumbered twenty to one with no hope of staving off the river of death brought forth by Voldemort’s followers. Surely the handful that had been ordered there that night knew they never could have saved a family he’d marked for death.

 

            Lena remained there in that field until the darkness thinned and became long shadows, the horizon showing a sliver of orange. Kara was still out cold so she gathered up her cloak and hauled her friend to her feet with some difficulty. She had a vague idea where Kara lived, looking Falmouth up on a map of Cornwall at home one summer, and focused on the destination before apparating there.

 

            The sky was lightening to a streaky pink and the early morning smelled of salt air as a warm front blew in off the coast. Focusing on the address Kara had shown her, written in her mother’s hand as Kara explained she was Secret Keeper, Lena tried to apparate there, shortening the distance she had to haul her friend. Of course, she couldn’t apparate into the house, but she found herself on a quiet street lined with grey cottages and watched as one seemed to melt out of the terraced row and felt relief rush through her.

 

            Walking up to the front door, she flicked her wand to open it and heard the clamouring of voices. Stepping over the threshold with Kara’s limp form draped over her shoulder, Lena paused.

 

            It was the soft smells of detergent and cooking bacon and mown grass that mingled in the entryway as the sea air rushed in behind her. A corner of the rug in the living room was flipped up as if someone had tripped and forgotten to smooth it back out. Too many plants crowded the place and a black cat mewed as it rose to its feet on the bottom step and arched its back, sauntering over to rub against Lena’s legs with familiar affection. Lena felt weak with the deep ache in her chest, entering a home for the first time in her life, some archetype brought to life before her very eyes.

 

            It was a tiny house filled with too many people, panic palpable in the air, so it only took a moment for someone to realise she was there. Looking into surprised dark eyes, Lena swallowed and watched the young woman set her glass down and rush into the hallway, quietly calling Alex over her shoulder. 

 

            Moving into the living room, Lena gently eased Kara down onto a comfortably worn sofa and turned just in time to face the wrath of Alex Danvers. Grabbing the front of Lena’s black robe, Alex hauled her to the narrow hallway and slammed her against a wall, pushing the tip of her wand into Lena’s grimy cheek. Lena had to admit, she didn’t look her best, and she was very suspicious indeed, showing up out of the blue with Alex’s missing sister as she bypassed the wards, which had the Auror looking so grey with terror.

 

            “Alex,” came the chiding sound of who could only be their mother, Lena’s eyes flitting over to her to confirm.

 

            “What the fuck are you doing here?” Alex snarled, ignoring her mother.

 

            Lena swallowed her fear, pressed up against the slim console and the brass-framed mirror. “Ask Dumbledore.”

 

            “How did you get in here?”

 

            “Ask Kara.”

 

            Alex stepped back, her shoulders slumping with confusion as she kept her wand against Lena’s cheek. Lena’s eyes slid past her to land on Kara, who was being fussed over by the dark-skinned girl who’d first seen her. Lena remembered her; she’d tried to stop them from duelling when they’d attacked Lena that first time. A muscle twitched in Lena’s cheek and she brought her eyes back to Alex’s brown ones.

 

            “Do me a favour; don’t tell her I was here.”

 

            Brow furrowed as she glanced back over her shoulder at her prone sister, Alex was momentarily distracted. Long enough for Lena to lash out, knocking her wand aside and throwing herself over the threshold of the door, apparating away before Kara’s sister could stop her.

Chapter 15

            Kara woke right after Lena left, groggy and feeling stiff and leaden as she sat up. She felt like she’d suffered the mildest full moon, her body aching and her mind foggy as she tried to piece together what happened. The door slammed shut as she sat up and she watched Alex stride across the room in three steps and grab a fistful of her robe, white-faced with fear.

 

            “What’s the name of my owl?”

 

            “I- wha- Maximus,” Kara spluttered, confused.

 

            Wrapping her in a tight hug, Alex smelled of mud and rain and blood, making Kara stiffen before pushing her back. Her sister has a few shallow cuts on her face and her hair was damp, but otherwise, she was unharmed. Kara’s stomach jolted as she looked around at everyone else, taking stock of the surprisingly full living room.

 

            “What happened?” Alex asked, flopping onto the sofa beside her.

 

            Kara raked a hand through her tangled curls, leaves and grass snagged free. “I- I don’t know. I was duelling with two Death Eaters and that’s the last thing I remember. Something slammed into me and then I felt like I was being stretched apart and  … I don’t remember anything else. What time is it? How long was I out?”

 

            “It’s just past six,” Winn said, glancing down at his watch.

 

            “We were out all night looking for you,” Imra said, grey with grief and exhaustion.

 

            “All night?” Kara echoed, shock flashing across her face. “What do you mean? How did I get here then?”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Alex moved over to their friends, the Order members who’d been there last night and had lost sleep over the thought of Kara being missing. Speaking quietly to them, Alex nodded and clapped shoulders, grabbed hands, and they all started to trickle away, a few ducking into the fireplace while the rest stepped out the front door and apparated away.

 

            Eliza ran a hand over her face and gave Kara a worried look. “Are you okay?”

 

            “Yeah, yeah, I’m fine,” she murmured, rolling her stiff shoulders. “I feel like the full moon was a couple of nights ago but nothing sleep won’t fix.”

 

            “I’ll fix you a cup of coffee,” Eliza said, kissing the top of her head and walking to the kitchen.

 

            Bastet leapt onto Kara’s lap and nuzzled her face before stepping in a circle and curling up in her lap. She stroked her soft fur and looked up as Alex stepped into the living room, raking a hand through her short hair.

 

            “The McKinnon’s,” Kara started, a hopeful look on her face, which was quickly dashed as Alex shook her head.

 

            Sinking down onto the pilled armchair and drawing her knees to her chest after kicking off her boots, Alex propped her chin on top. “Dead. All of them.”

 

            “Marlene?”

 

            Alex nodded and the air rushed out of Kara’s lungs as she sank back against the pillows. Her stomach plummeted with dismay and she closed her eyes, tilting her head back. Neither of them spoke for a moment and Kara thought about the brazen Gryffindor girl she’d been sharing wine with only a few nights ago at her flat shared with Imra and a few others. She swallowed with some difficulty, wondering how many more would be gone before this was over.

 

            “So, do you want to tell me what’s going on?”

 

            Opening her eyes, pale eyelashes fluttering, Kara raised her eyebrows a fraction. “Going on with what?”

 

            Hunched forward, fiddling with a Muggle lighter, sparking the flame and avoiding looking at her sister, Alex shrugged. Kara shifted further upright, careful not to jostle Bastet too much.

 

            "Why did Lena Luthor bring you home?”

 

            Kara felt like she’d been punched in the stomach, her insides actually hurting as she wordlessly opened and closed her mouth. It hurt as she swallowed past the lump in her throat and she sniffed, pushing her glasses up her nose.

 

            “I don’t know. I didn’t see her there.”

 

            She was telling the truth but something clicked into place. The spells tearing apart the two Death Eaters Kara had been duelling, the invisible thing that had seized her, Apparating her away from the fray. That’s what had happened, she realised. It made her stomach twist with confusion.

 

            “What happened there?”

 

            “I don’t know,” Kara murmured, her face clouding with a brooding look. “I already told you.”

 

            “Not last night; with her. She waltzed in here when she shouldn’t have even known where we live . Told me to ask you about it.”

 

            And then Kara burst into tears, startling the cat and curling in on herself as she nudged her glasses up and dug the heels of her palms into her eyes. She heard Eliza’s footsteps grow nearer and the smell of coffee assaulted her nose, mingling with something astringent, almost medicinal.

 

            “Here, sweetheart,” Eliza shushed her as she rubbed Kara’s back and pressed a hot mug into her hand. “You’re alright. It must’ve been a scary night for you.”

 

            She’d misunderstood Kara’s tears and sat beside her for a moment, urging her to take a sip. It was laced with whiskey to calm her nerves and warm her up, and Kara drained it all quickly, the lingering grit of sugar at the bottom dissolving on her tongue.

 

            “I might shower,” she hoarsely said as she climbed to her feet.

 

            The empty mug dangled from her fingers and she walked into the kitchen to set it in the sink before vanishing upstairs. In the tiny bathroom, she let scalding water wash over her, needling her back as she rinsed off the mud ground into the lines of her palms and the lingering staleness of dried sweat from the fear of the stakeout. 

 

            Hair damp and skin flushed pink, she dumped her dirty clothes in the laundry basket and made her way back into her room. Alex was already waiting for her there, stretched out on her bed as she toyed with her old Quaffle. Kara bit back a groan and dressed in clean pyjamas, the sweatpants showing her ankles and the T-shirt revealing her scarred arms.

 

            “Go on then,” Alex encouraged her.

 

            “There’s not much to say,” Kara mumbled, towelling off the ends of her hair as she sank onto the edge of her bed. “We were friends.”

 

            “Friends with a Slytherin?”

 

            Making a scathing sound at the back of her throat, Kara shook her head. “Don’t be so narrow-minded. How do you think you passed Potions?”

 

            Alex sat up, shock crossing her face. “That’s who you were talking about when you said you knew someone who could help? She’s the one who’s been sending you all those letters. Merlin, Kara. You really gave one of the most notorious Pureblood families our address without even considering that she might use it to hurt us?”

 

            “She wouldn’t,” Kara quickly defended her old friend’s honour. 

 

            “Then why was she there last night? She’s certainly not an Order member.”

 

            She didn’t have any counter-argument for that and her mouth thinned as she stared down at her lap. Alex was annoyed at her for the rest of the day and Kara stayed shut up inside their room, aching and trying to distract herself with the interview prep she’d been going over. Her interview was in three days and she was so nervous that she didn’t know what she’d do if she didn’t get the job. Kara had felt lost for so long but she’d been fixated on this career path for a few years now and it felt tangible and real.

 

            The day of her interview, she wore a secondhand suit she’d bought at The Junk Shop on a quick trip to Diagon Alley, the men’s cut a little baggy on her slender frame, but Kara made do, donning her deep blue robe over the tan jacket and pants. Her wayward curls were tamed as well as they could be and she polished her wire-rimmed glasses free from any smudged fingerprints.

 

            Eliza insisted on making her breakfast, despite her churning stomach, and Alex wished her luck before she went off to work for her Auror training, leaving Kara to navigate her way to the Ministry of Magic on her own. She’d been there before, of course, when she’d had to register her status as a werewolf, and she followed the familiar way, flushing herself in and stepping out of the wide fireplace.

 

            The tiled Atrium with its big fountain occupying the middle was an awe-inspiring sight, owls swooping past carrying messages or newspapers as all manner of witches and wizards hurried off to their departments and meetings. Kara had never been to the Department of Mysteries before and had to ask for directions as the Wand Weigher at the Security Desk set her wand down on a scale and let a small ticket churn itself out with the details. Vine with a unicorn hair core, eleven inches and pliant.

 

            Following the man’s directions, Kara rode one of the elevators down to Level Nine, the hallway she stepped out on tiled in the same black as above, the walls bare and windowless with only a door set at the opposite end. The door opened to the Department and Kara felt her throat go dry with nerves as she followed the hallway to it.

 

            Stepping into the Department proper, Kara was faced with a round room with a number of doors. The Entrance Chamber started to spin, disorienting and only mildly alarming. Standing just outside the spot where she’d entered, Kara looked around with interest as the doors stopped spinning. There were twelve of them, handleless and closed, and the dark marble floor was reminiscent of standing water as candles emitted cool blue light over the chamber.

 

            A door opened and a man stepped about, perhaps a decade older than Kara, his skin a little sallow and his eyes unsettling. He looked surprised to see her there and Kara gave her a wan smile, raising her hand in a slight wave.

 

            “Can I help you?”

 

            “I’m here to see Professor Saul Croaker. I have an interview.”

 

            “Oh. Yes, alright. Stay here.”

 

            He vanished again and Kara wondered what would happen if she tried to enter one of the rooms. Would the doors even open without any handles? Would they respond to magic? She wasn’t left to wonder for long as the door opened again and an older man stepped out, his face wrinkled and his tweed suit a little dishevelled, as if too preoccupied with more important matters to care about his appearance.

 

            “Miss Danvers?”

 

            “Yes, sir,” she said, sticking a hand out for him to shake.

 

            “Right, well, in my office, shall we?”

 

            He gestured to one of the doors and led her into an unassuming office. From an artificial window, a beam of sunlight highlighted spiralling dust motes and fell across the tiled floor. A desk monopolised most of the space and an open cabinet was crammed with hundreds of files and documents, and Kara was itching to know about what. The room smelled of paper and damp as she was directed into a seat across from the Unspeakable.

 

            “Now, Miss Danvers,” he said, settling down. “I have to say I’m impressed by your tenacity. I’ve never known a werewolf to attend school. Most of them are stuck on Ministry benefits.”

 

            She masked a wince and shifted uncomfortably. He continued to scan her application on the desk before him.

 

            “Hm. Very good Transfiguration marks. Good Astronomy, Charms and Ancient Runes. Potions … good, but we don’t use that much here. Good, good. You’ve taken all of the core requirements, and Alchemy, which is helpful. Now, tell me a bit about yourself.”

 

            Speechless for a moment, Kara launched into a glossed-over story of her life. Moving from America, her time in extracurricular clubs at school, her interest in theoretical magic and why she wanted to become an Unspeakable. Her throat was dry and her words were rasping after a while, feeling like she was trying to plead her case for a job. Kara could feel her cheeks turning rosy and her palms were clammy as she kept them balled up in her lap.

 

            “And your particular affliction,” Croaker said once she’d finished. “How will that impact your work if you were to get a job here?”

 

            Eyebrows rising a fraction, Kara cleared her throat. “Oh. Well, it’s really only the night of, which would be after work hours, and if- if I was … in bad shape, I’d be more than willing to make up for any work I missed. On the weekends, or staying back late. I- I know it’s not ideal, sir, but I’m willing to work hard if you give me a chance.”

 

            Leaning back in his seat, he eyed her for a moment and then picked up her essay on death that she’d written as part of her application. His eyes darted over her writing and he hummed.

 

            “Your essay on death is quite interesting. I take it you can see Thestrals?”

 

            “Yes, sir.”

 

            Pursing his lips he considered for a moment and then softly sighed. “You have the marks for it, so I’ll let you sit the test and we’ll see.”

 

            Perking up, Kara smiled brightly as he climbed to his feet, gesturing for her to follow. They ended up in another office, this one more communal with rows of desks and cubicles occupied by quiet Unspeakables puzzling through theories as they completed written reports on their findings. Kara was taken to the front of the office and seated at a desk with a quill and ink pot and test paper.

 

            “You have an hour,” Croaker informed her. “Good luck.”

 

            Kara immediately got stuck in with the questions, most of them philosophical in a way, where there were no correct answers but they wanted to know her interpretation. She finished before the hour was up and waited for Croaker to come back as the other Unspeakables eyed her from their desks, coming and going from the other rooms in the Department of Mysteries. 

 

            He collected her papers and shook her hand, telling her they’d be in touch with the outcome of her application, and Kara went back home to wait. It was an agonising three days, but an owl eventually came with a job offer and a request to start on Monday. 

 

 

            On the verge of starting her Seventh Year, Lena received a letter with a Head Girl badge enclosed along with the list of required textbooks. She didn’t tell her mother, but on the morning of the 1st of September, she emerged downstairs with her new tailored Slytherin robes on and sat down for breakfast, asking her mother if she’d finished with that morning’s copy of The Daily Prophet. Lillian’s eyes had lingered on Lena’s new badge pinned to her chest and her lips had twitched slightly at the corners before she nodded and then pushed a leather purse of money across the table.

 

            Eating her toast and drinking her tea as she mentally did the crossword and lingered on the article about the McKinnon’s, Lena was silent. Neither of them had much to speak about beyond Lena’s classes, and Lillian had already impressed the importance of her N.E.W.T.s on her daughter long before she’d ever set foot inside Hogwarts.

 

            Finishing up and brushing crumbs off her lap, Lena pushed her chair back and climbed to her feet. Pushing the chair back in, she made to leave. 

 

            “Kiss your mother goodbye before you go,” Lillian stopped her, tapping her cheek.

 

            Lena had long since tired of their games but obliged her, telling her she’d see her at Christmas. Gathering her trunk and her owl, Lena used the fireplace to Floo to Platform Nine and Three-Quarters and spent a good hour reading as she sat on top of her trunk, waiting for the train to screech into the station. As Head Girl, she was meant to sit in the compartment with the Prefects and her fellow Head Boy but she left after stowing her things. Most of the people she’d feigned friendly terms with had graduated, which meant Lena had to work her way into the confidence of some of the younger students, and she lingered in the long carriage at the end of the train, favoured by Slytherins, until the whistle blew and she retreated back to the carriage at the front. 

 

            Shaking hands with all of the younger students who’d received Prefect badges over the summer, she let the new Head Boy, a Ravenclaw, take the lead. The conversation was stilted and awkward and Lena wanted no part in it as she buried her nose in her book and waited for them to arrive at school.

 

            After the feast, she led the First-Years at a brisk pace down to the dungeons and left them at the doors to their dorms before vanishing off to her own. This year, courtesy of her status as Head Girl, she had a private room to herself. Pushing open the dark wood door, Lena looked around and found it comfortably worn, and not too dissimilar to the shared dorm.

 

            The bed was made up with the same hangings and heavy bedspread, with a few extra pillows for embellishment, but the headboard and posts were carved with snakes and filigree motifs. A plush emerald sofa was placed in front of the mosaic fireplace, depicting Merlin at his peak, and her uniforms and normal clothes were already stowed away in the wardrobe and her books shelved above the walnut writing desk stowed in the corner. A rug covered the chilly stone floor and Lena toyed with a few trinkets decorating the place, feeling a spark of relief that she’d be afforded some privacy this year. There was an adjoining bathroom as well with a roll-top bathtub and a sink and toilet and she was glad she wouldn’t have to make the extra effort to hide her scar.

 

            Her classes quickly swept her up in the busy course load of her final year, earning homework for every lesson on her first day back. Lena didn’t mind though, she welcomed the distraction and went up to her secret room for some privacy to get a heady start on it all. When she entered the room, she wound through the equipment to her window ledge and paused at the sight of the folded paper crane sitting there, as it had been all summer long.

 

            Throat closing up, Lena picked it up with shaking hands and turned it over, looking for some sign of a note. But it was just a folded crane, a parting reminder of the early days of their friendship, almost seven years ago now. She tucked it safely away in her bag and ended up brooding for the rest of the evening as she cast practical spells to vent her frustration. 

 

            Weeks slipped by quickly with frightening news greeting them every morning. It was difficult for Lena to remain locked away at the castle, knowing Kara wasn’t safe there with her this time. Every time word of an attack came her way, she reported it and willed Kara to not go, wondering if she’d see her name in the newspaper over the next few days. There were more than enough familiar names already and she couldn’t bear it if Kara Danvers showed up amongst the dead. Lena was barely sleeping, barely eating, by the time the end of October rolled around, her expression a permanent glower as she spoke to no one, her look alone deterring them.

 

            The news came the next morning, on the first day of November, that Voldemort had been defeated and Lena didn’t soften, didn’t cry like so many of the other students. There was still so much anger and coldness inside her. Raw hatred and so much betrayal and frustration and loss nestled in her chest for everything that had been taken from her over this war. But in that moment, she was free of it all and she felt the heavy weight of her responsibilities lighten, leaving her able to breathe properly for the first time in a year.

 

            It left a bitter taste in her mouth though, that everything had broken down only a year before it all ended. She’d tried her best to help, had successfully hidden it from everyone in her life, only to still be accused of helping out the wrong people. Kara didn’t even know the depth of how much danger Lena had put herself in, even on a small level of going home to a family that had no qualms about using the Cruciatus Curse on her as a trite punishment. What would her brother have done if he knew she was leaking information he’d unknowingly told her?

 

            And for it all to end a mere year later was almost laughable, in an empty way. Now, she was alone at Hogwarts, without even the mere pretence of friendship. Kara would have graduated anyway, but without the letters she would have sent, Lena felt the cold sting of loneliness. And that was all she had for company as everyone else celebrated the end of the bloodshed. She felt utterly alone, and while she’d always been afraid of being alone, she’d learnt to overcome her fears by dominating them, so Lena chose to thrive in her isolation.

 

            It seemed useless to spy now that the war was winding down, only a few fear-fuelled attacks by Death Eaters scrambling around without a leader reported in the news now, so aside from in relation to her classes, Lena didn’t speak to a single soul. She ate breakfast alone and focused on her work in class, and then ate lunch alone and went to the rest of her classes, before eating dinner alone and then studying alone in her secret room or the library. It was almost the same as it had been in her first weeks at Hogwarts, only now she knew what she was missing.

 

            Christmas approached rapidly and Lena was bundled up against the snow as she made her way home. It would undoubtedly be her last Christmas there and that was something to look forward to at least. Once she graduated, she’d move somewhere else, spend all her time at Healer School and never look back. This would all be behind her soon enough. Still, she had to get through Christmas first, and things were tense from the minute she stepped foot inside.

 

            “It’s fine,” Lex hissed, “they won’t be talking to anyone. They can’t.”

 

            He let out a cold laugh as Lena lingered in front of the fireplace, listening to the conversation between mother and son.

 

            “You’re reckless,” Lillian chided him. “You should have left revenge up to the others and waited to see if the Dark Lord’s truly gone. You should’ve played your hand better; if word gets out, you’ll be ruined, and for nothing.”

 

            “For loyalty.”

 

            “Loyalty? Loyalty to whom? I applaud your support while he was alive but this baby that supposedly killed him has put an end to this whole thing.”

 

            “He’s not gone,” Lex insisted, and Lena could hear him pacing, caged and seething. “Mark my words, he’ll be back. And he’ll reward those who stayed loyal to him.”

 

            Lillian scoffed loudly. “Think strategically, Lex. You don’t win at Wizard’s Chess by sticking to one piece. It’s the bigger picture, the long game that helps you win. These Aurors are well-respected, and now that the attacks are all but done with, they’ll be hunting down anyone with a mere rumour of implication.”
