            “They’re bound for a permanent ward at St. Mungo’s. It’s fine. The Lestrange brothers and that Black girl did the worst of it. Crouch and I barely cast a few spells. I have to say, they didn’t hold up nearly as well as expected. Even Lena doesn’t scream so much.”

 

            “Speaking of your sister, she should be home soon. We’ll have no more talk of this and you’d better destroy any evidence you were involved. They’ll come after all the old Pureblood Slytherin families and if the house is raided, I won’t go down for your mistakes.”

 

            Lingering in the living room as she heard her mother’s footsteps vanish upstairs and her brother’s head towards what she thought was their father’s old sitting room, Lena gave it a few minutes before making her arrival known. Banging her trunk along the floor and letting Morrigan’s cage clatter, the owl safely ushered out the window already, Lena walked into the foyer.

 

            “Do you have to make such a racket?” Lillian witheringly greeted her as she appeared at the top of the stairs. “You’re seventeen, use your wand.”

 

            “I’m eighteen now,” Lena corrected her, flicking her wand at her luggage, which floated.

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lillian sighed, “then you should know how to do a basic levitation spell. Take it upstairs. Quietly.”

 

            Obliging, Lena set her bags down in her room and immediately pulled out a piece of parchment, drafting a letter to Dumbledore inquiring about Aurors attacked and sent to St. Mungo’s recently. She had to wait for Morrigan to come back and was careful to keep the letter on her person just in case her brother came in and was nosy enough to start reading her mail. 

 

            When her owl tapped on the window later that night, a mouse clamped in her beak, Lena murmured an apology and tied the letter to her leg. After watching Morrigan fly off, Lena went to bed and woke in the early hours of the morning to a tap on her window with her owl bearing a response. It was the first time Dumbledore had responded directly to one of her messages and she paused as she stared down at the phoenix seal and opened the letter.

 

Do you have names of the people involved?

 

            Swallowing thickly, Lena sank down onto her desk chair and made a list of the names she’d overheard.

 

The Lestrange brothers

One of the Black sisters

Surname Crouch

 

            Then she hesitated, ink blotting the paper, and lowered the nib of the quill to the page and added one more.

 

Alexander Luthor

 

            Sealing the letter, she sent it off with Morrigan and anxiously awaited the outcome of her confession. Her brother was surly and aggressive over the next few days, a smug look of derision on his face as he lazed about, drinking as he exchanged letters with his friends, which Lena raided his room for when he went out to meet them. She always returned them to where he’d left them and avoided him as much as possible.

 

            It was only a few days before the manor house was raided by the Auror Office. 

 

            Lena had been reading up in her room when the sounds of banging and splintering wood greeted her with shouts. Bolting upright on her bed, her book tumbled from her hands and she walked over to her door, pressing her hand against it and closed her eyes as she listened. Footsteps filled the house, doors slamming and voices calling back and forth, and when Lena heard footsteps eventually near her door, she stepped back and raised her hands.

 

            The door burst open, breaking her lock and she blinked at the sight of Kara’s sister. Wand aimed at her, Alex paused as well, as if she hadn’t been anticipating Lena being home. Her lips twitched slightly and Lena arched an eyebrow in response, haughty but compliant.

 

            “Wand’s in my left pocket,” Lena murmured.

 

            “Don’t move.”

 

            Lena nodded and Alex stepped forward, pulling Lena’s wand out and then directing her towards the door, following behind.

 

            “Who’s here?” Alex asked.

 

            “My mum, my brother and Hope, our House Elf.”

 

            Snorting, Alex escorted her downstairs. “That’s oddly humane of you to consider your House Elf.”

 

            “Well, she’s the only person in my family I like,” Lena wearily sighed. “Is this a raid?”

 

            “I’ll ask the questions.”

 

            She didn’t actually ask any more though and Lena was led over to Lillian, who was rigidly immobilised in the foyer. Likewise immobilised, she watched as Lex was dragged downstairs by three Aurors, shouting his head off and cuffed, his dark eyes wide with disbelief. He looked at Lillian as they dragged him outside and he called out to her. Lena watched as her mother raised her chin a fraction, her face stiff and impassive as she ignored him.

 

            They searched the whole house, questioning mother and daughter individually and collecting evidence. When it was Lena’s turn to be interviewed, she sat at the long dining table in the dim room, a cooling cup of tea before her, courtesy of Hope, and answered the Aurors’ questions as best as she could. The evidence was already damning enough, and it was a mere courtesy to clear her own name. 

 

            While she sat there, a letter with a wax phoenix seal was brought in and set on the table. The Head Auror, a man in his late thirties with dark skin, who had shown her his DMLE badge after introducing himself, tapped it and raised his eyebrows.

 

            “Where did you get this?”

 

            Alastor Moody limped into the doorway and scoffed. “Really, J’onn? You bloody well know where she got it.”

 

            Keeping her expression neutral, Lena stared straight ahead and missed the confusion that rippled across Alex’s face as she stood on the fringes of the room and observed. 

 

            “Did you respond to this letter?” J’onn asked.

 

            Green eyes cutting to him, Lena hesitated and a rueful ghost of a smile twitched her lips. “I did, yes.”

 

            “What did it say?”

 

            “Just a list of names. Five of them.”

 

            J’onn glanced over at Moody, who nodded. Clearing his throat, the Auror seated to her left politely raised his eyebrows and nodded his head. “Just one more thing; your arm.”

 

            Blinking, Lena was slow to reply. “What about it?” she asked, her tone haughty and clipped.

 

            “I’ll need to see your forearm.”

 

            “Unless you’re a member of the Investigation Department and are investigating me as a suspected dark witch, I don’t believe you have any legal jurisdiction to demand that of me.”

 

            A ripple of laughter ran through the assembled Aurors and J’onn leaned back in his chair, lacing his fingers together as he smiled patiently. That made Lena bristle slightly, a prickle of damp sweat at her lower back as she considered that she might not be able to avoid this.

 

            Swallowing thickly, her low voice trembled slightly as she curled her fingers over the cuffs of her thick sweater sleeves. “You have the letter. You know who it’s from. Isn’t that enough proof?” she quietly pleaded.

 

            Leaning in closer, J’onn kept his voice down as well. “It’s not for my benefit. But you have nothing to worry about.”

 

            Raising his voice to be heard by the rest of the room, J’onn placed his hand out, palm up and fingers splayed expectedly. “The Investigation Department is a subdivision of the Auror Office, so I’m afraid I do have legal jurisdiction here. You’re not under investigation for any crimes, but it’s our due diligence to be thorough. Now, your arm, if you will.”

 

            She pushed her right sleeve up first and bared her pale forearm, setting it in J’onn’s rough, warm hand as he cast a series of spells, checking for any attempts to disguise it. Tugging the sleeve back down, she toyed with the left one and felt her stomach know itself with nauseous embarrassment. After a moment, she slowly pushed it up a couple of inches - not enough to show the scar - and set her left arm in his hand. 

 

            Giving her a funny look, J’onn pushed the sleeve up further and then froze at the sight of the scar. Nudging the sleeve up a tiny bit further to expose the whole thing, while keeping her arm blocked from sight by the rest of the room, his eyes drank in the meaning and then darted up to meet Lena’s gaze. Her eyes were trained on the table though, existing outside of herself as she willed it to be over.

 

            Clearing his throat, J’onn rolled the sleeve back down for her with surprising tenderness, until Lena sharply jerked her arm from his. Rolling the rest down, she covered the spot on her arm with her right hand, pale and rigid.

 

            “Alright, we’re done here.”

 

            The remaining Aurors lingering in the foyer all started to disperse and Lena remained seated at the table, ignoring all of the movement around her. A few sets of eyes burned into the top of her head as she kept hers bowed but she couldn’t bring herself to look up, couldn’t say a word to any of them. Apparently, a few knew of her status as a source for the Order, but she was still an outsider, still subject to suspicion in public. If she’d been more vocally objective, made more of a fuss about helping the Order in an official manner, they wouldn’t have had to go through the pretence of checking for a Dark Mark, making her reveal her shame to another person, a stranger no less.

 

            Lena was still sitting at the head of the table, in her mother’s usual spot, when Lillian walked in. Grey with weariness, arms folded over her chest as her pencil skirt and blouse looked pristine, despite the long day, her mother arched an eyebrow.

 

            “What did you tell them?”

 

            “Nothing. I didn’t tell them anything.”

 

            It wasn’t a lie. They already knew the truth, they’d already known she wasn’t a part of it and she hadn’t had to betray her brother any further than she already had. Her mother wouldn’t have to know she’d been the one to tip off the Order, the names relayed to the Auror Office, sending them out to raid the house. Lillian wouldn’t have to think any less of her daughter - if that was at all possible.

 

            “Good,” her mother curtly replied.

 

            “I didn’t have to. He damned himself.”

 

            Fixing her with a frosty look, Lillian raised her chin as her eyes narrowed. “Your brother can be proud of his loyalty. Remember that.”

 

            “Loyalty? To what? Growing up, you taught us that Purebloods were superior to others and that we were stronger and better than Muggleborns and Half-Bloods, but that was all a lie. This war was supposed to be about restoring us to our rightful place in the world, so everyone would know how great we are, but that’s not what they think. They hate us and he’s going to Azkaban for it. He wasn’t brave, he was … stupid. Stupid to think he wouldn’t get caught.”

 

            “You talk of bravery? Your brother is everything you’re not. Do you think that your discipline makes you better than him? You’ve had to work hard for everything your brother so easily takes, and that is what sets you both apart in this world. You will never measure up to his raw talent; you will always be second to him and it’s a shame. It really is.”

 

            Lena suppressed a weary sigh. Could Lillian not see how tired she was, how rote their arguments were? The same disdain, the same insults. They dredged it over and over, every time Lena was home from school, every time she so much as got a question wrong.

 

            “You could be brilliant but you’re a coward,” Lillian hissed. “I have tried my hardest to beat it out of you, but at the end of the day you’re just like your mother.”

 

            “Don’t talk about my mother,” Lena tightly replied.

 

            Lillian let out a light laugh, arching an eyebrow in a mannerism Lena had inherited from her in her upbringing. “You’re so defensive of her, yet all I earn is your derision when I am the one who raised you. Defend her and hate me all you want, but remember that it wasn’t me who tried to kill you. I can’t blame her though; perhaps if I’d had the chance, I might’ve done the same.”

 

            Lena quickly looked down, lowering her head as her chin trembled and her mouth went dry. She didn’t want to remember, closing her eyes as the dark memories of cold water rose to greet her. The feeling of fighting against the hand holding her head underwater, her lungs burning for air. One night her mother had taken her to a lake near their small house and only Lena had come home. She remembered the rippling current of what she now knew to be a Kelpie rising up from the gritty depths of the lake as mother and daughter sank with the weight of the stones hidden in Elizabeth’s pockets. She hadn’t been able to see, it had been too dark, but she’d felt it, the moment her mother had been dragged away by the creature and Lena had surfaced in the shallows, spluttering for air as the moonlight flickered on the inky surface of the lake. 

 

            Her father had found her the next day, damp and filthy and pale in their house she’d managed to find her way back to. Lena always said her mother drowned, and to this day she stood by it. She didn’t tell anyone her mother tried to kill them both, had filled the pockets of her robes with stones and waded into the lake with her four-year-old daughter in her arms, holding her close as the water closed over her head. If it hadn’t been for the Kelpie, Lena would’ve been dead too. But she already had one terrible mother, so she lied to herself because she didn’t think she could survive thinking anything else, knowing she’d been unwanted by everyone in her life.

 

            “Look at you. So weak. That’s her in you, that’s for sure. The only brave thing she ever did was rid the world of another Muggleborn; it’s just a shame I got left with you .”

 

            It wasn’t the first time Lena had heard Lillian wish she was dead in some capacity. After a while, she’d numbed herself to the emotional effects of how painful it had been to be unwanted, the trauma of witnessing another mother’s death and her own close encounter, only to feel the rejection of another on the heels of it. Over time, she’d lost contact with the origins of her trauma, her sense of self-worth deteriorating as she seemed to exist outside of what had happened to her, all of the hurt and anger swallowed and repressed over the years.

 

            There was so much trauma bottled up inside Lena that she’d had to stamp out any positive moment in her life to make room for it all, to keep her feelings contained. But she hadn’t even begun to feel the lasting impressions it had all made on her, and didn’t know just how much damage had been done yet. All she knew was that it was a sort of death in itself to feel like she didn’t even exist to her mother, Lillian’s indifference so hurtful that Lena wanted to beg for attention, even now.

 

            “If I’m weak then it’s your fault,” Lena snapped.

 

            “My fault? I tried my hardest to give your life some shape, some direction. Without me, you would have nothing. No drive to succeed, no ambition, no determination. Even now, after all my effort, you’re still a disappointment to me. You will amount to nothing because that is what you are. You're my greatest failure. Truer words couldn’t be etched into your skin.”

 

            “Then why didn’t you make me good so that you could’ve loved me?” Lena shouted, bright spots of colour in her pallid cheeks as she frowned, her teeth bared as she clenched them, trying to retain her composure.

 

            “Listen to you,” Lillian said with a quiet scoff of laughter, waving a hand at Lena as she shook her head. “Love. How trite. How pathetic. I’ve given you every resource to help further yourself in life, and at the end of the day, you beg for something so trivial and inconsequential as love. ”

 

            Bristling, Lena pushed the chair back and rose to her feet. “I do not beg. You’ve given me too much pride to do that.”

 

            “All the same, I do love you. It upsets me that you believe I don’t.”

 

            Lena was speechless, caught off guard by her mother’s self-pity, feigning wounded feelings as she tried to nettle Lena with guilt. Swallowing thickly, Lena paused and then brusquely brushed past her and ran upstairs to her room, slamming the door hard enough to make the window panes rattle in their frames.

 

            She went back to Hogwarts shortly afterwards and didn’t come home for the holidays again, seething with resentment and just a small bit of vindication as she read about Lex’s sentencing in the newspaper. A part of her felt guilty for turning him in but no one knew she’d done it; there wasn’t a single soul in the world for Lena to tell, and she found she preferred it that way. She wouldn’t exist as a printed name being hauled in The Daily Prophet for her help, she wouldn’t receive an Order of Merlin from the Ministry for all her spying. Lena would graduate and go to Healer School and this would all be a brief moment in her life, and she’d go on alone, as she’d always done.

Chapter 16

            Lena completed her work placement at St. Mungo’s shortly before her N.E.W.T.s and graduated from Hogwarts at the top of her year. Sitting in a sea of black robes as she wore the green and silver tie for the last time, her little Slytherin tie pin neatly held it in place as she waited for her name to be called. She’d never succumbed to the general air of dishevelment most students acquired over seven years at boarding school, and her uniform was pristine as she walked up to shake Dumbledore’s hand and received her certificate.

 

            “You should be proud,” he softly murmured as Lena grasped his aged hand.

 

            She didn’t feel proud. Lena didn’t feel anything except bitterness. She didn’t reply, didn’t offer him a thin smile or so much as a twitching muscle on her face, taking her certificate and walking off the stage to reclaim her seat.

 

            They’d allowed parents to come now that it was safe again and Lillian had shown up in a rare display of motherly duty. Lena had suffered a brief kiss on the cheek for show and allowed her mother to tell her how proud she was, brushing Lena’s hair out of her face and fixing the hood of her robe. She detested the whole thing, and once she arrived home the following day, Lena went upstairs and packed all of her belongings and then apparated to Camden, knocking on the door of the flat she’d been given directions to.

 

            Andrea opened it and gave her a pleased smile as if she hadn’t thought Lena had been serious about moving into the spare room. Lena would have moved into a cardboard box on the side of the road if it meant getting as far away from her mother as possible. There were four of them there; Andrea Rojas, Veronica Sinclair, Gayle Marsh and Lena. 

 

            She got the smallest bedroom, with barely enough room for a single bed and the dresser with the empty grate of an old fireplace. Lena didn’t mind though, she packed her things away with a light feeling in her chest, knowing she wouldn’t have to go home again if she didn’t want to. The flat belonged to Andrea’s father and Lena paid only a pittance in rent. She had her own vault at Gringotts, set aside by her father with a very generous sum, and Lena could have bought her own place but oddly wanted the company. She wasn’t even nineteen yet and had never lived on her own, never gone without being catered to, which was a slightly alarming prospect.

 

            Still, it turned out she was good at cooking, her affinity for Potions transferring across to following recipes as she made dinner for them all most nights, while Veronica brought home bottles of wine from The White Wyvern, where she was working with a desire to own a string of pubs in the future. While not the most sociable person, and the four of them being an odd collection together, Lena had to admit she rather enjoyed the nights when the four of them were home, drinking on the parquet floor before the living room fireplace, the mess of dinner and work and four girls living together cluttering the apartment as the warm summer air and sounds of London drifted in through the open window.

 

            Her acceptance into Healer School came in July with a start date of September, on the heels of her N.E.W.T. results, with an Outstanding in every subject. Lena felt only a small sense of satisfaction at getting in. While her friends all worked and went out for drinks, she spent most of her time studying over the summer, still in school mode with the intention of years of studying before her. It would be another two years before she stepped foot back inside St. Mungo’s, and another year of practical work on top before earning the title of a Healer, and Lena relished every moment of it.

 

            Lectures ran late into the evening and Lena spent all sorts of hours brewing potions and practising new healing spells in class with other students. It was highly competitive and by the end of her first year, barely half of them remained and she was beyond the skill of her other classmates. Some of them resented her for that but Lena kept her head down and spent most of her time at the student library in the draughty building in Kensington, two stone fireplaces always empty and floor-to-ceiling windows filling the stacks of books with an abundance of light in the daytime.

 

            Settling into her flat and her new school, Lena felt a sense of peace settle inside her, some of the old bitter resentment dulling with time. It still kept her up at night sometimes, and she couldn’t bear to wear anything but long sleeves, a fact which made her housemates make fun of her, although the two she’d slept with surely must have noticed that she’d never once removed her shirt. Sometimes, she forgot to think about Kara as well, and that was a relief because whenever she was reminded of her, it broke Lena’s heart just a little. 

 

            The last time she’d had any sort of visceral response to a thought of her had been towards the end of her Seventh Year, brewing Amortentia and breathing in the smell of books and fresh rain, and something else, something that had taken Lena a second to place, unsettling her with the realisation that it had been the smell of Kara. Whether it was her perfume or soap, Lena didn’t know, but she’d left Potions white-faced and irate.

 

            Two years passed by and Lena flourished. She was more confident, definitely more jaded, and wasn’t quite so closed off, although she enjoyed her space. Her friends - if that’s what they were - would take her out to Muggle spaces, to Camden Market and Hyde Park, the four of them sticking out like a sore thumb in varying fashions with Galleons and Sickles in hand. Lena was always a little more inconspicuous with her cigarette pants and shirts or turtlenecks, depending on the weather, but Andrea wore stylish cloaks everywhere in bold colours, and Veronica had recently been tattooed with a long snake that has the propensity to move on her skin, which she always bared as much as possible of to showcase the magical tattoo. 

 

            They taught her how to do her makeup and she got used to Andrea swearing in Spanish around the flat when she was in a mood. She was naturally closer to Andrea, actually considered her a friend and trusted her as much as Lena was willing to trust anyone these days, and she didn’t mind Gayle so much either, although she was always coming and going, working as a Curse-Breaker for Gringotts and frequently overseas. Neither of them were particularly interested in the war, hadn’t had any desire to join Voldemort and were only focused on their own ambitions. Veronica Sinclair was different and Lena never quite warmed to her, although she’d never let on she’d been using the young woman while they’d been at Hogwarts, and knew that she’d been an avid supporter with plans to join the Death Eater ranks as soon as possible. She supposed she’d never made it far up the ladder and had fallen silent since a toddler had wiped the Dark Lord out of existence.

 

            The four of them got used to each other, and it was almost like being at Hogwarts, in a shared dorm, just with more alcohol, freedom and work. The start of her practical placement in Healer School, and what would be her final year of study, saw Lena dressed in dove grey trainee robes with the Healer School crest stitched over the pocket and beige scrubs on underneath. Andrea was the only one up that morning, drinking coffee and smoking out of the window as the radiator popped and groaned beneath her. 

 

            “Morning,” she drawled, exhaling pink out the window, whisked away by the morning breeze.

 

            “You were loud last night,” Lena grumbled. 

 

            “Sorry, darling. I did try to cast Muffliato, but we’d been drinking all night and I was rather clumsy.”

            

            “Still that same man?”

 

            “Yes, Russell.”

 

            “I still don’t know which one that is.”

 

            “Well, he was a Hufflepuff - four years ahead of you so it’s no surprise you don’t remember him. Not like you knew any of the Hufflepuffs well, is it?”

 

            Lena hummed, her stomach twisting, and she moved over to Andrea, holding out a hand for her cup. Her friend knocked the dregs back and Lena refilled it and one for herself as well.

 

            “Ta,” Andrea murmured, eyeing Lena’s placement uniform. “All ready for today?”

 

            Quietly scoffing, Lena’s lips twisted derisively. “The worst part is going to be running into my mother.”

 

            “At least she’ll be too busy to be much of a bother. If you like, I’ll convince Veronica to say something to piss Gayle off and let them hex each other badly enough to need hospitalisation. Nothing too bad - maybe a few broken bones, a good curse.”

 

            Giving her a droll look, Lena’s mouth twitched at the corners and she looked down at her watch. “While I’d love to see who’d win that round, I’m sure it’ll be fine. I have to go.”

 

            “Alright. Well, The White Wyvern once you clock off? You can tell us all about it; drinks on me.”

 

            “Sure. I’ll see you later.”

 

            Nodding, Andrea returned to her cigarette and Lena picked up her black satchel, slinging it over her shoulder and then tossing Floo powder into the main fireplace. She went through to the lobby of St. Mungo’s and found a gaggle of other grey-robed trainees waiting there. 

 

            Her first day went well, with her only contact with her mother, who was Healer-In-Charge, being a quick introductory speech and a mirthful moment of eye contact as her pale eyes shone with amusement at the stony look on Lena’s face. After that, Lena was assigned to a second-year Resident Healer, Sam Arias. She was from Bristol and quite tall, with brown hair, hazel eyes and light brown skin. Her gentle way of talking caught Lena off-guard as she shadowed her for the rest of the day, answering her questions as they stood at a patient’s bedside, rolling gauze around wounds, smearing salves on burns and reciting textbook procedures for fixing broken bones.

 

            “Come on, let’s get lunch,” Sam said to her as her watch showed past twelve. “You have to take it when you can, or else you’ll starve all day. If you work here after your training, they’ll give you a cryptex like this with a Protean charm on it so it’ll burn to alert you to any of your patients.”

 

            She showed Lena the small wooden box with a number of round dials hidden within, denoting numbers and letters displayed in the small gap of the device. Sam pointed them out to her and explained the meaning, the first dial turning to the floor, the second to the ward, and then the remaining numbers denoting which bed. It was a system Lena would have to pick up, but she was vaguely familiar with it from her Hogwarts days.

 

            Sitting in a tearoom with harlequin black and white tiled floors and a number of wooden tables and chairs, the walls panelled with honeyed wood and a counter with trays and staff behind it, Lena took a bite out of her sandwich. Sam knocked back the two cups of coffee on her tray after emptying a potion into one to keep her awake, and Lena watched as she tipped her head back, eye drops going into each eye as she blinked rapidly.

 

            “You’re lucky they’ve only got you on the nine-to-five now, just wait until you’re pulling two days. My advice; don’t get pregnant. You’ll have little free time as it is, and a colicky baby is the icing on top when you’re on call all night.”

 

            Muffling a yawn, Sam shook her head and Lena smiled faintly, a bewildered v forming between her eyebrows. She liked Sam a lot and it took her a moment to realise that the other woman reminded her ever so slightly of Kara. Lena wasn’t sure whether it was the softness of her or the earnest way she spoke but there was something of her friend when she was younger in her and it made Lena stiffen momentarily like she’d been plunged into icy water. 

 

            Drinking her tea and finishing off her sandwich, Lena allowed the Healer to enjoy her break in relative peace, although Sam was warm and welcoming, asking questions, and telling her about the hospital and anything else that came to mind. After finishing off the dregs, Lena set her cup down and softly cleared her throat.

 

            “What do you make of the Chief?”

 

            “You mean your mother?” Sam said with a soft huff of laughter.

 

            Lena wrinkled her nose and her mouth thinned. Arms crossed over her chest, she sat rigidly on her chair and waited for Sam to continue. Most people at St. Mungo’s would have figured out Lena was Lillian’s daughter, by surname alone.

 

            “I haven’t had much to do with her, to be quite honest. She’s too concerned with running the place to have much involvement in Resident Healers. I take it that’s good news for you?”

 

            Shrugging, Lena’s lips twisted contemptuously as she straightened and curled inwards slightly. “Well, it’s not bad news.”

 

            “Well the Attendings have been gossiping about you all day and they say you’re something of a prodigy so you shouldn’t have anything to worry about.”

 

            “I’m not a prodigy,” Lena murmured. “I just study a lot.”

 

            Shrugging, Sam picked up her tray and rose to her feet. “You’re good, and that’s all they’re going to care about.”

 

            Sam was partially right, and no one paid her any attention other than open curiosity when she shadowed her Resident to patients overseen by an Attending. They would ask Sam questions and Sam would quiz Lena on it once they’d set off through the halls again, fetching Blood Replenishing potions or shoes squeaking as they ran to lend extra hands to particularly extreme cases. 

 

            By the end of her first day, Lena was only slightly overwhelmed by it all, saying goodbye to Sam and gathering her things from where she’d left them. She went straight out to the street level, standing outside the weathered shop named Purge and Dowse, Ltd. and walked through London to the entrance to Knockturn Alley. Her friends were already at The White Wyvern at their usual table, and Lena joined them as they peppered her with questions about her day as she knocked back her first glass of Bungbarrel Spiced Mead set before her.

 

            Lena’s life fell into the routine of three days of lectures and essays, two practical placements at St. Mungo’s and two days off to finish her essays, get blind drunk with her friends and wander around London. She picked up on Muggle fashion while walking the streets, buying boxy blazers and flared suit pants, leather trousers and wide-collared shirts tucked into her washed-out jeans. Everyone else tried out neon but Lena couldn’t abide by anything that wasn’t somewhat traditional, even though her mother would’ve had a fit at her leather trousers.

 

            She enjoyed her days at St. Mungo’s though, itching for a sea-foam green robe to replace the grey trainee one, wanting a permanent position at the hospital. Lena wondered whether her mother would grant her a spot immediately or whether she’d enjoy toying with her daughter, but Lena knew it wouldn’t be entirely up to Lillian, which was a small comfort. Working hard to ensure there was no reason to doubt her suitability for the role, she surprised everyone, except for herself, with how competent she was.

 

            There were days she was sent to the Alchemy Room to help Sam brew her quota of healing potions for the month, stirring cauldrons and labelling vials, doing stocktake and cutting the leaves or stems of varying plants, and hours spent filling out charts with the scratching nibs of their quills in an old administration office. The quiet of the office brought the same comfort as a library, a few planters of herbs blooming on top of filing cabinets, used teacups cluttering desks as exhausted Healers came and went. Lena enjoyed sitting there as sunlight streamed through the windows before she was dragged back into the challenging training.

 

            One day, Lena was surprised to find Jack Spheer occupying a bed with an ashen look on his sweaty face. His shoulders were lopsided but he still managed to give her a charming smile as their eyes met across the ward. “Lena Luthor, as I live and breathe. Or is it Healer Luthor now?”

 

            “Not for six months yet,” Lena wryly replied. She picked up his chart and raised her eyebrows. “Dislocated shoulder?”

 

            “I wish I could say it was from duelling or something cool, but I fell off my broom in three aside Quidditch.”

 

            Sam chuckled as she accepted his chart from Lena and pored over it. “Still living the glory days of the Slytherin Quidditch Team, hm?”

 

            “Too busy at the Ministry these days. Not like the fun you lot have here.”

 

            “What did you end up going into?” Sam asked.

 

            “Department of International Magical Co-Operation. The International Magical Trading Standards division. Absolutely riveting.”

 

            “Well, a dislocated shoulder will have you out of here quick enough to get back to your legislation. Luthor, would you grab his left shoulder and hold him still for me?”

 

            Lena cut her eyes at Jack and then away as she grabbed his left shoulder. Meeting Sam’s eyes, she nodded and then drew in a shallow breath. “So, were you at least winning?”

 

            He gave her a winning smile, reaching up to rake his dark hair off his forehead in a manner that Lena wasn’t quite sure was an intentional attempt to be charming or not. She wasn’t particularly weak to his charms but he was handsome and he’d grown a well-kept trimmed beard since leaving school, which she had to admit suited him. 

 

            “I was until Rogers slammed into me with his bloody Beater’s bat. Hey, isn’t he seeing your ex?”

 

            “My ex?” Lena echoed, confused as she’d never been in anything that could be considered a relationship, and the only person she’d ever loved had broken her heart without so much as a kiss exchanged between them.

 

            “Yeah, Andrea- ow, fuck.”

 

            Sam pulled his shoulder into place and then pressed the tip of her wand into the joint, murmuring quietly as she soothed the inflamed muscles. Smiling, she raised her eyebrows in a sweet manner.

 

            “All done. Luthor, will you get him an anti-inflammatory tonic? Maybe something for the pain as well.”

 

            Nodding, Lena fetched what she’d been instructed to and observed with Sam. The Healer left him there for an hour before filling out his discharge papers as Lena recited the doses they’d given him and the proper procedure for dislocations.

 

            “So, you know Jack?” Lena asked.

 

            “We were in the Gobstones Club together.”

 

            Snorting, Lena’s cheeks shallowly dimpled with amusement. Sam gave her a knowing look. “Don’t pretend that it’s lame; I know you were in the Chess Club. Didn’t you win the School Championship seven years in a row?”

 

            Shrugging evasively, Lena just smiled. “Something like that.”

 

            Her shift still had an hour left so she escorted Sam to check in on a batch of Skele-Gro and a Sleeping Draught. Lena was already trusted to brew potions by herself, given her affinity for it, but considering she wasn’t an actual employee, she didn’t have the authority. It meant that Sam got a quick reprieve, dozing on a stool with her head resting on the brick wall in the windowless room as Lena carefully tended to the cauldrons and followed the instructions.

 

            It was a bitterly cold January and she bundled up in her coat with a cloak on top before leaving, promising to bring Sam coffee on her next shift. Despite it being only just past five o’clock, it was already dark and she was planning on going home for some time to herself. Seclusion was something she enjoyed and she knew that Andrea was out with her boyfriend tonight, Veronica was bartending and Gayle was in Egypt for the rest of the week to undo a curse on a newly excavated tomb. 

 

            As she left, she found a tall figure leaning against the worn shopfront waiting for her, his hands tucked into the pockets of his woollen overcoat, a sleekly cut robe on top to fight off the chill of mid-winter. Lena paused at the sight of Jack and arched an eyebrow.

 

            “Are you waiting for me?” she sceptically asked.

 

            “Yes. Thought I’d see if you were free for a drink.”

 

            Adjusting the strap of her bag, Lena looked around and hesitated, “alright, but not at The White Wyvern.”

 

            “Don’t want to be seen in public with me?” he laughed, pressing a hand to his chest. “I’m hurt.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lena set off down the street with him. “I have too many nosy friends that’ll make a mountain out of it.”

 

            “Still not much of a social butterfly, then?”

 

            “No.”

 

            “And are you seeing anyone? Last I heard you were with Veronica Sinclair. A frightening woman.”

 

            “Merlin, no, I wasn’t with Veronica Sinclair. She’s one of my housemates,” Lena wryly replied. “And Andrea, which you probably know, seeing as you apparently know Russell.”

 

            Jack shrugged, stopping at a set of traffic lights and waiting as he watched the symbols. “Funny things, aren’t they? Muggles. Who comes up with this? Little men telling you when to walk.” They crossed once the lights changed and he carried on. “I wouldn’t say I know Russell well . Just through work, really. Different departments though.”

 

            They walked to Diagon Alley and stepped into The Leaky Cauldron and out the other side into the street. The Leaky Cauldron was always full and loud with witches and wizards coming and going, so they settled on The Hopping Pot in Carkitt Market instead. Lena had been there a couple of times and led the way through the maze of skinny streets that turned the bitter wind into something malevolent, patches of ice slippery underfoot as their breath turned to pale streamers in the cold. 

 

            They knew when they’d entered the market by the shift of brick and wood-panelled buildings crammed together haphazardly to the open outdoor arcade with the painted facades of shopfronts. Despite the hour and the darkness, lamps illuminated the stalls still operating as shoppers browsed the wares of hawkers. They made for the greenish front bearing the sign The Hopping Pot and stepped into the warmth. 

 

            Jack went to order - Dragon Scale for him and Wizard’s Brew for her - while she got the last two seats in a small alcove beneath a vaulted dome of tiles. It was warm and comfortable inside and her pink fingers thawed as Jack brought their drinks over.

 

            “So, how’s the cat?”

 

            “The cat?” Lena blinked, setting her pint glass back down. “Oh. The cat. Right. Um, well, it wasn’t for me. It was a gift.”

 

            He raised his eyebrows slightly, shedding his robe and coat. “Really? For who? I didn’t see it around afterwards.”

 

            Shifting awkwardly, Lena gave him an uneven smile. “Oh, um, someone in a different House.”

 

            Jack let out a scoffing laugh, “are you joking? You had friends in different Houses?”

 

            “Just one,” Lena shrugged, “and not so much of a friend. She liked cats though.”

 

            “Well … who was it then?”

 

            “No one,” Lena dismissively shrugged, taking another sip of her stout. 

 

            “That’s actually quite funny. We were at school together for years and this is probably the longest conversation we’ve ever had, but we all just assumed you didn’t talk to anyone. Not until Andrea managed to poach you after I’d gone. Why the sudden change of heart?”

 

            “I just … I had to focus on school. Expectations and all of that.”

 

            “I guess it’s paid off. Your mum must be proud.”

 

            Lena wrinkled her nose. She hated it when people assumed that. Lillian had never been anything but disappointed in her, no matter what she achieved or how much she excelled. Her supervisors at St. Mungo’s could very well be singing her praises right now, but Lillian would find some flaw to her, some fault in her work.

 

            “Well, it’s hard to be the family disappointment now,” Lena drolly replied.

 

            “I was sorry to hear about your brother.”

 

            “Why? He had it coming.”

 

            “Yes, but it must have been difficult for you.”

 

            She shrugged again. “Not really. I was back at school not long after.”

 

            “Right.”

 

            Finding herself awful at carrying the conversation as her natural inclination for defensiveness rose up, Lena let Jack navigate it, for the most part. Trying her best to not be too standoffish and prickly, she answered as best as she could and questioned him about work so he would talk about himself instead. He was nice though, understanding and easy to listen to, demanding nothing of her as they talked. He ended up buying Lena dinner at the pub and they stayed out late, copious amounts of ale and stout warming them against the cold when they eventually stepped outside.

 

            A few witches and wizards stumbled down the various side streets of the alley, all flushed and in some degree of inebriation and Lena hugged her robes to herself. She shivered slightly and thought of her bed and her warm room in the shared flat and then glanced up at Jack. He was looking down at her with lucid dark brown eyes, snowflakes clinging to his dark lashes as it started to snow and Lena wasn’t sure what she meant to say as her lips parted. Up until that point, she’d had every intention of going home.

 

            “Where do you live?” she asked instead.

 

            “I’ve got a flat in Notting Hill,” Jack replied, hesitating before raising his eyebrows. “Do you want to see it?”

 

            He was bold enough to ask so Lena was willing to say yes, although she didn’t see much of the apartment once they made it inside. There had never been a normal example of a relationship in her life, so Lena did what she did best and tried to manage her conflicted feelings the only way she knew how, by making a mess of things so she wouldn’t have to feel guilty when it all went pear-shaped. He didn’t question why she wouldn’t take her shirt off and Lena didn’t ask what it meant to him, and both were content to leave it at that.

 

            Jack made her a strong cup of coffee the next morning, which Lena thought was one of the best she’d ever had, sitting at the wooden table in the kitchen of his nice apartment. It was tidier than her place and made for one person, sleek and dark and masculine with leather and wood and muted colours of greens and deep browns. It reminded Lena a little of home, if the manor has been cosy in any sort of way. Truthfully, she didn’t mind being at his place at all and as he made her scrambled eggs she gave herself a tour and then showered in his bathroom.

 

            Feeling the awkward uncertainty of what came next, she said goodbye to him after breakfast and then apparated to Camden, in the alleyway behind her own apartment. Wandlessly opening the door, she crept inside and eased it shut, slipping off her shoes and padding barefoot to her room. Changing into clean clothes, she sank onto the edge of her bed and frowned as she took stock of things, her pale face reflected back at her in the tall mirror propped against the wall, her breaths shallow and slightly uneven.

 

            After a moment, she climbed to her feet and dragged the curtains shut, blocking out the grey sunlight and looked around her room. Her clothes were scattered around the place - a waxed Barbour jacket, a striped Slytherin scarf and faded flared jeans folded on the foot of her bed next to her broken-in leather boots. No one bothered her, although she could hear music playing in Veronica’s room and the sound of the shower running. 

 

            No one came into Lena’s room. They knew it was out of bounds, and while their rooms showed the lived-in signs of cluttered makeup and perfume, books, quills, robes, towels and cups, hers was always neat and relatively empty. Only Lena entered her room, even though the others were in and out and she often spent hours curled up on Andrea’s bed with her back to the wall and a book in her lap, her friend keeping up a stream of conversation as she painted Lena’s well-kept nails for her and let her borrow her clothes when they went out.

 

            She had a workshop just after lunch and left without seeing anyone, only to return in time for dinner, a Chinese takeout already ordered from down the road, and she rolled her eyes at the exclamations of shock and glee as she let herself in.

 

            “Look who decided to show her face,” Veronica snidely commented.

 

            “Go on then, who was it? You haven’t mentioned anyone,” Andrea said, nudging a clean plate towards the seat Lena favoured.

 

            Fetching herself a bottle of Gillywater, Lena unscrewed the cap and took a sip before sitting. “Never you mind,” she chidingly replied.

 

            “Oh, go on,” Andrea insisted. “We’re not going to make fun of you. I understand if it was a disappointment after both of us.” 

 

            “It would be hard to top that,” Veronica agreed, smirking as Lena flipped her off and picked up a container of fried rice. “Still, no need to be embarrassed. Out with it.”

 

            “And how do you know I wasn’t stuck at St. Mungo’s all night?” Lena evasively replied.

 

            They all scoffed until Lena relented. She didn’t care enough to keep it a secret; it was unimportant to Lena and if it provided them entertainment to know who’d managed to coax her home, then she didn’t mind sharing. Her real secrets were kept close to her heart, and she’d never divulge those. She’d made an oath.

 

            Normally, Lena didn’t like manual housework, but that night she rolled up her sleeves, just an inch, and washed the dishes by hand as a distraction. The kitchen sink looked out to the night through a window over it and the setting sun gilded her cheeks and nose as dusk was ushered in, until the full moon stood out starkly against the indigo backdrop of the sky.

 

 

            “Danvers.”

 

            Kara looked up from her arithmancy calculations, setting her quill down and quickly glancing down at her ink-stained fingertips. She was wearing a blue wool vest over a white shirt, tucked into brown tweed pants. Three spreadsheets were spread across her desk and she shot to her feet, almost tripping over her brown leather satchel at the foot of her desk.

 

            “Professor Croaker.”

 

            “You’ve finished your calculations for today?”

 

            “Yes, sir,” she said, scrambling to pick up the sheets of paper. 

 

            He didn’t take them, just nodded idly. “Good, good. You can leave early, considering … well, you know.”

 

            Relief flooded through Kara, who’d been feeling clammy and a little lightheaded all day, and she swallowed thickly. “Thank you, sir. I’ll see you tomorrow.”

 

            He gestured dismissively, “take the day. You’re never right afterwards; we can’t risk errors in your work. I’ll see you on Friday.”

 

            “Yes, sir. I’ll see if I can work on that Theory of Relativity. I’ve found another Muggle book which looks promising so far. A bit of heavy reading will get me through the morning.”

 

            He gave her a fleeting smile and nodded distractedly before checking his watch and saying goodbye. Kara watched him move to the door leading from the office to the Time Chamber and its abundance of clocks and the stock of Time-Turners. Kara had spent all morning checking the upkeep of them one by one. It was a menial task for the employees who weren’t new but weren’t allowed to work independently yet were saddled with, along with the brunt of the reporting and hand calculations. Every morning Kara was included in some sort of communal lecture about time or love or death, half a dozen Unspeakables scribbling notes and quoting heavy tomes while someone else wrote on an old chalkboard as they tried to puzzle through the theories of their department.

 

            Saying goodbye to a few of the coworkers she was on friendly terms with, she made her way out to the Entrance Chamber and then through the door to the hallway leading to the elevators. Riding it up to the Atrium, Kara exited onto the pavement outside the HM Treasury building. It was still relatively early but the streets were thick with fog and she doubled the scarf around her neck, the nimbus glow of the lamp posts and headlights giving the afternoon an otherworldly feeling. 

 

            It had been snowing a little last night and it had turned to slush in the gutters and the lonely splash of Kara’s boots in the dirty puddles followed her back to her apartment. She’d been living with Alex for two years now and when she opened the front door to the flat she found the place in its usual shabby disarray. Her sister had been and gone since Kara had been to work. They rarely saw each other at the Ministry, save for the occasional lunch taken together, but Alex was usually off rounding up residual Death Eaters while Kara was shut away in the bowels of the Ministry, unable to speak about her work with anyone.

 

            Lights seeped through floor-to-ceiling windows that looked over Diagon Alley and Kara set her satchel down on the dining table. Her books on space and time and science and philosophy cluttered the coffee table and the one in the kitchen as well, balled up pieces of parchment and broken quills littering the surface as well. It was all open with two bedrooms and a bathroom leading off, the place filled with furniture that looked like it was a century old, filling the space and making it comfortably homely.

 

            The first time Kara had visited the empty flat with Alex, it had seemed austere and empty, with big windows and honeyed wooden floorboards. From the front door, you could see out onto the Muggle street side, a train track rattling past, which had only reduced the amount they split for rent. All the curtains were drawn and the space was dim and cool until Kara lit a fire in the grate and went into her room. A sagging shelf of books sat against one wall, with a desk cluttered with yet more work and a few potted plants, gifted by Eliza to brighten up the place. Bastet was sleeping on the yellow blanket folded at the foot of the bed and clawed at it as she rose to her feet. Scratching her behind the ears, Kara kissed her head and made sure she had food and water before changing into a sweater and soft worn jeans and boots. 

 

            They were no longer as poor as they’d been with her and Alex working respectable jobs, even if they were lower on the rungs, but the flat was still sparsely furnished. It wasn’t uncomfortable, but ascetic in a way that they were used to. They still needed to find a rug for the living room and the walls in Kara’s room were blank, save for the photos she’d pinned up, one person glaringly missing whenever she looked at the groups of her friends.

 

            Her room had been painted a steel blue and in the wintry afternoon light, it felt like being submerged in the sea. She had a window that only let in patches of daylight and looked out into the fire escape of the building next door, the shop Cogg and Bell Clockmakers beneath it where Diagon Alley verged on Carkitt Market. Her bed was made up with beige cotton sheets and Kara listened to the rain that started up, feeling sweat bead on her forehead and the distant rumbling of thunder, wishing she could curl up with a glass of mulled mead and a book.

 

            After half an hour, she threw Floo powder into the fireplace and went through to St. Mungo’s, familiar with the way after so many years and going to admissions before heading to the Dai Llewelyn ward. Changing out of her clothes and into a hospital gown, she removed her glasses and set her wand on the nightstand and waited until a Healer came to fetch her. Even now, almost ten years later, Kara’s stomach still twisted at the thought of going down to those cells. It had gotten worse since leaving Hogwarts, needing the safety of the cell to ensure she didn’t hurt anyone, which only meant she hurt herself instead. Kara couldn’t even look at her body anymore, a crisscross of silvery scars, that Mike didn’t seem to mind so much when they’d met up again and started seeing each other. Her thighs weren’t so bad but she always kept her shirt on and the lights off.

 

            The Healers, who’d seen everything and worse than a werewolf, also made Kara self-conscious, ashamed of her body and her monthly transformations, even though she was a regular on the ward now. They were kind to her, but there was always pity in their eyes and Kara had to work to force a polite smile on her face, thanking them before they locked her into the stone cell.

 

            Shedding the gown, Kara sat on it to provide a barrier between the ice-cold stone floor and her bare skin. The hairs on her body stood on end and sweat started dripping down her skin in thin rivulets between the notches of Kara’s spine as the change slowly stole over her. Her neck ached a little from the knot that had plagued her all day, along with the faint headache behind her eyes, but which was a constant throbbing of palpable pain now.

 

            Breathing shallowly as the sun sank and the moon rose, Kara went rigid as her body started to crack and come apart, reforming itself into something monstrously and hairy. Kara’s mind went blank and she tried to stifle the screams by detaching herself from her body.

 

            She was twelve years old, laying in a field at dusk during the summer, the loud chorus of crickets a soothing sound as she breathed in the smell of fields and apples, reading her well-loved copy of Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them. She was twelve years old and hadn’t been bitten, was just another child enjoying the school holidays after her first year at Ilvermorny, still naïve to the terrors of the world. She was twelve years old and the feeling never went away.

Chapter 17

            A year later and Lena had started at St. Mungo’s as a qualified Healer, pulling 48-hour shifts and on call at all hours, throwing her schedules into disarray as she arrived home at two o’clock in the morning and woke when her friends had all gone out or to work or dinner. Lena didn’t spend so much time at the flat anymore, catching up on sleep in the on-call room in a bunk, feeling permanently exhausted as she reeked of blood and vomit and potions and potions. If she’d thought N.E.W.T.s and Healer School were overwhelming, it was nothing compared to being an Intern Healer, fighting against the others for the best cases, for the opportunity to see the inside of an operating room for the worst injuries. 

 

            So far, Lena had shouldered her way above the rest of the new Healers, always knowing the answer, always reciting the correct method or suggesting the best course of treatment. It was slightly alienating to be better than everyone else and scorned for it, but Lena was used to being on the outside of things and wasn’t there to make friends. She did have a friend though; Sam, the Resident she’d shadowed for her placement, had become a surprising constant in Lena’s life, although she was ahead of her in terms of career and skill. They got lunch together whenever they were both free at the same time, bought coffees or Gillywater and packets of Bertie Bott’s Every Flavour Beans for a sugar rush as they sat in the tearoom or one of the open-air courtyards in milder weather, dead-eyed and sagging from a long shift.

 

            For the first few years of their Residency, they rotated through the Departments to see where they’d like to specialise, and Lena was one of Sam’s Interns, which meant she shadowed her everywhere, assisting where she could and offered more opportunities to work independently on easier cases. These days, Lena spent hours doing the grunt work or splinting fingers, wrapping bandages and adding Dittany to shallow cuts, and slipping patients doses of potions for nausea, pain or sleep. It was menial work she’d already spent a year doing on her Healer School placement, but this time Lena was left unsupervised, like the other Intern Healers, as a test of good faith.

 

            “Bad news,” Sam sighed as Lena stepped up beside her to eye the packed chalkboard denoting which Healers were occupying which theatre. 

 

            Their names were nowhere to be seen, although Lena knew Sam had been scheduled for an internal Transfiguration mishap where the wizard’s insides had been turned into snakes, leaving him with no digestive system at the present. 

 

            “They took you off?”

 

            “We’re covering the Dai Llewellyn ward tonight. And it’s going to be busy . Full moon tonight.”

 

            Lena let out a soft sigh. No one liked covering the Dai Llewellyn ward, although they were sure to get a lot of hands-on action in the morning with all of the werewolf attacks and transformations. A lot of them went AWOL after being bitten, holed up in some forest or a secluded patch of the Highlands or other mountains across the U.K. but there were still the odd few who came into the cells for voluntary containment. Lena had never worked a full moon shift on the ward before, but she’d spent a few days on rotation healing bites from Fire Salamanders, venomous snakes, and on one occasion a particularly nasty bite from a Common Welsh Green, resulting in the witch nearly losing her arm. 

 

            After knocking herself out with a potion for a few hours of rest, already thirty hours into her shift, Lena woke feeling disgruntled and limp, until she drank a cup of coffee and added a tonic to a bottle of Tongue Tying Lemon Squash to perk her up, the tartness of it masking the bitterness of the potion. Splashing water on her face in one of the communal bathrooms, Lena found Sam stirring two sugars into her tea at the nurse’s station as she gathered the charts for the admitted patients.

 

            Hippocrates Smethwyck was the Head Healer of the Serious Bites ward and he brusquely greeted them as they entered the ward, half a dozen beds occupied. “Here, you take this one,” Sam said, handing a manila folder over to Lena. “She’s a regular and an old Housemate of mine, so be nice. She won’t be any trouble for you, poor girl.”

 

            Lena gave her a wry smile and quietly scoffed, “are you insinuating something about my bedside manner?”

 

            Sam just gave her a quick wink and drifted away as she spoke over her shoulder. “Moon’s up in an hour; better hurry with your assessment and get her downstairs.”

 

            Shaking her head, Lena moved over to the bed with the curtain encircling it, the metal rings rattling as she jerked it back slightly with one hand and stared down at the paperwork in the open folder, already going through the usual spiel before her brain even registered a name or a face.

 

            “Good evening, I’m Healer Luthor, I’ll be- oh. ”

 

            A head of blonde curls sprinkled with grey rose as wide blue eyes met Lena’s green. She froze, surprised to see Kara there, although logically she shouldn’t have been, and it was more surprising they hadn’t run into each other on other full moons, even just passing in the corridor, and she watched as Kara visibly blanched. Neither of them spoke for a moment and Lena’s mouth opened and closed as she tried to regain her composure. She hadn’t anticipated Kara being there, tried not to think of her every full moon, and hadn’t even considered that she was one of the few who locked themselves away once a month.

 

            “I, um, I just- I need to do a physical examination before I take you downstairs.”

 

            “Right,” Kara murmured, her voice rasping but shockingly familiar.

 

            Lena felt tension knot her muscles as she worked to swallow thickly. It shouldn’t have affected her so much, shouldn’t have unbalanced her to hear the sound of her old friend’s voice, a tangible ache starting in her chest. The sound of Kara’s voice split her in half.

 

            “Unless you’d prefer a different Healer. But we’re short-staffed so …”

 

            “It’s fine.”

 

            Nodding, Lena cleared her throat and plucked a self-inking quill from the pocket of her sea-green robe. Clearing her throat, she scanned the first page with Kara’s personal information, confirming her date of birth, her address - which Lena noted had changed - and that she didn’t have any allergies.

 

            “I’m just going to check your pupils,” she murmured, lighting her wand and stepping close to Kara. “Can you look straight ahead for me please?”

 

            She went to cup Kara’s chin and then let her hand hover midair instead as she flicked the light across her sky-blue eyes, watching the pupils as they constricted and dilated. Murmuring to herself in satisfaction, Lena pocketed her wand and then shook her sleeve back to expose her watch, hesitating before extending her hand.

 

            “I’ll need to measure your pulse.”

 

            Kara slipped her wrist into Lena’s grasp, allowing her to press her fingers against her pulse point, watching her watch as she counted the beats, a little rapid but regular. Writing the results in her file, Lena unwound a stethoscope from around her neck and put the ends in her ears. She felt awkward and uncertain as she stood before Kara and worked the metal disc under the thin hospital gown, pressing it against her chest and softly asking her to inhale deeply and exhale.

 

            She repeated it on the other side and then the back, pausing as she parted the gown to reveal a scarred back and the notches of her spine, rigid as Kara endured it. Finishing up after gently probing along the underside of Kara’s jaw, checking her lymph nodes and then making a few more notes on the pages, she closed the file and set it on the tray covering the foot of the bed.

 

            “I’ll need to take you downstairs soon.”

 

            Kara nodded, a flush creeping up her neck and into her cheeks, as she stared down at her hands, shivering slightly as her jaw was clenched tightly shut. Lingering a moment, Lena nodded to herself and dragged the curtain back across, her heart in her throat as she moved on to another werewolf, assisting the Head Healer to help speed things along, mindful of how much time she had left. There were only three of them this month, and Healer Smethwyk took one, Sam took the other and Lena was left with Kara in her charge. 

 

            “If you’ll come with me,” Lena murmured after pulling back the curtain, twenty minutes before the full moon was scheduled to rise.

 

            Climbing to her feet, looking gaunt and clammy with rosy cheeks, Kara obeyed. Her skin was ashen, nausea blooming in her guy as an ache permeated her skull, and she lurched alongside Lena to the elevator, letting the young Healer pull the metal grille aside before stepping inside with her. They both faced the grille as they descended through the hospital, a foot separating them as they ignored the stifling tension that fell between them.

 

            Reaching one of the basement levels, Lena led Kara to a cell that had been designated for her that night and awkwardly cleared her throat as she unlocked the heavy door and gestured into the dank cell. The stale smell of sweat and fear and blood lingered, despite the astringent smell of bleach, and it made Lena’s stomach turn as guilt well up inside her. There was nothing she could say though, so she didn’t say anything, waiting until Kara was inside before she locked the cell firmly behind her and swallowed the feeling of betrayal that welled up inside.

 

            She remained down there for a while, subjecting herself to the sounds that the thick cells and all their wards couldn’t mask. There was a small slot for Healers to look through, to check in on their patients, but Lena respected Kara’s privacy through the horrific transformation to not spy on her as her body splintered apart and reformed. They’d been made to watch it before on their placement, but it had been an older man, and it had been horrifying enough to witness then, let alone watching the young woman she’d been friends with suffer through it. 

 

            If she’d looked though, she would have seen the thin form of her friend writhing on the freezing stone floor, thrashing and struggling against some unseen force as her back arched and then took on an inhuman posture, the sound of snapping bones and guttural screams turning to rough, keening cries of something animal as she twisted, elbows snapping as the joints reformed backwards, trying in vain to elude her fate.

 

            When she went back upstairs, almost an hour later, Lena was ashen-faced and silent as she walked back onto the ward to help out with a bite from a Chimaera, the man shouting and thrashing on the bed as Sam, Smethwyk and two nurses restrained him. Not saying a word as she helped inject a Sleeping Draught into a cannula on the back of his hand, at Smethwyk’s direction, Lena stepped back as he went slack on the narrow bed and watched them treat the wound, pouring a Wound-Cleaning Potion into the bite and then casting Ferula to wrap his shoulder in a thick layer of bandages to let the potion work its magic.

 

            Faint moonlight fought through grimy windows as Lena stood back and waited to be of further use, her mind humming with thoughts of Kara and little else as she felt numb from the encounter. It wasn’t until they’d finished their rounds and were free to sit down for a moment and drink some coffee, perching on an unused gurney stowed in an empty hallway on a lower level, that Sam gave her a concerned look.

            

            “Are you alright? You look a little off. Even paler than usual.”

 

            Fighting to make her voice work as she fiddled with the paper cup in hand, Lena’s forehead pinched with unease. “I- Kara Danvers …”

 

            “Mm, she was a year below me. Nice enough but kept to herself. I didn’t realise why until she showed up on my first rotation on the Bite Ward. She was bitten when she was twelve, over in America. Such a shame.”

 

            Lena looked almost green then, her breaths shallow and her eyes bone dry, although she felt devastated. She couldn’t say why; she’d known all of this, known her friend was a werewolf, but now they weren’t friends and she was here and Lena felt helpless.

 

            “She, uh, I-”

            

            “Merlin, are you alright?” Sam suddenly exclaimed, straightening up. “You look like you’re going to be sick. ”

 

            “I’m fine,” Lena quickly ground out, closing her eyes and tipping her head back against the wall. “I just- I remember her from school.”

 

            “You get over seeing people you know soon enough. You should be glad you missed doing your placement while the war was still going on. So many familiar faces - most of them dead. It was awful .”

 

            Swallowing, Lena hesitated and then sat up from her slouched position. “I think I might lay down until sunrise. Page me if anything happens?”

 

            “Will do.”

 

            Slipping away to the nearest on-call room, Lena sank down onto the edge of a cot and buried her face in her hands, feeling restless and frustrated. Moving onto her back, she exhaled slowly and sank into the thin mattress, staring at the slats of the bunk above her as she tried to get her mind to quieten so she could catch up on sleep. That’s what it was - she was so far into her shift with only a few hours of rest to tide her over that her body didn’t know how to cope with the surprise. 

 

            But she didn’t sleep, didn’t rest or stop thinking about Kara for even a moment. Grey-faced and tense, she ended up in the tearoom, drinking coffee after coffee in the corner as the other Interns working the overnight shift cast her dubious glances. None of them approached and Lena was purposely unapproachable, brooding and surly as she marked the passing of the hours with a drink, until it was almost sunrise and she went down to the cells.

 

            Sitting at the base of the wall, she listened to the snarling and the exhausted yelps as the cold burrowed into her back, and went through a stack of her charts and files, ensuring everything was up to date. When footsteps grew louder, scuffing on the stone floor, she rose to her feet and met Sam’s hazel eyes. The sun was up and the cells were quiet.

 

            Nurses wheeled gurneys with stretchers on top of them and Lena yanked back the slot of the narrow window, and after confirming the transformation back to human, she opened the cell door, the grinding squeak of the hinges setting her teeth on edge. Even steeling herself for the sight couldn’t prepare her for the reality of it, the stench of blood and vomit stomach-turning as she stepped inside, her skin prickling with unease, the breath catching in her throat. Sprawled on her stomach, naked, filthy and unconscious, Kara looked like a fragile, broken doll.

 

            Crouching at her side, Lena tried to give Kara her modesty as her eyes restlessly refused to land anywhere on her body as she made a quick assessment, unwilling to touch her for a moment before she pointed her wand at the gash on the outside of Kara’s thigh and shakily muttered, “Ferula.”

 

            Bandages erupted from the end of her wand and tightly bound the wound, blood already spotting the white, and she draped a blanket over her old friend as the nurses set a stretcher down beside her. Lena allowed them to levitate Kara’s body onto it and then out of the cell and onto a gurney. She gathered up her files and then followed them up to the elevator, where they had to wait their turn.

 

            Helping push the gurney down the hallway, standing near Kara’s head, she was unable to take her eyes off her pallid face. Back in the ward, Kara was transferred from the gurney to the bed, before the stretcher was worked out from under her, and Lena hesitated, her eyes darting all over the limp body as she tried to separate herself from her memories. They were no longer friends and this was her patient.

 

            “I need two units of Blood Replenishing - intravenously,” Lena said as she jerked the wheeled trolley closer and started parsing through the supplies.

 

            Finding gauze and an antiseptic solution, she wiped the back of Kara’s hand and then inserted a cannula, her fingers shaking just a little. A nurse hung a bag of the wine red potion and Lena fastened the IV to the cannula and then cleared her throat.

 

            “Can I get one CC of silver in Dittany and two vials of Wound-Cleaning?”

 

            She carefully shifted the blanket up, examining Kara’s legs for injuries - aside from the one she’d already bandaged - and then lowered it back down, moving on to checking her arms and then hesitating as she quickly examined the rest of her, reminding herself that this was just another patient, this wasn’t someone she had any sort of personal relationship with. Not anymore, at least. It wasn’t a violation of Kara’s privacy to treat her properly, to provide the best care that she could, but Lena was quicker than she’d ever been, tugging the blankets down and up in the briefest examination before returning her attention to the bandaged leg.

 

            Vanishing the bandages, she laid surgical blankets around the two long gashes and watched as fresh blood welled up. “Talk to me, Luthor,” Sam called from behind the curtains of the next bed over, tending to her own patient.

 

            “Two lacerations to the vastus lateralis. Two units of Blood Replenishing have been hung and a standard course of action calls for cleaning the wound and sealing with silver and Dittany. Patient will be intravenously given a Sleeping Draught once the wounds have been treated.”

 

            “Good. Keep an eye on her consciousness; if she starts to wake up, it’ll make it harder to treat her.”

 

            Using a pipette to dropper on the cleaning solution, Lena nudged the edges of the claw wounds apart to thoroughly flush out the rent muscle. It was a slow process and Kara bled a lot, rivulets running down her sweat and vomit-stained skin to mingle with the already-dried patches of blood. Lena was gentle and as quick as she could be, her eyes burning with exhaustion as she worked. After she’d cleaned it out, she took the silver and Dittany solution and applied it to the wound, which smoked and hissed as the skin repaired itself, the edges helped together with Lena’s forceps until two neat parallel scars ran down Kara’s thigh.

 

            Once she’d taped gauze over the wound and pulled off the thin dragonhide gloves, she let out a breath of relief and administered the Sleeping Draught via a needle and cannula to keep her under for a few hours at least. A nurse approached with a basin of steaming water and a washcloth and Lena swallowed thickly as she held her hands out to take it. It wasn’t a Healer’s job to bathe the patients, but she couldn’t bear the thought of someone else touching her Kara. 

 

            “I’ll do it,” she rasped.

 

            The nurse opened her mouth but didn’t protest as Lena took the metal basin and set it down on the tray, jerking the curtain around the bed and dipping the washcloth into the hot water. Sniffing, Lena squeezed the water out and stared down at Kara’s face, soft with sleep, with an impassive expression. She felt anything but inside.

 

            Starting with her hands, Lena gently washed the dirt and blood and vomit from Kara’s knuckles, her fingers, her nails, working her way over the grooves of her palms and up over her wrists and forearms, biceps and shoulders. The water was filthy before long and she swished her wand at it, replacing it with clean water she heated in an instant until Kara’s skin was clean and bore no signs of the abuse last night. She left her face until last, her hands trembling as she wrung out the cloth and smoothed it along the curve of her jaw, over her round cheeks and pointed chin, her fingertips brushing against her skin as she gently wiped away the filth. 

 

            Once she was finished, Lena bandaged her leg over the gauze and managed to fit a robe on her, tugging the blankets up over her and tucking her in. She left everything for the nurses to clean up and made her way out of the ward, one of the outdoor courtyards, early December air burning her lungs as she breathed in rapid bursts, arms wrapped around herself as she bent over.

 

            Sam found her there twenty minutes later, blue and trembling. “You alright?”

 

            “Fine.”

 

            “Took you a while to finish up there.”

 

            Lena rolled her stiff shoulders and tipped her head back, looking up at the grey sky. Her ashen cheeks had turned rosy in the cold and there was a bright sheen to her eyes as she tried to stop her teeth from chattering.

 

            “I wanted to be thorough.”

 

            “Come on; breakfast is on me. I could murder a cup of tea.”

 

            Her friend clapped a hand on her shoulder and guided her inside without further questioning and Lena let her bowl of Pixie Puffs go soggy as she limply spooned them into her mouth at intervals. It was too sugary for Lena’s taste but she needed the pickup before her rounds started and accepted eye drops from Sam to take the redness out of her eyes. She went around to all of the patients for rounds before returning to the hallway just outside the Dai Llewelyn ward, lurking about in a manner that might have been suspicious if she wasn’t in sea-green robes.

 

            The cryptex went off an hour later to let her know her patient on the ward was awake, and Lena was inside the room immediately. Pulling the curtain back on Kara’s bed, Lena floundered for a moment before clearing her throat.

 

            “Good morning, Miss Danvers. How’re you feeling?”

 

            “Fine,” Kara curtly replied, her voice small and rough as she sat up, swinging her legs over the side of the bed.

 

            She reached for her glasses on the nightstand, turning them over in her hand, the lenses covered in greasy fingerprints that Kara tried to work out with the hospital gown. Lena wondered how she saw the world now, a drab blur of beige and white and brown until Kara popped her glasses on her face and blinked, the squinting look vanishing.

 

            “You should rest for a bit,” Lena pointedly told her as Kara started to climb to her feet, reaching for her overnight bag resting on a chair. “You sustained two lacerations- er, cuts to the thigh. You lost a lot of blood.”

 

            “I have work. Can you take this out of my hand, please?”

 

            Rooted to the spot for a moment, Lena stepped forward and started to detach the IV and the cannula, packing it all away on the tray as Kara pulled clothes out of her bag. She was pulling on odd socks and lacing up a pair of tan boots when Lena turned back around, taking in the burgundy sweater and flared jeans. Pulling on a brown vintage bomber jacket that was just a fraction too short, exposing Kara’s wrists, she climbed to her feet.

 

            “It’s my duty of care to tell you that I would advise you to stay longer,” Lena cautiously informed her, reaching for her file with the discharge paperwork for later. “I’ll need you to sign here declaring that you’re leaving against the recommendation of your Healer.”

 

            “Yep.”
