            Kara took the self-inking quill Lena plucked from her pocket and scribbled down her signature before hauling her bag up. Brushing past Lena, she limped from the ward without another glance back.

 

            From that day on, Lena made a special request to work every full moon on the Dai Llewelyn ward, which Smethwyck readily accepted, considering the lack of interest from other Interns, and which Sam thought was a bizarre waste of her time. Her Resident allowed it though, and after the next two, Lena made a point to stress how familiar she was with one of the regular patients and was assigned to Kara’s case every full moon, tending to her with such devotion that anyone who spared even a second to supervise her work would have seen the love that went into her care. 

 

 

            “Danvers, can I see you in my office?”

 

            Kara looked up at Professor Croaker and quickly climbed to her feet. It was a full moon tomorrow and she was already feeling the effects of it, her head feeling oddly heavy and a dull ache in her stomach as she trailed her boss to his private office.

 

            “Take a seat, take a seat,” he urged her, settling down behind his desk and lacing his hands together as she got comfortable. After a moment, he sighed heavily and his mouth thinned with regret. “You may have heard that there have been some budget cuts throughout all Departments here at the Ministry. Since Minister Bagnold has taken over, and with the end of the war, she’s allocated a lot of the funding to the Auror Office to locate any hiding Death Eaters.”

 

            “Yes, sir. My sister’s an Auror; she’s spoken about it a few times.”

 

            “Is that right? Yes, well, unfortunately, with our budgets being cut, we don’t have the funds to pay the salaries of so many employees down here. I’m afraid … due to your junior status as an Unspeakable, and your … certain affliction requiring so many days off, I’m going to have to let you go.”

 

            Stunned by the news as it completely blindsided her, Kara sagged in her seat, the air rushing out of her lungs. Mouth opening and closing soundlessly for a moment, she fought back against the stinging in her eyes and tried to keep her voice level.

 

            “Sir, I- I understand it’s been difficult to accommodate, and I appreciate the lengths you’ve gone to give me extra time off, but  … I can come in. I can come in the day after and work extra hours if-“

 

            “I’m sorry, Kara,” he said with genuine regret, “I just can’t afford to keep an employee who has to miss a day of work every month.”

 

            “But … what about the new hires? They don’t have as much experience as me. I know I’m still a junior, but I- I’ve worked here longer than them.”

 

            “They’re cheaper. I can get almost two of them for the cost of you.”

 

            Her chest ached as her lungs refused to draw in any oxygen for a moment, her vision furring at the edges. Squeezing her eyes shut as she gripped the arms of the chair, she floundered for a moment.

 

            “What if you paid me what they’re on? I could- I could take a pay cut. I just- I need this job, sir.”

 

            “There’s still the matter of your lycanthropy, I’m afraid. I- well, I didn’t want to say it, but a few employees have made their discomfort known to me.”

 

            A choked sound escaped Kara and she let out a shuddering laugh of disbelief, a red flush working into her cheeks, making her scars stark. Jerking her chair back, she lurched to her feet, unbalanced, swallowing the bitterness that filled her.

 

            “Well … um, thank you for your time, Professor. I’ve enjoyed working here and, um, I hope you’ll keep me in mind if- if things ever change.”

 

            “I really am sorry,” he earnestly replied. “You’ve been a great worker. Very bright and devoted. I’ll be sure to reflect that in my reference, and you’ll be paid your severance of course.”

 

            “Of course,” she hollowly echoed.

 

            He extended a hand and she numbly shook it, an odd feeling stealing over her as she left the room and packed up her desk. Then she went home to the apartment she’d shared with Alex until a few months ago, when Alex had moved in with Kelly after a year of dating, insisting that she’d be able to cover the rent by herself and use the spare room as an office for her work. Now she was unemployed with nothing to research and no money to pay for one bedroom, let alone two.

 

            Kara didn’t see anyone until the day after the full moon, after a night in the hospital studiously avoiding Lena, who seemed to be assigned to her every month now as an added layer of torment to her transformations. She’d come home to a letter from a Ministry owl with a payslip for a deposit into her Gringotts vault and a letter of reference that was surprisingly nice. That evening, as she heated up a tin of soup and scoured the newspapers for a new job, Alex knocked on the door and let herself inside.

 

            “Sorry I couldn’t come earlier. We’ve been busy with this case all week … anyway, I brought you some stuff to help.”

 

            Her sister set down a bottle of Peachtree Fizzing Tea and a block of chocolate from Honeydukes in an apology for not coming sooner. Alex always came over straight after work on the day after a full moon, playing chess with Kara and bringing her issues of an eccentric magazine called The Quibbler , which had started publication a few years prior and was entertaining, if not entirely factual.

 

            “What’re you doing?” Alex asked, dragging out a chair and sitting heavily, still in her long leather coat and a navy turtleneck, flecked with rain as it lashed the windows outside. 

 

            It was hard to believe they were in spring with the storms they’d been having lately and her sister pointed her wand at the empty grate and lit a fire to warm the chilly apartment. Kara tossed her quill down and her lips twisted derisively as she frowned. A touch of colour crept into her cheeks as shame and pride got the better of her.

 

            “I’ve been sacked.”

 

            “What?” Alex exclaimed, straightening in her seat. “What do you mean you’ve been sacked?”

 

            Shrugging as she pressed her lips into a flat line, Kara swallowed past the lump in her throat. “There’s, um, the budget cuts, so they can’t afford to keep me. And then there’s … you know.”

 

            She waved at her scarred face and Alex winced slightly before anger flushed her face. “They can’t just get rid of you like that. You’re good at your job.”

 

            Truthfully, no one had a clue how good she was at her job outside of the Department of Mysteries, considering she wasn’t allowed to talk about it. It still felt nice to have her sister defend her though as Kara unwrapped the bar of chocolate and broke off a corner. She nudged it to Alex, who scowled as she broke off a piece for herself.

 

            “Fuck, that’s unfair. What’re you going to do now?”

 

            “I don’t know,” Kara defeatedly murmured. “I’m looking for vacancies in The Daily Prophet but … I don’t want to be a- a dragon feeder. I got good grades! I should be able to get a good job but I know that none of them are going to take a werewolf on board - not if I have to disclose it. I was lucky enough to get hired as an Unspeakable but they’re going to want all the young graduates-“

 

            “You say that as if you’re not barely twenty-two. It’s fine, I’ll get you a job with me.”

 

            “No, no, it’s- it’s fine,” Kara insisted, “I’ll sort something out. I just … need a few days to process it. The old codger could’ve waited until after the full moon, at least.”

 

            But she didn’t find a job the following week, or the week after that, rejecting the offers of all of her friends to ask their respective bosses for any open positions. Perhaps she was being too proud, but Kara couldn’t let them do that for her, and it was all she could do to let Mike buy her dinner one night when they were all at The Leaky Cauldron, or Alex conveniently dropping by with groceries for her and her landlord telling her he was lowering the rent starting from next month.

 

            When a month passed by and she’d had to register with the Ministry for benefits, she’d been stammering and pink-cheeked, barely able to speak as she kept her head ducked down. The bored witch had told her she’d receive a payment of two Galleons, eight Sickles and twelve Knuts a week, making Kara wince as she mentally calculated her expenses. It wouldn’t be enough to keep the apartment and buy food without dipping into her modest savings.

 

            Another couple of weeks and she’d been rejected from half a dozen jobs and hadn’t been eating much, a meagre meal each day tiding her over until the next one. She saw Mike more frequently than she had before, spending nights at his flat, paid for by his mother as he doggedly pursued a Quidditch career, while only being an adequate player. The nights she spent at his were ones where she could count on a filling meal, picking up fish and chips near Blackpool Pier and watching the Muggle lights before heading back to his. He’d leave in the morning for Quidditch practice on the amateur team Lancashire had cobbled together from the British and Irish Team rejects. 

 

            She wouldn’t see him for days on either side of the full moon, which had caused Alex to change her tune and view him unfavourably, along with Kelly and Nia, but Kara found it a relief to not have to manage his emotions on top of her own. They weren’t really dating - only sort of - and they both knew it was out of Mike’s interest in her looks, although his comments about the number of grey hairs were getting more frequent, and Kara’s indifference to anyone else and lack of interest from other men. Neither of them viewed it as a long-term arrangement and she could never have felt comfortable enough around him to be herself. She couldn’t even undress in front of him, not since the first time, the mere idea of it mortifying. Kara would rather have flayed herself alive.

 

            Her indifference and carelessness made her blind to how she’d skipped her period, which she would’ve attributed to stress if she’d even realised it prior to a few days before the next new moon. She’d had the nagging thought for a day or two, and then she’d been sick and tired and endured another awkward encounter with Lena that made Kara want to rip her heart out of her chest. She was living in a cesspit of misery these days, the painful reminder of how she’d met Lena for the first time and felt that jolt of knowing someone, feeling so captivated by her and remembering everything about her, down to the subtle colours in her eyes. 

 

            Kara could never have known they’d go so long without speaking to each other, even seeing each other, realising just how much space Lena had taken up in her life. The world felt too big away from that secret room that had contained them both and all their promises and oaths and secrets swapped. It had felt too big until Kara had seen her again that evening at St. Mungo’s and realised it actually wasn’t big enough. But it had felt like coming up for air, something giving in her chest as she surreptitiously studied her old friend, noticing how her hair was a little bit longer and how she could look into her eyes instead of trying to remember the exact shade of green they were. 

 

            Those monthly encounters, as stilted and uncomfortable as they were, no small talk beyond the necessary medical assessments, were a moment of familiarity to Kara, in a sea of so much uncertainty. She started to forget that so much time had passed, that there had ever been a time when they hadn’t been familiar with each other. And she hated it because there was an insurmountable gulf between them. It wasn’t that she was trying to avoid Lena, but she felt a jolt of unrest each month she found her friend assigned to her, wondering what Lena had done to get stuck on the Bite Ward every full moon. Kara had underestimated how hard it would be to be around someone who was a stark reminder of better days.

 

            She showed up at St. Mungo’s for that full moon, underweight and gaunt, her lips chapped and her nails bitten down, as quiet and subdued as ever and just a little hungrier. She didn’t speak a word about the horrible nagging thought she’d had for the last couple of days, letting Lena lock her in a cell as she had every other time as they pretended like they didn’t know some of the biggest secrets and insecurities of each other, and woke in her hospital bed again, hooked up to an IV with a Blood-Replenishing Potion feeding into her arm and the feeling of bandages around her midriff. 

 

            Lena was sitting in the chair at her bedside, lavender bruises beneath her eyes and a solemn look on her face. Kara usually woke alone, minutes before Lena arrived, summoned to check in on her and inevitably discharge her as Kara hurried out of there. A part of her was terrified that if she stuck around long enough, she’d end up crying in front of her old friend, the ache for her in her chest too unbearable and her emotions volatile after the pain of the transformation and the cocktail of potions they’d pumped her with. No, it was always best to leave straight away, even if she could barely walk.

 

            “There was- there was a lot of blood this time,” Lena murmured, straightening as she inhaled. “I- was there- do you know if you were- if you were … pregnant?”

 

            Swallowing thickly, pressing a hand to her stomach, Kara blinked, her eyes dry and scratchy. She wasn’t sure, she might’ve been making too much out of it, but she knew that if she was, she wasn’t anymore. Her body was too inhospitable now, the transformation each month making it impossible for her ever to have her own kids.

 

            “Maybe.”

 

            “We’ll need to keep you in for a bit longer. For observation.”

 

            “I’d like to go home.”

 

            “It would be better if you stayed. Is there- is there someone I can send an owl to? Your mum, sister … a- a boyfriend-“

 

            Letting out a huff of laughter, Kara breathlessly echoed, “boyfriend? No, no, there’s- no, I don’t want you to write to anyone.”

 

            Sitting up, Kara let out a small gasp, residual pain tearing through her stomach where she’d clawed herself open, perhaps some animalistic part of her mind acting on those suspicions and trying to tear it out of her. The bandages compressed the healing scars but her whole body ached and she had to pause for a moment, her ears ringing as Lena haltingly explained her injuries and handed her a potion to take to make sure her body fully healed itself. 

 

            Fetching her bag, Kara fumbled with the IV tube until Lena sharply clicked her tongue and unhooked her, removing the cannula with gentle fingers. She was still chastising Kara as she picked up her bag and set it on the rumpled hospital sheets, pulling off the thin gown and tossing it onto the blankets.

 

            “May as well get past the false modesty,” Kara waveringly said, dumping a shirt and a knitted vest onto the bed and rifling through the bag for underwear.

 

            “I’ll give you some privacy-“

 

            “We’ve already seen the worst of each other,” Kara interrupted her, her voice thick with annoyance. 

 

            Lena realised she didn’t know her, not anymore. They’d both changed so much in a handful of years, almost the length of time that they’d first known each other. There was something washed out about Kara now, bleached of any hope and patience after years of horror that she’d only touched on while they’d been at Hogwarts together. What Kara would have given now to have the security of school and a forest to run through once a month, endless food and no worries about rent and income. 

 

            “It’s against my medical advice for you to leave, but seeing as you insist on ignoring me, you’ll have to wait a bit longer,” Lena said to her as she stared at the notches of Kara’s spine, faint scars crisscrossing her back. “The nurse will have to get your discharge papers ready; I’m off-duty now.”

 

            Kara paused, her arms through the sleeves of her shirt before she shrugged it the rest of the way on and fiddled with the buttons. She was tempted to ask what Lena was still doing there then but after a moment, the Healer left without another word. 

 

            It was perhaps the longest conversation they’d had since seeing each other again and Kara hated it. After all those times she’d felt Lena’s absence so keenly, she finally had her back in her life, but instead of relief, what Kara felt most was resentment. Resentment over the fact that it felt so uncomfortable between them, neither of them saying what they truly wanted to, both of them still angry and wounded. Gritting her teeth, Kara exhaled sharply through her teeth before tucking her shirt into her flared jeans and zipping them up.

 

            Twenty minutes later, bundled up against the rainy forecast, she was discharged from St. Mungo’s after signing against medical advice. Exiting onto the street level, she gulped down the cool mid-morning air. The rain from last night had cleared into a sullen day, everything drab and grey as Muggles swarmed around her on the pavement. 

 

            “You shouldn’t be walking.”

 

            Jumping slightly at the sound of Lena’s voice to her left, Kara exhaled sharply, her heart pounding in her chest. The shorter woman was wearing a sleek woollen overcoat with a deep green scarf around her neck - not Slytherin green, but a pine green that made her eyes pale like jade - and even as exhausted as she was from days at the hospital, she was still polished and put together, in contrast to Kara’s scruffy, sickly appearance.

 

            “I don’t need your help,” she dismissively replied, but her eyes were fevered, her skin at once sallow yet flushed, and Lena couldn’t help but think that she looked so frail, despite the size of her.

 

            “Yes, you do.”

 

            Before Kara could object, Lena grabbed her arm and Apparated them right off the sidewalk. Staggering as she landed, Kara felt her stomach flip and she sagged against the wall outside the building with her apartment above it, blinking in surprise.

 

            “How do you know where I live?” she hoarsely asked, a cold sweat beading on her brow.

 

            “I have your file.”

 

            Feeling stupid, Kara closed her eyes and breathed deeply for a moment before pushing off the wall and turning to the door leading upstairs. There were two flats up there on opposite sides of the landing, and she staggered upstairs and unlocked the door to hers.

 

            “I’m home. Satisfied?”

 

            “Am I not allowed inside?” Lena tersely asked.

 

            “I didn’t think you’d want to come in.”

 

            Lena let out a cool laugh, arching an eyebrow. Her bearing had only grown haughtier over the years and Kara swallowed, her mouth thinning as she eyed Lena.

 

            “Don’t you think we should talk?”

 

            “Talk? You want to talk now? Don’t you think it’s a bit late for all of that? It’s done. Whatever it was … it was done. I’ve spent years trying to figure out why I had to lose you but-”

 

            “You had to lose me?” Lena echoed, aghast at her audacity.

 

            Stepping inside, Kara pulled off her blue robe, the graduation gift from her mother and well-loved over the last few years as she wore it to work at the Ministry with pride. Up until a couple of months ago. Unwinding the scarf around her neck, she draped everything over the back of a chair and was left looking slight and untidy, her glasses winking in the wan sunlight streaming in and her outfit more suited to a librarian. 

 

            Lena eyed her broad shoulders gone bony beneath a shirt that ballooned out around her, wrinkled where it bunched up, messily tucked in. She wore men’s clothes that were several sizes too large to offset the years her clothes had been magically enlarged and worn out of shape, her trousers cuffed and her blonde hair as unruly as ever. Kara had an expression like she was permanently mildly surprised, but that could be attributed to Lena’s presence because she couldn’t remember her friend being so wide-eyed at Hogwarts. Kicking off her tarnished boots, she braced herself against the kitchen table and drew in a shuddering breath.

 

            Despite no invitation, Lena followed her inside anyway, taking in the old wooden floors, the colour of clover honey, the soft wallpaper in the open space, a hissing radiator in one corner and secondhand books scattered around the space. The window frames had warped slightly with time but the place still had that distinct air of being lived in, a home, and Lena looked around with interest.

 

            “Yes, I did. I did lose you because you- you’re the one that turned your back on me. I wanted to help you but you told me to go.”

 

            Kara felt that old burn just below her sternum as she slowly turned and looked at Lena. She’d worked so hard to detach herself from her personal feelings that her face was stiff and impassive now, that aloof air of a Healer unattached to her patient. Only her eyes betrayed her, and Kara only had to meet her gaze for a split-second to see all the pain and uncertainty there.

 

            “Don’t,” Lena cautioned her, her voice low and harsh, “don’t even begin to put the blame on me .”

 

            Visibly blanching, Kara looked away from her and stiffly moved away from the table. Softly sighing, Lena followed after her. Helping her over to the sagging sofa, Lena shed her coat and set it over the back of a kitchen chair before rummaging through the cupboards. Coming up with a tin of instant coffee with a few teaspoons of gritty powder left, Lena filled the tin kettle with water and set it to instantly boil. Finding two cups, one of them webbed with cracks inside, she pulled the sleeve of her sweater down over her hand and poured hot water into the two cups before carrying them over to the coffee table.

 

            “You should eat something,” Lena muttered, turning away and raiding the clunky fridge and the rest of the cupboards, finding nothing but a half-mouldy loaf of bread and a few slices of bacon.

 

            Trying her best, Lena fried the bacon and Kara found comfort in the bitter coffee as she held the chipped enamel cup between her freezing hands, the smell of bacon grease suffusing the flat.

 

            “I’m sorry,” Kara eventually rasped, as Lena set a sandwich down in front of her and picked up her own coffee.

 

            Taking a swig while standing, as if she couldn’t bear to get comfortable and let her guard down there, Lena hummed. “It’s fine,” she curtly replied. “It was a long time ago.”

 

            “Not long enough,” Kara said, taking off her glasses and running a hand over her weary face before putting them back on.

 

            Silent for a moment, her lips pressed into a flat line, Lena nodded her head at the limp sandwich. “Eat.”

 

            Sighing, Kara reached forward and picked up half, taking a bite. “You don’t need to stay. I’m fine.”

 

            Closing her eyes, Lena swallowed the lump in her throat. Sinking down onto the sofa, jostling them both as she held her coffee aloft, she kept a safe distance between them. “Who is he?”

 

            “Who?”

 

            Giving her a withering look, Lena’s eyelids shuttered and she took a sip from her mug. Exhaustion hollowed out her eyes and cheeks and Kara resisted the urge to reach out and press a hand to her face. She looked better than she had at Hogwarts, not as haunted by her mother Kara supposed, old guilt resurfacing as her eyes snagged on Lena’s left arm, remembering the words written there.

 

            “Mike Matthews,” Kara eventually replied.

 

            “What, that oaf with the plain face? Well …”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Kara swallowed her mouthful of bacon and sighed. “I’m not seeing him. It was an accident.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “I know I can’t have kids,” Kara frustratedly told her, pink-cheeked and peevish.

 

            Lena nodded in acknowledgement but didn’t reply. They lapsed into an uncomfortable silence and Lena pressed her lips into a flat line, staring down at the cup as her brow furrowed. “Are you alright?”

 

            “Fine,” Kara managed to squeeze out, although it was evident she wasn’t fine at all, her blue eyes glassy, her throat tight around her words. “Don’t tell anyone.”

 

            “Who would I tell?” Lena asked, mystified before sobering up as she softened. “Of course I wouldn’t. It would be a breach of patient confidentiality.”

 

            Exhaling roughly, Kara tipped her head back against the sofa and closed her eyes. Lena watched her pale eyelashes flutter and took another sip of coffee. “So, what’s it like being an Unspeakable? Are you allowed to tell me?”

 

            Shrugging, Kara’s mouth twisted ruefully as she smoothed the pad of her thumb over her eyelid. A headache bloomed behind her eyes and her whole body sagged with exhaustion. Her plan had been to come home and sleep until Alex showed up after work, and this was sapping the rest of her energy, but she wanted her to stay.

 

            “It was good , but I got sacked a couple of months ago,” Kara mumbled, vaguely embarrassed to admit it.

 

            Lena had grown up richer than Kara could even imagine, everything brand new and in abundance every year at Hogwarts, and she’d always been so sure of her own future, making it seem easy to become a Healer. And here she was, exactly as she said she’d be, changed out of her sea-green robes but carrying the success of her respectable career around with her without the fear of it being snatched away.

 

            Blinking in surprise, Lena looked crestfallen as her shoulders slumped. “Oh. Sorry. I- it was because of …?”

 

            She trailed off, letting the question hang in the air. Managing to nod, Kara swallowed a dry mouthful of bread and then set the plate down on the coffee table, reaching for her coffee and draining the cup. 

 

            “What’re you doing now?”

 

            “Nothing. I haven’t been able to find anything. I’m registered, so I get … benefits. ”

 

            “You get paid by the Ministry?”

 

            “Not a lot,” Kara said with a strained laugh. “Couple of Galleons a week.”

 

            Eyebrows rising a fraction as she blinked, Lena faltered. “You’re not serious, are you? That’s- how do you even live off that?”

 

            “I wouldn’t call it living ,” Kara mumbled, raking a hand through her scraggly curls. “It’s fine. I’m managing.”

 

            Lena thought about the near-empty fridge and the mouldy bread and wouldn’t have called it managing either. Pity knifed through her with a keen sense of worry, thinking about Kara’s increasingly thin figure that showed up every month. She hadn’t been eating, that much was evident, and she never stuck around at St. Mungo’s long enough to eat the breakfast they gave the patients. Kara prioritised avoiding Lena over eating and it left an ashen taste in her mouth.

 

            It was a dismal day and dark outside, the grey light spilling across the floors in gloomy patches that made the flat seem cold and inhospitable. Swallowing the last of her coffee, Lena got to her feet and crossed over to the table, taking her coat from the back of the chair and shrugging it on. Kara climbed to her feet as well, fiddling with her fingers as she watched her gather up her things, slinging the strap of her satchel across her body and winding the scarf around her neck.

 

            Pulling a vial from her coat pocket, Lena held it up and then firmly set it down on the table. “You need to take this. It’ll help with … that.”

 

            She gestured to Kara’s stomach and then buried her hand in her pocket, making for the front door. A shadow of pain and longing crossed Kara’s face as she followed after her, lingering back as they faced each other. She opened her mouth, inhaling sharply before cutting off. Lena waited for her to say it, finding it off to not know what was on Kara’s mind after being able to read her every expression and mannerism for so long.

 

            “Did you … ever think about me?” Kara asked, uncertainty clouding her face.

 

            Lena let out a sad, quiet laugh, her green eyes mournful and aching as she shrugged helplessly.  “I never learned how to stop.”

Chapter 18

            Lena left Kara’s place and apparated home to the flat she’d bought in Dublin when she’d moved out of Andrea’s a few months back. Shedding her coat and carrying it through to her bedroom with her wardrobe, carefully hanging it up and then putting away her shoes and scarf, she raked a hand through her hair and they pressed the heels of her palms against her temples. Eyes closed, she let out a long exhale.

 

            Moving back out into the kitchen, she glanced over at Morrigan’s empty perch and the open window beyond, where a breeze stirred fallen black feathers, and then fetched a spotless wine glass and a bottle of red. Pouring a healthy dose, she felt restless and her fingers itched to make themselves busy, to pull together the sides of an injury, to feel the pounding of someone’s heart, to apply a salve or brew a potion. Do something useful.

 

            Sipping her wine, rolling the taste around her mouth, Lena felt so overwhelmingly drained. After ten minutes of consideration, she found a box. Into the box went a bottle of aftershave, a packet of cigarettes, a tailored blazer and a book on Quidditch and anything else she found cleared away in various cupboards and drawers and shelves. In between, she polished off most of the bottle and basked in the hazy sluggishness brought on by the red wine.

 

            After she’d finished, she wrote a note and placed it on top of the box, setting them both outside her front door and then going to shower. Soft from the hot water, Lena dressed in comfortable pyjamas and dried her hair, painstakingly applying serums and lotions to her hands and face and then knocking back a sleeping draught to help her rest. She felt far too unsettled for sleep to come to her naturally, even as exhausted as she was.

 

            Passing out in her wide bed, Lena slept deeply, if not for long. A knocking on the door disturbed her a few hours later and she roused herself, heavy-lidded and annoyed. Padding through the apartment, she raked a hand through her sleek hair and yanked open the front door, her shoulders slumping immediately at the sight of Jack filling the door frame. He looked wounded as he held the box of his things and looked at her with sad black eyes. 

 

            “Really? That’s all I get?”

 

            “I’ve just finished a sixty-hour shift; I’m too tired for this.”

 

            He pushed past her and Lena closed the door, grinding the heels of her palms into her eyes. Setting his box down on the closest surface he turned around, a perplexed expression on his face and a weary set to his broad shoulders. He’d just gotten off work, deep blue robes on over a trim suit, the smell of his aftershave clinging to his clothes. She felt a stab of guilt.

 

            “Look, I know I was never anything more than the guy you regularly shagged, but don’t I deserve some sort of explanation?”

 

            “I don’t really have one,” Lena confessed, her voice rasping with sleep. “I just think maybe it means more to you than it does to me.”

 

            He scoffed loudly, half rolling his eyes and then rubbing his neat beard. “Bollocks. It’s been more than a year and I’ve never once brought up the fact that you’ve never said you love me. I'm fine with that. I know this isn’t about love for you; it’s about being wanted, isn’t it? I want you - or … I don’t want to lose you.”

 

            “You’re too kind for me to treat you this way. I’m sorry.”

 

            “Who is it?” he quietly demanded.

 

            Blinking in surprise, it took Lena a moment to reply, her face crumpling as her mouth twitched up at the corners with a confused smile. “What?”

 

            “You’ve been acting off for months now. Have you met someone else?”

 

            “No,” she quietly crowed. “No, I haven’t met someone else.”

 

            He gave her a searching look and Lena’s mouth thinned as a defeated look filled her green eyes. It wasn’t a lie - she hadn’t met Kara recently. She’d known her a long time, and it had brought back so many conflicting feelings that Lena had felt out of sorts for months now. Jack wasn’t wrong about that. But she wasn’t leaving him for Kara. She was leaving him - if that’s what it could even be called - because she was too tired to manage someone else’s feelings on top of her own, on top of an already busy life that was just getting more and more tangled up in the past.

 

            “It’s nothing like that. I care about you as much as I’m willing to care about anyone,” she honestly told him, pressing her pale hand to his warm cheek.

 

            He covered it with his own and smiled sadly, “I know. Some people just aren’t made for love.”

 

            If he hadn’t been holding her hand in place, Lena might have flinched back at the reminder of what she so clearly lacked. Letting out a sigh of regret, he dropped his hand and then wrapped her in a warm hug, and Lena pressed her cheek against his chest, wishing that something could just be easy for once. Perhaps Lillian had broken something fundamental inside her, because even after moving out, Lena seemed adept at causing strife for herself without her mother’s input. 

 

            “I’m sorry,” she mumbled again.

 

            “It’s alright. I honestly expected it sooner,” he said with a small laugh. “Is this the part where we say we’ll stay friends?”

 

            Lena pulled back and gave him a rueful smile, “we were never anything but friends.”

 

            “You say that about all the people you sleep with; I’m starting to think we have a different definition of friendship.”

 

            Smile growing a fraction bigger, Lena pushed herself up on her tiptoes and kissed his cheek, above the scratchy beard, and lowered herself back down. “You really are my friend.”

            

            Reaching out to push her hair out of her face, Jack smiled kindly, his fingers gentle. “Okay. Okay, Lena.”

 

            It was a little bit condescending but she deserved it. Wrapping her arms around herself, she bit her lip and watched him gather up his box of things and make for the door again. Trailing after him, Lena leaned against the door frame once he’d stepped outside, meeting his warm gaze when he turned.

 

            “Will you be coming to dinner on Friday with Andrea and Russell?”

 

            “Of course,” she softly replied. “I’m off that day.”

 

            He nodded and then hesitated, “I’ll see you on Friday.”

 

            Lena watched him go after that and felt a stab of relief. Not because she didn’t like Jack, not because she didn’t want to be around him, or the sex had been bad, or he’d treated her badly. Lena just felt relieved that she wouldn’t have to put in the effort to meet other people’s expectations - no matter how low they were. She could come home and sleep after work and make dinner for herself and not have to make small talk with a man whose only flaw was that he was too kind to her, and maybe she was too selfish with her thick walls, receiving, but not giving more than a sliver of herself. If that was the case, she was just fine being selfish; Lena couldn’t afford not to be. 

 

            She went back to bed afterwards, although the sleeping draught had mostly worn off, and managed a few more restless hours of sleep before waking up just past midnight, spreading hummus on a piece of toast and calling it a day. With a cup of tea and her breakfast, she curled up on the sofa and read one of the dozens of books on healing crowding the built-in bookshelves lining one of the walls. 

 

            Her flat was homely in a neat way, not a thing out of place as if no one even lived there. Yet the deep green walls and dark planks of the floorboards made the place feel comfortable, especially in the golden hour when light streamed in through the windows and picked out orange notes in the dark furniture. It was spacious and had one bedroom, a bathroom and office space, which was more than she needed, more privacy than she’d ever had in her life. 

 

            She’d been the one to move out first, when she grew tired of living with three other girls, and Gayle had gone shortly after, moving to Manchester to move in with some Gryffindor she’d been seeing, and then Veronica had moved out and Russell had moved in with Andrea. It struck her at times, how much they’d all grown up, how they’d gone from Housemates at school to housemates applying for jobs and messy dating lives, to being somewhat responsible and monogamous, depending on who you were talking about.

 

            A rift had appeared between Lena and Veronica and Gayle the moment they all weren’t cooped up in one apartment, but Lena didn’t mind so much. She’d never really considered them proper friends, only Housemates she’d gotten along with due to proximity and her short stint as a spy during the war, coaxing secrets and rumours out of Veronica without so much as a flicker of guilt for her manipulation. Lena had never really liked her, and she wasn’t all that cut up about the distance. Andrea had surprisingly become a very good friend though, perhaps her best friend, which was a shocking prospect to Lena, who’d always thought of Kara as her best friend, even though they hadn’t had any sort of friendship for years. 

 

            Thoughts of Kara made her broody as she drained her tea and then made another cup, a blanket draped over her shoulders and a weary slump to the set of them. Adding a splash of milk, Lena cradled her cup and stared at Morrigan’s empty perch with a troubling thought on her mind. When her owl came home, Lena immediately sent her off with a letter requesting the transfer of a small sum from her own account into someone else’s. 

 

            Milling about the flat until the sun came up, Lena got dressed and walked through Dublin, buying herself a coffee with the Muggle notes she’d become rather adept at using, and then taking a seat along the River Liffey as she watched the Muggles. The fresh air cleared her mind and was a welcome reprieve from the bleach and antiseptic smell of St. Mungo’s and the confines of its hallways. Three days cooped up inside there was enough to wear Lena out, although she loved the work and didn’t get enough sleep in the on-call rooms, and she ended up walking around aimlessly after finishing her coffee and then heading straight home.

 

            She was on-call that night and kept her cryptex close in case it burned with an alert for a patient, avoiding a glass of wine, even though she could’ve sobered herself up with a potion. It always left her feeling groggy, and Lena had had enough of that while still training, so she tidied up, flicking her wand at the dishes, sweeping the floors and making the laundry scrub itself in the claw-foot tub before making dinner for herself and enjoying her bowl of pasta at the table by herself.

 

            Called in just after eleven for a spell gone awry, Lena spent the better part of three hours helping to get rid of an extra leg that the woman had managed to grow out of her hip. By the time she was done, Lena was already weary and bought a strong coffee in the tearoom, pouring so much sugar into it that it made her teeth hurt. She was sipping it at one of the nurse’s stations when her cryptex started burning in the pocket of her beige scrub pants. The different numbers and symbols almost made her groan, and Lena pocketed it with a sigh before glancing down at her wristwatch and wondering how long she could reasonably make her mother wait.

 

            Lena hadn’t exchanged more than a dozen words with her since moving out, and then only at work, where her mother was far too important to spend much time with the Resident Interns. After finishing off her coffee, running her tongue over her aching teeth, she dumped the paper cup in the bin and let out a weary sigh as she walked through the hallways to the room she knew to be her mother’s office. Lena hadn’t been inside until that point and had wanted to avoid it at all costs, but she soon found herself outside, staring at the brass plaque engraved with Hlr. Lillian Luthor. Healer-In-Charge. Raising her hand to the wood, she knocked.

 

            “Come in,” came the muffled sound of Lillian’s voice from behind the closed door, giving Lena pause for a second as her mouth went dry.

 

            Drawing in a shaky breath, she squared her shoulders and then opened the door, stepping into the neat office and closing it behind her. Taking a few steps further inside, she clasped her hands behind her back and looked at the spot on the wood-panelled wall just above her mother’s head.

 

            “You wanted to see me?” Lena curtly greeted her.

 

            “I’ve had Healer Smethwyck in here lauding your abilities on the Dai Llewellyn ward every full moon,” Lillian contemptuously started.

 

            She was looking over a file and kept her head down, quill scratching as she made a note and then set it back in the inkpot. Slowly setting the piece of parchment back down, Lillian sat back in her chair and gave her daughter an appraising look, taking in the neat seafoam green robes, the pristine beige scrubs underneath, the dark hair neatly pulled back and the cool indifference on her face.

 

            “He thinks you’d make an excellent student under his tutelage if you choose to specialise in serious bites.”

 

            Meeting Lillian’s eyes, Lena felt wariness bloom in her stomach as her mother’s cold gaze pierced her. Fighting the urge to shift restlessly, still feeling like a child about to be punished for some invisible crime, Lena’s mouth tightened at the corners and she raised her eyebrows a fraction. 

 

            “That’s not going to happen. You’re going to specialise in Charms-based injuries, just as I planned for you. You’re going to stop this nonsense on the Bite Ward and focus on the career I have sacrificed so much to build you for. No more, do you hear me? I’ve groomed you to take over my position one day, and this is how you’re repaying my hard work. By squandering your time looking after werewolves every full moon. You’re been banned from the Dai Llewellyn ward. You’ll not step foot in there again or I’ll make sure you don’t see the inside of an operating theatre for the rest of the year. Have I made myself clear?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “Get to rounds,” Lillian dismissively told her, picking up her quill again and making a shooing motion.

 

            Pale face flooding with pink as she whirled around and opened the door, fighting not to slam it like a petulant teenager, Lena stormed through the hospital in a foul mood until she reached her floor, fetching patient charts and poring over them with a brooding look on her face. Sam appeared at her side, scooting a cup of strong tea towards Lena as she let out a weary sigh.

 

            “Morning.”

 

            “Oh. Thanks,” Lena murmured, glancing at the tea and then sideways at her friend.

 

            “What’s the matter with you today? Didn’t you just get here?”

 

            “I was on call all night. And then I had to speak to my mother,” Lena venomously finished, slashing the quill across the chart as she crossed off a section of the paperwork.

 

            Sam winced slightly and turned, elbows on the counter of the station as she watched Healers rush past. “What about?”

 

            “I’ve been banned from the Bite Ward.”

 

            “Oh. Well that’s not a bad thing, is it? A bit of special treatment, huh?” Sam lightly teased, bumping into her.

 

            At Lena’s grim expression, she cocked her head to the side and sobered up, turning back around and ducking her head in close. “What’s wrong?”

 

            Running a hand over her face, Lena swallowed, her mouth thinning. “Nothing. I just- it’s … nothing. I should get to rounds.”

 

            Nodding, Sam asked Lena to check that one of her patients in the Poisoning Department didn’t regurgitate the potion he was to be administered and went off to her own work. Making the rounds, Lena checked on the rest of Sam’s patients and had to give the man a second dose of his potion after he brought it back up in his lap and waved her wand to syphon the vomit off the sheets. 

 

 

            The next full moon passed by quickly and Lena stayed far away from the Dai Llewellyn ward. She had received a receipt from Gringott’s regarding her bank transfer a few weeks ago and hadn’t expected to hear anything more about it, thinking that she wouldn’t see Kara again, now that she’d been banned from treating her once a month. Until Kara showed up at St. Mungo’s out of the blue one day. 

 

            It had taken her a while to check her vault and see the small pile of Galleons stacked inside, the smallest amount Lena thought she might accept if she managed to overlook her pride, but the moment she’d realised and connected the dots, she’d apparated from Diagon Alley to the alleyway beside St. Mungo’s. However she’d envisioned Kara reacting to the money, Lena hadn’t anticipated her showing up at work with it all shoved into a purse, stubborn and embarrassed.

 

            She was filling in one of the charts at a nurse’s station on the Second Floor, just outside of the Magical Bugs ward, when Kara approached, her stride determined and bristling with irritation. Lena looked up and barely managed to blink before she was in front of her, only slightly less exhausted than she’d been the last time Lena had seen her.

 

            “Was this you?” Kara asked, holding up the leather purse of money.

 

            Lena blinked in surprise, only freezing for a brief moment, her expression unreadable as she closed her chart and set it down, taking her time to reply. “No.”

 

            Kara knew she was lying and scoffed, pushing the purse against her chest, “I don’t need your pity.”

 

            Bristling, Lena’s jaw tightened and she frowned slightly. “It’s not pity. It’s-”

 

            She trailed off and looked down, hand tightening around the purse. Kara stared at her, red-raw eyes flitting back and forth in an agitated manner as she stood unsteadily on her feet, so ragged with exhaustion that Lena considered fetching a wheelchair for her. 

 

            “It’s what?” Kara firmly demanded.

 

            Closing her eyes, Lena rubbed her eyelids, a pale lavender webbed with veins, too many hours into her shift to be dealing with the emotional turmoil of confronting an old friend. There was an ashen taste of old bitterness in her mouth, a bitterness she’d thought she was past, her heart scarring over from the damage inflicted by the waif standing before her, but she wasn’t. The truth was Lena didn’t know how to process things, every negative thought, feeling or experience stamped down as she ignored it. 

 

            “We made a lot of promises to each other,” Lena gravelly replied, frustration making her words clipped, “you might not have meant it, but I did. So this is me looking out for you.”

 

            “I don’t need you to look out for me. I’ve managed just fine without you.”

 

            Eyes drinking in the sight of Kara, Lena let out a small, light laugh of surprise. Her lips twitched ruefully and she swallowed back a sharp retort. “I have work to do.”

 

            “It’s fine, I only came to give you back your handout.”

 

            “You would’ve been better off taking it,” Lena murmured, pained by the terrible thinness of Kara’s face.

 

            They stared at each other for a moment, Lena aloof and Kara restless, as if she wanted to say something, a wounded look in her eyes. Lips parting slightly, she ended up pressing them firmly together and then abruptly turning and stalking off through the hallways.

 

            Lena was still standing there when Sam sidled up, shaking a handful of Bertie Bott’s Every Flavour Beans into her hand and grimacing at a liver-flavoured one. “What’s that all about?”

 

            “Hm?”

 

            “Thought you weren’t allowed to treat any of the werewolves anymore.”

 

            “I’m not. She was just … saying hi.”

 

            Humming dubiously, Sam held a hand out and Lena took one that she correctly guessed to be cinnamon. “It looked pretty serious for a hello. It’s got you all out of sorts.”

 

            “Don’t eat that one - it’s earwax,” Lena murmured, opening her chart and pulling out her quill to make a note of the potions she’d administered to one of her patients earlier.

 

            Sam ate it anyway and then wrinkled her nose. “Ugh, foul.”

 

            “I did warn you.”

 

            “How are you so good at guessing the flavours?”

 

            “Oh, um, trial and error with a friend. She’d try any flavour.”

 

            “Are you feeling okay today?”

 

            Rubbing her forehead, Lena squeezed her eyes shut and then shook her head to clear it. “Uh, yeah. Yes. Fine.”

 

            “Come on, let me buy you a cherry bakewell from upstairs to cheer you up.”

 

            Lena rolled her eyes and gave her a thin smile, “I don’t need cheering up.”

 

            “Okay, fine, you can still have a cherry bakewell because they taste nice. Rounds are over. I need something to eat, seeing as breakfast ended in a tantrum and porridge in my hair . I think I need a holiday. When’s the best time to go to France?”

 

            “I think I need one as well,” Lena said with a withering sigh.

 

            They ended up in the tearoom, Lena picking half-heartedly at the cherry bakewell Sam had bought them, although she didn’t eat much, sick of sugar for the day. They talked about their patients, Lena offered to babysit for a few hours on Tuesday before the sitter arrived and Sam told her about the date she’d gone on last week, which Lena had already heard a bit about, but they’d been sending letters since. Sam’s cryptex burned first, far busier than Lena, although Lena dutifully trailed after her, a cluster of campers in the Brecon Beacons arriving after a run-in with a Welsh Green, the skin all but melting off their faces.

 

            It was a long day, and Lena was grateful that she was only scheduled for a thirty-two-hour shift that time, washing the stench of blood and vomit and burnt flesh off her skin in one of the communal showers, a glamour on her arm to hide the scar, before changing into her plain clothes and heading to Diagon Alley. 

 

            She stepped into The Leaky Cauldron and nabbed a seat at a table tucked in beside the bar. Setting her satchel down and shedding her coat, Lena fished her purse out of her bag and walked up to the bar, waiting for her turn to be served.

 

            “What can I get- oh.”

 

            Lena’s mouth fell open as she found herself face-to-face with Kara, who had a cloth slung over the shoulder of her pinstriped shirt, the buttoned cuffs too wide around her skinny wrists. A muscle worked in Lena’s jaw and she swallowed thickly, arms on the scarred wood of the high bar as she frowned slightly.

 

            “You work here?”

 

            “I’m not behind the bar for fun,” Kara wearily replied. “What’ll it be?”

 

            “What brandy do you have?” Lena asked, suddenly needing something stiffer than the elderflower wine she usually drank there.

 

            “Dragon Barrel’s.”

 

            “A double, please. Neat.”

 

            Nodding, Kara turned and fetched a clean glass and a bottle of dark amber liquid. The shadows of the dim pub made the scars on her face starker and she was a little pink-cheeked, trying her hardest to ignore Lena, who was watching her things at her table as she likewise tried to ignore Kara. The glass was set down in front of her and Lena handed over a few coins.

 

            “Thanks,” she murmured, taking her change and dumping it into a glass with a few bronze Knuts at the bottom. 

 

            Carrying her glass over to the table, she took a large sip and pulled out a book and her diary. The brandy warmed her stomach and Lena bent her head over the pages, dipping her quill in ink and occasionally writing down a thought or a memory, alternating between chapters of the thick tome on the different ways to treat burns as she slowly emptied her glass. She ordered another and Kara didn’t quite meet her eyes, setting the double in front of her and then moving on to another customer.

 

            Lena stayed later than intended, ordering soup for dinner and forcing it down as she studied and drank and people-watched, while mostly casting furtive glances at Kara. She watched her wipe down the bar every so often, polish glasses and stack them on the shelves, fetch barrels of beer and mead and stout, laugh with regulars and suddenly furrow her brow as her eyes made their way back to Lena again and again.

 

            The Leaky Cauldron started to empty before midnight, until Lena was the only one left, her empty glass on the table and her attention trained on Kara, even as she feigned being busy, flipping pages and jotting down annotations in the margins of her book. Kara lazily waved a hand at chairs as they upended themselves and settled on the tabletops, the smell of lemon polish being rubbed into the grain of the wooden bar, the floors swept. Lena purposely avoided the hint.

 

            Eventually, Kara’s shadow cast across her table and Lena looked up with polite interest, setting down her quill. Eyebrow quirking up a fraction, Lena sat back on her chair and Kara’s mouth thinned. They both hated this game they were playing, but they didn’t know how to break out of the awkward rut they found themselves in.

 

            “We’re closed now.”

            

            “Alright.”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Lena gathered her things away and tucked them into her bag. Fishing out a few Galleons, she set the fat golden coins on the table and wound her way to the front door. Stepping out into London, she breathed in the dampness and pollution of Muggle cars. Sidestepping a puddle of brackish water in the alleyway, Lena apparated home to her flat.

 

 

            Kara had started working at The Leaky Cauldron two weeks prior, not long after she’d fallen too far behind on her rent to keep up and had all but been thrown out onto the streets. Packing up the things she’d accumulated since moving in there with her sister, Kara handed the keys to her landlord and apparated to Cornwall, arriving on Eliza’s doorstep with teary eyes and a truly defeated air about her. It had been a few days after the full moon and felt like being kicked while she was already down.

 

            Eliza had made her a strong builder’s tea and reheated a bowl of soup, concern etched into the lines of her face as she tried to reason with Kara, convincing her to stay a while, to take any job, to let her make her a proper meal. Everyone was always trying to help her and Kara hated feeling like a charity case, but it was a bit different when it was her own mother and she was back in her old home, feeling like she was eighteen and had just graduated from Hogwarts with her future hanging uncertainly before her. Only now it was so much worse.

 

            Buying them fish and chips from a local Muggle shop for dinner, convincing Kara to walk there with her and carrying the paper-wrapped bundle as the sting of salt and vinegar was sharp in the air, Eliza made her eat every scrap of it and then ran her a hot bath upstairs. Kara stayed until the water was almost cold, reheating it with her wand and then staying a bit longer, her eyes red from crying and her hair a dull brass as it hung around her face in limp tendrils. 

 

            Fresh out of the bath, Kara changed into worn pyjamas that were now far too big, a thick knitted jumper over a thin t-shirt and flannel bottoms that had pilled from wear and sagged at her hips. Eliza clicked her tongue as she set another cup of tea down before Kara, brushing damp hair out of her daughter’s face as her mouth turned down at the corners with worry.

 

            “Look at you,” she murmured, “no wonder you’ve been avoiding me.”

 

            “I haven’t,” Kara softly lied. “I’ve been busy. Job hunting. And then the full moon.”

 

            “I know, I know,” Eliza tenderly murmured, but Kara could read the anguish in her eyes. “I just wish you’d let me help more. I used to come to St. Mungo’s every month with you-”

 

            Kara ducked her head down, her cheeks warming in Eliza’s palms. “I’m not a child anymore, mum.”

 

            “You’re still my child, though. Go on, drink your tea. And write to your sister; she’s been sending me non-stop letters about how worried she’s been about you. She said you rejected her offer to move in again.”

 

            Giving Eliza a weak smile, Kara raised a shoulder in a small shrug. “I don’t really fancy living with my sister and her girlfriend.”

 

            Chuckling, Eliza gave her cheek an affectionate pat. “Well, you’re staying here. Drink your tea and then off to bed with you. You look dead on your feet.”

 

            Kara didn’t argue with her. The tea was scalding and warmed her from within as she curled up on the sofa and listened to the Wireless Wizarding Network , Bastet in her lap and Eliza moving around, watering the plants in a slow, methodical way that was soothing to Kara. It was dark outside now and Kara could’ve fallen asleep then and there. Finishing off the dregs and shifting the cat off her lap, she rose to her feet and kissed Eliza on the cheek before telling her she was going upstairs.

 

            While brushing her teeth in the tiny bathroom, Kara heard the front door open and voices downstairs. Spitting out a mouthful of toothpaste, she washed her hands and then slipped out into the narrow landing, eavesdropping. It was unmistakably Alex, although she couldn’t discern the words, and Kara hesitated just outside the bedroom door until she heard the first sound of a foot treading on the stairs. 

 

            Turning the handle, she lingered on the landing and met her sister’s eyes before ducking into the dark room. Flipping the light switch, Kara sank down onto her bed, across from the mess of her things spread across Alex’s unused bed and waited for her to follow her in. Shifting a pillow to the top of the bed, Kara turned and stretched her legs out, the right one aching where she’d clawed the calf muscle a few nights ago, and stared at the door. 

 

            “Hey.”

 

            “Hey,” Alex murmured, stepping inside and shutting the door, her eyes cautious. “What’s going on?”

 

            “Oh … you know,” Kara evasively replied, gesturing before folding her arms behind her head.

 

            Rolling her eyes, Alex nudged some of Kara’s stuff aside and gave her a pointed look before sitting down. Giving her a quick grin, Kara closed her eyes and exhaled forcefully. 

 

            “You could’ve just let me cover half of the rent. Or moved in with-”

 

            “I don’t want to,” Kara tightly replied, rubbing her forehead as a headache bloomed. “Thank you, but no. I’ll- I’ll sort it out myself. It’s … fine.”

 

            “The whole point in having family is that you don’t have to do everything yourself.”

 

            “Well, I’m moving back in, so … there. Satisfied?”

 

            “Don’t be an arse. We’re all worried about you. I’m worried about you. I’ve barely seen you in the last month, and I know you were home and just ignoring me.”

 

            “A lot’s been going on,” Kara mumbled.

 

            “Like what? You haven’t been working-”

 

            “I got fired.”

 

            “I know that, but … just take any job. Not everyone thinks that way about you. It might be shit, but at least it’ll pay more than you’re on now, right? What about going back to The Junk Shop for a bit?”

 

            Mouth twitching with annoyance, Kara sighed, “tried it. They didn’t need any extra help.”

 

            “Okay, well … what about a pub? The Hopping Pot? The Leaky Cauldron? Even a Muggle one-”

 

            “I am not working in a Muggle pub,” Kara scoffed, pummelling her pillow and then getting comfortable as she stared up at the ceiling. 

 

            Her cheeks were red and she felt an irrational flicker of anger towards her sister. Alex was only trying to help, but that’s all anyone ever did. Kara couldn’t stand their pity, their smothering eagerness to give her money, to let her sleep on a sofa or come over for dinner. James, Kelly and Lucy had all offered to put in a word for her at their jobs after Kara rejected Alex’s offer and maybe Kara had too much pride but she’d turned down their offers too. She was fine. She’d work something out, and she wouldn’t be at Eliza’s for long. 

 

            Only, a week turned into two and then she’d gotten a job at The Leaky Cauldron waiting tables, serving drinks and making beds. Tom was aware of her condition and didn’t judge her harshly for it, was as kind as she could expect a stranger to be to her. The pay wasn’t a lot either, but it was more than the Ministry benefits she’d been surviving on, which she was still receiving, still below the threshold that would disqualify her from receiving it.

 

            Every night she went home to Eliza’s, usually past midnight, and she’d go straight to bed, smelling of beer but full from a proper dinner, which Tom gave her for free every shift. In the mornings, she’d wake late and shower, heading downstairs to cold bacon or sausages and make herself sandwiches. It was getting warmer now, so she’d eat outside with a cup of tea and watch Eliza prune bushes and fertilise flowerbeds.

 

            Her cheeks filled out and her clothes didn’t sag quite so badly, and Kara felt somewhat okay. Her life wasn’t shaping up to be what she wanted, or even anticipated, but she’d hit rock bottom and clawed her way out after existing in a rut for a couple of months. Even the monthly encounters with Lena had come to an end, a small mercy that troubled Kara more than she cared to admit, the sullen Interns assigned to her each month were not nearly as kind, even with their messy history that had made things so tense between her and Lena.

 

            Kara saw her twice more at The Leaky Cauldron over the following weeks and wondered whether Lena was only showing up because she was working there, or whether she occasionally frequented the place before she’d started working there. It made no difference to her; Kara served her and went on with her life as if she hadn’t revealed every secret to the stranger on the other side of the bar at one point in time.

 

            Towards the end of her second month, when she’d been clearing out a storage room at the end of the third floor, a Room Thirteen that was too unlucky to be assigned to a boarder, Kara asked Tom if she could rent the place. He charged her a small enough fee that her money from the Ministry covered that alone, and she could scrape together enough from her wages and tips to amass a small amount of savings. 

 

            Eliza was wary about her moving back out, but Kara was excited for the first time in a while, and earnest about being back on her feet. It wasn’t much, but it was steady work and a private room for herself. A sturdy bed took up most of the space, and Kara made it up with her own sheets and quilt, a warm yellow that brightened up the room. A desk and wardrobe were also crammed in there, made from heavy wood and scratched with age but of good quality.

 

            She filled it with her things, with plants from Eliza and her photographs and books, the desk comfortably cluttered and her clothes often left out. Tom let her use the kitchens whenever she wanted to and Bastet had the run of the place, helping keep the old pub free from rats and mice as customers came and went. A train on the Muggle line rattled past every couple of hours, right outside the window that let in a draught of air, and the taps leaked and the walls were thin, but Kara felt a sense of independence again, instead of failure.

 

            Her friends all drank there too and she’d join them after her shifts or on her breaks, chiding them as they tried to leave the odd tip. Mike stopped showing up and Kara felt more relief than she imagined at that, her sudden indifference towards him earning her a rather nasty letter as she kept her reasons to herself. Kara didn’t tell anyone, still trying to figure out her own feelings about it. It might not have been anything, and even if it had been, it wouldn’t have been viable and she was overwhelmingly relieved about that, wondering if it made her an awful person to feel grateful that she wouldn’t have to raise a child with the genes of a werewolf and barely two Knuts to rub together. It was better to never have to find out, never have to worry that it would ever happen to her.

 

            Unfortunately, Kara’s mind didn’t have enough to occupy itself with to stop her from thinking about so many uncertainties in her life. What would it have been like to still be an Unspeakable? Would she have been assigned to the theory of death that she’d had a particular interest in? If she wasn’t a werewolf, would she have found someone to love her properly? Would they want kids, without the pressing danger of a war to make them rush into things? If she wasn’t a werewolf, would she have even met Lena before, if she hadn’t moved away from Wisconsin and Ilvermorny and her parents? Her mind was too free to dwell on the possibilities as she swept the floors of the pub with the heavy oak brook and then scrubbed them with lemon water and lit lavender candles to banish the smell of spilt beer.

 

            Life became monotonous for the most part. Easy. Finding her footing again, Kara went out for drinks with her friends and didn’t have to drag her belt in an extra few notches as regular filling meals did her a world of good. Eliza would meet her for lunch sometimes and Kara would go with her to sell her herbs and plants to various shops in all the stores and markets, and Alex would come on her days off to buy them ice cream at Florean Fortescue’s, leaving loose change scattered in unlikely places in Kara’s room at The Leaky Cauldron.

 

            It was May before she knew it, the beginning of summer affording a few extra hours of sunlight and mildly warmer weather. Kara browsed Diagon Alley to her heart’s content, making friends with the locals, and getting good deals on a new cloak, a new quill, and a new sturdy pair of shoes. She read The Daily Prophet as she ate breakfast in the pub’s kitchen as dishes went out to the guests staying there, and borrowed the owls to send letters to friends and the fireplace to Floo to Falmouth on her days off, helping Eliza tend to the flourishing garden, which was almost overgrown now, bending over flower beds as the back of her neck tanned and her hands grew a little calloused.

 

            The full moon was at the start of June, and with the heat and the exertion of the change, Kara took it extra hard afterwards. Sweating and flushed, she left a little later than usual, now that she didn’t have to avoid Lena, a pinstriped shirt tucked into flared jeans and scuffed boots as she made her way down to the street level. Outside Purge and Dowse, Ltd. she felt the heat on her face and felt sick, her shirt plastering to her back and the bandages wrapped around her left shoulder. 

 

            Nauseous and faint, Kara blinked back dark spots as she lurched into the alleyway beside the entrance to St. Mungo’s and braced her hand against the cool brick wall. Her hair was pulled back into a bun, but her wayward curls escaped it and clung to her pink, sweaty cheeks as she drew in ragged gasps of air, feeling as if she was going to vomit.

            

            “Are you alright?”

 

            A groan escaped her and Kara closed her eyes as her glasses slid down the clammy bridge of her nose. “Go away.”

 

            “Let me help,” Lena murmured, her voice quietly pleading and tender.

 

            Her hand fell on Kara’s arm and then she was subjected to the disorienting trip of Apparition, winding up on the doorstep of her old apartment. Blinking as her stomach lurched, Kara glanced at the door and then at Lena - who was somehow still managing to wear a grey tweed coat over her linen shirt in the heat, and standing too close to Kara for comfort - and then vomited all over her chest.

 

            Lena’s mouth fell open as she stiffened, blinking, and Kara clapped a hand over her mouth. Mortification slammed into her in a wave and she tried to mumble an apology through her fingers as Lena’s mouth thinned and she reached for her wand.

 

            “I’m so sorry, I-“

 

            “It’s fine. This happens at least three times a day,” Lena exasperatedly assured her, vanishing the vomit and then casting another spell to thoroughly clean her clothes. “Drink some water once you’re inside; it’ll be the heat.”

 

            “I don’t live here anymore,” Kara rasped, her face red at the awkwardness of the moment prolonged.

 

            Blinking, Lena faltered for a moment, a crease forming between her eyebrows as she crossed her arms over her chest, and leaned forward slightly as if she’d misheard Kara.

 

            “Pardon? What do you mean you don’t live here anymore?”

 

            “I was evicted,” Kara peevishly admitted. “Now, if you don’t mind, I’m going to my actual home.”

 

            Sighing, Lena gestured vaguely and rolled her eyes. “Well, where’s that? I’ll apparate; you’ll get splinched in your state and it’s a nasty business to fix.”

 

            Pausing, reluctant to give her anything personal, Kara’s mouth twisted derisively. Finally, she caved and gave Lena a disgruntled look.

 

            “The Leaky Cauldron.”

 

            “Yes, I know you work there-“

 

            “I have a room there.”

 

            “Oh. Oh, alright then. May I?”

 

            Kara gave her a flinty look. “Now you ask?”

 

            Giving her a thin smile, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction, “I recall you being a lot more insistent without asking - once upon a time.”

 

            Blustering for a moment, Kara couldn’t formulate a response and Lena wearily sighed. Grabbing her arm, she apparated then to the Diagon Alley side of The Leaky Cauldron. Kara was white-faced and damp with sweat, her skin taking on a ghastly grey tint, and Lena slung an arm around her shoulder as she helped her inside.

 

            Making her way upstairs, Kara had to lean heavily on the other woman and hated her own weakness. It was doubly embarrassing to be staying at the pub she worked at because she hadn’t been able to afford rent, and the comfortable shabbiness of her room didn’t seem quite so charming when Lena’s polished form stepped foot inside, oozing wealth and privilege, down to the perfume wafting off her.

 

            “I’m fine. You can go,” Kara dismissively told her, setting her bag down beside her desk and gripping the back of the wooden chair for balance.

 

            Taking in the place, Lena met her gaze and raised her eyebrows a fraction. “You’re welcome.”

 

            Scoffing, Kara flushed and then felt irritable. “I’m not going to thank you for following me around-“

            

            “I’m not following you.”

 

            “Then why are you everywhere?” Kara demanded, her voice breaking slightly with defeat. “You are … everywhere , and you never used to be, but now I’m constantly reminded of-“

 

            “Of what?” Lena haughtily asked, stepping further inside so she could firmly shut the door. “What do I remind you of? How you treated me? Are you ashamed? I am - for ever letting you treat me like that.”

 

            “Like what? What did I ever do to deserve this- this hatred from you? All I did … all I did was try to help you. And you told me to go.”

 

            Lena’s lips twisted as she let out a huff of defeated laughter. “You were my only friend. You had other friends but I only had you , and you didn’t believe me.”

 

            “And you never forgave me for it.”

 

            Trying not to sound childish, Lena made a choked sound at the back of her throat. “You never even said sorry.”

 

            “And I’m paying for it even today. We’ve barely seen each other in five years and it’s still hanging over us. We were fucking kids, Lena. There was a war and I was terrified for you.”

 

            “You should pay for it for the rest of your life . For making me believe that we were friends, that you gave a shit about me, and then pulling the rug out from under me. For giving up on me when things got hard. I never gave up on us. But you did,” Lena snapped, her eyes bright with anger. “We made a promise but you assumed the worst of me. Do you have any idea how fucking lonely I was? You have no idea what I’ve been through.”

 

            Kara let out a hollow laugh, irritably moving a strand of hair out of her face. “I could say the same thing.”

 

            “No, you couldn’t; I kept tabs on you, I kept you safe . You had your friends, you had your family and the people that cared about you, despite what you are. I knew what you were going through every month, but you had no idea about me. The things that … happened to me on the holidays,” Lena’s voice turned thick and uneven then, gravelly as she tried to speak about it. “I hated going home. I hated it so much, and I didn’t have anyone I could talk to about it. Who had I ever had to love me? My mum-”

 

            “You can’t blame everything on her,” Kara quickly cut her off. “You can’t blame her for what you did. You think my mom didn’t make me into something too? I was abandoned but I- she didn’t get to choose the person I became. I chose for myself the kind of person I wanted to be, and so did you, but you chose to be the same as them. You chose to have the blood of those people on your hands-”

 

            Scoffing, Lena shook her head and turned to the brass door handle. “Fuck you.”

 

            Her footsteps thudded away from Kara, who wilted, devastated all over again, although she wasn’t the one leaving this time. She’d always felt undeserving of Lena’s love and had never been able to act on her feelings out of a deep-rooted shame and feeling of inadequacy. But she didn’t want her to go and this time she wasn’t too proud to say it.

 

            “Please don’t go,” Kara quietly begged, looking at her with pleading eyes. 

 

            Hesitating, Lena turned and blinked, swallowing with some difficulty. “You should be resting.”

 

            Leaning heavily on the back of the chair, Kara felt something cave in her chest as she tried to still the pitching feeling in her stomach. Choking on a sob, she ducked her head, sandy blonde curls falling in her face as she squeezed her eyes shut, teeth bared as she tried to stifle the tears, the pain of it all.

 

            Helping her onto the edge of the sagging bed, Lena stepped back and crossed her arms over her chest, disgruntlement making her features harder and her eyes sharper. She’d shut the door again but didn’t look pleased to be there, a coldness to her face as she clenched her teeth.

 

            “I’m sorry. I know your mum treated you cruelly - well … I know that now. You never told me-“

 

            “No, I didn’t,” Lena curtly agreed. “I didn’t want to. I didn’t want your pity, but, in hindsight, that might’ve been preferable to your accusations. You assumed the worst of me, Kara, and you never even knew the truth. You didn’t know half of what I did and why, but your friends didn’t like Slytherins and that was enough, wasn’t it? Our little secret, our promises, broken over a suspicion that I never once deserved.”

 

            “You knew about the attack at Hogsmeade and told no one ; it was deserved.”

 

            “Hogsmeade,” Lena softly crowed, bitter and bright-eyed. “Do you want to talk about Hogsmeade? I couldn’t tell you then, I couldn’t talk about it with anyone, but what’s the harm now? Hm?”

 

            Rain speckled the windows in a summer shower and Kara’s face was grey, her vision blurring slightly with angry tears as her head pounded. Lena was just getting started, her words sharp and rough, each one laced with venom as if she’d harboured it all inside her for years, waiting to let it out. She probably had been doing just that.

 

            “You were right that I knew. You hated all those people I became friends with,” Lena flatly laughed, a sarcastic edge to the word friends before she continued. “But most of us had someone on the Dark Lord’s side, someone who was showing off and leaking information to their younger siblings, smug about how much they knew, how trusted they were. It was easy to gather it all up and feed it right to Dumbledore, just like he’d asked me to. So easy to spy for him, to tip him off about the attack ahead of time. Did you think those Aurors immediately showed up out of mere coincidence? I thought he’d cancel the trip, I thought- I thought he’d protect everyone, but … it wasn’t until after , when I went to him, that he said he couldn’t risk them knowing they had a spy. He let those people die and called in Aurors and the Order so I could keep feeding him more information. When he didn’t cancel the trip … I begged you to stay, not because I was on their side, but because our side did fuck all . And I … I couldn’t risk you.”

 

            Kara’s breaths were sharp and quick and she folded in on herself on the lumpy mattress as she pressed the heels of her palms into her eye sockets, nudging the glasses up. She trembled, already weak but now utterly blindsided by the revelation.

 

            “No,” she hoarsely whispered, “no, he wouldn’t do that.”

 

            “You would believe some doddering old man with a secret agenda over the person who was your best friend?” Lena softly challenged.

 

            “I- no . But … you- how?”

 

            Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “You know me.”

 

            “I did - once,” Kara softly murmured.

 

            Flinching at the past tense, Lena cleared her throat and ran a hand over her face. “I hated everyone until I met you,” Lena said with a small, sad laugh, her lips twisting into a rueful smile. “But I … cared about you so much that I tried to understand your reaction even while you were hurting me. I couldn’t even hate you properly because … I was supposed to be convincing, so how could I blame you for falling for it?”

 

            Kara drew in hitching, breathless sobs on the bed, her shoulders shaking as she tried to stifle the sound with the cuff of her shirt sleeve.
