            “What a year it has been, another host of bright minds sent out into the world to make the most of their potential. That’s all we can really do, isn’t it? Give people the opportunity to prove themselves on their own merit.”

 

            His meaning wasn’t subtle and Kara shifted uncomfortably, setting down her trunk and her briefcase, keeping a tight grip on Bastet, tucked under her arm. “Thank you, Professor Dumbledore. Thank you for the opportunity you gave me. Not just now but allowing me to come to Hogwarts. I don’t want you to think I’m ungrateful-”

 

            He held up a hand, silencing her as his expression softened with understanding. “I don’t think that. I understand that we must all carve our own path through life, that there are things we must do alone at times.”

 

            Nodding as she meekly lowered her head beneath his kind understanding, she vaguely mumbled her gratitude and buried her fingers in her cat’s fur as she tried to resist the urge to fiddle.

 

            “Are you taking a carriage?”

 

            “No, I think I’ll walk. I’d like the time to think.”

 

            “Then this is goodbye. If at some point in the future, you decide you’d like to return to teaching, you’ll be very welcome back at Hogwarts, Miss Danvers. In any capacity.”

 

            “Thank you, sir,” she murmured, shaking his offered hand and then hoisting her trunk.

 

            Without another word she set off down the long path to the gates, the air holding a faint chill, as high up as they were, but the sun shining and the fresh greenness of the surrounding nature invigorating. She was sorry to leave it behind.

 

            Once she reached Hogsmeade Kara apparated to Cornwall, lugging her belongings to the front door and letting herself inside. She could hear Celestina Warbeck on the radio and Bastet let out a mewling cry, twisting from her grasp in her haste to seek out her usual haunts around the old cottage. Filling the doorway, Kara toed the heel of her brogues and slipped them off before setting down her briefcase and slipping off her cloak.

 

            “Mum?”

 

            She could see straight through to the open back door and deduced that Eliza was outside. Floating her trunk upstairs to the tiny bedroom, Kara remerged and walked downstairs, pushing up her shirtsleeves as she stepped out into the sunlight. It was warmer in Cornwall, although it was cloudier there, and she shaded her eyes against the brightness, catching sight of her mother on her knees, pruning one of her cherished plants.

 

            “I’m home.”

 

            Eliza turned, squinting against the brightness before a smile graced her face. Climbing to her feet, grumbling about old joints, she wiped dirt off her hands and held her arms open to embrace her daughter as Kara padded barefoot across the grass. Feeling Eliza’s arms around her, Kara had to bite back the urge to let everything spill right out of her in a breathless torrent, holding her tightly in return.

 

            “Hi, sweetie,” Eliza said, pulling back and brushing Kara’s grey-peppered hair out of her face, taking in her appearance with approval.

 

            “Need a hand?”

 

            “No, no, you go on in. I’ll be in in a minute. We can have some tea. Are you hungry?”

 

            Kara’s expression softened with a smile, “no, I’m alright. I’ll boil the kettle while you finish up.”

 

            She slipped back inside and pottered around in the kitchen until she’d put together two cups of tea and some of the gingersnaps Eliza had in the cupboard, already on her third by the time her mother appeared. They sat at the scarred kitchen table, a breeze drifting in from outside as they left the door open, and talked about Hogwarts and Kara’s year and Eliza’s business as they refilled their cups and enjoyed the rest of their morning.

 

            It was a lazy day and Alex was due over for dinner with Kelly later on and Kara knew she was going to have to tell her family sooner or later that she’d resigned and that she didn’t know what she was going to do anymore but she quite fancied the idea of travelling. The thought of being alone and outdoors, hiking mountains in search of magical creatures or visiting the libraries and ministries of other countries to sate her curiosity, learning different types of magic from local communities and immersing herself in other cultures, was something that sparked an interest. Kara had always enjoyed discovering new things, an endlessly inquisitive child that had enjoyed running barefoot through fields in Wisconsin, and that was a big part of why she’d applied for the Department of Mysteries in the first place, wanting answers to the big questions. Now her dreams were smaller and she just wanted answers to the little ones.

 

            They had a leg of lamb for dinner, spooning roast potatoes and carrots onto their plates, glasses of red wine poured that reminded Kara of a different bottle of wine smashed on the wooden floorboards not altogether that long ago. She ate slowly and grew tenser as she steeled herself to finally come out with it but waited until the opportunity presented itself.

            

            “So … first year of teaching out of the way then,” Alex said, raising her eyebrows. “Be honest; how bad was it?”

 

            “It wasn’t bad,” Kara said with an awkward laugh. “Some of the kids are troublemakers. Most of the Gryffindors are a handful like you were, but they’re not bad. There are some real characters though. I like the funny ones.”

 

            “At least you know what you’re getting yourself into next year,” Kelly said with a smile. “I really felt for our Defence Against the Dark Arts Professors. A new one each year - they never stood a chance.”

 

            Kara shrugged noncommittally, grimacing as she moved food around her plate. Alex nudged her with her foot, leaning back in her chair and raising her eyebrows when Kara met her eyes. “What?”

 

            “Nothing, I just- I’m- I’m not going back. I mean … I quit.”

 

            “What do you mean? I thought you were enjoying it,” Eliza softly exclaimed, surprise crossing her face.

 

            “I was but … it’s just not what I thought it would be. Um … I think I just- I need some time to process things. Some more independence.”

 

            Eliza’s mouth opened and closed as she was left speechless for a moment, blue eyes full of surprise and an anxious set to her face. “Independence? You’re going to be living at home again.”

 

            “Just for a little while. I thought I might go abroad,” Kara mused, “see some of the world, you know? I don’t know when I’ll ever have the money to do it again, given my condition. May as well make the most of it, right?”

 

            “Go abroad,” Alex echoed, confused at the mere idea of it.

 

            “Now seems like the right time to do it.”

 

            “Kara … come on. What’s gotten into you? You quit your job and now you’re trying to up and leave?”

 

            Rubbing her cheek, Kara shrugged, shoulders hunched and defensive. “I just feel a bit suffocated here.”

 

            “You- there is no way you’ve just had a sudden change of heart. What happened? You were fine up until a few weeks ago so don’t act like you haven’t been behaving differently because something is clearly wrong.”

 

            “You don’t know everything, you know,” Kara churlishly replied, “and I’m allowed to not tell you things. I’m allowed my privacy and to make my own choices, okay? I’m not a child, I’m not- I’m not helpless just because no one wants to give me a job because of- of what I am.”

 

            “No one is saying that,” Alex sighed, rolling her eyes, “but this is a bit out of the blue. All you’ve done is go on about how great it is to be back at Hogwarts, how much you like the work, your own office and the feasts and Quidditch and … everything. And now you’re so fed up you want to leave the country? I don’t buy it.”

 

            Scoffing, Kara stabbed a fork at a potato, “is it so hard to believe that maybe I want some more freedom in my personal life? Being a teacher does complicate those sorts of things. It’s not as easy as just Apparting to the pub after work for a drink with friends. I can’t … invite people over.”

 

            “You want me to believe you’re giving up a good job for some … hypothetical boyfriend?”

 

            Cheeks flaming, Kara huffed, setting down her cutlery and reaching for her pumpkin juice as she leaned back in her chair. “No. I’m just saying … it’s not a sustainable lifestyle for what I want.”

 

            “And … The Leaky Cauldron was?”

 

            Eliza hushed Alex and clicked her tongue, her mouth thinning with exasperation. “Alex, leave her be.”

 

            “Mum-”

 

            “Travelling is a good experience. If that’s what Kara wants to do then she can; she’s a grown adult. She can figure things out once she’s back.”

 

            “You must be having a laugh,” Alex scoffed, shaking her head. 

 

            But her annoyance was just a mask for the worry in her brown eyes as she studied her sister, recalling how thin she’d gotten, how bad it had been, how she’d been broke and unemployed and homeless. It was different for them - Eliza did the best that she could but they were nowhere near well-off enough for them to have a family fortune to fund their lifestyles. Alex made decent money as an Auror, and Kara had been as a Professor, more money than they were used to, but she knew her sister wouldn’t take a single Knut from her once her savings ran out. Alex loved her sister dearly but she was stubborn as anything and too proud to accept her help. It had been infuriating to watch her scrape together money for rent when Alex and Kelly had a cluttered spare room they’d offered for free. And now Kara was on the verge of putting herself back in that exact same situation.

 

            The rest of dinner was mostly silent and awkward, Eliza and Kelly doing their best to keep the conversation flowing, the mood light, while the two sisters were quiet and somewhat sullen, drinking their wine and avoiding each other’s eyes. Kara couldn’t tell Alex the truth and Alex was upset at the thought of Kara going so far away. It had been bad enough with Kara squirrelled away at Hogwarts for most of the year, seeing her sister when she could; being on different continents would be even worse. 

 

            After they’d cleaned up dinner, Alex went out into the garden while Kelly followed Eliza into the living room, discussing some policy or another from work, while Kara wiped down the counters. She caught a flicker of a cherry red coal in the dark as her sister lit up a cigarette and rinsed her hands off beneath the taps before stepping out to join her.

 

            Alex didn’t say anything as she slowly paced back and forth on the grass, a warm breeze sweeping in with the hint of salt, trees rustling and the sound of garden gnomes ferreting about filling the peaceful silence. Leaning against the stone of the cottage wall, Kara hugged her arms to herself, soft flannel beneath her fingertips as she tipped her head back and gazed skywards. It was a cloudless night, the stars visible against the darkness, and she listened to the grass crunch as Alex walked over to her.

 

            They stood in silence for a long while, Kara breathing in the clove and leather smell of her sister and her cigarettes and long coat as she paced beside her. It was what she associated with her now and she committed it to memory, knowing she’d miss her terribly while she was gone. As she thought about it, she felt she owed her some sort of explanation, some sort of truth, even if it wasn’t entirely related to the reason why.

 

            “I was pregnant a while ago,” Kara quietly confessed.

 

            Alex’s restless pacing paused and Kara could feel her eyes on her. She closed her own, a thin smile on her lips as her throat constricted.

 

            “Obviously it would’ve been impossible …”

 

            She trailed off, leaving the rest unsaid. Footsteps scuffed the patio and Alex’s coat brushed against the stone wall as they stood shoulder to shoulder. An arm was slung around her and Kara let her head fall onto her sister’s shoulder, letting out a heavy sigh.

 

            “Are you okay?”

 

            “Yeah. Don’t tell mum.”

 

            Alex exhaled a stream of smoke, lit cigarette held aloft, and then kissed the top of her sister’s head, a silent vow of secrecy. They stayed that way for a few minutes longer, listening as the crickets started up and a breeze ruffled their hair. Alex’s voice was barely audible as she spoke, small and uncertain.

 

            “I’ll miss you if you go.”

 

            “It’s not forever.”

Chapter 23

            Packing a secondhand tent into her battered briefcase, along with her clothes and an assortment of camping equipment bought cheaply at The Junk Shop , Kara prepared for her trip with a flicker of excitement bringing back some of her almost forgotten enthusiasm. It had been a long time since she’d looked forward to something so much, the idea of walking and flying and Apparating from place to place with only her thoughts and Bastet for company already allowing Kara to shed some of her worries.

 

            Donning jeans, a thin cotton shirt and her sturdy scuffed boots, Kara pulled on her beloved blue cloak and picked up her briefcase. Her footsteps felt heavy and apprehensive on the stairs as she made her way down, Alex gripping the back of a dining chair, while Eliza wrapped bundles of food in waxed paper, things that would keep and could be cooked over a campfire or the small gas burner Kara had bought. Her throat closed up at the sight of her family and Kara’s heart stuttered in her chest with the realisation of just how much she was going to miss them.

 

            They’d all had dinner together the night before, with Kelly and Kara’s friends crowding into the kitchen, and Alex had stayed the night, insisting on seeing her sister off. Kara had woken up early and they’d all eaten breakfast together before she’d finalised the meagre belongings she’d be taking with her, selected from her already rather meagre pile of worldly belongings, and gotten dressed. Now there was nothing else to do but get on with it.

 

            Coaxing Bastet from the kitchen counter, where she was curled up around a potted Mandrake seedling, Kara perched her on her shoulder and then let out a forceful breath, squaring her shoulders as she faced her mother and sister. Shrugging slightly, the cat shifting with the movement, she gave them a wavering smile.

 

            “Well, time to be off then.”

 

            “You take care of yourself,” Eliza sternly warned her. “And make sure you eat. Especially around the full moon. Send letters when you can and don’t forget to place wards around your tent when you set up camp.”

 

            “I will,” Kara promised, wrapping Eliza in a tight hug.

 

            Alex sighed when Kara turned to her, opening her arms as her mouth thinned with dismay. “I’ll kill you if you don’t come back. But … have fun, okay?”

 

            “Yeah,” Kara whispered, breathing in the smell of leather and smoke. “You look after each other too.”

 

            “Look after yourself.”

 

            A laugh got stuck in Kara’s throat and she swallowed thickly. “I’m trying.”

 

            Patting her back, Alex inhaled sharply and then sighed, pulling back and giving her a wry smile. Squeezing her arms, she nodded and Kara’s cheeks dimpled with her answering smile.

 

            “I’ll miss you.”

 

            “You too.”

 

            “I should get going.”

 

            “Remember your offensive spells,” Alex cautioned her.

 

            Nodding, Kara let out a huff of laughter as she started drifting down the hallway to the front door. “I will.”

 

            “Bring me back something cool.”

 

            “You got it.”

 

            Stepping outside, early summer bringing a clear day, Kara inhaled deeply and then squared her shoulders before turning to smile at her family lingering in the doorway. Shading her eyes from the sun as she squinted, she swallowed past the lump in her throat and said a wavering goodbye.

 

            “I’ll see you soon.”

 

            Intending to walk for a while, to enjoy the coastal walks that Cornwall was known for, Kara turned and started off down the street, pausing near the end, while the cottage was still in sight, and raised her hand in a wave. After that, she turned on her heel and Apparated a few miles west, coming out near a pocket of rocky coastline, the waters a deep navy and the beaches golden sand. Damp seagrass was soft underfoot as she breathed in the bracing briny air and started to walk.

 

            It was peaceful and the morning passed by quickly, Kara enchanting her briefcase to drift behind her, the weather warming as she shed her cloak and tossed it over her shoulder, Bastet on the other one until she leapt down to ferret out mice in the burrows they made in the low shrubbery and jumped at Cornish Pixies as they chattered about, teasing her and plucking at Kara’s hair and robes until she tired of their antics and immobilised them, leaving them drifting around, bug-eyed and blue. 

 

            Setting up camp that evening along the grassy cliffside overlooking cerulean waters, watching the sunset over the horizon, Kara warded the worn tend and the surrounding area as she lit a woodless fire with her wand and made a stew in her small cauldron. Bastet wandered around, pouncing at a butterfly, stalking through long grass and rubbing up against Kara’s shins as she sat on her briefcase, knees to her chest. 

 

            She ate her dinner and made a cup of tea and read outside until the light failed before she coaxed Bastet inside and readied her bed. It was a small camp bed with a thin mattress and while it wasn’t much, Kara enjoyed the idea of living simply. It felt deliberate, as opposed to the last time she’d been homeless, and she lit the small lamp with her wand and turned the radio on and ate a few biscuits with a second cup of coffee and continued to read until it was time for bed.

 

            The next morning she packed up camp and continued her walking, her feet gaining blisters and the day warmer than it had been yesterday. Every few miles she Apparated, until she grew tired of the coast and set her sights westwards. She camped in Wales, hiking partway through the Brecon Beacons and then Apparting up to Snowdonia, waking to early morning views over the mountains and lakes. That was where she had her first brush with a wild dragon, heating a kettle over the campfire and warming her hands until a deafening roar that seemed to shake the world almost knocked her off balance. 

 

            With her camera in tow, Kara crept through the trees, her breath pluming before her despite the start of summer, and she stumbled upon a Common Welsh Green stretching its wings and long neck, the dappled colours of the forest making it blend in so well with the landscape that she wasn’t surprised the Muggles didn’t know they existed. Snapping a photo of it before it launched itself skywards, the rippling airwaves buffeting Kara to the ground as the trees almost bent in half by the force, Kara returned to her breakfast somewhat shakily and smiled at the photo.

 

            Apparating across to Ireland, she encountered a Hag and a Banshee on two separate occasions, hiking across bogs and through glens and thinking of Lena the whole time as she wondered where her house was. In Dublin, Kara found a magical pub, disguised to look like a littered alleyway from the front, and she managed to cinch a room for the night before carrying on her way. She visited the Cliffs of Moher and Giant’s Causeway, camping amidst a fine drizzle and walking through the sunny patches of summer days.

 

            On to Scotland, which was somewhat familiar from school, Kara hiked partway through the highlands and spent some time outside Inverness, catching sight of Selkie’s in the great lochs and almost falling for a Redcaps trap on a foggy evening. Apparating down to Yorkshire, Kara spent a night with Winn and showed him her photos over dinner, sleeping on his sofa before she was off again the next morning.

 

            After exhausting the U.K., Kara was restless and eager to get as far away as possible, so naturally, she chose Australia. Forking over a few Sickles, she got a Portkey to the other side of the world and Apparated to Uluru, a breathtaking sight that she brought her broomstick out for to view from above. She camped in the Outback on red dirt and beneath a grey sky, the beginnings of winter leaving her considerably cooler than she’d anticipated, and she managed to catch a Quidditch game between the Thundelarra Thunderer s and the Wollongong Warriors while she was passing through. On her last night camping in the tropical regions of Queensland, she was stung by a few Billywigs, the sapphire insects hovering around, and Kara was faced with the grim prospect of levitating for a few hours until the effects wore off and she could apply a dab of Dittany to the little raised bumps.

 

            New Zealand was lush and green but was too much like the U.K. for her to linger too long before getting a Portkey to Indonesia after her quick attempt at catching sight of an Antipodean Opaleye dissolved into homesickness. There were many ghosts in Indonesia and they made good company, although Kara couldn’t understand Indonesian, and she found that many of the Muggles there seemed to be more perceptive of the magic around them as she heeded warnings from a guide she’d found at a magical market to stay out of sight as much as possible or risk being discovered. Hopping from country to country, she passed through Singapore to Malaysia, Cambodia and Vietnam, Thailand, Laos, Philippines, Myanmar and Taiwan. 

 

            In Japan, Kara spent a week at a wandmaker’s shop in Osaka in exchange for board, sorting out fibres of unicorn tail hair and polishing wands made from cherry and ginkgo wood, drinking green tea and sweeping floors in her spare time as she watched customers come and go, young witches and wizards buying their wands for the new school year. After camping around the various islands she went across the sea to Korea, staying south as she hiked through the mountains and then spent two days in Seoul where she paid an aurologist to assess her aura. The outcome was a rather bleak but accurate assessment that left Kara flushed and annoyed as she left the narrow building and went to buy herself a cup of ginseng tea and watched the thriving city pass her by. 

 

            In China, she went on a hunt for the Chinese Fireball, encountering the volatile dragon after linking up with two witches and a wizard who were Magizoologists, one of them a specialised Dragonologist. They camped together and shared their congee with her and after they’d shared in the delight of finding one of the elusive dragons they invited her to their quest to locate a Phoenix for their new book. It took two weeks of climbing through mountains and forests before they located one near the peak, all of them quiet and careful as they took in the sight of the large, radiant bird. It wasn’t anything new to Kara, who had met Fawkes on numerous occasions in Dumbledore’s office, but they were beautiful birds and it was another thing altogether to see them in the wild. Afterwards, she spent a few days in Hong Kong, researching the acclaimed Alchemist, Dzou Yen, one of the pioneers she’d studied at Hogwarts, sating her curiosity on old scrolls in a dusty library.

 

            From Hong Kong, she travelled to Tibet and spent two weeks at a monastery filled with magical folk from all around the world. They drank potions and meditated on the philosophies of magical theories, focusing inwards on their own bodies as they learnt about correlating magical energy and linguistics with spells and how to enhance their own abilities. It was a freeing experience and Kara felt rested and more aware of herself after her stay, delving off into the wilderness to seek out a Yeti. She managed to enrage one and came away with a souvenir of white fur and a panicked, shaky photo as it barrelled towards her the moment she clicked the button on her camera, and Kara had to fix a few broken ribs after she lost her balance and slipped over the side of an incline, catching herself on a rock on the way down.

 

            In Borneo she accidentally stumbled upon a nest of Acromantula in the rainforest, white beach ball-sized eggs clumped together, while a few of the freshly hatched ones scuttled around, three feet wide at the thorax and with far too many legs for Kara’s liking. A few of the bigger ones hung in large webs and were instantly on alert at the presence of human flesh. Kara filled the rainforest with the bright colours of offensive and defensive spells as she fled through the foliage, slipping on patches of rotting leaves, clambering over mossy logs and pushing through hanging vines as she left a few curled-up corpses in her wake from the spells cast over her shoulders. 

 

            In Egypt, she explored a few of the old Pyramids, reading the curses on the walls, and explored the ruins encountering a Sphinx, which left her feeling uneasy as she was confronted with three riddles before she managed to escape its games. In Turkey, she camouflaged herself and soared up with the hot air balloons, enjoying the sight of the colourfully striped balloons with the Muggles gathered in the little swaying baskets, snapping a photo from high up as the sun rose over the arid landscape and she breathed in the cool, dusty air. 

 

            She disturbed the resting spot of a Chimaera in Mykonos as she hopped around the Greek islands, and Kara knew their danger well enough to Apparate out of there immediately as the lion-headed creature pounced towards her, jaws opening. Abandoning Europe for now, with plans to come back later, Kara returned to the north of Africa and swept her way down the country, camping amidst a herd of Erumpents on the open savannah, keeping Bastet close by even though her wards allowed Kara to watch the magical creatures from a close distance without being spotted. Although, by the twitch of a female’s ears she thought they might have sensed her there anyway and was wary of the monstrously huge beasts trampling her tent in the night.

 

            Travelling from Ethiopia, Chad, the Ivory Coast, Mauritius, Nigeria and Uganda, she visited the magical communities located there, clipping Abyssinian Shrivelfig and drying them out so she could mail the seeds to Eliza, encountering the small, rotund Diricawls and watching them Apparate in and out of sight. The weather varied depending on where she was - humid as she explored pockets of mangroves on the coast, arid in the deserts of the Sahara, with nothing in sight but undulating sand dunes, and quite cool in South Africa at night as she photographed the bioluminescent waters with wonder.

 

            Afterwards, Kara hopped continents to South America, exploring the ruins of the Amazon and studying Fire Slugs that she found there. She drank too much tequila that had the effect of spouting steam from her ears and got a brief gig boxing up quills at a factory in Argentina that belonged to the father of a girl she’d gone to Hogwarts with - that Slytherin she’d once tried to hex. Getting a Portkey from the bottom of Brazil up to the northern regions of Canada, Kara rented a small cabin and promptly passed out on the comfortable bed, waking in the morning to step outside to the most vivid-green ryegrass as it extended all the way out of sight to the end of the property, a pine forest visible in the distance and the sky a heavenly, cloudless blue overhead. That far north, spring still had a sharp bite to it, snow blanketing the peaks of mountains and dusting some of the hills and capping the mountains as she took in the great expanse of the outdoors. She stayed for six nights, waiting up until dawn as she tried to spot the aurora, finally packing up once she saw it, feeling tiny and insignificant in comparison to the glowing ribbons lighting up the night.

 

            Stopping in Seattle to pouring rain, Kara hiked - or part-way hiked - Mount Rainier to find a Thunderbird at the top, bringing the coalescing storm that darkened the overhead sky as rain lashed the surrounding wilderness and grey cities. In the Appalachians, she found an abandoned cabin and heard strange noises all night before she woke with a start to the keen yowling of a cat and the dim shadow of a Lethifold creeping over her body, intending to smother her in her sleep. Kara managed to free herself and Bastet’s fur was on end, the cat practically inconsolable as Kara sat up for the remainder of the night, running her fingers through the dark fur and hushing her. 

 

            Eventually, she found her way to New York City, a hub of activity, congregating witches and wizards almost blending in with the oddities of the concrete jungle in their flapping robes and mismatched outfits that didn’t seem so out of place amidst the 80s riot of colours the Muggles were sporting. It was a place she could have envisioned herself living in another life, if she hadn’t been bitter and hadn’t left America, so much knowledge and culture crammed into one place that she would’ve been drawn there like bees to honey. Kara wondered if her mother would be at the MACUSA building situated there but wasn’t curious enough to wander in and see for herself, terrified that she would find her there.

 

            Kara’s first stop was Wizard Broadway, buying a ticket for the next showing of Big Foot’s Last Stand. It wasn’t something of interest in particular, but she’d always wanted to see a show on Broadway, and as the place filled up with all manner of magical people and creatures, Kara sat in the dimly lit room with a Gigglewater and watched the production with delight. Still, she fell asleep near the end, as exhausted as she was, and woke to a raucous round of applause as the auditorium rose to their feet, some of the patrons setting off colourful sparks as the cast and crew bowed and the front row conjured flowers to toss onto the stage.

 

            After securing a night at a cheap hotel, the noise outside spilling in, Kara followed the directions she’d gotten from a witch she’d stopped in the foyer of the theatre to a speakeasy and jazz club called The Blind Pig . Accessing it through a large advertisement on the wall, Kara was assaulted by the loud noise of music and felt like a giant as she walked through the space largely occupied by Goblins. She’d been assured it was a regular haunt for magical folk looking for cheap drinks and Kara found an empty table tucked away in the corner and ordered herself a beer. She was halfway through it when someone said her name - her old name.

 

            “Kara El?”

 

            Looking up from her drink, Kara blinked as she found herself staring at a tall Asian man that was vaguely familiar. Dark hair neatly brushed back, the collar of a white oxford shirt peeking out from beneath a navy sweater and deep violet robes over the top with a crest on the breast. It took her a second before Kara realised who it was.

 

            “Kenny?” Kara said with a similar surprise, slowly rising to her feet.

 

            He smiled and stepped forward, hesitating then as he half-raised an arm as if to hug her. Uncertain and awkward, Kara paused for a moment before meeting him halfway, hugging him and feeling an odd sensation in her chest at a sliver of her old life showing up out of the blue. 

 

            “This is such a surprise,” he said, pulling back. “I thought- well, we all heard about what happened to your dad. And then you never came back to Ilvermorny.”

 

            “No,” Kara haltingly replied, fiddling with her fingers. “I, uh, I moved to England. Ended up finishing school at Hogwarts.”

 

            “Hogwarts? Really? Well, isn’t that something? Can I get you a drink? Are you here with someone?”

 

            “No, no, I’m here by myself. Please, sit.”

 

            He set down his satchel and the copy of The New York Ghost that he had clamped under his arm, nervous and a little clumsy in his haste, so like Kara that she smiled slightly as she remembered why they’d been friends. Asking what she was drinking, he walked to the bar and ordered before carrying two glasses back over and setting them down. Shedding his robe, he took a seat and shuffled the chair in, giving her a nervous smile.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            “Wow, you sound so … English. ”

 

            Wrinkling her nose as she blushed, Kara laughed at her lap as she adjusted her glasses. “I always feel so obnoxiously American over there.”

 

            “How do you like it?” he asked, taking a sip of his beer.

 

            “Oh, um, yeah, it’s good. Different. They, uh, they don’t have Quodpot over there. The sweets are different too - the candy,” she quickly corrected herself, laughing nervously and swallowing a gulp of her drink.

 

            Clearing her throat, she set her glass back down and shifted. “Sorry, I’m just … nervous. I haven’t seen anyone from back here since I left.”

 

            He scooted his chair in a little more and opened and closed his mouth, looking uncomfortable but curious as he spoke. “There were rumours at school after you left. Someone’s mom apparently worked at the same MACUSA department as yours.”

 

            “What rumours?” Kara asked, her voice barely audible over the noise of the bar.

 

            Kenny’s face crumpled with a ginger expression as he rubbed the back of his neck. “That Alex Danvers’ mom took you away. That’s why you both weren’t at school for the next year.”

 

            “Oh, well … that’s true. She’s, um, she’s my sister now. Her mum took me in when my- my mom - when she- I’m sure you know what happened,” she murmured, gesturing to her face.

 

            “Only that your dad died and … some other things.”

 

            A spasm of pain flashed across Kara’s face and she brushed her hair back, trying not to feel so self-conscious about the scars as her cheeks burned red, only making the scars more livid.

 

            “Right.”

 

            She raked a hand through her wild curls and gave him an embarrassed smile, thin and grim, expecting more questions and was pleasantly surprised when Kenny just nodded and took a sip from his beer. 

 

            “I’m really sorry.”

 

            “It was a long time ago,” Kara rasped, her throat tight around the words.

 

            She didn’t feel nearly as dismissive about it as she was pretending, although he didn’t know the true depths of her torment. Each month a new horror, even though she’d grown to expect it, grew accustomed to the pain and the disjointed memories, the blood, the scars, the vomit, the exhaustion. Half of her life had been given over to it once a month; it wasn’t anything new, but a secret to this man who’d once been a boy who’d been her only friend in the world. 

 

            “You didn’t write,” he said after a pause, his brow furrowing.

 

            “No, I didn’t. It was a lot to go through at once. New home, new country, new school, new name, new mum, new sister.”

 

            “Right. Right, of course. So, um, moving back or …?”

 

            “Oh, no, I’m just- I’m travelling around a bit. Taking a break from work and life, you know.”

 

            “And what are you doing for work?”

 

            An uneven smile graced her lips. “I was an Unspeakable for the Department of Mysteries. A Ministry job in research. Then I taught the Study of Ancient Runes at Hogwarts for a year.”

 

            Kenny nodded, curiosity filling his dark eyes, his gaze warm and gentle as they didn’t linger too long on Kara’s scars. “Interesting. Do you enjoy it?”

 

            “I did. What about you? What do you do?”

 

            “Astronomer,” he sheepishly replied, spreading his hands in a helpless manner.

 

            Kara laughed, her eyes creasing at the corners. She fondly recalled nights spent stargazing with him when they should’ve been safely tucked away in bed, and he’d always seemed to be lugging around a telescope, jostled about by the rowdier students as he skirted through life on the outskirts with Kara, never quite fitting in. Now, he seemed confident and more sure of himself, but still a little sheepish about the nerdier aspects of his personality he’d never grown out of.

 

            “Oh, really? That’s so cool. You always did love the stars.”

 

            “Mhm, and now I get paid to stare at them all night for a living,” he said with delight.

 

            “So, what have you been up to? Aside from the stars?”

 

            They talked over their drinks, the years falling away and reminding Kara of why they’d been friends all those years ago, two curious kids who didn’t quite fit in so much. They’d both changed a lot since then, Kara quieter and more introspective, Kenny more confident, and they both looked like entirely different people too, the years stretching them taller and leaner and older. Kara bought the next round of drinks and Kenny bought the two after that, and when they were done for the night he nervously asked if he could see her again before she left for her next stop. Being bold for a moment, Kara asked if he wanted to go back to her hotel instead. 

            

            Once there, they were clumsy and awkward as if they were still teenagers, and despite their childhood friendship, they were practically strangers to each other. They were both a little drunk and he kissed her clumsily, pulling off her cloak. That was all Kara would let him take off and she was tongue-tied and furiously red in the face as she looked down and told him she didn’t want to take off her clothes, her mind straying back to Lena’s words with the sharp twist of a knife in her chest. Even now, with someone else, she was all Kara could think about.

 

            It almost felt out of spite as she kissed him back and unbuttoned his shirt beneath his robes, Kenny spluttering with surprise before he hastily helped speed things up. In the end, she managed to shed her corduroy trousers and keep Kenny’s hands over the soft cotton of the long-sleeved shirt she wore, the rest of her hidden beneath the covers and in the darkness of the room as she turned the lights out. 

 

            It was quick and awkward, out of rhythm and a little stiff as Kara’s mind wandered, unable to stay focused in the present when all she could think about was the past. The past with gentle hands tracing her scars, hot lips kissing them softly, the voice that haunted her dreams and was at the root of all of her regrets, making Kara conscious of how wrong it all was. Afterwards, in the dark, she lay on her side, fighting the urge to cry as a keen sense of loneliness filled her.

 

            “Kara?” Kenny whispered in the dark, stretched out beside her beneath the covers, his voice wary and awkward.

 

            “Hm?”

 

            “Your scars-” he started before faltering. Clearing his throat, he tried again. “The rumours …”

 

            “What did the rumours say?” she whispered.

 

            She could practically feel him cringing beside her. “That when your dad … you got mauled by it.”

 

            Kara almost bristled by the inhumane way he spoke of Serena, the woman who had ruined her life. Rubbing at the tender spot above her eyebrow as her eyes burned, Kara swallowed dryly.

 

            “I wasn’t mauled,” she whispered. “I was bitten.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            He didn’t say anything after that and Kara pushed back the blankets, fumbling around in the dark for her underwear and pants, blindly putting them on as she heard the mattress shift and the rustling of fabric as Kenny searched for his own clothes. Flustered and pink-cheeked, Kara hovered in the dark as she listened to him get dressed, not wanting to confront the mistake she’d just made. He’d never been one for gossip but would confirmation of those old rumours now fly within their old circles of classmates who probably barely remembered her beyond that?

 

            She gestured off-handedly to the lamp on the nightstand to wandlessly light it after a few minutes and Kenny paused halfway through putting on his shoes. Running a hand through her hair and then tucking in the hem of her shirt, Kara cleared her throat.

 

            “I’m really sorry.”

 

            His solemn expression softened with surprise. “It’s okay.”

 

            Finishing getting dressed, he shrugged on his robes and picked up his satchel before moving to the door. Kara went with him, a lump stuck in her throat as she kept her head down, eyes trained on the worn carpet of the cheap bed and breakfast. Opening the door, Kenny paused and Kara raised her eyes to the crest on his uniform.

 

            “It was good seeing you again,” she mumbled.

 

            “Could I see you again?” he asked, a hopeful note in his voice.

 

            A spasm of guilt ran across Kara’s face and she opened and closed her mouth for a moment before plucking up the courage to meet his dark eyes. “I- you’re really nice, but … no, I don’t think so. Sorry.”

 

            “That’s alright,” he said with a lopsided smile. “It was good to see you again too. Take care of yourself, okay?”

 

            Her lips twitched ruefully and she was surprised when he quickly pecked her cheek before saying goodbye and leaving, so painfully American in his open honesty that it made Kara feel a little homesick. At the same time, it made her ache for a certain repressed Irishwoman who could never talk so openly about her thoughts and feelings, who took everything to heart and hurt so easily. It was hard to move on when you were still wrapped up in pining after somebody else.

 

            Continuing on her way, she went from state to state, discovering plants and meeting new people, learning new spells and finding work plucking dirigible plums at an orchard in California, rounding up Hippogriffs in Colorado and camping in Yellowstone, waking for the sunrise as she brought out her broomstick, left Bastet on the ground, and soared through the peaks of the sprawling park with awe. Renting a Niffler from a guy running a prospecting business in Utah, Kara went off with the creature and let it burrow through the earth in search of anything precious, spending the day reading in the baking sun as it brought back a few nuggets of gold and tiny emerald, which she sold back to the guy when she brought back her Niffler. Pockets padded a little, she stretched out her thin budget for a few more weeks in the States before it would be time to tackle the rest of Europe before her funds ran dry.

 

            She spent a night of the full moon with a pack of werewolves - some of them previously Muggles until the bite - who’d congregated in the Bayou of New Orleans, all of them changing together with cries of pain and baying howls, running through the swampland with reckless abandon in a pack. Kara woke the next morning at the base of a twisted elm, filthy and bloody, copper in her mouth and red beneath her nails, and vomited up the flesh of a rabbit she remembered tearing apart, some lingering animalistic feeling lingering as she tried to clear her head. She found her way back to the shacks in the middle of the swampland, white-faced and weak, and reclaimed her belongings and rejected the offer of a greasy breakfast with these people who were so different from her but showed her a part of herself that she was afraid to give into, and moved on to the next place.

 

            Eventually, Kara’s travels brought her to Wisconsin, almost as if it had been inevitable. She’d made a silent, stern decision to stay away but found it unavoidable, the idea of seeing her mother again too tempting. Kara wasn’t sure how she’d react or what she’d say, what feelings she had towards her after so long, all of them stamped down as a different mother - a better one - had stepped in to fill the space. 

 

            Still deliberating whether or not she should attempt to see her, Kara decided to walk there from a few miles out. The fields were golden and the trees were vivid green and Kara enjoyed the bracing chill as she trampled through the picturesque landscape, spotting farms and nearby towns. Eventually, the landscape became familiar, the spot where Kara had tried to find Mooncalves, the lake where she’d caught tadpoles and garden gnomes, the trees verging on her family’s property where she’d climbed trees to root out Bowtruckles and common owls, insisting that she’d catch one to deliver her letters for her. 

 

            And then at dusk, she reached the spot where she’d stood as a werewolf stalked her and she’d been bitten, her dad’s throat torn out and blood staining the grass. She hadn’t been back there in thirteen years; it was longer than she’d ever lived there. It left Kara feeling odd and she was rooted to the spot as the day bled into the night and the sky darkened around her.

 

            Looking at her mother’s house in the clearing between the trees, the house where she grew up, she saw the light come on in the kitchen and just for a second Kara still lived there and her father was still alive. She could envision it so clearly, her mom in her work robes at the kitchen table, her father standing in the doorway calling her home, the smell of dry grass and greenery swept in on the cool breeze. For a moment there was no werewolf and no abandonment and she knew it wouldn’t last forever but it made her feel safe - just for a moment.

 

            Tightening her hand around the handle of her briefcase, Kara made the difficult decision to step forward, tense as her stomach swooped and she felt faint and hollow, a weakness creeping into her limbs as she pushed onwards. Her boots thudded on the back porch steps, which creaked with old age, and she stood before the peeling door and hesitated before raising her hand to knock.

 

            Her face was pinched with painful unease and her throat closed up as she listened to the muffled scrape of a chair and the footsteps growing nearer before the door was pulled open. There was a prolonged moment of surprise on both ends, the sound of crickets in the dusk filling the silence as they took each other in. Alura had aged gracefully, brown hair streaked with less grey than her daughter’s, a few lines at the corners of her eyes and her complexion paling as her lips parted. Kara was taller than her now, by inches, a shock in and of itself, and she couldn’t help but wonder what her mother thought when she looked at her, this nondescript, washed-out, dusty-haired young woman in patched clothes.

 

            The moment stretched beyond stunned silence to plain awkward and was broken by Kara as she shifted uncertainly on her feet, boots scuffing the worn planks, a restless agitation that had been instilled in her since birth, always itching to be running off somewhere barefoot, always eager to trip over her tongue in her haste to dispel any discomfort. Only now, she didn’t know what to say, and so her restless shifting broke it for her.

 

            “Kara,” Alura eventually got out, her voice hoarse, her expression slack as if seeing a ghost instead of the daughter she’d willingly abandoned.

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Kara made a small choked sound at the back of her throat. “Mom.”

 

            “You’ve grown.”

 

            A huff of surprised laughter at her mom’s audacity escaped Kara, a painful tightness in her chest as she clenched her empty hand into a fist to stifle the trembling. Bastet was curled around her neck like a scarf and nuzzled against Kara’s ear at her evident discomfort, feeling the rapid pulse at her throat. She wasn’t sure if what her mom meant was that she looked so old, signs of her Lycanthropy making her seem years older, even though it was clear she was still young if you looked close enough.

 

            “Of course I have,” Kara said with forced levity, her voice and face flushed with agony, “it’s been thirteen years.”

 

            Alura’s face rippled with pain and she had the decency to look ashamed. “What are you doing here?”

 

            “I’ve been travelling so I thought I’d come and see you; there are things I’d like to talk about.”

 

            “Oh. Well, come in.”

 

            Stepping aside as she held the door open, Alura invited her daughter inside the house she’d grown up in, memories assaulting Kara as she looked around at the place, relatively unchanged save for a few pieces of decor. Her father’s cloaks no longer hung on the hooks inside the hallways, her shoes no longer littered the floor as she kicked them off and ran around outside barefoot. She wanted to run upstairs, to step inside her childhood bedroom and see her things - if they were even still there - she wanted to sit on the peaked roof above her bedroom window and watch the stars all night, have pancakes with her dad on a Sunday morning, have her mother love her again. It was painful how tangible the memories of her childhood felt there, back in the house she'd never been allowed to come back to after that night. Her whole life had vanished in the time it took for the werewolf's teeth to clamp down on her shoulder and Kara felt the weight of that like gut punch.

 

            Bastet jumped down and stretched her legs, tail waving in the air as she nosed about curiously. Kara set her briefcase down to the left of the front door but kept her robes on as Alura closed the door behind her, shutting them in on the awkwardness clouding the air between them. Her mother went through to the kitchen and Kara followed after her, hovering on the threshold for a moment before stepping over it. Dragging a chair out, Kara took a seat and Alura reclaimed the one she’d occupied before answering the door. There was a palpable hum of anxiety to her mother as she nudged back a glass of wine she’d been drinking, no offers for a glass for her daughter, and as Kara stared at her, Alura studiously avoided meeting her eyes.

 

            “How are you?” Kara haltingly asked.

 

            Surprise flashed across her mother’s face and her head jerked up, taking in her daughter’s wide-eyed face, still so much like that child she’d abandoned, but horrifically scarred. Alura swallowed with difficulty.

 

            “Dear me, you sound so English . I suppose that’s what I get for letting her take you over there.”

 

            “You didn’t let her do anything. You abandoned me. You left me there, at the hospital. I waited for you to come back for me.”

 

            A tremor crept into Kara’s voice and she swallowed thickly, devastation softening her face. Alura heaved a sigh and ran a hand through her brown hair, mouth turning down at the corners. While Kara favoured her father’s looks more, there was something of her mother in her mannerisms and Kara’s heart broke just a little.

 

            “I didn’t just lose my dad, I lost my mom too. And everything else besides,” she continued, anger warming inside her now. “I know it must have been hard for you but … you didn’t have to leave me as well.”

 

            “You’re not a mother; you wouldn’t understand.”

 

            “Neither are you,” Kara softly replied with scorn. “Did you even care? Did you even … think about me? Think about coming back?”

 

            Alura didn’t reply for a long minute, tense and horrible as they sat there, but eventually, she let out a resigned sigh and faced Kara, reaching for her glass of wine and knocking it back. She set the glass down on the edge of the table and softly cleared her throat.

 

            “No, I didn’t. As far as I’m concerned, my daughter died the same day as my husband.”

 

            Pain knifed through Kara’s chest, rippling across her face as Alura confirmed what Kara had already known, and she let out a hoarse laugh. Climbing to her feet, Kara sniffed and cleared her throat, staring down at Alura through a haze of tears as she fought to stop her bottom lip from wobbling. 

 

            “I should go. I’ve taken up enough of your time already.”

 

            “You haven’t asked your questions yet.”

 

            “I just wanted to see if there was anything salvageable, so thank you for answering that for me.”

 

            She strode out of the room, clicking her tongue for Bastet to come wandering back over from wherever she’d gotten off to, and stooped to pick up her briefcase. The cat trotted over and sprang into her arms before working her way up onto Kara’s shoulder. Blinking until her eyes dried, Kara yanked open the back door and hesitated on the threshold before she turned back, knowing Alura had followed after her. 

 

            “You didn’t have to come back for me,” Kara said, wiping tears from her cheeks as she grew angry with herself for revealing so much. “You could’ve answered her letters though.” 

 

            Nodding, Alura’s mouth thinned and Kara turned away again, stepping out into the night. Something caught the sleeve of her robe and she glanced down at her mother’s hand clenching the fabric before she looked up at her face.

 

            “Are you happy?”

 

            Hesitating, Kara’s mouth felt dry and she rubbed the scar on the bridge of her nose as she answered. “Happiness isn’t for the likes of creatures like me; you taught me that. But … she’s a good mum and I love my sister. You did me a favour, in the end.”

 

            Looking as if she wanted to say something else, Alura opened her mouth and then snapped it shut, her daughter’s words sinking in and leaving her with nothing else to say. They weren’t a family anymore, hadn’t been in so long that Kara didn’t even feel anything but old pain and confusion about it, thinking that closure would help but now doubting her decision to come there. They didn’t know each other at all and Kara was left with the urge to see her family again, to have dinner with Alex and Eliza, to play Gobstones with her sister and listen to her collection of Weird Sister albums in their tiny bedroom in Cornwall. For all its familiarity, Wisconsin wasn’t home anymore.

 

            “Goodbye, Alura,” Kara murmured, refusing to call her mom any longer, and she plodded down the stairs and Apparated out of the backyard.

 

            She got as far away as she could in one jump, coming out in a field of grass, shoulder-high and dry from the sun beating down on it. Kara had no idea where she was but she pitched her tent and crawled inside, the bunk with the thin mattress and rumpled quilt already set up with the lantern beside it, and she sank onto the edge of it, knees practically drawn up to her chest, and buried her face in her hands as she cried.

 

            Getting it out of her system, Kara felt better afterwards and chalked it up to the full moon in a few days, her hands shaking as she heated a tin of soup with the tip of her wand and ate it straight out of the can before making instant coffee. She listened to her wireless radio and lay in bed, exhausted and a little heartbroken and determined to never feel like that again. The next morning, she packed up and Apparated to New York City.

Chapter 24

            Using a few of her remaining Dragots, Kara booked herself in on the next Portkey out of the country, fortuitously whisking her away to France, a few miles outside of Paris. Making her way into the city, Kara found her way to Place Cachée , an infinitely more refined and grander version of Diagon Alley, everything built with the creamy limestone of the ornate Parisian buildings, and she accessed it through the bronze statue in the Montmartre district of the city, at Rue Richer and Rue Girardon. Her first stop was the bank, exchanging Galleons and Dragots and other currencies she’d picked up along the way for Bezants.

 

            Sitting at a small table at Café Abringer , shedding her robe in the summer heat of the city, Kara cuffed her sleeves once and spread parchment over the table as she sipped a hot chocolate and penned a letter to her sister. After sealing it, she finished off her drink and went to the post office to hire an owl to send it before fumbling through a conversation with the clerk there for directions to Hotel De Ginestou where she rented a room for the night.

 

            It was cheap but clean and Kara collapsed onto the bed with relief, her body aching and tired, especially after the Portkey. With the time difference, it was already past midnight on American East Coast time and Kara slept a while, waking just in time for the quiet dusk descending over Paris, purple skies overhead and the sound of an accordion drifting up from the plaza below.

 

            Stomach rumbling, she made her way out, leaving Bastet curled up on the rumpled bed sheets, and wandered the Place Cachée until she found what looked to be a pub with a sign reading Griffon Buveur . It was faded and homely, stone floors and plastered walls, polished wood and a murmur of French as witches and wizards, Veelas and ghosts and goblins congregated. Some were smoking over glasses of wine, others tittering over bowls of soup and Kara tucked herself away in the corner with a glass of Chardonnay and ordered the chicken in a cream sauce. 

 

            Finishing off every bite, feeling the usual shakiness of an approaching full moon, her body aching and her face clammy and pale, Kara pulled a small book out of a pocket and read quietly over a second glass of wine. Then she went back to her room at the hotel and slept again until morning when there was a loud knock on the door and she opened it to reveal her sister standing on the threshold. 

 

            Kara’s face split into a smile and she almost bowled Alex over as she barrelled out of the room, engulfing her in a hug. Laughing and patting her back before giving her a tight squeeze, Alex sighed softly with relief.

 

            “Hi, you.”

 

            “It’s good to see you,” Kara whispered, her voice a little ragged.

 

            Pulling back, Alex studied her face as she clapped her hands down on Kara’s shoulders. Giving her an uneven smile, Kara nodded and then turned, stepping back into the room and rubbing her face to get rid of the imprint of the sheets marking her chin. She was dressed in a long-sleeved shirt with a hole in the neck, her feet bare on the old floorboards, and ran a hand through her messy curls as she blinked owlishly, fishing for pants on the bedroom floor.

 

            “You’re looking well,” Alex noted. 

 

            “Yeah, thanks,” Kara replied, buttoning up her jeans and then patting Bastet’s back as she tried to ignore how much everything hurt - her knees, her joints, her bones. “How’re you?”

 

            “Good. Although you were supposed to be back by now.”

 

            Turning, Kara gave her an uneven smile. “I didn’t specify how long I would be going for.”

 

            “Well, I miss you.”

 

            “I’ve missed you too,” Kara said with a small laugh, catching her sister in another hug. “How’s mum?”

 

            “Same as ever. You haven’t missed much. Except for this.”

 

            Alex held up her left hand and rolled her eyes to the ceiling as Kara gasped at the ring on her finger and grabbed ahold of her hand to get a better look.

 

            “When? How? Why didn’t you tell me?”

 

            “You’ve been a hard person to get a hold of. Very elusive, almost as if you’ve been running from something.”

 

            “I’m sure Maximus could’ve tracked me down.”

 

            “Sure, let me send my owl across the Atlantic to drop off my mail, you dolt. It’s fine, it was only a month ago. And we wouldn’t have gotten married until you were back anyway. Now, tell me everything. I got your letters but you’ve been holding out on me, I can tell. You really do look good, by the way.”

 

            “Oh, um, yes, well, it’s been good for me. I’ve done a lot of thinking, a lot of meeting new people and new places. I, uh, I went home recently. Yesterday, in fact - I think. Time differences, you know?”

 

            “Home? Home home? You mean with-”

 

            Kara gave her a thin smile, sitting on the edge of the bed as the mattress groaned. “Alura, yes.”

 

            Scoffing at her name, Alex walked over to the narrow floor-to-ceiling windows that opened to the tiny enclosed balcony that was scarcely big enough for her sister to stand in, leaning against the wrought-iron railing as she patted down her pockets for cigarettes. Shaking one out, she lit it with a flame between thumb and forefinger and let out a stream of blue.

 

            “How is the old hag?”

 

            “Unclear.”

 

            “And how are you?”

 

            Shrugging noncommittally, Kara scuffed a toe along the floorboards. “Got what I asked for, didn’t I? If I tickle a sleeping dragon, I can’t moan when I get burnt.”

 

            Alex sucked her cigarette down quickly, making a sound at the back of her throat as she exhaled smoke into the morning and flicked the butt over the railing. A torrent of French cursing drifted upwards and Alex choked, smoke escaping her mouth.

 

            “Oh, fuck. Sorry! Er, pardon,” she called over the railing, ducking back inside and shutting the windows.

 

            Crossing over to Kara, she cupped the back of her head as she dropped a kiss down on top, and the smell of tobacco and leather and clove made Kara’s eyes sting with tears. Jostling the bed as she sank down beside her, Alex leaned back and stared at Kara before prodding her arm.

 

            “It’s alright. She doesn’t matter anymore.”

 

            “I know. I’m glad.” Rubbing her face and fixing her glasses, Kara sighed and glanced down at Alex, a smile curling her lips. “I’m glad you’re here. Now, let’s get some breakfast; I’m starved.”

 

            They went to the café Kara had gone to the day before, eating butter croissants with jam, scrambled eggs and black coffee on the sides, her sister chain-smoking through it as they chatted away, Alex answering Kara’s dozens of questions while she elaborated on the stories she’d included in her letters when she’d sent them. There were photos as well, developed film of moving creatures and people and places thumbed through as they bent their heads together.

 

            “So, what do you want to do while you’re here?” Kara asked.

 

            “Didn’t you say you had the rest of Europe to see? I’m coming too.”

 

            “I- but what about work?”

 

            Alex shrugged and gave her a quick grin, exhaling smoke from the corner of her mouth. “I have three weeks of paid leave so I’m ready for some adventuring.” She pitched forward in her chair, clapping her hands together. “Where are we off to first?”

 

            Kara just laughed and they started plotting. First up was Spain, a day in San Sebastian by the sea, another in Seville as they toured old buildings and sat at small tables in the sun lining the street, drinking beer at a tapas restaurant as their skin reddened. Barcelona was full of music and they spent a few restful days in Portugal, stretched out on the beach, Kara fully covered to hide her scars while Alex worked on her tan and exasperatedly tried to coax her sister into a pair of her shorts and a tank top instead of the neck to ankle ensemble she was wearing.

 

            In Berlin, Alex dragged Kara to underground clubs they could hear the thumping bass two blocks away from, colourful strobe lighting making Kara feel disjointed as she drank too much vodka and swayed unsteadily on her feet, the press of bodies around her. In Amsterdam, they met two witches who shared mushrooms with them, which Kara had naïvely not realised were enchanted hallucinogens until the walls had started melting in a riot of neon colours, and they’d found a nasty troll under a bridge on the way home, Alex stumbling about as she tried to stun it. Kara caught the edge of its club in her stomach, driving the air from her lungs, and slept until noon the next day, rising with a banging headache and a sore body that even the hangover potion Alex gave her couldn’t cure.

 

            In Romania, they camped out in the barren rocky foothills beneath a dark, star-scattered sky, playing Exploding Snap and drinking Butterbeer around the campfire as the radio played music and advertisements and news segments. They enjoyed each other’s company as Kara regaled Alex with stories she hadn’t included in her letters, while Alex filled her in on the things she’d missed with their friends. The next morning, they went hiking, Kara’s briefcase filled with their belongings and Bastet perched on her shoulder like an owl. They spotted blackened ruins in the distance, a gothic-spired estate that lingered in shadows, and when Alex insisted they explore. Their grave mistake ended up rousing two vampires, ashen skinned with coal-red eyes appearing out of the gloom in blurs of motion as the sisters presented themselves as meals delivered right to their doorstep. 

 

            Only Alex’s offensive spells and Kara’s quick thinking to grab a fistful of rice grains from her briefcase saved them the fate of being drained of their blood and left to decompose in the crumbling building. Scattering them over the floor, Kara dragged her sister back to the hole in the wall where the doors had been, and they watched as the vampires paused, seized by the impulse to count. While they were distracted by the handful of rice grains that they’d be able to quickly count, Alex blasted a hole in the high roof of the foyer, letting in a swathe of pale sunlight, and the sisters ran outside before Alex Apparated them all the way to Russia.

 

            In Russia, they camped on the shores of Lake Baikal, cold despite summer, and watched the Merpeople flouncing around. Kara made numerous attempts to try and talk to them but she didn’t speak Mermish and they either didn’t know English or were purposely ignoring her. It was beautiful and the lake was bigger than they could even conceive as they flew over it, laughing as they tossed a Quaffle back and forth, sparkling blue spreading out in every direction, as far as they could see.

 

            They made their way to St. Petersburg, where Alex booked them both on a Portkey to Greece, having a mind to drink and sunbathe for a few days. They saw the ruins in Athens and they went to a few islands Kara had previously visited. In Cypress, they encountered a herd of suspicious Centaurs but Kara managed to convince them to let them stay for a night of stargazing and deciphering the meanings as the herd bickered and debated what it meant if Mars was so close and if Orion’s Belt looked brighter that night.  

 

            In Venice they ate gelato and saw the sleek rainbow shadow of a Hippocampus winding through the canals, knocking gondolas as Muggle tourists let out cries of alarm. Kara convinced Alex to ride in one with her and they enjoyed the sunny afternoon before heading back to their hotel and changing for dinner, eating too much pasta and drinking too much wine as they enjoyed the slow pace of life.

 

            Eventually, Alex’s leave was up though and they found themselves back in Paris, in the hotel with the same room Kara had stayed in before. They took turns sleeping on the floor, the narrow bed only big enough for one, and a few days later Alex said it was time to leave. It took Kara about twenty minutes to realise that Alex had lumped her in with that sentiment, and Kara realised she wasn’t ready yet. 

 

            “I think I’d like to stay a bit longer,” Kara hesitantly confessed.

 

            “Oh,” Alex softly murmured, disappointment deflating her. “I thought- right, well-”

 

            “Just a little bit. A few months, maybe. No more than a year. I just- I think I need to work for a bit and get back into a normal routine before I come home again.”

 

            Sighing, Alex cupped the back of Kara’s neck as they walked along the Seine, and she gave her a thin smile. “Just … try and visit for Christmas. Mum would really like that.”

 

            Grinning, Kara kissed her sister’s cheek and then linked their arms together, more relaxed as they walked along the murky river and stopped at Muggle stalls of books and souvenirs, remarking about how dull they were in comparison to the enchanted things they could buy at the Place Cachée. They ended up returning to the confines of the magical market and Alex picked out a few gifts for Kelly and Eliza, while Kara wrote letters and included a few photos of the two of them on their travels around Europe for Eliza’s perusal. 

 

            Alex left the next morning at a Portkey outside of Plaisir, waving to Kara, who hung back, as she grabbed onto the old milk bottle with four other people booked in and was whisked away from her sister for the foreseeable future. Kara Apparated back to Paris and returned to her hotel room, opening the windows and sitting cross-legged in the small alcove as she penned out a few ideas for jobs.

 

            The start of the school year was approaching and Kara’s first stop was at Beauxbatons Academy of Magic, hidden up in the Pyrenees, and Kara was a little daunted by Madame Maxime’s height as Kara shook her hand and tried to fumble through her heavily accented French as she felt the interview fall flat even while she was still seated before her.

 

            “I have written to Professor Dumbledore and he gives you a glowing recommendation, but tell me, Kara, how is your French?”

 

            “Oh, um, I don’t- I don’t speak French,” she admitted, her cheeks turning rosy. “I mean, I know a little, but I’m willing to learn.”

 

            “Ah, shame. Tell me, why did you leave Hogwarts?”

 

            Shifting on her seat, her shirt clinging to her back as Kara grew flustered, she leaned forward slightly. “I, um, I wanted to do some travelling. But I enjoyed the job very much, and Professor Dumbledore was very kind to me. I’m not sure if he told you about my … condition-”

 

            “Condition?”

 

            “I’m- well, I have- I have Lycanthropy,” Kara said with a wince, “but it’s easily managed and it- it doesn’t impact my work, I assure you. Just one day of recovery a month.”

 

            “A werewolf? Merde.”

 

            The interview was practically over from there and Kara hurried out of the gilt palace of a school with hunched shoulders, bypassing trimmed lawns and strutting peacocks and knowing that she would have been so out of place there anyway in her shabby clothes and scarred face. Putting it behind herself, she interviewed at a few other places - the Apothecary, Dr Aziz Branchiflore, the Astronomy shop,  Luna et Aurore Jumelle, and then gravitating towards the French Ministry of Magic, hoping for some international relations position as she entered the Wallace fountain in the grounds of Place de Furstemberg , coughing as the roots of the surrounding trees rose up into an elevator resembling a birdcage and then descended into the ground.

 

            She had no luck in international relations, nor even the mailroom, passing down hallways lined with portraits who liked to chatter away, and Kara wasn’t interested in the Bureau des Aurors or Beureau de la Justice Magique. Eventually, she found her way to a towering set of Art Nouveau doors carved to look like oak trees. 

 

            Inside was the Records Room, managed by an older witch who introduced herself as Madame Melusine, the head Archivist of the sprawling room. There was a desk guarding the doors and the Archivist had an ancient book laid open with the name of every family who had access, referring to it to grant anyone permission to enter the room beyond. 

 

            “Ah, bonjour,” Kara nervously greeted the white-haired woman with a nervous smile. “Parlez-vous Anglais?”

 

            The woman gave her an amused smile. “Oui, how may I help you, mademoiselle?” 

 

            “I’m Kara. I’m- I’m looking for a job. I was wondering if you had any positions available.”

 

            “You are living in France?”

 

            “Yes. At the Hotel De Ginestou.”

 

            The woman held out a hand and beckoned, “what are your qualifications?”

 

            “I completed my N.E.W.T.s at Hogwarts. I’ve worked as an Unspeakable at the Department of Mysteries at the British Ministry and as a Hogwarts Professor. Study of Ancient Runes,” Kara babbled as she withdrew her papers, handing them over for the woman to read through. 

 

            “Ah, a Professor. Well, you are far from home. Tell me, how is your French?”

 

            “Not … good. I can help with shelving, though. And fetching. I’m- I’m a good worker, Madame. And I learn quickly, so I’m willing to try and pick it up as quickly as possible.”

 

            Reading over the record of Kara’s results and experience and her letter of recommendation from Dumbledore, the old woman hummed and then gave Kara a shrewd look as she handed back her papers.

 

            “Your scars, how did you get them?”

 

            “I- they’re self-inflicted, Madame. I’m a werewolf.”

 

            “Ah, well, you are pretty otherwise, but we shall put you at the back, I think. My name is Melusine.”

 

            Relief washed through Kara and she almost went weak at the knees as she blinked in surprise. Mouth opening and closing, she struggled to reply for a moment. “Oh, um, you- does- does that mean that I have the job?”

 

            “That remains to be seen. Come. We shall test the merit of your hard work.”

 

            The room was very dark and had acres of shelves carved to look like trees holding records. It was almost akin to a library, the smell of dust and polish and leather and wood greeting Kara as she wandered inside, but there were artefacts as well. Rolls of parchment, leather-bound tomes, prophecies and little boxes, but most overwhelmingly books.  

 

            Melusine led Kara through the space, explaining how the system worked. The old woman had been there for decades and explained how it had turned into more of a library over the years, with only small pockets dedicated to the prophecies and personal effects of ancient families. Kara trotted along and listened to the rapid-fire history of the place, of what Melusine and the other Archivists did, staring around with wonder as a hush descended over the cavernous gilt room.

 

            “You are in luck; my eyesight is starting to fail and my knees are no good for climbing ladders these days. I could use some assistance as there are only four of us here. Tell me, Kara, is a werewolf strong?”

 

            “I- yes, Madame, I think I am. I was a Beater on the Hogwarts Quidditch team, so I like to think I have some muscle on me, even if I don’t look like it.”

 

            “I cannot pay much. Only fifteen Bezants a week.”

 

            “That’s fine.”

 

            “And the work will be quiet and dull.”

 

            “I’m quite used to occupying myself,” Kara said with a crooked smile.

 

            The old witch softly laughed and clicked her tongue, “well, it is hard to come by anyone volunteering for a position here so I must admit I must take help where it is offered, even by an English werewolf.”

 

            “I’m actually an American witch,” Kara said with a self-conscious laugh, “the rest came afterwards.”

 

            “Semantics, no? You are not French and that is perhaps even worse than you being a werewolf. But we all must make do. Come, let us return to the atrium before I am missed.”

 

            Their footsteps echoed softly in the spacious room and Kara felt some of the nervous tension dissipate, although her hands still shook slightly as she clutched her briefcase in both hands. Following Melusine to the front, Kara watched the woman settle herself behind the desk and pick up a quill, jotting down Kara’s name in the thick visitor’s ledger and then setting the quill back in the ink pot. Steepling her fingers, she gave Kara a shrewd look and then sat back in her wooden chair.

 

            “I shall see you tomorrow morning. Eight o’clock. Don’t be late, oui?”

 

            “Yes. Oui. Merci, Madame.”

 

            Looking faintly amused, Melusine sighed softly and shook her head. “We shall work on that.”

 

            Flushing, Kara ducked her head in a quick nod and backed away. She said goodbye and made her way back up through the building with a smile on her face, a prickle of excitement in her chest at the prospect of starting a new job. Her travels had led to some interesting work on the side, sometimes a day or two here, a week there, but something stable and consistent would be good for her to put away a bit of money before she drained her savings and get back into the routine of normal life while delaying her return home for a while longer.

 

            The next morning, she skipped breakfast out of nerves and Apparated to the Ministry, following the stream of cloaked individuals through to the opulent atrium and then down to the Records Room. Melusine was already there even though Kara was ten minutes early, and the French witch rose to her feet, knees stiff, and beckoned Kara after her.

 

            Her days started to follow a similar routine of hours spent shelving and dusting and fetching and trying to pick up some phrases as quickly as she could. There was dark coffee and ham and cheese in fresh baguettes for breakfast, lunch and dinner most days, all she could afford on top of rent at the hotel and the occasional dinner at the pub. Melusine was patient but honest and Kara was eager to please and a quick learner, and the job wasn’t particularly mentally demanding. In the quieter hours, Kara browsed the shelves and read over laws and registers and papers that were shelved there, replacing them once she was done but soaking up as much of the new information as she could. It was a wealth of knowledge, most of it in French and requiring a translation spell for her to get through the dense texts, but Kara was eager to learn all that she could while she was there.

 

            Five months passed by in the blink of an eye, her French vocabulary expanding, even though her accent was atrocious and any French person she spoke to looked at her with amusement, as if it was endearing she should try. Work was enjoyable and offered her the freedom to explore on the weekends, visiting Prague and Amsterdam and Florence for quick trips to other libraries or magical markets or pockets of magical communities nestled away in mountains, deserts or fjords or in underground networks.
