            Blinking in surprise, Lena considered lying for a moment, her face crumpling with beseeching pain as her shoulders slumped and she let out a weary sigh. “No,” she confessed.

 

            He looked shocked by the admission, dark eyes widening with aching pain as Lena felt guilt twist her stomach. Her mouth felt horribly dry, that taste of Firewhisky cloyingly sweet at the back of her throat, and it took a moment for her to break the stunned silence that fell over them.

 

            “Look, I didn’t mean to hurt you. We were just- we were never going to work out, even without her in the picture.”

 

            “Why? What is it about me that you just can’t seem to love? I- I’ve been patient, I’ve given you everything you could want, I’ve never asked you for anything, except to marry me. I have a good job, I have enough money to take care of you.”

 

            Lena let out a strained laugh, “it’s not about any of that. You’re nice . I know that you’re nice, you don’t need to prove that to me. I just- you’re not …”

 

            “What a werewolf?” Jack scoffed. “Am I not enough of a monster for you? Do you need someone who is poor and hideous and unambitious so you can feel better about yourself?”

 

            Shock flashed across Lena’s face at his words and Jack’s anger faltered as his expression fell, sheepish and apologetic. “That’s not what I- that wasn’t very nice. To you or her.”

 

            Lips twisting ruefully, Lena shrugged. “Say whatever you want about me. I don’t care.”

 

            Letting out a hollow laugh, Jack gave her a waveringly thin smile, bitter and irate. “Just not her?”

 

            Nodding, her green eyes bright with anger, shoulders tense, Lena folded her arms over her chest. Raking a hand through his perfectly styled hair, Jack blew the air out of his cheeks and shook his head. “Well … that’s it then. I guess I should be grateful, shouldn’t I? At least you spared me the embarrassment of a divorce, even if I have to live with the fact that I came in second to a werewolf.”

 

            “Don’t-” Lena roughly started.

 

            “Do me a favour,” Jack cut her off, his wounded expression hardening. “Have the decency to at least stay away for a while. It’s the least you can do.”

 

            “The least I can do? We ended things months ago-”

 

            “You ended things.”

 

            “Fine. I did. Now it’s such a big issue because you find out I’ve moved on?”

 

            “Yes. Yes, it’s a big issue when it’s with the woman you told me not to worry about.”

 

            Huffing, Lena gestured widely, “it wasn’t anything to worry about. When you asked me about her, I didn’t even think I was ever going to see her again. I hoped that I wouldn’t.”

 

            “That doesn’t change anything.”

 

            “Yes, it does. It changes everything. If it hadn’t been for you-”

 

            She cut off, her mouth thinning as she ducked her head beneath his vindicated stare. “Go on,” he ordered her. “May as well be honest, now that it’s all coming out.”

 

            “If it hadn’t been for you … I would never have sent her away again. Because even though I hated her then, I still loved her more than that.”

 

            “More than me.”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            Mouth thinning, old heartbreak brought forth anew, Jack’s anger softened into grim resignation as their eyes met. Lena didn’t know what else to say, didn’t know whether to apologise would sound falsely hollow, whether the cold comfort she could give him would just be salt in the wound. In the end, she didn’t have to say anything.

 

            “Go to hell, Lena.”

 

            The breath came out of her like she’d been punched in the stomach, a muscle twitching in her jaw as she wiped the rain out of her face, dark hair hanging in a damp curtain around her shoulders. Jack jerked open the door to The White Wyvern and stalked back inside, the sound of voices and laughter spilling out for a brief moment with the sour smell of beef and stale smoke. 

 

            Muttering curses beneath her breath, Lena turned the collar of her grey robe up and scowled at the rain. It would’ve been an easy thing to Apparate home but she found herself reluctant to return to the company of her flat when she was so tense, needing to vent her frustration first. Drinking was out of the question so she settled for a walk, taking a few steps forward before the raucous sound of the pub swelled momentarily and a hand fell on her.

 

            “Hey.”

 

            “What?” Lena snapped as she whirled around at the grip on her arm, bristling with frustration.

 

            Blinking in surprise, Andrea jerked back slightly before she pouted, brow furrowing. “Don’t you take that tone with me or you’ll have soap bubbles coming out of your mouth for the next week .”

 

            Raking a hand through her wet hair, eyes shifting sideways, Lena rankled at her friend’s scolding. Still, the sight of Andrea’s wand casually twirling in her friend’s fingers was enough of a warning to dial back her anger; Andrea was a fierce dueller, Lena knew that much at least.

 

            “I’m not in the fucking mood.”

 

            Patting down her pockets, Andrea pulled out a packet of cigarettes as Lena hunched her shoulders against the late October chill and scuffed her shoe over the glistening cobblestones. Fishing one out of the packet, Andrea fixed Lena with an appraising look and jerked a hood up over her head.

 

            “Let’s walk a bit.”

 

            Nodding, Lena turned and set off through Knockturn Alley, the dark narrow streets and puddles of dirty rainwater making her eager to escape to the more savoury parts of the magical warren of streets. It didn’t take long for them to near Diagon Alley and Lena was still brimming with tension as the rain lightened a fraction, cutting her wand through to air to create a barrier to keep it off them.

 

            “What’s going on with you?” Andrea mumbled around the filter of her cigarette as she lit it with a finger and glanced sidelong at Lena.

 

            Shrugging, hands buried in her robe pockets, Lena furrowed her forehead as her mouth turned down at the corners. “You heard.”

 

            “Blimey. Well … she must be one hell of a ride to have your wand in such a knot over a few jokes. What else do you expect for fucking a werewolf?”

 

            A scathing sound of annoyance escaped Lena as she gave Andrea a warning look. “Save it.”

 

            “I’m just saying, you’re awfully defensive about it. If you were looking for a quick shag, you might’ve picked someone who wouldn’t piss off two other people. I guess I can see why though, for curiosity’s sake. She’d be pretty if it wasn’t for the scars.”

 

            Lena came to an abrupt halt as a flash of anger and resentment swept through her, throat tight and her expression surly. “It wasn’t just … a quick shag. We’ve been seeing each other for a couple of months.”

 

            “Oh. Right,” Andrea murmured, bewilderment crumpling her face. “How’d that happen?”

 

            Running a hand over her face, Lena’s mouth thinned as she started walking again, stumbling over her words. “I told you we were friends at Hogwarts and we had a falling out. I just left out the part where we were sleeping together a few years back. I was still mad at her but I’d- I’d always- things between us … she was the- remember when I kissed you?”

 

            “Of course. I was your first; how sweet.”

 

            “I only kissed you because I couldn’t kiss her ,” Lena confessed with a shaky laugh, looking sheepish.

 

            A startled laugh escaped Andrea, her face creasing with a grin. “You cheeky cow. And here I thought you fancied me.”

 

            Giving her a wry look, Lena sighed. “Well, you weren’t a bad alternative, I’ll say. Anyway, that’s beside the point. The point is, I’d always felt … some sort of way for her and even when I was mad I couldn’t help myself. We haven’t had the easiest time together. It- it hasn’t always been good between us but I- she and I- the way we’ve felt about each other …”

 

            Softly sighing, Andrea put her arm around her friend’s shoulder as they passed by Florean Fortescue’s, closed for the night like most of Diagon Alley. She smoked her cigarette down to the filter and tossed it underfoot, grinding out the cherry red embers and then slipping her wand out to vanish it. Then she brought them to a stop and laughed quietly.

 

            “Why is it always so bloody difficult with you?” her friend murmured with confused amusement as she smiled wryly. “Just tell me you fucking love her.”

 

            “I do,” Lena quickly agreed, surprising her friend, who was so used to being met with a brick wall.

 

            Reaching out, Andrea gave her cheek a quick pat, her voice warm with fondness as she smiled. “Good girl. Next time, I’ll be terribly cross with you if you don’t tell me straight away.”

 

            Lena just rolled her eyes and carried on walking, some of the weight on her shoulders alleviated, the tension bleeding out of her with some breathing room after the corner Veronica had backed her into. She’d known it wouldn’t be well received and had anticipated Jack and William’s scorn and the mockery of her other friends, but it was a relief to have Andrea take it in stride, even if her friend was apprehensive about the whole thing. 

 

            Busy tapping out another cigarette, Andrea lit it and took a drag before narrowing her eyes as she gave Lena an appraising look. “She’s the one who broke your heart?”

 

            “A few times,” Lena admitted.

 

            Andrea let out a huff of laughter, exhaling yellow smoke and flicking ash off the tip before she drew in a shuddering breath and looked at Lena. “Tell her if she does it again, getting sacked will be the least of her problems.”

 

            Surprised laughter escaped Lena and she gave her friend a wry smile, “why didn’t you sack her when you found out?”

 

            “You mean aside from your threats?” Andrea asked, giving her a wry look. “There are worse things in the world than werewolves, right? And you’ve never asked me for anything so … I thought something - I’m not sure what - but something was going on.”

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            They were silent for a moment, walking side by side, the rain pattering about around them as Lena kept it off them, and Andrea let out a laugh as her eyes cut sideways to Lena. “You’re both a good match, I think.”

 

            Quietly scoffing, even though she felt a prickle of satisfaction sweep through her, Lena rolled her eyes. “Oh, yes? Because you know Kara so well.”

 

            “She is my employee. I may not know her half as well as you do but you both lied to me. Gave me the same lie, in fact. That alone should have tipped me off.”

 

            “What do you mean? What did she say? When?” Lena demanded.

 

            Sighing, Andrea tossed her dark hair off her shoulder and looped her arm through the crook of Lena’s elbow. “Back after the Lake District. It was at work. She also said the two of you had been friends and had a falling out.”

 

            “It wasn’t a lie; I told you, it’s what happened.”

 

            “Right. You both just failed to mention you were both pathetically in love with each other and pretending to be in love with other people.”

 

            “I don’t think she was pretending to be in love with William; they barely knew each other.”

 

            “Semantics. Anyway, it’s good to know I can trust my best friend and my employees to be honest,” Andrea sarcastically pressed on, a flicker of annoyance in her eyes.

 

            Lena clicked her tongue and grimaced. “Don’t be like that. You know perfectly well why I didn’t tell anyone.”

 

            “Ashamed, were you?”

 

            Face quickly clouding with anger, Lena pulled her arm free. “I have never felt ashamed about my feelings for her.”

 

            Giving her an exasperated look at her bristling defensiveness, Andrea pulled her closer again so she could loop her arm back through. “Pipe down, darling, I’m not saying you should feel that way. I was merely asking if you had. Otherwise … well, you could have told me. ”

 

            Lena only felt a prickle of guilt as she patted her friend’s arm placatingly. “It wasn’t personal; she’s been my secret since I was a First-Year. She was my first friend, my best friend-”

 

            “Well, now I’m really offended.”

 

            Laughing, Lena leaned into Andrea, making them stagger sideways before she studied them. “She was before you. And then she was gone. And then she was back and I just- I didn’t want to have to deal with … tonight.”

 

            “Be honest, do you really give a shit what Veronica thinks? Gayle? William?”

 

            “No. I don’t care about them. I was only ever friends with them because of school - and you. I don’t even really care what you think but … I would care more about your opinion.”

 

            “You know that I don’t think that way.”

 

            “I’d hoped.”

 

            Scoffing, Andrea gave her a look of irritation. “Come on, Lena. When have I ever given you the impression that I would? I kept her on after finding out. You’re a half-blood witch from a purity-obsessed House and you’re still my best friend. I was never that interested in You Know Who’s ideology; we were some of the few. Yes, maybe we’re too comfortable around people who do believe that but … it’s us. We’ve always been cleverer than everyone else so I know you haven’t gone daft on me. If you mean it, if you genuinely love her, what else is there to say? Except perhaps now I suppose I need to make an effort to like her.”

 

            “It shouldn’t be too hard.”

 

            “No? My first impression of her was a hex sent my way. She apologised for that at work - how funny. Anyway, I don’t have much of an opinion of her at all, except that she works without complaint and she’s been the centre of scandal in our group twice , so maybe she’s more interesting than I originally thought. I suppose I should give her a pay rise now.”

 

            Lena snorted, “don’t tell me about work. I don’t want to get dragged into her job.”

 

            Andrea hummed and they continued walking for a moment longer, almost on the verge of Carkitt Market now. Glancing down at her watch, Lena sighed. “Speaking of, I should get to work.”

 

            She would be early but there was nothing else for her to do, given the lateness of the hour and her evening with her friends gone sour. Jack was right - it probably would be good for her to stay away for a while. Andrea was right as well, that Lena didn’t really care what any of her friends thought, was only really friends with the majority of them through some nostalgia from their Hogwarts days, where she’d ingratiated herself into their group to spy and then been left amidst them like a cuckoo once the war had ended. It was no skin off her back to put some distance between them now, except for Andrea. She was still the only one Lena had ever genuinely thought of as a friend - and maybe Jack, if she hadn’t worn out his welcome by breaking his heart twice. 

 

            Walking Andrea back to The White Wyvern, Lena watched her vanish into the pub and then Apparated to the alleyway beside the entrance to St. Mungo’s. A few hours early, she holed herself up in an office and spent some time working on Belby’s paper, revising paragraphs and referencing old documents on previous research for a cure to Lycanthropy. He’d set a deadline to have it in the December issue of a potion-making publication and with the concrete progress they’d made over the last three months, they would have something worth publishing to include and Lena painstakingly made notes on the maths and method for him to finetune for the final copy.

 

            Emerging an hour before her shift, Lena went to fetch herself a potion to banish the effects of her drinking and bumped into Sam on the way to the tearoom for a pre-shift coffee and a bowl of soup to warm her through. It was cold in the hallways and she was still dressed in her robe and clothes, damp and distracted, almost walking past her friend until Sam fell into step beside her.

 

            “You’re here early.”

 

            Glancing up at her, Lena smiled wanly, “as ever. How’s it been?”

 

            “I’ll not be jinxing us, thank you very much. Six new admissions on the Charms Ward since tea time though.”

 

            Sharing an exasperated look, they made their way into the tearoom and claimed a rickety table before Lena went to buy them coffee and soup, sitting across from each other as they dipped bread and sipped the gritty bitter beans the hospital stocked. It was adequate at best but it warmed Lena through and perked her up as the start of her shift loomed closer.

 

            “Been working on the report?” Sam asked, looking down at Lena’s ink-stained fingers.

 

            “Mm. Drinks finished up earlier than expected,” Lena wryly explained. “Thought I’d make good use of my time.”

 

            “Full moon last night,” Sam continued. “Seeing as we swapped shifts, I thought I’d see you up on the Bite Ward. Kara wasn’t a patient there though. Second month in a row.”

 

            “Mm.”

 

            “You sure you know what you’re doing?”

 

            Giving her a quick smile over the rim of her coffee cup, Lena swallowed a mouthful and set it back down. “Don’t I always?”

 

            Looking unsure of herself, Sam just hummed dubiously and moved her spoon around in her bowl before giving Lena an exasperated look. “You’ll ask if you need help?”

 

            “You’ll be the first,” Lena promised. “It’s alright, though. I’ve brewed it perfectly. Not so much as a scratch on her in months now.”

 

            She kept her voice low as she gleefully bragged, her green eyes bright with delight and victory at having helped mitigate some of Kara’s pain and outsmarted her mother in the process. Managing a thin smile, Sam nodded but her hazel eyes were full of concern.

 

            “That’s good but … it’s not Kara I’m worried about.”

Chapter 34

            A few days later, Lena was glancing down at her watch, counting down the minutes until she was off the clock. Dinner plans had been scheduled with Kara, despite the long shift Lena was about to finish, and she was eager to finish up and head straight home. 

 

            She still had just over an hour left and sighed as she sat slumped on the gurney lining the hallway, a textbook open in her lap for some downtime studying as she waited for her cryptex to alert her to a patient. A ham and cheese sandwich was set beside her and she took an unenthusiastic bite from one half.

 

            “Got somewhere to be, have you?” Sam asked, climbing onto the bed beside her.

 

            “I do, actually,” Lena distractedly replied, fishing her quill out of her pocket to underline a sentence and then tapping it. “See here, Anapneo for choking victims. Do you think that could be used for blockages in arteries?”

 

            Craning her neck to stare at the text, Sam hummed, opening a packet of crisps. “What’s the etymology? I breathe?”

 

            “Yes, but it’s for blockages and blood carries oxygen so … say in the case of hypoxemia due to a stroke from a blood clot … logically, you should be able to use it to clear the blockage to help them breathe.”

 

            “Logically … yes,” Sam slowly agreed, wariness in her hazel eyes. “I don’t know how you’d test that though. Want one?”

 

            She shook the packet and Lena glanced down. “Prawn cocktail?”

 

            “Mhm.”

 

            Taking one, she put it in her mouth and offered Sam the other half of her sandwich as she chewed. Jotting a few notes in the margins of the page, Lena reached for her sandwich and paused at the sound of her name being called.

 

            “Healer Luthor.”

 

            Blinking, she stared at her mother, who stopped in front of the gurney, eyeing the two of them sitting together. Lips twitching with a telltale sign of annoyance, she gave her daughter a piercing look.

 

            “Seeing as you seem to have a lot of free time on your hands, Theatre 2 in twenty minutes.”

 

            “I finish in an hour.”

 

            “Then you’d better hope it’s a quick procedure,” Lillian dismissively replied before her eyes cut to Sam. “Arias, why don’t you go and catch up on your potion quota for this month, or do you think we pay you to sit around drinking tea?”

 

            “Of course, Chief, I’ll- um, I’ll head straight down now.”

 

            Blanking her, Lillian just gave Lena a long look and then turned, striding off in her insufferably elegant manner that made Lena’s blood boil. Staring daggers at her mother’s back, Lena’s face pinched with bitterness.

 

            “Cow.”

 

            “What’s got her wand in a knot?”

 

            “She’s punishing me.”

 

            “Punishing you? With surgery? That’s special treatment.”

 

            Lip curling with annoyance, Lena looked down at her watch again. “If it came from anyone else. She’s still bitter that I managed to get around her little ploy to have me stood down.”

 

            Climbing off the gurney, Sam’s eyebrows rose and she shoved her packet of crisps in her pocket, ham sandwich in hand as she gave Lena a dubious look. “What, she’s still being nasty about you and Kara?”

 

            “This is nothing,” Lena scoffed. “No one holds a grudge quite like Lillian. It’s alright though, I won’t let her get to me. I’ve suffered worse than scut and overtime.”

 

            “And how is it going with Kara? You’re awfully tight-lipped about her, you know. And here I thought we were friends. ”

 

            Sam trailed after Lena, who gave her a small smile, green eyes brightening with amusement. “Sorry, it’ll have to wait until next time. I need to report to the old hag before she puts me on probation for tardiness. You know what she’s like.”

 

            Hurrying through the hallways, she stowed her book and wolfed down the rest of her sandwich before removing her green robe and stethoscope and shoving it in her locker. Quickly making her way up to the Theatres for the more advanced healing, Lena pushed open the heavy wooden door to Theatre 2’s scrub room. Donning a green scrub cap, an outer robe and mask, she washed her hands beneath the hot water for the length of time it took her to run through the ingredients in the Wolfsbane Potion and was then helped into sterilised dragonhide gloves.

 

            Her mother was already in the Theatre with two other Residents, three Interns and various other healing staff, from the witch who kept the patient asleep to the nurse administering intravenous potions. As an Attending, Lena was above them in terms of experience and she stood at the patient’s side and looked down to find herself staring at their open abdomen. Intestines were shredded and blood welled up quickly even as one of the Residents kept banishing it while the nurse hung another Blood Replenishing unit. 

 

            “Nice of you to join us,” Lillian snippily greeted her. “Someone fill her in.”

 

            One of the Interns leaned in and whispered an explanation of the case and Lena watched as the Resident continued to siphon blood away, alternating between his wand and the growing pile of bloody gauze. Apparently, the patient had ingested one too many Exploding Bonbons without chewing and the Coconut Dynamite had ripped through the lining of his stomach as soon as he’d started to digest the sweets. 

 

            “What do you think the recommended course of action should be?”

 

            Lena ran through the scenario in her head, answering quickly as she mapped out the procedure. “Check for gastrointestinal perforation in case there’s-”

 

            “This is a learning hospital, Healer Luthor. Anyone else?” Lillian cut her off.

 

            One of the Residents glanced sideways at Lena and then haltingly held up a hand. “Um … check for gastrointestinal perforation?”

 

            “Why?”

 

            Lena’s jaw tightened as the Resident looked at her again as if waiting for her to give him the answer. “Um …”

 

            “Anyone else?”

 

            Folding her arms over her chest, Lena was silent until her mother’s eyes landed on her. “Risk of sepsis if the large bowel has ruptured into the abdominal cavity.”

 

            “And?”

 

            “Peritonitis.”

 

            “You. Here,” Lillian bluntly ordered her.

 

            Stepping forward, Lena warily met her mother’s eyes across the body of the patient. “Check the length of his intestines for perforation. His stomach is already shredded so we can guarantee bile in the abdominal cavity.”

 

            Hesitating, Lena reached out for the mess of intestines and started the arduous process of inspecting every single inch for any ruptures that may have been caused by the explosion, as if she were a Resident again, tasked with the menial healing work. It was agonisingly slow work but she could feel the envious eyes of her coworkers on her back as she got to help in what should have been their learning opportunity. They would mistake it for favouritism but she knew the truth.

 

            Lillian kept up a stream of questions, which none of the Residents or Interns could answer, and Lena bore the brunt of her mother’s criticisms of her technique as she assisted through the slow process of repairing the man’s digestive system. Exhausted from her already long shift, Lena’s thoughts were starting to become a little muddled as one hour stretched into two, then three and four. She’d stepped back into line once she’d finished her inspection hours ago and since then her mother had been content to make her watch for the sake of it.

 

            As the hours passed by, her mother slowly managed to piece the stomach back together with complex charms that required multiple hands to staunch the bleeding and carefully move the internal organs as she worked around the mess. Lena hated to admit it, even to herself, but it was impressive work and informative as she watched Lillian’s hands steadily move through the magic. 

 

            By the time she’d been awake for thirty hours out of what had become a fifty-hour shift, Lena was bleary-eyed and impatient. Despite her mask, she couldn’t hide the yawn that stole over her, eyes squeezed shut.

 

            “Are we keeping you awake, Healer Luthor?” Lillian drawled, naturally catching sight of it.

 

            “No, Chief.”

 

            “Then why are you yawning in my Theatre?”

 

            “Sorry, Chief. It’s been a long shift.”

 

            “It’s been a long shift for all of us. If you can’t manage your time efficiently enough to sleep in between rounds and healing, perhaps you’re not cut out for this line of work. Even the Interns are managing better than you; I expect better from an Attending.”

 

            “I didn’t say I couldn’t manage my time,” Lena bitingly replied. “You asked me a question and I answered it. I’ve been here for fifty hours already - longer than you .”

 

            Silence filled the Theatre as she bristled where she was standing, hands curling into fists inside her gloves. The tension was unbearable and Lena’s cheeks flushed as her coiled muscles went slack, regret sweeping through her as she knew she’d just made a terrible mistake by rising to Lillian’s bait in front of a room full of her peers.

 

            “Healer Luthor, you’re dismissed,” Lillian softly informed her, her hands steady as she moved her wand in a slow circle over the wound, keeping a tight grip on the clamp in the other.

 

            Lena stared at her, rooted to the spot as she blinked in surprise. Words burning on the tip of her tongue, she managed to swallow them as frustration nettled her. When she still hadn’t moved a moment later, Lillian paused and looked up, her pale blue eyes frosty over the mask covering the lower half of her face.

 

            “Get out of my Theatre,” her mother snapped with more vitriol this time.

 

            Letting out a huff of laughter, Lena turned on her heel and barged through the door. Tearing the scrub cap and mask from her face, she tossed them into the cart of the other used ones and then rammed the cart into the wall as her anger got the better of her. Tearing off the outer robe, she wadded it into a ball and dumped it in as well with the gloves before barging out of the scrub room.

 

            She made her way through the hospital to her locker room, the Attendings arriving for their shift getting changed while a few others were finishing up. Lena was hours later than she should have been but no one seemed surprised to see her there as she swept inside, roughly jerking her scrub top over her head. Keeping the long-sleeved cotton shirt she wore underneath on, she pulled off her pants and grabbed the corduroy flared trousers from her locker.

 

            “You.”

 

            Turning from her locker, Lena pulled the waistband of her pants up and buttoned them, fixing her mother with a flat look, surprised she’d left someone else to close up but not that surprised. The other Healers in her locker room all looked around uneasily, eyes flitting between mother and daughter, high up in the hospital’s hierarchy but still nothing beneath Lillian’s quickly assessing gaze as she swept a cutting look around the room.

 

            “Everyone out,” Lillian barked.

 

            There was a quick scramble for the half-dressed Healers to make themselves decent before they filed out of the changing room. Stepping inside, Lillian shut the door behind her, her heels clicking on the old tiles.

 

            “If you’re expecting me to apologise, I won’t,” Lena calmly told her. 

 

            Her mother crossed the space between them quickly and Lena had to force herself to remain rooted to the spot instead of shrinking up against the row of lockers. Trying not to look too insolent, she raised her chin a fraction to look her mother in the eye.

 

            “You are walking a very thin line,” Lillian snapped, holding her thumb and forefinger a fraction apart as she loomed over Lena. “I’m this close to losing my patience with you. If you don’t fall into line and do exactly as I say, I’ll have you sacked before you can lift a finger.”

 

            “So that’s it? Because you say so, I’m supposed to tuck my tail and do what I’m told?”

 

            “I’m Healer-In-Charge; that’s exactly what you’re supposed to do. Don’t forget you’re here because of me-”

 

            “I’m here because my work is exemplary . I’m miles above half of the senior Attendings even.”

 

            “Look at the ego on you. You have the skill of a Resident,” Lillian berated her. “If this is the manner of your work, you have no place in this hospital. You’re impatient and short-tempered and that is not the quality of a good Healer.”

 

            A caustic laugh worked its way up Lena’s throat. “And what is? Hurting children? Should I torture my patients or-“

 

            “Torture. You have such a vivid imagination; do you really believe I was that cruel to you?”

 

            Lena’s face went slack with disbelief, devastation cutting deeply through her. Green eyes bright with wounded anger, she swallowed thickly, curling her hands into fists. “I didn’t imagine anything.”

 

            “It hurts that you would say things like that when I have given you everything. ” 

 

            “It upsets you more for me to say it than it did for you to do it. Funny.”

 

            Scoffing contemptuously, Lillian’s face hardened. “You’re ungrateful and spoiled. Do you know how easy you’ve had it? Just ask your friend, Arias. A single mother without the advantages you had; no doubt she would’ve leapt at the chance to have the training and resources I gave you.”

 

            “No one in their right mind would leap at that chance. I could have you-” Lena snapped before lowering her voice, trembling with barely restrained anger. “I could have you in Azkaban for the spells you used on me.”

 

            “That was your brother. How fortunate for you he’s already there.”

 

            Staring at her with a stony look on her face, even paler than usual as her stomach lurched with the uneasy feeling that perhaps Lillian knew Lena was the one who had turned him in, Lena pressed her lips into a hard line. She couldn’t have though, and Lena knew her mother would not have let her walk around unpunished for her disloyalty if she knew Lena had been the cause. 

 

            “I have to go.”

 

            “You’re not dismissed.”

 

            “My shift ended five hours ago.”

 

            “And you’re still not dismissed,” Lillian lightly crowed, amusement on her face before she hardened. Folding her arms over her chest, she arched an eyebrow. “I’m in charge here, in case you have forgotten.”

 

            “How could I forget when you’re always so quick to remind me?” Lena replied, her voice hoarse and droll as she swallowed thickly.

 

            Letting out a soft huff of laughter, lips twitching with cold amusement, Lillian looked her up and down. It was a scrutinising look that made Lena feel vulnerable and self-conscious, her forearm prickling as she resisted the urge to scratch at her old scar.

 

            “I’m not to be trifled with.”

 

            “I know,” Lena stiffly replied, “but neither am I. I’m not your plaything to let you bully at work for your satisfaction because you’re mad you can’t control me at home anymore.”

 

            “You’ve gotten awfully mouthy recently. Is your werewolf rubbing off on you? All that anger and resentment; they are a nasty breed.”

 

            Anger flashed through Lena, hot and sudden, making her stiffen. “Don’t you talk about her.”

 

            “Enjoy your little act of rebellion if you will,” Lillian dismissively replied, turning and walking a few steps away as she waved her hand. Turning again, she fixed Lena with a hard stare. “But you will not let that girl ruin our hard work. Do you hear me, Lena? She may not be on the trial any longer but I can make life very difficult - for both of you. I say jump, you ask how high. I tell you you’re assisting me on a procedure when you’re about to clock off and you thank me for the opportunity and make sure you’re wide awake, even if you’ve been here all week . Am I clear?”

 

            Rankling at the mere idea of answering her mother’s every whim, Lena took a moment to respond and only managed to swallow her pride at all for Kara’s benefit. “Yes, Chief.”

 

            “Get your things.”

 

            Turning, Lena hurriedly pulled a jumper over the thin long-sleeved shirt and then pulled her cloak over the top. Shoving her worn scrubs into her satchel with her green robe, she straightened her locker for tomorrow and then shut it, resisting the urge to slam it.

 

            Slinging the strap of her satchel over her shoulder, she put her wand in her pocket and moved towards the door. Lillian didn’t move and as Lena passed her by, her hand shot out to grab her arm tightly. Pausing, Lena looked up at her.

 

            “I’ll see you tomorrow,” Lillian murmured, still gripping her daughter’s arm. Reaching up, she ran a hand over Lena’s sleek hair, a faint smile on her lips. “Have a good night.”

 

            It was almost mocking in the way she said it as if she knew she’d derailed Lena’s plans. It was a form of punishment in itself, and Lena didn’t like the way it was playing out, with Lillian holding all the cards and her at her mother’s beck and call. She’d never wanted word of Kara to get out and she cursed herself for how stupid she’d been to think Diagon Alley was a good place for them to go out together, even if it had only been once or twice.

 

            “Goodnight,” Lena replied, the word clipped but clear.

 

            Letting her go, Lillian was silent as Lena continued to the door. Jerking it open, her eyes swept around the nurse’s station, where the Interns and a few Healers and other staff were trying not to appear too nosy as they’d listened to the muffled argument behind the closed door. Clenching her jaw, Lena feigned indifference as she stepped outside and was pulled up short by the sound of her name behind her as Lillian stepped into the doorway.

 

            “Lena?”

 

            Half-turning, she raised her eyebrows a fraction and her stomach jolted at the hint of mirth on her mother’s face.

 

            “One more thing; you’re banned from the Theatre for a month.”

 

            Face flushing with anger and embarrassment as her eyes darted around to all the witnesses watching her mother have the last laugh, Lena pressed her lips into a flat line and squared her shoulders before continuing onwards. She didn’t waste time making her way to the waiting room, stepping outside and Apparating home with a shaky feeling inside her as she tried to squash her anger. 

 

            Inside her apartment, she let her satchel thump heavily to the floor and closed her eyes. Sighing heavily, Lena ran a hand over her face, feeling limp and wrung out, her body aching for sleep. Dinner was supposed to have been hours ago now and she hadn’t even had time to write Kara a letter to explain her absence. The thought of her knocking to no answer cut through Lena and she hurried through to the kitchen, quickly rummaging through her potion cupboard and coming up with a Reinvigorating Draught. Knocking the contents back in one mouthful, she perked up with the false boost in energy that rushed through her.

 

            It was a slippery slope to sustain herself on potions like that and she normally only used them at work, doses handed out with cups of tea and coffee to keep the Healers on their feet through the long hours of their shifts but she didn’t normally take them outside of work hours. The thought of disappointing Kara was enough for her to take the edge off a little, although the haggard look of exhaustion on her face couldn’t be masked by the potion.

 

            Without shedding her cloak or changing, Lena Apparated from her apartment to the doorstep of Kara’s home in Cornwall. Swaying a little unsteadily on her feet, she took a moment to collect herself and then knocked. Warm yellow light spilt out of the windows of the grey stone cottage and she could hear voices inside. One got louder as it approached, gentle and the accent tempered by long years in England, and something in Lena’s chest loosened as she listened to the rattle of the lock as Kara opened the door.

 

            “Oh, you’re here,” Kara softly exclaimed, surprise softening her face.

 

            Her warmth made Lena’s eyes sting, although they never filled with tears. Her throat closed up and she let herself get wrapped up in a tight hug, the press of Kara’s lips on her cheek making her sag slightly. Pulling back, Kara smiled tenderly at her and Lena took her hand.

 

            “I’m sorry I’m so late,” Lena murmured, an aching look of apology on her face as she gripped Kara’s fingers tightly. “I was called into a procedure right before I was due to clock off and I-”

 

            “It’s okay. I figured when you didn’t answer that something must have come up. I left a note under your door-”

            

            “I didn’t see it. I came straight here.”

 

            Face creasing with a grave look, Kara cupped Lena’s face in her warm palms. Closing her eyes, Lena’s lips twitched slightly at the touch of her and she sighed heavily.

 

            “You’re tired.”

 

            “I’m okay. I took a potion.”

 

            “You need to sleep,” Kara softly urged her.

 

            “I needed to see you more.”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Kara gave her a searching look for a long moment. “Bad day?”

 

            “I-“ Lena started before faltering, averting her gaze as she swallowed thickly. Ducking her head down, she rubbed her forehead. “It’s been a long shift.”

 

            “My mum put some leftovers aside for you; let me grab it. I hope you like beef casserole.”

 

            Lena didn’t have time to respond before Kara slipped back inside, walking down the hallway to the kitchen. Hovering on the doorstep, Lena listened to the comforting sound of muffled voices before Eliza’s head poked around the corner of the kitchen door and creased with a warm smile.

 

            “Hi, sweetheart. Come in, it’s cold out.”

 

            “Oh, um, hi Eliza,” Lena haltingly greeted her, stepping inside and shutting the door behind herself.

 

            It muffled the worst of the wind and Lena stood huddled in her cloak as Eliza walked down the hallway. She wrapped an arm around Lena’s shoulder and squeezed gently as she smiled. “Happy birthday.”

 

            “Thank you - and for the jumper.”

 

            “You’re very welcome. Come on, come into the living room.”

 

            “Mum, it’s alright, I’m going to take it with us,” Kara called.

 

            “It’s nine o’clock, Kara. Just heat it up before she starves to death,” Eliza called back, sighing.

 

            Helpless as she was shepherded into the living room, Lena could barely get out a stammer of surprise before she found herself obediently sinking onto the sofa. Eliza took her cloak and Lena looked around in a daze, Bastet climbing to her feet and arching her back as she moved over to Lena, rubbing against her legs, a log popping in the fireplace as the comforting smell of smoke drifted from the fire with a wall of heat.

 

            “Sorry,” Kara sheepishly whispered as she stepped inside with a steaming plate and a glass of pumpkin juice. “She likes to fuss.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Lena’s face crumpled with bewildered amusement as Kara set the plate in her lap and the glass safely on the coffee table. Scooping up her cat, she set her in her lap and gave Lena a crooked smile.

 

            “You don’t have to stay long but at least you’ll have gotten a proper meal in you.”

 

            “I’m sorry.”

 

            “Don’t apologise,” Kara murmured, reaching out to brush a lock of hair out of Lena’s face. “It’s work. I know you work a lot, it’s alright.”

 

            “I just- I was … really looking forward to dinner.”

 

            Smiling sweetly, Kara gave her arm a gentle squeeze. “Next time. I think you need to go home and sleep.”

 

            Humming in agreement, Lena smiled thinly and ate a forkful of the casserole. Eliza rejoined them a minute later with her shapeless knitting and Lena reassured her the food was delicious, eating quickly as silence blanketed the room. Unlike her family’s house, it wasn’t an uncomfortable silence and she felt some of the residual tension bleed out of her as she ate.

 

            Kara occasionally asked a question in between bites as she stroked the white patch on Bastet’s forehead and Lena gave her vague answers about her day. She was in the following evening, just for an eighteen-hour shift, so they made plans for breakfast the day after, with two scheduled days off. Lena hoped she didn’t get paged in then, needing a break and wanting some uninterrupted time with Kara.

 

            She finished her dinner and pumpkin juice and made to carry her empty plate to the kitchen to wash it when Kara stopped her. Making her stay put, Kara vanished and Eliza suggested tea, following after her daughter. Sitting on the sofa, Lena listened to the running of the tap in the next room, the sounds of Kara washing up oddly comforting, joined by the faint whistling of the kettle.

 

            Full and heavy-lidded, the fire making her even sleepier than she felt, Lena sank into the sofa and waited for the other two women to come back. When Kara filed in after Eliza with two mugs, she paused at the sight of her girlfriend, fast asleep with a faint softening of her face which made her look even younger than she was.

 

            “Oh,” Kara murmured, hesitating before she set down the two mugs. 

 

            “Poor thing, she must be exhausted,” Eliza gently clicked her tongue. “Leave her there. Let her sleep a bit.”

 

            Carefully sinking back down onto the sofa, Kara snagged the blanket from the back of the sofa and gently draped it over Lena. Sipping her hot tea, her eyes kept sliding back to Lena, quietly fascinated by watching her sleep, and Eliza silently immersed herself in her knitting as the night slipped by.

 

            “I should wake her,” Kara eventually whispered as she set down her empty cup.

 

            “Just put her in Alex’s bed.”

 

            Chewing on her bottom lip, Kara hesitated. “She might prefer to go home.”

 

            “Maybe but she looks so peaceful. Merlin, they make those Healers work long hours, don’t they? And you said she’s all alone?”

 

            “She doesn’t … get on with her mum.”

 

            “You should invite her over for dinner more. Make sure she eats properly.”

 

            “Okay. I’ll go and put her to bed.”

 

            Nodding as she counted her stitches, Eliza adjusted the tension and then continued with the quiet clicking of another row. Climbing to her feet, Kara removed the blanket and then stooped down to wriggle an arm behind Lena’s shoulders. 

 

            Guiding her to her feet, Lena’s eyelids fluttering as she mumbled incoherently, her mind desperately clinging to unconsciousness, Kara kept an arm around her waist. “Hey, come to bed,” Kara lightly whispered.

 

            “Mm.”

 

            “Come on.”

 

            Sinking back down onto the sofa, Lena made another humming sound at the back of her throat. Letting out a quiet laugh, Eliza set her knitting down and climbed to her feet. “Here, you get the bedroom door. I’ve had to put you to bed more than once and the best way to do it is with a levitation charm.”

 

            “You’ll wake her up,” Kara fretted.

 

            “Sweetheart, she’s exhausted. She’s not going to move for the next ten hours.”

 

            Hovering nervously as she wrung her hands, Kara relented and took the stairs two at a time and opened the bedroom door, turning on the light and pulling back the covers of Alex’s bed. Standing in the middle of her room, hyper-aware that Lena would wake up in it tomorrow morning, Kara quickly started grabbing things, stuffing worn clothes into a laundry basket and shoving a stack of drafted articles into the desk drawer.

 

            Eliza guided Lena into the room a moment later, her feet a few inches off the carpet until her mother guided her back down. Kara wrapped her arms around her before Lena could sag and eased her onto the bed. Pulling off her shoes, Kara made her comfortable and covered her with the quilt.

 

            Pausing, she turned and switched the light off, easing the door shut and leaving Lena to sleep. It was an odd sensation for her to be downstairs as her girlfriend slept upstairs in her room and Kara was jittery and distracted for the rest of the night, which was already late so she didn’t stay up much longer. 

 

            Locking up when Eliza headed up, Kara followed after her and got ready for bed before stepping into the bedroom. Trying to be quiet, she made for her bed and sank onto the mattress, removing her glasses and getting comfortable. Her eyes adjusted to the dark and she stared unseeingly at the ceiling as she listened to the sound of Lena’s slow, even breaths. It did something funny to her chest to listen to her sleep from the other side of the room and Kara was lulled to sleep shortly after.

 

            When Lena woke the next morning it was to a bedroom that was only vaguely familiar, although it looked different in the morning light. Sitting up, she rubbed her eyes and looked around, face puckering with confusion as she found herself still wearing her clothes and very much not in her bed. It only took her a brief moment to deduce it was Kara’s room.

 

            It was still surprising as Lena looked around, taking in the photos, the old Hufflepuff banner and posters of Quidditch teams and celebrities. There was one of Gilderoy Lockhart, who Lena vaguely remembered as a pompous Ravenclaw from school who had recently shot to fame, and she snorted at the idea of Kara having him on her wall, making a note to tease her for it later.

 

            Climbing out of bed, noticing the one against the opposite wall was already made, Lena paused at the sight of a folded origami crane. Reaching out to pluck it from Kara’s pillow, she unfolded the paper bird and read the message hidden inside.

 

Good morning! Sorry, you fell asleep on the sofa and we didn’t want to wake you. Looked like you needed the rest. 

 

I’ve already gone to work but my mum is home. She’ll probably harass you about breakfast so a word of advice, it’s easier to just let her cook for you. 

 

I know you have work tonight but stay as long as you want. I’ll see you at breakfast xx

 

            Smiling to herself as she refolded the crane, Lena made the bed and lingered a few minutes as she eyed the photos on the wall. There were a few of her in their hidden room in the Astronomy Tower and Lena knew they hadn’t been there last time as she tried to recall her previous glimpse of Kara’s room. A small smile twitched her lips and she refrained from snooping as she put on her shoes and made her way downstairs.

 

            Pausing at the bottom of the stairs, she looked into the living room and found it empty before peering around the end of the bannister to look into the kitchen. It seemed empty as well but she could see the back door was open. Consulting her watch, Lena found that it was almost noon and she ran a hand over her face, a little hesitant at the prospect of being alone with Kara’s mum, no matter how nice she seemed. Lena didn’t have a good track record with mothers.

 

            Still, she didn’t have to linger long, with her day already half eaten up and a shift to prepare for that evening. Mustering her courage, she walked down the hallway and into the kitchen, letting the momentum carry her past the table and out into the garden, where Eliza was kneeling beside a carefully cultivated flower garden, pulling weeds and pruning plants.

 

            “Morning,” Lena haltingly called out.

 

            It was a grey day and Lena hugged her arms to herself as she hovered with uncertainty, a wavering, doubtful smile on her face as Eliza turned her head. Her face softened into a smile and she finished cutting off the green shoot of a new branch on an Alihotsy tree.

 

            “Morning sweetheart. Sleep well?”

 

            Nodding as she raked a hand through her hair, Lena looked around at the garden as she fumbled for something to say. Removing her dragonhide gloves, Eliza pushed herself to her knees.

 

            “Why don’t I make you some coffee? Or are you a tea person? You lot this side all seem to be tea drinkers.”

 

            “Tea, please.”

 

            She toyed with the cuffs of her jumper as she stood just outside the door, her expression wary as Eliza approached her. Lena could feel her shoulders tense involuntarily and she swallowed thickly, looking down.

 

            Stepping into the kitchen, Eliza moved around the space as she filled the kettle, grabbed a clean mug and a teabag and the milk. Standing just inside the door, as if she was ready to flee at any moment, Lena watched her from the corner of her eye as she pretended to be interested in the potted plants scattered around the room.

 

            “I don’t bite, you know,” Eliza lightly intruded on her thoughts, glancing up from the cup as she poured boiling water and gave Lena a quick smile. “You can sit down.”

 

            “Oh, um, no, I- I know, I just …”

 

            She faltered, her shoulders slumping slightly as she gestured helplessly. Setting the tea down on the table, Eliza drew out a chair and then stepped in front of Lena, squeezing her arm gently.

 

            “Why don’t I make you something to eat?”

 

            Remembering Kara’s advice, Lena smiled weakly and took a seat. “That would be lovely, thank you.”

 

            Her response seemed belated as Eliza was halfway through raiding the fridge. Sipping her scalding tea as she watched Kara’s mother make her a bacon and egg sandwich, questioning her on how she liked her egg cooked and what sauces, Lena slowly forced herself to relax. Eliza seemed content to leave her be and Lena stopped expecting the harsh judgement that would have come from her own mother under the same circumstances.

 

            “There you go,” Eliza softly proclaimed, setting a plate down before her.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Taking a bite, Lena chewed slowly as she watched Eliza clean up, feeling compelled to say something. Swallowing her mouthful, she took a sip of tea.

 

            “Was that an Alihotsy tree you were pruning?” she shyly asked.

 

            Glancing over her shoulder, eyes creasing at the corners, Eliza nodded. “Yes, I sell the leaves to apothecaries for potions. It’s also used in fudge.”

 

            Lena let out a quiet huff of laughter. “Yes, we’ve had to treat a few people who’ve eaten too much of it.”

 

            “Do you enjoy your work?”

 

            Pausing, Lena considered the question. “Yes. I think- it’s difficult but it’s rewarding.”

 

            “Your mom’s a Healer too?”

 

            “Yes, she’s Healer-In-Charge at St. Mungo’s.”

 

            “Well, she must be proud to have you following in her footsteps.”

 

            A laugh got stuck in Lena’s throat and she took another bite to avoid answering. Pride would be the last feeling Lillian held for her and she was perhaps the only reason for any discontent Lena might have felt about her job. 

 

            “You’re working again tonight? Kara said.”

 

            “Yes, only eighteen hours this time. Unless something goes wrong.”

 

            “Dear me, you must be exhausted all the time. I’m surprised you’re even up this early.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose as amusement stole over her, Lena finished off one half of her sandwich and washed it down with tea. The differences between Eliza and Lillian couldn’t have been more apparent and Lena wondered what it must have been like to grow up in a house of love. Just the way Eliza’s voice softened with tenderness on her daughter’s name spoke volumes about how much she loved Kara.

 

            “I guess it’s the same for Alex.”

 

            “Not quite. I think she mostly does regular day shifts unless there’s a big bust or an emergency. She certainly doesn’t work as much as you.”

 

            “It’s almost a given that we’ll be doing eighty-hour weeks.”

 

            Clicking her tongue, Eliza shook her head, “I hope you look after yourself properly when you’re off. Sleeping enough, eating well. If you ever need something for dinner, I can dish you up something to take home. Of course, you’re welcome here anytime as well - whether Kara’s home or not.”

 

            “Oh,” Lena murmured as surprise made her blink. Her expression clouded with confusion but her response was earnest. “Thank you.”

 

            Drying her hands, Eliza gave her a warm smile. “I need to get back to work.”

 

            Nodding, Lena finished the rest of her sandwich and tea in the kitchen before washing up and stepping back into the garden. She hesitated on the narrow strip of the paved patio before crossing the neatly trimmed lawn.

 

            “Can I help?”

 

            “Oh, you don’t have to do that.”

 

            “I actually miss Herbology. I only get to handle dried plants now for brewing potions.”

 

            Giving her a quick smile, Eliza hesitated and then handed Lena the little pair of shears. “Alright then. Just prune what you think; maybe leave the Venomous Tentacula, it can be temperamental.”

 

            Nodding, Lena sank to her knees beside Kara’s mother and started moving aside branches and leaves, the tight buds of plants that were shrivelling up in anticipation of the coming winter. The wind was brisk but it was a calming process, freeing up Lena’s mind as she worked methodically along the flowerbed and Eliza split open a bag of dragon dung fertiliser and started applying a thin layer.

 

            An hour passed by shockingly fast and the weak sun was overhead when Eliza paused, brushing hair out of her face with her forearm. She glanced sideways at Lena and smiled slightly.

 

            “You should probably head off soon.”

 

            Glancing down at her watch, Lena hummed in agreement. She finished pruning the Flutterby bush and then rose to her feet, dusting off her knees, and handed the shears to Eliza with a small smile.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            “Thank you. ”

 

            Another smile twitched Lena’s lips and she ducked her head in a quick nod. Removing her gloves, Eliza dropped them to the grass and put an arm around Lena’s back to herd her towards the back door.

 

            “Wash your hands and have a drink first.”

 

            Rinsing the green tang of plant sap and leaves from her hands, Lena dried the suds from her wrists and then accepted the glass of lemon squash from Eliza. She stared out the back door at the quaint garden as she sipped, feeling warm from her work despite the dreary day - it looked like it might rain soon.

 

            “Thank you for having me,” Lena haltingly murmured as Eliza took her empty glass from her.

 

            “Anytime, sweetheart.”

 

            “Um … I’ll see you again next time.”

 

            Nodding, Eliza followed her to the door and Lena took her cloak from the hook and folded it over her arm before stooping to scratch Bastet beneath the chin in a parting farewell. Saying goodbye to Eliza, Lena stepped outside and Apparated back home to her flat.

 

            Opening the door, Lena paused on the threshold as she bent to pick up a slip of parchment that had been pushed beneath the trim. Reading the quick note from Kara, Lena smiled as she moved further inside, Morrigan ruffling her feathers at her arrival as Lena made a beeline for her. The owl clicked her beak and nuzzled her palm, eyes closing as she softly hooted, and Lena fussed over her for a moment before she went through to the bathroom and ran the hot water.

 

            Moving on to her bedroom, she hung up her cloak and fetched clean clothes for work before taking a long, indulgent shower. The hot water scoured her skin and she washed her hair as well, lingering beneath the hot water as steam filled the bathroom until she shut it off. Wrapping a large towel around herself, she brushed her teeth and spent a painstaking age drying her hair with her wand, until it hung sleek and straight with the product she worked through it.

 

            Once she was dressed, she read the latest copy of The Daily Prophet on the sofa as she nursed a cup of herbal tea, avoiding too much caffeine as she saved it for her shift. She had a few hours to herself and after finishing off the word search in the newspaper, Lena tidied up a bit, setting the broom to sweep the floors and the dishes to wash themselves in the sink as she wrote a grocery list and sent Morrigan off to place the order with a few Galleons slipped into the small purse attached to her leg.

 

            Leaving the window open for her return, Lena gathered her things together for work and pulled on her cloak before Flooing into the waiting room at St. Mungo’s. It was a calm chaos inside, patients lined up on worn chairs as they waited their turn, a woman who looked like she’d taken a wrong dose of Polyjuice Potion sitting beside a child who’d accidentally transfigured his nose into a pig’s as his magic manifested, a man who’d splinched himself bleeding through his paisley shirt as two Healers fussed over him as he sank onto a wheelchair to be whisked away for treatment. 

 

            Making her way through to her locker room, Lena changed into clean scrubs and donned her green robes, stowing her satchel and removing her stethoscope, looping it around her neck. She made her way through to her ward, doing a handover with the Healer whose shift was ending, before diving straight into work. Nights were typically quieter at the hospital but it was still hours of getting through patients with charms-based injuries before there was a lull.

 

            Once it quietened down a bit, Lena secluded herself in the Alchemy rooms as she checked up on the cauldrons, reading the notes and timestamps left by previous Healers and continuing to the next step for those applicable. It was almost midnight when her cryptex burned in her pocket, the runes spelling out a summons from Sam and Lena finished crushing up beetles to add to a potion before she slipped out of the room and made her way upstairs to the tearoom.

 

            Sam was already nursing a cup of coffee, looking haggard as she inspected a spoonful of yoghurt and Lena bypassed her table and went to buy another two cups of coffee and a fruit salad for herself. Slumping onto a chair across from her friend, she nudged one of the cups across the tabletop and gave her a tired smile.

 

            “Long shift?”

 

            “Mm, oh, yeah, always . You alright?”

 

            Blinking, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction. “Fine, why?”

 

            “I heard about your mum. That’s rough.”

 

            Sighing, Lena sank into her chair, taking a sip of coffee. “Can’t keep secrets in this place, can you?” she grumbled. “To be fair, it was in front of a good chunk of the on-duty Healers and nurses. Which is why she did it.”

 

            “What’d you do to deserve that?”

 

            “Yawned in the Theatre.”

 

            “Yawned?”

 

            “Mhm. I told you, she has it out for me.”

 

            “Because of Kara, right,” Sam nodded before kicking Lena’s shoe under the table. “How is Kara? Go on, spill. I want to hear everything.”

 

            “She’s fine. It- it’s going well, you know, us and the potion,” Lena said, lowering her voice. “Lillian doesn’t like that, of course. I think she thought I’d allow her to bully me into dumping her but … well, she was sorely mistaken if she thought I was going to roll over and take it. And it’s purely because she’s a werewolf as well; my mum wouldn’t give a shit otherwise. We don’t talk, we don’t get along, it’s all just about appearances. ” 

 

            Lena’s mouth twitched with bitter amusement and she gestured off-handedly. “Hence the punishments. I’ll be doing scut for the rest of the year if I piss her off again. I’m worried this isn’t all of it though; I’m not sure what she’ll do next but it’s not going to just be petty torment, I’m sure.”

 

            Wincing, Sam spooned yoghurt into her mouth and then set down the empty container. “The downside of working with family, I suppose.”

 

            “It’s not so bad. I don’t have to see her here much, unless she goes out of her way.”

 

            “Well, I’m happy for you. I was only a little bit friendly with Kara at school but she was sweet.”

            

            “She is.”

 

            “We should get dinner again soon,” Sam suggested, smiling brightly at the prospect. “Normally I’m stuck with your old Housemates so it was nice to outnumber you for a change with one of mine.”

 

            Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes, “I’ll say, she doesn’t have a single Slytherin friend so, naturally, they all hate me.”

 

            “You’ve met her friends already?”

 

            “I’ve met her family too,” Lena replied, trying not to sound too smug before her expression turned surly. “And my friends found out. Not how I would have liked it to come about but … well, it went as you would expect.”

 

            “I can’t imagine why,” Sam sarcastically replied, “it’s not like a bunch of Slytherin fanatics would have an issue with you dating a Hufflepuff werewolf.”

 

            Sighing, Lena took a bite of her melon and gave her friend a withering look. “Very funny. They’re not all fanatics, and they did already know about her. She works for Andrea, actually. And William - I don’t think you ever met him - is her ex.”

 

            “Oh, she’s the one who caused that little tiff with you all.”

 

            Face crumpling with disgruntlement, Lena’s cheeks warmed slightly. “Yes. Don’t tell anyone but she kissed me while we were on that trip away. I didn’t tell Jack that but it … it was sort of downhill from there and he’s not happy at the way it’s all turned out.”

 

            “Merlin, you’re messy.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Lena took a swig of coffee. “You don’t know the half of it. But I should get back to work - before my mum finds another reason to punish me.”

 

            Sighing as a grave look of worry crossed her face, Sam set her coffee down. “Lena … be careful. Don’t do anything to antagonise her, okay? I know she’s your mum, and maybe we both have shit mums so I’m biassed when I say that mothers and daughters rarely get along, but … I don’t know, don’t let that be the reason for your rash decisions.”

 

            Quietly scoffing, Lena gave her a crooked smile. “Rash decisions? Come on, Sam, it was one decision and it was made for Kara, not for her. It was in retaliation to her but … as far as I’m concerned, she stopped being my mum the day I left home. And she was a shit one before then so …”

 

            “I know,” Sam regretfully murmured, although Lena had never divulged any of the reasons why she felt that way to her friend. Those secrets belonged solely to Kara. “I just … I’d hate to see you get sacked or get your heart broken because of all of this.”

 

            Heaving a sigh, Lena’s eyelids shuttered and she smiled thinly. “She’s not going to sack me; she’s going to make me the Head of Charms one day. If you asked her about it, she’d tell you all about how much time and effort she put into me. She’s not wrong, she did, and Lillian doesn’t waste her time on lost causes. I can handle a lot worse than she can throw at me at work because I know over her dead body would she let me give up what she wants; it’s outside of work that worries me.”

 

            “What could she do outside of work?”

 

            Eyebrows furrowing together, Lena’s mouth flattened into a grim line, green eyes clouded with concern as she sipped her coffee and set down her cup, turning it on the tabletop as she brooded. “I don’t know,” she eventually murmured, pushing her chair back and climbing to her feet. “But I have a feeling I’m going to find out.”

 

            She went to check on her patients and treated a few new admissions, watching Interns dole out Skele-Gro to a kid that had fallen off her broom, checking on them as they fumbled through the treatment options and dosages, critiqued their work in her cool, professional manner, as free with her praise as her criticisms. Banned from the Theatre, which all of the Healers seemed to know about as the gossip spread through the hospital, Lena was haughty as she treated the patients she could, her cut-throat ambition giving her an edge as she demanded the patients she wanted for herself as they came through the waiting room. 

 

            It may not have been as arduous, treating awry jinxes and bad hexes and all manner of magical ailments, as it was to operate but Lena was run off her feet and chafed at the restraints put upon her, wishing she was up to her wrists in the bloody insides of an unconscious wizard, fixing a heart that had been charmed bigger, vanishing bones that had shredded muscle and restructuring the body cavity for new ones to grow, removing the thorny flowers from a witch’s lungs. Lena had been raised for this job and Lillian knew it, knew it would eat away at her that she was banned from doing what she loved, from using her fine-tuned skill that countless hours had been poured into. Still, her shift passed by quickly, a few hours of sleep stolen in an on-call room in the early hours of the morning before she worked the morning shift and then left before lunch. 

 

            Heading home, she indulged in a long bath, the long hours of the last week catching up to her as she kept her head above the shallow depth of her steaming bath, dark hair like a sheet of silk around her shoulders as she stared sternly at the bathroom wall. Brooding over the unknowable future, Lena stayed until the bath was almost cold. Emerging in a fluffy towel, her skin soft and perfumed from her lavender soap, she dressed in warm pyjamas and pulled a robe over the top before she topped up Morrigan’s water and food and murmured tenderly to the owl that gave her a half-lidded look of annoyance.

 

            It was early afternoon by the time she sat down with a cup of tea and something to read, whittling away the next few hours as she unwound. Cooking dinner for herself, she ate alone at her table as she had so often that it was comforting, and then had an early night, in bed before the early sunset could even finish descending over Dublin. Sleeping long, Lena didn’t wake until past six the following morning, the fourteen hours of rest making her groggy as she dragged herself out of bed, making coffee for herself and standing near the window left open for her owl as she breathed in the chill air of late October, the smell of the rotting leaves and damp concrete mingling with the exhaust fumes of Muggle cars. 

 

            An owl arrived with her copy of the day’s paper and she made herself another cup of coffee before settling in to read over the news, clicking her tongue and scoffing at some of the articles, smiling at the sight of Kara’s name on one of the bylines of a column piece. It was a small report of the sight of a Hippocampus seen in the channel, a rare occurrence to be noteworthy and worth the time of a junior journalist and Lena felt a small swell of pride as she removed the page and safely folded it away to safekeeping. 

 

            Rousing herself to get ready for breakfast, she Apparated to Cornwall for breakfast at a Muggle cafe that Kara was fond of, the wind blowing a gale off the coast as she wandered the streets of Falmouth until she arrived at her girlfriend’s front door. Kara was barrelling outside, the wind tossing her blonde curls as she tried to fasten her cloak one-handedly, calling over her shoulder as she pulled the door shut with the other.

 

            “Bye mum! Oh.”

 

            Kara was brought to an abrupt stop by Lena’s hands on her shoulders, stopping them from colliding. Blue eyes creasing warmly, Kara reached up to cup her chin. “Hi, you.”

 

            “Morning,” Lena coyly murmured, leaning in and kissing her quickly. “And where are you off to in a rush?”

 

            “Trying to beat you to breakfast so I could pick up some flowers,” Kara sheepishly replied, putting a hand behind her back and then producing a handful of Aconite, summoned from Eliza’s neat garden, the purple flower buds in full bloom. “These are fitting enough.”

 

            Laughing, Lena took the fistful and traced a light fingertip over a petal. “I’ll make good use of them in the next Wolfsbane batch once they dry out.”

 

            “Perfect,” Kara whispered, leaning in to kiss her again and pausing at the shout coming from the back garden of the cottage.

 

            “I- wha- Kara. Did you decimate my Aconite plant?” her mother’s stern voice drifted over to them.

 

            Wincing as she shared an impish look with Lena, Kara cupped her mouth and called back. “Sorry! I’ll fix it later!”

 

            Snorting, Lena looped her arm through Kara’s and towed her away from the cottage. “Come on, before your mum starts conspiring to split us up as well, if only to preserve her garden.”

 

            Letting out a quick laugh, Kara cupped Lena’s cheek as they walked and pressed a kiss to it, almost tripping over the curb as they walked down the street. “My mum loves you.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, Lena narrowed her eyes against the glare of the white sky, watching a Muggle car pull into the road and set off, her thoughts on the matter dubious at best. Kara studied her expression and cocked her head to the side.

 

            “What?”

 

            “What?”

 

            “What’s that face for?”

 

            Shrugging, Lena smiled ruefully, “nothing, I just- I told you, mothers don’t particularly care for me.”

 

            “Ah, well, that was more to do with them than you. Believe me. And if you don’t believe me, I have this for you.”

 

            Kara dipped into the pocket of her robe and withdrew an envelope with Lena’s name written on the front in an elegant hand. She handed it over and Lena juggled her handful of toxic flowers to take it, turning it over to stare at the wax seal before looking at the front again.

 

            “What’s this?”

 

            “Alex and Kelly’s wedding invitation. They’ve set a date for March. You’re invited, if you can make it of course, because my family likes you.”

 

            It filled her with a disconcerting feeling, to think about being liked by someone’s family. Lena, who had been liked by so few people in her life. Of course, she was more well-liked than she thought, her cool demeanour and aloofness keeping people at bay, at her own design most of the time. 

 

            Blinking, Lena looked up at Kara and then frowned slightly, slipping it into her pocket. “Oh.”

 

            Giving her a crooked smile, Kara jerked her head towards the near-distant town centre. “Come on, let’s have breakfast.”

Chapter 35

            October bled into November, which swiftly gave way to December, rain turning to sleet and then snow in turn. Lena never mentioned that night with her friends and Kara was oblivious to what had come out, what had been said, except for the unsettling feeling of William’s increasing contempt for her. It made no difference to her though, going about the mundanity of her clerical work at The Daily Prophet , coming home every day smelling of ammonia from the ink, her neck and shoulders aching from hunching over her desk, her head filled with nuggets of information and facts as she took the opportunity to pore over dozens of books and papers and essays in research of the journalists she helped out.

 

            Over the course of those weeks, the Wolfsbane trial came to an end with a published report on Belby’s findings, Lena’s name showing up in it and the quick dismissal of all of the participants who’d shown up monthly at St. Mungo’s to be experimented on. Belby was quite satisfied with his findings, content with the outcome of the Wolfsbane Potion and what it entailed. It cured no werewolves but it kept everyone else safe. The only person involved in the research who was frustrated by the outcome seemed to be Lena, the fact that her girlfriend was still subjected to the transformations each month a glaring failure on her behalf to put an end to it. She accepted that in stride though, brewing her own batches as she continued her research and scouring of books and journals from decades ago in hopes of seeking the answer she’d committed herself to finding when she’d been a young girl with a sick friend who’d been too frightened to tell her the truth.

 

            Christmas rapidly approached and Kara had finished her gift shopping in Diagon Alley on late nights after work, walking through the damp streets as it rained, witches and wizards bundled up in their robes, carrying parcels wrapped in brown paper. Garlands and enchanted candles festooned the place, the smell of cinnamon and pine needles perfuming the air through the smell of rain and wet stone, and Kara spent more than one night inside The Leaky Cauldron with a mug of warm Butterbeer and a stack of presents beside her. 

 

            The full moon was on the twenty-third of that month which meant that she was feeling well enough to attend the work Christmas party at the office in Diagon Alley on the twenty-first, a faint headache and the flu-like symptoms creeping up on her as she perched on the edge of her desk. The smell of ink and parchment was heady, fresh paper being stamped with the latest issue as the charmed printing press got a headstart on tomorrow morning’s issue. 

 

            Everyone was dressed warmly in jumpers and tweed jackets, the cold seeping in through the glazed windows, the office floor draughty with the tall ceilings and the little windows left open for the owls that came and went. Brandy and Firewhisky were passed around in little glasses and Cat Grant was brief with her thanks and well-wishes for the holidays and Andrea gave a lengthier speech, all smiles as she charmed them with her good humour, her effortless confidence. Kara didn’t mind her as one of her bosses, finding her fair, if a little cool at times, and although she was Lena’s best friend and Kara had spent time around Andrea through association with William and Russell’s friendship, she wouldn’t have said they were really friends in any capacity. 

 

            The last few weeks, she had caught Andrea watching her though, shrugging off the interest as some open curiosity about her Lycanthropy, the crisscrossing scars and the way her complexion turned greyish and waxy as the full moon approached. As Kara nursed her glass of brandy, she stood apart from the rest of the office, not quite fitting in with the junior journalists, definitely not the smattering of interns that had joined in July, and not the well-seasoned veterans who wielded red ink with reckless abandon whenever the report from a rookie came across their desks. It wasn’t that she didn’t like any of them, it was just Kara’s natural inclination to cling to the fringes, knowing that if they knew the truth about her, she would make their skin crawl.

 

            And then, of course, there was William. He was the darling of the office, Andrea’s favoured reporter due to his status as Russell’s best friend, and even Cat Grant had a soft spot for him on account of him winning a few awards for The Daily Prophet . He was friends with everyone, a natural charmer, which was perhaps why Kara had allowed herself to go along with the attention he’d given her at the start of the year. Now, his eyes seemed to pass over her, although there was a certain venom to his stare lately, as if her being there angered him, his criticisms harsh enough to warrant a few gentle chastisements from Andrea, who always looked exasperated by it.

 

            Kara kept all of this to herself, not wanting to burden Lena with the petty dramas of past flings and the drudgery of her job. Still, when they’d all had a few drinks and a few of the employees who hadn’t put their names in a hat at the start of the month had left, the remainder of them drew in closer near the stack of wrapped presents beneath a tall Christmas tree that had been put up and decorated by the House Elf that cleaned the office. 

 

            “Alright, who’s up first?” Andrea mused aloud as she selected the first present and read off the name written on it.
