            They went through a series of people collecting their gifts and trying to guess who it was that had gifted it to them. There was everything from a packet of Jelly Slugs for a senior journalist who was always eating some form of sweets, to many quills in a variety of colours, sizes and bird species, little notebooks and bottles of alcohol. Kara had selected the name of a woman who reported the daily horoscopes and had purchased a new set of tarot cards for her.

 

            It was towards the end of it that Kara’s name was called, Andrea holding out a rectangular wrapped gift that looked very much like a book. Stepping forward, Kara took the gift from her boss and unwrapped it to reveal a book, as assumed, and she scrunched up the wrapping paper as she read the title. Emerett Picardy Lupine Lawlessness: Why Lycanthropes Don’t Deserve to Live.

 

            Her stomach swooped and she felt a hollow shakiness in her stomach as her head jerked up. Meeting William’s gaze as he stood tall, arms folded over his chest, there was a flicker in his eyes that let Kara know it was him. Of course it was him who had picked her name and chosen such a gift.

 

            “What did you get?” Andrea prompted, waiting for her to show it off, to guess who it was from.

 

            “A book,” Kara rasped, attempting to clear her dry throat as she felt a flush creep up her neck. 

 

            “A book?” William echoed. “Go on then, what’s the title?”

 

            “It’s-” Kara tried, faltering and then clearing her throat again as her ashen face reddened. “It’s about werewolves.”

 

            “Werewolves?” William replied, his voice laced with false bewilderment. “That’s an odd choice for a book. I didn’t know you were interested in werewolves, Kara.”

 

            Caution crept into Andrea’s features and she stepped forward. “William-”

 

            “Who would send you that?” he continued, rubbing his chin. “Surely they’re not- do you think they’re trying to say something about your scars? Or how you’re always off after every full moon? It is every full moon, isn’t it? But a werewolf would never be hired to work somewhere like this, right Andrea?”

 

            “That’s enough,” Andrea firmly replied, her composure slipping slightly as her blue eyes flashed a warning.

 

            A few of the employees shared a glance, a couple of others frowning, looking confused or perturbed, most of them looking at Kara with renewed interest. Of course, they’d all been curious about the young scarred woman whose hair was prematurely greying, who was evasive whenever her coworkers skirted around the question of what had happened. A few of them looked angry as they quickly connected the dots and Kara ducked her head, cheeks flaming with the telltale sign of the truth as she avoided the looks of revulsion.

 

            “You’re not serious, are you?” Siobhan Smythe, Cat Grant’s personal assistant, asked after a moment.

 

            The silence was tense and then someone else muttered something and someone contemptuously spat out a curse and Kara could feel the burning stares as her heart pounded, her skin prickling with a cold sweat. Without a word, she tossed the ball of paper in the trash and kept a white-knuckled grip on her new book as she forged towards the assembled group of employees, most of whom scattered as they tried to avoid being close to her. 

 

            Walking over to her desk, she grabbed her briefcase with a shaking hand and popped it open, swiping her arm across her desk to slide all of her belongings into it. She had little there anyway, just some ink pots, quills, a coffee mug and paper. Quickly rummaging through the drawers to make sure she had everything, she tuned out the sound of raised voices, grabbed her cloak in one hand and hurried out of the office, her shoulders hunched against the rain.

 

            There was an ache in her chest, her eyes prickling slightly as she swallowed thickly, feeling the heaviness of her bones, the itch of her scars as she welcomed the cold rain against her heated cheeks. She considered Apparating away immediately but Kara didn’t want to go home to Eliza, brimming with so much tension as frustration overwhelmed her. Instead, she set off down the street, pausing beneath the awning of Florean Fortescue’s to shrug on her robe before she continued.

 

            “Hey!”

 

            Kara didn’t even register the voice behind her as she walked, hoping it would sober her frustration, temper it a little so she could go home without the defeated slump to her shoulders and the soft devastation of someone who had been unfairly fucked over once more. The click of hurried heels on the cobblestones caught up with her though.

 

            “Hey,” Andrea loudly intruded on her thoughts as she grabbed Kara’s arm, yanking her around.

 

            Blinking in surprise, Kara brushed her damp curls out of her face and frowned. “Don’t even worry about it,” she choked out. 

 

            “Hold on a minute. I- look, I’m sorry it worked out this way but … can you come and see me tomorrow? In my office?”

 

            Letting out a quiet laugh, Kara gave her a crooked smile, her rain-splattered glasses slipping down her nose slightly. “Really? You want to make me come in so you can fire me?”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, guilt was bright in Andrea’s eyes and she let go of Kara’s arm, stepping back slightly. Sighing, her shoulders dropping, Andrea gave her a grim look. “You understand that I have no choice, right? I- William shouldn’t have … done that but-”

 

            “I know,” Kara snorted, raising her briefcase. “Don’t worry, I packed my things already.”

 

            “Right. Um … I’ll give you a good reference. And I’ll have your Christmas bonus and final pay paid into your Gringotts account. Redundancy pay too.”

 

            “You don’t have to-”

 

            “I’d like to. For the trouble.”

 

            Forcing herself to swallow her pride, knowing Lena’s friend could afford the loose change to cover Kara’s lost wages for a few weeks, she nodded and mumbled a thank you, still not entirely rooted in the reality of losing another job. She’d already burned through so many options that Kara didn’t think she could stomach the dreaded search for another one. 

 

            She turned to go on her way but Andrea stopped her again with a hand on her arm. Turning to look at her, getting annoyed now, the intense embarrassment and shabbiness of her person in the face of someone so polished, so pretty and put together, so much like Lena that Kara felt so inadequate, knowing she’d have to go home to her mother’s with nothing to show for herself.

 

            Giving her a pleading look, Andrea winced. “Can you- can you not tell Lena? Please.”

 

            “Lena?” Kara flatly echoed. “What’s she got to do with any of this?”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Andrea smiled thinly. “I know about the two of you, it’s alright. So does William. Everyone, really. I think … maybe that’s why he did it, with what happened at drinks.”

 

            Kara was scrambling to keep up, blinking cluelessly as she listened. “Right.”

 

            “She told me before that I- that I’d better not fire you but … you can see why- I mean, we overlooked it before, I really tried to make it work for you because she asked but with everyone knowing-”

 

            Face softening with a crooked smile, Kara swallowed thickly and nodded. “Of course. Lena knows it was never going to be permanent, anyway. I am grateful to you though, for keeping me on before.”

 

            Nodding, her eyes slightly wide with worry as she wrung her hands, Andrea faintly returned the smile. “I’m sorry. Really, I am. I just- I would hate for this to ruin my friendship with Lena but I know that she loves you.”

 

            “It’s okay,” Kara whispered, her voice wavering slightly. “Consider this my resignation. There; now you don’t have to fire me.”

 

            “Kara-”

 

            “You should get back to your party.”

 

            “Right. I want you to know that I think, given enough time, you would’ve been a good journalist. It’s not about your work, it’s just-”

 

            “Me,” Kara finished, her voice cracking as she gave Andrea a wry smile.

 

            Shrugging helplessly, Andrea grimaced. “Unfortunately. But, hey, if you enjoy it, if it’s what you want to do, you could check out The Quibbler. Xenophilius Lovegood runs it. He’s a bit of a kook but … well, maybe he’ll have no problem working with a werewolf.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose slightly as her pale eyebrows drew together, Kara let out a strained laugh, amused at the suggestion. “Thanks. I’ll, uh, I’ll keep it in mind.”

 

            Nodding, Andrea let out a weary sigh and grimaced. “I really am sorry.”

 

            Waving a hand dismissively, behaving far more indifferent about it than she really felt, Kara gave her a crooked smile. “It’s not your fault. I should get going though. You have a good Christmas.”

 

            “You too.”

 

            Turning around, she swiftly walked away after that and Apparated out of Diagon Alley, the weather milder in Falmouth as she hurried up the short path to the front door and let herself in. The wall of heat chased away the freezing chill in her bones as soon as she crossed the threshold, and Kara fell back against the door, her pallid cheeks rosy from the cold, her blonde hair plastered to her skin, and she took a moment to compose herself. Swallowing thickly, she went through the motions of kicking off her shoes, hanging up her damp cloak, setting down her briefcase and ruffling Bastet beneath the chin as the cat came to greet her.

 

            “Is that you, sweetheart?” Eliza called from the living room. 

 

            Stepping forward so her mother could see her through the doorway, Kara gave her a forced smile. “Hi.”

 

            “You’re earlier than I expected. I thought you had your work party tonight?”

 

            “Oh … well, it was more of just a quick drink and a thank you speech from management.”

 

            “Ah, okay. Have you eaten yet?” Eliza asked, pushing herself to her feet, clicking her tongue as she gave Kara a concerned look. 

 

            “It’s alright, I’ll fix myself something now. You sit.”

 

            Lowering herself back down onto the sofa, Eliza picked her book back up and Kara deliberated before making her way upstairs and changing into something warm first, pulling her damp hair up and then padding back downstairs. Eliza had made chicken pot pie and Kara reheated herself a slice of it and sat on a dining chair with her knees pulled up to her chest, picking at her dinner as she ate slowly. 

 

            Eliza came out to make some tea as she was still picking at her food and Kara looked up at her mother as Eliza stroked her damp hair in passing. Filling the tea kettle, Eliza boiled it and made two cups, setting one down in front of her daughter, who was eating without her usual relish.

 

            “Are you alright? You look all funny.”

 

            Shrugging half-heartedly, Kara’s mouth thinned at the corners. “Full moon in two nights.”

 

            “Have they said when they’re going to stop the trial? Now that it’s been published,” Eliza anxiously asked, worry flickering in her blue eyes.

 

            Kara’s eyes strayed to the cut out of the article stuck to the front of their fridge with a magnet where Eliza had snipped the copy out of the journal it had been published in. It was stuck there with Lena’s name in the byline, towards the end of a dozen other names involved in the research, a place of honour in the Danvers household, alongside Kara’s first article clipped from The Daily Prophet, an article detailing Alex’s first big arrest and Kelly’s laws she pushed through, in between a smattering of moving photos and souvenirs from Kara and Alex’s travels. 

 

            “Um, I think they’re going to let the participants keep receiving their doses,” Kara lied. “You know, as an ongoing basis for test subjects. And as a way to thank us, I guess. It’s a pretty difficult and expensive one to brew.”

 

            Relief crossed Eliza’s face and her shoulders dropped slightly as she nodded. “Right, well, that’s good. It’s good that they take care of their patients.”

 

            “Mm.”

 

            She made herself eat the last few bites of her dinner as Eliza hovered and then slid her chair back, climbing to her feet and setting her plate into the sink to wash themselves. Giving her mother a fleeting smile, Kara crossed back over to the table.

 

            “I think I might take this upstairs,” Kara said, picking up her tea. “I’ve got a new book I want to get started on.”

 

            “Alright, goodnight.”

 

            “Goodnight,” Kara murmured, pausing to let Eliza kiss her cheek as she passed her by.

 

            Upstairs, she set her tea down on the edge of her desk, snapped her fingers at the lamp and then climbed into bed, pulling the quilt up to her chest and picking up the glossy book that had been spitefully gifted to her. Nothing if not a masochist, Kara opened it to the first page and devoured a third of it in between mouthfuls of tea before she fell asleep with the lamp on and her glasses askew, the bone-leaden imminence of the full moon calling for an early night.

 

            She woke at her usual time but had nowhere to be, no job to show up for, so Kara went back to sleep for an hour, the peaky pallor of her face making her look ghostly as she buried her head in the pillow. When she woke again, the room was still dark from the late dawn, mid-winter deep grey and the drumming of rain on the shingled roof as she sat up. There was a chill seeping in through the glazed windows, the faint whistle of the wind, and Kara dragged a fleece on over her jumper and slipped her feet into slippers as she got out of bed, feeling like a young girl in an old woman’s body as her joints ached.

 

            Shuffling downstairs, she walked into the kitchen rubbing the sleep from her eyes and her pillow-creased cheek. At the sound of Kara’s slippers slapping against the floor, Eliza glanced over her shoulder as she washed her hands, soap suds covering her wrists, and raised her eyebrows with surprise. “Oh. You’re still here.” 

 

            “I don’t feel too great,” Kara murmured, which wasn’t entirely a lie but usually wouldn’t have stopped her from going to work. 

 

            She’d always felt like she had to prove herself, be strong enough to overcome the effects of her Lycanthropy, aside from the next day, where she’d usually been ripped apart and exhausted. Now, she only had residual aches from the transformation and wasn’t as tired after curling up in Lena’s office and sleeping away the night but she still allowed herself the singular day to recuperate. Kara didn’t have to worry about that anymore though.

 

            Clicking her tongue, Eliza dried off her hands and walked over to her daughter, beckoning her closer as she approached and then cupping Kara’s face in her hands, turning her this way and that as she fussed. Even though she’d endured the transformations for years, Kara still indulged Eliza in her fussing, knowing it was an act of love and occasionally needing that confirmation that yes, she was loved by people, despite what she was.

 

            “Go and lay down in the living room and I’ll make you something to eat. Coffee too. Go on.”

 

            Obeying, Kara slumped as she plodded into the living room, sinking onto the squashy sofa and curling up on herself. The fire was lit and the room was warm as Kara burrowed down onto the pillows, dragging a blanket over her and making room for Bastet as the cat jumped up, kneading the blanket on the side of Kara’s thigh before she made herself comfortable. The house was peacefully quiet and Kara listened to the sounds of her mother moving around in the kitchen, the kettle whistling, the scrape of drawers opening and closing, until Eliza carried in a plate and a cup of coffee, her own drifting behind her, and set the breakfast down in Kara’s lap. A slice of toast and a buttered omelette, the smell of it heavenly but Kara’s stomach so small without her appetite that she felt faintly queasy.

 

            Making herself eat it all, knowing she needed her strength, knowing that brooding over her misfortune wouldn’t be the way to manage things, she wolfed it down with her sweetened coffee and thanked her mother. Eliza whisked away her empty plate and brought her another cup of coffee before kissing her clammy brow and telling her she had to get back to work. From the living room, Kara listened to her mother trim her harvested herbs and plants at the kitchen table, the snick of the scissors, the scrape of unfurled package paper as the bundles were wrapped a soothing routine in the background as she allowed herself to be lulled to sleep.

 

            She woke at lunch and ate a bowl of steaming soup with her mother at the kitchen table, a little feverish as she shed her fleece and pushed the sleeves of her jumper up over her scarred forearms, dipping pieces of bread into the soup. Afterwards, she helped Eliza with her work, grinding plants into a fine powder with the pestle and mortar and measuring out doses with the set of brass scales and little weights, storing them in little glass jars and sealing them with hot wax. She did the grinding, for the most part, her hands shaking slightly as she tried to shake out the powder, melt the wax, pour it into the jars. 

 

            After an hour, Eliza thanked her and then sent her off to bed to rest and Kara took a cup of tea with her, finishing off the rest of her book as the afternoon breezed by. Lena was working so Kara was left home that night, Alex and Kelly coming over for dinner, bringing bundles of fish and chips from their local, the sharp sting of vinegar wafting in as they carried in the soggy newspaper-wrapped packages and spreading them over the table. Kara said little and listened to the talk of wedding planning, the small affair intended to be casual but her sister’s excitement still evident as she told Kara she’d seen a nice blue dress for her. 

 

            They talked about their Christmas shopping and the plans for dinner, for what time they’d be there to exchange gifts, if they’d bought enough alcohol and if the Christmas ham was enough to feed them all. Lena had to work Christmas Eve and half of Christmas Day but Kara had invited her over for dinner and she’d accepted with wary surprise. She didn’t have to explain her trepidation; Kara knew from their Hogwarts days that Lena had never gone home for the holidays, and knowing what she knew now, she wondered if her girlfriend had ever had a Christmas at all. When she’d asked Lena about her holidays over the last decade, Lena had told her she’d worked every time, picking up shifts so Sam or other Healers with family could spend the time at home. What difference did it make to someone who had no family ties and only a smattering of friends, who had their own families anyway?

 

            Kara was determined to make it different for her this year, although she secretly lamented the fact that Lena would miss out on Christmas Eve and the next morning. They usually had eggnog and flannel pyjamas, fresh gingerbread biscuits filling the house with their smell, the decorated tree in the living room with a small pile of presents beneath it. In the morning, they’d congregate there to open them all, colourful paper strewn across the floor, gratitude and delight at their new things, still a rarity for them, despite Eliza no longer being the sole income for their family of three. They’d eat breakfast together and prepare lunch and play Exploding Snap and Gobstones on the living room floor as the day dragged on, bundled up warm against the cold outdoors. Kara loved Christmas. 

 

            She stayed home again the next day, having the good excuse of the full moon that night and feigning a head cold when Eliza questioned her on staying home two days in a row. Kara really did feel like shit though, her head aching, her body aching, her mood low and the desire to stay in bed too tempting to pretend that she was off to work. Kara didn’t want to tell Eliza she’d lost another job, to see that worry flare to life, the tender assurances that something better would come along, that she was clever and strong and her Lycanthropy wouldn’t hold her back. It always did though. 

 

            Sleeping away most of the day, she eventually got up and packed a bag, pretending she was off to St. Mungo’s, wincing internally as the lies stacked up. If she told her family Lena was brewing the potion for her, the instructions stolen from Belby and replicated in secret, while Kara curled up in her office each full moon and slept the night away outside of a cell, they would have been aghast at the recklessness and risks of it all. But Kara had always believed in Lena more than any person should have, perhaps not everything about Lena but certainly her intelligence, an almost infallible conviction that Lena could do anything.

 

            Kissing her mother goodbye, Kara pulled on a tweed coat and Flooed through to Lena’s flat, murmuring the address as she tried not to let her mother hear. Ducking out of the fireplace, covered in soot and feeling like her knees were going to buckle as vertigo stole over her, Kara was steadied by a pair of gentle hands. Eyelids fluttering, Kara’s face creased with a quick grin and she breathed in the clean smell of soap, toothpaste and peppermint tea of Lena’s after-work routine. Dusting her off, Lena wrapped Kara in a hug and Kara’s chin dug into her shoulder as she let out a heavy sigh.

 

            “Hello.”

 

            “Hi,” Lena murmured, stroking a hand over Kara’s wayward curls. “Let’s get you settled in.”

 

            Sinking onto the firm sofa, Kara tipped her head back against the cushions and sank into it, her body grateful for the reprieve of being upright. They talked about their lives over the last few days since they’d seen each other, Lena’s schedule keeping them apart, and Kara purposely omitted her new status of unemployment as she tried to sort things out first. She didn’t want Lena to pity her, didn’t want her to feel obligated to fix her problems for her. 

 

            Lena ordered them Chinese for dinner and once they’d tidied up Kara walked into the office and stowed her wand and glasses in the desk before stripping off and drinking down her last dose of the potion. Locked inside the room, the wintry air making her bare skin ripple with goosebumps, she waited as the transformation crept over her, ragged gasps of pain choked out as her bones snapped, skin and muscles stretched and she felt every second of the agony before falling onto four paws.

 

            That was the worst part of it, Kara thought, the awareness. Sure, she always remembered everything the next day but she’d always been spared the oblivion of mauling herself, her monstrous destruction and that skin-crawling feeling of being inside the wolfish form. Now, she wasn’t spared that self-awareness, even though she was spared the rest of it. Kara could feel the way her legs bent unnaturally, the length of her muzzle, the fur that covered her body. Curling up, the motion awkward and clumsy, she rested her head beside her paws and closed her eyes, tired as her inhuman body allowed sleep to take her.

 

            She woke as the transformation reversed itself, torn from the relative peace of her vague dreams to the pain of feeling her body ripped apart, the animalistic whimper escaping her as she writhed on the rug, elbows splintering and reforming back the other way, hunched shoulders deflating, ending up on her knees, shivering as her heart pounded, blood pumping through her with the adrenaline of the agony. 

 

            Lena found her there a few minutes later, bundling her up in a blanket, giving her time to come around. There were potions and gently murmured words as she found the energy to climb to her feet, coltish on her weak legs, a hollow shakiness inside her. Running a bath, Lena helped her in it and set sausages on to sizzle, making them sandwiches and coffee before they both crawled into her bed and slept like the dead.

 

            They slept the rest of the morning and then Lena was up, showering, dressing for work, cutting apples into slices as she snacked on them and made Kara eat her own wedges in bed as she insisted she stay. When her girlfriend left with a lingering kiss tasting sweet like the fruit, promising to see her tomorrow for Christmas dinner, Kara stayed beneath her warm sheets for a while longer before tidying up the place, feeding Morrigan owl treats and then Flooing home with her packed bag. 

 

            Eliza didn’t fuss so much and Alex made her a cup of tea before the four of them holed up in the living room, Kelly sitting at Kara’s feet with the blanket draped over the two of them as she discussed work with Alex, who was steadily making her way through a plate of fresh gingerbread. Their mother was anxiously working away at the last few rows of a scarf, the forest green hue leaving no doubt who it was for. There was a similar pile of yellow socks waiting for the ends to be woven in, maroon fingerless gloves waiting for the same, and a deep blue cable knit jumper pinned for blocking with a small raven embroidered over the breast. With more people to knit for, Eliza had less time to finish everything and refused to let the needles clack away by magic, deeming it cheating.

 

            It was a quiet afternoon, Kara dozing on the sofa in between bouts of conversation as rain gave way to sleet, an early dusk darkening the sky outside. As it grew later and she’d recovered some of her strength, she ate some of the foil-wrapped chocolates in a dish on the coffee table and helped Kelly and Alex with a puzzle while their mother finished off her knitting and vanished to the kitchen to wrap the gifts, returning with an armful of colourful presents for beneath the tree. Alex fetched the eggnog and they sipped little glasses of it and changed into flannel pyjamas as the fire crackled, the radio tuned into Christmas carols, before picking at a platter of cold cuts, soft cheeses, pickled vegetables and crackers. 

 

            Tired from the residual discomfort of the transformation, Kara fell asleep on the sofa as Eliza and Kelly had a game of Wizard’s chess and Alex flipped through a battered copy of the July issue of Witch Weekly their mother had bought. Christmas was typically a quiet affair for them, spending time together as a family, the three women who’d moved there together as close as a family could be. Kara didn’t move until Alex shook her awake before midnight, coaxing her upstairs, where she put Kara to bed and let Kelly take her own bed, returning downstairs to take her sister’s spot on the sofa.

 

            Waking before dawn the next morning, Kara shook Kelly awake, that childish excitement for Christmas creeping up on her as she blearily smiled, smoothing down her curls as she waited for her sister-in-law to fully wake. Knocking on Eliza’s bedroom door, Kara continued downstairs, where the smell of bacon came from the kitchen, Alex smoking by the open back door as the damp air swept in and she got a start on breakfast. Sucking down the rest of the cigarette, she tucked the butt back in the packet and shut the door on the cold, moving over to the skillet and turning the sausages and tomatoes. 

 

            “Merry Christmas,” Alex grumbled, turning her head to kiss Kelly, “we got snow last night.”

 

            “Really?” Kara perked up, eagerly crossing over to the door, nudging the little curtain aside as she stared out the small glass window at the thin, pale crust on the lawn. 

 

            Eliza came in, knotting a dressing gown and looking grim as she caught Alex’s words. “Good thing I brought the Mandrakes upstairs last week. They’d be miserable in this weather.”

 

            “I hope you’re sleeping with earmuffs on,” Alex snorted, “Merry Christmas.”

 

            The sentiment was echoed by everyone else and tea and coffee was made, chipped mugs in hand and the four of them crowding in the kitchen. They all pitched in, toasting bread, buttering the toast, frying eggs in spitting oil, and they sat down for breakfast first, chattering excitedly until their plates were scraped clean and the two sisters were restless with excitement for their presents. They cleaned up quickly and assembled in the living room, Alex’s rumpled blanket from the night before pooled at one end of the sofa, a fire already lit.

 

            Taking turns opening their gifts as they were all handed out, they each amassed a small pile, new knitted items from Eliza, at least one book each, sweets for Kara, quills and ink for Kelly and records for Alex. Kara scrunched up fistfuls of colourful wrapping paper as they went and eyed the few remaining presents for Lena that remained under the tree once they were done. With her armful of gifts, she kissed everyone’s cheeks and took it all upstairs to put away before showering and dressing in her new jumper and a pair of soft-worn jeans. 

 

            Alex and Kelly left shortly afterwards, heading home first to get ready for lunch with Kelly’s family, and Kara helped Eliza take care of the plants left outdoors, the crunch of the melting snow underfoot making her smile as her breaths came out white and her cheeks reddened. One of the things she missed about America, and Hogwarts, was Christmases with thick snow drifts and she relished the chance to have even the scant layer blanketing their garden, the air still and frosty as she helped melt off the worst of the ice covering leaves, readjusting hessian sacks covering the sensitive plants, evicting Garden Gnomes from where they were trying to shelter in the roots of plants, feeling sheepish as they gave her dirty looks, filing off to burrow elsewhere. 

 

            Her fingers were pink and numb inside the gloves by the time she’d finished, although she was warm enough with her jumper on, toiling away over the garden beds. They were back inside in time for lunch, making sandwiches with the Christmas ham that had just come out of the oven, and then Kara rolled her sleeves up and helped peel vegetables, ice the fruit cake, almost burnt herself on three separate occasions as she turned the roast potatoes, handled the kettle for the jelly to help make the trifle. 

 

            By the time she was done, she had little to do except go back upstairs and enjoy her Christmas. That entailed pulling out that little book William had gifted her, searching back through it for certain passages, and ruminating on the meanings, the facts of it all. That was where Lena found her a couple of hours later, Kara oblivious to her arrival until she was standing on the threshold of the room, knocking on the open door to catch her attention.

 

            “Merry Christmas,” Lena greeted her, giving her a tender smile as she crossed into the room.

 

            “Merry Christmas,” Kara replied, straightening up. “How was work?

 

            “Long. Do you know how many idiots come out of the woodwork on Christmas Day?” Lena sighed, stopping in front of her and leaning down to kiss Kara. Pulling back, she cocked her head to the side, trying to read the title of the book in Kara’s hands. “What are you reading?”

 

            Kara covered the front with her pale hand, a deep-throated noncommittal hum in response as Lena sank down onto the bed beside her. Reaching out, her girlfriend moved her hand and tugged the book free, staring down at the cover as her expression slowly darkened.

 

            “Why do you have this?” Lena softly asked.

 

            “It was a Christmas present,” Kara murmured, messing with her fringe as she stared at the sheets of Alex’s old bed.

 

            “Who gave it to you?” Lena asked, her voice brittle as she tried to stifle her anger, to keep her words from wavering.

 

            “It doesn’t matter,” Kara muttered, setting the book aside and running a hand through her hair.

 

            “Who?”

 

            Lena’s voice was firmer that time, flatter, colder, a thin layer of composure masking the brittle anger beneath. 

 

            “Someone from work.”

 

            “Who?”

 

            Giving her a strained smile, Kara let out a quick laugh. “What, are you going to hex them for me?”

 

            “Too fucking right I will.”

 

            Closing her eyes, Kara shook her head slightly, the corners of her mouth twitching with amusement. “It’s alright. I, uh, I did quit, though.”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Lena was silent for a moment. “Quit or were you fired?”

 

            Opening her eyes, Kara glanced sideways at her, raising a pointed eyebrow. “Why? Going to force Andrea to take me back?”

 

            “Not if you don’t want to go back,” Lena diplomatically replied.

 

            Turning to face her properly, Kara gave her a searching look. “What happened at drinks?”

 

            “What drinks?”

 

            “With your friends? Something happened. Andrea told me. William’s not pleased or-”

 

            “So, it was that gutless coward,” Lena mused aloud, drawing conclusions. Giving Kara a rueful look, Lena rolled her eyes and then stared up at the ceiling, sighing heavily as her shoulders dropped. “Veronica … she saw us getting drinks with Sam. Um … she couldn’t wait to let that slip so … well, they all know. Jack didn’t take it well. Neither did William. Honestly, I don’t really care anyway, so …”

 

            Struggling to speak for a moment, her throat closed up, guilt and shame welling up as her cheeks turned pink and she stared down at her lap, Kara fiddled with the hem of her pilled jumper. Swallowing thickly, she chewed on the inside of her lip and swallowed again, forcing the lump down.

 

            “I’m sorry. I know you didn’t want to tell them yet. I didn’t mean to cause problems-”

 

            Tensing as she shifted closer to Kara on the mattress, jostling it as their knees knocked and she grabbed Kara’s cool hands, a muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw. “Don’t. I’m not- I’m not ashamed of you. No matter what anyone says. I just- it makes me angry. I feel so angry when people treat you this way.”

 

            Letting out a strained laugh, coming out awkward as she smiled unevenly, Kara shrugged half-heartedly. “I’ve had worse.”

 

            “One day it will be better,” Lena firmly told her. 

 

            Brushing aside her fringe, Lena kissed her forehead and Kara’s eyelids shuttered, the comforting peace of Lena’s presence seeping through her, alleviating some of the tension. Pulling back, Lena glanced down at the book in her lap and tapped a finger on the cover of it.

 

            “I’m taking this with me.”

 

            “Why? I-”

 

            Giving her a knowing look, Lena’s lips curled in a thin, pained smile. “You took my quill so I couldn’t use it. I’m taking your book so you can’t read it. I know that both of us would be incapable of resisting the temptation to hurt ourselves otherwise. We’re too good at that.”

 

            “Yes, we are,” Kara murmured in agreement, a furrow forming between her eyebrows before her expression turned solemn. “Have you- have you wanted to use the quill?”

 

            “No,” Lena truthfully replied.

 

            Although, she knew in her bones there would come a day when she would feel that burning desire, the itch to carve open those old words. Just not yet. Not in the last eight weeks, at the very least. Lena didn’t know what she would do in that eventuality, she just knew she couldn’t beg Kara for it back, and wouldn't have been given it even if she had begged. Eyes darting around the room, she made a quick assessment of the space and wondered where it was hidden. It would undoubtedly be inside the small bedroom.

 

            “Good,” Kara whispered before cupping Lena’s chin and leaning in to kiss her chastely. “Keep the book, then.”

 

            She said it with the same bravado Lena had mustered when she’d relinquished her quill. There was something familiar in dwelling in the awful pit of self-loathing that they both experienced in different ways and they both sought comfort in that. Except, now they wouldn’t let each other do it, the strangeness of their relationship, how fiercely protective and intense it all was so much different than any other kind of relationship either of them had experienced before. They would each have suffered tenfold to spare the other one an ounce of pain; it hadn’t always been the case, inflicting pain upon each other by pressing on their hidden wounds, but they had never been good at expressing themselves clearly.

 

            “Come and open your presents,” Kara said after a moment.

 

            Tucking the book into the pocket of her oversized houndstooth blazer, Lena climbed to her feet and Kara followed after her. Alex and Kelly were just arriving and they could hear them downstairs as they descended, Kara taking the lead, slipping into the living room and ferreting out Lena’s presents from beneath the tree as her girlfriend was subjected to a hug from Kelly and a rather warm greeting from Alex, who hated to admit she was fond of the old Slytherin but did secretly think so. 

 

            Lena fetched her bag too, producing two bottles of wine, an entire cooked chicken that she cradled in a baking dish, still warm from her oven, half a dozen neatly wrapped presents with the printed holly and mistletoe lined up along the seam and velvet ribbon tied around them and an enchanted mouse that she dropped on the floor for Bastet to chase. 

 

            They all stood around or sat in various places within the living room or hallway beyond and Lena handed out her own presents to everyone before looking surprised at the little pile for herself. It wasn’t that she’d never received Christmas presents before - anything she’d ever needed had been provided for her - but they had always been just that, things she needed. Lillian had never gifted her frivolous things that weren’t functional in some capacity. She would never buy Lena books that weren’t applicable to her education, clothes that weren’t what she’d picked out, jewellery amounting to the little Slytherin emblazoned heirlooms. Her mother didn’t knit her a jumper in burgundy with the thought it would complement her complexion, as Eliza told her once Lena had finished unwrapping it, along with the green scarf, her favourite colour. 

 

            There were a couple of books from Alex, Kelly and Kara, as well as a perfume Kara had picked out for her, a planner to schedule her days, a new type of tea for her to try, personalised stationery and hand lotion for all the time she spent wearing dragonhide gloves at work. Lena bought everyone a gift that she thought they’d like from past conversations - rare seeds imported from overseas for Eliza to plant in her garden; a law book Lena had found interesting and had spoken to Kelly about; a vinyl she’d enjoyed that Alex had mentioned she hadn’t listened to before. For Kara, she bought her a new pair of brogues, the leather polished and sturdy, brand new, a pair of little gold earrings and a few pots of coloured ink, knowing her girlfriend would like the novelty of the different hues while writing in her diaries. Lena also bought her a little brass photo frame and had put a picture of them taken on Kara’s camera inside it, thinking she’d put it on her desk, planning on revealing that she’d told her friends at the same time. That idea was no longer possible but Lena knew Kara would get another job soon enough.

 

            With the excitement of someone who knew what it was like to be poor, Kara had her new earrings in, her new shoes on, despite her dislike for anything on her feet whenever she could avoid it, and the new jumper from her mother, bundled up in her Christmas presents as Alex likewise wore her jumper and was in the middle of putting on her new vinyl record. Carrying the rest of her things upstairs, Kara neatly put it all away and kissed Lena deeply as her girlfriend followed her upstairs, changing into her new jumper as well as she abandoned her blazer and black turtleneck on Kara’s bed.

 

            Back downstairs, they prepped dinner, Alex setting plates onto the table as Kara pulled out one of the chairs covered in books, old mail, garden shears and a wooden sewing box where Kara had been fixing a lost button on a pair of pants. Music drifted in from the living room and the kitchen was warm with the heat of the old oven, the back window fogged with steam, the glass velvety and blue, as they all sat down for dinner, the sound of voices overlapping as the wine was opened, dishes were picked up and portions added to plates. 

 

            If Kara sometimes seemed quiet and awkward, with her messy, greying curls, her clumsiness, and her scars hidden behind her glasses and oversized clothes, she became a different person at home. More confident in herself, more at ease within her skin, she talked animatedly with Alex and Kelly about a Quidditch match they’d listened to on the radio, carving chicken and setting some on Lena’s plate for her as Lena picked up the bowl of buttered peas and returned the favour. 

 

            It was the best Christmas Lena could remember having, even better than the relief of solitude at Hogwarts. They had crackers they tore open, and while she’d watched the few students and the Professors at school indulge in the novelty of the paper hats and little gag gifts inside, Lena had never done so but found herself sporting a blue one as Kara read the joke from her one and Alex set off the firecrackers from her own with a snort of laughter. 

 

            After dinner, they congregated in the living room with tea and gingerbread baked the day before, playing charades and having to frequently pause as Kara and Alex bickered over broken rules. They moved on to Exploding Snap for a while before the night started to wind down, the music turned off, the cottage quiet around them, solid with its nailed-down floorboards, the warm orange glow of the fireplace, the quiet gardens as sleet poured down, the heaviness of a good meal and the comfort of being indoors on such a night leaving them all relaxed. 

 

            Lena finished off her second cup of tea, idly stroking Bastet in her lap as she listened to the trio talk about plans for New Year’s Eve as Alex tidied up. James was throwing a party and Lena had been invited as well, as an extension of Kara. Pausing in front of her, Alex scoffed at the cat.

 

            “Why does that bloody cat like you so much?”

 

            “I don’t know. Maybe she remembers me from when she was a kitten. I got her for Kara.”

 

            Pausing, Alex gave her a mildly surprised look. “You gave her the cat?”

 

            “Mhm. For Christmas one year.”

 

            “Oh. She never said. ”

 

            “I can hardly imagine why,” Kara wryly murmured as she turned over another card and set it down on top of the growing pile. 

 

            Kelly turned over the next one and added it on top, Alex took Lena’s cup from her and raised her eyebrows. “So? Are you coming to the party? Or are you working?”

 

            “Working New Year’s Day,” Lena replied, her eyes straying over to Kara. “Um …”

 

            Turning over another, Kara let out a sharp laugh at the matching pair and went to slap her hand down, just slow enough for the half deck of cards to blow up, scattering everywhere. Chuckling, Kelly tapped the remainder of her deck on the coffee table and grinned.

 

            “You really are awful at this.”

 

            “It’s snap. It’s pure luck,” Kara grumbled, shuffling cards back into a pile and reaching beneath the coffee table for a few escaped ones. “And Lena doesn’t have to come if she doesn’t want to. She does have her own friends, you know.”

 

            “Well, she can bring them along too,” Alex rolled her eyes, shrugging helplessly. “Liven up the party a bit. Revive a bit of school drama, for old times’ sake. That’s a joke , Kara. Don’t get your wand in a knot.”

 

            Snorting, Kara rolled her eyes and restarted the game with a prod from Kelly. “You know, you should invite Sam. And Andrea, if you’d like.”

 

            She said the latter with reservation, watching Lena’s blank expression as she stiffened slightly. Shrugging noncommittally, Lena made a vague comment about asking and Kara hoped that she did. Even though she’d met all of Lena’s friends before, she’d never spent time with them as her girlfriend and that was an important distinction to make. Her thought was that it might make things easier for everyone if they tried to integrate their lives a little bit, instead of keeping everything so separate. And it wasn’t that she didn’t like Andrea, only that she’d gotten the impression that the other woman wasn’t too fond of her, although it turned out she’d been secretly biting her tongue at Lena’s request and that made Kara think a little better of her. 

 

            The conversation moved on and Alex and Kelly left a while after that, and then Lena took her leave as well, thanking Eliza in her quiet, earnest way as she held her satchel with her carefully stowed gifts and a plate of leftovers to ensure she ate dinner the next day. Walking her to the front door, Kara lingered on the doorstep as she held Lena’s hand, kissing her fingertips and giving her a soft smile.

 

            “Thanks for coming.”

 

            “Thank you,” Lena said, the words more weighted when she said them, more solemn and meaningful. “Really. It- I’ve never had a Christmas like that before. It was … nice. ”

 

            “Oh. Well, I guess you’ll just have to get used to it,” Kara said with a crooked smile. 

 

            “Will I?” Lena coyly replied, stepping in closer and toying with the cuff of Kara’s jumper as she ducked her head slightly.

 

            “Of course.”

 

            Lena smiled slightly, raising her eyes to meet Kara’s. She swallowed thickly and lifted her hand to gently trace the scar on Kara’s chin. “Thank you for my presents.”

 

            “Thank you for mine. And think about New Year’s.”

 

            “I will. I’ll see if Sam is free,” Lena assured her as she wrapped her in a hug, kissing the edge of her jaw.

 

            “Don’t be angry at Andrea,” Kara whispered as they swayed slightly in each other’s embrace. “It wasn’t her fault; she’s been very nice to me.”

 

            “I just … I want so much more for you,” Lena hoarsely murmured into her shoulder, a lump catching in her throat. “I wish- I wish other people knew you like I do.”

 

            Kara let out a choked laugh. “If they did, I think they’d like me a lot less. Maybe- maybe they’d think they have even more reason to hate werewolves.”

 

            “Remind me to tell you why I love you at some point,” Lena instructed her with a weary sigh, pulling back and giving her a firm kiss before patting the pocket of her blazer with the confiscated book. “It’s a long list. And you won’t find any of it in a book.”

Chapter 36

            The days between Christmas and New Year blurred together and Kara spent a chunk of her free time at Lena’s when her girlfriend was home, curled up on the sofa with parchment and a quill, dipping the tip in ink and hesitating long enough to leave dots of indigo on the page, repeating the process in between the occasional scribbled word as Kara tried to plead her case. Lena helped her when asked, otherwise keeping her mouth closed as she let Kara puzzle through the petition for work at the Department of Mysteries, although she was quietly, firmly supportive of it. They’d spoken before about how much Kara missed her job, had enjoyed that one the most out of all of the ones she’d had, and Lena would have paid any sum, any bribe to fund the Unspeakables, pay Kara’s salary if she knew it wouldn’t be a nail in the coffin of her relationship. This was something Kara needed to do alone so Lena proofread and edited the letters to Professor Croaker and then lent Morrigan to Kara to send it on New Year’s Eve. 

 

            They were getting ready in Lena’s bathroom, makeup, hair potions and clothes strewn around the place and the bedroom, Kara’s blue eye shadow and Lena’s vivid red lipstick, the ease of moving around each other within the confines of the space. Lena dabbed perfume at the base of her throat and on each wrist, the one that Kara had bought her for Christmas. Lena had invited Sam, as instructed, and had ignored Andrea, still angry about the whole situation, even though Kara tried to reason that she’d quit. It didn’t seem kind to Lena to let William get away with his poor behaviour and she didn’t have it in her to confront her friend about it then, letting her anger cool and feeling grateful that she’d fucked things up with Jack so spectacularly that she hadn’t spent much time around her friends recently anyway.

 

            Sam got a sitter for Ruby and met them at the party James was hosting at his flat, a spacious two-bedroom that he’d recently moved into, decorated with dark wood and a lot of leather and filled with all manner of people as music played loudly and drinks flowed freely. Lena didn’t go too heavy on the drinking because she had work the next morning and wasn’t too keen on the effects that a hangover potion just couldn’t quite mask, so she drank lemon squash for the most part and tried her best to integrate into Kara’s friend circle, Sam helping with that somewhat with her natural warmth and earnestness. She had always reminded Lena of Kara in a way, which had made the early days of their friendship a painful thing.

 

            At midnight, they had Muggle sparklers and someone else had bought a pack of Dr Filibuster’s Fabulous Wet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks to set off through the window, a haze of smoke and sparks choking the room, and Lena kissed Kara and tasted the ale she’d been drinking, her blue eyes glazed and happy. She took her home in the early hours of the morning, escorting the stumbling, coltish form of her girlfriend into the bedroom and making her drink a hangover potion and a glass of tepid water as Lena tugged her boots off for her and then tucked her in. She woke first for work, tired but pleasantly so, cooking sausages in the pan and getting ready for work before leaving a note behind for Kara with the sausages left in the fridge for her.

 

            She worked until the following evening and then was called back in again a couple of hours after getting home, eventually getting to sleep off her shift and then met Kara for breakfast at a Muggle cafe, her girlfriend restless with excitement as she lurched to her seat at the sight of Lena entering, the loud scrape of her chair legs and the bizarre assortment of clothes she was wearing drawing all attention to Kara. Pink-cheeked beneath her scars, Kara kissed Lena and then thrust out an already-opened letter before they could take their seats.

 

            A letter from Professor Croaker relenting to her request and offering her an entry-level position as an Unspeakable again, outlining the salary, which Lena thought was shockingly low for someone of Kara’s skill but was more than Kara made anywhere aside from Hogwarts, and stable office hours, Monday to Friday, with the agreement for days off according to the full moon. Kara obviously accepted the offer and Lena watched her come back to life in a way Kara hadn’t been since Hogwarts, the quiet, defeated air that she’d dragged around since Lena had been treating her at St. Mungo’s slowly receding. 

 

            It was something of a relief for Lena too, the nights and weekends she had off now spent with Kara without that pall of dissatisfaction hanging over her girlfriend. She couldn’t tell Lena what she did at work, strictly confidential, but there was more drive to her, that old curiosity for learning, more animation to their discussions about various areas of magic that gently hinted at what Kara was working on. Lena directed her to the broad collection of books in her office, not solely dedicated to healing but a variety of other areas of magic as well. Through the ensuing weeks of cold weather, as January flew by, Kara was often found curled up with a book and working on old theories she hadn’t given up on.

 

            February rolled around and Lena was off the morning of Valentine’s Day and met Kara for an early lunch break at Madam Puddifoot’s in Hogsmeade, the place identical to all those times they’d met there during school with Lena in disguise. This time there were no disguises, just the two of them and a pot of tea to share, paper hearts in pink and red strung up around the place, scones with jam and butter to go with the tea. They’d bought each other flowers and Kara gifted Lena a book on Muggle medicine and Lena gifted her with a bursting bag of sweets selected from Honeydukes that morning.

 

            Before they knew it, it was March and Lena was still purposely avoiding her friends and spent increasing amounts of time with Kara, Sam and Kara’s friends. Sam had slipped into the group with far more ease than Lena, still somewhat stiff and aloof with a few of them, and them with her, wary of the odd relationship between the purported Pureblood Slytherin and werewolf. It didn’t matter to Lena what anyone thought, though, and she was content for the first time in her life, the ease with which she and Kara had managed to carve out their own private relationship, while not feeling the need to keep it a secret, something of a surprise to Lena, who had never thought she’d see the day.

 

            Alex and Kelly’s wedding was on the 18th of March, the Saturday before the next full moon on the 22nd. It was a small affair, the couple’s family and closest friends congregating at a scenic spot in the Cranbore Chase for the ceremony, Kara in her sky blue dress and dress robes, standing at her sister’s side while James stood at Kelly’s side in a navy suit and robes. It was a cool day but the sky was mostly blue and the sun was out, the ceremony quick amidst the scenic backdrop of nature and the magically conjured wildflowers dotting the field. 

 

            They all made their way back to Kelly’s mother’s house afterwards, the neat little stone house that had once been a gatehouse set on an acre of neatly tended grounds, a marquee erected with tables set up beneath it, alcohol and food free-flowing as the afternoon wore on. Kara was in good spirits and Lena left her to wander freely amidst her friends, enjoying the sunny day and the social opportunity as she chatted animatedly about her job and pointed out Lena to a few acquaintances who hadn’t met her girlfriend. Lena mostly sat at a table with a seemingly bottomless glass of wine, sweet smiles offered up to all those who paused to speak with her, Eliza checking in every time she caught sight of the Healer sitting alone. Lena didn’t mind being alone, it allowed her to observe and think, enjoying the reprieve from work, although her cryptex was safely tucked in an internal pocket of her indigo robes in case she was paged.

 

            After dinner, the drinking was well underway and a jazz band started up, enchanted globes of colourful light drifting over the dance floor, the marquee charmed to keep out the cold as a light rain pattered down outside, making the gardens smell fresh. Kara found her later on, after the cake had been cut, carrying two slices of chocolate cake covered in vanilla icing and sinking onto the chair beside Lena. She leaned in and gave Lena a quick kiss, her faintly glazed eyes creasing behind her glasses.

 

            “Hi,” Lena murmured, her arm going around Kara, soothingly rubbing her back. “Having fun?”

 

            “Mhm. Are you?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “Here,” Kara said, nudging one of the plates closer.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            She picked at her slice of cake, good but too rich and sweet for Lena’s taste, and then gave Kara the rest of it. Watching her girlfriend closely, the makeup masked the beginnings of Kara’s peakiness, the full moon far enough away for Kara to not feel the effects of it, even if her complexion was starting to pale. By the following Tuesday, she’d be practically ghostly and Lena drew in a shallow breath.

 

            “Don’t forget to take your dose,” she reminded Kara.

 

            “I won’t,” Kara said with a smile, patting her pockets. “I’ve got it right here. Doesn’t go too well with chocolate cake though, I’d imagine.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, Lena hummed in agreement. “Probably not - with wine or beer either.”

 

            “I won’t forget. I’ve still got … a couple of hours.”

 

            “Right, just maybe don’t leave it until the last minute,” Lena wryly instructed her.

 

            “Yes, Healer Luthor,” Kara lightly replied, kissing Lena as her eyes shone with amusement before she climbed to her feet and held out her hand. “Now, come and dance with me.”

 

            Shrinking away slightly, wary surprise crossing her face, Lena scoffed. “Dance? When have you ever known me to dance?”

 

            “Once. In our tower.”

 

            “One time too many,” Lena wryly replied. “My left feet don’t have your Quidditch grace.”

 

            “Ah, but you’re forgetting one very key promise I made you back then; I won’t let you fall.”

 

            Rising to her feet, slipping her hand in Kara’s, Lena gave her a stern look, a little apprehensive. “You also promised not to laugh.”

 

            “I was too preoccupied to laugh even if I’d wanted to.”

 

            “And why was that?”

 

            Towing her to the edge of the dance floor, Kara paused, her lips near Lena’s ear to make herself audible over the sound of the jazz music, Kara’s voice was flushed with amusement and a sort of wry exasperation for the past.

 

            “That was the first time I wanted to kiss you.”

 

            Lena remembered that night vividly, the two of them dancing to no music, the awkward fumbling in a slow circle as her heart pounded quickly and she felt the tension between them, the anticipation of it. It had been unbearable , waiting for that kiss that had never come. She’d been so sure and then had been forced to reevaluate everything afterwards, after that meek, friendly peck on the cheek and hasty exit. 

 

            “Why didn’t you?” Lena asked, her voice hoarse, her face furrowing with bewilderment, that old agony and embarrassment over how confusing that period of her life had been flickering to life.

 

            Kara likewise seemed to be struggling with resurfacing feelings, her face flushing, her scars a livid silver against the high colour as she looked down, their foreheads almost touching. Swallowing thickly, audibly, Kara stammered slightly as she tried to get the words out, drunk and honest and slurring her words together as she wrestled with getting them out.

 

            “I- I almost did, I- but then … I couldn’t. We were- we were dancing and I- I loved you so much and then … I almost did. I almost - almost - kissed you and, um, then we- we turned and I-”

 

            Cutting off, letting out a huff of frustration as she failed to get the words out, Kara grabbed Lena’s hand and wound through the wedding guests milling about, leading Lena straight out into the drizzle. She quickened her pace and Lena had to take small, hurried footsteps to keep up with Kara’s longer stride as they hunched their shoulders and walked through the dark.

 

            They didn’t go far, just to the back of the house, the lights of the party reflected in the dark glass of the windows, providing enough light to see their reflections looking back at them. Or, rather, Lena’s, as Kara kept her head ducked down.

 

            “We were dancing and then we turned. And I saw my reflection in the window, like this, and I- well, I’ve never- I’ve never liked how I looked, you know that, and, um, I guess … I just- it hit me then; how was someone like you ever going to love someone like me? So I didn’t kiss you. How could someone as perfect as you want to be kissed by someone who looks the way I do? Except, the funny thing is, I had fewer scars then. So what must I look like now?”

 

            “Look,” Lena softly ordered her. 

 

            Raising her head, damp curls brushed out of her face as Lena cupped her cheeks, watching Kara’s face take in her reflection with a fierce intensity in her green eyes. Mouth twisting derisively, Kara swallowed and looked at Lena, shrugging half-heartedly.

 

            “I know what I look like, as much as I avoid it,” she said with some bitterness. “I just- I- I hated myself so much back then and … it wasn’t half as bad.”

 

            “It’s not bad at all,” Lena murmured, her fingers tracing Kara’s scars, her gaze tenderly soft, the pupils blown slightly wide. Her mouth was dry and the breath caught in her throat as she followed the line of a scar to the edge of Kara’s jaw. “Not in the slightest. You’re mesmerising to me. I wanted you to kiss me that night too. I can’t begin to describe how disappointed I was that it was only on the cheek. I loved you so much as well, so much that it hurt. But I have never thought you were anything less than beautiful.”

 

            Kara’s expression was brooding, her cheeks cradled between Lena’s cold palms. Her lips were almost a pout, eyes so vulnerably doubtful that Lena let out a strangled laugh, a quick smile unevenly twisting her mouth. 

 

            “You don’t believe me?”

 

            Hesitating, Kara shook her head in Lena’s grasp, mumbling some vague dismissal. Clicking her tongue in a wryly chastising manner, Lena heavily sighed, her fingertips gliding over Kara’s wet skin, tracing her temple and chin around the arm of her glasses. Then she straightened and held out her hand, arching an eyebrow slightly.

 

            “Kara Danvers, will you dance with me?”

 

            Quietly snorting, Kara took her hand and guided it to her shoulder before she cradled Lena’s waist and pulled her closer. Letting out a soft sigh, she propped her chin on Lena’s shoulder and closed her eyes.

 

            “Now, where do I begin?” Lena murmured, almost as if to herself.

 

            They swayed slowly, rotating in a small circle on the wet grass, the fine drizzle settling in their hair, lightly beading on their robes, but they were wrapped up in their own little bubble, the wedding fading away for a minute. Lena drew back slightly, raising her eyebrows, and Kara let out a quick laugh, wrinkling her nose with bewildered amusement.

 

            “The crinkle right here when you wrinkle your nose,” Lena whispered as she reached out to touch the spot. “The lines right here when you smile - yes, like that. This scar right there on your chin; you had that one at school and I used to think about what it would be like to touch it, to kiss it, the way it would move when you smiled. This one on your cheek that makes it look like you have a really deep dimple when you smile as well. Your hands … well, I was positively obsessed with them. I think the practicality of things is often overlooked and your hands, well, they just seemed so capable. You had callouses, right along here, from Quidditch training, from holding your broom and your Beater’s bat, and I used to love watching you do things. Moving a chess piece, holding a quill, turning a page. I would fantasise about touching the little scars on your knuckles. You know, silly teenage things you do when you fancy someone. The slope of your shoulders when you were trying to make yourself smaller, shorter, unnoticed. Your curls - I had to stop myself from brushing them out of your face so often that it’s a miracle I never made a fool out of myself - and your mouth, Merlin, I’d daydream about kissing you so much I had to kiss someone else to try and get you out of my head when you wouldn’t kiss me. And perhaps best of all, your eyes.”

 

            Lena fell silent for a moment as they stopped their abysmal attempt at dancing, staring into Kara’s eyes with the helpless look of someone completely besotted. Her smile was rueful as she gave Kara a wry look. “I hate the water but that’s a shade of blue I would happily drown in.”

 

            “None of that … makes sense,” Kara slowly replied, confused as she tried to take stock of it all.

 

            “No?” Lena said with surprise. “Well, that’s because I haven’t told you why I love you. It’s not for your looks, you know, although that alone would do it, I think. I’d tell you now but, well, I’m a bit preoccupied with more important things, like dancing, so you’ll have to remind me to tell you some other time.”

 

            Laughing, Kara pressed her face into the side of Lena’s neck, her breath warm and her lips soft as she kissed her jugular, and Lena felt her throat close up, her eyelids fluttering closed. Pulse elevated, Lena’s hands knotted in the fabric of Kara’s robes and when Kara straightened up, the salted curls of her fringe sticking to her forehead, she smiled impishly and cupped Lena’s face in her hands.

 

            “One day you’ll tell me,” Kara sighed.

 

            “Eventually. If you- if you wanted to stick around to hear it.”

 

            “If you’ll have me.”

 

            “Of course I will. I would never want anyone else.”

 

            “Not- not someone … prettier? With fewer scars? Someone who- who isn’t a- isn’t like me?”

 

            “Well, they wouldn’t be you and I don’t want anyone but you.”

 

            “That’s nice,” Kara whispered, touching their foreheads together, their noses brushing. “That’s really nice. Thank you.”

 

            Lena let out a quiet huff of laughter, her fingers brushing Kara’s jaw, feeling her warm breath fanning over her lips as they stood close together. “You’re going to have a banging headache in the morning.”

 

            “Mm. It was a good day though. I’m glad you came.”

 

            “Me too.”

 

            “I know that … these things aren’t easy for you. Thank you for coming.”

 

            Squeezing her arm, Lena gave her a wavering smile and then guided them back into their gentle swaying, “it’s been a good day. I’m glad Alex and Kelly invited me. This is actually the first wedding I’ve ever been to.”

 

            “Really? You didn’t go to any during the war?”

 

            “No. No hasty elopements for any of my friends; we were all too young. I, uh, I was actually the first …”

 

            “Oh. Right. Well, I guess there was a high chance your first wedding would have been your own,” Kara said with a light laugh. “Is it wrong for me to be happy it wasn’t?”

 

            Lena cupped the back of Kara’s neck, thumbing the feathery hairs at the nape of her neck as she smiled. “No, I’m happy it wasn’t as well.”

 

            “You don’t- you don’t want to get married?”

 

            Stiffening, making Kara stumble slightly as she anticipated the next step in the small square they were wearing on the grass, Lena stopped and gave her girlfriend a clouded look of wariness. 

 

            “I- well … I didn’t want to marry Jack. I don’t think I really know what I want. I mean … I want you but that’s about all I’m sure of. I guess I just- I never got to make my own decisions or had a lot of control over my life until I left school, and then … it sort of happened to me and I’m still trying to figure things out. Is that- is that … okay?”

 

            Blinking in surprise, jerking back slightly, Kara let out a shuddering laugh, the sound slurring together with sheepish amusement as she cupped the back of Lena’s head and kissed her temple. “You’re asking the wrong person. If it’s okay with you, it’s okay with me.”

 

            “But … what do you want?”

 

            “I- well, no. No, I never thought- I was so young when I was bitten that … it very quickly changed a lot of things for me. Um … I- I don’t know. Since then I’ve just never imagined anyone would want to so that just- it made my mind up for me, I guess. In a different way, I haven’t been able to make my own decisions or had a lot of control over my life either.”

 

            “What a pair, hm?” Lena murmured.

 

            Kara laughed, cupping Lena’s face in her hands and giving her a serious look as she swayed a little unsteadily in her heels. Hesitating, she leaned in and kissed Lena firmly, her lips cold but soft, the drizzle starting to soak into their robes now, leaving them a little damp and masking a few shivers. Lena’s teeth chattered slightly and a muscle twitched in her jaw as she clenched it and pressed back against the kiss. Slightly taller and a little enthusiastic after one too many drinks, Kara slipped on a wet clod of grass and pitched forward, driving the two of them back a few steps as Lena broke off the kiss and let out a soft yelp as she pitched over backwards into a rose bush with Kara following after her.

 

            “Ow, fuck,” Lena softly swore as she tried to pick herself up, robes catching on thorns, a few of which she could feel the score lines of as she dragged herself out of the bush. 

 

            Kara had landed next to her and was struggling more as the thorns kept her pinned amidst the crumpled bushes. Lena had to laugh, that haze of the precipice where tipsy gave way to drunk making it seem funny as she tried to haul her girlfriend out of the bushes. There were a few ripping sounds and their muffled laughter as Kara came free and staggered towards Lena, who steadied her with her hands as they staggered back a few steps, heels digging into the soft ground.

 

            “I have a thorn in my arse,” Kara mumbled with a snort of laughter.

 

            Muffling her own laughter, Lena shook her head. “What am I going to do with you? Come on, let me take a look.”

 

            She grabbed Kara’s hand and dragged her towards the house, the downstairs mudroom lit with the yellow glow of a light to help the guests find the bathroom. Inside, safe from the rain, Lena bypassed the ajar door to the toilet and continued down the hallway to a small living room, waving her hand to light the sconces on the wall and guiding Kara over to the loveseat. 

 

            “Take off your robe,” Lena said as she gave Kara a once over, plucking two thorns and a leaf from her curls, her updo starting to come undone, and then assessing the damage once the robes were off.

 

            Kara sagged onto the sofa, the slit of her satin dress baring her scratched legs, part of the dress torn and shredded from the momentum of her fall, and she gave Lena a heavy-lidded smile. Sinking to her knees before her, Lena took Kara’s palm in her own and smoothed a thumb over the bloody prick where a rose had caught her, healing it with wandless, non-verbal magic, the minor cut a trivial thing at her skill level. 

 

            Taking full stock of the red lines of rose thorn scratches on Kara’s shins, calves and thighs, Lena let her fingers glide over them, healing them all with ease, her eyes kept on her girlfriend’s face, expression darkening as her lips parted, fingers skirting higher. Leaning forward, Kara cupped Lena’s face in her hands and kissed her firmly, Lena pushing herself up higher on her knees, pressing back against her, her hands gripping Kara’s thighs. 

 

            In hindsight, that was probably the biggest mistake of the evening, wrapped up in each other as they lost track of time in what was supposed to be a quick tryst. It was a miracle they weren’t caught, Lena forgetting to lock or ward the door, what she’d intended to be an innocent check for scratches and caught thorns quickly transitioning into sex on Kelly’s mother’s sofa while the wedding party raged on outside. If they had only checked for thorns and scratches, they would have rejoined the party a lot sooner, and Kara might have noticed the dose of Wolfsbane Potion earlier when patting down her pockets as they left the room in the same state they’d found it in. 

 

            But they’d lost track of time and she found the dose too late, not knowing the time, not realising it was just past midnight as she hurriedly knocked the bitter potion back, thinking she still had plenty of time, and hastily followed after Lena. They were pleasantly drunk and quietly enamoured with each other, their fleeting touches, secretive glances as they sipped wine or beer, did shots of Firewhisky with the newlyweds and friends and endured the puffs of smoke as the photographer snapped photos of everyone before Alex and Kelly were sent off with showers of colourful sparks from the dozens of wands held aloft.

 

            The party went until the early hours of the morning and most of the guests were put up by Kelly’s mother, including Kara and Lena, who woke up in the morning sharing a quilt on the living room floor, sore and tired with hangovers setting in. The newlyweds were back for breakfast and Lena found herself frying bacon as Kara scrambled the eggs, a dozen of them crammed into the admittedly spacious kitchen, although it wasn’t made for that many people to be standing in at once. Lena inconspicuously started to pull out hangover cures from the little enlarged purse she’d brought with her, handing one to Kara first and murmuring to her.

 

            “Did you take your potion last night?”

 

            “Mhm,” Kara said with a wan smile. “Found the empty vial in my robe pocket this morning.”

 

            “Good. Get this one in you as well and you’ll be right as rain.”

 

            She knocked one back herself and continued to pull them out, making a neat row on the countertop as she flipped the bacon, catching Alex’s eye across the room and jerking her head towards them. Lurching to her feet with relief, Alex quickly crossed the room and let out a rough exclamation of relief, clapping Lena on the shoulder hard enough to startle her.

 

            “You know, I usually only feel this way about you at St. Mungo’s but thank Merlin you’re here, you’re a lifesaver.”

 

            “Don’t grow too fond of me,” Lena quietly drawled, rolling her eyes as she smiled thinly. “Or it might become a conflict of interest and you’ll have to find someone else to heal you.”

 

            Alex let out a quick laugh and gave her shoulder another quick pat before carrying a potion off to her wife, announcing to the rest of the room that Lena had brought enough for everyone. As they served up breakfast, going down the line of plates and pans, everyone collected a potion as well - including Eliza, Lena was surprised to see - a chorus of thanks sent the Healer’s way as everyone seemed to perk up a little.

 

            Lena had booked that day off as well and was content to spend it doing little else but enjoying the quiet congregation of people as they ate and talked and sipped too much tea, dispersing through the house and grounds. She found Eliza near the rose bush Lena had found herself in last night with Kara, trying not to look too sheepish as she nursed a cup of tea and watched the Herbologist coax it back to its former glory.

 

            Eliza cast Lena a fleeting look, her face warming with a smile before turning her attention back to the bush, clicking her tongue. “I don’t know what was going on out here last night but the state of these rose bushes …”

 

            “Can I help?”

 

            “Oh, no, you enjoy the fresh air, sweetheart. I’m just indulging myself in this beautiful garden.”

 

            “Some coffee or tea then?”

 

            Hesitating, kneeling with her elbows on her thighs, Eliza smiled. “Go on then, I’ll have a coffee.”

 

            “Milk and one sugar, isn’t it?”

 

            “That’s it.”

 

            Nodding, Lena vanished back indoors and busied herself in the kitchen, making small talk with Nia and Querl as she made the cup of coffee and then stepped back out into the pale sunshine. Rejoining Eliza, Lena handed her the coffee and was a little shy at the delight and gratitude of Kara’s mother, hanging around as she sipped her tea and caught sight of Kara approaching from the other side of the gardens.

 

            “Hi, where were you off to?” Lena asked.

 

            “Just stretching my legs; this garden is massive . Imagine living here, mum, you’d have so much room to work.”

 

            “Mm, that would be nice, wouldn’t it?”

 

            Lena didn’t reply, thinking of where she’d grown up, the monstrously big manor house set on acres of neatly cultivated land. It didn’t hold the charm or comfort of the Olsen’s childhood home though, or even that of the little cottage Kara lived in, and Lena knew it was from a warped perception when she silently thought she would have traded houses with Kara in a heartbeat. Looking around, Lena thought about how nice it would be to buy a house like that for herself one day - her and Kara. It caught her by surprise to think of the prospect of them living together one day, even though she was twenty-six and in a relationship. Lena hadn’t even lived with Jack, not even after he’d proposed, valuing her space too much to share it with someone else, and she turned her head quickly to look at Kara, almost shocked at her train of thought.

 

            “What?” Kara asked, raising her eyebrows as she nudged her glasses up her nose.

 

            “Nothing,” Lena quickly replied. “Just thinking how nice it would be.”

 

            “You probably grew up somewhere just like this,” Kara snorted, crossing over to Lena and wrapping her arms around her.

 

            Humming noncommittally, Lena narrowed her eyes, a brooding look on her face as she sipped the dregs of her tea. “Something like that.”

 

            Kara’s lips were close to Lena’s ear as she whispered a response. “And you never have to go back again. I’ll make sure of it.”

 

            Squeezing her arm, Lena gave her a rueful smile and then extracted herself from Kara’s embrace. Taking Eliza’s cup, Lena carried both of them in and helped tidy up, people starting to depart, Kara setting the dishes to wash themselves and turning to hug her friends goodbye. Alex and Kelly would be going to Greece that evening for their honeymoon and Lena was invited back to Kara’s for lunch, sitting in the living room with a plate balanced on her lap as she ate her tuna sandwich and watched Alex and Kelly go through the pile of gifts while Kara kept a running list of who had bought that what. 

 

            From Kara and Lena, there was a gilt photo frame for a wedding photo, a bottle of champagne for them to share on their honeymoon and a new trunks each with their initials stamped on the leather. Lena had forked over her half of the cost to Kara and then left a secret purse full of Galleons on the laden table after the reception without a tag or any mention to Kara. She wasn’t as sneaky as she thought she’d been though, Kelly holding up the purse and looking around amid the mess of opened boxes and wrapping paper.

 

            “This one doesn’t have a note. Did it come with a card, Alex?”
