The tension of her frustration quickly gave way to the tension of desire, and she found her hands on Kara’s back, beneath her sweater vest, tugging up the hem of her tucked-in shirt.

 

            Raising her head, Kara kissed Lena, the taste of Firewhisky on her tongue, and Lena softly moaned into it, her hands pulling everywhere, trying to get Kara undressed. With the mess of the full moon and the Werewolf Capture Unit carrying Kara off, coupled with long, consecutive days of work leaving her away from her girlfriend for so long, what Lena wanted most right then was to touch her, remind herself that everything was okay, that she still knew every inch of her body intimately, and nothing had separated them. Impatient, Lena cast a non-verbal spell that had Kara’s clothes unravelling at the seams as she pushed her towards the bedroom door, squawking indignantly as each piece fell off.

 

            Afterwards, she idly ran her fingertip over the silvery scars latticing Kara’s skin, her head on her chest as she listened to her heartbeat while Kara lazily stroked her dark hair. Loose-limbed and pleasantly exhausted, Lena had her eyes closed as she felt by touch alone, some of her knotted frustration spent but not enough to banish the worry that crept in.

 

            “You’re quiet,” Kara murmured.

 

            If Lena hadn’t been so skilled at Occlumency, she might have thought Kara had read her mind. Humming contentedly at the back of her throat, she stilled her idle tracing and pressed her palm flat against Kara’s stomach.

 

            “I’m thinking.”

 

            “You’re worrying. What can I do to help you stop?”

 

            “Nothing,” Lena whispered, afraid to speak any louder in case her voice shook. “I always worry about you.”

 

            “Don’t worry about me. Go to sleep.”

 

            With a soft laugh, Lena pushed herself up and kissed Kara. They went to bed then, leaving a candle burning and the window cracked open to let in the cool breeze as they wrapped themselves up in the blankets. Lena slept uneasily though, tossing restlessly throughout most of the night as she worried over the next full moon, about what Lillian might do and Kara back in a cell. She had to slip out of bed the other side of midnight to fetch a potion to knock her out, just so she could get enough sleep to compensate for how long she’d been awake. It did the trick and she didn’t move until mid-morning.

 

            Kara was sitting on the sofa with Morrigan on her shoulder, sharing a piece of toast with the owl as she thumbed through one of the books from Lena’s extensive collection, and she smiled at Lena around a piece of toast sticking out of her mouth and let out a muffled sound of surprise as the owl took the rest from her. They didn’t speak about anything they’d discussed the evening before, didn’t mention the full moon at all, just enjoyed a lazy morning around the flat and a walk through Diagon Alley to get ice cream from Florean Fortescue’s before Kara went home.

 

            They tiptoed around it for the next few weeks as well, an unease between them until Lena naïvely thought Lillian had forgotten about her threats, and in turn, thought she could talk Kara out of going to St. Mungo’s if she wasn’t there. They forgot about their unease as the rest of the month passed by with relative normalcy; Alex and Kelly came back from their honeymoon with stories and souvenirs, their annoyance at being momentarily dragged home abated with the time spent back in Greece, Lena’s busy work schedule leaving her with less time than she would have liked, with all of the Hogwarts students on the summer holidays, leading to an influx of accidents and magical mishaps, and there were numerous dinners and breakfasts at the cottage and her flat, drinks at The Leaky Cauldron with Sam and Kara’s friends and shopping trips in between, as well as the odd walk through Dublin while the nice weather held. 

 

            June passed by quickly and all too soon the next full moon was upon them again with a jitteriness to both women as the unease they’d managed to squash reared back up. With Lillian’s silence on the matter, Lena tried on numerous occasions to talk Kara out of it, but she was stubbornly insistent that she go to St. Mungo’s, that it was safer for everyone. Unfortunately, Eliza and Alex were supportive of Kara’s decision, eager to avoid any future dealings with the Werewolf Capture Unit, and Lena felt the wounded sting of being on the losing side as she was outnumbered by the Danvers women, despite her insistence that as a Healer, she knew better than anyone what Kara needed.

 

            The day of the next full moon, Kara spent the morning and afternoon at Lena’s flat, napping on the sofa as Lena studied old books and essays on Lycanthropy, scouring the texts for anything she might have missed in the past as she jotted down notes. For all the help the Wolfsbane Potion had been, Lena hadn’t lost sight of her true cause - finding a cure. Even something to stop the transformations entirely would be enough for her, and ambitious in its own right, with how difficult merely allowing a werewolf to keep its mind while transformed had turned out to be. She was committed though, and passed by her day with ink-stained fingers and a thoughtful furrow on her face as she left Kara undisturbed until it was time to take her last dose of the potion and get ready to leave.

 

            Flooing to St. Mungo’s with enough time to allow for a quick assessment and to get her down to the cells in the basement, and hopefully avoid Lena’s mother as well, they dusted the ash from the fireplace off their clothes and Lena carried Kara’s bag as she pressed a hand to her back to guide her along. They didn’t make it more than a few feet before Kara pulled up short at the sight of a blonde woman sitting in the waiting room amidst patients waiting to be admitted.

 

            “Mum,” Kara said with surprise. “I- what-”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Eliza looked relieved to see her as she reached out to rub Kara’s arm, but there was a tightness to the corners of her mouth. “I wanted to be sure.”

 

            Wincing as her cheeks reddened, Kara rubbed her scarred chin. “I’m not a child.”

 

            “Well, you’re my child, Kara Danvers, and after the stunt you two pulled last month-”

 

            “Okay, okay,” Kara quietly interrupted, peeved but eager to wrap things up before a passing Healer overheard her mother reveal something that could incriminate Lena. “I need to get ready.”

 

            The three of them stepped onto the Dai Llewellyn Ward and the Healer assigned to Kara directed her to a bed, drawing the curtain around. Eliza took the seat set off to the side and Lena folded her arms over her chest as she watched Kara get undressed and change into the hospital gown. Neatly folding her clothes and setting them in the bag she’d packed, Kara set her wand on the nightstand and sank onto the thin bed. A few minutes later, the Healer was back to check her vitals and Lena had to bite her tongue as she watched the Resident nervously fumble through the routine under her intimidating stare.

 

            They were quiet, the Ward relatively empty this full moon, and Lena was agitated, hating that Kara was putting herself through this. If they’d just been a bit more careful with timing, none of it would be happening, but at least Lena could comfort herself with the knowledge that Kara had taken every dose of the Wolfsbane Potion this last week, and one more before coming to St. Mungo’s, so even if she transformed inside the dank hospital cell, it wouldn’t be to mindless rage as she turned on herself. She would be able to go to sleep, the conditions less than ideal but as good as they could be for now. Lena would continue to try to talk her out of it.

 

            As she brooded over what could have been different, Lena tuned out the sounds of the Ward as she kept her eyes on Kara, her attention so far elsewhere that it startled her when the curtain was torn open. Blinking, she stared at her mother and felt her stomach plummet with dread. Ignoring mother and patient, Lillian’s piercing stare landed on her daughter.

 

            “You,” she coldly singled her out and sharply pointed to the next bed bay.

 

            Swallowing thickly, Lena unfolded her arms and made her feet move, her eyes lingering on Kara a moment, seeing the unease there, before she gave her a shallow nod and turned. Eliza watched the exchange with a furrowed look of confusion on her face and Lena didn’t look at her as she slipped through the curtain to the next bed. 

 

            Her mother followed after her and Lena felt her pulse jump as the curtain was pulled back around, closing them off from sight. An uncertain Intern stepped through with a hospital gown and warily held it out.

 

            “You’re having a laugh,” Lena hissed.

 

            “You’re being admitted as a patient. This is what all patients must wear. Get changed.”

 

            “Are you really going to go through so much effort just to embarrass yourself when I prove you wrong?”

 

            “I can assure you, it won’t be me who comes out of this embarrassed. Get changed.”

 

            Tearing the curtain open, Lillian stepped outside, followed by the Intern, and Lena could feel her cheeks burn with anger as she roughly shrugged her coat off. Untucking her shirt, she unbuttoned it and paused at the sight of her left forearm, mouth thinning as her mind raced. The hospital gown had short sleeves, a mortifying prospect for Lena, and she hurriedly cast a glamour over her skin, making it appear smooth and unblemished. It was still there, and deeper than the surface of her skin, but at least the Intern wouldn’t instigate a fresh batch of rumours.

 

            Kicking off her loafers and shedding her jeans, Lena unclipped her bra and then slid on the rough hospital gown, the sturdy cotton cold against her bare skin as she tied the back closed. She was folding everything into a neat pile on the chair when the curtain was opened again. Straightening, she gave her mother a blank look and watched as the Intern stepped past her.

 

            “I just need to check your vitals, Healer Luthor.”

 

            Letting out a scoff of laughter, Lena smiled thinly and moved to the edge of the bed. The whole thing was a farce but she complied with a haughty lift to her chin as the Intern checked her blood pressure, heart rate and pupillary response before sheepishly feeling her glands and checking her throat. The whole time, Lena was straining her ears to keep track of what was going on with Kara, wishing she was at her bedside and cursing her mother for her pettiness in keeping them apart.

 

            “Take her blood as well,” Lillian instructed the Intern.

 

            “Why?” Lena exclaimed, her temper rearing up.

 

            “It’s standard hospital practice to screen the blood to help with diagnostics, as you well know. Who knows what you’ve taken.”

 

            “Well, given the reason you’re subjecting me to this, you know regardless of what I’ve taken you’ll get your answer. There’s no cure for Lycanthropy.”

 

            Her throat tightened around the last part, a deep ache in her chest. Giving her a faint sneer, Lillian arched an eyebrow. “It’s standard practice.”

 

            Grinding her teeth together, Lena stared daggers at her. “Fine.”

 

            The Intern vanished for a moment and then returned with a tray, setting it down and stepping in closer. His hands shook with nerves as Lena held out her right arm, noticing her mother’s gaze dart to the left and then back to the right with nothing more than the faintest twitch of her lips, and he fumbled with the tourniquet for a moment until Lillian clicked her tongue with impatience.

 

            “You should already know this,” she berated the young man, taking the tourniquet from him and wrapping it around Lena’s bicep, cinching it tight. “Here, it’s not difficult. Hand me a wipe.”

 

            Mumbling an apology as he held out the wipe, he backed away as Lillian swiped it across the crook of Lena’s elbow. She curtly ordered him about as Lena rigidly sat on the bed, her skin clammy at the feeling of her mother’s hands on her. Lena couldn’t look anywhere else but at them, the slender fingers digging into her skin as she angled Lena’s arm and was handed a needle. Lillian wasn’t gentle as she stabbed it beneath the skin but Lena barely felt the sting, her ears ringing faintly as she felt a tightness in her chest. 

 

            Her mother worked efficiently and Lena watched as vivid red blood was drawn, quickly filling a couple of vials and then whisking them off for testing. Letting the Intern press a cotton ball to the crook of her elbow, Lena listened to the beat of her heart drum in her ears as she stared at the gap in the curtains where her mother had left.

 

            Hand clamped over the cotton ball, Lena climbed off the bed as the Intern tried to caution her against it. Giving him a firm look, Lena pushed through the curtain to Kara’s bed and felt her cheeks flood with pink as both women looked up at the intrusion. Quietly seething, Lena tried to feign nonchalance as she gave Kara a grimace of a smile.

 

            “Sorry about that.”

 

            “She’s really making you go down there?” Kara asked, horrified.

 

            “Of course,” Lena lightly murmured, green eyes glittering with anger.

 

            Eliza looked between the two of them cluelessly. “What’s going on?”

 

            “It’s nothing. Just a quick check-up.”

 

            Giving her a blank look, Eliza just rubbed her forehead and closed her eyes, murmuring something with a sigh. Shifting restlessly from foot to foot, the cold radiating through the soles of her socks as she kept her arms folded over her stomach, Lena smiled thinly at Kara, who looked pale with worry - although the more likely probability was the approaching full moon was starting to get to her. Even as Lena watched, she could see Kara’s hairline growing damp, the circles beneath her eyes seeming more prominent.

 

            Walking over to her bedside, Lena reached out to check her pulse, glancing down at her wrist and then clicking her tongue as she unclasped it and set it beside Kara’s once she was done. “Your pulse is a little fast.”

 

            “You’re not on duty.”

 

            Lena gave her a fleeting glance as a smile twitched the corners of her mouth. She knew that Kara was worried, that it had been a long time since she’d had to confine herself to a cell, not since all those months ago when she’d still been on the Wolfsbane trial. The sight of Lena in a hospital gown wasn’t helping either and Kara’s eyes anxiously strayed to her left forearm, surprised to see nothing but smooth skin there.

 

            Perching on the edge of the bed, Lena tried to make idle chit-chat to pass the time but Kara was looking queasier with each passing minute, and Eliza was tense as she waited. It would be a long night for them all and Lena felt a prickle of guilt for letting things get so far out of hand that Kara’s mother had been dragged to St. Mungo’s for the night. As soon as she was allowed back up, she was determined to get her to leave, stubbornly insistent that she could watch over Kara alone. After all, Lena had done it on and off for years with relative success.

 

            Fifteen minutes later, they were roused by the arrival of Kara’s Healer and Lillian, who caught sight of Lena through the parted curtains and gave her a sharp look, her meaning clear. Suppressing a sigh, Lena climbed off the bed and kissed Kara’s cheek, murmuring a reassurance as she squeezed her hand. 

 

            “I’ll see you in the morning,” she promised.

 

            Nodding, giving her hand a squeeze in return, Kara’s expression was serious as Lena turned away, making her way back to her own bay. Sitting on the edge of the bed, she gave her mother a sullen look as Lillian stepped back inside.

 

            “Well?”

 

            “Normal.”

 

            Raising her eyebrows slightly, a goading look, Lena gave her mother a tight smile. “As expected. Anything else to drag it out?”

 

            “No,” Lillian curtly replied before a smugness coloured her voice, “it’s about time to take you down.”

 

            “If we can hurry it up, then.”

 

            Looking amused, Lillian gestured for Lena to go ahead. Pausing a moment, Lena got to her feet and made sure she’d left everything in a neat pile before she brushed through the curtains with a stubborn set to her jaw and shoulders. The air was cool and she hugged her arms to herself as she walked out the doors and down the hallway with her chin raised, her sharp gaze meeting the eyes of a nurse or two as she walked to the elevator.

 

            The cage rattled to a stop and she drew back the metal grill door to step inside, pressing the button for the sub-basement as her mother stepped inside and drew the grill back across. Silence hung heavily between them as they descended through the hospital, making only two stops for a Mediwizard to climb in and get off on the ground floor before they reached their floor. 

 

            The smell of damp stone wafted towards them as Lillian dragged the grill door open and stepped out. She walked down the long, dark hallway with Lena in her wake, unease already knotting her stomach at the dimness of the place, before Lillian gestured to a heavy cell door to open and gave Lena an expectant look. Feeling nothing but resentment for her mother, Lena silently stepped inside, determined to abide by whatever silly thing her mother made her do, if only to prove that she was wrong. 

 

            Inside the cell, the stench of blood, sweat and fear couldn’t be eclipsed by the scouring with bleach and disinfectant the place was given by the cleaners after every inhabitant left, and Lena breathed shallowly through her mouth. It was unpalatable and she was impatient for it to be over. 

 

            “Undress,” Lillian instructed her.

 

            Lena let out a choked laugh of panic. “Seriously?”

 

            “It’s hospital policy for Lycanthropes.”

 

            “Don’t quote hospital policy to me,” Lena contemptuously replied.

 

            She roughly tugged at the ties of her gown, pulling it free and shoving it at Lillian. It was cold enough as it was in the stone cells, and she folded her arms over her chest and hunched her shoulders as the frigid air made her skin ripple with goosebumps.

 

            “And the rest.”

 

            “You’re being absurd.”

 

            “It’s hospital policy for-“

 

            Lena angrily pulled off her socks and underwear and added them to the pile, her skin crawling at the feeling of her mother’s eyes inspecting her. Silently fuming as her heart pounded and her skin turned clammy with panic, Lena looked at her mother through her lashes, eyes dark and surly in the low lighting.

 

            “No obvious bite marks,” Lillian softly noted.

 

            “None at all.”

 

            “We shall see.”

 

            She stepped back through the doorway and waved a hand, hinges screeching as the heavy door closed, punctuated by the loud sound of bolts and locks sliding home before a slot was drawn across to reveal a glimpse of the hallway and her mother’s watchful gaze. It was even darker then, the air feeling close, the odour of the room stronger, and Lena very much wanted to get out of the cell as quickly as possible. 

 

            It couldn’t be more than ten minutes until sundown then, the required time for all infected patients to be locked up upon them, and she stayed rooted to the spot, shivering slightly with her arms wrapped around herself for warmth as she waited it out. Through the slot in the door, she saw Healers lead patients to their cells and had to stop herself from pressing up against it at the sight of Kara passing behind her mother, eyes trying to pick her out as she passed by Lillian. It was too dark and the slotted window too narrow though and Lena felt a deep ache and a newfound empathy for her girlfriend and how it felt to be on the other end of the parts they’d played for so long.

 

            Despite the thickness of the walls and doors, spelled so thoroughly that there would be no hope of a werewolf escaping, Lena heard the first hair-raising screams as the moon rose. Breaths turning shallow as a cold sweat sprung up on her skin, Lena was almost desperate in her need to know which cell Kara was in and if she was okay. She knew she would be, of course, but without seeing her safely to her cell herself, Lena wasn’t reassured.

 

            Listening to the awful screams turn into strangled snarls and then keening howls, oddly beautiful and gut-wrenchingly melancholy, she stood a few feet from the door, completely human. Her mother hadn’t moved an inch and Lena could just make out the glint of her eyes in the dim lights of the hallway, watching her daughter prove her wrong, as they’d both known she would.

 

            “Satisfied? Is this proof enough for you? You can let me out now.”

 

            “I’m afraid not,” Lillian drawled, spiteful delight lacing her words. “It’s hospital policy for patients admitted to these cells for Lycanthropy to be contained until sunrise. As a precaution. I’m sure you know all too well the risk of a werewolf getting out.”

 

            “You can’t leave me here all night.”

 

            “You’ll find that I can.”

 

            Panic knifed through Lena’s chest as she stumbled towards the door, mouth opening and closing. She really didn’t want to beg and she could see her mother was hoping she would. Not that it would have made even the tiniest difference if she had; Lillian would only get enjoyment from it and Lena would end up all the weaker for pleading.

 

            “I- well, can I at least get a blanket? A candle for light?”

 

            “No. Patients in the cells aren’t permitted anything that can be a hazard.”

 

            Seething, a muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw and she let out a cold huff of laughter. Shaking her head, she turned her back on her mother and paced a few steps, back stiff as she tried to rein her anger in, to bite her tongue.

 

            “See you in the morning,” her mother mockingly replied, followed by the sound of the slot window being drawn shut, plunging Lena into full darkness.

 

            Blinded by the pitch black of the cell, Lena lost all sense of depth perception as she whirled around and slammed the side of her first against the door. Pain blossomed and the door didn’t so much as shudder, the loud thump quickly giving way to deafening silence.

 

            Drawing in quick, shallow breaths, Lena blinked a few times, willing her eyes to adjust, to pick out even the merest prick of light around the doorframe or the window slot. But there was nothing, just a blinding darkness as she staggered back a few steps, the soles of her bare feet scraping over icy stone. Feeling her chest constrict as her fear of the dark obliterated almost every other feeling, she shivered, the cold sweat on her skin only served to make her feel even colder, bare-skinned with nothing to wrap around herself for warmth.

 

            Pacing away from the door, Lena inhaled and felt sick as the tang of blood and sweat emanated from the very walls and floors. Inhaling through her mouth to fight the stomach-turning odour, although she felt nauseous for reasons beyond the mere stench, she paced back the other way. Lip trembling as she let out a shaky breath, almost mistaken for a sob but anything but that - she wouldn’t cry, not over that, not over her childhood fears she’d sworn would never get the better of her again - she scratched at her left forearm, feeling the shiny little letters carved in her arm, invisible to the eye with her glamour masking it but very much tangible.

 

            In the dark, cold and sightless, she clung to the comforting feeling of the old scar. Pacing back and forth, trying to reassure herself, whispering quietly to herself in the dark, her voice shaky and cracking faintly, Lena scratched and scratched until the skin was tender, and then raw, deep gouges as she dug her nails in. Time passed slowly as she tried to quell her fear of the dark with the sting of her nails as she split the skin.

 

            Hours passed, and her anxious pacing dissolved into wracking shivers as she sank to her haunches, crouching on the sterile stone floor with her shoulders hunched, trying to warm herself up. All the while, she worked at her arm, not stopping even when she felt the sting of breaking the skin, not even when she felt the stickiness of blood, or deeper still when the stickiness became wet and warm. 

 

            Eyes gritty with exhaustion and body stiff from the cold and fear, Lena had to fight to keep her gorge down, so queasy and light-headed she almost wished she’d pass out so she didn’t have to endure the remainder of the night. Swallowing the taste of bile, staring blindly into the dark as air sawed in and out of her lungs in rasping breaths, she didn’t even know where she was situated in the room, had no sense of the four walls, only the radiating cold of the stone like ice through her bare soles.

 

            It felt like an eternity before she heard the strangled whines and muffled cries of werewolves transforming back into humans whispering through the basement. Staggering to her feet, teeth chattering and feet clumsy as her stiff joints ached, Lena blindly searched for the door, hearing the heavy scrape of it unlocking echo through her cell a minute later as she stumbled towards it. The door opened, the brightness of the dim hallway suddenly so bright that her eyes stung, and she practically bowled over the Healer silhouetted in the doorway in her haste to get out, breathing heavily as she tried to clear her senses of the close air tainted by her sweat and fear. 

 

            A blanket enveloped her as a familiar voice softly reassured her. “It’s okay, just take a moment.”

 

            Blinking, she scraped her hair out of her face and met Sam’s wide-eyed look. A shiver ran through Lena and she clutched the blanket tighter around herself. “I’m fine,” she rasped, her throat dry and tight. “Kara-”

 

            Turning, looking down the length of the hallway as she tried to spot which cell her girlfriend was in, Lena felt her stomach twist with worry. “She’ll be alright. Let them do their job; you can wait for her on the Ward. I brought your clothes for you.”

 

            Sam crouched to pick up the pile of clothes Lena had left up in her bay and held them out. Reaching for them, Lena hastily dressed as she watched the activity in the other cells, patients being brought on stretchers. She was distracted as she spoke, fumbling with the buttons of her shirt. 

 

            “You’re a Charms Attending; what’re you doing down here?”

 

            “Healer Parker was leaving as I arrived and filled me in on your mum’s stunt.”

 

            Lena hummed at the back of her throat, rubbing her tired eyes as she tried to take stock of things, trying to ground herself. The Healers were levitating stretchers to the lift then and Lena was quick to fall into step beside one with a blonde woman fast asleep. Kara’s lashes fluttered and she looked pale in the low lighting, the blanket hiding her body from view but the Wolfsbane Potion surely leaving her unscathed, as usual. Lena stubbornly insisted on riding in the same lift and the Resident assigned to Kara was too meek to object to the two Attendings.

 

            “Get her to her bed and then help one of the others,” Lena instructed the Resident as they made their way up through the hospital.

 

            They stopped at the ground floor and then continued upwards as Lena kept the grill door shut, glowering at the Intern and visitors before they carried on, the lift spitting them out on their floor. The Bite Ward was a flurry of activity and the Resident did as Lena bid, Eliza climbing to her feet as the curtain parted to admit them. Lena had her blanket wrapped around her shoulders as she rattled off instructions to the Resident.

 

            “Get me a Reinvigoration Draught. I need hot water and a clean gown as well.”

 

            “You,” Sam firmly said as the Resident hurried off, “need to sit down. You’re not on the clock, and more importantly, your mum will have a fit if she finds out you’re working on the Bite Ward. Not to mention Healer Smethwyck will kick you out if you don’t behave.”

 

            “They’re the least of my worries right now,” Lena darkly muttered as she picked up her watch and pressed two fingers to Kara’s fluttering pulse.

 

            Eliza was confused by the whole thing, her eyes darting from Kara to Lena and back again. “Lena, I- what happened? Where were you? You look- you’re bleeding. ”

 

            Slowing at Eliza’s soft exclamation, Lena looked down at her hands, spreading her fingers as she looked down at the bloody nails of her right hand. Her attention moved to the long sleeve of her left arm and the stain where the old blood was seeping into the cotton, a faint flush colouring her pale neck as she cleared her throat.

 

            “I’m fine. Must have caught myself on a nail on the cell door.”

 

            “Let’s see-” Healer Smethwyck started as he opened the curtains, making the rounds of each patient and the Intern or Resident unfortunate enough to end up on his rotation during the full moon. Cutting off at the sight of Lena and Sam at Kara’s bedside, he made a sound of surprise, bristling indignantly. “Healer Luthor, Healer Arias, I don’t remember either of you being called for a Charms consult. Where’s my Resident?”

 

            The Resident chose that moment to reappear, arms full of potions, gauze and bandages, a hospital gown and a basin of water floating behind him. Lena glanced at Smethwyck and moved to take the Reinvigoration Draught from the Resident but halted as the man spoke.

 

            “Healer Luthor, this is my patient and you, yourself, are currently a patient. I kindly ask that you remove yourself from the Bite Ward or let my Intern discharge you.”

 

            Chafing at the polite line drawn in the sand, Lena let her hand fall back to her side and rounded the bed, pulling the curtain to her bay all the way back so she could clearly see Kara. Sitting on the edge of her bed, Lena curled her hands into fists in her lap and watched them work on her girlfriend. Kara was just sleeping for now, no sign of injuries as they assessed her, and Sam sat beside Lena for a short while, before she was paged, the two of them silent and tense as they waited for everyone to state the obvious, that Lena have been brewing a potion that hadn’t been made accessible to the public just yet.

 

            “She’ll need to sleep,” Smethwyck told Eliza, casting Lena a sideways glance. “Other than that, she’s miraculously unharmed. You can take her home once she wakes up.”

 

            Eliza quietly thanked him and he made his way to Lena’s bed, her file from the Intern Lillian had assigned to her in his hands. He gave her a kindly stare, pointed enough to let her know that he knew. “Well, you are not infected with Lycanthropy, so you’re free to go as soon as you’d like to.” Hesitating, he cleared his throat. “And if - if, mind you - there had been any involvement in Miss Danvers’ care by someone who has contributed greatly to the Wolfsbane trial, well … I’m sure that would be no cause for me to concern myself with. I’ve been treating her since she was a child, you know.”

 

            “Thank you, sir,” Lena murmured, a small smile at the corners of her mouth. “I’m sure if that had been the case … it would be very much appreciated.”

 

            He nodded and signed her paperwork and then tapped her left shoulder before leaving. “Take care of that cut.”

 

            Running a hand over her face, Lena sank onto the bed and stared up at the ceiling, closing her eyes to the lights overhead as she felt the dull throb of her arm. She wouldn’t be able to see the damage she’d inflicted on herself until she removed the glamour, and she couldn’t remove the glamour without some privacy and getting up to close the curtain now would only seem suspicious. Palm pressed to her forehead, she tried to think, tired and still cold and her emotions all over the place as her body tried to regulate itself. 

 

            The sound of a chair being drawn up to her bedside made her open her eyes, tensing as she raised her head off the pillows. It was just Eliza and she sank back against the mattress with a soft exhale. There was a moment of silence as Eliza studied her before she spoke.

 

            “You can tell me it’s none of my business but … what happened?”

 

            “There was talk of me being bitten. She just wanted to make sure I wasn’t.”

 

            “Your mother?”

 

            Lena’s face rippled with pain, her mouth turning down at the corners. She didn’t say anything else, feeling her face heat, and dug the heels of her hands into her eyes. Hearing the chair scrape, she didn’t move, just listened to Eliza’s footsteps move away from the bed and then return.

 

            “Auguamenti.”

 

            Opening her eyes, Lena turned her head to the side to take in the basin of water that had been left beside Kara’s bed, now refilled with fresh water. As she watched, Eliza tapped the rim of the basin with her wand and steam started to rise from the surface. Without speaking, Eliza produced a clean handkerchief and dipped it into the hot water, reaching out to take Lena’s hand, blood dried into the palm, and gently wiping the dried flakes away.

 

            “You don’t need to talk about it,” Eliza said after a long minute of silence. “I sense there’s more to it than you’re letting on, and you always try to put on such a brave face, but … it’ll be alright. The pain will pass.”

 

            Lena felt her throat close up and it hurt to swallow. Brow furrowed in a severe look, she stared up at the ceiling as she let Eliza wash her hand, and then the other one, before her fingers touched the cuff of Lena’s bloodied sleeve. Stiffening, Lena reached out to touch the back of Eliza’s hand, stilling her, and pushed herself up slightly as she attempted to clear her throat twice.

 

            “I’ll do the rest. Um … can I get you a cup of coffee?”

 

            She just needed a few minutes alone to pull herself together, to wash away the blood and heal her arm in an on-call room, or a supply closet. Just a minute to set herself straight and bury it all deep inside so she could be okay when Kara woke up.

 

            Relinquishing her handkerchief, Eliza patted the back of her hand and smiled. “I’ll get it.”

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            “Back in a tick.”

 

            Sitting up, Lena slowly rolled her sleeve up and removed the glamour, taking stock of the damage she’d inflicted on herself. It wasn’t bad; deep gouges that had broken the skin, in the clear shape of crescent nail marks, the blood dried in them and bruises mottling the site from the strength it had taken to do that to herself. Sniffing, Lena swallowed thickly and dipped the handkerchief into the basin, wringing it out and wiping at the blood.

 

            She heard Kara shift from her bed and slowed, keeping her head ducked down as she dabbed at the words scarring her arm. The bed creaked again and she caught sight of Kara sitting up from beneath her lashes, shoulders tensing.

 

            “What happened?” Kara rasped.

 

            “It’s just a scratch.”

 

            Her vague explanation wasn’t enough for her girlfriend and Lena sighed as Kara pushed back the blankets and staggered to her feet. Pale with exhaustion and seeming to sag where she stood, Kara shouldn’t have been out of bed, and Lena told her as much.

 

            “Get back in bed. You need rest.”

 

            “I slept all night,” Kara reasoned, although the dark circles beneath her eyes revealed it for the lie it was.

 

            She slowly crossed over to Lena’s bed and reached out to take her arm. With another sigh, Lena tipped her head back, eyes on the ceiling, and felt her pulse in her throat as it tightened. A small sound of panicked surprise escaped Kara and her eyes lifted to Lena’s face

 

            “What happened?”

 

            Her voice was softer this time, breathless with horrified concern. A strained smile crossed Lena’s lips and she seemed to chew on her words for a moment, clearing her throat and inhaling. Nothing came out and she tried again.

 

            “She made me stay in overnight. It was … the dark. I didn’t like it.”

 

            Embarrassed to admit it, that at her age she could still be brought low by a childhood fear, Lena ducked her head and ran a hand over her face. Kara didn’t see it that way though, knowing how deep Lena’s torment had gone, that it wasn’t just the dark, but a collection of things that had occurred in the dark that led her to such extremes when caught somewhere similar once again.

 

            “It’s nothing I can’t heal in a second.”

 

            “That doesn’t make it okay.”

 

            “I know, I just- I panicked.”

 

            “Not you, I mean- how can she do this? How is she allowed to be Chief and do this to her employees? No, she isn’t your mum here, she is your boss.”

 

            Reaching out, Lena cupped Kara’s cheek in her palm. “She’s still my mum. That will always be a factor, and she’ll say she’s harsher on me because of that, but we both know this is nothing compared to how it used to be. But I get to go home after this and she won’t be there and that’s enough of a relief to make me not care about the rest of it.”

 

            “I’ll put in a complaint-“

 

            “No, you won’t-“

 

            “I-“

 

            “It’ll be a waste of time, nothing will come of it. She followed hospital policy, she was very careful about that. I did this to myself.”

 

            “That doesn’t mean it’s not her fault.”

 

            “I know that. It just- it is what it is.”

 

            Dropping her hand as Kara’s expression sourly furrowed, any angry purse to her lips, Lena smoothed her thumb over her forearm. The skin knitted itself back together with only the old scar to show for it and Lena tilted her arm for Kara to see.

 

            “See? It’s like it never even happened.”

 

            “But it did.”

 

            Shrugging as she started to get annoyed, Lena rolled her sleeve down and buttoned the cuff. She would deal with the bloodstain later. Staring at her as if waiting for a response, ready for an argument, Kara’s stare was unwavering and her pale face flushed. Eyes sheepishly darting up, Lena’s mouth thinned and she reached out to cup Kara’s shoulders in her hands, trying to turn her.

 

            “Back into bed with you.”

 

            “Oh, so it’s fine for you to worry about me , but I can’t do the same?”

 

            “Our situations are different.”

 

            Lena steered her back to her bed, and despite her irate protesting, Kara climbed back in and let Lena tuck her in, quietly stewing in her frustration. Taking up a seat at her bedside, Lena crossed her legs and took in the hard set to Kara’s jaw, clearly put out by Lena’s dismissal of doing anything to make Lillian suffer the consequences. It wasn’t that Lena didn’t want that - she would love to see her mother pay for what she’d done - only that she didn’t want to get dragged into it, have to give statements and divulge everything she’d endured. They were still sitting in tense silence when Eliza returned, two cups of coffee in hand.

 

            She handed one to Lena and then fussed over her daughter as Kara sheepishly endured it, pink-cheeked as she repeatedly insisted she was fine, she was ready to go home. It was another hour before she was discharged though, after a quick assessment by her Resident Healer, changed into clean clothes and looking in dire need of more sleep. She looked how Lena thought she must look, dry-eyed and despondent. The two of them trudged after Eliza and Lena let her grip her arm and Apparate them to her cottage, a balmy day in Cornwall, the sky a clouded blue and salt on the wind blowing in off the coast. 

 

            Inside, Lena stifled a yawn and stooped to scratch Bastet beneath the chin. Eliza was already moving through to the kitchen, calling back over her shoulder about breakfast. The three of them were soon wedged into the small kitchen, sitting at the table with bacon and egg sandwiches and cups of tea, quiet as they sat with their tiredness - and a slight discomfort at unfinished business between Kara and Lena - and Eliza shooed Lena away from the dishes when she’d finished eating, insisting she go upstairs and sleep.

 

            Deliberating between saying goodbye and going home to sleep in her own bed or following Kara upstairs, the glance Kara gave her over the bannister as she walked up a few steps, coupled with the desire to know she was okay, made Lena follow in her wake. Inside Kara’s bedroom, Lena stood in the narrow space between the two single beds and watched her girlfriend stoop to rummage through the drawers and fetch pyjamas for them both. Undressing, Lena changed into them and then took Kara’s bed, the softly pilled sheets smelling of her, a comforting presence as she pressed her face into it, hugging it tightly. 

 

            “Budge over,” Kara murmured.

 

            Rolling onto her side, facing the wall, Lena shifted to the far side and felt the mattress jostle as Kara slid in alongside her. It was cramped but she felt the knot in her chest loosen as her girlfriend enveloped her in her warm embrace, kissing her shoulder. Eyes closed, Lena’s mouth twitched at the corners and she felt an ache in her throat.

 

            “I know you’re just trying to help,” she whispered to the wall, her jaw stiff as she squeezed her eyes shut, a furrow between her eyebrows. “I’m sorry if you feel like I don’t appreciate it. I do, I just-”

 

            “It’s okay. You don’t have to explain yourself. I know- well, there’s a lot I don’t know, I just- she hurt you and now you’re hurting yourself …”

 

            “It was just the dark.”

 

            “I know, that doesn’t mean that it doesn’t worry me, that you could- you could do that to yourself.”

 

            “Don’t worry about me. Go to sleep,” Lena wearily murmured as she used Kara’s words against her, a faint note of amusement colouring her voice.

Chapter 40

            It was August soon, their first anniversary coming around with surprising speed. Perhaps because they’d known each other so well, harboured feelings for far longer than either of them had let on, and had crossed that line a few times before, but it felt as if it had been longer than a year. They were both working in the day but they had plans for the evening and Kara came home from work with an eager smile on her face as she swept in the front door, calling a hello to Eliza as she bounded up the stairs with a bouquet in her hand.

 

            Hastily showering, she washed off the ink and the lingering odour of the foul-smelling deep green potion that her current assignment on the mysteries of thought left her brewing for the brains they kept in large tanks. It wasn’t a particularly coveted job, and there were many complaints from the entry-level Unspeakables, but Kara was uncomplaining, grateful for anything that put her ahead, anything that got her a step closer to some of the bigger projects. She was still angling to research the mystery of death, but that was still a project that Professor Croaker didn’t think she was ready for. At the very least, her accurate calculations and imaginative theories had allowed for a two Galleon pay rise per week and a little more trust in the Department of Mysteries to assist some of the Senior Unspeakables in their research.

 

            Changing into a navy check shirt and a pair of dungarees, she tied her hair up and grabbed the bouquet, pausing to spray herself with perfume and grab the wrapped gift she’d bought her girlfriend, before she took the stairs two at a time, shouting goodbye on her way out the front door. Apparating on the doorstep of the cottage, she appeared outside Lena’s front door and knocked, checking the time on her watch, satisfied that she wasn’t late. Jerking the door open, Lena smiled at the sight of her and Kara swept in to kiss her, grinning as she propelled her backwards, stepping over the threshold of the flat.

 

            “Happy anniversary.”

 

            “You sound like you’ve been dying to say that all day,” Lena said with a laugh. 

 

            “I have.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose as she smiled, Lena reached out and cupped her chin. “Happy anniversary to you too.”

 

            “These are for you,” Kara said as she produced the bouquet, and Lena took them, giving her a coy look through her lashes as she put her hand behind her back and summoned the bouquet she’d bought for Kara from the kitchen. A dozen red roses. Kara took them from her with another, lingering kiss. “Thank you.”

 

            Tugging on her hand, Lena raised her eyebrows suggestively. “Come and open your gifts.”

 

            Kicking the door shut, Kara trailed her girlfriend to the kitchen, watching as Lena filled a vase with water and arranged the burgundy dahlias she’d bought her. There were two wrapped gifts on the counter and Kara set Lena’s down beside them, waiting for her before she opened them. They’d agreed on something small but Kara was a little apprehensive about that, wondering what Lena would consider small . Lena finished arranging the flowers and gave her a quick smile, gesturing to the gifts.

 

            “Go on, open them.”

 

            Smiling as she picked up the one that looked a lot look a book, Kara unwrapped it and found a brand new brown leather diary in the style she was partial to, ever since that first one Eliza had gifted her for her thirteenth birthday. The brand was a little pricey but it was a nice gift and Kara brightened at the sight of it, thumbing through the new pages and then turning her attention to the other gift, which was a slimmer box holding a nice quill for her to write with. Kara thanked Lena and leaned across the kitchen island to kiss her before she slid Lena’s gift across the counter to her. It was a rare book on the history of potion-making that Kara had ordered from America but she’d thought Lena would find it interesting and was proved right by that assumption as Lena eagerly started to flip through it. She’d also bought her a little packet of Fizzing Whizbees, a nod to the first gift she’d ever bought Lena, and her girlfriend grinned as she popped one in her mouth, both of them laughing as she levitated a few inches off the ground.

 

            Kara had a bottle of Lena’s favourite elderflower wine with her as well, upholding her end of their plans for a picnic, while Lena had arranged the food. She had a wicker basket and a chequered blanket waiting on the counter, and she stubbornly refused to tell Kara where this picnic was taking place, her secrecy only serving to make Kara even more curious about it. It had been Lena’s idea for the picnic and Kara couldn’t help but wonder if it was so Lena could spare Kara her pride of having to let her pay for an expensive dinner at a fancy restaurant. A picnic suited her just fine though, and the weather had seemed fine when she’d left Cornwall only minutes before.

 

            “Ready?” Lena asked once they’d finished opening their gifts, raising her eyebrows suggestively, the small wicker basket looped over her arm. 

 

            Kara took her other arm and Lena Apparated them to the secret destination. Leaving behind the Dublin flat, Kara felt the breeze of the outdoors and found herself standing knee-deep in a field of grass. After a moment, she realised it wasn’t a field but the overgrown back garden, perhaps an acre in size and bordering on a forest. There was a house there too, limestone walls and slate roof, a jumble of the original building and a few extensions over the last couple of centuries. Kara had never seen it before and wondered if it belonged to someone Lena knew.

 

            Turning in a slow circle, Kara took in the breathtaking views of green as far as she could see, the property nestled in a dale, a glimmer of water at the bottom and the sloping, grassing sides of the shallow valley dotted with trees and mossy rocks. The forest arced around, sparser on the fringes of the garden, but thick and sprawling as it stretched away behind them. Birds called in the trees and the wind was a little brisk but not unpleasantly so. It was a peaceful, secluded area and she was pleased with the decision to come for a picnic.

 

            Spreading out the blanket, they sank onto it and Lena started to unpack a selection of foods. She had ripe grapes and strawberries, tuna and cucumber sandwiches cut into triangles, scones with jam and cream, soft cheeses and cured meats, boiled eggs and olives. They spread everything out and picked from it as they lounged on the blanket, sipping elderflower wine and enjoying the day. Kara had brought her old camera with her and snapped photos, both of them laughing and a little giddy with the delight of an anniversary, as if they were still two teenagers at Hogwarts. Lena had packed Wizard’s Chess as well and they played a few games as the afternoon wore on, the sun setting late and the day retaining its lingering warmth, a rare nice day before the autumn chill set in.

 

            “So, where are we?” Kara asked after they’d consumed most of the food and finished their second game of chess, confused and intrigued as she looked around.

 

            “Ah,” Lena murmured apprehensively, taking a sip of her wine and then clearing her throat. “Right, well, this is a property that’s been vacant for a while that I’ve been thinking about a lot.”

 

            Perplexed, Kara’s brown wrinkled as she picked up the bottle of wine to refill their glasses. “A property? What, to buy? I didn’t know you wanted to move.”

 

            “Well, that’s why I brought you here. So you could look at it first before … anything is decided .”

 

            “Me?”

 

            Shifting on the rumpled blanket, her legs tucked to the side, Lena brushed her hair out of her face. “I was thinking … well, maybe I should show you and then we can talk.”

 

            Wariness wound through Kara but she mumbled in agreement, pushing herself to her feet and dusting off some crumbs. Taking her hand, Lena ran her thumb over the back of it and towed her towards the house. Crossing the overgrown lawn, Kara stared at the house with curiosity. 

 

            Nearing the back doors, Lena paused and looked right. Kara followed her line of sight and saw a set of wooden doors, slightly angled against the bottom of the wall, leading down to a cellar. The wood was worn and damp, curling up at the corners, and a rusting lock held them together. Gesturing to the back door, Lena unlocked it and Kara felt a flicker of panic, reaching to touch Lena’s arm.

 

            “Lena, we can’t go inside someone’s house.”

 

            “It’s fine, no one lives here.”

 

            “But still …”

 

            “Trust me,” Lena said with a wry smile. “And indulge me a little.”

 

            Rolling her eyes as she smiled, Kara followed her through the back door. Eyes adjusting to the gloom, she found herself in a spacious kitchen. A massive oven took up the right wall, set into an alcove, sooty bricks arching above it, dusty jars of desiccated foods and herbs set on wooden shelves, tarnished pots and pans hanging from hooks. Plant pots sat on the windowsill overlooking the garden they’d just come in from, the window thick with dirt, a porcelain sink hosting dead flies and evidence of mice.

 

            A table and chairs had been broken to pieces, broken china on the floors, leaves and dust and dirt piled in corners. Rafters held evidence of herbs and things that had once resided in nets and baskets hanging from them, and Kara looked around with interest, bewildered and wary but getting a small thrill out of breaking into the old place. It was plain that no one had lived there for years.

 

            They moved through the space to enter a comfortably sized living room, everything shabby and dirty now. The space eddied with dust motes and Kara took in the musty sofa, a wobbly lamp and an upholstered armchair, faded navy velvet worn through in places. There was a fireplace with ashes in the grate, an age-spotted mirror above it, and the stubby remains of ivory candles stuck to the mantel with melted wax. As Kara studied the place, she felt uncertainty wash through her, taking in the sofa with the sagging cushions, the stuffing bursting from one of them, and a yellowed and faded newspaper sitting on one of them. She thought she already knew what publication it was from before she picked up the brittle pages bearing The Daily Prophet on the top.

 

            “Oh, I thought it was a Muggle house,” Kara mused aloud. 

 

            “No, it used to belong to a witch.”

 

            “Did she … in the war?”

 

            Kara made her own assumptions and Lena was quiet for a moment, her voice a whisper as she responded. “No.”

 

            Proceeding onwards to another sitting room, this one at the front of the house, filled with bookshelves sagging beneath heavy tomes, the leather spines swollen and split from the damp, pages gnawed on by mice. A desk was set in front of the murky window and Kara made a lap of the room, a rug covering the stone floors, muffling her footsteps as she left tracks in the film of dust. There was a mudroom on the right side of the house, old boots set beside an empty cauldron, the bottom rusted through, a few cloaks draped on wall pegs, a door with a window opening to the stretch of grass and the fringes of the forest when Kara gave it a good shove with her shoulder, the warped edges getting stuck. 

 

            At the wooden staircase leading up, Lena paused outside a door at the back of it, opening it to reveal steps leading down into darkness. The wan daylight seeping into the old house guided them down the first few steps, but Lena lit her wand at the bottom so they could see. At the glow it cast, mice scattered into the dark crevices of work tables and cabinets, the startled shout of the two witches filling the space before they dissolved into laughter. The room fell silent again as soon as they did, although there was an audible drip of water from a leak somewhere. The cellar was larger than she’d expected and ice-cold, the size of the entire ground floor of the cottage combined. 

 

            Light filtered in around the cracks of the doors set in the base of the wall outside, the faint whistle of the wind coming through, and Kara looked around with interest. There were cauldrons on a few of the work tables, smashed vials littering the floor with glass, the dank smell of water and shelves of smashed pots that had once contained herbs and ingredients. Kara had a sneaking suspicion as to why Lena wanted her to look around the place, and she turned to face her, but Lena hadn’t moved from the bottom of the stairs.

 

            They didn’t linger down there long and Lena gestured to a downstairs toilet before leading them up the rickety staircase, steps groaning beneath their weight. Upstairs, there were three bedrooms, a large bathroom and a linen closet, and Kara briefly toured them. There was a large bed in the main bedroom, the old sheets perhaps white once, but now water stained and dusty, water damage darkening the walls as a sliver of the sky was revealed through a gap in the roof tiles that had been exposed through the crumbling clapboard, bare rafters overhead. The dresser had a few framed photos, too layered in grime for Kara to discern any details, a vase of dried lavender beside it and a smattering of candles. Another room was sparse, with no furniture inside, a battered steamer trunk and a few folded sheets of fabric in one corner with packed boxes, tins of paint and rolls of unused wallpaper in the middle of the wooden floorboards, as if it was being used for storage amid renovations. The last was a room with pale blue wallpaper, peeling at the seams from the damp, a wooden rocking horse carved like a hippogriff beside the dresser, a mobile of stars and planets hanging from the rafters above the bed, a children’s cauldron on top of the dresser and a copy of The Tales of Beedle the Bard alongside a few other children’s books.

 

            “You might have guessed why I’ve brought you here,” Lena started, pacing in the middle of the room.

 

            “You want to buy the place?”

 

            Smiling thinly, Lena fiddled with her fingers. “The cellar … it could be turned into a nice spot for the full moon. We could make it comfortable, and if anything ever happened … the forest is there for you to run through. There aren’t any Muggles for twenty miles, at least.”

 

            “No,” Kara firmly murmured before gaining more confidence to speak plainly. “Thank you for wanting to help, but … you can’t buy a house just for me to transform safely. That’s just- that’s-”

 

            “That’s not the only reason.”

 

            “What do you mean?”

 

            Shoulders slumping, Lena let out a huff of laughter, crossing the space between them and taking Kara’s hand. “I might not be good at relationships but … I think at a certain point, you’re supposed to decide if there’s a future there.”

 

            “Oh,” Kara softly exclaimed, surprised by the turn in conversation. She backed up a few steps to sink onto the dusty bedsheets of the narrow bed. “You want me to move in with you?”

 

            Taking a seat beside her, Lena let out a resigned sigh. “I can see you haven’t given it much thought, um … there’s no rush of course, but if I’m going to move houses, it’s something to consider. Is this the sort of place you’d like to live one day? Can you see yourself living here?”

 

            “I- yes, it’s nice, it’s perfect, I just- I can’t buy a house! I make more money than I have since I was teaching, but still, my savings aren’t enough for a deposit on a house.”

 

            “I’m not asking you to buy it-”

 

            “I can’t let you buy it!”

 

            “Of course you can’t,” Lena muttered, “even though it’s not a matter of money-”

 

            “You know, it’s only people who have money who think it doesn’t matter. I just- I don’t have much. I’m sorry.”

 

            Giving her an aching smile, Lena cupped the side of her face, running her thumb over the scar on Kara’s cheek. “You’re right, you don’t have much, but you’ve given me the best thing you have and that’s yourself. And I’m not being dismissive when I say it’s not a matter of money; the place is already mine.”

 

            Surprise was quick to cross Kara’s face. “You’ve already bought it?”

 

            “No,” Lena corrected her, looking down as a shadow of grief crossed her face. “No, I didn’t buy it, I inherited it. .”

 

            “You-” Kara faltered, shock rendering her speechless as she floundered for a moment. Her throat felt suddenly very tight and dry as she struggled to form a coherent thought. “Your mum-”

 

            “Yes,” Lena wearily sighed, pushing herself to her feet and crossing over to the window with the moth-eaten curtains, parting them as she peered through the grimy glass. “This was my house when I was little. This was my bedroom. And that is the lake where she drowned, tried to … well you know.”

 

            She said it all with forced levity but soft devastation still cut through Kara as she stared at her across the room, crestfallen for her. Turning away from the window, Lena’s eyes were wide and she chewed on her lower lip, anxious and uncertain, as if she was struggling with how she felt. Pushing herself to her feet, Kara crossed over to her and swept her up in a hug, enveloping her narrow shoulders as she held her tightly, one hand cupping the back of Lena’s head as she propped her chin on her shoulder. They didn’t speak for a long minute, Kara swaying them slightly as she soothingly rubbed Lena’s back, until Lena pulled back and gave her a faint smile, kissing the tip of her nose.

 

            “I know I’ve kept too much to myself, so … all cards on the table,” Lena told her. “No expectations, just … something to think about.”

 

            Nodding emphatically, Kara rubbed her scarred cheek, a divot between her brows as she thought. “I will think about it.”

 

            “I know you will. Probably too much.”

 

            With a scoff of laughter, Kara rolled her eyes, cheeks shallowly dimpling. “Probably.”

 

            “Come on,” Lena murmured, touching the back of Kara’s hand gently. “Let’s get back to our dinner.”

 

            There were a thousand questions on the tip of Kara’s tongue but she let them all die to spare Lena the arduous task of recounting painful memories or facts of the past. Being brought to the home she’d lived in for the first four years of her life had been the last thing Kara had expected and she knew to handle it delicately. Lena wouldn’t show how much it hurt, how it agonised her to miss a mother who had treated her as poorly as the second one she’d wound up with, but Kara knew that she’d always been a deeply sensitive person - she’d just been forbidden to show it.

 

            Descending through the dusty house, they went through the backdoor and Lena cared enough to lock up behind them, even though Kara was sure the place was warded from sight, before trampling across the overgrown garden to reclaim their abandoned picnic. Sinking to her knees, Kara watched Lena flop down, drain her glass of wine and then reach for the bottle. Picking up a sandwich, Kara bit off the end and cleared her throat.

 

            “How often do you come here?”

 

            Lena’s eyes slid to her face, piercing and aloof for a moment before she cast off the shadow of memories better left forgotten. “This is only the second time since. The first was after I could Apparate; I didn’t know it had been left to me until my dad died and the deed and will were found in his office but I’d had no way of visiting before. I was … curious.”

 

            “Do you remember it much?”

 

            “More than I’d like to. I remember the kitchen; she was always baking and the backdoor was always open. We had a cat that would sleep on the windowsill and chase the gnomes away. I used to help as well - she liked to be outside a lot, especially by the water. Otherwise, I’d be in the cellar with her, where she brewed her potions. Um … I remember that she was sad a lot. She’d come into my room at night and sit on the edge of my bed while she cried. I think maybe that’s why … she did what she did.”

 

            Reaching out, Kara put her hand on Lena’s knee, stroking gently as she gave her a sympathetic look. Drawing in a rattling breath, Lena shrugged and took another sip of wine before plucking a grape off the bunch and popping it in her mouth.

 

            “It’s in the past now, I suppose. No point dwelling on it.”

 

            “I- we could find somewhere else if it’s too much,” Kara awkwardly managed to speak. “I can … compromise on how we split things, or we could maybe wait a little bit longer and I can save more or work more or we could just stay in your flat if-”

 

            “It’s okay,” Lena cut her off, a small smile on her lips. “I- that wouldn’t be fair.”

 

            “What wouldn’t?”

 

            “To put more stress on you, to make you move into my flat. You said it yourself, it’s my flat. I don’t want you to move into a place that’s already mine, that’s decorated how I want it to be, that has a whole history already. I think … if we were to move in together, I’d want it to be somewhere new. Okay, I’ve lived here before and it’s mine by inheritance, but … it’s a dump right now. We can pick … paint colours and furniture together. Decide which bedroom we want ours to be and what kind of rug should go in the living room. I don’t know … I guess I just-”

 

            She sighed, her shoulders dropping slightly as she closed her eyes. Kara stroked her knee, cocking her head to the side as she studied her, taking in the way her dark lashes fluttered, how she frowned ever so slightly, mouth thinning at the corners.

 

            “You what?”

 

            “I never loved anyone until you, and I never cared about anything like this before, never wanted someone in my space or to change anything in my home. But now I do, and it should be as equals. I know we grew up differently, but I just- maybe it’s time to start thinking about what we want, and how to get it. There’s no rush, of course, but it’s better to know what we’re expecting.”

 

            “The only thing I want or care about is you , and I already have you, so everything else is secondary to that,” Kara said with a crooked smile, her cheek dimpling as she leaned over to clumsily kiss Lena’s cheek. “If you’re happy, I’m happy. And if moving here would make you happy, then you should do it no matter what I say.”

 

            “I know, but I care about your opinion.”

 

            “I really will think about it. I’ll work out some numbers as well, see what I can afford.”

 

            At the quick inhale, Kara laughed and raised her eyebrows, reaching over to cover Lena’s mouth with her hand. She kissed the tip of Lena’s nose and laughed again at the furrowed look on her girlfriend’s face.

 

            “That wasn’t me asking for a solution. Let me figure some things out by myself and I’ll let you know as soon as I can.”

 

            Pulling her hand away, Lena pressed a kiss to her palm and smiled. “Alright. But take as long as you need; I can be patient, and I’d rather you make the right decision for yourself than rush into one because it’s what I want. I won’t be offended if yours is different from mine. No expectations, remember?”

 

            “Come here,” Kara murmured, shifting onto her knees as she set aside her glass of wine and moved the containers of olives and strawberries and the chess set safely out of the way. 

 

            Lena moved to meet her without a word, her lips firm and eager as she gripped Kara’s thigh tightly. The afternoon had faded to dusk, the sky purple and a host of moths and gnats surrounding them, the lit candles wavering in the breeze. Tipping her head back as Lena’s lips found her neck, Kara’s eyelids fluttered as she looked up, and she saw the waning moon floating in the sky, missing a sliver, ten days past the full moon. As engrossed as she was in the pleasant feeling of her girlfriend’s lips skating lower, towards her collarbones, Kara was equally struck with the thought of full moons in such a peaceful place, yes, in a cellar, but also in the spacious garden or expanse of the forest if push came to shove.

 

            Afterwards, laying on the rumpled picnic basket, the remains of their dinner claimed by the ants where they’d kicked plates and dishes into the grass, Kara stroked Lena’s dark hair, the fingers of her other hand tangled in Lena’s, a spare blanket covering them both. She’d lost her glasses somewhere along the way with her clothes and was too lazy to find them, content to stay there all night, amidst the long grass and the cloudy sky. Lena had cast a spell to ward off any rain and Kara brushed her lips against Lena’s temple as she basked in the feeling of being outdoors, her feet bare to the cool breeze, and wondered if they would have plenty of nights like this. She’d almost certainly made up her mind.

 

            Drowsy and comfortable, they both fell asleep somewhere in the middle of their ongoing silence, Kara’s fingers stilling in Lena’s hair, Lena’s hand limply pressed against her chest, both of them breathing slowly and deeply. An owl hooted, the grass rustled with the wind that picked up, and the two witches remained fast asleep, all through the night, the candles guttering and the melted wax solidifying, a fox scurrying over to steal a triangle of a sandwich before it vanished back into the darkness.

 

            It wasn’t until the sky started to lighten that Kara stirred first, confused for a moment at the sensation of cold air on her feet sticking out from the bottom of the blanket. Pushing herself up, blearily blinking as she looked around, fumbling for her glasses, she was greeted by a perfect sunrise, the deep blue tinged with orange and pink as clouds streaked the horizon. The cottage was a buttery yellow, aged but solid as it stood on the edge of the forest in the shallow dale. Kara was alone with her thoughts as Lena slept through the exhaustion of her long shift the day before, and she was preoccupied with thoughts of Lena’s offer.

 

            Finding her clothes, she dressed and tucked Lena in, stepping over the remains of their scattered picnic as she did a slow lap of the house. She hadn’t seen it from the front yet and she rounded the left side of it, counting windows, looking up at the lichen-speckled roof of the rooms that had been added on over the years, ivy that was on the verge of turning orange and red creeping up over the limestone and thicker as she neared the front of the house. Backing up until she could fit the front facade in her field of view, Kara buried her hands in the pockets of her dungarees and studied it. Ivy covered the entire front, a wide wooden door weathered and scarred set in the middle, and it created a charming picture. Kara could envision smoke trickling out of the various chimneys, their wellies by the front door, Bastet curled up in the window inside and the smell of something cooking. It could be as homely as the cottage in Cornwall if given the chance.

 

            Standing in the morning light, Kara stared at the cottage and watched shafts stream in through the old, moth-eaten curtains, trying to imagine Lena there as a child. A child so small and different to the Lena she’d met at Hogwarts. She could imagine her mother singing in the kitchen, the smell of bread proving, freshly picked herbs littering the counters, the cedar of the burning wood and the laughter of a little girl. How badly Kara wished her life had remained that way, that her mother had never tried to drown her or killed herself, and Lena had never wound up at the Luthor mansion. It all would have turned out so differently if she had. Perhaps she would have been in Ravenclaw too, and they would have been friends from the beginning, and Lena would have been happier and unscarred, and wouldn’t have had to bear the guilt of things that had never been her fault and shouldn’t have been her responsibility to bear. She stood there for a long time imagining that and considered that maybe she could bring her a little bit of that peace by continuing what should have been and moving into the cottage with her.

 

            The sound of her name tore her away, and Kara padded barefoot back around the house and through the long grass to find Lena buttoning up her shirt, expression softening at the sight of her. They packed up their things and Kara suggested breakfast before they went home, prolonging the morning, knowing she had to get ready for work but having enough time to spare. Apparating them to Diagon Alley, they walked to the south side hand-in-hand in yesterday’s clothes, taking seats at a table outside a café, a red umbrella shading them as they perused their menus.

 

            They had just finished eating when Kara caught sight of Andrea stepping out of The Daily Prophet’s office and making straight for the café before working hours started. Her gaze flitted to their occupied table and Kara saw recognition flash across her face, her pace slow slightly as she deliberated between pretending she hadn’t seen them and passing them by or turning around. Lena was still oblivious to her old friend approaching behind her and Kara still felt a prickle of guilt for what had come between them, knowing that it wasn’t Andrea’s fault and wishing Lena had believed her when she’d said so. Seizing her chance, Kara raised a hand and waved, as Lena finished her last bite, frowning slightly.

 

            “Who are you- oh,” she murmured as she twisted in her seat and caught sight of Andrea.

 

            “Andrea, hi.”

 

            Caught out by the direct greeting, Andrea was forced to continue onwards, changing her trajectory to warily approach their table. Lena’s mouth tightened at the corners and she sank down in her chair, arching an eyebrow at Kara, who sheepishly met her gaze and then quickly looked away.

 

            “Ah, Kara, hello … Lena.”

 

            “We were just going to get another coffee, you should join us.”

 

            “Oh, no, it’s-”

 

            Shifting her chair back, Kara gestured for Andrea to take one of the empty seats. “Please. I’ll just go and order. What do you-”

 

            Chair grating on the cobblestones, Lena shot to her feet. “I’ll order.”

 

            She rounded the table and Kara grimaced with exasperation as Andrea paused and then dragged out the chair. Sitting, she cleared her throat. “Well …”

 

            “Sorry. I just- she has so few people who genuinely care about her. I don’t want her to lose one of them forever over something so … unimportant.”

 

            “That minimises what happened to you just a little, don’t you think? Maybe she’s right and I should have vouched for you or … did something . I don’t know, I don’t think it was handled well. I’m sorry for that.”

 

            “I didn’t want you to handle it. It all worked out in the end.”

 

            “Did it? I mean … you’re doing well? Working?”

            

            Giving her a pleased smile, Kara nodded. “Mhm. Back at the Department of Mysteries again. And we’ve made it a year together now, so I’m the best I’ve ever been really.”

 

            “Oh. That’s good, I’m glad.”

 

            “And how’s the Prophet going?”

 

            “Good. William is no longer employed there; there were a few other issues so he left for America. I’m not sure if you heard.”

 

            “Oh. No, I didn’t hear that.”

 

            Andrea nodded, lips pressed into a line, and Kara awkwardly cleared her throat, wondering if it would be better or worse when Lena came back. A minute later she was, her fingers brushing Kara’s shoulder before she retook her seat. Kara watched her fix Andrea with a piercing, level look and raised her eyebrows as she folded her arms over her chest.

 

            “So …”

 

            “Work’s well?” Andrea asked, unruffled, used to Lena’s aloofness.

 

            “Mhm.”

 

            “Kara was just telling me you’ve been together a year now. That’s good.”

 

            “Mhm.”

 

            “Are you still with Russell?” Kara asked, trying to help steer the conversation away from hummed responses.

            

            “Yes. Yes, we’re still together.”

 

            Nodding, murmuring a vague nicety about it, Kara was spared having to respond by the arrival of their coffees. Stirring three sugars into her cup, she took a sip and ventured a few more questions as she kept the conversation going with Andrea, a little awkward considering the two of them had never been particularly close, and had mostly interacted at work with Andrea as her boss, but she slowly managed to draw Lena into it. Recounting stories and pretending to forget facts that Lena supplied as she sipped her black coffee, and it wasn’t so palpably awkward then. 

 

            After fifteen minutes, Kara excused herself to the bathroom and was relieved to find they hadn’t remained in uncomfortable silence the whole time, Andrea midway through telling Lena that Gayle was back with her old Gryffindor ex-girlfriend she’d seen for a little while after they’d graduated from Hogwarts, which turned out to be Imra. Kara had never pieced that together before, friendly with Imra but not overly invested in her personal life beyond catching up at parties or group get-togethers, and it put her out a little to know that someone tangentially linked to her friend group had dated a Slytherin as well, with no backlash or dramas involved. Perhaps no one else had been aware either, Kara thinking hard about whether that bit of gossip had ever reached her ears before, but she was sure they were all only aware of the few years she’d spent with Mike. Regardless, things were always harder for her and Lena than they were for everyone else. 

 

            Eventually, Kara had to leave, checking her watch and draining the lukewarm remains of her coffee as she lamented about being late. Lena went with her, finishing off her drink and parting ways with Andrea a little awkwardly, and Kara took her back home to her flat, picking up her gifts and kissing her goodbye. Lena had work later that evening, which ruled out dinner, so they wouldn’t get to see each other until tomorrow night, at the very least. With the promise of a letter via Morrigan, Lena kissed her again before Kara left and rushed to get ready for work.

 

            Hastily showering and pulling her hair up, Kara pulled on a pair of wide suit pants, an ivory shirt, too big, even with the sleeves rolled up and the hem tucked in, and a matching suit vest over the top. Picking up her briefcase, she laced on a pair of brogues and dashed downstairs, snagging a cloak off the hook and yelling goodbye to her mother, who was out the back. Flooring to the Ministry Atrium, Kara ducked out of the fireplace and dashed through the crowd of employees, nodding to various familiar faces, waving to James as she caught sight of him Flooing out of a fireplace a few down from hers. She piled into a lift and waited as it stopped at every floor until reaching Level Nine.

 

            The black-tiled walls and pale blue light of the torches greeted her as the metal grille parted to spit her out. Hurrying down the hallway, Kara slipped through the black door to the Entrance Chamber with a few minutes to spare, slightly breathless as she smoothed down errant curls and made for the door to the main office. She said hello to a few colleagues as she made her way to her desk, an organised mess of papers, files, quills and ink. Her new quill joined the cup of them set beside a framed photo of her and Lena, right alongside one of her, Alex and Eliza. She went to the small kitchen at the back corner and made herself a cup of tea before settling in with her calculations.

 

            It was a mentally engaging activity, if a little rote from the familiarity, running the numbers, flicking across the beads of her abacus and staining her fingertips with ink as she worked tirelessly. She took a break for another cup of tea and a few biscuits and was just finishing up with her calculations when she was asked to measure the brains in the Brain Room.
