            She was no Healer, but she’d had to do a field course as part of her Auror training, so Kara trusted her sister not to heal it crookedly. It was an effort for Kara to push herself to her feet, as if her whole body weighed a tonne, legs threatening to buckle beneath her as she shakily rose and let Alex guide her through the house, her hands a warm brand between Kara’s shoulder blades.

 

            In the kitchen, a chair dragged itself out and Kara collapsed into it, fresh tears welling up, a seemingly inexhaustible stream of them. Lights on, Alex tipped her sister’s head back and eyed the bridge of Kara’s nose, while Kara cried and Kelly fixed her a cup of tea. She heard the sound of the kettle boiling, of Kelly moving around and the tingling in her nose as Alex healed it, her face a terrible mess. 

 

            The tea was put in front of her, but she didn’t drink it, staring at the mug for the better part of an hour as she let out quiet gasps, trying to stop crying as she breathlessly apologised, over and over again. Alex and Kelly sat in the kitchen with her, the three of them crowded around the table, her sister’s arm around her shoulder as she tried her best, but there was nothing to be done for Kara’s broken heart. And the worst part was knowing that it wasn’t from a lack of love, wasn’t because either of them had wanted things to end, but out of a sense of obligation, to do what they could to make it safe for them to be together again at a future date. But all Kara was worried about was Lena’s safety, crying and crying as she thought of how much danger she was putting herself in, walking into the dragon’s den because of her morals. And Kara couldn’t even tell anyone. She couldn’t laud her girlfriend’s bravery, the sacrifice she was making. Instead, she had to drag her name through the mud and hope that they both made it through it all alive so she could clear it one day.

 

            It was two o’clock in the morning when Kara asked if she could shower, her voice wavering and rough after hours of coming undone but trying to keep it together. There was no asking if she could stay the night, already a given, but she could still taste blood at the back of her throat, and she could feel the mess of her face, just wanted to scrub the night off and pretend it hadn’t happened. 

 

            Alex rose with her, and Kara wearily plodded upstairs, the breaths still hitching in her chest as she made her way to the bathroom. Her sister fetched her a clean towel and summoned Kara’s bags from where she’d dropped them before leaving her to it. Shedding her clothes as the shower heated up, Kara stepped beneath the scalding stream and let it sting her bare skin as she cupped a handful and splashed it over her face. It hurt, her nose still stinging somewhat, her eyes still bruised black, but it was refreshing, rinsing away flaking blood that had dried and smudged, until her face was clean, even if it was horribly blotchy.

 

            Eventually, she had to get out, drying off and fishing out clothes from her extended bags, pausing when Bastet jumped out with an annoyed yowl, snubbing Kara’s attempt to apologise with a scratch behind the ears. Bundled up in soft-pilled pyjamas, smelling of the laundry detergent that she and Lena used to wash their clothes together, Kara swallowed the painful lump in her throat down, her eyes stinging fiercely again. Gathering up her bags, dirty clothes shoved back inside with her shoes, Kara slipped on her glasses, wincing slightly as the metal frames pressed into her bruises, and opened the bathroom door.

 

            The cat wandered out, cautious to be in an unfamiliar home, and Kara saw the door to the spare bedroom open, the light on, and her sister sitting on the edge of the bed as she waited for her. Clearing her throat, Kara crossed the landing and stepped inside the room, setting her bags down and then sinking onto the edge of the mattress beside Alex. After a moment, she tipped her head to the side, resting it on her sister’s shoulder.

 

            “Here,” Alex mumbled, uncurling her fingers to reveal a tub of a bruise salve.

 

            Kara took it from her, rolling it in her palm as her mouth twitched at the corners. “Thanks.”

 

            “Let me.”

 

            She let Alex take it back and removed her glasses, setting them in her lap and turning to her sister. Eyes closed, Kara let her smooth the thick paste over her eyelids and the tops of her cheekbones, smearing it over the dark bruises as she tried to be gentle. Screwing the lid back on, Alex set it on the bedside table and then let out a soft sigh. They sat silently beside each other, Bastet wandering in and jumping up onto the covers, bumping her head against Kara’s arm, and Kara could sense that Alex wanted to say something, but she didn’t want to talk anymore. She was so tired , the full moon only a couple of nights before, still recovering from that ordeal, and now saddled with the loss of her relationship on top of that. Kara didn’t think she’d ever felt so drained in her life.

 

            “I’m sorry,” Kara rasped before Alex could speak, steering the conversation in a different direction.

 

            “It’s okay. None of this is your fault.”

 

            With a shrug, Kara swallowed a laugh. Thumbing her eyelids, forgetting about the salve, she quietly cursed, rubbing it off on her pants, and then sighed. “You should get to bed too.”

 

            “Mm,” Alex hummed, not moving an inch. “So … what happens now?”

 

            “Well … I’ll go to mum’s tomorrow. My name wasn’t- wasn’t on the title for the house, so … and it’s probably a good thing for someone to stay with mum, with the way things are going.”

 

            “Right.”

 

            “Um … could you do me a favour? Don’t tell her about … this,” Kara mumbled, gesturing to her face, lips twitching slightly. “I’ll tell her about the rest, but … well, I’d just prefer it if she didn’t know. Um, I don’t want to upset her.”

 

            “Okay, I won’t tell her.”

 

            “Thanks. I think I might sleep now.”

 

            With a sigh, her sister patted her arm. “Okay.”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Alex dropped a kiss onto the top of Kara’s damp hair and then left the bedroom, easing the door shut behind her. Sitting in the yellow glow of the lights, Kara tried to quell the feeling in her chest, as if her heart was being squeezed, toying with her glasses as the cat curled up beside her. She sat there for a long while until the thought crossed her mind that perhaps the glow of the light around the door frame might keep Alex and Kelly awake. 

 

            Eventually, she made herself move, the lights off, the blankets pulled back as she slipped beneath them. She slept very little, her mind too full of worry for Lena as she tossed and turned, no longer sobbing even as tears continued to slide down her cheeks, down her temples when she lay on her back, staring up at the dark ceiling. Kara had to be up for work as well, rising just after five, unable to pretend that she was resting any longer. No one else was awake, trying to catch up on lost sleep, and she quietly dressed in the spare room, making up the bed and leaving Bastet behind with her bag, before she picked up her briefcase and Flooed to the Ministry.

 

            Bumbling her way through the workday, Kara could barely string a thought together, terrible bags beneath her eyes, which were still faintly bruised, another layer of the salve applied that morning before she left her sister’s, and while Croaker attributed her appearance to the full moon a few days prior, that was no excuse for her knocking over her cup of coffee, spilling it right into her lap, or for the blank sheet of paper that sat before her all day, a pile of open books ignored as she idly tapped the nib of her quill against the desk and bounced her knee. Still, even though she accomplished nothing but fretting all day, Kara worked some overtime, staying late, no reason to be home on time, no one and no home to go to.

 

            That wasn’t quite true, though, and once the clock hit seven, she packed her desk up and went to Alex’s house, letting herself in, finding her sister absent and Kelly drinking tea in the living room. Her sister-in-law quickly rose to her feet, her voice gentle as she said hello, a look of sympathy and sadness in her dark eyes as she stood before Kara, soothingly rubbing her arm. Kara couldn’t look at her, eyes darting around restlessly as her voice wavered, rubbing the back of her neck as Bastet wound around her legs. She ended up fetching her things from upstairs, packing the cat back into the bag before giving Kelly a brief hug, insisting that she was fine before she took a pinch of Floo powder and vanished in a swirl of emerald flames.

 

            Emerging into the cramped living room of her mother’s house, Kara locked eyes with Eliza, who looked up in surprise, her face softening with a smile as her eyes creased at the corners. She was knitting, the radio a quiet hum, tea on the coffee table, and she lowered her project back to her lap.

 

            “Hello, sweetheart, I wasn’t expecting you.”

 

            “Hi,” Kara murmured, setting down her bags and skirting around the coffee table to stoop down and kiss her mother’s cheek.

 

            She sank onto the sofa at Eliza’s side, her hands in her lap as she looked down at them, unsure what to say then, how to break the news to her mother. But Eliza was more perceptive than that, reaching out to cup Kara’s cheek, trying to urge her head up.

 

            “What’s the matter?”

 

            Her gentle question was all it took to unravel the composure Kara had managed to hold onto all day, letting out a hitching breath as her eyes immediately flooded with tears and her shoulders shook. Collapsing into her mother’s lap, burying her face in her folded arms, Kara sobbed as her exhaustion caught up with her. Letting out a sound of surprise, Eliza rubbed her daughter’s back as she straightened on the sofa, smoothing back blonde curls as her face furrowed with concern.

 

            “It’s alright, come on, what’s got you so upset?”

 

            It was a few more minutes before Kara could gather herself enough to sit up, her head ducked down, wiping her face on the wide sleeves of her robe. Eliza had her head cocked to the side, eyeing her with worry as she rubbed her arm, waiting patiently for Kara to speak. Kara had always been her most sensitive daughter but had always shut it all away too, and Eliza knew that she’d open up if she gave her the time she needed to collect her thoughts. 

 

            Letting out a pitiful sound as she swallowed another sob, Kara drew in a hitching breath, her voice so full of misery as she spoke, more tears running down her cheeks. “Lena … finished with- with me … last night.” 

 

            Eliza’s lips parted in surprise, blue eyes widening a fraction as she slowly shifted back from her daughter, looking at her with bewilderment, as if trying to comprehend what she’d heard. She didn’t speak for a moment, and Kara kept her head down, chin wobbling as her face flushed.

 

            “I- what happened?” Eliza softly exclaimed, disbelieving.

 

            “Did- did Alex tell you about- about her brother? We … had a fight about him, um … I guess she just- she’s … not the person I thought she was. I guess … our opinions on a, uh, a few things are just … too different to overlook, so …”

 

            Still floundering, understanding Kara’s veiled meaning, Eliza tried to process that piece of information, fitting it in with the quiet and polite woman who she’d folded into her family and treated like a daughter for the last seven years. Lena had always been somewhat reserved, a little aloof, but she’d always been unfailingly loyal to and protective of Kara, and it had been a comfort to Eliza to know that Kara had found someone who loved her completely. She’d hoped they’d get married at some point, seven years long enough for her to lament about a wedding and grandchildren over family dinners, but Kara was crying on the sofa, telling her they’d split up. The anguish of it deepened the lines at the corners of Eliza’s eyes and mouth as she grimaced, her shoulders slumping. 

 

            “Right,” Eliza eventually replied, nodding as she accepted what was said at face value and then reached over to smooth Kara’s hair back and cup her face in her hands. Giving her a rueful smile, she squeezed her cheeks slightly, and Kara gave her mother a weak smile, bloodshot eyes briefly meeting hers. “It’ll be alright, darling. It’ll all work out for the best, I’m sure.”

 

            Kara hummed, sniffing as she closed her eyes. “Is it alright if I- if I come back here for a bit?”

 

            “Of course it is. Go on, you put your things upstairs and I’ll make us some tea.”

 

            Nodding, Kara pushed herself to her feet and stooped over her bags, opening the one with her belongings to let the cat spring out, before she carried everything upstairs. Leaving it on her bed to unpack later, she went into the bathroom to wash her face, the skin pink and flushed. The bruises around her eyes had healed completely after another application of the salve at lunchtime, but she still looked awful. Still, the cold water from the old taps made her feel a little more put together as she stopped crying and patted her face dry with a towel.

 

            She changed into pyjamas before heading back downstairs, her mother sitting at the kitchen table with two cups of tea steaming in the cool air before her and a plate of shepherd’s pie. Eliza nudged the plate slightly as Kara appeared in the doorway, looking drawn and pale, urging her daughter to eat some dinner. Pulling out a chair, Kara sank onto it and quietly thanked her mother, picking up the knife and fork and staring at the plate of food. She didn’t feel hungry in the slightest, but she knew her mother would worry, and that Lena would worry if she knew too. The only way Kara would be able to get through this was for Lena, for the future they were trying to provide for each other, one that was safe so they didn’t have to be apart for their own protection. Even if it was for their own good, it didn’t feel that way.

 

            Pushing her food around and slowly picking at it, she answered Eliza’s hesitant questions with a mumbling response, unsure of what she was even saying. She cleared half of her plate and drank her tea, the kitchen quiet as her mother studied her for the most part, keeping her company until Kara thanked her and then excused herself, nudging up her glasses as she rubbed her eyes, saying that she was tired. And she was, but she didn’t want to sit in the living room for another hour with her mum looking at her with worry and sadness in her eyes. 

 

            Wearily plodding upstairs, Kara shut the bedroom door and turned on the lamp before drawing the curtains. Then she started to unpack her things, pulling out clothes and putting them in the drawers, stowing her diary, quills and ink on the desk, a few books alongside them, a bag of toiletries on the desk chair and a few other essentials strewn across her bed. She hadn’t packed much, most of her things still in their house, not of much use to her then, able to wait for her return. 

 

            And there, at the bottom of the bag, where it had fallen through the folded clothes and pairs of shoes as everything had gotten jumbled up, was a folded crane. It made the breath catch in Kara’s throat, her chest tightening painfully as she plucked it out, vision blurring with tears before she’d even managed to unfold the note. They’d agreed not to talk for a long time, but Lena had left her a parting letter. She unfolded it with shaky fingers as she sank onto the edge of the bed to read it.

 

Kara, 

 

I just wanted you to know that I’ve been so happy during these last seven years with you, that I have never been so happy in my life, and that I already know I’ll never be so happy again unless it’s with you.

 

Yours always,

Lena x

 

            A breathless sob worked its way past Kara’s lips, and she pressed the letter to her chest, hunching over as she cried quietly. She could have stayed like that all night, feeling the keen pain of her girlfriend’s words, but ten minutes later, she heard her mother’s footsteps on the stairs, heard her hesitate on the landing and approach Kara’s room. The light rap on the door had Kara hastily wiping her face before she called out goodnight, careful to keep the tears out of her voice, shoulders slumping with relief as Eliza responded through the door and went to bed. 

 

            That first day was one of the hardest of Kara’s life, and she quickly went to bed after that, leaving the lamp on to keep the dark at bay, a habit, as if Lena was there with her. Under the blankets, face pressed into a pillow that didn’t smell of her girlfriend, Kara eventually fell asleep with the crumpled note clutched tightly in a fist, clinging to the slightest sliver of her Lena she had left.

Chapter 52

            Despite the lack of sleep she got that night, still awake as pre-dawn light filtered into her room, Lena was up and dressed before eight o’clock, her hairline damp from a shower, passing over the variety of Eliza’s knitted jumpers to select one that would hurt a little less, before she made herself presentable and exited the bedroom. Her face still bore the shadows or bruises, her eyes gritty and raw with a heaviness behind them, and the stairs groaned beneath her footsteps as she descended through the house, still as a morgue.

 

            Making for the dining room, she paused in the open doorway, taking in the rather ordinary scene of her mother and brother sitting at the dining table. A fire was lit and the curtains were open, but the room was still gloomy and held a chill as Lena stepped inside, her brother looking up while her mother kept her attention on that morning's copy of The Daily Prophet . She sat at the head of the table with Lex to her right, and Lena was forced to take the seat to her left, putting her across from her brother. Fortunately, it was a large table, so they were still somewhat spread out, Lena taking the napkin from the set place and draping it across her lap as she murmured her good mornings to them both.

 

            Wary and tense, her wand tucked up the sleeve of her jumper for easy access should she foil her plans so soon, Lena reached for the tea tray, fetching a clean cup and saucer and lifting the teapot. Strongly steeped tea poured into her cup in a stream of amber, and she added a splash of milk, taking a scalding sip before she heard the apologetic squeak of Hope to her left. Glancing down at the little House Elf, Lena blinked as she shifted her teacup out of the way so Hope could set a plate with two boiled eggs and triangles of toast before Lena. It had been her preferred way to have eggs when she was younger, and she felt a flicker of old fondness and guilt steal over her as she ignored the House Elf, not wanting to display any softness in front of her family.

 

            “Are you working today?” Lex asked her as she worked the top off her first egg.

 

            “This afternoon.”

 

            Lillian cleared her throat, still not looking up from the newspaper as she shook the pages out. “If you need the day off, I can make your excuses.”

 

            Lena held the small silver spoon in hand and paused, her eyes lifting from the bright yolk of the egg to give her mother a poorly concealed look of surprise. She couldn’t remember her mother ever allowing her to take a day off for the sake of it, Lena having to book annual leave or get Sam to cover a shift if she ever needed time off, and she was shocked that she’d even suggest it, always so hard on Lena, always so unyielding. Clearing her throat, Lena licked her lips.

 

            “Thank you, but I’ll manage.”

 

            “You’d better sort out those bruises before your shift starts, then,” Lillian curtly ordered her, turning the page, her pale gaze briefly flitting up to her daughter’s as she reached for her coffee and took a sip.

 

            Nodding, Lena dipped the spoon into the runny egg and kept her head lowered through breakfast, a tense set to her shoulders as she silently ate, refilling her tea and then her brother’s when he nudged his cup forward, giving her a quick wink as she obliged. It was strange to sit there with him, Lex’s dark eyes bright with satisfaction, a smugness to his expression as he lounged in his chair with no concern over being a wanted man. Lena suspected it would only be a day or so before they should expect a Ministry raid on the estate, or however long it took to get a warrant approved by the Wizengamot. 

 

            Mealtimes had always been a rather quiet affair growing up, so it was nothing new for her to sit there with that uncomfortable silence, the sounds of cutlery and china filling it, Hope bringing in more toast, a fresh pot of tea, but it was a bitter blow to be thrust back into it. Over the last seven years, she’d gotten used to breakfasts in her cottage, the radio or a record filling the place with music, Kara cooking them bacon and eggs, chatting animatedly as they ate. There had been dinners in Eliza’s cramped kitchen, five of them - sometimes more - with a roast dinner on the table, all of them elbow-to-elbow as they jostled for space, laughing and talking over each other. She felt nonexistent, as if she could’ve been a ghost, sitting at the dining table in her childhood home, her presence barely acknowledged.

 

            It wasn’t until they’d all finished that her brother spoke again, eagerly pushing himself to his feet as Lillian stalked out of the room and Lena pushed her chair out but remained seated. Looking at him, an eyebrow slightly arched, she climbed to her feet and dropped the napkin onto the table.

 

            “I fancy a walk in the gardens. Care to join me?”

 

            She couldn’t say no, of course, no matter how desperately she wished to put the length of Ireland between herself and her brother. Masking her hatred, Lena smiled faintly. “Of course. I could do with some fresh air.”

 

            Following their mother out of the room, they crossed the foyer, shoes loud on the checkered marble, and Lex led them through a door beside the staircase, down a hallway and to a set of French doors opening onto the rather bleak garden. It was damp and green where it wasn’t bare, but was primarily still deep in the throes of winter, stark branches and bushes reflecting the austere nature of the Luthor manor house. Stepping outside, Lena shivered slightly in the cold, the dreary sky speaking of rain, and the air like a knife in Lena’s throat.

 

            Setting off down the ice-rimed stone path cutting through neat hedgerows, barely waist high, Lex had his hands in his pockets, perfectly at ease. Folding her arms over her chest as she scowled against the grey day, still somewhat in shock at the sudden change in her circumstances, Lena followed a few paces behind him. They passed by lichen and moss-speckled statues scattered along the path until they came to a fountain, the water greenish and full of rotting leaves, and her brother took the path around it, heading for the maze. 

 

            He slowed at the mouth of it, the frosted hedgerows taller than he was, plunging the path through it into shadow, turning to let Lena catch up to him. He took his hands out of his pockets and grabbed her arm, looping it through his and giving her hand a fond pat. He dragged them into motion, the two of them listening to birdsong in the barren branches of the trees scattered throughout the expansive gardens, the wind lessened with the barrier of the hedgerows, and something akin to peace blanketed them. Lena’s pulse was racing, though, even if she didn’t show her unease, the mask for her emotions she’d cultivated in her childhood back in place now that she was home again.

 

            “So,” Lex said after a few minutes, walking the familiar route through the maze, “what’s all this mum’s been telling me about you and a werewolf?”

 

            Fighting her body’s urge to go rigid, Lena’s mouth thinned, and she narrowed her eyes against the glare of the pale sky. “Well, it was the easiest way to get under her skin,” Lena blithely replied, a tightness in her chest. “And it served a dual purpose as well; easy access for research.”

 

            He let out a huff of laughter. “Research? I thought you were the Head of Charms.”

 

            “Yes, but I helped develop the Wolfsbane Potion as well. Belby didn’t even find a proper cure, so … well, I did my due diligence and found myself one of them to experiment on. No luck in ridding us of their kind yet, though, I’m afraid.”

 

            “Mum said you were living with her, that you’ve been with her for years.”

 

            Glancing sideways at him, the corner of Lena’s mouth twitched with a weak smile. “Well, a cure isn’t an overnight process . I admit, I might’ve led the creature to believe I cared for her, but it wasn’t particularly difficult to come up with the ruse when her prospects were rather slim. Pissing off our mother was merely an added incentive to continue with my research.”

 

            “Mm, well, I hope you’ll put any further dalliances with beasts behind you. It’s not fitting for one of our status to debase ourselves, even for the pursuit of knowledge, and least of all out of pettiness.”

 

            Lex’s tone was clipped, somewhat frosty as he spoke quietly. It was phrased as a suggestion, but Lena recognised it for the warning it was, her stomach lurching as she let out a soft laugh, breath misting before her in the cold air. She gave his hand a pat, cheek dimpling with her forced smile.

 

            “Don’t worry, I put an end to it the moment I heard you were out. I know where my priorities lie, and it’s not in chasing notoriety for the advancement of magic. I have missed you, you know.”

 

            “I missed you too,” he replied, leaning in to kiss her temple, bringing them to a halt for a step. “There’s much I’ve missed.”

 

            “What was it like?” Lena dared to ask, apprehensive as she gave him a wary look, her voice small.

 

            Amusement softened the hardness of her brother’s face, but when his eyes met hers, Lena felt her stomach lurch, something not quite right about it, something almost manic in his expression. There had always been something off-putting about her brother, more apparent to her as she got older, saw the casual cruelty beneath his arrogant nonchalance, but she felt the breath catch in her chest as she wondered just how sane he was now.

 

            “It was a constant torment,” he murmured, a muscle twitching in his jaw, anger blooming in his eyes as he cast his gaze ahead, bearing them left at the next intersection. “But it will all be worth it.”

 

            “Have you- have you seen him yet?”

 

            “No, but I will. And he will reward me for my loyalty.”

 

            Swallowing the lump in her throat, Lena nodded. “Just … be careful. Please.”

 

            He laughed, the sound loud in the stillness of the morning, sharp and chilling as Lena flinched slightly. “I have nothing to fear. Word is spreading, and while the Ministry denies the Dark Lord’s return, he grows stronger every day. When the time is right, when he summons me to his side, I’ll be protected by his power.” Hesitating, Lex glanced at his sister. “You should come with me. You’ll need to prove yourself first, but he would welcome another loyal servant into his circle.”

 

            Knowing it would be too obvious to leap at the chance, Lena licked her lips, hesitating before haltingly replying. “I’m not sure he would; I’m not a Pureblood.”

 

            Waving a hand dismissively, Lex smiled, knife-sharp. “There are a few who aren’t, but they’ve all proven their worth is beyond the weakness in their blood. The same would go for you, so long as you were loyal to his cause.”

 

            “Well, I only came home for you,” Lena hedged.

 

            With a small laugh, Lex brought them to a stop and reached up to grip Lena’s chin in a vice-like grip. Stiffening, Lena didn’t move a muscle as her brother held her face in a firm grasp, and she was unsure whether he even knew that he was hurting her, or even intended to, just swallowed as she watched him smile, lips twisting into a crooked smile.

 

            “Ah, little Lena, always so loyal , so eager to be wanted,” he practically crooned. “You’ll do well in his circle. Trust me. Once you meet him, you’ll love him wholeheartedly - more than you love me .”

 

            Lena didn’t tell him that her whole heart already belonged to someone else, no room for anyone else in it, just let the faintest hint of a strained smile twitch the corners of her mouth. “I doubt that,” she murmured. “My family will always come first.”

 

            She just forgot to mention which family she was talking about. Still, even though he interpreted her words to mean him, perhaps Lillian to a lesser extent, his face hardened, and he held her face a little tighter, almost squeezing her chin. She felt a prickle of fear, felt the tip of her wand pressing into her bent wrist as her fingers toyed with the cuff of her jumper’s sleeve, ready to arm herself if he didn’t let go. 

 

            “You will do as you’re told,” he coldly replied, his voice soft but something chilling about his face. 

 

            He let go of her chin then, relooping her arm through the crook of his elbow, and pulled her along. Stumbling into motion, Lena swallowed thickly. “Of course. I only meant … well, you’re hard to replace.” 

 

            She gently bumped him, and he chuckled, shouldering her back. “Fortunately, I’m back now, and the Dark Lord will change everything. For the better, you’ll see. We won’t have to demean ourselves by coexisting with those beneath us. He’ll elevate us to our rightful places.”

 

            Lena didn’t respond, keeping her expression neutral as they continued through the maze, reaching the middle a minute later. There was a sundial statue in the middle, weather-worn and old, the edges of stone softened by time, and Lena ran her finger over the lichen-speckled face of it, the day too overcast for the sundial to work. Walking around it, Lex eyed her with a shrewdness that she pretended she didn’t see, changing the topic to other things as she tried to make herself seem harmless.

 

            They spoke about some of his old friends, of other people who’d been caught that he hadn’t heard of, of what he’d missed. Lena had eagerly promised to fetch him some of his favourite chocolate from Honeydukes the next time she had a day off and could make the trip to Hogsmeade. Only then did Lex turn his attention to her, tiring of talking about himself, or perhaps trying to dissuade any suspicions instilled in him by Lillian.

 

            “So, what about you? You were still at school before I … went away. Now, you’re a qualified Healer and Head of Charms , to boot. You grew up.”

 

            “It doesn’t feel that way,” Lena said with an awkward laugh. “Especially not being back here now. Mum always has the knack of making me feel like I’m fifteen again.”

 

            “Ah, don’t worry about her. She’ll be pleased to have you back; you know how much she’s always prioritised family coming first, about the Luthor name succeeding.”

 

            “Mm, well, if things go well, hopefully we’ll surprise everyone and come out on top.”

 

            “I don’t doubt that we will,” Lex agreed, misconstruing Lena’s words once more. He gave her a sharp smile and then jerked his chin to the gap in the hedges. “Come on. It’s bloody freezing out here; let’s have a cup of tea and a game of Wizard’s Chess for old times’ sake.”

 

            Walking arm-in-arm with him back through the maze, her lungs burning and a headache pounding behind her eyes, Lena didn’t feel like playing chess, didn’t feel like sitting in her brother’s company, her whole body coiled in anticipation of his outbursts, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Still, somewhat helpless to let it happen, going along with things without complaint, hoping to get something out of it.

 

            Back inside, they retreated to the main living room, a chessboard on the dining table, Lena taking white and moving first. Her brother was a good player, had frequently versed her growing up, but Lena was better. She spotted several missteps, multiple avenues to checkmate in two or three, but she let him win, not wanting to wound his ego. When he finally checkmated her after she left her queen and a rook hanging in succession, he chuckled to himself, a smugness to his wide smile as he met her gaze.

 

            “It looks like you haven’t lost your edge in there,” Lena conceded the loss, giving her brother a crooked smile as she extended her hand across the board for him to shake.

 

            “And you clearly haven’t played in years.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, letting out a sheepish laugh, Lena shrugged. “Too busy with work.”

 

            He reached for his teacup, brought in by Hope earlier on in their game, taking a sip as Lena gestured for the board to reset itself. Setting it back down, he glanced down at his wrist, a watch - their father’s, she realised with a jolt of surprise - showing the time, and then smiled at her.

 

            “Time for another game?”

 

            Draining her own dregs of tea, Lena nodded as she indulged him in another round, once more letting him lose as she watched his ego inflate, never believing for a second that she was going easy on him, purposely blundering. It was almost laughable - Lena had been better at chess than he since she was a child, but he thought so much of himself that he never even considered that she was fooling him. After that, she excused herself to get ready for work, applying more of the bruise salve to her face, packing her satchel with comfortable shoes and then donning her green Healer robe before she Flooed through to the reception at St. Mungo’s hours before her shift started.

 

            Changing into scrubs and swapping her shoes out, Lena stowed her bag and got to work. She spent the following three nights there, sleeping in the on-call room, eating sandwiches, pasties and bowls of Cheeri-Owls in the tearoom between copious amounts of tea and coffee, the cereal making her sad as she thought of Kara’s penchant for the sugary treat. It was a difficult three nights, working herself to the point of exhaustion, racking up hours in the Theatre, snippy and otherwise quiet as she worked with the aid of potions, until she felt like she might drop. She saw Sam several times, her friend’s shifts coming and going while Lena remained at the hospital, avoiding speaking to her, afraid that she would reveal too much, that her misery would be too apparent. She didn’t spend more than a handful of minutes with her friend the entire time, finding some excuse to rush off whenever Sam caught her, full of guilt for that, too.

 

            Eventually, she couldn’t avoid going home. Her mother cornered her after she’d finished a procedure, removing her dragonhide gloves and washing her hands at the sink when Lillian had stepped inside the scrub room, informing Lena she’d be home for dinner that night. It wasn’t a question, wasn’t an invitation, merely stated as a fact. Quiet in her disgruntlement, dark circles ringing her eyes and a baleful look in her eyes, Lena curtly assured her that she would be there and was left to it. Finishing off the remainder of the day in the Alchemy Room, assisting a few Residents with their brewing hours, wearily coaching them through mistakes she wouldn’t have even made at Hogwarts , she Apparated to the gate of the Luthor estate just after five o’clock, making the long trek up to the front door and stepping inside.

 

            Dry-eyed and wound tight with tension, Lena showered and changed into normal clothes before making her way downstairs. Her mother and brother were enjoying wine in the main living room, a fire lit in the wide hearth, and she helped herself to a glass, answering questions when spoken to but itching for bed. It was a relief when they went through to the dining room to eat, the table laid with shining silver platters filled with food. Eating sparingly, her appetite avoiding her, Lena occasionally spoke but mostly focused on sipping her wine, feeling so very drained that all she really wanted was to go to bed. Instead, she made it through the drawn-out dinner, mother and son leisurely talking and sipping wine in between bites of food, Lillian’s gaze doting and full of pride, something Lena had never experienced from her mother before. Dinner ended just before eight o’clock, and Lena wearily excused herself from a nightcap in the drawing room, ignoring her mother’s snide comments about her work ethic as she kissed her brother’s cheek and then vanished upstairs.

 

            Falling into bed with barely a minute spent changing into pyjamas and cracking the window open for Morrigan, who ruffled her feathers and shifted away from Lena, evidently offended by three days of no attention, Lena was mercifully asleep almost instantly. She didn’t dream, her body heavy and unmoving as she slept deeply, waking eleven hours later and still feeling tired. Remaining holed up inside her room for a while longer, trying to prolong her peace, delay interacting with her family, she read in bed and then got up to shower and dress before eventually heading downstairs, a grim set to her mouth before she pulled herself together on the threshold of the dining room.

 

            Lex was still there, reading a newspaper, the remains of his breakfast before him with a fresh cup of coffee. He smiled as he glanced up from the article he was reading. “Ah, good morning. I thought you might sleep the whole morning away.”

 

            Suppressing the urge to roll her eyes, Lena glanced down at her watch. “It’s barely nine o’clock.”

 

            “Well, mum had a lot to say about it.”

 

            “Of course she did,” Lena dismissively replied, sitting across from him.

 

            Hope was there in an instant, wide-eyed with nerves but seeming to relax somewhat at Lena’s side, meekly glancing up at her as she set a toast stand on the table with a fresh pot of tea. Her voice was squeaky as she informed Lena that her boiled eggs would only be a minute longer, Lena’s face softening with a smile as she quietly thanked her, reaching for the teapot and filling a cup.

 

            “Anything interesting in the news?” Lena asked, jerking her chin to the newspaper still in her brother’s hand.

 

            “The usual drivel. I haven’t missed that . Mother said you’re still friends with the Rojas girl.”

 

            “Yes, we see each other fairly often when I’m not at work.”

 

            “Who else?”

 

            “Oh, um … well, one of the Attendings at work is a good friend. There’s also … Veronica Sinclair, Gayle Marsh, um, I was good friends with Jack Spheer,” she scrambled for Slytherin names, of friends she hadn’t seen in years, trying to entrench herself in the Pureblood circle she’d been schooled alongside.

 

            “A good friend? Mum told me you were engaged to him-”

 

            “Is there anything mum hasn’t told you?” Lena bitingly cut him off.

 

            He fell silent, giving her a flat look. She stiffened slightly in her seat, dragging her saucer closer, head ducked down as she toyed with the handle of her cup. The tension was palpable and fraught with danger, and Lena fought to clear her throat, her voice rough and meek as she ran a hand over her face.

 

            “Sorry. I’m just- I’m tired. Work has been busy, um … I probably should’ve slept a bit longer.”

 

            Rubbing her dry eyes, Lena exhaled softly, and Lex continued to stare at her for a long moment, raising his cup of coffee to his lips, drinking slowly as his dark eyes continued to pierce her. She didn’t look up, not even when Hope brought in her eggs, and she jumped slightly when her brother set his cup down heavy-handedly. Chair legs scraping the floorboards, he climbed to his feet, folding the newspaper and slapping it down on the table.

 

            “I’ll leave you to your breakfast in peace. I’ll be in the living room, once you’ve finished.”

 

            Nodding, Lena kept her eyes closed a moment longer before letting out a soft sigh and taking the top off a boiled egg. She ate as slow as possible, drawing out her breakfast as she had a third cup of tea, picking up the newspaper and making her way through the main articles and her horoscope, eating up another hour of her morning before she finally scooted her chair back and made her way through to the living room.

 

            Lex was reading, lounging on the sofa, the picture of ease, and Lena dropped down at the opposite end of the sofa. “Is mum home?”

 

            “She left for work just before eight.”

 

            Nodding, somewhat relieved to have to manage only one family member, Lena sank back against the cushions and closed her eyes. After a few minutes, Lex snapped his book shut and set it down between them, and Lena opened her eyes, turning her head slightly towards him. Pushing himself to his feet, he grinned down at her.

 

            “Come on, let’s have a game.”

 

            She glanced at the chessboard and suppressed a sigh, pushing herself up straighter as Lex rounded the coffee table to sit across from her. Lena had white again, moving her pawn forward to initiate the game, both of them remaining mostly silent as they played in the cool room, the heat of the fire doing nothing but stave off the cold of the outdoors, but adding a cosy ambience. It hadn’t snowed since Lena had come back home, but the windows were rimed in ice and fogged up, so they were fortunate that the estate was warded when they were disturbed twenty minutes later.

 

            A bell enchanted with the Caterwauling Charm started to clang loudly, alarm shooting through Lena as she looked up from the chessboard, eyes immediately going to her brother, who climbed to his feet, doing up the button of his suit jacket. Lena was on her feet as well, pulse racing as she rounded the coffee table, their game abandoned, and craned her neck to catch a glimpse through the tall, fogged-up windows. She couldn’t see anything distinct through them, but she knew her assumption of a raid had been correct.

 

            “Go,” she urged her brother, shooing him towards the fireplace.

 

            Grabbing a fistful of Floo powder, Lex hesitated as he made to step into the wide grate, glancing over his shoulder with a flicker of uncertainty. “Where-”

 

            Lena blurted out the address of her Dublin flat and watched Lex toss the powder into the fireplace, echoing her words and vanishing in a whirl of emerald flames. She no longer had any use for the Dublin flat, was happy to send him off there, where none of her personal effects were, to keep this ruse up for longer than a few measly days. It would be a bitter disappointment and embarrassing defeat to come out of this less than a week later with no information to show for it, and it would bind Lena closer to her brother, strengthening the trust there.

 

            Still, she so badly wanted the Aurors to come inside and take him away, whisk him back to Azkaban, or somewhere that hadn’t been breached yet. Instead, she stepped away from the fireplace, backtracking to the chessboard on the coffee table and then feeling the spike of panic as she realised they would question her too, suspect her, as intended. That would mean letting them inspect her arms, and her face paled at the thought. There was no possible enchantment that could hide the evil magic of a Dark Mark, but she could hide her scar, so Lena quickly slipped her wand out of her pocket and pushed her sleeve up.

 

            Listening for the door, she quickly glamoured her left forearm and then cast a quick spell to light a lamp so her last spell wouldn’t tip them off to a glamour. The sound of the front door bursting open sounded then, multiple sets of footsteps on the marble, voices calling out, overlapping as instructions were given. A man called out to announce the arrival of the Auror Department with a search warrant for the property, and Lena was still standing near the chess set with her wand in hand when Alex entered the room first.

 

            There was a slight pause, barely a heartbeat as their eyes met, before Alex’s face hardened and she straightened her raised wand arm, firing off a non-verbal spell as she stormed forward. It struck Lena in the face, the sound of her nose breaking making her blink, the sharp pain quick to follow as blood ran over her lips and chin. It dripped to the floor as she raised a hand to cup it, head awkwardly ducked as her wand was torn from her grasp by a follow-up disarming spell. Then Lena’s body went taut as she was jerked a few inches off the ground, her hands dragged to her sides, immobilised as Alex approached, her eyes trained on Lena as she called over her shoulder for backup, which was already coming, two more Aurors in the doorway as they watched it play out.

 

            “Give me a hand here,” Alex said as another woman stepped up next to her, wand also pointed at Lena. Jerking her chin, Alex continued. “Fetch her wand. And check her arms - both of them, just in case.”

 

            Mouth clamped into a flat line, blood in the creases of her lips, Lena gave Alex a blank look, trying to feign indifference. Her heart was pounding in her chest, though, and she knew that Alex’s spell had been intentional, clearly under the assumption that Kara’s broken nose had been Lena’s doing, as they’d intended. Lena didn’t mind; she would’ve expected much worse if she’d actually laid a finger on Kara. Still, the worst part was looking into Alex’s eyes, expecting the anger, which, yes, was there, and seeing wounded betrayal as well. 

 

            The reality of it struck Lena then, that it hadn’t just been Kara she’d left, that there had been other people she cared about and who cared about her too, other people who she’d hurt by allowing this charade to play out. She hadn’t even said goodbye to Alex, hadn’t given any reason or excuse, which was out of necessity, but it still made her feel sick with guilt to see the hurt in her sister-in-law’s eyes as they stared at each other now. She knew Alex was stubborn to a fault, and there was the voice at the back of her head that whispered that she’d never be forgiven for what she’d done, even though it was all a lie. Alex didn’t forgive that easily.

 

            Lena’s wand in her hands, the other Auror - Vasquez, Lena realised as she dragged her eyes away from Alex and stared at the familiar witch, present at many parties thrown by Alex over the years - approached her. Alex kept her held in that taut, floating position while Vasquez jerked up one sleeve of her jumper, finding it bare, and then onto the other, also bare. Dropping her arms, leaving the sleeves pushed up, Vasquez turned to Alex, whose eyes were trained on Lena’s pale forearms.

 

            “All clear.”

 

            “Watch her,” Alex muttered, ending her spell as Lena’s body went limp before gaining control of itself as her knees buckled.

 

            She managed to save herself the indignity of collapsing to the floor, and pulled her sleeves down as she watched Alex brusquely leave the room without another word. Lena felt shame prickle in her face, clearing her throat as she wiped her wet chin and then stared down at her red palms. Looking up, she found Vasquez giving her a wary look and licked her lips, her throat hoarse as she spoke.

 

            “May I fetch my handkerchief from my pocket?”

 

            “Slowly,” Vasquez conceded with a warning.

 

            Nodding, Lena’s hand moved towards her pocket, fetching out the square of spotless white cotton, quickly stained red as she wiped her mouth and chin and then pressed it to her nose. After a moment, she moved towards the sofa, sinking onto it and leaning back against the cushions. Closing her eyes, Lena listened to the sound of footsteps passing back and forth through the house, floorboards creaking overhead, distant doors slamming shut, voices calling back and forth. It dragged on while she was left under the guard of Vasquez, whose wand arm had developed a tremor, until another Auror stepped into the doorway.

 

            “Thank you, Vasquez, I’d like to have a word with Healer Luthor.”

 

            “Sir.”

 

            Lowering her wand as she nodded, taking Lena’s wand with her as well, Vasquez strode towards J’onn and passed by him, closing the doors behind her. Lena stared at J’onn, only vaguely acquainted with him but relieved by his presence; he’d known she was helping the Order in the first war, and she was hoping to have an ally in him now, someone she didn’t have to lie to. He quickly put her at ease, crossing the room and dropping onto the low armchair set across from the sofa, the coffee table and unfinished chess game between them.

 

            J’onn twirled his wand in both hands, nodding at the chess set. “Playing by yourself?”

 

            Lena’s mouth twitched with a faint smile. “Did Kara-”

 

            “Yes, she got your message through to Dumbledore. He sends his gratitude and would like to meet with you at some point soon, once you’re sure your movements aren’t being watched.”

 

            Nodding, Lena wiped her nose and swallowed the coppery taste caught at the back of her throat as she balled the handkerchief up in a bloody fist. “How should I send word? I used to use my owl while I was at school, but now that I’m older, I think that might be more suspect.”

 

            “Dumbledore would like to limit the number of people who know you’re a spy, naturally. Seeing as you already told Kara, he’s suggested she carry messages.”

 

            “But … we broke up. I had to end things to make it believable-”

 

            “Yes, she told us, but is there a way you can get information to her without compromising yourself?”

 

            Thinking a moment, lips pressed into a flat line as a divot furrowed her brows, Lena wrinkled her nose, pain flaring up as her broken nose objected to the movement. “I- well, I told her I was staying at my flat in Dublin, and she was going to her mother’s house in Cornwall, so our home is empty. I could- I could leave letters there for her to collect, but she’d need to know when there’s something to pick up; it could be time-sensitive.” 

 

            Pausing a moment, Lena patted her pocket, where the Cryptex was stowed, the little box with the dials and symbols burning hot and beeping when she was on-call and needed to be contacted to rush to St. Mungo’s. Pulling it out of her pocket, she fiddled with it and then held it up between thumb and forefinger. 

 

            “We use these at work. A simple Protean Charm to link them. I could do the same with an item, say … a Gobstone, a bracelet, just something ordinary we can keep in our pockets or wear. If I transfigure the colour of it or the pattern, it’ll burn while it changes.”

 

            “That could work. I’ll speak to Dumbledore and we’ll get something to you both.”

 

            Nodding, Lena raked a hand through her hair. “Thank you.”

 

            “Now, to business; your brother …”

 

            “I’ve seen him,” Lena hedged, still aware that J’onn was an Auror first. “I imagine Dumbledore would like him to remain free so I can spy effectively?”

 

            “Yes, that would be more useful to us, personal feelings aside.”

 

            Lips twitching with another smile as her green eyes flickered with amusement, Lena hummed in agreement. “Yes, personal feelings aside. There’s nothing to report yet; he’s lying low, of course, and I need to build trust first. My mother will be harder to convince, but she’s not the one with a mark on her arm, so I can handle that.”

 

            “Right, well, unfortunately, they’ll be doing a full sweep of the place, and all personal items, so while we wait for that to end, is there anything you can think of? Anything at all that you’d like me to pass on to Dumbledore?”

 

            Considering it, touching the bridge of her nose as it continued to throb, Lena was silent for a minute. “My brother intends for me to go to meetings, to meet the Dark Lord himself, once I’ve shown my loyalty. I’d like it known to Dumbledore that I won’t be branded with a Dark Mark, no matter how many lives it might save down the line to ingratiate myself so deeply with the Death Eaters.”

 

            Shifting in his seat, J’onn nodded, crossing one ankle over the opposite knee. “I think that’s understandable.”

 

            His eyes flitted to Lena’s left forearm, and she was struck with the embarrassing notion that he hadn’t forgotten about the scar he’d seen there so many years ago, when she was still a teenager, in over her head and too helpless as she was forced to let him see it. Gripping her arm, she dug her thumb into the wool of her jumper, right over the scarred words. Clearing her throat, feeling the warmth creep up her neck, Lena tried to keep the colour from flooding her cheeks.

 

            “But I’ll attend what meetings I can. Frequent the same places he used to go to last time, see if any of his old acquaintances are still around. I know of a few who I’m sure will at least be openly sympathetic with You Know Who’s cause, even if they don’t bear a mark.”

 

            “Your mother?”

 

            “Well, that’s undeniable,” Lena softly laughed, “although, I haven’t spent enough time with her since graduating from Hogwarts, so I’m unsure of her current sentiment on the topic. I do know that she still holds a deep prejudice towards blood purity; she’s not very fond of me, or werewolves, so …”

 

            “At this stage, any information you can provide is vital. Even just known sympathisers we can tail would be beneficial.”

 

            “Who do you have on your list so far?”

 

            “Rookwood, Dolohov, Black, Malfoy, Crabb, Goyle,” J’onn rattled off the top of his head, spreading his hands pragmatically. “The main suspects from last time. Any shared connections of theirs who are undoubtedly complicit.”

 

            “There were a few I went to school with. Namely, Veronica Sinclair, out of those I was well acquainted with. Mercy and Otis Graves were close friends of my brother back in the day; I didn’t hear that they were branded Death Eaters last time, but I’m sure they’d leap at the chance. Rumours were circulating through school in my Seventh Year, right after it ended, of others who were supposedly involved, or friends of friends, extended family. Morgan Edge - he was a bit older - and Maxwell Lord and John Corben, too.”

 

            Lena listed everyone she’d ever heard a rumour about, whether there was any validity to it or not, and she watched as J’onn jotted down the names. She wasn’t sure how outdated all of that was, unsure how deep the bigotry of those she’d named had gone last time, whether those sentiments had festered over the years since Harry Potter had defeated Voldemort, but it seemed safer to cast suspicion on them than to err on the side of caution.

 

            Her palms were clammy, her heart still beating somewhat fast, despite knowing that she had an ally in the room, that she hadn’t done anything to incriminate herself, save for in the eyes of her sister-in-law. Lena cared a shocking amount about the opinion Alex had of her, knowing that this had been her intention, to put an insurmountable gulf between herself and the kindhearted people who’d been a better family than the one she’d grown up with, to make sure that her actions and choices in this budding war couldn’t be misconstrued. And yet, she was filled with that bitter dismay that it had worked so well, any fondness she’d garnered immediately severed by a lie and a broken nose. She’d known it would work, that it would be effective, and yet, it still hurt, a similar sting to the betrayal of Kara all those years ago, not believing Lena when Lena had purposely misled her into thinking badly of her. It was to a lesser extent now, though, because at least Kara knew the truth this time. Lena could live with the rest.

 

            Touching the bridge of her nose again, she shrugged nonchalantly, staring at the chess set. “That’s all, I think.”

 

            Pocketing his notebook and quill, J’onn nodded. “Thank you. I’ll pass this on, and we’ll go from there. I’ll look into that Protean Charm as well.”

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Hesitating, J’onn cleared his throat and ran his palms over the thighs of his pants. “Dumbledore also would like me to, ah, ensure that you’re willing to take the risk associated with this. Obviously, you’d be risking your life by aiding the Order, and with no real protection from us, and your brother is well-known for his cruelty. I’m assuming you know that better than anyone, and the fact that you’ve willingly come back is a testament to your dedication to the Order, but … well, Dumbledore would like to reiterate that you’re under no obligation-”

 

            “Thank you, Auror J’onzz,” Lena interrupted him, sniffing as she tried to wipe the drying blood off her palms, eyes cast down. “I know the risk I’m taking, but it’s what must be done. I’ve already made promises to get myself out if it becomes too big of a risk, and I intend to keep that promise. But you can tell Dumbledore that I’m committed to this path for the foreseeable future.”

 

            “Alright, then. And my apologies for the, uh, the nose,” he gestured to Lena’s face.

 

            Waving a hand dismissively, Lena weakly smiled, eyes closing for a moment. “Think nothing of it. I hope you won’t punish her for it, seeing as I was armed, so it should be considered an act of self-defence.”

 

            “You’re a good witch, Lena,” J’onn sighed, grimacing slightly. “It’s a very brave thing you’re doing, and the Order is lucky to have you on our side.”

 

            Nodding, his words a cold comfort to Lena, she remained silent. After a few minutes of sitting there, a certain tension blanketing them as the muffled sound of the search continued, J’onn pushed himself to his feet. Looking down at her, he cleared his throat.

 

            “Thank you for your help.”

 

            She nodded, fiddling with the handkerchief as she hunched her shoulders, mouth twisting with dismay. Walking to the door, J’onn opened it and stepped back out into the foyer, calling out orders, catching Aurors to ask them to check for certain things in particular, while Lena was left on the sofa, a different Auror filling the tall doorway to keep watch over her. With a soft sigh, Lena leaned forward and picked up a white knight from the chessboard, turning it over in her red palm before she moved it by hand, checkmating her brother and watching as his king toppled over.

 

            It was almost another two hours before they started to file out, coming up with nothing but a few questionable books they confiscated and leaving with disgruntled looks on their faces as they gave her her wand back, J’onn giving her a curt nod as he stepped into the doorway of the living room and then vanished from sight. Left alone, Lena went limp, a cold sweat prickling her skin as she sank into the sofa and breathed slowly for a few minutes, before she made herself stand, a little weak-kneed, and walked over to the fireplace.

 

            Picking up the pot of Floo powder, glad she’d never had her flat removed from the Floo Network, she dashed a handful into the grate and Flooed to her flat, the pot still cradled in the crook of her arm as she stepped out. Lex was leaning against the kitchen counters, looking unbothered, bored of waiting, and he arched an eyebrow at her appearance as she held the pot of Floo powder aloft.

 

            “They’re gone.”

 

            Approaching, he reached out to thumb her chin, streaked with dried blood. “Bastards.”

 

            “Nothing I can’t fix,” she weakly smiled, her nose dully aching.

 

            “Thanks for that. Quick thinking,” he nodded, looking around the bare place.

 

            “Here.”

 

            He took a handful of powder and Flooed home, Lena quick to follow, setting the pot back on the mantle. Crossing back over to the chessboard and taking a seat, Lex eyed the game for a moment, noticing the checkmate, and then swept everything off the coffee table. Startled at the sudden outburst, Lena backed up against the fireplace, staring at his back, watching him run a hand over the bald pate of his head before he got to his feet again and stalked out of the room without another word. 

 

            Heart in her throat, Lena remained rooted to the spot for a minute before she tidied up the mess of his tantrum and then slipped upstairs. It was Saturday, and she had work later anyway, deciding to feign getting called in if Lex caught her on the way out, quickly healing her nose in her bathroom mirror and then getting her things together before she Flooed to St. Mungo’s and fetched a potion to wake herself up more. Dressing in clean scrubs, she hesitated before making her way to her mother’s office, drawing in a deep breath before knocking and entering when ordered to.

 

            Lillian glanced up, raising her eyebrows. Easing the door shut and clearing her throat, Lena met her mother’s stare, keeping her chin jerked up a fraction. “I’m sure he’ll tell you when you go home, but I thought you should know now that the house just got raided.”

 

            She watched her mother’s face ripple with surprise, lips parting as Lena caught her off-guard. A rare occurrence. “Lex-”

 

            “I sent him to my flat,” Lena quickly reassured her. “They didn’t find anything. Well, the library is missing a few books, perhaps, but other than that … nothing.”

 

            “And did they question you?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “And what did you tell them?”

 

            “What I needed to to make them leave. I imagine they’ll be back, though.”

 

            “Did they have a warrant?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “Very well,” Lillian nodded, shifting in her seat, the tension in her body fading now as she cleared her throat and motioned to the door. “You can go.”

 

            She hadn’t expected anything more than that, no gratitude or pride in her quick thinking, saving her brother from being caught again so soon after his escape, and Lena was glad to have the exchange over. All she’d wanted to accomplish from that was to showcase her loyalty to family, hoping to garner a little more trust from her mother, even if it was only a sliver. Moving back through the floors of St. Mungo’s, she checked the charts of the currently admitted patients and started delegating tasks to the Residents on duty. 

 

            Working all through the night, she was glad for the distraction of it, tirelessly going from patient to patient and catching Sam near midnight for a brief reprieve in the tearoom. She had a coffee, strong and bitter, and shared a sandwich and packet of crisps with Sam, both of them stifling yawns, talking very little as Lena remained silent, playing it off as exhaustion. Draining her coffee, she excused herself under the guise of being paged on her Cryptex and left the tearoom to go and do a lap of the Charms Ward.

 

            It ended up getting busy for a brief spell, Lena dragged from bed to bed, into the Theatre a few times for mercifully quick procedures as she monitored the Residents she let take the lead on them. After her latest procedure, she emerged from the Theatre pale-faced with a slight stoop to her shoulders as she made for the nurse’s station, still working her robe on. It was mid-morning on Sunday, and she was jotting down notes, leaving sections of the charts for the Interns to manage, when she heard her name called. It was a soft rasping voice, but as familiar to her as her own, even though it wasn't the usual warm tenderness she was accustomed to. She looked up on instinct, her brain still processing everything, trying to keep up with her new reality, and stared at Kara, looking grey and drawn, her eyes bloodshot and bottom lip trembling.

 

            Lena froze at the sight of her, as her mind caught up, lips parting, taking every bit of her strength not to reach out, to cup Kara’s face in her hands, stroke her scarred cheeks and let her gaze soften as she tenderly asked her what was wrong. Of course, Lena knew what was wrong - they weren’t allowed to do that - but there was a desperate anguish in Kara’s tearful eyes as she kept walking straight for her, not stopping until there was little more than a foot between them.

 

            “I need to talk to you,” Kara murmured, her voice wavering as she barely held it together. 

 

            “You shouldn’t be here,” Lena muttered, quickly averting her gaze, a stiff set to her shoulders as she looked down at the chart she’d been reading through, not seeing the words and numbers, not seeing much of anything, adrenaline pumping through her whole body as she held herself back.

 

            “Please. Please, Lena, I-” Kara grabbed her wrist as she begged, and Lena jumped slightly at the contact.

 

            Feeling a tightness in her chest, aware of other staff around, of Kara’s rasping words, louder as she pleaded, Lena hurriedly shut the manila folder and grabbed Kara’s arm. Dragging her along, a little rough in her urgency, Lena briskly hauled her down a hallway and then made a left and a right before opening the door to an on-call room and steering Kara inside. Slipping in after her, Lena shut the door, her eyes flitting to the empty bunks to double-check they were alone, before her eyes landed on Kara.

 

            “You shouldn’t be here,” Lena repeated, her voice cracking as her heart raced.

 

            “I had to,” Kara breathlessly insisted, taking an urgent step forward and then pulling up short when Lena shied away.

 

            Turning her head aside, Lena felt a prickle of shame as Kara faltered, blinking in surprise, before she forged on again, as if her reaction had been a mistake, reaching out for Lena. “Alex-”

 

            Catching her wrists, Lena gently but firmly pushed Kara away, putting some distance between them again. “Don’t. Please. I don’t want this to be more difficult than it already is.”

 

            Hurt flitted across Kara’s face as her shoulders slumped, glassy eyes filling with more tears as she floundered for a moment. It hadn’t even been a full week yet, and nothing had changed in their feelings, not in the slightest, so it felt wrong for them to not be able to touch each other, for Lena to kiss the scars of Kara’s cheeks, and Kara to smooth a thumb over the dark circles beneath Lena’s eyes. It all felt so horribly wrong, and yet, Lena didn’t waver, a hard set to her jaw as she kept her eyes down on the floor, hands balled into fists.

 

            “You told me you went to Dublin,” Kara managed to get out after a moment, her voice thick with agony and doubt. Lena didn’t respond, and after a beat of silence, Kara continued. “But Alex said- she said they raided your family’s estate … that they went through your things, in your room.”

 

            Rubbing the bridge of her nose, Lena’s mouth was a flat line as she continued not to speak, the sound of Kara’s quick, shallow breaths filling the on-call room. She couldn’t look at her, guilt needling Lena as she stared at the floor, her throat tight around any excuse she could’ve made, mentally cursing Alex out for telling Kara. She’d intended to keep that to herself, if only to spare Kara the knowledge.

 

            “Tell me that’s not true,” Kara brokenly demanded, the breath hitching in her throat.

 

            “It was the only way-“

 

            “No.”

 

            The fierceness of her response made Lena soften, but when she looked up at the flicker of movement, she had to slam that wall back into place. Kara reached out and touched her face, and Lena turned her head aside, shrugging off her touch.

 

            “Please,” Kara whispered, her tears falling now as she cupped Lena’s cheek again, stepping in close. “Don’t do this. You can’t-“

 

            “It was always my intention,” Lena murmured, reaching up to cover Kara’s hand with her own before she peeled it away from her face and urged it back down to her girlfriend’s side. “It’ll all be okay.”

 

            “No, you can’t- you weren’t supposed to go back there. I was supposed to keep you safe . You can’t do this, please, don’t do this. You need to come home. Come home with me, and we can- we can join the Order together, and- and-“

 

            Setting her hands on Kara’s shoulders, Lena forced her away, a determined set to her jaw as her brow furrowed over brooding green eyes. She was trying to be strong, but Kara’s cheeks were wet with tears, and her eyes were red and full of devastation. Lena withdrew her hands and looked down at the floor, hand in the pocket of her Healer robe as she fiddled with the Cryptex.

 

            “I’m not coming home with you. I’m sorry.”

 

            “I- wha- but … you- this wasn’t the plan. This wasn’t what we said-“

 

            “It was the plan - my plan. It was my decision,” Lena firmly cut her off.

 

            Wiping her face with the sleeves of her robe, Kara drew in a hitching breath before she let out a breathless sob. “But we said- we said that- you weren’t supposed to go back there. You said you’d get out if you were in- in danger. They're going to hurt you.”

 

            Closing her eyes, covering them with a hand, Lena shakily exhaled. “I always planned to go home, Kara. I just- I didn’t want to tell you that. I didn’t want to upset you.”

 

            Mouth opening and closing as more tears ran down her cheeks, Kara shook her head. “No, you can’t just- you can’t just lie to me and think I’ll accept that as- as an okay excuse.”

 

            Her cheeks were reddening now, and Lena cringed as she briefly glanced at her, hating to make Kara look the fool, but thinking it had been her best option. She thought it would take her longer than a week to figure out that Lena wasn’t at the Dublin flat, and that perhaps some of the anger at that would be dimmed by then.

 

            “Well, you have to accept it,” Lena softly snapped, getting frustrated now, wanting the interaction to be over before she caved. It was what she wanted to do more than anything, but she’d made her decision, and she’d ended things with Kara for this reason. She hadn’t achieved anything worthwhile yet, and she knew she had to keep going. “I was going to do this whether you approved or not. I made my decision, and I’m sorry that it upsets you, but I’m doing what’s best-“

 

            “Not what’s best for you,” Kara hotly interrupted, wiping her face. “When will you put yourself first? I didn’t want you to do this, but I didn’t think that- I thought you’d at least be safe most of the time. Not- not sleeping under the same roof as them. I- have you lost the plot?”

 

            “Maybe it’ll be over quicker this way,” Lena tried to reason.

 

            “You’re going to get hurt,” Kara sobbed, taking a stumbling step forward. “Please don't do this, please don’t let them hurt you. I can’t let anything bad happen to you, okay? You’re the love of my life; I just- I want you to come home with me. I’ll do anything for you to change your mind. Anything. I’ll- I’ll beg.”

 

            She sank to her knees before Lena, reaching out to grab fistfuls of her robe as Lena looked down at her with agony. Loudly weeping as she hunched over, Kara breathlessly pleaded with Lena, and Lena felt that self-hatred that had been buried for so long rear its head again. She didn’t like to make Kara cry, and even the other night, when they’d both fallen apart together before leaving, it hadn’t been like this. It hadn’t been Kara on her knees begging her to stay, crying her eyes out, the sounds of her sobs cutting through Lena; that had been a mutual heartbreak.

 

            But this time, Lena was watching Kara unravel as she stood there, white-faced and tormented by it. Every bit of her wanted to collapse to the floor and wrap her in her arms, stroke her hair and tell her it would be okay, but she didn’t. Lena just remained standing, ashen and nauseous as she shifted with agitation, a tightness in her chest as she struggled to breathe, not sure what to do as she quietly urged Kara to get up.

 

            “Come on, darling, get up off the floor,” Lena softly pleaded, her voice wavering. “Please, just get up.”

 

            “Please, don’t. I don’t understand why you’re doing this,” Kara sobbed, still clutching the hem of Lena’s robe in one hand.

 

            The door cracked open behind Lena then, and she glanced over her shoulder before relief washed through her. Sam poked her head inside, confusion furrowing her face as she held her Cryptex in her hand, where Lena had secretly paged her to the room with the Cryptex in her own pocket.

 

            “Hey, what’s- oh.”

 

            Quickly taking stock of things as she slipped into the on-call room, Sam looked from Kara to Lena with surprise. Looking up, uncaring about the mess of her appearance, Kara let out a ragged sound of relief as she clumsily staggered to her feet.

 

            “Sam. Sam, you have to- you have to talk to her,” Kara urged her, reaching out for the Healer’s robe, her eyes wide and full of tears. “Please, tell her not to do this.”

 

            “I- wha-“ Sam stammered, her eyes darting to Lena.

 

            Raking a hand through her hair, her distress evident, Lena’s voice was thick with regret and guilt as she gestured to Kara. “Can you get her out of here? Please.”

 

            Blinking in surprise, floundering for a moment, Sam looked back at Kara, reaching out to gently take her arm with no further questions or explanation needed. “Alright, it's time to go.”

 

            Mouth falling open with indignant surprise, Kara spluttered, “but-“

 

            “Look, I’m sorry, but we’re working , so you can’t be here right now, okay?” Sam tried to reason, gently but firmly. “I don’t want to call security-“

 

            Letting out a scoff of disbelieving laughter, Kara looked at Lena, who had one hand on her hip, the other cupping her brow. Sniffing, wiping her face, Kara couldn’t keep the tremor out of her voice as she gave Lena an aching look.

 

            “This is what you want?”

 

            “Yes,” Lena whispered, unable to meet her gaze.

 

            Kara let out a pitiful sound, and Sam tugged on her arm, using her vulnerable state to forcibly steer her out of the room. The second they were in the hallway, Lena firmly shut the door, hands braced against the wood as she let out a breathless, choked sound. Feeling like she might be sick, she walked over to the bottom bunk and sank onto it, elbows on her thighs and face buried in her palms.

 

            Drawing in shallow breaths as she tried to stamp her feelings down, Lena was sitting in the exact same position twenty minutes later when the door opened again. She didn’t move a muscle, knowing that it was Sam without looking up when no apologetic stammering for an Intern or Resident greeted her. The door clicked shut, and Lena felt her friend’s stare drilling into her.

 

            It was quiet for a minute until Sam moved over to the bunks to sit beside her, clearing her throat. “So, are you going to tell me what that was all about?”

 

            With a weary sigh, Lena dropped her hands from her face, tipping her head back as she kept her eyes closed. “Kara and I split up at the start of the week.”

 

            “You what?” Sam exclaimed. “Why?”

 

            Raking a hand through her hair, Lena helplessly shrugged. “We just- we had a row. One thing led to another. Um … things haven’t been right for months now, so I think- well, it was only a matter of time. We both knew it; she’s not taking it well, though, obviously.”

 

            “Right, yeah, I just spent fifteen minutes trying to console her in the alleyway outside before she finally left. But … are you okay? I mean … the two of you have always been … I don’t know, it was odd, but it felt right. Is that- is that something you want to just … throw away?”

 

            “I don’t know,” Lena murmured, staring at the black wall ahead. “I haven’t really had time to think things through yet. I have more important things to worry about right now.”

 

            “I- right, well … and has she moved out, or where are you staying?”

 

            “I still have my Dublin flat. It’s a bit … bare, but- well, I think she’s gone to stay with her mother, anyway. I’m not really sure; I haven’t spoken to her since Monday.”

 

            “So that’s why you’ve looked like shit all week. I thought you were doing more overtime than usual, but I- well, I just thought it was a distraction from this thing with your brother.”

 

            Lena hummed absentmindedly, rubbing her chin as she felt exhaustion wash over her. Sam watched her for a moment, silent as she waited for any further explanation from Lena, pity swimming in her hazel eyes, before she sighed and forged onwards.

 

            “Okay. Well … she wanted me to give you this.”

 

            Sam held out a little paper butterfly, and Lena’s shoulders caved as she reached out to pluck it from her friend’s palm. “Thanks.”

 

            “What time are you off? We should go for a drink. You definitely need one.”

 

            “I’ll be here all night. Maybe tomorrow, or when are you off?”

 

            “I can do tomorrow night - if you’re up to it. You really should get some sleep, love, you look like you might keel over at any moment.”

 

            “Mm, maybe I’ll have a lie down for a bit.”

 

            “Are you going to be alright? Do you want to go home?”

 

            Shaking her head, rubbing her tired eyes as she smiled thinly, Lena swallowed the lump in her throat. “No. No, I- that’s the last thing I want to do. I’ll be okay, though. I’ll come and find you for a cup of tea once I wake up, alright? And … thank you for that. She- well, it’s complicated and I didn’t want to hurt her.”

 

            Giving her back a quick rub, Sam nodded sympathetically. “I can’t say I understand what’s gone on, but you know I’m on your side, no matter how much I like her. If there’s anything else I can do, just ask.”

 

            Lena gave her another wan smile, nodding, and Sam squeezed her arm before climbing to her feet. Slipping out of the on-call room, she left Lena alone with the little folded butterfly. With a defeated slump to her shoulders, Lena’s fingers shook slightly as she unfolded the piece of parchment and took in Eliza’s address written in her hand, and then the scribbled note beneath it in Kara’s handwriting.
