Alex made my mum change her to the Secret Keeper. Please come if you’re in trouble. I’ll be waiting for you, my secret. I love you xxx

 

            Feeling as if her chest had been split open, Lena turned, tipping onto her back as she pressed the note to her heart, eyes closing to the slats of the bunk above. It felt hard to breathe, knowing that she’d hurt Kara by withholding the truth, that she’d given her little say in the matter, kicking her out of St. Mungo’s so she couldn’t change Lena’s mind. And how badly Lena wanted her mind to be changed, to be selfish and choose her own happiness for a change. It was seeing Kara pleading on her knees that had almost been her undoing, because she would do anything to make sure she wasn’t in pain, and it was so obvious that Lena was hurting her, was the cause of her heartache. 

 

            And yet, she’d held it together long enough for Sam to do her dirty work for her. It didn’t make it any easier to bear, but she was grateful that Kara had let her make her own decision. Lena just hoped they wouldn’t see each other again so soon, and hoped even more that it would all be over soon, so she could hold Kara in her arms and apologise until she ran out of ways to say it.

Chapter 53

            The following weeks were the most miserable of Kara’s life. Over the years, almost a third of her life ago now, the fear and pain of being bitten and losing her father had dimmed, the memories of it somewhat hazy, and so, to Kara, losing Lena was a fresh agony that eclipsed any other bad thing that had ever happened to her. It was like a shock to her system, the sudden loss of her girlfriend, who was still very much alive and still very much in love with her. And yet, Kara was back at home, in her childhood room in Cornwall, sleeping in the narrow bed in the tiny bedroom she’d once shared with her sister. From one day to the next, everything had come apart, and she was struggling to process it, despite knowing it was temporary, that it was a choice she’d always known was a very real possibility. But when it happened, it hadn’t felt real.

 

            It had been a hard first week, made even harder when Alex had shown up at the Black house in Islington after her shift one evening, mentioning the raid that had been conducted on the Luthor estate. Kara had sat rigidly near her sister, staring down at the worn tabletop in the dim kitchen, her whole body taut as she listened to her sister’s account of it, bitterly coming up empty-handed. The only piece of information that had been worthwhile was Lena’s presence there, the futile search of her room, and that had finally made Kara look up, her gaze sharply landing on her sister as her lips parted in surprise. Kara had known she would have to listen to the ignorant judgment of her friends and family, who weren’t supposed to know any better, but she hadn’t anticipated hearing from her sister that Lena had moved back home.

 

            What else could she do but show up at St. Mungo’s and beg Lena to come home with her? It hadn’t gone the way Kara had hoped, in tears, on her knees, trying to reason with her love as Lena barely looked at her. It had been confusing, such a cold front, familiar to Kara but not for many years, not since she’d been young and accusatory and mistrustful of her best friend and had lost her for a long time. It was like stepping back in time, except they were no longer twenty and Kara hadn’t expected that reaction from Lena. She hadn’t expected to be escorted out by Sam either, crying in the alleyway on a dismal, grey day as rain soaked her hair and clothes, a note in her pocket that she’d had to hand over as a last resort to ensure Lena’s safety.

 

            Weeks had passed since then, with no sight of Lena. The loneliness was gut-wrenching, leaving a pit in Kara’s chest as she moved through her days in a daze. At work, she’d started to arrive early, regularly arriving at the Department of Mysteries at six o’clock to let out the Order member who had been on guard duty, working through until everyone else had left to let in the person on guard duty that night, staying behind even longer, sometimes to seven or eight o’clock, or taking guard duty herself, gritty-eyed and dull the next day as she drank copious amounts of coffee to keep her going until that evening. 

 

            It became a more frequent thing, allowing Kara to distract herself as much as possible. If she wasn’t working, she was helping the Order; if she wasn’t helping the Order, she was at home with her mother, usually in bed, catching up on sleep. It was all so very exhausting, but it was better than the alternative of being left to her thoughts, left to brood over the gaping holes in her life that Lena had used to fill. Kara missed her so badly that on the first full moon without her, she dutifully drank her seven doses of the Wolfbane Potion collected from their cottage and still made her way to St. Mungo’s that afternoon to check herself in, if only to catch a glimpse of Lena in the hallways, to know she was alright. She didn’t see her, but then, she had been asleep in the hospital bed the next morning when a figure had hovered outside the doors to the Dai Llewellyn ward for a minute, just to catch a glimpse of her.

 

            The first month dragged, despite how busy she kept, February arriving with damp, foggy mornings as Kara found herself in the back garden, trimming hedges with her mother, although she couldn’t remember agreeing to it, pruning shears in hand and a gold ring on her finger with a white stone set in it. She’d been pulled aside two weeks after splitting up, after an Order meeting, the ring pressed into her palm with a quick summary of the codes, or what was expected of her. A Protean Charm had been cast on it to change colours; if the ring burned and turned green, a letter had been left for her to collect from the cottage at her earliest convenience, if it was amber, it was somewhat time-sensitive, and if it burned red, it was urgent and required her immediate retrieval. Likewise, if a letter was given to her to pass on to Lena, she changed the colour on her ring to the matching code for Lena to read. So far, it had burned once - green - at five o’clock on a Saturday, and Kara had retrieved it almost instantly, hoping to catch Lena for just a moment, but the cottage had been empty when she’d arrived, the furniture draped with white sheets, nothing stirring.

 

            Since then, nothing, although she was sure more was to come. There was always more to do with the Order anyway, as Kara found herself thrust back into the middle of the eclectic group of witches and wizards - some familiar from the first war, others new or young - all of it quite secret. If she saw most of them on the street, she wouldn’t even be able to acknowledge that she knew them, as covert as they tried to keep their allegiances. It was not the same Order she’d once been a part of, though; there was less scurrying through bushes this time, less drama to it as they all had their respective tasks, quite mundane compared to the thrilling danger of her youth. Kara wondered if perhaps the early years of the first war, which she’d been too young to be involved in, had been similar, and if this brewing second war would devolve into outright chaos as it progressed. She hoped it wouldn’t; she didn’t have the vigour of her eighteen-year-old self to chase down Death Eaters in the dark and then spend all night drinking away the relief of coming through it with nothing more than scrapes and bruises.

 

            Already, the new routine of her life was taking its toll on her. Even when it wasn’t the full moon, Kara looked pale with exhaustion, her long days and little sleep whittling away at her as Eliza chided her for not looking after herself properly. Her misery was palpable, although no one knew the truth behind it, chalking it up to a bad breakup, and Kara felt utterly alone in it, working herself hard enough that she was rewarded with a promotion at work. It hadn’t been her intention, but with Bode taking up permanent residency on the Janus Thickey ward at St. Mungo’s, and subsequently dying because of a Devil’s Snare plant, there was an opening as a Senior Unspeakable in the Time Room. Kara had aspired to become a Senior Unspeakable one day, still somewhat on the younger side to assume such a role, but she couldn’t even feel any pride in the achievement, taking it with little fuss, grateful for the pay rise and the freedom to pursue her own research. 

 

            She was far from happy, but she managed, she coped. Alex incessantly worried about her, dragging her out of the cottage in the rare moments Kara wasn’t occupied with something else, taking her out to drink pints of Dragon Scale, coaxing her out of her loneliness as best as she could. Kara was too resigned to even object, tagging along with her sister and friends to a Quidditch match one weekend, staring vacantly out at the pitch as her mind was more preoccupied with thoughts of Lena’s safety, about what her family could be doing to her, than the score of the game. She had never been particularly exuberant, too nervous in herself, but now she was downright stoic, which vexed more than one of her friends, who believed Kara was better off without a girlfriend who, at best, sympathised with Death Eaters, if not one herself. Kara preferred the time she was home with her mother, no explanation needed for her solemn mood, Eliza so gentle with her daughter’s feelings as she constantly proclaimed her delight to have her at home again for company. Kara often wondered if Eliza was as lonely as she was, if perhaps there was that pit in her mother’s chest that had persisted in the long years since her husband’s death. She only hoped she wouldn’t have to find out how long that feeling could linger.

 

            On the last Thursday of February, Kara was early to work again, dark circles beneath her eyes as she entered the department, her briefcase in hand, and the moon watch on her wrist showing it was a little before six. The Department of Mysteries was dimly lit as she made her way across the Entrance Chamber and through to the Time Room, the sound of so many ticking clocks a familiar din that no longer bothered her, barely even acknowledged as it made an almost comforting ambience. Bypassing her desk, Kara moved through the crowded room to the door leading through to the Hall of Prophecy, where she called out, her voice carrying through the cavernous room.

 

            “James?”

 

            Slow footsteps grew nearer after a couple of minutes, her friend appearing at the end of a row of shelves. He gave her a tired smile, shoulders sloping and eyes bloodshot from a lack of sleep, and she weakly returned it as he met her at the door. 

 

            “A quiet night,” he assured her, giving her back a reassuring pat as she moved back out into the Time Room ahead of him. 

 

            Nodding, Kara clutched her briefcase in hand as he stepped out after her, shutting the door, and trailed her through the narrow path between desks, shelves and clocks. “I’ll take it from here.”

 

            “Who’s got tonight’s watch?”

 

            “Tonks, I think.”

 

            “Right. Well, I’m in desperate need of a strong brew and a kip before work,” he said, stifling a yawn as they went straight through to the Entrance Chamber, Kara leading him out without the disorienting experience of rotating walls. “Will you be at Grimmauld Place tonight?”

 

            With a sigh, rubbing at tired eyes, even though she’d only gotten out of bed not yet an hour ago, Kara shrugged. “We’ll see.”

 

            “It’s not good for you to brood, you know,” he said, not unkindly, with a faint smile.

 

            Rolling her eyes, a smile of her own growing on her lips, Kara gave him a withering look. “Don’t believe everything you hear from Alex. Or Kelly - she obviously gets it from my sister.”

 

            “I don’t hear it from them - much. You just- you don’t seem like yourself anymore. I know it was hard for you, but-”

 

            “Aren’t I allowed more than six weeks to grieve the last seven years?” Kara quietly interrupted, her voice flushed with genuine bitterness. And it was bitterness directed at Lena, too, because for all the necessity of secrecy, of allowing people to believe things had ended badly, Kara had still been left, and knowing the real reason didn’t soften the blow.

 

            “I- of course you are, but you could talk to us about it, you know. I know it’s hard for you to wrap your head around, and I had my doubts about her at first, but even I have to question if she’s lost the plot, and, well, my point is, we’re all here for you.”

 

            Softly sighing as she reached for the door, jerking it open, Kara rounded on him and gave him a tired smile. Propping the door open with her foot, she pushed herself up onto her tiptoes to wrap her arms around James’s shoulders, giving him a firm hug and patting his back.

 

            “Thank you. I’ll be alright, though. You know me.”

 

            He returned the hug, giving her a quick squeeze. “I do, so I know you’re putting on a brave face.”

 

            “We’ve got more important things to worry about.”

 

            “Mm, I just hope Dumbledore’s wrong for a change.”

 

            Kara snorted, a crooked smile flitting across her face. “I’d wager he’s been wrong more times than we know. I just- I hope it’s all over soon.”

 

            “Me too. Alright, I need to run. See you later, yeah?”

 

            “Bye.”

 

            She watched him go, making for the lift at the end of the hallway, before she shut the door. Moving back through to her desk, she set her briefcase down and made her way to the little kitchen, boiling water and heaping instant coffee into a mug to get her through the morning. Stirring in milk and coffee, Kara made her way through to her desk, settling in as she pulled out papers and a quill, unscrewing the ink pot, thumbing through the stack of books on her desk for the one she’d been referencing. Taking a sip of her coffee, she hummed to herself, the sound drowned out by the ticking of clocks, leafing through the pages of her cramped writing, sections scribbled out, words circled or underlined in red ink, Kara skimmed through her proposal, spreading the pages across her desk as she tried to conclude her case. She’d worked hard over the last few weeks to put it together, years of curiosity leaving her with more questions that needed answers, and it had been a good distraction for her, something to focus on at work so she didn’t spiral while thinking about Lena too much.

 

            Kara was on her feet, nursing her coffee as she utilised the chalkboard situated behind her desk, the scrape of chalk swallowed by the clocks as her palm became coated in white dust, and she was so absorbed by her brainstorming that she didn’t hear the door open. It was often hard to hear much over the ticking in the Time Room, so that wasn’t unusual, but she lost track of time as she worked and didn’t notice she wasn’t alone until a voice cut through the peace of the Time Room.

 

            “Oh, Kara,” Professor Croaker said with mild surprise, startling her as she turned, almost spilling her coffee as she dropped her chalk. “Another early morning?”

 

            “Professor Croaker,” she breathlessly greeted him, stooping to snatch up her chalk, her scars livid as her cheeks flushed. “Morning, sir. Um, yes, just … working on my proposal.”

 

            He nodded, tilting his head to the side. “You’ve been clocking a lot of overtime recently. I know you’re a hard worker, but this is … a considerable amount. Is everything well?” 

 

            Moving over to her desk, Kara set down her mug and wiped her chalk-dusted hand over her thigh, instantly regretting doing so as she left a large white smear on her pants. Clearing her throat, colour high in her cheeks, she kept her gaze down as she produced a spotless handkerchief and wiped her hand. 

 

            “Oh, um, there have been some … personal changes recently. Nothing that will affect my work, sir, I promise. It just- I split up with my partner a few weeks ago, so I’ve been moving and … processing it. I just- I’d rather be at work than be alone with my thoughts.”

 

            “Oh. Well, I’m sorry to hear that. Lena Luthor, wasn’t it? A clever woman, from my conversation with her. Well, it’s all well and good for you to occupy yourself with work, but I’d hate for you to wear yourself out, Kara. Especially with … you know, your condition. Now, with your new promotion, if you think that it might be too much to handle on top of-”

 

            “No, no, it’s not,” Kara quickly insisted, her stomach lurching as she thought about losing the only good thing that had happened since Lena had left. She’d worked hard for years for this opportunity, and she was struck with panic at the thought of having it taken away from her. “I’ve already come up with a proposal. I’m still drafting it, but you- you can take a look, here.”

 

            Shuffling her pages into a pile, tapping them against the desk to neaten the stack, Kara handed it over to Croaker, whose curiosity got the better of him. He took her papers and planted a hand on his hip as he skimmed over the first page, turning to the second page and then glancing up. He hummed thoughtfully as he handed it back over.

 

            “Ambitious.”

 

            Anxiously biting her lip, Kara looked at her boss with wide, wary eyes as she reached out to take back her proposal. Croaker gave her a slight smile before continuing.

 

            “But an interesting approach. I’d normally be sceptical about approving overlapping research between two Rooms for a new Senior Unspeakable, but with the right team, you should be able to piggyback off of existing research to make it more manageable. Have the full proposal to me by the end of next week, and I’ll consider it.”

 

            Deflating slightly as relief washed through her, Kara felt a flicker of triumph as she clutched her pages in both hands, a small smile on her lips. “Thank you, sir.”

 

            “And for Merlin’s sake, go home early, Danvers. I don’t have the money in the budget to pay you to be here morning, noon and night.”

 

            She let out a strained laugh, nodding as her cheeks dimpled slightly. “Yes, sir.”

 

            He glanced down at his watch and shook his head, sighing. “I have a meeting with the Auror Department at eight, so I need to get moving. Oh, would you mind speaking to Snapper about your proposal? I don’t want any stepping on toes, and he’s very protective about what goes on in the Death Room. It’s a good thing he’s fond of you, eh?”

 

            That was news to Kara, who’d always found Snapper Carr rather irate and dour when she’d previously been working in the Death Room. She’d envisioned focusing her research in that area, but after transferring to the Time Room to aid the Order, she’d become interested in the overlap between time and death, primarily how the consciousness perceived both and how they correlated. She imagined at some point she’d need to rope in someone from the Brain Room too, with more experience on the theory of consciousness and thought, but that was of lesser importance to Kara as she sank back onto her seat with her pages in hand.

 

            Feeling a little more emboldened by how pleasantly surprised her boss had seemed, Kara was filled with the determination to finish her proposal and make her case well. Still, Croaker was right - she was feeling drained, and could very easily burn herself out if she didn’t take better care of herself. Even then, her eyes were already burning, a heaviness to her body as she sat slumped in her chair, running a hand over her face, pushing her glasses up and thumbing her eyelids. After a moment, she straightened up and slid open her desk drawer, reaching inside to pull out a small brass frame. 

 

            Cupped in her palm, Kara stared down at the photo of Lena, taking in the reserved smile, the way her green eyes softened as she kept glancing past the frame, at Kara, who had taken the photo, a certain shyness to Lena’s movements as she flicker her hair off her shoulder, glanced down as she cheeks dimpled, something coy about her gaze. There was a keen pain in her chest, and longing suffused her as her expression softened, tender and aching, and she so badly wished she could physically lay eyes on Lena, just to make sure she was okay, just to know that she was safe and unharmed. After a minute, Kara slipped the little frame back into the drawer and shut it before reaching for her coffee.

 

            Her day passed by quickly, working on her proposal and assisting the other two Senior Unspeakables in the Time Room with the work they’d all split after Bode’s hospitalisation. Coffee kept her going, and she would’ve killed for an Invigoration Draught by the time it hit lunch, but Kara kept herself buried in her books or talking through theories with the small group working on current projects under her. It was methodical and monotonous, but she enjoyed the routine distraction it provided, eating her way through some biscuits with yet more coffee, until it was early afternoon and the ring on her finger startled her by burning. 

 

            Dropping a ginger newt, scattering crumbs across the pages, Kara’s eyes were immediately drawn to her right index finger, taking in the amber stone as her pulse raced. Time-sensitive, but not urgent. Still, she didn’t know how long it would take to relay that information to Dumbledore, so Kara erred on the side of caution. A glance at her watch revealed it was nearly four, and Croaker had instructed her to leave early that day, so she swept crumbs into the rubbish bin beneath her desk, packed up her briefcase and said goodbye to anyone she passed by on her way out. She would have to leave it up to one of the Aurors in the Order who’d wrangled clearance to come and go in the Department of Mysteries to let Tonks in later that evening.

 

            Making her way up to the Atrium, Kara Apparated out of the Ministry and wound up at the edge of their property, the dark cottage greeting her as she felt a pang of homesickness strike her. It was the middle of the afternoon, and the light was already failing, clouds blotting out weak sunlight and a fine drizzle misting on her cloak as she hurried up the damp garden path, letting herself inside with a pit in her stomach. The cloth-draped furniture made it seem so austere, the empty grate radiating a chill as Kara walked straight through to the kitchen table, finding a letter sealed with wax waiting on the dusty table. She slowed at the sight of it, exactly the same as the last one she’d come to fetch, and she picked it up with a faint tremor in her hand, a lump in her throat, smoothing her thumb over the folded parchment, the deep green seal, putting her fingers where Lena’s had been not so long ago.

 

            Pocketing the letter, still gripping her briefcase in the other hand, Kara spared a glance at the gloomy kitchen before heading back through the living area and out into the rain. Apparating to an alleyway in Islington, she briskly walked through damp streets and puddles with an oily sheen on top as Muggle cars passed by and the lampposts started to come on, casting a wan, orange glow over the glistening pavement, until she reached the row of townhouses on Grimmauld Place and made for number 12. The house seemed to push in between its neighbours, and she plodded up the stoop and let herself inside with more familiarity now, not waiting for someone to let her in, and knowing better than to use the brass knocker and set off the painting of Walburga Black.

 

            Slipping down the hallway, Kara descended the stairs to the kitchen, appearing with damp hair and rain-speckled glasses as her curls started to frizz slightly. There were a few gathered there already, always at least a few of them, and Kara exchanged solemn nods with the familiar faces.

 

            “Winn, Sirius, Emmaline, Lucy.”

 

            Pulling a chair out beside him and sitting, Winn smiled at her. “Alright?”

 

            Dropping down onto the seat, Kara set her briefcase down on the floor and nudged her glasses up as she ran her hands over her face. “Long day. Will J’onn be showing any time soon? I’ve got something for him. It’s, um, about what’s going on in my department.”

 

            Lucy was reading a folded-up newspaper, mottled damp at the edges, and she tossed it onto the table as she looked at Kara. “What about what’s going on?"

 

            “Well, I can’t really say. Um … it’s probably better to wait for him to relay it to Dumbledore to decide if it’s important, isn’t it? It is time-sensitive, though, so … the sooner the better.”

 

            “Roger,” Lucy smiled, giving her a quick wink before pushing her chair back and standing. “I’ll send word to J’onn myself.”

 

            “Ta.”

 

            Pulling the letter from her pocket, Kara set it on the table before her, taking stock of the plates with the remnants of sausage sandwiches and cold cups of tea, lit candles that had started to melt, the wax dripping like tears. The kitchen was almost stuffy with the lit fire and it made Kara feel sleepy as her clothes dried, the smell of wet wool surrounding her, and she sat with slumped shoulders.

 

            “Are you staying? I’ll make some tea,” Winn said, already moving, Kara’s response not seeming to matter much.

 

            She felt so very tired, though, so she remained seated as he pottered about, Sirius slinking out of the room with a brooding look on his face, leaving the other few together. Mumbling her thanks as a cup of tea was set before her, Kara sighed.

 

            “So, anything new?”

 

            Shrugging, Winn took a sip of his tea. “Mike and I have been tailing another name that’s on Dumbledore’s list, but nothing’s come of it yet. Just a lot of drinking at The White Wyvern from what we can tell. Um … have you spoken to Mike?”

 

            “No, why?”

 

            “Oh. It’s just- well … we saw Lena there. A few times, actually.”

 

            “Oh. Did she see you?”

 

            “Not in Knocturn Alley, but … well, you know Mike. He couldn’t stop himself from having a go at her the other day in Diagon Alley.”

 

            Kara had to school her expression into something akin to indifference, a faint tightening at the corners of her mouth as she gritted her teeth, clutching her cup of tea tightly. “She didn’t hurt him, did she? I mean, she’s a nasty dueller, so … I’m not sure what she’s gotten mixed up in since … but, um, who knows what magic she knows.”

 

            “I’m well aware,” Winn grumbled, rubbing his sternum, as if any trace of the cuts Lena had once inflicted upon him still lingered. “No, she, uh, she didn’t do anything, didn’t even say anything. Mike just- well, he spat on her, had a right go of it, and one of the ones she was with - Veronica Sinclair, you remember her, right? - got in his face a bit, but Lena just left. Um … well, it’s Veronica that we were tailing.”

 

            “Well … it makes sense,” Kara diplomatically replied, her blood boiling to hear even the most harmless of insults being cast upon Lena and having to sit there and lie to keep her cover. “Lena was friendly with Veronica in school. A bit more than friends, actually.”

 

            “Right, yeah, I remember that. Funny though, I thought she was only friends with Andrea out of the Slytherin crowd. I don’t remember her inviting anyone else to your parties. I mean, Gayle, sure, but she was only there because of Imra.”

 

            A wan smile crossed Kara’s lips as she raised the tea to her lips, holding it in both hands to stop the cup from shaking, and then softly cleared her throat, feeling more than a little uncomfortable. She wasn’t nearly as good at masking her emotions as Lena was, and she supposed it was a good thing she hadn’t gone with her to spy as well. Kara would surely have given them up immediately. Yet, she supposed she was allowed to feel uncomfortable, talking about the woman she’d spent the last seven years with, had loved for even longer, and how she’s supposedly turned her back on the morals everyone had thought she had.

 

            “I guess she went crawling back to like-minded people,” Kara murmured with a nonchalant shrug. “It’s- well, it’s not my business anymore, is it? I guess that’s why Dumbledore hasn’t had me tailing anyone she knows.”

 

            “I’m actually surprised he hasn’t had you tailing her. She’d lead you straight to her brother. That’s Dumbledore for you, isn’t it? I guess he doesn’t keep all of his dragon eggs in one basket.”

 

            Shifting in her seat, Kara didn’t meet his eyes as she smiled thinly again. “I suppose he doesn’t trust me to do a very good job of it. After all, she fooled me the entire time and I … I didn’t suspect a thing. Clearly, I have my uses elsewhere.”

 

            “It can’t all have been a lie,” Winn reassured her, face furrowing with bewildered concern. “Surely what she felt for you … it must’ve been real. Seven years. And you were friends for years before that. Whatever my opinion of her is, I don’t believe she was leading you on the whole time, that she just … was that good at pretending she wasn’t a bigot.”

 

            “I don’t know. She must’ve been. You don’t just- you don’t side with people obsessed with blood purity and think that a werewolf is fine. I’m … the bottom rung of the ladder, I’m the one that even the most tolerant witches and wizards have a hard time accepting. All I can think is … she needed someone to help her with her research, and I was an easy target because we’d been friends at school. Maybe she didn’t find me as repulsive as others, but … she grew up in a Pureblood family, and that has to have left a mark. A bigger mark than anyone could see.”

 

            For all her years of fretting that she wasn’t good enough for Lena, for believing what others thought of her and thinking poorly of herself, Kara was lying through her teeth. It had taken a great deal of time and trust to change the way she viewed herself and to believe that she was loved so deeply, in every way possible, by someone else, and she knew it hadn’t been a lie, knew that Lena loved her enough to keep her safe, the same way Kara loved her. Still, she played her part well enough, all the doubts and insecurities she’d gone to great lengths to get past so easily surfacing when she needed them to. She hated to paint Lena as such an awful person, wanted to rush to her defence, to obstinately refuse to condemn her as nothing more than a bigoted Slytherin, but she had little choice in the matter. And she wasn’t lying about everything , because there had been marks left on Lena that no one else could see, marks that went deeper than words carved into an arm, but it had only made Lena kinder , more empathetic, even when that same grace wasn’t returned. Kara just hoped the mistreatment Lena endured now would be atoned for when everyone found out the truth, and she hoped it wouldn’t go so far that Lena would let herself be hurt beyond untrue words spoken out of ignorance.

 

            “Maybe you’re right. I’m sorry, anyway.”

 

            “I should be apologising,” Kara murmured, frowning as she stared down at her cup. “I should’ve seen her true colours when she first attacked you. Even when we got together, years later, everyone told me my instincts were wrong, and I let her in like a cat among the pixies. If I’d listened then … none of this would’ve happened.”

 

            “We can never know the truth until it’s too late. Look at Pettigrew and what he managed to do with his lies. At least no one is dead because of Lena. Not yet, anyway.”

 

            Masking a wince, Kara quickly drained the rest of her tea and scooted her chair back. Setting the cup down, she cleared her throat as she climbed to her feet. “I need to go. You’ll make sure J’onn gets this?”

            “Of course. Lucy will be back in two ticks, I’m sure. Are you sure you won’t stay and wait?”

 

            “Oh, no, that’s okay. I’ve had a long day; I should get home to my mum.”

 

            She picked up her briefcase and said goodbye, making for the stairs as Lucy appeared, her Floo message relayed via the living room fireplace. Reaching the top, Kara was leaving just in time to watch a few others arrive after work, windswept and wet from the worsening rain. Nia came in, folding down an umbrella and cursing out Walburga Black, who was shrieking her head off, with Querl right behind her. Giving them both quick hugs, apologetic and evasive as they asked how she was and mentioned how missed she was at drinks, Kara was eager to be on her way, the three of them lingering in the doorway, the exit blocked. Before they could even shut the front door properly, Arthur Weasley was pushing inside with J’onn on his heels.

 

            J’onn’s eyes landed on her, and Kara felt a flicker of relief, which must have shown on her face. “J’onn! A letter for you; Winn has it in the kitchen. It’s, uh, time-sensitive, but I’ll leave that for you to relay. If I need to pass a message on to- to work, um, just send a Patronus and I’ll come pick it up.”

 

            Pushing her way through the now rather crowded hallway as she spoke, Kara was out the front door and in the rain before he could question her further, and Kara Apparated to the end of her mother’s street. Normally, she would’ve still been at work, and would’ve lingered at Grimmauld Place a while longer if more people were there, wedged in beside her sister as they sipped Firewhisky and exchanged gossip and information with other Order members, but hearing Winn talk about Lena had caught her off guard, and Kara wanted to go home to think it over. Little information about Lena had come her way since the last time she’d seen her at St. Mungo’s, and Kara craved any scrap, any mention of how she was, how she looked, what she’d said, if only to dissect it, to recount it all and reassure herself that she was okay.

 

            She felt a little sick, walking down the street, strong winds sweeping in off the coast as dark grey clouds hung low over Falmouth. A Muggle car rolled past, and Kara’s brows were furrowed together over storm-blue eyes as she hugged her cloak around herself and made for her mother’s front door, the paint salt-stained and wearing away. Letting herself inside, Kara set her briefcase down and kicked off her shoes, listening to the sound of Eliza in the kitchen.

 

            “Is that you, sweetheart? You’re home early.”

 

            “Croaker let me leave early,” Kara called back, shedding her cloak and then stooping to pick up Bastet.

 

            Cooing over the cat, she walked down the short hallway and gave her mum a small smile. Eliza was in her old towelling dressing gown, slippers flapping against the stone floor as she rounded the table, holding a cup of coffee in hand. Giving the contented cat a quick squeeze, Kara set her down and walked over to Eliza, taking her mum by surprise as she hugged her, burying her face in her shoulder. Eliza made a small sound at the back of her throat as she held her mug aloft, while wrapping her other arm around her daughter’s shoulders, then reaching up to smooth a hand over Kara’s hair.

 

            “Are you alright?”

 

            “Yeah,” Kara whispered, a pain in her throat as her eyes stung. “I just miss her a lot today.”

 

            Holding her close a little longer before giving her a quick squeeze, Eliza kissed her temple and then drew back with a pitying look of understanding on her face. Kara was grateful that her mum wasn’t so vocal about her opinions on people, that she wasn’t quick to judge either, that she understood the complexity of Kara’s situation and didn’t try and lecture her about Lena’s apparent betrayal. Eliza just let her miss her ex, knowing that Kara had loved her, and it was no easy thing to get past that, no matter what truths had come out. And Eliza had always liked Lena and had more compassion for her, perhaps because she wasn’t directly involved in the Order, despite her support of them. She wasn’t at the regular meetings, hearing whispers and intel about what the Death Eaters were doing, Kara’s friends lumping Lena in alongside her brother, and Kara was glad her mother was removed from it all because it meant that she could be honest and seek out the comfort she so badly wanted.

 

            “Go on, change into something dry, and I’ll make you some coffee. I’ve got stew on for dinner; it’ll be ready soon.”

 

            Nodding, a defeated air about her, Kara did as her mother instructed, padding back downstairs five minutes later with fuzzy socks on her feet and the latest jumper from Eliza hanging a little loose from her lanky frame. She could see the way her mum’s eyes caught on the thinness of her face, the concern that always seemed to plague Eliza, worrying about her youngest daughter the most. Her coffee was set on the coffee table, and Kara thanked her mum before curling up beside her on the sofa, watching Eliza pick up the shapeless red thing she was knitting as she got lost in her thoughts.

 

            “It’s okay to be worried,” Eliza said after a few minutes of silence, pulling Kara out of her thoughts. 

 

            “Hm?”

 

            “You’re allowed to worry about her. I know your sister is very righteous , and there’s nothing wrong with that, but you’ve always been softer-hearted than her, which isn’t a bad thing either. So, Alex might be quick to tell you to move on, to forget about her, but you don’t have to, sweetheart. You loved Lena so much, and you don’t know where she is or what she’s doing, so it’s okay to be worried about her. Just make sure you’re looking after yourself too. These late nights aren’t doing you any good; you look exhausted. And goodness, you need to eat more, Kara. The full moon takes enough out of you as it is.”

 

            “I know, I know,” Kara sighed, leaning into her mum, resting her head on her shoulder. “I just- I’m having a hard time adjusting to not having her in my life. I miss her. I miss her so much.”

 

            “It’ll get easier. The more time passes, the easier it gets,” Eliza sighed, patting her knee. “Now, let’s eat. And then you can have an early night; tomorrow will be a new day.”

Chapter 54

            Weeks passed by, a month giving way to two, until it was March and Lena could barely cope with the way her life was. She kept going around and around the painful memories of her old life, of how it had been with Kara and her family, their friends, unable to let go of it. All of that had been replaced with a life that would’ve been unrecognisable to her if she hadn’t grown up exactly the same.

 

            Lena had spent years trying to heal from what her mother and brother had done, trying to move past it, to be whole and happy, instead of haunted. And now she had undone it all, putting herself back in that house with them, and while they hadn’t laid a hand on her yet, it made her skin crawl just to be in the vicinity of them. It was like being thrust back into time, to when she was fifteen on the summer holidays, forced to be at home, walking on eggshells as she waited for one of them to snap. 

 

            And it was worse in so many ways now, because Lena had gotten herself away from that, had secretly put her brother behind bars and had tried so very hard not to need to hurt herself, to love and trust Kara and build a life that she deserved. But she’d given that up for the stifling feeling of having her every move watched, barely able to go anywhere but work or home, constantly plagued by the feeling that she was seen as suspect by Lillian, and maybe even Lex too. They never said anything, never made their doubts known, but she could sense that they were waiting for her to slip up, or waiting to make her an offer she wouldn't be able to refuse without betraying her true feelings. She was yet to be invited to a meeting with any Death Eaters, not even one of the hopefuls, let alone meet the Dark Lord himself, but she knew if she waited it out, she’d have her chance. And that would benefit the Order in the long run. 

 

            Still, it was exhausting to keep up the pretence, and it was only because Lena was so accomplished at Occlumency that she’d managed to keep it up for so long. But having to ensure her mental shields didn’t slip for even a second , when she was at home or when she was at St. Mungo’s at the same time as Lillian, was mentally draining, and the fatigue was starting to wear away at her. Pale-faced and thin, a morose air about her, Lena tried to unobtrusively go through her days, taking meals with her family, after dinner drinks in the drawing room, games of Wizard’s Chess with Lex, and strolls through the garden. And the whole time, Lena just thought about how remarkable it was that you could get used to anything. A year ago, she would never have believed she could stomach being back in her childhood home, sleeping beneath the same roof as the people who were responsible for so much of her pain, and yet, she endured it with a vague sense of boredom to the monotony of her days.

 

            It might’ve helped if Lena hadn’t isolated herself so much, but it had been deliberate and necessary, as hard as it was. She regularly saw Sam at work, taking coffee breaks together, chatting in the Attendings Lounge or over patient notes, and more recently, outside of work as Lena begged a favour, but she’d essentially cut off every other person in her life, in exchange for less savoury acquaintances. Even Andrea had invited her for coffee soon after her split from Kara, the two of them huddled inside a café in Diagon Alley as Lena was immediately confronted by her friend, who’d heard of the split, of Lena’s return home, and her visits to The White Wyvern, where Veronica was still bartending. Andrea had been confused at first, and then angry, berating Lena over her cappuccino, until Lena had left without finishing her coffee and hadn’t seen her since. 

 

            It wasn’t easy, but Lena was committed to doing what she could to make it as believable as possible. Alienating herself from anyone she’d been close to before, anyone Lillian might’ve known about, was a good start, even if it meant she was so lonely. Fortunately, she worked with Sam, and it was that workaround that left her sane. Still, Lena was wary of being anywhere her mother or brother weren’t for too long, just in case they grew suspicious, so even her occasional meetups with Sam were brief, and she was glad about that, knowing that if they spent more time together, they might end up a few bottles of wine in, and Lena didn’t want that, knowing it was very likely she might burst into tears if she got too many drinks in her and blurred that line between her feelings and the front she was putting on.

 

            Instead, she mostly stayed at home, ingratiating herself with Lex’s friends, who frequented the house, their arms marked, contempt and arrogance in every word they spoke as they lounged about with drinks in hand, all so familiar to Lena’s Housemates that she felt as if she was back at Hogwarts. In many ways, nothing had changed since then, back to spying on her brother, feeding information back to the Order, and surrounding herself with people she would rather not socialise with. Except, this time, they weren’t younger siblings, children or cousins, they were direct Death Eaters, her brother’s friends, people who made her skin crawl as she lounged on the sofa with them after a long day of work, as if she belonged.

 

            None of them would rat him out to the Auror Department, and Lex was at ease as he adjusted to life outside of Azkaban. His cheeks were still somewhat hollow, but not quite as skeletal as he’d been before, the dark circles vanishing from under his eyes, which were no longer so deeply set in his skull. Regular meals of quantity and quality, a soft bed and being away from the influence of Dementors did wonders for him, and in that vein, it whittled away at Lena, whose face was drawn and dolorous, who slept fitfully unless she used a potion, and who could barely stomach the food Hope prepared, her stomach in permanent knots.

 

            She would have spent all of her time at St. Mungo’s if it wouldn’t have been to the detriment of what she was hoping to achieve. As it was, Lena worked long hours, which was a blessing, so the rest of her time had to be devoted to spying, if only to end it as quickly as possible. But it was slower than anticipated, only a handful of notes left in her cottage, homesickness striking her every time she stepped inside, leaving a sealed letter on the table and changing the colour of the stone in her ring before she left. They had all been greens and ambers so far; nothing urgent.

 

            Lena made a few trips to Knockturn Alley as well, purposely avoiding Diagon Alley if possible, although she had bumped into Mike the one time she’d been there, and she restocked her personal potion supplies to brew the Wolfsbane Potion, taking a few minutes in between clocking off and arriving home at the manor house to pore over the cauldron in the basement of the cottage, leaving bottled doses for Kara, a folded butterfly or crane beside them with no words. But even those nights spent drinking at The White Wyvern didn’t help her unwind, her ears tuned into the conversations around her as unsavoury folk drank and flogged illegal wares, swapping gossip in the process. And there was always Veronica, manning the bar, relishing in the information that came to her, passing it onto Lena in an almost gloating manner, as if she was smug that she knew more. Lena let her have that upper hand, every piece passed on to Dumbledore, and a nice tip left on the bar.

 

            March was almost over when there was a palpable shift in her relationship with her brother. It was that cruelty again, which he was quite adept at hiding, exuding confidence and charm when he wanted to, but the cruelty was always there, simmering beneath the surface since he’d been indoctrinated as a teenager. She hadn’t seen it at first, and he’d been somewhat nice to her throughout her childhood, although he wasn’t home enough for them to be close, but whatever he’d been before he’d laid a hand on her was overshadowed by the horrifying amount of pain he’d inflicted upon her. Still, he’d been rather affable since they’d both returned to that house, as if he was still buoyed by his release, but really, Lena knew things were just going his way, so he had no reason to lash out.

 

            But they’d raided the house again, Lena not home that time but her mother informing her over dinner that night, and Aurors showing up the following morning with court documents and a record of their Floo Network usage, the address of her flat flagged for a second time upon the immediate arrival of Aurors to raid the property as Lex had remembered her address. Lena was haughty but compliant, her arms folded over her chest as her mother lurked nearby, the Aurors speaking to Lena as they waved about their documents, signed by Wizengamot officials.

 

            “Well, yes, I’m still under ownership of that property, as I’ve already said,” Lena tersely said. “I can show you the deed, if you’d like.”

 

            “No need. We have a warrant to search the premises; department Aurors are undertaking that task as we speak.”

 

            Lena gave the man a tight-lipped smile, arching an eyebrow. “You won’t find much there.”

 

            “Then may I ask why you’ve been frequenting the place?”

 

            “Two trips in a few months are hardly frequent. But if you must know, I’ve recently gotten out of a long-term relationship, around the time of that first visit, actually, so I’m … in between places at the moment. I’m staying with my mother while renovations are completed on my old flat, and then I’ll be moving back in.”

 

            The Aurors exchanged a look, and Lena raised her chin a fraction. “By all means, check every corner of the place - although, there’s not much in there. The place is halfway through being painted.”

 

            She wasn’t bluffing, but her pulse was racing, her skin prickling with a cold sweat as she avoided looking at her mother, the tension thick in the air. Lex was upstairs; it was early in the morning, and he hadn’t had time to come downstairs and Floo through the fireplace before the Aurors were at the front door. It was fortunate that he hadn’t Flooed through to her flat, whilst simultaneously unfortunate Lena silently thought, or it would’ve put her brother right into the hands of another set of Aurors, and it would’ve logged another trip to the flat at the first hint of Aurors arriving at the estate. Still, all they would have to do was go upstairs, and they’d find him wedged inside the servant’s stairwell on the second floor, Lillian’s wand in hand, just in case, his own in possession of the Ministry. It was a tense minute of silence before the Auror nodded, clearing his throat.

 

            “We’ll be in touch if we have any further questions.”

 

            Lena nodded, feeling her pulse hammering at her temples, a prickle of relief stealing over her as they started making for the door. She shadowed them, eager to get them out, so she didn’t have to be caught in the middle of two groups she was lying to, knowing that anything she said could get her in trouble with the Ministry or her family. Opening the front door, she stood aside as the two Aurors filed out, weak sunlight spilling into the dingy foyer of the gloomy house.

 

            “Oh, and one more thing,” the Auror said before turning back to her, Lena’s stomach lurching at the look on the man’s face. “The first time the property was raided, you were here, were you not?”

 

            “Yes. Auror J’onzz can corroborate that.”

 

            “Yes, I believe he has. So, who was it who used the Floo Network that time? It couldn’t have been you, could it? Not for painting.”

 

            “It was a friend,” Lena tightly smiled. “She’s the one helping me paint; she left to get on with it, while I spoke with the Aurors.”

 

            “And the name of this friend?”

 

            “Samantha Arias. She’s a colleague of mine; she’ll be able to confirm what I’ve told you.”

 

            The man jotted it down in his little notebook and pocketed his quill before nodding. “Well, thank you for your time, Healer Luthor.”

 

            She nodded, watching them walk down the front steps, gravel crunching underfoot as they started down the long path to the gates. Neither she nor her mother moved until they watched the two men pass through the gates and Disapparate, and only then did Lena ease the groaning door shut, enclosing them in the dimness of the foyer once more. And then Lillian stormed forward, her heels clicking on the marble floor as she hissed, her face twisted with anger.

 

            “You foolish girl. Lying to Aurors? They’ll be back with more of them next time, and probable cause to detain you for questioning. Do you think you’d be immune to Veritaserum?”

 

            “I didn’t lie,” Lena softly replied, a little curt but standing her ground. “Well, except partially about Sam, but I’ll ask her to-”

 

            “And you think she will lie to Aurors for you?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “And what about the rest of it? This painting business? They said they have Aurors there as we speak-”

 

            “And they’ll find a half-painted flat,” Lena interrupted, giving her mum a tight smile. “I had thought they might check the Floo Network records at some point, albeit not so soon, so I took precautions.”

 

            “What?” Lillian demanded.

 

            “If you’ve wondered where I’ve spent my admittedly slim spare time, I’ve been painting my flat with Sam. I am clever enough to think ahead, you know. All they’ll find are drop sheets, tins of paint and an unfinished job.”

 

            Pausing, Lillian cocked her head to the side, eyeing her with her usual piercing stare. After a second, she made a small sound of grudging respect at the back of her throat, and Lena’s lips twitched with a ghost of a smile. Then there was the distant sound of a door closing, followed by the tread of Lex’s feet on the stairs, before he materialised at the top, their mother’s wand in his grasp as he ran a hand over his shaved head.

 

            “Well, that was close, wasn’t it?” he said with amusement.

 

            “A bit too close,” Lillian grumbled as she watched her son descend the rest of the steps. “You will need to be more careful. They suspect too much.”

 

            He waved a hand dismissively, rolling his dark eyes. “Oh, they’re like the blind leading the blind, they are. Don’t worry , mother, they’re not going to catch me.”

 

            “That’s not my only concern. You might escape, if cornered, but I will be left to explain why you are here. I’d prefer to avoid a cell in Azkaban as much as you would.”

 

            “As would I,” Lena murmured, lifting her eyes to her brother’s, the corners of her mouth curling slightly.

 

            He gave her a wide smile, walking forward and cupping the side of her face. “ You are too cunning to wind up in a cell, dear Lena. Thank Merlin for your foresight and cleverness; I had wondered why the place smelled of paint yesterday.”

 

            “How did you-”

 

            Pulling something out of his pocket, Lena couldn’t determine what the flesh coloured coil was as Lex held it up, the long string unravelling. Arching an eyebrow sceptically, Lena looked from it to her brother. “And what is that , exactly?”

 

            “An Extendable Ear. Lockwood’s son bought a few at Hogwarts. Apparently, two of the Weasleys are quite creative. Anyway, it’s good for eavesdropping, so I heard every word.”

 

            “Hm.”

 

            “Well done,” Lex said, giving her another smile.

 

            “Don’t encourage her,” Lillian snapped, giving her son an irate glance. “I won’t tolerate this deceit . Do you hear me, Lena? You are conniving and manipulative, and I don’t trust you for a second. If I find that you have ulterior motives, if you do anything to harm your family, I swear you will regret it. Azkaban will be the least of your concerns.”

 

            Lena felt a pit in her stomach, her hands balled into fists at her side as she looked down at the floor, trying to school her expression into something neutral. She knew her mother was watching her too closely, and Lena had done everything she could so far to not rouse suspicion, but even though she’d just saved her brother’s hide, Lillian would be questioning what else she’d secretly planned. Wrapped up in her worried thoughts, she flinched slightly at the sharpness of Lillian’s voice as she continued.

            

            “Look at me when I speak to you. You know I loathe that sullen expression you use,” Lillian scathingly hissed.

 

            Looking into her mother’s eyes, Lena made her face soften slightly, an edge of amusement touching the hard lines of her face. “I would never do anything to hurt my family, I can promise you that.”

 

            And Lena wouldn’t; she would do anything for Kara, for Alex and Kelly and Eliza. They were her family, the ones she chose, the ones who’d loved her, and Lena would suffer at the hands of the people she’d been raised with if it meant keeping the people she loved safe. She just needed to buy herself more time, to go undetected for as long as possible, to give everyone the best chance that she could. If it meant a little pain in exchange for information that might change the trajectory of the brewing war, the rising tide of bigotry and suspicion so close to boiling over, Lena would gladly subject herself to it, and if it meant a lot of pain to keep Kara alive, Lena would bear it with her head held high.

 

            Running a hand over her face, realising it was trembling slightly and then burying it in the pockets of her pressed pants, Lena cleared her throat. “I should go and speak to Sam.”

 

            “See that you do,” Lillian tersely replied before stalking off to the dining room to return to her now-cold breakfast.

 

            With no desire to finish off her own, Lena went upstairs to grab a robe and her satchel before heading back downstairs, tossing half of the handful of Floo powder into the grate, arriving in the St. Mungo’s reception area and then tossing the handful in to Floo to Sam’s home. She’d frequented the flat so often in the years of their friendship that Lena didn’t feel quite so apprehensive to intrude, although it had been a couple of months, with her purposely avoiding it. Considering it wasn’t quite the Easter holidays yet, Ruby was away at Hogwarts, so Sam was alone in the flat, drinking coffee at the kitchen table as she read that morning’s edition of The Daily Prophet.

 

            At the sight of Lena in the narrow mouth of the kitchen, Sam’s eyebrows shot up as she almost spilt her coffee. “Bloody hell, you might make a sound next time. You frightened the life out of me.”

 

            “Morning. Sorry,” Lena sighed, brushing soot off her shoulders as she stepped into the spacious kitchen, the arched windows overlooking Victoria Square as Bristol bustled below them.

 

            She took a seat, and Sam got up to make her a coffee, setting it down in front of Lena, who quietly thanked her, before she took a seat and stifled a yawn, eyeing her friend as she waited a minute to see if Lena would explain her presence. Lena didn’t, picking up the hot coffee, taking a sip as warm steam made her face prickle, and eventually, Sam grew impatient enough to ask, her voice soft and curious, hazel eyes full of concern.

 

            “Is everything alright?”

 

            With a half-hearted shrug, Lena set her mug down and gave her a grim look. “It could be better.”

 

            “Mm. I’m worried about you, you know.”

 

            “Why?” Lena laughed, aiming for bewildered amusement and falling short.

 

            Exasperated, Sam tossed the newspaper she wasn’t even reading aside, folding her arms over her chest as she cocked her head aside. “You know, I can’t remember the last time you came over. Not since you and Kara split up, that’s for sure. And you still haven’t really explained what that was about, which is fine, that’s not my business, but I just- I don’t understand what’s going on. Because you told me you’d moved back into your flat, but that’s clearly not the case, because we’ve been painting it and there’s not a bloody thing in the place, and I’ve been waiting for you to tell me why-”

 

            “Would you believe me if I told you it was to keep you safe?” Lena cut her off, arching an eyebrow.

 

            “Believe you? Of course I’d believe you, but that only makes me question what the hell is going on. What trouble have you gotten mixed up in now? And where are you staying?”

 

            Lena gently bit her bottom lip as she deliberated over how much to tell Sam, meaning it when she said she wanted to keep her safe. Sam would be no better at ingratiating herself with Lena’s current circle than Kara would have been, and Lena already regretted dragging her into it by lying to the Aurors, but that was as far as she would risk her friend’s involvement. She wouldn’t let anyone she cared about come to harm because of her own decision to spy, but she couldn’t explain that to Sam, who wasn’t even an Order member, who probably didn’t even know it had reconvened, even though she would’ve been sympathetic to the cause.

 

            “Um … I’m back with my mum for a little while,” Lena started, immediately cut off by Sam’s outburst.

 

            “You what? Lena, have you gone mad? You can’t stand her.”

 

            “I know. It’s not going to be long-term, it’s just- with the way that she is … well, you know how strict she’s always been, and I guess … with everything going on with my brother as well, I’m a little too suspect with the Ministry right now, so I wanted to keep you out of it. I’m sorry for not coming around, really, I just- I don’t want to drag you into anything, but … I’m afraid I have. Um … I can’t fully explain it, but if you have Aurors show up at your door, enquiring about painting my flat, will you tell them you Flooed there from my mum’s house?”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Sam gave her a questioning look as they sat in silence for a few minutes, before she nodded, her mouth thinning with dismay. “Okay. But you’re going to tell me why-”

 

            “I can’t,” Lena shook her head.

 

            “You’ll tell me why one day. If I’m going to lie to the Ministry for you, I want an explanation at some point, okay? I mean … fuck, Lena, I’ve got Ruby to think about as well, you know.”

 

            “I know. I wouldn’t ask you if- if it wasn’t important.”

 

            Snorting, Sam rolled her eyes. “Yeah, I know that’s true. And what the bloody hell do you think you’re doing living with Lillian again? Why didn’t you just ask me? Ruby’s not here; you could have her bed and-”

 

            “Thanks, but … it’s necessary. Um … maybe one day I can explain that to you as well,” Lena murmured, a crease between her brows as her throat tightened. 

 

            With a sigh, Sam shook her head. “And you can’t tell me, not you won’t tell me?”

 

            “Can’t,” Lena agreed.

 

            “Buggar.”

 

            They sat in silence for a long minute, Sam’s barn owl cracking an eye to give them a disgruntled look from its perch, while Lena took another sip of coffee. Then Sam sighed again and gave Lena a warm smile.

 

            “Hungry?”

 

            Thinking about her abandoned breakfast, the shift ahead of her, which was actually fairly short, and how sorry she was for essentially avoiding Sam outside of the hospital unless she needed her, Lena said yes. They were both used to eating whatever was quickest, so they settled on plain old toast, Sam handling the loaf of bread while Lena buttered the slices and slathered jam over them as well. They chased their coffees up with cups of tea, and Lena felt a little bit of the heaviness in her chest abate as they chatted and ate breakfast, wishing that she had more time for this without feeling like her absences were being timed. If Sam wasn’t such a good person, it would’ve been easy, but she was, and so Lena had to sit with the grim knowledge that she wouldn’t be able to be a good friend for a while yet.

 

            Still, she stayed to supervise the dishes as they washed themselves, asking about Ruby while Sam directed her clean laundry to fold itself, and then it was time for her to go to work, taking a pinch of Floo powder and stepping into the reception area once more. It was a rather uneventful day, consulting on a few cases, ordering around the Resident on her case and managing to squeeze in two minor procedures before she left only an hour later than anticipated. Knowing her mum was checking her timesheets, having been questioned by Lillian a few times about the gaps between when she finished and when she got home, now explained by painting, Lena was quick to go home that day, if only to relay that Sam would twist the truth for her.

 

            Showering once she got home, Lena dressed in clean clothes for dinner and made her way downstairs, evening already darkening the day, the cold creeping into the cavernous house. Her mother and brother were in the sitting room, nursing their drinks, and she cleared her throat as she stepped inside, drawing their attention.

 

            “I’ve spoken to Sam. She’ll corroborate what I told them.”

 

            “Good,” Lillian nodded, swirling her Firewhisky in her glass. 

 

            “See that she does,” Lex followed up, and Lena had to school her face into a neutral expression as a chill ran down her spine. 

 

            Nodding, she hovered for a moment before fetching herself a drink, draining the glass in one mouthful. The three of them moved through to the dining room then, the table laid by Hope, a shoulder of lamb carved into thin slices in the middle of the table, steam rising from a silver gravy boat, platters of roast potatoes and vegetables spread about. Lena waited for her mother and brother to dish themselves up first and helped herself to a small portion, her usual lack of appetite of late plaguing her as she picked at her plate. She drank a glass of elderflower wine, though, the conversation minimal, a fire casting an orange glow over them, that only served to make deep shadows of her mother and brother’s faces. It was stiff and uncomfortable, as usual, and Lena was surprised when Lex dabbed a napkin at the corners of his mouth and pushed his chair back as soon as he was finished.

 

            “I should get going. Your wand, mother?”

 

            Lillian slipped it from her pocket and handed it over as Lena’s eyes darted between the two of them, stomach lurching. “Going where?”

 

            “I have business to attend to.”

 

            Her mouth opened and closed for a moment, and Lena felt her heart stagger in her chest, adrenaline sweeping through her as she tried to feign nonchalance. “Can I come?”

 

            “No,” he curtly replied, buttoning his suit jacket and making for the door.

 

            Lillian hesitated momentarily and then followed after him, and Lena quietly followed suit, hovering just inside the doorway of the dining room as she listened to her mother’s quiet words, laced with worry.

 

            “Are you sure this is a good idea? Surely someone else could go? What about Malfoy; he’s trusted enough, and he isn’t a wanted man.”

 

            “The Dark Lord asked me to go, mother. If he wanted someone else to go, he would’ve asked them. You shouldn’t worry, though, it’s only a trip to some town in Yorkshire. Little Hangleton, he said it was called. It shouldn’t take longer than half an hour.”

 

            The sound of the front door groaned open then, and Lena hurried back to her seat, cutting into a piece of lamb when Lillian cut across the foyer, to the doors of the sitting room directly across from the dining room. She glanced back to catch a glimpse of her daughter still eating, and then vanished into the room. Only then did Lena quickly dart out of the room, rushing upstairs as quietly as she could and calling out for Hope. She asked the House Elf to bring her a pot of tea in half an hour and then ushered her through the door, quietly shutting it behind her. Then Lena opened her window and felt her skin prickle as little black feathers sprouted, and she started to shrink, managing to take her clothes with her this time, her ability as an Animagus somewhat rusty but more familiar over the years as she became more adept. Still, as she hopped about as a raven, it was a daunting prospect for one afraid of heights to swoop through the open window and glide to the edges of the property, where Lena promptly turned back into a witch and fixated on the thought of Little Hangleton, Yorkshire and her brother as she Apparated.

 

            While she’d never been there before, nor even heard of the place, the thought of her brother there made her destination a little too close for her own good. Standing in a field on the outskirts of the small town, Lena sank to a crouch as she peered through the dark, trying to take stock of her surroundings and figure out where her brother could possibly be. Before her eyes could adjust or before she could move, a hand seized her by the collar of her jumper, dragging her to her feet and roughly shoving her away.

 

            Staggering a few steps, Lena turned and watched her brother approach, a dark shadow that was briefly illuminated as a cloud passed the moon and silvery light showed the cold anger burning in his eyes. He grabbed her by the throat, fingers digging in painfully as the breath caught in Lena’s throat, a small whine of panic escaping her as she went rigid, and Lex’s mouth twisted derisively.

 

            “Why are you following me?” he demanded, his voice harsh.

 

            Blinking silently for a second as panic jolted through her, Lena tightened the fortress of her mind as she tried to speak past his tight grip. Her voice was a painful rasp as she choked out her pre-planned excuse.

 

            “I want to- to … help. I want to … be useful.”

 

            Lex’s grasp slackened, although he didn’t let go, and he scoffed contemptuously, haughty amusement crossing his face. “You’re too impatient for your own good. And foolish. The Dark Lord asked me to do this; me, not you. Now go. Go home; we’ll speak of this when I return.”

 

            Lena managed a weak nod, and he finally uncurled his fingers, gesturing dismissively to her. Stumbling back a step, Lena drew in a grating breath and then turned on her heel, Disapparating, although she only envisioned herself a mile away. She had to know what he was doing, had to report her brother’s every move to Dumbledore, unsure what was useful and what wasn’t. If it was something Voldemort had asked Lex to do himself, then it was clearly valuable information.

 

            A mile away, in a different field, Lena transformed into her Animagus form once more and took to the skies. She stayed quite low, soaring on the wind currents, wary of crashing, and while her vision wasn’t that of an owl, she could see much better in the dark than she could as a human. It made it that much easier to spot her brother as he circled around Little Hangleton, his eyes darting about as he surveyed the houses, and she couldn’t tell what he was there for, what he was looking for, but he must’ve known something. It wasn’t until he stopped outside a rundown shack that she seemed to realise he was there for that. 

 

            Gliding to perch in a nearby tree, Lena shifted along the branch as she tried to give herself a good view of what he was doing. Lex opened the door and was inside for a handful of minutes before he stepped back outside, no sound of voices drifting out while he was in there, no visible sign of a package on him, and Lena kept still as she watched him lock the door and then Disapparate. 

 

            Alarm shot through her, and Lena quickly fluttered down from her perch, transforming back to a witch and Apparating to the back hedgerows of the Luthor estate. There, she promptly turned back into a raven and flew as quickly as she could over the expansive gardens and up to her open bedroom window. Inside, she transformed back again and hurriedly undressed, feeling cold, the smell of the outdoors on her, fetching pyjamas and a deep green dressing gown belted over the top before she sank to her desk chair.

 

            Hope knocked on the door a minute later, bearing the tea tray Lena had requested, and Lena thanked her, her voice hoarse and pitching unevenly, before the House Elf left. Pouring herself half a cup of tea with a shaking hand, Lena added a splash of milk and leafed through her notes on the Wolfsbane Potion, her research not forgotten or given up, even with her change in circumstances. Her hand shook slightly, and she burned her tongue on a quick gulp of tea, trying to steady herself as she heard the heavy tread of footsteps on the stairs five minutes later.

 

            The door burst open, and Lena jumped slightly, her face pale, a flicker of panic in her eyes as she pushed her chair back, the legs scraping over old floorboards, and climbed to her feet to face her brother. Lex’s angry stride carried him across the room as Lena stood, and she’d no sooner faced him than he struck her across the face, so fast that Lena never saw his hand coming. The blow rocked her, but she managed to remain upright, cheek smarting as her dark hair fell around her stiff face in a curtain, all the better so he couldn’t see her anger. It wasn’t a surprise to her, her brother’s violence always simmering just beneath the surface, but it was humiliating all the same.

 

            “I told you you weren’t to come,” Lex quietly raged. “I specifically said you weren’t allowed to, and you still defied me. You defied him. Until you prove yourself to the Dark Lord, until you have a mark on your arm, you have no right to come. Do you hear me?”

 

            She knew that tone, the one that thinly veiled his threats, telling her there would be consequences if she didn’t step carefully. If things were different, if she’d been in a place where she could’ve burned the whole world down to see her brother jailed again, she might have risked his wrath, but he was a small nuisance in the grand scheme of things. Still, when she raised her head to look at him, she hated his face, with his boorish cruelty, hard with anger, and she knew that if not that day, there would be a day when she would get her vengeance. Perhaps not justice, but vengeance all the same.

 

            Giving him a curt nod, her throat so tight she couldn’t speak, Lena couldn’t quite look him in the eyes. His anger was palpable, and her heart raced, wondering whether he’d leave it there or take it further. His hand twitched slightly, but if he was still in possession of Lillian’s wand, he didn’t reach for it, just stared at her for a long moment and then abruptly turned and stormed out of the room. As her door slammed shut, shuddering in its frame, Lena sagged to the floor, quietly gasping as she reached to press her cold fingers to her red cheek, her throat already bearing a light ring of bruises, sure to be worse in the morning, and she felt weak with something that wasn’t quite relief, but the knowledge that she’d managed to make it through another day undiscovered.

 

            After fifteen minutes kneeling on the hard floor, a brisk wind making the room considerably colder as the window remained open, Lena pushed herself to her feet and moved to shut the window most of the way, leaving it slightly ajar for Morrigan when she returned from her hunting. Sitting at her desk again, Lena pushed aside her notes, drained her cup of tea and poured a fresh one, and then penned a short note. The details were sparse, and she was unsure of the importance, deciding she’d relegate it to green when she delivered it in the morning, sealing it with a blob of green wax once she’d finished her account of Lex’s strange behaviour.

 

            Then, with the letter under her pillow, she went to bed and slept fitfully, rising early, when the sky was still dark. Dressing warmly, she grabbed her satchel, intending to head to work straight from her errands, and carried her cloak over her arm as she made her way down to breakfast. Her mother was already there, casting her a dismissive look, and Lena made her way through half a bowl of porridge, her throat feeling a little raw, dark bruises ringing her throat beneath the turtleneck, despite the bruise salve she’d applied after she’d showered that morning. It would be a few hours and another application before she’d be able to go to work and wear scrubs, but it would see her through the morning at least.

 

            “I need to visit Mulpepper’s for some supplies,” Lena quietly broke the silence as she finished off her cup of coffee and set it down on the saucer. “Was there anything you needed?”

 

            “No.”

 

            Nodding, Lena set her napkin on the table and climbed to her feet, fetching her cloak from the back of the chair beside her and draping it around her shoulders before fastening it at the neck. Picking up her satchel, she cleared her throat, casting her mother a cursory glance.

 

            “I’ll see you tomorrow.”

 

            Lillian behaved as if she hadn’t even spoken, and Lena walked out of the room without another word, crossing the foyer to the front door and stepping out into the bitter morning. Dew coated everything, and a thin fog lingered over the estate as she walked down the long gravel path to the gates, passing through them and then Apparating to Knockturn Alley. Her first stop was a branch of Mr. Mulpepper’s Apothecary, which was relatively understocked as she came away with only half of the supplies she would’ve liked, and had to make the grim trip to Diagon Alley to finish off her shopping. If it hadn’t been a restock of potion ingredients for the Wolfsbane Potion, she might not have bothered, but of course, she would brave anything for Kara. 

 

            Still, as the morning had brightened to a cloudy London day and Diagon Alley had started to open for business, Lena was wary of the shopkeepers and staff who moved purposely down the cobbled streets, and at the sight of Andrea heading to work, Lena was quick to duck into the nearest open store. It just so happened to be a teashop, a quick glance at the sign above the door reading Rosa Lee Teabag, a reassurance to Lena, who ordered a pot of tea for one and whittled away at an hour, hoping that would make any encounters with familiar faces less likely. Once she’d drained her tea to the dregs, she stepped back out and made her way to Slug & Jiggers Apothecary , buying a few moonstones, a bag bursting with Sopophorous Beans, and a blue bottle of Syrup of Hellebore. Paying at the counter and waiting for the shopkeeper to wrap the parcels in brown paper and twine, Lena was thinking about Kara, about the most recent full moon, and the next one, and how much she missed her, and whether she was safe or if she was being too reckless to help the Order. 

 

            Almost as if the thought of Kara had summoned a portion of her life, Lena thanked the shopkeeper, gathered up her parcels and made for the door, coming to a stop as it was opened to reveal a familiar blonde woman. Not Kara, but Eliza, and almost as painful. Worse in some ways, because if it had been Kara, they might’ve stolen a painful moment, but known the truth, whereas, Eliza knew nothing but what Kara had told her, and as much as she hated it, as shameful as it was, Lena hoped what she’d been told hadn’t been very nice. 

 

            Eliza pulled up short, her kind laughter and apologies petering off into surprised silence as Lena stood firmly rooted to the spot, every inch of her screaming to run. But Eliza was blocking the doorway with a few parcels under her arm, presumably supplies to sell to the shopkeeper, and there was no way for Lena to escape as her eyes darted everywhere but to her mother-in-law’s face. It didn’t matter that they weren’t married, or that she wasn’t with Kara, that was still how Lena viewed the other woman, who had only ever been good to her. And she was good to her now, her voice small but still soft, and unusually sad.

 

            “Oh. Lena.”

 

            A muscle jumped in Lena’s jaw as she ducked her head slightly, trying to swallow, her face twitching slightly at the rawness in her throat. She couldn’t speak, didn’t even know what to say, and the silence dragged on a split-second longer before Eliza continued, reaching out to cup Lena’s face in a rough, warm hand.

 

            “Look at me.”
