            At the gentle urging, both physically and verbally, Lena was helpless to obey, raising her head and letting her eyes meet Eliza’s. They were shockingly blue and full of worry as they took in the dark shadows beneath Lena’s eyes, the pale thinness of her face, her expression tense and haunted. She saw Eliza deflate slightly, dismay flitting across her face, the faint lines of ageing deepening.

 

            “This isn’t you,” Eliza murmured, shaking her head with bewildered concern. Her eyes dipped to catch sight of a dark bruise on the underside of Lena’s jaw, where Lex’s thumb had pressed, unhidden by her turtleneck like the rest of them, and she saw grief and distress cross the older woman’s face before she met Lena’s eyes again, her voice a soft plea. “We can help you. I know you’re struggling through something at the moment, but we’ll help you.” 

 

            Lena turned her head aside, gently shrugging off Eliza’s touch, her mouth thinning at the corners. And while she still didn’t speak a word, she hardened herself as she faltered momentarily, stepping forward to force her mother-in-law to step aside. With a soft sigh, Eliza did step aside, but she gently grabbed Lena’s arm as she brushed past, and her words rang in Lena’s ears as she hurried out of the shop.

 

            “You can come home when you’re ready.”

 

            With a shakiness in her chest and a hollow feeling in her stomach, Lena Apparated right from the doorstep of the apothecary and hurried up the path to the front door of the cottage. Inside, she stumbled straight through to the kitchen, dumping her parcels and her satchel on the table, and then pressed the heels of her palms into her eyes as she drew in shallow, ragged gasps, which were more like sobs as her eyes stung with tears that wet her hands as she tried to keep it together. 

 

            It hurt more than anticipated, like pressing on an old bruise, and it took Lena a good fifteen minutes to calm herself down, her eyes bloodshot and cheeks slightly blotchy when she finally pulled out the note she’d come to deliver and left the cottage with the ring on her finger charmed green.

Chapter 55

            After work, Kara went straight to Grimmauld Place with the letter she’d picked up from her home in her pocket, socialising with the other Order members as she sipped elderflower wine with a pit in her stomach, the taste reminding her of Lena, who favoured that as her drink of choice. It was a good hour and a half crammed into that basement kitchen, pretending she was there to glean any information from the others, some bearing scratches and bags under their eyes from their own covert assignments, drinking coffee and itching for bed. So far, Kara’s tasks had been little more than what she’d been doing before rejoining the Order: letting Order members in and out of the Department of Mysteries, taking the occasional watch herself, and ferrying messages between Lena and Dumbledore, although it was mostly ones from Lena that came through. So far, she’d only had one to pass back to her, charming her ring to the appropriate colour, itching to make it red and stay to see her, just for a minute, even just a glimpse , but Kara didn’t take advantage of the Protean Charm and just did her duty.

 

            There hadn’t been any urgent messages yet, either, the one in her pocket relating to the ring on her finger that had turned green. Not urgent, not time sensitive. It meant that Kara could sit in the kitchen at Grimmauld Place, drinking her elderflower wine and waving off the offer of dinner, while waiting for one of the direct links to Dumbledore to pass the letter in her pocket off to. An hour and a half passed, three glasses in her, before Kingsley swept in with Alex and Tonks, all fresh from the Auror Department, looking a little windswept and morose as they filed down the narrow staircase. 

 

            Spotting her sister at the table, Alex walked over to her, clapping her hands on Kara’s shoulders and kissing the top of her head. “You alright?”

 

            “Mhm. Everything okay? You look …”

 

            “Yeah,” Alex sighed, flopping onto a chair beside Kara, eyeing her fourth glass of elderflower wine and accepting it when Kara nudged it towards her. Downing the glass in two mouthfuls, Alex raked a hand through her hair. “It’s just the Ministry. You know how it’s getting. Fudge is making it harder for us to investigate … certain things. Kelly’s copping it as well; we got her to sign off on another warrant to search- well, there were a few estates, um, but someone in the Wizengamot reported it, so now we’re being told to lay off. And it’s all just Fudge turning a blind eye, so he doesn’t have to admit that Dumbledore’s right . Did you see the paper this morning?”

 

            Nodding, Kara let out a soft sigh, running a hand over her face, nudging her glasses up as she rubbed her tired eyes. “Yeah, I have half a mind to speak to Andrea myself. Not that it would do much, I think. Still, she’s too under the Ministry’s thumb, and I can’t imagine Cat Grant is happy about that either.”

 

            “Best leave them to it for now,” Alex said, patting her shoulder. “You on duty tonight?”

 

            “No, no, I’m just- I needed to speak to Kingsley about something. Um, work-related.”

 

            “They’ve not got someone on the inside again, have they?”

 

            “No, nothing like that. Just … something Dumbledore asked me to keep an eye on.” Glancing down at her watch, Kara ran her palms over the thighs of her pants and cleared her throat. “I should speak to him and get home. You know what mum’s like.”

 

            “Okay, well, we might go to The Leaky Cauldron on Thursday, if you want to come.”

 

            “Sure, I’ll meet you there after work.”

 

            Squeezing her sister’s shoulder, Kara’s eyes landed on Kingsley Shacklebolt, and she quietly asked to speak with him upstairs. Shut inside one of the dingy drawing rooms, Kara handed the letter over to Kingsley and informed him it was non-urgent, reassured he would get it to Dumbledore, and then left to go home. The sky was a dark blue as she stepped through the front door of Grimmauld Place and then Apparated to Falmouth, the salt air hitting her as she stood on the pavement outside the cottage, hurrying up the short front path to let herself inside.

 

            Her mum was banging around in the kitchen, and Kara found Eliza wrestling with a freshly potted Venomous Tentacula, a few vines wrapped around her arms, face red as sweaty as she ducked to avoid its bite. A few Chizpurfles crawled on the tabletop, and Kara paused in the doorway to observe the chaos.

 

            “Need help?”

 

            “Oh, hi, sweetheart. Best you stay right there a second, while I sort this one out.” 

 

            Kara smiled faintly, leaning against the doorway as she watched Eliza feed the plant the Chizpurfles, keeping her fingers away from the thorns. Quietly crooning as she stroked a finger over the head of the plant, Eliza coaxed it into unwinding its vines and then carried the plant over to the fridge, setting it on top, out of the way.

 

            “What in Merlin’s name are you doing with another one of those?” Kara laughed as her mother dusted off her hands, looking a little dishevelled, dirt covering the front of her overalls, a few scratches on her forearms, her shirtsleeves rolled up to her elbows. “They are actually venomous, right?”

 

            Waving a hand, Eliza chuckled, moving to the sink to wash her hands. “Ah, they’re misunderstood. They’re just a little temperamental. Ten galleons a leaf, though; can’t argue with that. I only wish I’d been able to afford more seedlings when you girls were younger. Wouldn’t it have been nice to have new school robes every year and a pile of Christmas presents, huh?”

 

            “We had everything we needed,” Kara murmured, a soft smile on her lips, her fingers brushing over the wool of the knitted vest Eliza had made her a few Christmases back.

 

            Looking over at her as she dried her hands, Eliza smiled and then seemed to sober up. Setting the tea towel down, she softly sighed, her mouth turning down at the corners. Inside the kitchen now, Kara was lifting the kettle off the stovetop, rounding the table to step up beside her mother and fill it at the tap. She didn’t catch the flicker of hesitation on Eliza’s face, but she stiffened as soon as she spoke.

 

            “I saw Lena today.”

 

            Nearly dropping the kettle, Kara rounded the table again, setting the water on to boil as she kept her back to her mother. “Where?”

 

            “Diagon Alley. We were both at the apothecary.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “Kara,” her mum started and then faltered. Pausing, Kara made herself turn around, gripping the edge of the counters as she stood beside the stove, raising her eyebrows slightly. With a grave look on her face, Eliza’s shoulders drooped as she softly sighed again. “I- are you sure that you’re right about her?”

 

            “Yes,” Kara tightly murmured as she looked at the floor.

 

            “Because … I don’t think she’s okay.”

 

            Head jerking up, Kara wasn’t very good at masking her worry, that flicker of panic that ran across her face. But then, less than three months wasn’t long enough to get over years of love, and her mum knew how devastated she was, so she didn’t have to pretend, didn’t have to act like she didn’t care. “What do you mean?”

 

            Struggling for a second, Eliza’s face furrowed as she shook her head, reaching up to gently brush her fingers over her throat. “It looked like she’d been … hurt. Bruises, I think. If she’s in any trouble … well, we can help her. I know her family aren’t-”

 

            “You shouldn’t speak to her,” Kara cut her off, swallowing the lump in her throat, making herself turn around. 

 

            Palms clammy, her heart raced as her face prickled with numb panic. She had visibly paled, and her hands shook as she reached for a cupboard with the mugs, pulling out two, settling on tea as she busied herself with lifting the just-bubbling kettle off the stove, pouring hot water into each mug. She could feel her mum’s perturbed gaze on her back, feeling hot around the collar of her shirt, and swallowed thickly.

 

            “Do you still love her?”

 

            “What?”

 

            “Do you still love her?” Eliza repeated, a little more ire in her voice now.

 

            “I- yes, of course I do,” Kara murmured.

 

            “Then you should be helping her. Why are you giving up on her without a fight? I understand she might’ve gotten herself mixed up in things that are- no good person would want to be involved in that, but I don’t believe she’s a bad person. You can bring her back from it.”

 

            “I can’t. She made her choice. She left me . I’m just respecting that decision. It’s because I love her that I’m doing that. I’m not- I’m not responsible for anything that happens to her because of it,” Kara firmly replied, keeping her head ducked down, staring at the rings of the stovetop as she felt her throat close up.

 

            “Kara,” Eliza exclaimed, quietly outraged.

 

            Running a hand over her face, Kara stood there with her shoulders hunched for a moment, shame washing over her, that pit of panic in her stomach growing bigger. And she wished she could tell someone, she wished she could tell her mum that Lena was better than any of them, that she wanted to be sick with worry, that every day was agony, that in a couple of days it would be April, and they would’ve spent nearly three months apart, lying to everyone while Lena risked her life. 

 

            And it was never supposed to be like that, and Kara could feel the way her breath turned shallow, the pressure building behind her eyes, and she knew she had to get out of that kitchen instead of arguing back. Especially not when she agreed with everything Eliza said, and that if that had been the case, Kara would fight for Lena this time. She wouldn’t have repeated the same mistake again. Except, Kara couldn’t tell her that, so she left her tea cooling on the counter as she turned, head down, and made for the mouth of the hallway, Eliza’s hand ghosting over her arm as she silently tried to stop her. Walking straight to the front door, leaving her cloak on the hook, her shoes amidst the jumbled mess of wellies, slippers and boots, Kara stepped outside and Apparated.

 

            She went straight to their cottage, because of course she had to know she was safe, no matter what she told her mother. Anxiously pacing back and forth for a few moments, agonising over the improper use of her ring, Kara changed the colour to red and sank to the base of the front door, hugging her knees to her chest as she waited. It wasn’t long, a handful of minutes, and she wondered what Lena was doing, whether she’d had to sneak out of her family’s estate, whether she’d been at some Death Eater party, scrambling for an excuse to bolt. The answer was so ordinary that Kara should’ve expected it, watching as a figure in a pair of green Healer robes popped into sight.

 

            The shadowed figure rushed up the garden path, not noticing that Kara was there until she unfolded herself, the moon coming out from behind the clouds to illuminate her as she rose to her feet. Lena came to a stop, and Kara could see her expression in the moonlight, the wariness in her eyes, the way her face crumpled, the corners of her mouth quivering slightly. She didn’t come any closer, and Kara had to hold herself back from throwing herself at Lena, fear constricting her chest as she breathed quickly, hands balled into fists at her side as her eyes started to fill with tears.

 

            “You should go,” Lena rasped, her voice soft and wavering slightly.

 

            Kara felt the sound of her voice like a kick in the chest, inhaling sharply as her shoulders sagged. Wiping her eyes, she sniffed, mouth turning down at the corners, and her expression was one of pure agony. 

 

            “There’s no message,” Kara tearfully admitted, her throat painfully tight.

 

            Hesitating, licking her lips, Lena could barely look at Kara. “Then I should go.”

 

            “Wait.”

 

            Already shrinking back a step, trying to put some more distance between them, Lena paused. She made herself look up, and Kara met her eyes, pleading, heartbroken. Her fingers flexed, reaching slightly before falling limply back to her sides. Wiping her eyes on the cuffs of her shirt, Kara cleared her throat, trying to compose herself.

 

            “Are you okay?” she quietly asked, her voice breaking.

 

            Shoulders slumping, Lena gave her a pained look, eyes closing as a thin smile twitched her lips. But she seemed to sense Kara’s desperation, taking a slow step closer, her eyes fluttering open again as she reduced the space between them. Kara watched her throat bob with the effort it took to swallow, and she had to stop herself from lurching forward, grabbing onto Lena, holding her closely, tightly, with the intention to never let her go. She blinked away more tears before they could fall.

 

            “I’m okay,” Lena whispered, a foot from Kara now.

 

            And she did look okay, no bruises evident, except for all the ways she didn’t look okay. Dark circles beneath her eyes, her face ghostly in the moonlight, a slight thinning of her cheeks. Lena looked tired , and Kara’s chest tightened, ached. But she could see how reserved Lena was being, perhaps because of the last time they’d seen each other, Kara begging on her knees as she sobbed, and she held herself back, not wanting to make it harder for her this time. Kara knew there would be no hope of changing her mind.

 

            “Come here,” Lena murmured after a moment, reaching for her, asking for what Kara wouldn’t.

 

            But Kara wanted that so badly that she stepped in immediately, her arms going around Lena, holding her tightly, cradling the back of her head in a hand, breathing in her perfume, cherishing the way she fit in her arms, that she was safe. It was everything she could do not to start sobbing into Lena’s shoulder, and by the feeling of her chest quickly rising and falling through her Healer robes, Lena might’ve been struggling with the same. It was still so shocking to Kara to know that was a possibility, having watched Lena fall apart before her very eyes after so many years of stoicism. But Lena didn’t cry, held herself together as she usually did. But still, she clung to Kara, drinking in every bit of her in their limited time together.

 

            When Lena pulled back, Kara still reached for her, cupping the underside of her jaw, her eyes flitting over her face, finding no marks, no signs she’d been hurt. That didn’t mean that they hadn’t existed, though, that Lena hadn’t healed herself, and she knew that they would’ve had to be somewhere on her face for Eliza to have noticed. Covering Kara’s hand with her own, Lena raised her eyebrows slightly, her face achingly tender.

 

            “What’s wrong? Why did you-?”

 

            She didn’t have to finish her question. They both knew the rings weren’t toys, that they were to discreetly pass information, and that one of them would only charm it red if it was urgent. But Kara had said she didn’t have a message, which would mean that there was something wrong.

 

            Kara couldn’t stop staring at her, not wanting to look away for even a second, cherishing the chance to lay eyes on her and know she was safe. Even as she floundered, mouth opening and closing, she kept looking at Lena, who looked fine, and didn’t know how to voice her fears. Kara didn’t know how to explain the terror that filled her, how even the merest suggestion that she was hurt was too much for her to bear, too much to stay away.

 

            “My mum said she saw you,” Kara admitted, her voice fraught with worry.

 

            Swallowing thickly, Lena averted her gaze, her hand reaching up to cup her throat, before she quickly dropped it. But Kara recognised it for what it was, her stomach dropping as she reached out to cup the side of Lena’s neck, her thumb gently pressed to the underside of her jaw as she made her tip her head back, exposing the pale length of her throat. Not a mark in sight, clear skin and a few freckles all the way down to the v-neck of her scrubs.

 

            “What-”

 

            Kara couldn’t ask, her throat closing up, eyes stinging, although they remained dry. She drew in a few short, quick breaths, feeling her anger suffuse her, hot but quiet. Lena’s cool fingers brushed her flushed cheeks, and while she wouldn’t meet Kara’s eyes, she cupped her face in her hands, softly shushing her.

 

            “I’m okay. Really. It was nothing.”

 

            “Don’t say that.”

 

            “You don’t have to worry,” Lena murmured, leaning in, her nose gently bumping against Kara’s. “I promise. The only thing I’m in danger of is a broken heart when I have to leave you again.”

 

            Kara let out a small laugh, hoarse and full of pain. Her eyes closed then, leaving in to close that inch between their lips, kissing Lena with all of the pent-up longing and love inside her. She never wanted that kiss to end, would have gladly stayed there forever, let the war go on without them, realising that she had been wrong for feeling caught between her frustration of sitting it out and her desire to protect Lena. The correct answer would always be protecting Lena, at the cost of anything else, including her morals. Unfortunately, Lena was so self-sacrificing that she’d convinced Kara otherwise.

 

            “You don’t have to leave.”

 

            Lena laughed, the sound pitifully small and full of regret, and they both knew it was a long shot anyway, that Kara didn’t believe she’d come with her, no matter how badly Lena wanted to. “I do.”

 

            “I’ll kill him one day,” Kara whispered a hairsbreadth from her lips.

 

            Lena laughed again, stealing a quick kiss, a soft brush of their mouths. “You leave my brother to me, alright? Now, did you take your doses of Wolfsbane with you yesterday?”

 

            “Yes. Thank you.”

 

            “Good.”

 

            Lips twitching with a smile, Kara hugged her again, pressing her close to her body, feeling her heart break a little more. “If he touches you again, I swear I’ll- you can’t let him hurt you, okay? I don’t care if it exposes you to fight back, you do it and you come home, okay? Just … come home to me. Please.”

 

            “I wish I could promise that,” Lena sighed, “but I won’t leave over a few bruises. You and I both know I can tolerate more than that.”

 

            “Just because you can tolerate it, it doesn’t mean you should .”

 

            “I know, but- just … trust me. Please. I know my limits.”

 

            “Lena, I-” Kara started, a pain in her chest as she cut off, her face rippling with pain and worry. “I love you.”

 

            Pulling back slightly, Lena gave her a brilliant smile, genuine and warm for the first time in months, and reached out to tuck a wayward curl behind Kara’s ear, her fingers following the shell of her ear, resting on the corner of her jaw. She leaned in and kissed Kara, hard and full of urgency.

 

            “I love you, too. I’m sorry we didn’t have more time.”

 

            Kara reached for her hand, the one that she still nervously flexed sometimes, and kissed her fingers. Then she let her go, and Lena backed away a few steps, her expression pained, before she Disapparated, vanishing from sight as Kara was left alone in the front garden. Tears stung her eyes, and she ran a hand over her face, taking a moment to compose herself before she removed her glasses, slipping her wand out of her pocket and steeling herself. Eyes closed, teeth gritted together, Kara hexed herself in the face, as she’d done in January, except last time she’d gotten Alex to keep it from Eliza, and this time, it was for Eliza’s benefit. Kara had to make her mother believe that there was no redemption for Lena, because Kara couldn’t risk Eliza complicating things by trying to reach out to Lena herself, thinking she was helping but compromising her cover.

 

            The crunch of her nose breaking was loud in her ears, the gush of blood hot and fast as it spilt over her lips and chin, dotting her knitted vest, and Kara could feel it in her eyes as well, the way they were quick to swell, until she could barely see. Her hands shook, and she pocketed her glasses before she turned on her heel and Apparated back home. Stepping inside with a bloody nose, two quickly forming black eyes, already bluish beneath the red swelling, Kara found her mother still in the kitchen, browning sausages on the stove.

 

            She turned at the sound of her daughter coming home again, and let out a small cry of alarm as Kara stepped into the kitchen. Squinting through swollen eyes, licking her lips, tasting wet blood on her tongue, Kara cleared her throat twice before she could make her voice work, unable to see the white look of shock on Eliza’s face.

 

            “There’s nothing I can do for her,” Kara gravelly explained.

 

            “Wha- I-” Eliza stammered, snatching up a tea towel as Kara spoke, rushing over to her daughter, of a height with her, and pressing it to her nose as she continued to make soft sounds of disbelief, of panic.

 

            Covering her mother’s hand with her own to take the tea towel, Kara kept it pressed to her nose, glad that most of her face was covered as she felt her cheeks burn with shame. She’d wanted to avoid this last time, had wanted to spare Lena’s false reputation from one person, at least, but she could see now why it was necessary for people to believe that she was someone who would be capable of doing horrible things, of believing in the same ideology as the people Kara claimed she was affiliated with. And it wasn’t fair, it wasn’t right, but it was necessary , which made it worse to bear.

 

            “You need to go to St. Mungo’s,” Eliza fretted, trying to urge Kara out of the kitchen, towards the living room.

 

            “No,” Kara thickly objected. “No, I can’t go there. She-”

 

            Trailing off, she shook her head, a dull pain radiating from the centre of her face. She’d given Lena no warning to expect the accusation of hexing her, breaking her nose again, and Kara could imagine her expression if she Flooed into the waiting room covered in blood. Lena was so fiercely protective that she would just about pass out, or have a fit, and that wouldn’t corroborate what Kara had implied to Eliza. And Kara didn’t think she could see her again then, because it was hard , and she didn’t think she’d be able to pretend very well in front of other people. Lena had been right about that; it had to be a real separation, because they wouldn’t be able to pretend well enough if it wasn’t.

 

            “It could be broken. You need a Healer to set it and-”

 

            “Alex can do it.”

 

            Clicking her tongue, pale-faced and shaken, Eliza continued to shepherd Kara towards the living room. “Your sister can’t-”

 

            “She did last time.”

 

            “Last time?”

 

            Barely able to see through the swollen slits of her black eyes, the muscles around them tender and puffy from her up close hex, Kara moved unsteadily as she tipped her head back, trying to stem the flow of blood, and fumbled with her other hand for the sofa. She almost sat on the cat as she collapsed onto the cushions, Bastet letting out a disgruntled yowl before she started clawing at Kara’s pants, rubbing against her arm and then curling up in her lap.

 

            “She’s done this before,” Kara whispered, ashamed all over again as she made herself force the lie out, her throat tight around her reluctance.

 

            “She- Lena?”

 

            Wincing at the horror lacing her mother’s voice, Kara managed a weak nod. Aghast, mouth opening and closing, Eliza ran a hand through her hair, still in her dirty overalls, as she stared at her daughter with devastating disbelief. Clearing her throat, Kara ran her hand over the thigh of her pants and then moved the tea towel away, the flow of blood slowing, sniffing and wincing at the tender pain as she hung her head.

 

            “Kara,” Eliza whispered, helplessly confused.

 

            “Only once,” Kara felt the need to elaborate, not wanting her mother to think badly of Lena, of the years they were together and openly in love. It was one thing to hurt each other in a duel over an ended relationship, but another altogether to let people believe this had been a common occurrence during their relationship. “When we split up. I- well, I … left her in a bad way, too. I didn’t- I didn’t want to tell you. I knew you’d worry.”

 

            Quickly moving over to the old cabinet crammed into the corner of the small living room, Eliza shakily wrote a note and folded it in half before walking over to the fireplace. With a pinch of Floo powder, Eliza thrust her hand with the letter into the emerald flames, dropping it onto the floor on the other end, and then pulled her hand back through, the flames extinguishing as she stepped away. Moving back over to the sofa, she sat beside her daughter and ran a hand over Kara’s wayward curls, ducking her head to look at her face, to see the extent of the damage.

 

            At her mother’s gentle, urging fingers, Kara raised her head, closing her mostly shut eyes, the skin feeling tight as it ached dully. Reaching up, she probed at her nose, hot to the touch and smarting as her eyes pricked with tears, and Eliza swallowed thickly, her heart hurting for her daughter, reeling with the shock and guilt of pushing Kara to help someone who had only hurt her, a person Eliza never believed would’ve hurt her.

 

            “Let me get a bruise salve for you,” Eliza murmured after a tense minute, “I can sort out the rest while we wait for your sister to get my letter.”

 

            Nodding, Kara’s mouth was a thin line of regret as she dabbed the tea towel against her nose. Sitting on the sofa with the cat in her lap, she listened to the sound of her mother moving about, cupboards opening and closing, water running, a glass clinking. Eliza came back with a few things levitating in her wake, carefully setting them all down. First up, she gave Kara a glass half full of Firewhisky, making her knock most of it back to dull the edges of her pain, and then she dipped a cloth into the bowl of warm water to help wipe her face clean, blood half-dried to Kara’s chin and fingers.

 

            Eliza was quick and gentle, and Kara clenched her teeth as she closed her swollen eyes and let her mother tidy her up. Then Eliza worked a charm to help reduce the swelling, before applying a thick layer of a bruise salve around Kara’s eyes, the tingling effect of it almost immediate as it got to work. Then her mum made them fresh cups of tea, the ones Kara had made now cool in the kitchen, and they sat side by side on the sofa as they waited for Alex to show up. Usually someone who always had an appetite, Kara rejected the offer of dinner three times as they waited, the sausages Eliza had been frying left in the kitchen, slightly burnt where they’d been forgotten about until the bruise salve was fetched, and it was an hour and a half before Alex ducked out of the fireplace, wide-eyed and hard-faced.

 

            “What happened?” she demanded, rounding the narrow gap between the coffee table and sofa, sinking to her knees as she stared at Kara’s face.

 

            The bruises had slightly faded, the swelling gone down, and without the blood, Kara didn’t look nearly as ghastly, but her nose was slightly crooked and red. Alex cupped her chin and gently turned her face from side to side as Kara drew in a shaky breath.

 

            “I saw Lena-”

 

            “She did this? Again?”

 

            “You might’ve told me about the first time,” Eliza softly berated them both.

 

            Quietly fuming, Alex observed Kara’s face while her sister kept her eyes closed, wincing slightly when she straightened Kara’s nose, a muffled sound of agony behind closed lips as Kara squeezed her eyes shut, jerking her head back. Tears leaked from her eyes, and she drew in a shaky breath before letting Alex cup her face again, holding her steady so she could finish setting it properly.

 

            Afterwards, Kara rubbed the sore bridge of it and reached for the rest of her Firewhisky, careful not to disturb Bastet, gulping down the rest of it as it seared a path down her throat. Coughing slightly at the burning sensation, her eyes streaming, Kara wiped her eyes on her sleeves and drew in a few gasping breaths. Rising to her feet, Alex fumbled for the inside pocket of her leather duster and pulled out a little notepad and a self-inking quill, flipping to a new page.

 

            “What happened?” she asked tightly.

 

            Kara remained silent, pressing her fingers to her lips, chin cupped in her palm with a distant look in her eyes. The bruises still ringed her eyes, the salve battling against the still-developing injury, and Kara looked tired, sad , as Alex stared at her, waiting for some sort of response. It was Eliza who had to answer for her in the end.

 

            “I saw Lena today. She didn’t look well. I thought- I thought maybe there was a chance-”

 

            “She’s a Death Eater, mum,” Alex snapped.

 

            Kara sighed, cupping her forehead in her hand as she closed her eyes. “She’s not-”

 

            “Yes, she is. She might not have a Dark Mark, yet, but in every other way, she is. We all have to accept that, whether we like it or not, okay? And this, ” Alex gestured helplessly to Kara, running a hand over her face as she shook her head. “Merlin, Kara, that’s not okay. So, tell me what happened-”

 

            “What’re you going to do, huh?”

 

            “It’s assault. What do you think I’m going to do?”

 

            “Make it worse,” Kara snapped. “Just like these- these constant raids on their estate. It’s making things worse.”

 

            “It’s my job-”

 

            “No, it’s not. Not this. This is you making things personal. And I’m telling you I don’t want to press charges, so this isn’t your job. Don’t make things harder for me. Please. ”

 

            Opening and closing her mouth, Alex silently seethed, a muscle twitching in her jaw, before she roughly pocketed her notepad and quill with a scowl on her face. Folding her arms over her chest, Alex continued to scowl for a few moments as the living room was filled with a tense silence, before she huffed, a pained look softening her face.

 

            “Stay away from her. Or I’ll be forced to make things very hard - for her.”

 

            A thin smile crossed Kara’s face. “Well, I won’t be trying again, so …”

 

            “Good,” Alex murmured, hesitating before she nodded, walking over to their mother and kissing her on the cheek before she said goodbye and went home.

 

            With a sigh, Kara lingered a moment longer before picking Bastet up, cradling the cat in her arms as she stood. “I’m going to shower and have an early night.”

 

            “You should eat something.”

 

            “I’m not hungry.”

 

            “Sweetheart-”

 

            Eliza moved to cup her shoulder, but Kara angled away from her touch, moving out of the open mouth of the room and making for the stairs. She felt a prickle of guilt for her abruptness, her cold shoulder, but she just wanted to be alone with her misery for a few minutes. Taking the stairs two steps at a time, Kara carried the cat into her room and set her down on Alex’s bed before fetching pyjamas for herself.

 

            Locking the bathroom door, she stood beneath the hot water and washed the lower half of her face, rinsing away any blood her mum didn’t get, before drying off and changing. Back in her room, she paused at the sight of a cup of tea on the desk wedged between the beds, and a plate with a sausage sandwich beside it. A lump got caught in Kara’s throat, and she felt a heaviness in her chest as she walked over to the bed and sank onto the mattress. 

 

            Wallowing in her misery, Kara dutifully ate the sandwich in between sips of tea and then got beneath the covers and turned off the lamp, her glasses and wand sitting on the desk as she went to bed. She found tears in her eyes, although she didn’t cry, lying on her back with a fading ache in her nose, trying to shut her mind off as she focused on breathing slowly. It was an age before she managed to fall asleep.

 

            Up early for work, another application of the bruise salve slathered over her eyes by her mother as she endured it with some grumbling, half a sausage sandwich in hand and her shirt untucked. Insisting that she was fine, Kara finished her breakfast, drained her coffee and was Flooing to the Ministry early enough to let out the Order member on duty that night. No one else was at the Department of Mysteries yet, so Kara snuck Lucy out before she settled in at her desk.

 

            It was a long day, and towards four o’clock, Kara received an internal memo, the folded piece of paper swooping overhead before landing on her desk. Reading her sister’s familiar handwriting, she parsed the meaning fairly easily, the message a seemingly innocuous invitation to a dinner party after work at Padfoot’s house. Of course, it was her sister’s way of informing her that she needed to go to Grimmauld Place as soon as she clocked out, which last time had meant that Kara had a letter to deliver to Lena.

 

            No overtime in store for her that day, she wrapped up her paperwork, returned her books to their spots in the stacks, and then said goodbye to her team before hurrying up to the Atrium. Exiting to street level, Kara Apparated to Grimmauld Place, landing on the stoop and using the brass knocker. Waiting patiently to be let inside, the day grim and damp, Kara looked around as she hugged her robes to herself, her briefcase clutched in hand as she heard the wailing of the portrait beyond the closed door.

 

            The door was opened by Remus Lupin, a fellow werewolf, whom Kara had been acquainted with during the first war, and befriended this time around. He was a few years older than her and looked it, his sandy hair full of grey and his pale face scarred as he quietly greeted her, letting her inside. She was about to follow him downstairs to the kitchen, but the door to the front sitting room was open, and she saw Dumbledore speaking to J’onn and glancing out into the hallway. He gave the Auror’s arm a quick pat, their murmured conversation wrapping up, and made for the door.

 

            “Miss Danvers, I’m glad I caught you. J’onn? I’ll take that letter, if you please.”

 

            Slipping a letter out of his pocket, J’onn handed it over and made for the door, stepping out into the hallway, moving on with Remus, while Kara was left standing there. She felt a flicker of resentment rise as the old man smiled kindly at her, holding the letter in his hands and then raising it.

 

            “For you, to pass on to our friend.”

 

            “Could we discuss that matter in private for a moment, sir?”

 

            Dipping his head, he stepped out of the doorframe and gestured her inside. It was where they’d had their previous meeting, when Kara had rejected his offer to join the Order and told him to leave Lena out of it, and she hovered just inside the closed door, holding her briefcase, a somewhat surly look on her face as she swallowed thickly.

 

            “Is there something I can assist with, Kara?” he politely inquired, moving towards her to hold out the letter for her to take.

 

            “She’s not safe , sir,” Kara managed to get out, her voice wavering as her eyes stung. “You need to make her come home. Please.”

 

            A shadow of regret passed his face, and Dumbledore softly exhaled. “I’m afraid I can’t do that. You must understand how invaluable the information Lena is passing on to us is. It is-”

 

            “She is invaluable. She’s not some- some disposable thing.”

 

            “Nor do I view her as such,” he calmly insisted. “I understand this is difficult for you-”

 

            “With all due respect, sir, you don’t understand. You don’t know how- how difficult it is for her to be back in that house.”

 

            “Lena has discussed the limits of what she’ll endure. I respect her decision to uphold her own boundaries and won’t ask more of her than she is willing to give. I know she’s expressed her reluctance to receive a Dark Mark-”

 

            “Yes, because it would be traumatising for her to have that on her arm,” Kara hotly interrupted, her eyes stinging. “You don’t know-”

 

            “I know more than you think,” Dumbledore softly countered. “I know of the other mark she has.”

 

            Kara floundered for a moment because she was sure Lena had never told anyone else. It had been hard enough for her to talk about it with Kara, and that was many years after they’d known each other, years after Kara had shamefully dragged up her sleeve, expecting a Dark Mark and finding something just as evil instead. There was no way Lena would have willingly let anyone else know about it.

 

            “She wouldn’t have told you about that.”

 

            “No, she didn’t. But I have been informed of it. You forget that during the first war, she was still suspect, despite not being old enough to have participated in it. That involved interviews by the Auror Department and her arms being inspected. I have my assumptions about where such a mark came from, and I suspect I am correct, so I understand the magnitude of Lena’s sacrifice, to be back at home with her family. It’s no small thing, and I appreciate the risk she’s taking-”

 

            Eyes swimming with tears now, her face flushed pink as she ducked her head, Kara had to clench her jaw to stop her chin from wobbling. “Just not enough to stop it.”

 

            “I’m afraid not. It could be the difference between winning this brewing war or losing it.”

 

            Swallowing thickly, Kara was silent for a moment as she tried not to cry. She’d known it was a long shot anyway, that all the things Lena had told her about Dumbledore were undeniably true, that he’d sacrifice the few for the many. It didn’t make it any easier to bear, though, and she had to take a few deep breaths to retain her control, her anger simmering just below the surface. 

 

            “For the greater good.”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “I just don’t think that makes you a good person ,” she murmured, still looking down.

 

            He didn’t reply, and she lingered for a few moments before making her way to the door. Her hand fell on the doorknob when Dumbledore softly called after her, and she roughly jerked the door open as anger flashed through her.

 

            “Amber, this time, please, Miss Danvers. The message is quite time-sensitive.”

 

 

            It was before dinner when Lena’s ring started to burn on her finger, a quick glance down making her stomach drop at the sign of amber. She hesitated momentarily and quietly swore as she felt torn. Her mother and brother were both home, and Hope would be serving dinner soon, the afternoon dimming towards dusk. It didn’t give her much time, and Lena wondered whether it could wait an hour or two. Amber was time-sensitive but not urgent, but they hadn’t exactly set parameters on what the timeframe was for picking up time-sensitive messages. So far, Lena had been lucky enough to be the one passing messages, for the most part, so it hadn’t complicated her life too much, trying to sneak away from difficult situations. It had all been relatively easy, quite boring, in fact, as was much of spying.

 

            Relegating her retrieval to after dinner, Lena leaned her head back against the rim of the bath, staring up at the ceiling as she lazily trailed her fingers through the steaming water. She could feel the knots in her shoulders and neck, a result of weeks of tension, of walking on eggshells around her family, under constant surveillance. Sitting up, she sighed roughly, scooping water up to wash her face, feeling ragged from a long shift, which had mercifully run into overtime, back-to-back consults as half of the Wizarding World seemed to have a Charms-based injury that needed her opinion on. 

 

            Lena just wanted to sleep; she felt as if she never had time for it these days, or when she did, it wasn’t so restful as it used to be. She’d never slept well, always needing some light to chase away the terror of the dark, but even then, she used to sleep fitfully, waking fairly often from a bad dream, and it wasn’t until she’d slept beside Kara that she was able to find any peace. Seven years of that had been ripped away from her, albeit at her choice, and now there was little comfort to be found in sleeping in her childhood bed, the old house radiating malice as her unconscious mind couldn’t forget that her mother and brother lived within those walls too.

 

            Pulling the plug, she climbed out of the tub and dried her face on a towel, avoiding her reflection in the mirror, and then wrapped the towel around herself before she stepped into her room to get ready for dinner. The room had a chill to it, despite the small fire crackling in the small grate, and she made for the outfit she’d already laid out on the made bed, almost jumping out of her skin at the sound of her brother’s voice coming from behind her.

 

            “You took your time.” 

 

            “Fuck,” she quietly ground out, scowling as she turned around, finding Lex lounging in the armchair set before the fireplace, twirling her wand in his fingers.

 

            “What are you doing in here?” she asked, her heart hammering, running a shaking hand through her damp hair.

 

            “I’m bored, dear Lena. Being cooped up inside is starting to wear on me. I thought you might provide some entertainment, at least, but you spent so long in there, I almost thought you’d drowned,” he drawled, a curl of amusement to his lips.

 

            Climbing to his feet with a sigh, Lex tugged down the cuffs of his dress shirt and smiled at her, still holding her wand, seeming to enjoy the tense set of Lena’s shoulders as she clutched her towel to herself with a look of annoyance on her face.

 

            “Don’t worry, I kept myself amused.”

 

            Her heart skipped a beat as her eyes darted around, taking stock of the orderly room, mind scrambling as she tried to remember if she’d brought anything with her that could incriminate her. But she’d only brought clothes and her Wolfsbane research with her, so there was little for him to hold against her. 

 

            “I can’t imagine there’s anything that interesting in here,” she murmured, turning back to her clothes, gathering up her thin jumper and pants.

 

            “Oh, well, I had a good snoop. That was the only amusing part, though; you’re rather boring. And it was getting quite cold in here with the window open, so I took the liberty of starting a fire for you.”

 

            She felt a lump in her throat, on edge as she licked her lips. “Thank you.”

 

            “I hope those papers in your desk weren’t important,” he continued, his dark eyes watching her intently. “They made excellent kindling.”

 

            She felt the blood run from her face then, unwilling to face him as she felt dread pool in her stomach. Lena knew exactly which papers he was talking about, because she’d already mentally inventoried her belongings, nothing more than clothes and her research. Trying to keep her voice even as her head pulsed with blinding anger, she drew in a few short, sharp breaths as she closed her eyes, trying not to think about how many years’ worth of research that had been. And the worst part was he knew what they were, knew how important they’d been, because they’d spoken of it in the garden when she’d come home, when she’d dismissed her relationship with Kara as little more than a tool to help her research, hell-bent on finding a cure at any cost, merely another ambitious Slytherin, instead of a woman in love.

 

            “It’s fine,” she managed to say, her voice rasping. “Um … I’m going to get changed.”

 

            Hurrying back into her bathroom, she shut the door and let out a shuddering breath, falling back against it as her face rippled with pain. She dropped her clothes and the towel to the flower and then curled in on herself, hands digging into her eyes as she drew in ragged breaths for a moment, anger flushing her cheeks red, the loss of so much of her time and effort burning to cinders in the fireplace beyond, and she knew it wasn’t the end of the world, that she’d read and reread her research a thousand times over the years, remembered enough, knew even more to get by, to rewrite it all, but it was so spiteful that she only felt hurt. But Lena hadn’t expected anything else. Her brother was a spoiled child who’d grown into an entitled man, and his boredom, his fickle moods, had always led to her pain.

 

            Making herself get dressed, she raked damp hair out of her face, folded the towel and then drew in a shaky breath, squaring her shoulders and raising her chin a fraction. Stepping back into her room, she cleared her throat and held her hand out for her wand, raising her eyebrows a fraction as Lex studied her. After a tense moment, wondering if her lack of reaction would anger him further, he stepped forward and handed it over with a smirk, reaching up to give her cheek a quick pat. Lena had to stop herself from flinching, unsure whether the pat was going to be a slap. 

 

            Pocketing her wand, she sank onto the foot of the bed and pulled on her socks before working her feet into her loafers. “We should get down to dinner.”

 

            Nodding, Lex stalked out of her room, and she followed on his heels, shutting the door behind her and walking downstairs, stewing in her bitterness. Taking her seat at the dining table, Lena ate in silence, a hard set to her jaw as she drank her wine and cut into her roast lamb with stiff movements. Her mother and brother said little as well, but when they did, it was only to each other, just the way Lena liked it, but dinner still dragged on, and she hadn’t forgotten about the ring on her finger, her task for later that night.

 

            After dinner, she took a drink in the drawing room over a game of Wizard’s Chess, trying to placate her brother so he might leave her alone after she retired to her rooms. Feeling her exhaustion weighing her down, Lena really did want to go to bed, and if it hadn’t been for the message awaiting her, she would’ve stayed in her room when retiring, but when she finally did so, it was to throw the window open and transform into a raven, swooping across the expansive garden, until she was over the border hedge. Then, she Apparated to her home, finding it dark and empty as she let herself into the still cottage, finding a letter waiting for her, and beside it, a little folded butterfly. 

 

            She opened the butterfly first, finding it blank, no message awaiting her, merely a reminder that she was loved and missed, before refolding it the same way Kara’s nimble fingers had hours ago. Then, Lena opened the sealed letter and quickly read the message, asking her to meet at the cottage tomorrow morning, at nine o’clock. Brow furrowing with confusion, wondering what Dumbledore could possibly want to discuss that warranted a meeting in person instead of sending a message, Lena crumpled the letter and set it aflame before walking back outside and Disapparating.

 

            Flying back up to her open window, she hopped onto her desk and transformed back into herself, lowering herself off the windowsill and quickly changing into her pyjamas. Easing the window shut, Lena safely stowed the little paper butterfly in her desk drawer and then moved over to her bed, climbing beneath the covers and leaving a candle lit as she closed her eyes and willed sleep to come. She had to fetch a potion from her work satchel in the end, knocking it back to help her sleep, to rest properly for her evening shift tomorrow, and for the meeting in the morning.

 

            Rising early, she showered and dressed down, flared jeans and a cotton button-up shirt, intending to lie and say she was painting that day. Now that her mother and brother had been clued into her lie, it was easier for Lena to claim she was there with Sam, ensuring that her brother wouldn’t come through and expose himself, and her mother most likely wouldn’t either. After breakfast, she informed them of her plan for that morning, sipping tea, although she really could’ve used the caffeine to wake her up more. She already felt nervous enough about meeting Dumbledore, though, so she didn’t need to make herself even more jittery.

 

            Taking a pinch of Floo powder in the drawing room, she tossed it into the fireplace and Flooed through to her flat, before taking a pinch of the Floo powder stored on the mantle there and then Flooing through to her cottage. Ducking out of the fireplace, Lena brushed some soot off herself and peered through the gloom to see what the time was. She was ten minutes early and spent that time wisely in the cellar, poring over her simmering Wolfsbane Potion, already working on the next batch of it. When a knock on the door sounded, she wiped her hands on a cloth and left the unbalanced scales with the powdered moondust and little weights, the stairs groaning slightly beneath her footsteps as she felt her stomach twist with unease.

 

            Opening the front door, she found herself staring at the unchanged face of her old Headmaster, looking as old as he ever had, but not any older, despite the years since she’d been at Hogwarts. He had that ever-present faint smile on his lips, layers of embroidered robes donned, and his white hair and beard long and neat, blue eyes twinkling behind half-moon glasses. Lena’s mouth went dry at the sight of him.

 

            “Professor Dumbledore.”

 

            “Healer Luthor,” he politely greeted her, hands clasped behind his back as he raised his eyes to look up at the facade of the ivy-covered cottage. “A charming home. I imagine you are quite eager to return to it.”

 

            “Quite.”

 

            “It’s a pleasant enough day. Shall we walk along the lake while we talk?”

 

            Nodding, Lena stepped outside, shutting the front door behind herself, and folded her arms over her stomach as she narrowed her eyes against the glare of the pale sky. Walking away from the cottage, following the sloping path down towards the sparkling lake, trampling through long grass and the beginnings of early spring buttercups and daisies, they didn’t speak for a long minute, and Lena felt somewhat awkward to be at her home with her old Headmaster.

 

            “Are you well?”

 

            She looked over at him with a mild look of surprise on her face, lips twitching with a wry smile. “Well enough.”

 

            “I spoke with Kara yesterday, while she was picking up my letter for you. She was concerned.”

 

            Expression softening as she looked back towards the lake, Lena’s shoulders slumped slightly. “She worries a lot.”

 

            “It’s good to have someone worry about your safety. Although, I hope you are staying safe. Remember, you’re under no obligation to remain in harm’s way if you feel unsafe.”

 

            “I’m fine, sir. Kara doesn’t like it much, but I can tolerate a lot more than she’d prefer I do.”

 

            “As long as you understand the risks and know your limits.”

 

            “I do.”

 

            He nodded, and they continued to walk in silence for another minute, the lake drawing nearer. Clearing his throat, Dumbledore reached into the pocket of his robe and pulled out a letter, unfolding it to reveal Lena’s handwriting, before he handed it over to her and spoke.

 

            “I imagine you know my desire to meet with you today wasn’t solely out of concern for your safety.”

 

            “I suspected.”

 

            He smiled slightly, casting her an amused glance, before nodding to the letter. “I was interested in your last letter, about your brother’s visit to Little Hangleton. I was hoping you could tell me more.”

 

            Slowing, glancing at her brief summary of where Lex had gone, Lena frowned, her mouth thinning at the corners with bewilderment. “I didn’t see much, sir. All I know is that my brother was asked to visit. Directly by- by him.”

 

            “And he visited a house there?”

 

            “More of a hovel, really,” she shrugged a shoulder, giving him a crooked smile. “I couldn’t go in, of course, but it didn’t look like much. He wasn’t inside for very long, either.”

 

            “Did he see you?”

 

            “I followed him there. I was … a little lax in my approach, but I Apparated a mile away and … caught up with him. I kept my distance then, and he didn’t see me.”  

 

            “I suspect there’s more to your method than that.”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “Do you think you would be able to show me which house he was visiting in particular?”

 

            Hesitating, she nodded, and Dumbledore offered her his arm. A flicker of surprise crossed Lena’s face as she realised he expected her to take him there now, and she apprehensively took his arm and closed her eyes, envisioning the hovel in Little Hangleton and Apparating them both there.

 

            Weak morning sunlight washed over them, and Lena opened her eyes to the hovel she’d observed from the tree just behind them, the place seeming far dingier in the daylight. It was obviously abandoned, with rust on the door hinges, the stones dirty, roof tiles missing, and the windows cracked or glass missing in portions, and she stared at the house for a moment as her hand slid from the crook of Dumbledore’s arm.

 

            “Thank you, Lena. That will be all for now. You’ve been of great assistance,” he said as he turned his face towards her, but kept his eyes trained on the hovel.

 

            Face crumpling with confusion, she wondered what was so special about that place that it warranted him asking her to meet in person, solely for her to take him to it. The place was a dump, and she wanted to question his interest in it, but knew she wouldn’t find any answers forthcoming. Closing her mouth, she nodded at the obvious dismissal and then Apparated to the landing of her flat, letting herself inside with a twitch of her fingers to unlock the door. With her meeting over and done with far quicker than she’d anticipated, Lena spent an hour inside the flat painting the walls, just to lend more authenticity to her lies, paint on her fingers and a general air of dishevelment about her when she Flooed back through a little after ten and walked through the drawing room with her mother’s eyes tracking her as Lillian read that morning’s copy of the newspaper from the sofa.

 

            Showering and making herself lunch alone in the expansive kitchen, watching the House Elf rush about, doing the ironing, prepping dinner, hurriedly making biscuits to go with Lena’s tea, despite Lena’s insistence she didn’t want any, she set the dishes to wash themselves, much to Hope’s panic, and then vanished upstairs to her room. Spending the rest of the afternoon transcribing as much of her research as she could, Lena’s hand was cramping and she was low on ink by the time she had to get ready for work, heading off early and catching Sam in the tearoom as she bought them both coffees and agreed on drinks at The White Wyvern the next time they both had a night off. 

 

            A few days later it was April, and then another full moon on the fourth, lingering in the stairwell off the corridor of the Creature Induced Injuries section of the first floor, hoping to catch a glimpse of Kara through the small window set in the heavy wooden door, but getting paged to an emergency before she could. A few more days after that, word started to spread that Dumbledore had been sacked, and Lena was surprised by that, Andrea running another article in The Daily Prophet and receiving a strongly worded letter from Lena with her concerns for her friend’s safety listed, while St. Mungo’s was rife with the gossip. She heard through those whispers that some Ministry lackey called Umbridge, who’d been teaching there this year, was appointed the new Headmistress, and Lena could feel the shift in things, the way all of these actions were going to have ramifications that would shape the Wizarding World in the coming months, perhaps even longer. 

 

            One such ramification was of her own creation, and rather small in the grand scheme of things, but upsetting nonetheless as she was reminded once more of the consequences of her choices. It came almost two weeks into April, by way of a Charms consult, Lena answering the page on her Cryptex as she parsed the symbols and made her way to the ward, finding a bloody and bruised Alex on a bed. Lena’s stomach lurched, and she took a step forward to assist, an Intern, two Mediwizards and a nurse already dealing with her, and two Aurors hovering nearby with panicked looks on their faces.

 

            At the sight of Lena, Alex was off the bed, pushing the Intern and a Mediwizard away as she lurched unsteadily on her feet, a head wound bleeding freely, and her shredded shirt soaked with blood from a Laceration Curse. Lena knew the words for that one well enough and wondered which Death Eater her sister-in-law had clashed with, knowing only a Slytherin would have been privy to Snape’s dangerous creation. She’d gotten it from Lex all those years ago, when she’d naïvely used it on Winn, and she knew that it would require a few units of a Blood Replenishing Potion to replace what had already bled out of Alex. 

 

            But Alex didn’t seem too bothered by her injuries right then, her expression livid as she made a beeline for Lena, grabbing a fistful of her Healer robes in hand, while she slipped her wand out from her sleeve. Alex had been brought to the first bed on the left of the doors to the ward, and she propelled Lena backwards, pinning her up against the wall and pressing the tip of her wand into Lena’s cheek, while the Intern, Mediwizards and Aurors leapt to defuse the situation, voices overlapping as a panic went through the ward. Lena didn’t even reach for her wand, holding a hand up to stop the nurse, who had voiced their intention to fetch security. 

 

            “You! You stay the fuck away from my sister, do you hear me?” Alex hissed, so much anger in her eyes that Lena felt as if she was missing something. 

 

            She had to step carefully, knowing that any objection might lead to further issues down the line, difficult questions she or Kara couldn’t answer, inconsistencies that would make things even more confusing. Although Lena suspected she wouldn’t be believed anyway, that whatever she said that countered Kara’s version of the truth would be chalked up to another untrustworthy Slytherin lying through their teeth. But still, she wondered what had happened to solidify Alex’s hatred of her. Last time they’d been face-to-face, her sister-in-law had looked wounded, had been upset by Lena’s apparent betrayal, and angry that she’d supposedly harmed Kara, but there was no bewildered hurt this time, only a fierce protectivness that Lena was grateful for, knowing that Alex would die for her sister if needed, and feeling glad that Kara still had people around her who loved her unconditionally.

 

            “You so much as lay a finger on her again and I’ll come up with a curse so fucking painful, they’ll make it the fourth Unforgivable. Do you understand?”

 

            Blinking, Lena swallowed thickly, Alex’s wand tip still pressed into her cheek, and she had to take a moment to quietly clear her throat, make her voice work. “Yes. Now, I’ll have to ask you to get back into bed, or we’ll have no choice but to call security and have you escorted out,” Lena curtly informed her, keeping her voice down, trying not to antagonise Alex, but giving her no reason to think that Lena wasn’t her enemy.

 

            With a scoff, Alex let go of the fistful of Lena’s robes and removed her wand from her cheek, giving her a scathing look of pure hostility as she backed up. A little unsteady on her feet, pale beneath the blood, she stumbled a little, sagging, and Lena reached for her at the same time as the Intern and an Auror. They caught Alex before she could fall, but Alex wrenched herself further backwards, her lip curling as she glared at Lena, who was still reaching for her.

 

            “Get your filthy hands off me,” she spat at her, straightening somewhat with a hand pressed to her abdomen as she panted, yet admirably still had the energy for her animosity, to make Lena’s life difficult as she pointed accusingly at the Healer. “She isn’t coming anywhere near me. I want a new Healer.”

 

            Rubbing her tired eyes, Lena let out a quiet huff and then glanced at the Intern. “Page Healer Arias. I think it would be … best for everyone if she did the consult.”

 

            Without another word, Lena walked out of the ward with her eyes stinging and her cheeks burning with embarrassment, eyes watching her go. And she knew that within the hour, word would already be spreading through the hospital, with people making their assumptions about what she’d done. The only silver lining would be her mother catching wind of it, because even the best actor wouldn’t be able to be so convincing in their hatred of Lena as Alex had been in front of a host of the hospital’s staff, so she would have to believe it was genuine. And that had been the entire point in Lena’s leaving in the first place, except it didn’t feel quite so victorious to have pulled it off so well that someone she’d come to view as a sister believed it too. It would be almost a year before the ramifications of that would be felt, but for now, Lena went to check on a different patient and tried not to let it bother her that her sacrifices had made her a pariah.

Chapter 56

            It was June before Kara knew it, the month flying by, half a year without Lena at her side and a knot of worry in her chest that only worsened with every passing day. They hadn’t seen each other since her moment of worry a week into April, fretting over bruises Lena had already healed, doing what she could to widen that rift between her family and Lena, hating every bit of it, and Lena still hadn’t come home. Kara had to view that as a good thing, that Lena hadn’t been discovered or didn’t feel as if she was in so much danger that she needed to get out, but she also knew that didn’t mean she wasn’t being hurt.  

 

            Every morning, she rose with a pit of dread in her stomach, the uncertainty of Lena’s safety a constant worry at the back of her mind, leaving her with near-permanent bruises beneath her eyes, which only worsened with the toll of each full moon, the transformations at St. Mungo’s wearing her out, even though the Wolfsbane Potion meant she did not harm to herself. Six months without her was almost unthinkable, so much time apart not transpiring since the days when Kara had made so many mistakes and pushed Lena away at every turn. They’d grown past that, and it felt so wrong for them to have missed out on so much time together. There were days when she didn’t think she could cope another hour without seeing her face, hearing her voice, holding her tightly in her arms.

 

            Kara persevered, though, knowing there was nothing she could say or do that would change Lena’s mind. Not even begging Dumbledore to pull her out had worked, and that only stoked Kara’s resentment towards the man even more, although she aided the Order without question, doing what was asked of her, even as she quietly voiced her discontent to her sister and closest friends. They didn’t understand her doubts, and she couldn’t explain them beyond her logical reasoning that no one was infallible, and Dumbledore was as human as the rest of them, just as prone to mistakes and moral ambiguity. But he was their best chance, and she knew it as well as everyone else did, so her grumblings offered nothing more than a way for her to vent some of the tension that plagued her nonstop.

 

            Towards the end of June, she was at the Ministry early, as usual, letting out the night watch and getting a headstart on the menial tasks that filled the first hour of her work, reading missives left on her task, penning replies, fetching a stack of books she wanted to reference and stopping in the breakroom for another coffee and a few biscuits. Chatting with the other Unspeakables as they trickled in, Kara then retreated to her desk, and worked diligently for the next hour, assigning tasks to her Junior Unspeakables, requesting statistics and research she’d assigned a few of the more seasoned Unspeakables at the start of the week, and then managing to get a quick break to return to her desk, where she found an internal memo on her desk. She briefly thought it might be another request to go to Grimmauld Place and pick up a letter Dumbledore had left there for her, but a quick glance at the writing revealed an invitation from Nia to get coffee at ten o’clock.

 

            Glancing at her watch, Kara saw that it was ten to, considered her empty coffee cup and the need to stretch her legs, and fished her coin purse out of her briefcase. Shifting her chair back, she strode through the Time Room and out into the Entrance Chamber and crossed over to the entrance, making her way down the dark passageway to the lift and taking it up to the Atrium as a few familiar faces from other Departments climbed in along the way. A few minutes early, Kara crossed the Atrium to the coffee cart and placed her order before standing off to the side and looking around, waiting for Nia to arrive.

 

            Looking a little frazzled, Nia brusquely greeted her and placed her order, distractedly answering Kara’s questions about her morning with vague comments about some sort of issue in the Spirit Department with a troublesome poltergeist. Kara didn’t think that was what was bothering her friend, but she didn’t press the matter, unsure whether she was aware of her broodiness. Asking if she was going out for drinks for James’ birthday tomorrow, Kara was given another absentminded response and a bewildered smile crossed her face as her name was called, stepping in to thank the barista and take her coffee as she studied Nia for a moment, and couldn’t help but ask, just as the barista called Nia’s name.

 

            “Is everything alright?”

 

            “I just- I had such a bad sleep last night,” Nia grumbled, taking her coffee from the barista working the cart in the Atrium and taking a swig. She rubbed at a tender spot above her eyebrow and gave Kara a worried look. “I kept having a dream about the Hall of Prophecies-”

 

            “Alright, well, keep your voice down,” Kara cautioned her in a hushed voice. “You’re not supposed to know what that is.”

 

            Glancing about with a furrowed look of concern on her face, Kara took her friend by the elbow and led her towards the Fountain of Magical Brethren. Perched on the edge of the fountain, money sparkling in the clear water, she gave Nia a grave look of concentration, a bad feeling in her stomach.

 

            “I have a bad feeling,” Nia quietly confessed, the worry in her dark eyes filling Kara with apprehension.

 

            “In what way?”

 

            “I don’t know. I just- I had a dream. There were Death Eaters down there. They must’ve broken in.”

 

            Considering her words, Kara took a sip of her coffee and tried to silence the nagging thought at the back of her head. “Maybe you’re just … projecting. Too many nights on watch.”

 

            Her words rang false even to her own ears, and Nia slowly shook her head, her mouth thinning. “No, it’s more than that. I’ve never dreamt about it before, and I’ve been taking watch shifts since Dumbledore started this whole thing. I don’t know how to explain it. You know I get these feelings sometimes …”

 

            “I know,” Kara murmured, pressing her lips together for a moment before she let out a breath. “Do you remember that Hogsmeade weekend when we were at school? You had a bad feeling about that, too, and people died. Is it- is it like that?”

 

            A shadow passed over Nia’s face, and she swallowed thickly, looking unsettled, anxious. “Yes. It’s exactly like that.”

 

            Closing her eyes, Kara nudged her wire-rimmed glasses up to rub her eyes, thinking for a moment. “Then you should get word to Dumbledore. It could be important.”

 

            “You’re on watch tonight, aren’t you?”

 

            Kara nodded, feeling a twinge of unease in her chest. “Yeah.”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Nia’s face was grave as she restlessly shifted her weight. “Be careful.”

 

            A faint smile curled the corners of Kara’s mouth, and she nodded again, standing and giving her friend’s arm a quick squeeze. Walking back towards the lifts down to her floor, Kara glanced back to watch as Nia walked over to one of the large fireplaces filling the Atrium and left for Grimmauld Place to report her uneasiness to the Order. It might’ve just been nothing, could’ve been bad dreams as everyone walked around on edge, unsure who to trust, or what to expect, but Kara knew that Nia had strange dreams sometimes, or weird feelings. More than once, some harmless comment from Nia had been strangely prophetic, dismissed as something she’d dreamt of, but no one could be too careful these days, and Kara knew that if she was having prophetic dreams, Dumbledore needed to know. The question was whether he’d do anything about it.

 

            If it was a prophetic dream, the other problem was when the events of it would occur. Nia wasn’t a registered seer, hadn’t created any prophecies that had wound up in the stacks of glowing orbs that Kara had spent many hours carefully dusting with layers of PPE as a Junior Unspeakable, but Kara trusted her intuition. She just didn’t know what the timeframe on her sort of dreams would be, and whether she should be concerned about her watch that night, or perhaps the warning would apply to someone on watch in a week, or next month. Either way, Kara would hold to her guard duty, as she’d promised to do for the Order, and whatever came next, she would deal with in turn.

 

            She fretted all through the rest of the morning, eating her ham sandwich at her desk, eyes nervously flitting around as she switched from coffee to tea, already feeling too jittery for more caffeine. A Junior Unspeakable almost frightened her out of her skin when the young woman intruded on her thoughts, Kara kneeing the underside of her desk, scattering a few pages and books as they leapt off the desk as she blinked herself back to the present, murmuring an apology to the startled employee as she found herself staring at some calculations she’d assigned that morning. Thanking her and picking up her mess with rosy cheeks, Kara shook her head and ran through the calculations with her head in her hand, barely comprehending the complicated arithmetic sequences she’d requested with some urgency, and not even considering how they would work with the theories she’d been primarily focused on researching.

 

            Feeling a headache grow, her temples aching, a heaviness to her eyes, Kara tried to snap herself out of it. She was on watch that night and didn’t have time for stress headaches or worrying about her friend’s dreams. The afternoon passed by slowly, and despite her best attempts, Kara did worry, barely paying attention as she remained at her desk for the remainder of most of her shift, attempting to distract herself by visiting the Death Chamber, posing a few questions to the Unspeakables there working on different projects relating to death, feeling an eerie chill steal over her at the whispering coming from the archway on the dais as she stood at the top of the amphitheatre and eyed it with wary curiosity. She went to make herself another cup of tea then, and when four-thirty rolled around, she went upstairs to go and buy something for her dinner, hiding it in her desk drawer and then pretending to continue her work as the others eventually started to drift off at five o’clock, a few ambitious Unspeakables fitting in some overtime, before they trickled out too.

 

            By six o’clock, Kara was all alone. She made another cup of tea in the communal breakroom, sneaking a few more biscuits, and distracted herself with a book as she remained at her desk. It was fortunate she was located in the Time Room, although that had been the entire purpose of her request to transfer there, because it meant that she didn’t have to go into the Hall of Prophecy, and could sit at her desk for the most part. The sound of so many clocks ticking did start to grate after a while, especially after a full day of the noise, which hadn’t helped her headache, so Kara did spent forty minutes in the blissful silence of the Hall of Prophecy, walking up and down the dimly lit row 97 with no issues, until her stomach started to rumble.

 

            It was twenty-five past eight by that point, and she sat at her desk, a cold cornish pasty and a packet of crisps making up her dinner, and ate slowly, the clock inching towards nine, and then past it, a stillness over the room that was only disrupted by the ticking of the hundreds of clocks crammed into the cavernous space. She made another lap of the rows of orbs and then went back to her desk again, where she had a deck of Exploding Snap cards in her drawer and absentmindedly started to create a house of cards to pass some more time, finding the night watch boring on occasion, cycling through Wizard’s Chess played against herself, Gobstones and reading, walking up and down every single row of the Hall of Prophecy and trying out new origami creatures over the months she’d been taking watch down there. The deck blew up three times, and she’d just finished putting them away, almost midnight now as she eyed her empty mug and thought about making a coffee to take on another lap of the Hall of Prophecy, when the ring on her index finger burned.

 

            Glancing down, Kara did a double-take and felt her stomach lurch at the sight of red. Hesitating a moment, deliberating over the importance of standing her watch or fetching an urgent message for Dumbledore, the latter won out. That had always been Kara’s priority to the Order; her instructions from Dumbledore were quite clear that any information Lena had to pass on, especially anything that required a red alert, was invaluable to their efforts against Voldemort. Still, Kara had a bad feeling about abandoning her post that night, remembering Nia’s warning and wasting a few precious seconds as she remained seated, before she eventually leapt from her seat and took off at a run. Through the Entrance Chamber and in the lift, she ran across the dark wood floors of the Atrium, making for the row of fireplaces for departures and Apparating straight to her cottage.

 

            Inside, the house was dark, a letter was left on the table, and she imagined the paper was still warm from Lena’s handling. She’d barely snatched it up before she was rushing back outside and Apparating to Grimmauld Place, her banging on the door disturbing Walburga Black as the lateness of the night dawned on her. It was still and dark outside, and her watch showed it was only just on the hour, midnight rolling into the next day, and she wondered who, if anyone, was there at that time of night. Mike answered the door, and Kara burst inside, breathless and a little frantic as she rushed towards the staircase leading down to the basement kitchen, almost falling down them in her haste, before she righted herself at the bottom and found a few worried Order members eyeing her. Present were Kelly, Winn, Mad-Eye Moody, Emmeline Vance, and Sirius Black, of course.

 

            “I need to speak with you,” she addressed Moody, thinking he’d be the best bet for getting the letter to Dumbledore as quickly as possible.

 

            They all knew he’d been ousted from Hogwarts, but his whereabouts were unknown to most of the Order, occasionally crossing paths with him at the Black house if they were lucky enough to be around, but otherwise, entirely at his whim. Most of his instructions came through Moody, Shacklebolt of J’onn, and Kara trailed after the grisly Auror, back up the stairs to the empty hallway, and held out the letter with a shaky hand.

 

            “This one’s urgent,” she said in a hushed voice.
