She wasn’t sure what he did with half of the information she gave him, but she had to believe that it was useful.

 

            It was the only thing that kept her there, in that house, enduring the suffocating silences, the constant surveillance, the simmering violence. If not for the purpose she served, she would’ve left the moment she’d stepped foot back inside the walls of the manor house, she would never have even gone back in the first place. Every day, she silently prayed that he’d be arrested, that they’d send him back to Azkaban, and she could give up this pretence, but until then, Lena wouldn’t leave. Not even as she watched her brother smash the bottles of liquor and crystal goblets, kicking chairs over and tearing up pillows. That was nothing, it didn’t even frighten Lena, even if it sent her heart racing, palms clammy, waiting for him to turn that rage on her. But he’d barely laid a finger on her so far.

 

            That didn’t mean she escaped his attention, though, and Lena spent more time than she would’ve liked sitting rigidly in a seat after he’d snagged her attention. Fortunately, she worked long hours and even more overtime, but she did wonder what information she missed out on while she was at St. Mungo’s. It made it difficult for her to pass up any opportunity to be around him when she wasn’t at work. 

 

            Unfortunately, late November, she came home to one of his gatherings, the sounds of voices drifting into the foyer as she shut the front door and glanced towards the shaft of light spilling across the dark floor. At the quiet thud of the door closing, she heard her brother’s voice cut through the conversation, self-satisfied and authoritative. Clearly, he was in a good mood, and Lena felt she should be grateful for that; still, she wished she could just go to bed. Instead, she found her feet moving towards the door, answering his summons.

 

            “That’ll be her now. Lena! Come here.”

 

            Stepping into the open doorway, still in her Healer robes, her satchel slung over a slumped shoulder, Lena raised her eyebrows in a politely enquiring manner, her expression mild as she looked at her brother. Lex was sprawled on the sofa with a goblet of some dark wine, his suit jacket flung over the arm, his shirtsleeves rolled up to show off his Dark Mark. There were a handful of others there too, including two known Death Eaters - Rowle and Yaxley - as well as Veronica Sinclair and Otis and Mercy Graves. The latter two were a sibling duo who had been old lackeys of her brother during their Hogwarts days, but the presence of Veronica Sinclair surprised Lena. So far, despite being at several gatherings at other people’s homes, she hadn’t been extended an invitation to the Luthor manor, her brother’s trust not so freely given, even to those hopefuls wishing for a mark on their arm, too. As a rule, Lex only truly trusted fellow Death Eaters not to run to the Ministry or divulge information if caught.

 

            “Ah, there she is!” her brother exclaimed, letting out a cold laugh. “Our little hero. Come, join us.”

 

            Forcing a thin smile to her face, Lena nodded slightly. “Just give me a moment to get changed.”

 

            He waved a dismissive hand in her direction, and Lena slipped away, hurrying upstairs, foregoing a much-needed shower in favour of haste. He didn’t like to be kept waiting, so she quickly shed her robe and scrubs, changing into comfortable pants and a dark knitted jumper, made for her by Eliza a few years ago. Arranging her hair up, sticking her wand through the bun, Lena fetched some slippers and made her way back downstairs, walking into the living room with casual confidence as she made straight for the newly stocked liquor cabinet.

 

            “Would anyone like a refill?” she said over her shoulder, choosing an open bottle of cherry wine and deducing that’s what her brother had been drinking.

 

            Filling her goblet, she levitated the bottle after her and took a seat at the opposite end of the sofa, nearest to her brother and Veronica, whom she was fairly confident she could handle. The others made her skin crawl, a feeling she couldn’t get past, no matter how much time she spent in their company. Settling in, she nodded to the others as the bottle of wine set itself down on the coffee table, and she cocked her head slightly at Veronica, arching an eyebrow as the woman she despised but befriended out of necessity exhaled a haze of smoke, cigarette sandwiched between her fingers, and mirrored Lena’s expression.

 

            “I didn’t think you’d be home so soon,” Lex filled the silence as Lena took a sip of her wine, trying to make herself unwind, to not seem so stiff. Alcohol would help, given enough of it.

 

            “If I spent any more of my time there, I might as well move in.”

 

            “You’d spend less time there if you only dealt with those worthy of your time.”

 

            Otis let out a quick laugh, giving Lena an eager smile. “Now that’s an idea, huh? Let the Mudbloods heal themselves; we’d have less of them to concern ourselves with then.”

 

            Lips twitching slightly, Lena shrugged dismissively. “Unfortunately, my oath is to all. Even our mother wouldn’t change hospital policy to turn away Muggleborns and beasts.”

 

            “She would if the Dark Lord instructed her to,” Lex quietly corrected her, his eyes flashing to Lena’s face with a hard look.

 

            Conceding to him, Lena smiled a fraction. “Of course. If he asked it of her, I’m sure she would.”

 

            “Well, it’s fortunate for Lena that he hasn’t,” Veronica snidely interjected. “She so enjoys looking after the beasts, don’t you? How’s that little werewolf of yours? I heard from Siobhan that she got very lucky the other month. What a shame.”

 

            “Well, she’s not my werewolf,” Lena cut in, giving her a thin smile as her eyes flashed dangerously, stomach tying itself into knots as she was reminded of September. Word had gotten back to her at one of the gatherings that Siobhan and Rowle had almost cornered her after work one day at the Ministry. Just the news that they’d been unsuccessful had made Lena’s hands shake so badly she’d had to sit on them, pulse racing. As far as she knew, no one else had managed to tail her since. “I was merely … conducting some research.”

 

            “Oh, is that what they call it these days?” Veronica laughed.

 

            She could feel the others watching her, including her brother, and tried to feign nonchalance. With a sip of wine, slouching slightly on the sofa, crossing her legs at the knee as she leaned back against the cushions, Lena gestured with her goblet, rolling her eyes a fraction. “It’s shocking how low the self-esteem of a creature like that can be. But, I made the selfless sacrifice to endure it in the hopes of ridding monsters like that from our society,” Lena affably replied, a smirk on her lips. “Of course, ideally, the only good werewolf would be a dead one, but in a pinch, a cure would do nicely. At least we’d be able to eradicate them for good without losing good Pureblood stock.”

 

            “I’m not sure I’d let even a cured one put their hands on me,” Mercy derisively replied, her face twisting with disgust. “How revolting.”

 

            “That’s where we differ,” Lena shrugged, draining the rest of her glass and reaching for the bottle of wine on the coffee table. “My ambition far outweighs my qualms about those beneath me. A dragon doesn’t concern itself with the opinion of sheep.”

 

            “Ambition? Fat lot of good that’s done you,” Veronica cattily remarked. “If you were so ambitious, you’d already have a mark on your arm.”

 

            “I don’t see one on yours either,” Lex coolly cut in, his eyes dark and unnerving as he fixed his attention on the other woman, his voice hardening. “And as my sister said, a dragon doesn’t concern itself with the opinion of sheep; she’ll bear the Dark Lord’s mark soon enough - sooner than you - so I’d play nicely if I were you, Sinclair.”

 

            Lena’s stomach lurched at the thought of a Dark Mark on her arm, and the rim of the wine bottle clinked against her goblet as her hand trembled slightly before she forced herself to still it. Pouring herself a fresh glass, she set the bottle down and took a big gulp of wine, trying not to show her panic. It was the one thing Lena was opposed to doing for the Order, and she hadn’t even met Voldemort yet to even be anywhere close to receiving one, which had been a cold comfort amidst so much bleakness, but her brother’s words were like ice down her spine. Lena just hoped he was posturing for her sake, but that was unlike Lex; he only cared about how things reflected on him, how things could be used to his advantage. Draining her glass of wine, Lena didn’t speak, didn’t ask him to clarify what he meant, and she was glad that Veronica wisely kept her mouth shut as well, looking disgruntled and a little put out at Lex’s defence of his sister.

 

            It had already been past dinnertime when Lena had arrived home, and while she’d been prepared to go straight to bed without dinner, she hadn’t anticipated staying up until the early hours of the morning, sipping her wine slowly once the initial glass and a half took the edge off her stiffness. Still, she never drank enough to make her lose her senses, to forget to tread carefully. Clever and sharp, she played along with the others, indulging them in their usual tirades, trying to endear herself to her brother, who hated witless dullards almost as much as he hated blood traitors. It was relief when Yaxley left first, and then Veronica not long after, followed by Rowle. A little after two o’clock, Lena considered it safe enough to retreat to bed, leaving her brother in the company of the Graves siblings as she found sleep hard to come by, fretting over the thought of a Dark Mark.

 

            It was a frigid day in early January before there was any merit to his words. In those weeks since that night, Lena had stopped fretting about it too much, too preoccupied with work and spying to devote too much time to the thought of being branded by Lord Voldemort, and she continued to comfort herself with the knowledge that she’d have to at least meet him to make that a possibility. She just hadn’t anticipated that actually happening so soon after Lex had mentioned it, so when she arrived home from work one evening, eating dinner in silence with her mother and brother and then attempting to retire to her room to work on her research, Lena thought nothing of his firm instruction that she was accompanying him somewhere that night. Anticipating drinks at some Death Eater’s house, or even one of his daring trips to The White Wyvern, swaggering about with his his reckless satisfaction, she donned a robe over her clothes and followed her brother out of the manor house and beyond the boundary of the estate, before taking his arm and allowing him to Apparate them to their destination.

 

            She’d never been to the Lestrange’s home before, so she didn’t know her location until Lex informed her of it, standing on the pavement outside the small estate. In the light of a lamppost, she could see the stately Georgian-style home, red bricks, a hipped roof and multi-pane windows. The front door was painted black, and Lex jerked open the wrought-iron gate and started up the short path to it, grasping a silver snake knocker and pounding it against the metal plaque. They waited a few minutes before it was opened, and Lex seemed pleased with himself as Lena kept glancing sideways at him, trying not to betray her brimming anxiety as her breath plumed white before her in the dim light, until Snape opened the door and looked from Lex to Lena. As it happened, neither of them knew the other was a spy for the Order, as Dumbledore intended, and Lena had no cause to believe that he wasn’t just a coward, going back and forth between whichever side had the advantage. Snape’s gaze lingered on her just a moment too long before he glanced back at Lex.

 

            “I don’t recall her receiving an invite, Luthor.”

 

            “Well, perhaps you’re not kept so closely in the Dark Lord’s confidence as you think, Snape. It’s all above board, I can assure you. Unless you’d like to take it up with our master?”

 

            Silent for a moment, blocking the doorway, Snape eventually turned, his dark robes dramatically fanning out around him as he walked back down that hallway, and Lex stepped over the threshold perfectly at ease. With a little more apprehension, Lena followed him inside, out of the bitter cold as the air burned in her lungs. She thought it might snow any day soon, and wondered where they were in the U.K. for it to be so freezing. It was colder than their estate in Ireland, that much she was sure of as she rubbed her hands, trying to get some warmth back into her fingers from her brief stint outside.

 

            Trailing her brother down the wide hallway, the house cold but grandiose, with tall ceilings and moving portraits on the walls, Lena heard low voices drifting towards them, piquing her curiosity. Whatever the gathering was, it seemed as dignified and dour as much of Slytherin House had always composed themselves, and it wasn’t until she was inside a large sitting room, bare of any furniture but a large chair set before a lit fireplace, that Lena felt herself waver slightly. And just like that, the mental fortress of her mind tightened as her whole body went numb, her heart racing in her chest as her blood ran cold. And she knew what it was then, knew who sat in that chair, a place of honour, a place of deference, as only ratified Death Eaters stood stoically gathered in the room.

 

            “My Lord,” Lex submissively called out, ten feet away from the chair, his hands clasped behind his back as he ducked his head slightly.

 

            That in itself was baffling to Lena, whose impression of her brother had always been one of a man self-satisfied and egotistical. She wondered that he was able to behave so deferentially to anyone , but his awestruck fanaticism had always had a certain obsessive quality to it, and she knew that her brother’s ambition would always lead him to claw his way to the top in any manner necessary. She imagined with a bit more power at Voldemort’s behest, Lex would be able to enact many of the brutal pleasures he sought, and could see how he would easily flock to like-minded people to let his ambition be stoked. She’d just never envisioned herself there in the midst of the madness of it all.

 

            And yet, there she was, hanging back, her face shockingly white in the gloom of the room as she curled her hands into tight fists, every inch of her body screaming at her to flee. She didn’t want to be in that room, didn’t want to be around those people. Briefly, Lena considered running, slipping outside, packing her bag and going to Kara. But this had been her goal, to ingratiate herself so completely into Lord Voldemort’s inner circle that she would be privy to the workings of his plans. Her brother had merely been a stepping-stone to that eventuality.

 

            “Alexander,” a whispery voice sounded loud in the stifling silence of the room.

 

            Eyes darting around, panicked and frightened, Lena took in the sight of as many faces as possible, all dressed in Death Eater robes. Perhaps most shocking was the pale face of a teenage boy with platinum blonde hair, looking so young and haggard. Lena felt a sliver of pity for him, correctly deducing that he was Malfoy’s son, and wondered that any parent would let their child that young join. His robe covered his forearms, but she knew there had to have been a mark on his arm to warrant his presence, which begged the question: why was she there?

 

            Returning her attention to the quiet conversation between master and servant, Lena’s throat was dry with fear as she kept trying to swallow. She could barely make herself pay attention to the brief report her brother was giving to the figure sitting in the chair, facing the fire, his features hidden from Lena. She prayed she’d be allowed to remain where she stood for the rest of the night, that she would never have to lay eyes on this man who had inadvertently ruined her life. Unfortunately, she’d barely had that thought before her brother half-turned to her, his stare firm and voice brooking no disobedience as he spoke.

 

            “Lena. Come.”

 

            It took her a moment to make her feet work, almost tripping over them as she walked over to her brother, bizarrely shrinking to his side for comfort, before Lex grabbed her shoulder and shoved her forward. A ripple of chuckles flitted through the assembled Death Eaters, but Lena didn’t have it in her to flush with embarrassment, too fixated on the danger she was in. She was no coward; she wasn’t going to run, not right then, but every nerve was screaming at her to. Still, Lena couldn’t bear herself to look up as she righted herself and warily approached the side of the chair, sinking to her knees with her wide eyes cast down on the floor.

 

            “Closer,” that soft voice ordered her. 

 

            Shuffling closer on her knees, until the hem of a black robe came into sight, Lena’s dark hair fell around her face in a curtain and she balled her fists in her lap and set her jaw to stop her chin from wobbling. She was no coward, but she would’ve been lying to say she wasn’t afraid. But she was brave despite that fear, and that made all the difference as she made her voice work, managing to keep it steady.

 

            “My Lord.”

 

            Cold fingers pressed beneath her chin and urged her head up, and Lena was helpless to obey, raising her eyes to look upon Lord Voldemort for the first time. Despite what she’d heard, looking upon him was something she wasn’t prepared for. His skin was pale white, eyes scarlet in the firelight, and his nose was snake-like slits. The hand that cupped her chin was large, his fingers abnormally long, and there was an endless pit in Lena’s stomach as she stared up at him with repulsed fascination. She schooled her expression into something akin to awe, though, her lips parting slightly as her green eyes widened a fraction, breathing shallowly as she hardly dared to believe the appearance of the wizard before her. It was so much worse than she’d anticipated, and she felt almost certain then that she was staring her death in the face. How was she supposed to get herself out of this if it all went sideways?

 

            “Ah, quite the beauty. And clever, too, your brother assures me.”

 

            Lena didn’t respond, not to agree or disagree, staring at him as her body brimmed with tension. She was as good as dead if she stepped wrongly now, and Lena knew what was coming, her mind scrambling for a way out of it without making the situation worse. And as she stared into his eyes, she tightened her mind against his, his expression unreadable as he kept his gaze locked on hers.

 

            “And are you as loyal as your brother, Lena?”

 

            “Yes, My Lord,” she whispered, her lips barely moving.

 

            “He has informed me you wish to serve our cause.”

 

            “Yes, My Lord. In any way that I can.”

 

            She wasn’t sure what he was looking for, if he was watching for a flicker of doubt, whether he was waiting for the fortress of her mind to buckle so he could see her true thoughts. It was a long minute before he dropped his hand from her chin and reached into the folds of his layered robes to pull out a wand. 

 

            “Hold out your arm.”

 

            Stomach lurching, Lena licked her lips, ducking her head submissively as she scrambled for careful words. “You honour me, My Lord, but … I feel I am undeserving of such an honour.”

 

            “Do you question my judgement?”

 

            His voice didn’t change at all, still as soft and sibilant, but she felt a cold finger of fear trail up her spine. She was kneeling in front of Voldemort, after almost a year of spying to get to that position, and she felt as if she was wasting the opportunity, but couldn’t bear the thought of a Dark Mark on her arm. The thought of having it made Lena want to flay the skin from her bones to be rid of an evil thing like that, and she wondered if she was better off using her newfound chance to try and kill him. He was right in front of her, and he didn’t know how much she despised him, and she had her wand. If she could kill him, which was a big if, she would never make it out alive, but surely that was a worthy sacrifice? Lena wasn’t deluded into thinking she was any sort of hero, but she could be a sacrifice. 

 

            “No, My Lord,” Lena murmured, her brow knitting together as she tried to articulate her reasons well. “It would be an honour to bear your mark, but I don’t believe I have done anything worthy of deserving to bear it. It would feel … undeserved to bear your mark without having done anything to earn it. I should like to prove my worth to you first, on my own merit.”

 

            He surprised her by laughing, the sound uneasily echoed by those others gathered in the room, and Lena felt the fabric of her shirt clinging to her back, her skin prickling with sweat. Hands still curled in her lap, she dared to glance up through her lashes, trying to gauge his expression.

 

            “She has your shrewd charm, Alexander. I find I must agree with your sound logic; your ambition is admirable, as is your pride. I believe we have another fledgling member in our midst, my friends. See that she is given some robes. We shall see about my mark next time we meet.”

 

            “My Lord,” Lena breathlessly whispered, shuffling away on her knees as she kept her eyes down, until she pushed herself unsteadily to her feet and backed away. 

 

            Bumping into her brother, she felt his hand encircle her arm like a vice, and she could feel his anger radiating from him, a quiet but palpable thing. If there was one thing she had faith in, it was her brother’s cunning vindictiveness. It was a small relief that he wouldn’t be able to lash out at her then, that she would be spared the humiliation of an audience, and she quietly hoped that he would see Voldemort’s acceptance of her request as proof that she was right as well. Rooted to the spot, feeling his fingers dig in hard enough to bruise, Lena’s throat was tight, and she didn’t dare speak or move until Voldemort spoke again, one of his long-fingered hands gesturing dismissively.

 

            “See her out; we have important matters to attend to.”

 

            Silently cursing herself, wanting to know what they were discussing, wanting to gather that valuable information and pass it on to Dumbledore, Lena had to swallow her frustration as Lex dragged her to the door and shoved her out into the wide hallway. Shutting the door in her face, his eyes hard and full of anger, Lena was left alone and wondered briefly if she should stay or go. If she’d had an Extendable Ear on her, she might’ve risked staying to eavesdrop, but she didn’t, so she continued down the hallway and out into the bitter night, her breaths coming short and shallow, hanging in the frigid air before her as she stumbled down the short path and onto the street. Disapparating, she went straight home, passing through the gates and walking up the long gravel driveway to the front door, her teeth chattering, her skin crawling, and dread filling her.

 

            Inside, Lena went upstairs to her room and quickly shed every scrap of clothing before getting into the shower, the curtain drawn around the tub as she stood beneath the spray of hot water and scrubbed herself clean. Except, she didn’t feel clean, the thought of his hands on her chin making her shiver with disgust, the scar on her arm itching at her failure to have achieved anything that night. What a wasted opportunity. And yet, she couldn’t have done it. It didn’t matter how badly she felt that she’d failed at her task; having another permanent mark on her skin was more unbearable than the thought of being a failure. Still, she couldn’t stop herself from scrubbing herself clean until it was almost raw, trying to wash away the feeling of being touched by him, scratching at her skin and her scar until livid red lines crisscrossed her body.

 

            When she finally got out, Lena changed into pyjamas and climbed into bed, trying to quiet her mind enough to sleep. It was already late, and she felt exhausted, but couldn’t make her body let go of the tension, until she had to get out of bed and take a potion to knock herself out. It was effective and she sank into sleep with relief, her body going slack as she tried to pretend that everything was fine, that she had nothing to fear from her brother.

 

            The sky was grey when he returned home, smelling of smoke and damp from a night spent outdoors in the middle of winter. Lena didn’t hear him come into her room, a night spent seething over her actions, giving him plenty of time to stew in it, until it was all he could think of when he finally came home. Oblivious to her bedroom flying open, Lena remained fast asleep, thanks to her potion, until Lex flicked his wand at the bed, the covers yanked off her, before he flicked his wand again, and Lena was dragged out of bed by invisible hands as the door rebounded off the wall with a loud bang.

 

            Startled awake by the sound, the sudden cold, and the motion, confused and panicked, Lena was aware that she was being dragged out of bed by her ankles, flailing for a second before she crumpled to the bedroom floor, the back of her head smacking into wooden floorboards. Blinking back black spots as she drew in a wheezing breath, Lena scrambled for her nightstand, for her wand, but her fingers just grazed it before Lex seized her by a fistful of her dark hair and dragged her to her feet. His face was twisted into a snarl, and Lena was suddenly outraged, shoving him away, despite him still having a hand fisted in her hair.

 

            “You little bitch,” he spat at her, jerking her head back so she was forced to look up at him. “You ungrateful , sly cunt. After everything I’ve done for you-”

 

            “I haven’t earned it,” Lena hoarsely cut him off, the back of her head throbbing, her heart pounding in her chest as she tried to reason with him.

 

            “I don’t give a fuck what you think-”

 

            “Well, he certainly seemed to agree with me. Unless you think you know better?”

 

            Blustering for a moment, Lex scoffed, tightening his grip in her hair. “You undermined me.”

 

            “No, I didn’t. What makes you look better - having to ask for your sister to be let into his confidence, or having a sister worthy of being in it? It makes us both look weak if the only reason I have a mark is because my brother had to beg for one for me.”

 

            “It makes us look weak that my Half-Blood sister has a reputation for fucking filthy half-breeds,” he shouted in her face, shaking her sharply.

 

            Lena let out a frayed laugh, baring her teeth slightly as she raised her eyebrows a fraction, almost goading him. “Oh, that’s what this is about, is it? You’re angry because of what other people will think?”

 

            “I’m angry because of what I think. And because my sister is so intent on dragging the Luthor name through the mud. Are you sure of where your loyalties lie? Because you’ve made a poor effort to please the Dark Lord. Even those desperate bottom feeders hanging around have done more to help our cause than you. And yet, you throw the opportunity for power, for status, back in my face? You’re a disgrace .”

 

            He pressed the tip of his wand into her cheek, lips pulled back over his teeth in a snarl, and gave her a contemptuous look. “And now you stand here, feeling brave. I still remember the sounds of your screams; I wonder if you’ll be so brave if I take you back down there and don’t hold back this time. Should we see how much the Cruciatius Curse hurts when I really mean it? Hm?”

 

            There was a struggle for a moment, as he let go of her hair and grabbed a fistful of her pyjamas, Lena trying to pry his hands free, trying to pull away, before she landed a firm slap across his face. She froze, then, pressing her fingers to her lips as she wordlessly stammered, her stomach lurching as her hand tingled. Lex’s head had whipped to the side, and he reached up to touch his reddening cheek, moving slowly as if he couldn’t believe she’d actually hit him. 

 

            “I’m sorry,” she whispered, quickly trying to remediate the situation as she took a step forward. “I didn’t mean to-”

 

            He grabbed her by the throat and squeezed tightly, so the blood congested inside her head, and, much to Lena’s surprise, it was her mother who interjected. Her voice was sharp and firm from the doorway, having risen from bed early to see what all the noise was about.

 

            “Lex. Enough.”

 

            Without turning to look at Lillian, he let Lena go, roughly shoving her away. Stumbling, Lena hit the bed frame and then the nightstand when she tried to right herself, knocking off an unlit candle, her wand rolling off and clattering to the floor. Bracing her hands against her mattress, she hunched over slightly, drawing in ragged breaths as she tried to steady herself. Running a hand over the bald pate of his head and his neatly trimmed beard, Lex eyed her darkly and then walked over to her, grabbing her chin and forcing her head aside to look at him.

 

            “You’d better show your worth, and soon . The Dark Lord isn’t prone to second chances, and neither am I,” he warned her. “I’d start by finding that creature and putting her down like a dog, if I were you.”

 

            Letting go of her, he walked towards the door, where their mother watched with blank indifference, and slammed the bedroom door shut behind him. Running a shaky hand over her clammy face, Lena turned and sank heavily onto the edge of the mattress. It would’ve been wise to run then, she thought, but Lena knew she’d just bought herself some time. Not a lot, but perhaps enough to stretch out a few more weeks before anything drastic needed to be done. No matter what her brother suggested, she could never even pretend to go after Kara, not wanting other to get involved, to potentially assist, but she knew she would need something to prove herself, to show her value to Lord Voldemort, if she was to infiltrate his inner circle and relay useful information back to the Order. Lena just didn’t want to compromise herself in the process, already in such a morally ambiguous area that the thought of going too far frightened her. And she knew she could never do anything that would make her unredeemable to Kara and her family, but Lena was left with the sinking feeling that, before she was done, they would think worse of her than they already did.

Chapter 58

            The end of February was bitterly cold, snow and frost riming the grass, sedge and heather as a werewolf with sandy colouring peeking through the grey barrelled through the Cairngorms under the light of a full moon. She wasn’t alone, running with a pack as they chased down a red deer across the moorland, howls filling the early hours of the morning as they ran wild through the national park. They were hunting across snow-covered hills when the deer was caught, vivid red looking black in the darkness as blood spilt across white, teeth and claws tearing through the hide and into flesh. Mindless of what she was doing, the sandy-haired werewolf joined in, snapping back at others in the pack as they fought over food, feral and possessive, until they left behind a carcass and continued to stalk through the snow and heather until the sun started to rise across the bleak, wintry landscape.

 

            Kara woke with a splitting headache, her cheek pressed against something cold . She didn’t know where she was, momentarily dazed by the pain filling her body as her heart pounded in her ears. It took her a moment to push herself up, the febrile tension of her body leaving her arms shaky as she breathed in the earthy scent and pushed herself up off the snow. Tasting blood in her mouth, she spat it into the grass, red spattering over the crust of snow, and Kara looked down at herself, her body scraped down to something painfully thin over the last couple of months, and found something dark coating her chest as she pushed herself to her knees, her mind still a little bleary, her vision making it hard to make out anything in particular. 

 

            In the gloom of dawn, her breath pluming before her in the frigid air, Kara weakly got to her feet, the motion making her head swim, clenching her teeth as she felt bile claw up the back of her throat. Eyes narrowed as she tried her hardest to see past her poor vision, she flexed her fingers, feeling something dried on her palms, the tang of copper strong to her sensitive nose. Naked and shivering, she didn’t have her wand on her to Apparate, and was forced to try and find her way blindly in the slowly brightening day, her toes frozen and feet numb as she staggered over heather and gorse, knowing that she had to be somewhere near where they’d all transformed the night before. Even in her state, there was always a sliver of awareness that led her back home; in this case, home was a bothy they’d all crammed into for the winter.

 

            She’d originally started out in Wales, taking over from Remus by seeking out the group hiding out in an abandoned mine in the Brecon Beacons. That hadn’t even lasted a month, the dampness of the old coal mine in the middle of December making a miserable time of it, all of them fighting over blankets and food, mistrust rife throughout as they’d refused to warm to her. Kara wasn’t sure whether it was their fear over her wand, many of the werewolves previously ordinary Muggles, who’d been warned away from wizarding folk, or her appearance, too clean and well-fed to have been suffering. They didn’t know the years it had taken for her to make a stable life for herself, to be healthy, despite the toll on her body every month. Even with the scars crisscrossing her skin, Kara wasn’t able to ingratiate herself with the group and had to move on.

 

            Conferring with Dumbledore in his office over more tea, looking a little dishevelled, already thinner, it was decided that Scotland would be their next best bet. This time, Kara had left her wand at Alex’s house, on the outskirts of Inverness, on the fringes of the Cairngorms, too, so close and yet so far away from where Kara had wound up. She’d had to walk almost ninety miles over a few days before she’d found them and tentatively asked to join them, the scars on her face, the dirt and dishevelment, the lean edge of hunger, speaking for themselves. The scruffy pair she’d found had taken her back to the bothy, miles to the east of where she’d been walking, and she’d remained there since the start of January, a dozen of them holed up against the cold. So far, Kara hadn’t had much luck swaying their opinion to the Order’s cause, but she was still trying.

 

            Walking two miles through the wintry moorland, stark naked as the sky brightened, hunger raking her stomach, Kara was able to make out a patch of coniferous woodland, a dark stain against the austere hills. She felt a prickle of relief flash through her, sure that it was the woodland that held the bothy. Another mile, and she was stepping into the chill shadows of the trees, frosted pine needles forming a soft carpet underfoot, and Kara moved through the trees until she found a cloak hanging from a branch, pine needles caught in the damp wool. Pulling it on over herself, she let out a hoarse cry of relief, wanting to sink to the ground right there, curl into a ball and huddle for warmth, but she kept going. The robe smelled of smoke and sweat, but she didn’t care; anything better than the biting cold of being exposed, and she was grateful for whoever had left it out, hoping they’d already made it back to the bothy and found their clothes, else she was sure that would cause a fight.

 

            Wrapped tightly in the cloak, Kara continued to stumble through the Scots pines until she caught the smell of smoke on the wind, turning her face towards it with some urgency now, relief and exhaustion giving her a desperate edge. Walking into the clearing five minutes later, she caught sight of Manchester Black sitting on a log in a beam of weak sunlight, smoking a hand-rolled cigarette, an enamel cup full of tea at his feet. He gave her a quick grin, confident and at ease, seeming none the worse for wear, despite the ordeal of the full moon. He was relatively new, only a werewolf for the last two years, so his face showed minimal signs of premature ageing, and only one set of scars, claw marks scoring his right cheek. Despite that, he’d managed to make something of a leader of himself, the others flocking to him for decisions, for approval and acceptance, exuding a natural charm.

 

            “Linda,” he mumbled around his cigarette, giving her a nod. “You look rough; where’d you end up?”

 

            “A few miles east.”

 

            “Ah, got left behind by the rabble? Don’t worry, you haven’t missed breakfast, but I’d get warmed up first if I were you, unless you want to lose a couple of toes.”

 

            He gave her a wink, and a ghost of a smile touched Kara’s lips as she nodded, the cloak wrapped around herself like a blanket, and made for the door of the bothy. The bottom third of it was pale stone, and the rest was wooden slats, the chimney of a wood burner sticking through the roof with a trickle of smoke trailing from it. Stepping inside, she found it mercifully warm, compared to outside, and took in the cramped quarters as she picked her way over sleeping figures in dirty sleeping bags on the hard, dirt floor. There were two sets of triple bunks against one wall, tattered curtains covering grimy windows as weak sunlight struggled to get in, illuminating the lucky few who’d managed to get proper beds, even if the wooden slats were no more comfortable than the ground. After a black eye during her first week there, Kara had decided it wasn’t worth fighting over the bunks and had relegated herself to the floor, stretching out with a sleeping bag wherever she’d fit.

 

            Knackered, she wished for nothing but the same right then, but sleep would have to wait a little while, heeding Manchester’s advice and getting warmed up first. They had a barrel of water they all helped haul buckets into from a nearby stream, and Kara filled an empty saucepan with some before grabbing her old school backpack and walking back outside. Heading away from the bothy, Kara crouched at the base of a tree and rummaged through her bag for clothes and her glasses, setting the latter aside and finding a ratty towel that had seen better days. With a bit of wandless magic, she heated the pot of water and dipped a corner of the towel into it, before she started on her feet. The skin was a waxy-looking white beneath the dirt, where the cold had been so intense that it had restricted the blood flow. It hurt, and Kara worked quickly, drying them off with the dry end of the towel, before she climbed to her feet and worked on her underwear, a pair of socks and some boots.

 

            Washing her face next, hot water sluicing down her chin and neck, running red from the blood of the deer she remembered eating, it washed off some of the blood on her palms too, the tip of Kara’s nose stinging from the heat. Slipping her glasses on, everything came into focus, and Kara was able to work with more precision, forced to shed the stolen cloak as her skin rippled with goosebumps while she wiped crusted blood off her chest. Finishing up, she emptied the pot over her hands and scrubbed them clean, before shaking out a pair of thermal tights, kicking off her boots and working her legs into them. Flannel pyjama pants followed over them, and then a long-sleeved top, an old knitted jumper from her Hogwarts days, now worn out of shape, and a fleece layered over each other, before she zipped a down-filled coat over the top. Layering another pair of socks over her bruised feet, Kara put her boots back on and rubbed some warmth back into her hands, still shivering as the icy air burned her lungs.

 

            Packing everything back into her bag, Kara picked up the pot and the cloak and made her way back to the bothy, pine needles crunching underfoot as her breath hung heavily in the air, the temperature so low that she still wasn’t warm, even in all her layers. Stepping back into the cramped building, damp and smoky, Kara made for the wood burner, where a few who weren’t asleep huddled, and she joined them there, dropping her bag and crouching in front of the open door, tasting woodsmoke past the stale blood. One of the men, only referred to as Hat, passed her a cup with some gritty coffee powder at the bottom, and Kara thanked him as she reached for the kettle, which was still hot. Filling her cup, she waited for the coffee to dissolve and took a sip, rinsing her mouth before swallowing.

 

            Breakfast was a few sausages sitting in a pan as they cooled in their fat, wedged in a slice of bread that was starting to grow mouldy. Kara couldn’t choose to be picky, removing the bad pieces and wolfing down her meal before she finished her coffee and got to her feet. A woman called Pamela was getting up already, rubbing her eyes, and Kara took her spot, crawling onto the top bunk as her bruised body protested, the space so narrow that there was barely room between the bunk and the rafters, and she finally lay down with a sigh, too tired to wallow in the misery of it all.

 

            Wishing for a potion, wishing she was in her bed, whether that was her bed at her home with Lena, or at her mother’s, in her childhood bed, Kara shivered inside her sleeping bag as she shut her eyes and eagerly waited for sleep to come. It didn’t take long at all, her body so drained that her mind was happy to give in to it, casting her into oblivion as the aches and pains, the collection of bruises, scrapes and scratches, faded to nothing. Sleeping through the rest of the morning, she woke in the evening to someone grabbing her leg over the sleeping bag, almost headbutting the beam overhead as she jerked awake, bleary-eyed and confused, her body stiff from the cold.

 

            “Lee,” Manchester said, giving her leg another shake. “You’re going with Mo to fetch supplies.”

 

            Humming, rubbing the bridge of her nose, Kara kicked her way out of the sleeping bag and slithered out of the bunk, boots thumping hard on the packed ground of the bothy. Raking a hand through her tangled hair, old blood dried there, leaves and pieces of bark snagged in her wayward curls, Kara glanced at the other man, his old face so scarred that his face was permanently wrenched in a glowering sneer. He wasn’t so bad, though, a little grumpy but made of stern stuff, and more importantly, a wizard. A wizard with a wand.

 

            She’d been unable to hide that she was a witch, not wanting to embroil herself in too many lies that she might lose track of them, but she’d made the excuse that she’d never had a wand or any formal education, turned too young. That seemed to work well enough, and Mo had taken pity on her, letting her use his wand sometimes as he taught her the words for spells he assumed she’d never learnt. Of course, whenever she asked to use his wand, it was usually because the ring on her finger had turned a different shade, and more than once, she’d had to sneak out when they were sleeping, stealing the man’s wand and hoping no one would notice she was gone. 

 

            They all came and went, though, sometimes venturing miles away, slipping into Muggle towns to steal warmer clothes from washing lines when the cold days were clear enough for it, filling pockets and bags with food from their shops, rifling through the dumpsters behind them for any out-of-date produce. Kara was usually good at making use of her escapades with the borrowed wand, fetching Lena’s letters and delivering them to Dumbledore directly as she used a secret passageway into the castle and then fetched as much food from the kitchens as she could bear. Suspicious but grateful, no one ever questioned where the fresh pasties, sandwiches, biscuits, tarts and scones came from, just glad to have something that wasn’t from a can. Although a couple of the Muggles did debate over whether she’d robbed a Gregg’s.

 

            Hat was a wizard too, but he didn’t trust her at all, watchful and quiet, so Kara didn’t try to borrow his wand, didn’t try to convince him of how much better things would be if they joined the Order, instead of Voldemort. He already knew what it was like for them, and Kara wasn’t sure how old he was when he’d been turned, but she knew the years wouldn’t have been kind to him since then. One thing she did know was she’d been a werewolf for the longest out of them all, although there were a couple of older teenagers amongst them. One was an eighteen-year-old boy who’d been changed by Greyback, and the other a fifteen-year-old Muggle girl from Glasgow who’d been missing for eight months. Kara pitied them both more than any of the others, knowing how difficult it was to be cursed so young. And she kept thinking of Lena, and the cure she’d always vowed to find. For the sake of these kids, Kara hoped she’d do it one day. For the sake of herself, too.

 

            Following Mo out of the bothy, Kara let him Apparate them to an alleyway in the middle of Aberdeen, miles east of the Cairngorms. She walked with him into the city centre and then they split up, Kara walking towards some of the wealthier streets as the sky darkened, the evening cold as heavy clouds rolled in. Bieldside offered plenty of cars parked along the roads, and it was a simple thing, even without a wand, for Kara to break into them, raiding the centre consoles, dashboards, doors and the gaps between the seats for spare change. Going from car to car, locking them up after herself, she filched enough to fill her pockets with gold Muggle coins, smaller than Galleons but useful in the brightly lit supermarkets she used them in. Filling a trolley with the cheapest options, she bought tins of sausages in beans, rashers of bacon, boxes of oats, long-life milk and bags of elbow pasta. They didn’t have the luxury of being fussy, or very nutritious either, and she tallied the amount in her head against the coins she’d stolen, getting as much as she could, tins of coffee and boxes of tea bags, sachets of soup, which only needed water added to them, anything that would be filling, anything to get them all through the next week. 

 

            At the till, she hovered nervously, the cashier casting furtive glances at her, taking in the mess of her hair, her poorly washed face, the dirt beneath her nails when she counted out coins onto the counter, leaving a pile in front of the bewildered young woman. Everything bagged up, Kara thanked the woman and heaved her shopping into her hands, tottering out of the grocery store and into the rain that had started up. Head ducked down, she hurried through the streets, back to the alleyway, where Mo was huddled in his long coat, scowling as he stamped his feet to keep them warm.

 

            “You took your bloody time.”

 

            “Sorry,” she breathlessly apologised, letting him take half of the bags from her. “I got loads, though. Look, I even got this for you.”

 

            She pulled a pack of mostly full cigarettes from her coat pocket and tossed them to him. He opened it and counted how many were inside, before grunting slightly, which she took as thanks. He pocketed them and picked up the bags he’d filled with stolen produce, using magic to Accio more expensive items from various stores around town, like cheap whiskey at the off-licence, ripe apples and oranges from a greengrocer with crates of produce outside, new pairs of socks and gloves from a department store, all of it shoved into a bag so small that no one would accuse him of shoplifting with it. 

 

            “We should get back.”

 

            He offered her his arm and Disapparated them away from Aberdeen, back to the bothy. Half of their group was gathered outside, a campfire keeping them warm as they threw more wood onto the pile, the smell of smoke working into everyone’s hair and clothes. A couple of the more eager ones leapt to their feet to see what they’d nicked, including Manchester, and they carried their handfuls of plastic bags into the bothy, dumping them on the floor. They had a battered cooler charmed to stay cold, and Kara started handing things out of the bags to go in there: the packages of cheap bacon, cheap cuts of meat, loaves of bread. Everything else was just piled in the corner, an assortment of tins, boxes and sachets stacked or wedged in alongside the remains of their last trip.

 

            Mo shared a couple of the cigarettes with Manchester, who then had to break up a fight between two of the hotheaded young men, one of them already sporting a bloody nose as they fought over a little bar of Galaxy chocolate Mo had pinched. With a few shoves and a sharp order, he had everything in hand, putting a cigarette between his lips as he turned his attention to Kara.

 

            “Anything secret hidden in your pockets, Lee?” Manchester asked, raising his eyebrows.

 

            “No,” Kara mumbled, her brows furrowing together.

 

            “You’re a funny one, you are,” he remarked with a smile. “I’d never have taken you for being so good at stealing. Go on then, this is yours.”

 

            He tossed her the Galaxy, and Kara hesitated, opening the packaging and breaking off a piece. The chocolate melted on her tongue, the sweetness welcomed after a draining day, and she broke off two more pieces, tossing one each to the two young men, before she handed the rest of it back to Manchester. He cocked his head to the side, watching her with curiosity, but didn’t say anything, just tossed the rest of the chocolate bar to Pamela. Others were roused from their beds to see what else had been brought, someone eagerly choosing something for dinner, separating ingredients from the pile. They were all hungry, but they knew how to ration their food, even if they fought over what they had, some of them nasty and brutish as they took rations from others. Most of them weren’t so selfish as to hoard things for themselves, but then, they hadn’t been outcasts from society for so long. Kara couldn’t blame those who’d had to fight over scraps for years when she’d only been subjected to it for a couple of months.

 

            Still, the weight had dropped from her, not enough food to go around, too much walking as they traipsed around the national park, sometimes a couple of them going off to a different bothy when things got too heated, division amongst themselves. Kara had stuck to Manchester’s side, doing whatever he planned, knowing he was her best bet for getting them all to work together, to organise and hopefully side with the Order. There had been several discussions so far, and he’d listened to her make her case for why it would benefit them all to side with Dumbledore, but so far, he’d remained noncommittal, and Kara had been left trying to pretend like that wasn’t her sole purpose for being there. A part of her made her think he suspected that’s why she was there, so she held true to the lie that she was just another outcast werewolf with no job prospects, no family, nothing but a battered backpack of belongings to her name and a Ministry stipend.

 

            Sitting around the campfire with the others, she sipped cheap whiskey from an old soup can, repurposed as a cup, and let the smell of smoke infuse her hair and clothes, nodding at a few others who roused themselves for dinner. In a slightly rusted cauldron, a woman in her sixties, who Kara couldn’t remember the name of, made a dinner of tinned tomatoes and fried bacon, slices of bread doled out to mop up the hot meal, and then most of them turned in early, nursing aches and pains and debilitating fatigue. There was the usual bickering over bunks, and Kara snagged a sleeping bag and took a spot in the middle of the room and away from the door, having learnt that it was best to stay away from the walls and where any draughts of air could come inside. Stretching out, worming her way into the sleeping bag, Kara felt bone tired as she listened to the rustling sounds of others getting ready for bed. It was so cold that she slept in her coat, although she took off her boots and tucked her glasses safely inside them, leaving them at her feet. 

 

            There was a sense of peace and camaraderie in the group that she found odd, that notion that she wasn’t alone in her suffering, that they’d all endured the same full moon, and they were all there together, tucked inside the bothy, outcasts of society, whether that was Muggle or magic. Listening to the sounds of rumbling snores from a couple of the others, the deep, even breaths of the others, Kara’s eyes quickly grew heavy, and she fell asleep in the company of her own kind, feeling sorry for them all and wishing the full moons were kinder to them. She’d come to know the shifting moods of the motley gang, who was petulant, who was helpful, who was quick to anger and who was too cowardly to pick a fight, and for all their flaws, Kara couldn’t see any of them as monsters. One of the most scarred of their pack, she only saw herself in them all, even in the ones who were vocal with their rage, who were selfish and churlish, and blamed everything but themselves. They were, all of them, victims of a terrible condition, and there were parts of her in all of them, and while she didn’t like them very much, Kara empathised with them so greatly that she couldn’t blame a single one of them for anything. Not even when they stole, not even those who’d infected each other, so much of it out of their control, a matter of their circumstances.

 

            Sleeping peacefully throughout the night, she woke relatively early, the sky still grey outside, although she knew it must’ve been almost seven o’clock, working herself free of the sleeping bag and putting her glasses and boots on. Kara slipped outside and grabbed two empty plastic buckets and made for the nearest stream, the cold like a slap in the face as she crunched pine needles underfoot, rounding coniferous trees as she followed the now-familiar route to fetch more water. They all had little to do, but what chores they did have were shared amongst them, and Kara didn’t want to give them any reason to shun her from the group, and it couldn’t hurt to gain the support of the others too, in her crusade to convince Manchester.

 

            Hauling two brimming buckets back, trying to slosh as little as possible over the sides, Kara set them outside the door as she nodded to a couple of early risers, already gathering around a freshly lit campfire. Someone had a kettle boiling over it, and Kara accepted a cup of tea when it was ready, the milk powder clumping together slightly, but fine all the same as it warmed her belly. It was a cloudy day, the sky white overhead, and Kara was content to sit by the fire, striking up conversation as they all stayed warm, someone producing a coin and flipped it as everyone bet heads of tails, a few more coming out, wrapped in pilled blankets, yawning in mismatched clothes and wellies, taking cups of tea or coffee as they were offered up. Kara liked how, even though they all clashed, and no one seemed to fit right together, they all looked after one another. She thought it was a shame that other people didn’t see that in them, that the only traits attributed to werewolves were ones of violence and anger. But as someone started mixing up porridge in a clean pot, and Hat repaired the broken zipper on someone’s sleeping bag, and Mo tried teaching the teenage boy how to play chess, it all felt so ordinary. Nothing was frightening about any of them.

 

            A couple of weeks only made Kara more sympathetic with their plights, and frustrated as she seemed to get nowhere with Manchester. He made good counter-arguments to her points, and Kara didn’t know how to convince him that Voldemort wasn’t going to give him the respect that he wanted, the equality he deserved. If she knew anything, it was that people who believed in the same ideology as he and his Death Eaters weren’t likely to believe that werewolves, at the very bottom of the social ladder, should be elevated in society. But Manchester didn’t seem to believe her that much, had explained that Fenrir Greyback had visited a couple of times, had made promises to them that Kara knew he wouldn’t keep, and while Manchester didn’t seem to care so much for either side, he stopped to listen to a werewolf like Greyback. She supposed someone who was undeniably a monster, every bad thing said about their kind rolled into one beastly person, was a more reliable reflection of what society thought of their kind than a well-spoken former witch, who was still pretty, even with her scars.

 

            Kara didn’t tire of her effort, though, making a little more headway there than she had in Wales, so she stayed and helped, stealing away early hours one morning with Mo’s wand to deliver a message to Dumbledore and returning with another armful of bundles wrapped in tea towels. She’d had to ask the House Elves to give her ones without a Hogwarts insignia on them, not wanting to tip anyone off, and she was rather popular at breakfast as muffins, quiches, croissants and danishes were wolfed down. She caught a few suspicious glances, curious and a little mistrustful, but no one openly questioned her after she shrugged off the initial ones, and Kara hoped the pastries would do more good than harm for her reputation amongst them all.

 

            By the next full moon, their numbers fluctuated a little, the Muggle girl heading back to Glasgow, homesick and confident she’d be able to manage it herself, while a spat between a few members of the group led to a couple who’d shacked up right before Kara arrived decided to leave and find somewhere else. Kara informed them of the group hiding out in the Brecon Beacons and suggested they seek community there, if they weren’t going to stay, so their numbers were down three when they all shed their clothes and walked through the patch of woodland as the full moon rose. The evening was filled with the sounds of their screams of agony, which petered out into howls and then the yips and growls of werewolves sniffing each other out in the dark, some playful, some irate, others angry. A couple snapped at each other’s muzzles, until the larger werewolf with a little more black to its pelt got its teeth around the other’s throat, eliciting a whine, and a few others joined in on the scrap, clawing at each other and growling as muzzles pulled back over sharp fangs. But they were easily distracted too, snapped out of animalistic behaviour as they gave in to the hunt, chasing after each other, wild moorland stretching around them for miles and miles.

 

            The snow had petered out over the course of the month, so when Kara came to, transforming back into her human form with a groan of pain, she was spared the threat of frostbite as she rose shivering from the mud. Rain pelted her bare skin, hard and stinging against the already tender flesh, and it felt like it was being flayed from her body. A storm covered the sky overhead, lightning flashing as thunder stuttered and rumbled, and Kara wiped wet hair out of her face as rain sluiced down her body. It made the moorland marshy and muddy as she staggered through it, feet sinking into heather and moss as she forged onwards, trying to follow the cardinal directions based on which way the sun was rising to make her way back to the bothy. They’d had to move to a different one recently, a little smaller but more remote. They were right near a loch, fewer trees for cover there, but a beautiful, if a little austere, landscape surrounded them as they nestled in the heart of the Cairngorms. It took Kara an hour of weakly trampling through the sedge, grass and heather before she arrived back, shivering from the rain that turned her skin red, arms crossed over her chest, shoulders stiff as she hunched against it, and mud splattered up to her thighs. It wasn’t as cold as last month, though, even though she was soaked through and could feel the ache in her joints and bones, and she arrived back at the bothy as the sun made it over the horizon.

 

            Washing in the loch, rinsing away the mud as the water made her body hurt, the intensity of the cold painful, Kara nodded to a few of the others as they came staggering back, in a similar shape to her. All of them were thin and dirty, and Kara eagerly changed into her clothes, warm but filthy, despite her attempt to wash as few items in the loch. Warmer, she made her way inside and practically collapsed to the floor. There were no bunks there, and the wood burner couldn’t be used much, very little to burn in the vicinity of the bothy, but someone had started a fire without wood; a little bit of magic afforded them in the wake of the full moon. Heavy eyes closing as her head pounded, Kara shivered in her sleeping bag until her body heat warmed her through, and only then did she sleep. Until a commotion woke her far too soon, no more than an hour or two passed, as she peeled reluctant eyelids open and sat up.

 

            Noticing that she was awake, Manchester beckoned for her, and Kara frowned through a near-sighted squint, struggling out of the sleeping bag and stepping into her boots as she shoved glasses onto her face. Stepping around sleeping figures, she moved towards the door as Manchester stepped through and held it open for her, rain-swollen wood scraping over the ground as she pushed it shut behind herself, listening to him explain.

 

            “Pamela found a hiker last night.”

 

            Stomach lurching, Kara blinked in surprise, raising her eyebrows. “Did she- I mean … are they okay?”

 

            His mouth thinned, and he shook his head, running a hand over his unkempt facial hair. “Even if she hadn’t carved him to bits, we don’t have enough Dittany or silver left to close up wounds that big. He was already dead when she transformed back, anyway.”

 

            “Oh.”

            

            “We need to hide the body.”

 

            A flicker of surprise crossed Kara’s face as she quickly pieced together why he’d gestured for her to follow him once he’d seen she was awake. Manchester stared at her, taking in the way her face changed, blue eyes widening a fraction behind grimy lenses, blonde brows rising slightly, lips parting. 

 

            “We protect our own,” he reminded her.

 

            Kara swallowed whatever judgement she felt, whatever moral failing she saw in this, covering up a crime, and Manchester clapped her on her shoulder, the gesture weak, both of them tired from the full moon, no potions to prop them up and fill them with energy. It was fortunate they were both still standing, if a little shakily on unsteady legs, but Kara wasn’t sure she had the energy to bury someone. Still, she nodded, a hollow feeling in her chest, and curled her hands into fists as she followed on his heels. Approaching the edge of the loch, she saw Hat standing on the shore, while Pamela stood shin-deep in the icy waters, covered in mud and blood. When she turned, Kara saw it sheeted down her chin, neck and chest, dried on and dark against her pale skin. Stomach lurching, she fought a wince and felt pity for the other woman. She didn’t know her that well, but she was good with animals, usually a menagerie of creatures in hand, whether it was a bird perched on her shoulder or a stoat or mouse cupped in her palms. It was frightening what the full moon could do to a person.

 

            Looking away, swallowing thickly, Kara followed Manchester, walking miles through the moorland again, sweating and pale-faced, dark hollows beneath her eyes as she wished she were still asleep. It was only mid-morning, and the sheeting rain soaking them through, until Kara’s flannel pyjama pants were plastered to the thermals underneath, mud in her boots, and rain down the back of her coat. Uncomplaining, she stomped onwards, her mind focusing on things like trench foot and a late breakfast as she tried not to think about what she was about to do. Manchester seemed to know the area well enough to know approximately where the body was, the ground sloping uphill through rocky hills, until a sharp whistle faintly cut through the din of rain and wind. Mo was waving to get their attention, directing them to it, and they changed their trajectory, walking along a steep path before they joined the old man, who was smoking a damp cigarette.

 

            “That way,” he jerked his thumb over his shoulder. “I’ll join you shortly.”

 

            Manchester forged onwards, and Kara followed in his footsteps, rain stinging her reddened cheeks as she tasted it in her mouth. A couple of minutes later, she could make out a body sprawled awkwardly in a patch of grass, mud and blood mingling beneath it as the rain made a puddle. Approaching, feeling nauseous, although that could’ve been from the full moon anyway, Kara glanced down at the face of a man in his early forties, eyes vacant, throat torn out. He had a pack on his back, and the shell of his windbreaker was slashed to bits by sharp claws. Dismay caved Kara’s shoulders as she stared down at the dead man.

 

            “Get his pack,” Manchester told her.

 

            Glancing at him in shock, aghast, Kara baulked at the prospect of robbing a corpse, but she knew she couldn’t make a sound enough argument to protest. They needed supplies, and they were about to bury him in the middle of nowhere, so he wouldn’t need them. Swallowing bile, Kara sank to a crouch and gingerly reached for the man, rain pelting the shell of his jacket, which rustled as she tried to move his arm to work it through the straps of the pack. He was stiff, and it took some force, quiet, gasping breaths drawn in and out as Kara couldn’t bring herself to look at his face, her stomach swooping with panic as her hands shook. Trying to be careful, trying to be respectful of this Muggle man who’d been innocently following a path through the Cairngorms, she worked the pack off him and dragged it away, mud and blood staining the wet fabric. 

 

            She glanced over at Manchester as he started to undo the man’s hiking boots, a sharp look of disapproval briefly crossing her features, before she schooled it into a hard look of determination. Mercifully, he left the man in his clothes, although that might’ve been purely because it had all been shredded by Pamela’s claws, and Mo joined them then, the damp butt of his cigarette clamped between scarred lips as he exhaled grey smoke. He pulled his wand out and tried to think of a spell to move the dirt, and Kara had to stop herself from offering up the correct words, waiting for him to fumble through a spell to cut a chunk out of the ground and then levitate it. While he held it, Kara was tasked with grabbing the man’s arms, while Manchester got his feet, and carrying him into the hole, trying to be gentle as she waited for Manchester to drop his legs before she lowered his torso. He was heavy, and Kara was sweating from the brief exertion of it, her limbs feeling limp as they trembled to keep her standing. 

 

            Letting the dirt fall back down, Mo pocketed his wand and then tossed his cigarette butt aside. Kneeling beside the fresh grave, Kara reached out and started to pat the dirt down, compacting it, making sure he was properly buried. It left a dark stain on the patch of green, but there was nothing to be done about it. They were in a place so remote that by the time anyone searched the area, it would most likely already be reclaimed by the grass and sedge in the area. Trying to wipe the wet earth off her hands, smearing it over the knees of her sodden pyjama pants, Kara climbed to her feet and sniffed, stooping to heave the pack up. It was so heavy her knees almost buckled beneath her, but Manchester steadied her. Glancing at Mo, he jerked his chin.

 

            “Take us back.”

 

            Wand remaining in his pocket, Mo took their arms and Apparated them back to the bothy. They filed inside, the other ten of their party still asleep, and Kara dropped the pack off near the wood burner and found her bag, rifling through it for dry clothes. Stripping off all of her layers, no room for self-consciousness in their circle, she worked on a pair of jogging bottoms, a long-sleeved top and a sweatshirt someone had brought back from a secondhand store last month, leaving her wet clothes to air dry as she worked on two pairs of socks and then tiptoed back to her abandoned sleeping bag, getting back into it and rubbing her tired eyes. She was wet, cold and dirty, but Kara didn’t have the strength to worry about that then.

 

            She slept until the middle of the afternoon, waking to the whistle of the battered kettle, and shoved her glasses onto her bleary-eyed face, creased with lines from the sleeping bag. Wishing she had something to tie her greasy hair up with, Kara just raked it out of her face, the curls so snarled and knotted she feared it would become matted soon if she didn’t get a brush through it, and made her way over to the wood burner. Checking on her clothes - still damp - she saw that the hiker’s pack had already been combed through, picked over, and the pack left deflated on the floor. Finding an empty cup, Kara made herself some coffee, black this time, out of milk powder, and stepped outside, the cold stinging her face as she cupped her hands around the cup, leaching as much heat from it as she could, no coat to fend off the piercing wind.

 

            “Linda,” Manchester called out, perched on a rock with a wrinkled copy of The Daily Prophet folded over in his hands as he smoked, using it to beckon her over.

 

            Walking towards him, she sank to a crouch beside the rock, her breath faintly misting, blue eyes clouded as she looked across the loch. The wind rippled across the surface, and she took in the scattered werewolves, passing the time how they fancied. 

 

            “How’re you faring?”

 

            “Fine,” she murmured, taking a sip of coffee, turning her head to look up at him.

 

            He nodded, stubbing his cigarette out against the damp moss and tossing it aside, before he shook out the newspaper. “You get anything to eat in you yet?”

 

            “Not yet.”

 

            “Make sure you do. You’ll need to keep your strength up. Sorry for dragging you along earlier; I saw you were awake, and you seemed a good choice. I don’t fancy many of the others would be up to that without a fuss.”

 

            “No, I don’t fancy they would,” Kara murmured.

 

            Fumbling in his pocket for the pack of cigarettes, he offered them to her and then took a new one for himself when she shook her head. Lighting it, he took a drag and then turned his gaze down to the newspaper, tapping it.

 

            “Hat said a few of your lot showed up while we were gone. Witches and wizards. He said they were all followers of You Know Who. Not very high up, but doing the grunt work.”

 

            “Trying to persuade you again?”

 

            “No, not this time. He said they had a couple of names they wanted to run past us. Had a good look at everyone’s faces, too.”

 

            “Yeah? What names?”

 

            “One for a bloke called Remus Lupin. They reckon he was hanging around in Wales for a bit. You were there before, weren’t you?”

 

            Masking her surprise well, Kara rubbed her chin as she pretended to consider it. “Mhm. No one by the name of Remus that I can recall, though.”

 

            “And a witch called Kara Danvers. Maybe a few years younger than you, from what Hat said.”

 

            Feeling her heart lurch in her chest, Kara took a sip of coffee, hoping the faint tremor in her hand wasn’t noticeable. Forcing herself to swallow, she hummed thoughtfully and then looked up at Manchester.

 

            “No, I don’t think I ran into her, either.”

 

            “Ah, well, tough luck for them, then.”

 

            “Did they say what they wanted?”

 

            He refolded the damp newspaper, sniffing as he scratched the side of his nose. “I don’t know much about your war, but I think we both know what they wanted. Hat said there was a woman with them, though, said she seemed more angry about how they hadn’t found the woman than about the man.”

 

            Dread pooled in her stomach, and Kara couldn’t hide the tremor in her hand that time, cupping it in both as she remained crouched. She was fortunate it was the day after a full moon, because it excused the greyish pallor of her pale face, and Kara had to work hard to keep her voice level.

 

            “Well … for their sake, I hope she doesn’t find them,” she murmured, draining the rest of her coffee.

 

            “Depends on what they’ve done, doesn't it? Hat said they were saying both werewolves went to that magic school. Hogwarts? Yeah, apparently they think they’re better because they’re proper educated in magic and all that, but they’re just werewolves like the rest of us, end of the day, innit? Might be they killed a few of You Know Who’s lot, and now they want revenge. Nothing wrong with that, as long as they take it as far away from us as bloody possible.”

 

            “You haven’t reconsidered siding with Dumbledore?”

 

            “Nah,” he gestured dismissively. “What’s one wizard to another? I might not have grown up on that side of things like you, and Hat, and Mo, but I know enough to know we won’t fit anywhere. Greyback makes a good case, but I don’t trust him. Something ain’t right with him, but that doesn’t mean I’m going to go throwing my lot in with some old man.”

 

            “Those ones they were after … if they went to Hogwarts, it’s Dumbledore who let them in. Maybe he’s trying to change things, after all.”

 

            “Yeah? Why didn’t he let you in, then?”

 

            Kara smiled wryly, eyes flitting sideways to Manchester. “I was born in America. My name wasn’t on the books for Hogwarts.”

 

            “Oh. I thought you sounded funny sometimes.”

 

            Humming, Kara pushed herself to her feet, stomach in knots and gnawing with hunger as she clutched her empty cup in one hand. “Well … I’m going to get something to eat.”

 

            He nodded, taking another drag of his cigarette, and Kara walked back to the bothy, taking a sachet of dried pasta from their stores and boiling water to cook them through in a large can. She made herself another coffee as well, gritty and bitter, and waited for her meal to congeal into something edible before she ate quickly while it was hot and then spent some time sitting by the edge of the loch, skipping stones across the surface with a few others. Lost in thought, Kara considered reporting to Dumbledore that Death Eater lackeys were looking for her, but they’d already been on her tail before she’d come to proposition werewolves. That had been part of the reason why she’d come in the first place, not having much to give up. 

 

            Keeping it to herself, Kara buried her fear deep down inside. She wasn’t sure if the woman was Siobhan Smythe, or maybe it was Lena herself, having heard about Kara’s new pursuit of danger. But she merely had to send a letter and change the colour of the ring, if that were the case, so Kara knew it wasn’t her. Still, that was the safest option, even though she knew it was wrong. Trying not to worry about it, she pushed all thoughts aside and comforted herself with the knowledge that they only knew her as Linda Lee here, that she wasn’t well acquainted with the werewolf community for anyone to know her from before she’d joined them. She hadn’t needed to know them; she’d had a family. A family who loved her, whom she missed dearly, wishing she could have a Sunday roast at her mother’s house, drinks with her sister at The Leaky Cauldron , go to a quidditch match with her friends, parties for birthdays and weddings, even just a sandwich break in the Atrium of the Ministry of Magic. Kara would give anything for that; she would give even more for Lena. Just a minute with her, to know how she was, to set eyes on her living, breathing body and make sure she was safe.

 

            Instead, she had to swallow the longing in her chest and go on. With the full moon at the end of March over and done with, April was ushered in with more wet, early spring days, and Kara couldn't envision an end to this existence, stealing from Muggles and quietly listening to everyone bicker and argue over belongings, growing lean on rations as she waited for the next full moon and the hope that Manchester would finally agree with her. She was already considering another option, one of the werewolves mentioning another group of them in Northumberland, tucked away in the expansive Kielder Forest, but she wasn’t at the stage yet, still hoping to encourage her present company to heed her warnings. Then she’d need to move on to the next group, and hope she didn’t get to them too late.

 

            She needn’t have worried, though, things having a horrible way of turning out for the worst for her in every instance. It seemed inevitable in a way, the knowledge that she was being hunted leaving her a sitting duck, when she should’ve left, gone to her sister and fetched her wand, abandoned Dumbledore’s task as impossible and helped the Order however else she could. But she’d stayed, so of course it all caught up with her again. Kara’s only regret was that she hadn’t had time to say goodbye to anyone. But she didn’t have to worry; she was going to get the one thing she wanted more than anything soon enough.

 

            Oblivious to what was in store for her, she’d been off hunting a red deer with Mo and Pamela, the latter’s knack for tracking the herds quite useful, and they’d hauled it home, the beauty of the animal marred by the wrong twist of its neck from a well-aimed spell. They were at a new bothy that month, one along a river, graffitied concrete and damp water stains making for a dismal new home, and they had to navigate a valley of pines to access the wide clearing it stood in, so Kara didn’t have time to see what lay ahead. The sounds of voices that drifted towards her could’ve been anyone’s, and she thought nothing of it until she was following Mo, Pamela and the levitating deer around a final tree and stepping into the clearing.

 

            The sight of two figures in dark Death Eater robes made her stomach lurch with sudden panic, and Kara slowed mid-step, hanging back as she tried to identify them both.
