            “Probably better than we’ll fare with a nice Killing Curse sent our way before then,” Kara grumbled. 

 

            “How optimistic of you,” Alex sarcastically replied, and Kara folded her arms over her chest, ignoring her as she looked at Lena.

 

            “Can we go?”

 

            Suppressing a sigh, Lena gave her a pleading look as she approached, and Kara put her socks and shoes back on as Lena said goodbye to everyone, pulling on her coat as they lingered in the hallway, the conversation prolonged for another five minutes before they could get out of the door. Lena Disapparated them, and Kara stepped inside the cottage and went straight up to their room, shedding her socks and jeans and flopping onto the bed on her back as she sighed. Coming in after her a few minutes later, delayed by the act of straightening up the pile of shoes inside the door and taking her coat off downstairs, Lena sank onto the edge of the bed and gave her a searching look.

 

            “You could be a little less abrupt with her.”

 

            Softly groaning, nudging her glasses up so she could press the heels of her palms to her eyes, Kara felt a flicker of annoyance shoot through her. “We’re dealing with Death Eaters, and she’s making jokes about blowing them up.”

 

            “Cut her some slack. She’s trying to lighten the mood, and we could all use it. In case you haven’t noticed, everyone’s been a bit miserable of late. Including your grumpy arse.”

 

            “I hate this,” Kara whispered. “I hate this.”

 

            “I know.”

 

            “How much longer do you think we can go on?”

 

            Considering it for a moment as she quietly hummed, Lena looked up at the ceiling. “Well, it depends on what sort of outcome you’re hoping for. Something has to give, eventually, and Dumbledore put all of his trust in the Potter boy, so we have to give him time to do … whatever it is he’s expected to do. If we’re hoping to win this thing, we probably need to nip it in the bud within the next year, before too many of our numbers are killed off - which is happening faster than we’d like - because there aren’t enough kids who’ll graduate and join our cause. Especially not with the Death Eaters inside Hogwarts, now. They’ll be doing all sorts to them, making all sorts of threats to keep them obedient.”

 

            “Wow. Now you’re being optimistic,” Kara mumbled.

 

            “It’s the truth,” Lena gently replied. “You know I don’t assign emotions to logical thinking; I’ve thought about this a lot, and I know we’re running on limited time. And we don’t have a clue what we’re supposed to be doing, except trying to stay alive and keep as many other people alive as we can. Um … but if the outcome is that he wins … well, then I suppose people will just endure. People have always endured, even if it’s not very pleasant. I know I have. Um … I guess the difference is … how long I can endure. Being hunted, that is. I can’t endure that forever; I know that much.”

 

            “I won’t let him touch you.”

 

            “I believe you, if it’s up to you to decide that,” Lena quietly replied, leaning down to kiss the tip of Kara’s nose.

 

            Dropping her hands from her face and then reaching up to shift her glasses back down onto the bridge of her nose, Kara gave her an unwavering look. “But it won’t be up to me.”

 

            “No,” Lena agreed, “it won’t.”

 

            “I hate this,” Kara said again, her voice wrenched with painful yearning for it to all be over. “Every day it’s just- we can’t keep going on like this. I can’t sleep properly. I can’t eat. It’s just- it’s agonising waiting to see if we’re going to make it through the next day alive. I just want to have our life back. I want everyone to be safe, and for us to go back to work, and for things to be normal. I feel so- so trapped. And how lucky we are to still be alive. Well, I don’t feel very lucky.”

 

            She let out a frayed laugh, closing her eyes and shaking her head. Leaning down, Lena gently kissed her cheek and smoothed down the little curls at her hairline, softly shushing her. “It’s alright. I know it’s frustrating and that it feels like we’re living the same day over and over again, but it’ll end. It’ll end eventually, and we have to keep going to make sure that we survive it. Just … come downstairs and cook dinner with me, and then we’ll have a game of chess, and we can have an early night. You must be knackered from this morning; it’ll all seem better after a good sleep.”

 

            Exhaling forcefully, Kara stared up at her wife, a bleakness filling her that even Lena’s reassurances couldn’t fill. “I’m sorry,” she whispered, reaching out to take Lena’s left hand, kissing the engagement ring on her finger and thinking about the wedding bands tucked in the ring box in the desk drawer. “I don’t mean to complain; it’s not your fault. And I do feel lucky. I’m lucky to have you. No matter how frustrating everything else is, I don’t take that for granted. Not for a second.”

 

            “I know you don’t. You can be as frustrated as you like; I feel the same way.”

 

            “You’re much better at hiding it, though,” Kara said with a small laugh.

 

            “Mm,” Lena hummed, leaning down to kiss her slowly before she pulled back. “I’d be a shit spy if I couldn't hide my emotions very well, wouldn’t I?”

 

            “You don’t have to hide them from me, though.”

 

            “Well, I’ve never been too good at that, anyway. You’ve always been able to see right through me.”

 

            “Not always.”

 

            Lena gave her a small smile. “Yes, always. You might’ve gotten the wrong impression, but you always knew when something was wrong. You’re too perceptive for your own good sometimes.”

 

            “Come here,” Kara softly ordered her.

 

            Obliging, Lena shifted and sprawled heavily on top of her, making Kara laugh, slightly breathless as Lena accidentally winded her. Still, it was a pleasant feeling to have her wife’s weight pressing down on her, her head tucked in beneath Kara’s chin, and she wrapped her arms around her, letting out a slow breath as some of the tension abated.

 

            “My Lena,” she said with relief. “What would I ever do without you?”

 

            “You already know the answer to that,” Lena’s muffled reply came.

 

            Letting out a soft huff of laughter, Kara turned her head slightly to kiss the top of her dark hair, humming in agreement. “That’s right; I’d be completely lost.”

 

            “Stay by my side, then. We’ll be okay.”

 

            “Of course we will,” Kara agreed with false bravado. “How could I not be with you beside me?”

 

            They stayed that way for a few minutes, Lena listening to Kara’s steady heartbeat, while Kara basked in the feeling of peace that came from being with her wife. It was a balm to her frustration, to the agitation she felt at being so helpless, but Lena had always been the bright spot in Kara’s life, and vice versa, and she knew that whatever happened, she could bear it a hell of a lot better than she could alone. Thinking back to a year ago, spending the winter in Welsh valleys with werewolves, Kara knew she was infinitely better off at her mother’s home with Lena in her arms and the comforting knowledge of secret wedding vows nestled in her chest, no matter how bad things got. There was always that comfort, that reassurance. It was the thought of losing it that made her start to get in her head about it all.

 

            Eventually, Lena coaxed her downstairs to make dinner, and Kara obediently peeled potatoes and carrots for a stew, letting her wife take the lead in the kitchen as they listened to the radio. Music this time, not the despairing news, and the windows fogged up, velvety blue as the afternoon darkened, the smell of herbs and seared beef filling the small space. Eliza left them to their cooking, retreating to the living room with the glass of wine Kara poured her, and it was a slice of normalcy after the events of that morning and the ensuing worry of the day.

 

            The phantom pain in her leg had disappeared by then, and the wine made her feel warm, things seeming a little less dire as she sat at the kitchen table with her wife and her mum. They talked about ordinary things as they ate, Lena discussing Mandrakes with Eliza as she dipped bread into her soup, and Kara recounting some trivial information she’d heard on the radio the day before. They tidied up afterwards, setting the dishes to wash, putting leftovers in the fridge for lunch tomorrow, and then Lena poured them more wine as Eliza went back outside to do a little more work by wandlight, the evening already dark.

 

            Sitting on either side of the coffee table, they played a game of Wizard’s Chess, Kara playing as black, and it was quiet and cosy, the fire lit and the sips of wine in between their moves making their worries seem smaller and smaller. They were evenly matched, although Kara suspected Lena was going easy on her, usually the stronger player, but it was nice to put her attention to something, even if it was as unimportant as a game of chess. It was a long game, with fewer pieces on the board as it dragged on and longer pauses between their moves as they tried to catch each other out, and it was Kara’s turn when Lena startled, her eyes darting down to the ring on her finger.

 

            Kara stopped studying the board to look at her. “What is it?”

 

            “My ring’s amber,” Lena slowly replied, wariness in her voice as her expression furrowed.

 

            Kara felt a stab of worry but tried to console herself as she ran her palms over the thighs of her flannel bottoms. “Not urgent, then. That’s good.”

 

            “Mm,” Lena hummed, already shifting to push herself to her knees. “I should still go now, though. Just to be safe.”

 

            “You mean we.”

 

            Giving her an exasperated look, Lena smiled faintly. “Yes, we.”

 

            Nodding, placated, Kara stood up and then paused, reaching down to move a piece. “Check.”

 

            “Oh, for fuck’s sake,” Lena sighed. “Priorities, perhaps.”

 

            Shrugging, Kara gave her a crooked smile. “Just before I forget. You can get out of it when we get home.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lena moved over to the collection of shoes by the front door and shoved her feet into a pair. “Should we tell your mum?”

 

            Eliza was outside, bundled up against the cold as she worked enchanted coverings over the plants before the weather worsened, and Kara bit her lip for a moment, deliberating. “No, no, it’s fine; it was amber, so it’s nothing dangerous.”

 

            “I’m not sure Sam understands the significance of the colours as we intended them,” Lena grimly replied.

 

            “I think she got the gist of it after you lectured her about it last time.”

 

            “Right, well, put your shoes on, then. We shouldn’t keep them waiting, just in case …”

 

            Lena trailed off, not wanting to speak her thoughts aloud and jinx them. While she would’ve been quite content to go barefoot, always finding shoes a bit claustrophobic, Kara put on two different shoes in her haste to go and snagged her wife’s hand, dragging her outside and Apparating them to her sister’s house. The front door was already open, Alex leaning against the frame of it with a sense of panic about her. She straightened at the appearance of them, a mere few feet away, and her shoulders slumped with relief. Her eyes went to Lena, though, and Kara frowned, watching Alex take a small step forward, anxiously wringing her hands.

 

            “Sorry to use the ring, I just- it’s not urgent, but I thought you’d want me to fetch you as quickly as possible. Without making you panic. Um … she showed up here five minutes ago. I couldn’t get a word out of her,” Alex breathlessly explained, her brown eyes a little wide as if she was surprised by the turn of events.

 

            Kara could hear the sound of someone loudly sobbing, and her expression fell as she pressed a hand to Lena’s back and urged her inside, following closely on her heels, Alex moving out of the way to let them in. Shutting the front door, Kara followed the sound to the living room and paused, as Lena likewise momentarily paused, before she was spurred onwards at the sight of Andrea sitting on the sofa, sobbing as Sam tended to her face. If she wasn’t so identifiable by her hair and side profile, Kara might not have recognised the swollen features, blood covering the bottom half of her face, and she touched her fingers to her lips, drawing in a soft gasp of surprise. Lena hurried to her friend’s side and dropped to her knees, talking quietly to her.

 

            “What the hell happened?” Kara quietly asked Alex, who stood beside her in the living room doorway, observing.

 

            “I’m not sure. She showed up here looking like that and said she didn’t know where else to go; it was Lena she was after. I thought I’d better send word.”

 

            “Yes,” Kara distractedly agreed, although she was mildly surprised that Andrea had come seeking Lena. From what Lena had told her, they hadn’t parted on the best of terms when the truth had all come out.

 

            Nudging her, Alex jerked her head. “Come give me a hand with some tea. I might need to sneak something into Andrea’s to calm her down. We won’t get anything coherent out of her in this state.”

 

            “Do you have a Calming Draught? Anything?”

 

            Shaking her head as she led her sister down the hallway, Alex sighed. “No, that potion was low priority on the list; I’m out of anything useful at the moment.”

 

            Humming, Kara didn’t respond further as they stepped into the kitchen. She fetched mugs as Alex filled the kettle, and they lingered in a beat of awkwardness for a moment, her leaning against the kitchen counters, while Alex folded her arms over her chest and rocked on her heels. 

 

            “How’re you doing?” Alex broke the silence.

 

            Shrugging indifferently, Kara grimaced. “Fine.”

 

            “And Lena?”

 

            Gesturing towards the hallway, Kara shrugged again and let out an awkward laugh. “You’d have to ask her. But she’s coping okay.”

 

            Nodding, Alex swallowed. “You guys are good? That’s good. Good.”

 

            “Mm.”

 

            “Have you decided on a new date for the wedding?”

 

            Rubbing the bridge of her nose, Kara felt a flicker of guilt. “Um … haven’t made any plans for the ceremony yet, no.”

 

            “Oh. Pity. We could probably use a bit of cheer at the moment,” Alex murmured, the kettle starting to faintly whistle on the stove.

 

            “Mm. I’m surprised you’re in a hurry to deck yourself out in pastel pink robes, though,” Kara said with a crooked smile as she looked up at her sister.

 

            Rolling her eyes, Alex softly sighed. “I know you picked that colour for me on purpose.”

 

            “I did,” Kara agreed, smug with her satisfaction.

 

            “But I’d happily wear it if it meant I was Maid of Honour at your wedding. Given … everything that happened … well, I wasn’t sure I’d get an invite from you.”

 

            “Oh, you would’ve,” Kara said with an amused huff, pushing off the counter as Alex removed the kettle from the hob. “Lena would’ve murdered me if I refused to invite you.”

 

            “Yeah, well, I kind of wish you wanted me there because I’m your sister. Not just because your fiancée wants it.”

 

            Kara winced slightly, pink creeping into her cheeks, and she could hear the raw pain in her sister’s voice at admitting that aloud. Fetching the milk from the fridge, she stepped up beside her and added a splash to the mugs and cleared her throat with an air of discomfort.

 

            “I did. I do,” Kara corrected herself. “It’s just- I needed time. Things still don’t feel right. And it’s just- we don’t have the time to be sorting out our feelings right now. But it’s not just you; it’s … everything. I told you I could never forgive you for what you did, and that was true, but … I’m moving past it, and if things were normal, it would be a lot easier, but it’s just- it’s constant doom at the minute.”

 

            “I know,” Alex quietly agreed. “I just miss my sister. It seems like the only time I see you these days is with everyone else around, which makes it impossible to talk properly, or in the middle of some sort of fight, and getting out of it alive is more pressing than my trying to make amends for being a twat.”

 

            Laughing slightly, Kara spooned a teabag out of a mug. “A huge twat.”

 

            “Yeah,” Alex chuckled.

 

            “We should go and check on her,” Kara murmured, jerking her head back towards the hallway as she dumped another teabag in the bin. “Find out what happened.”

 

            “Yeah,” Alex quietly agreed. “But we’re alright, aren’t we? I mean, you’re not still mad - well, not not mad, but-”

 

            “Yeah, I’m not mad,” Kara wearily told her. “I’m just … too preoccupied to get past the awkwardness right now.”

 

            “Okay. Good.”

 

            Nodding, Kara picked up two mugs, levitated the third, and left Alex to bring the others with her. Briskly walking down the hallway, the sobbing hadn’t subsided even a little, but Andrea looked marginally better. Kelly had fetched a flannel, soaked in the sink of the downstairs toilet, and Lena was mopping at her face, which was no longer lumpy from the disfiguring curse, but was still slightly swollen as she cried her eyes out. Hushing her, Lena tried to calm her down, but Andrea couldn’t get any words out past the frantic, hitching sobs that wracked her.

 

            “It’s okay, you’re safe,” Lena gently reassured her, wiping tears away with the blood. “I just need you to tell me what happened. Is Russell okay?”

 

            Andrea choked on a sound of utter pain, the sob even louder as she curled in on herself, her dark hair curtaining her face. Wincing at her tact, Lena dipped the flannel into the water and glanced up as Kara set the mugs down on the coffee table. Kara was thinking perhaps they should’ve gone with something a bit stronger than tea, but she didn’t say a word as she met Lena’s gaze and backed away from the coffee table, her own mug of tea cupped in her palms as the heat burned right into her.

 

            “Maybe we should give her a bit of privacy,” Kelly suggested, looking around at the room full of women.

 

            Hesitating, Kara nodded, meeting Lena’s gaze again and then nodding more firmly as her wife gave her a reassuring one in response. Kara’s relationship with Andrea had always been strange; she’d been jealous of her at Hogwarts, when Lena had started to drift towards other friends - although, Kara now knew the real reason why - and then she’d been glad Lena had her when she knew the truth of the matter, knew that she’d left Lena alone because of her worst assumptions, and Andrea had been there to fill that loneliness. Then she’d been Kara’s boss and had been forced to let her go when her disease had been revealed. She’d never been particularly close with Andrea, but was friendly enough with her for Lena’s sake, and she knew that whatever pretences had started Lena’s friendship with Andrea, she was one of her longest friends, and she would see her through whatever had brought her to Alex’s house in such a state so late at night.

 

            Slipping out of the room without another word, she found herself sitting at the kitchen table with Alex, Kelly and Sam, the three of them nursing their tea and exchanging questioning glances as they dwelled in silence for a bit. Kara was the first to speak, keeping her voice low as she stared at the surface of the table.

 

            “Russell didn’t come with her?”

 

            Alex hesitated, a grim set to her face. “No, she showed up alone.”

 

            A spasm of pain crossed Kara’s face, and she nodded, thinking the worst. Andrea had been with Russell for almost as long as Kara had known the woman, virtually since she’d graduated from Hogwarts, and she knew Andrea would’ve gone to him first if she’d been attacked in such a way. The fact that she’d come to Lena instead only made dread pool in Kara’s stomach. She liked Russell, for all she knew him, and she hoped she was wrong in her assumption, but she knew that hope was a small thing those days.

 

            “She’s safe, though. That’s good, at least,” Sam murmured, running a hand over her face.

 

            No one really said much as they lingered around the table, exchanging glances, trying to eavesdrop, with the loud sobs turned into garbled conversation, difficult to decipher. The sound of mugs being set down gently on the tabletop as they sipped their tea was the only thing to cut through the tense silence, and it wasn’t until Lena emerged, pale-faced and grim, that anyone spoke.

 

            “Is she-”

 

            “What happened?”

 

            Rubbing her tired eyes, Lena softly exhaled. “I stunned her once I got it out of her. Sorry, she’s laid out on your sofa. I don’t think I can move her at the moment.”

 

            “That’s alright,” Kelly quickly assured her, pushing her chair back. “Let me get some extra blankets so she doesn’t get cold.”

 

            Nodding, Lena went with her without answering any of their interrupted questions, and they had to wait until she stepped back into the kitchen to get a response. Sitting heavily on one of the empty chairs, she put her head in her hands, elbows propped up on the table, and Kara reached across to touch the bare skin of her wrist peeking out from beneath the cuff of her jumper. Raising her head, dropping her hands from her face, Lena gave her a bleak look, her thin smile strained.

 

            “Death Eaters.”

 

            “But she’s a Pureblood,” Sam replied, face crumpling with confusion.

 

            “Doesn’t matter. It’s her usefulness they’re after. The Prophet. They’ve nabbed Russell, too.”

 

            “That’s why she-” Kelly winced as Lena nodded.

 

            “He went to work this morning. Never came home. Couple of Death Eaters showed up and wrecked their house, left her in that state with a warning for her to get back in the office and start printing what they want in the Prophet,” Lena grimly explained.

 

            “So, he’s …” Kara apprehensively spoke.

 

            “Alive, I think, was implied. Leverage to blackmail Andrea into doing what they want.”

 

            “Do we know where they’re taking their hostages?” Sam asked.

 

            Alex shook her head, palms flat on the table, a displeased downturn to the corners of her mouth. “No one’s managed to figure out where their headquarters are. And even if we did, I don’t think the Order’s really in a position to be storming their nest at the moment. Um … not really any guarantee they’re keeping anyone they take alive, either, is there?”

 

            “They’re probably toying with them before they kill them,” Lena murmured, a vacant look in her eyes for a moment, before she blinked and looked around the table. “It’s what they’re like. It’s all for sport.”

 

            “You’re right,” Kelly sighed, “but I don’t even want to think about what they’re doing to those poor people.”

 

            Lips faintly twitching, Lena hummed. “Mm, you don’t.”

 

            The way she said it caused a small disturbance in the ruminating preoccupation of the assembled women, and Kara cringed slightly at the understanding in Kelly’s dark eyes, the shock on Sam’s face, the grim resignation on Alex’s, as they all reacted differently to the meaning behind Lena’s words. And Kara knew better than any of them what it meant, the implications of being caught by a Death Eater. It would’ve been a kindness to be killed quickly, but they were notoriously unkind people, so they would never show their prey such mercy. It sickened her, her stomach in knots, to think about what she’d sustained for half a day being amplified, dragged out over days or perhaps even weeks, as they tormented those they dragged from their homes or offices. 

 

            The thought of Lex resurfaced, and Kara clenched her hands into fists. It had been more than six months ago now, and yet it still haunted her. It was stamped down and buried beneath more recent memories, but it was still there, and it always would be. Even showing up to fight made Kara’s chest feel tight when she thought about being captured again, enduring it all over again with no hope of Lena walking through the door to save her again. But she could live with that, just as long as it was her that was taken. She knew that whichever Death Eater captured her would probably make relatively quick work of her once they realised she’d give them nothing, and was less than nothing, with her scars so clearly marking her as a werewolf. They’d want her dead quickly. But Lena would be handed over to Lex, or perhaps even Voldemort himself, a plaything to torture for her spying, and Kara knew there would be no rush to kill her. From what she knew of Lex and how he’d dragged out the torture of her for his own enjoyment, knowing what she meant to Lena, he would eke out every moment of his sister’s agony until she wasn’t his sister anymore. The thought filled her with dread, but she couldn’t speak it; the words were locked away inside her as she stared at her wife and silently prayed to the Muggle God, to anything out there, that it wouldn’t be the case.

 

            “We should let you get to bed,” Kara whispered, breaking the awkward beat of silence.

 

            “I’ll stay up,” Sam replied, draining her tea and then climbing to her feet. “Just in case she wakes.”

 

            Gratefully nodding, Lena pushed her chair back. “I’ll come and check on her in the morning. We can figure out what to do next then.”

 

            “I’m not sure there is anything to do,” Alex mused, slowly raising her mug to her lips and then pausing. “Sorry, not to be a pessimist, but Death Eaters invaded her home and took her fiancé; she can’t go back, and we don’t have a clue where he is. Does she have any other family?”

 

            “Her mother’s here,” Lena replied, “but they don’t speak. Her father’s in Argentina; she won’t go there.”

 

            “Then she’ll stay with us,” Kelly decisively replied.

 

            “You can’t take in all of my friends,” Lena scoffed, looking a little guilty, a little agitated, as if she were the imposition.

 

            “Well, it’s a good thing you don’t have any others,” Alex blithely teased her, “so this should be the last of them.”

 

            Lena offered her a weak smile in response, rolling her eyes, and Kara just shook her head and softly smiled. Finishing her tea, she stood with a leaden feeling in her body, so defeated by their worsening circumstances, and took Sam’s empty mug from her, rounding the table to put them in the sink. Raking a hand through her wayward curls, Kara turned back around to face everyone, grimacing.

 

            “Don’t tell her there’s nothing we can do for him, okay? Don’t ruin her hope like that.”

 

            “It won’t be doing her a kindness to lie,” Alex darkly replied, softening when Kara opened her mouth. “But I’ll tell her the Order is working on finding him. That much will be true; I’ll put the word out to J’onn and Kingsley. They might’ve heard something from their eyes and ears if he had been taken directly from the Ministry. See if there’s any hope for him.”

 

            “There’s always hope,” Kara firmly insisted, reaching out to take Lena’s hand and rubbing her thumb across her knuckles, trying to soothe her as she echoed her wife’s words from earlier that day. “We’ll just- we’ll talk about it in the morning. Everything will look better after a good night’s sleep.”
